But, with us, it is now more frequently used for the effect of such transgression; or the losing some <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a>, privilege, estate, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a>, office, or effects, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> thereof; than for the transgression itself. Forfeiture differs from *confiscation*, in that the former is more general; while confiscation is particularly applied to such things as become forfeited to the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>'s exchequer; and goods confiscated are said to be such as nobody claims. Forfeitures may be either in civil or criminal <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a>. I. With respect to the first, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> that hath an estate for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> or years, may forfeit it many ways, as well as by reason of felony; such as alienation, claiming a greater estate than he hath, or affirming the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVERSION">reversion</a> to be in a stranger, &c. When a tenant in tail makes <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEASES">leases</a> not warranted by the statute; a copy-holder commits waste, refuses to pay his rent, or do <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUIT">suit</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>; and where an estate is granted upon condition, or non-performance thereof, &c. they will make a forfeiture. Entry for a forfeiture ought to be by him who is next in reversion, or remainder, after the estate forfeited. As <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> a tenant for life or years commits a forfeiture, he who has the immediate reversion or remainder ought to enter, though he has the fee, or only an estate-tail. II. Forfeiture in criminal cases is twofold; of real, and personal estates. 1. As to real estates by *Attainder* in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TREASON">treason</a>, a man forfeits to the king all his lands and tenements of inheritance, whether fee-simple or fee-tail; and all his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a> of entry on lands and tenements, which he had at the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of the offence committed, or at any time afterwards, to be for ever vested in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>; and also the profits of all lands and tenements, which he had in his own right for life or years, so <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> as such <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> shall subsist. This forfeiture relates backwards to the time of the treason committed; so as Comment, to avoid all intermediate sales and encumbrances, but not those before the fact: and therefore a wife's <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOINTURE">jointure</a> is not forfeitable for the treason of her husband; because settled upon her previous to the treason committed. But her dower is forfeited, by the express provision of statute 5 and 6 Edw. VI. c. xi. And yet the husband shall be tenant by courtesy of the wife's lands, if the wife be attainted of treason; for that is not prohibited by the statute. But, though after attainder the forfeiture relates back to the time of the treason committed, yet it does not take effect unless an attainder be had, of which it is one of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>; and therefore, if a traitor dies before judgment pronounced, or is killed in open rebellion, or is hanged by martial law, it works no forfeiture of his lands: for he never was attainted of treason. But if the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> of the king's <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BENCH">bench</a> (the supreme coroner of all England) in person upon the view of the body of him killed in open rebellion, records it and returns the record into his own court, both lands and goods shall be forfeited. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> justice of the forfeiture or confiscation of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a>, for treason, is founded on this consideration: That he who hath thus violated the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FUNDAMENTAL">fundamental</a> principles of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, and broken his <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the original <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRACT">contract</a> between king and people, hath abandoned his connexions with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>, and hath no longer any right to those advantages which before belonged to him purely as a member of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMUNITY">community</a>; among which social advantages, the right of transferring or transmitting property to others is one of the chief. Such forfeitures, moreover, whereby his posterity must suffer as well as himself, will help to restrain a man, not only by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> of his duty, and dread of personal <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a>, but also by his passions and natural affections; and will interest every dependent and relation he has to keep him from offending: according to that beautiful sentiment of Cicero, "nec vero me fugit quam sit acerbum, parentum sceleratiorum paenit ut; sed hoc praclare..." Forfeiture, praecipue legibus comparatum est, ut caritas liberorum amiciorum parentes reipublicae redderet." And therefore Aulus Casellius, a Roman lawyer in the time of the triumvirate, used to boast that he had two reasons for despising the power of the tyrants, his old <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> and his want of children; for children are pledges to the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of the father's obedience. Yet many nations have thought, that this posthumous punishment savours of hardship to the innocent; especially for crimes that do not strike at the very root and foundation of society, as treason against the government expressly does. And therefore, though confiscations were very frequent in the times of the earlier emperors, yet Arcadius and Honorius, in every other instance but that of treason, thought it more <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a>, ibi esse ponam, ubi et nova est; and ordered, that "peccata suos teneant auctores, nec ulterius progrediatur metus, quam repertiarum delictum;" and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTINIAN">Justinian</a> also made a law to restrain the punishment of relations; which directs the forfeiture to go, except in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> of crimen majestatis, to the next of kin to the delinquent. On the other <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, the Macedonian laws extended even the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> punishment of treason, not only to the children, but to all the relations of the delinquent; and of course their estates must be also forfeited, as no man was left to inherit them. And in Germany, by the famous <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> bull (copied almost verbatim from Justinian's code), the lives of the sons of such as conspire to kill an <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTOR">elector</a> are spared, as it is expressed, by the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a>'s particular bounty. But they are deprived of all their effects and rights of succession, and are rendered incapable of any honour <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> and civil: to the end, that being always <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a> and necessitous, they may for ever be accompanied by the infamy of their father; may languish in continual indigence; and may find (says this merciless edict) their punishment in living, and their relief in dying." In England, forfeiture of lands and tenements to the crown for treason is by no means derived from the feudal policy, but was antecedent to the establishment of that system in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>; being transmitted from our Saxon <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a>, and forming a part of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Scandinavian <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a>. But in certain treasons relating to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COIN">coin</a> (which seem rather a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of the crimen falsi than the crimen læse majestatis), it is provided by some of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> statutes which constitute the offence, that it shall <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> no forfeiture of lands, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAVE">save</a> only for the life of the offenders; and by all, that it shall not deprive the wife of her dower. And, in order to abolish such <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEREDITARY">hereditary</a> punishment entirely, it was enacted by statute 7 Ann. c. 21, that, after the decease of the late pretender, no attainder for treason shall extend to the disinheriting of any heir, nor to the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PREJUDICE">prejudice</a> of any person, other than the traitor himself. By which the law of forfeitures for high treason would by this time have been at an end, had not a subsequent statute intervened to give them a longer <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DURATION">duration</a>. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of this <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> is somewhat singular, and worthy of observation. At the time of the union, the crime of treason in Scotland was, by the Scots law, in many respects different from that of treason in England; and particularly in its consequence of forfeitures of entailed estates, which was more peculiarly English; yet it seemed necessary, that a crime so nearly affecting government should, both in its essence and consequences, be put upon the same footing in both parts of the united kingdoms. In new modelling these laws, the Scots <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> and the English <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of commons struggled hard, partly to maintain, and partly to acquire, a total immunity from forfeiture and corruption of blood; which the house of lords as firmly resisted. At length a compromise was agreed to, which is established by this statute, viz. that the same crimes, and no other, should be treason in Scotland that are so in England; and that the English forfeitures and corruption of blood should take <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in Scotland till the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of the then pretender, and then cease throughout the whole of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>: the lords artfully proposing this temporary clause, in hopes (it is said) that the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRUDENCE">prudence</a> of succeeding parliaments would make it perpetual. This has partly been done by the statute 17 Geo. II. c. 39, made in the year preceding the late rebellion, the operation of these indemnifying clauses being thereby still farther suspended till the death of the sons of the pretender. In petit treason and felony, the offender also forfeits all his chattel interests absolutely, and the profits of all freehold estates during life; and after his death all his lands and tenements in fee simple (but not those in tail) to the crown, for a very short <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> of time: for the king shall have them for a year and a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>, and may commit therein what waste he pleases; which is called the king's year, day, and waste. Formerly the king had only a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> of committing waste on the lands of felons, by pulling <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> their houses, extirpating their gardens, ploughing their meadows, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> down their woods. And a punishment of a similar spirit appears to have obtained in the oriental countries, from the decrees of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEBUCHADNEZZAR">Nebuchadnezzar</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CYRUS">Cyrus</a> in the books of Daniel and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EZRA">Ezra</a>; which, besides the pain of death inflicted on the delinquents there specified, ordain, "that their houses shall be made a dunghill." But this tending greatly to the prejudice of the public, it was agreed in the reign of Henry I. of England, that the king should have the profits of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> for one year and a day in lieu of the destruction he was otherwise at liberty to commit: and therefore <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MAGNA_CHARTA">magna <a cla</a>ss="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CHARTA">charta</a> provides, that the king shall only hold such lands for a year and a day, and then restore them to the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a> of the fee, without any mention made of waste. But the statute 17 Edward II. de prerogativa regis, seems to suppose, that the king shall have his year, day, and waste; and not the year and day instead of waste: which Sir Edward <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COKE">Coke</a> (and the author of the Mirror before him) very justly look upon as an encroachment, though a very ancient one, of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PREROGATIVE">prerogative</a>. This year, day, and waste, are now usually compounded for; but otherwise they regularly belong to the crown: and after their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPIRATION">expiration</a> the land would naturally have descended to the heir (as in gavelkind <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TENURE">tenure</a> it still does) did not its feudal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> intercept such <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a>, and give it by way of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ESCHEAT">escheat</a> to the lord. These forfeitures for felony do also arise only upon attainder; and therefore a felo de se forfeita no lands of inheritance or freehold, for he never is tainted as a felon. They likewise relate back to the time the offence was committed as well as forfeitures for treason, so as to avoid all intermediate charges and conveyances. This may be hard upon such as have unwarily engaged with the offender; but the cruelty and reproach must <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> on the part, not of the law, but Forfeiture of the criminal: who has thus knowingly and dishonestly involved others in his own calamities. 2. The forfeiture of goods and chattels accrues in every one of the high kinds of offence; in high treason, or misprision thereof, petit treason, felonies of all sorts whether clergyable or not, self <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDER">murder</a> or felony de se, petty larceny, standing <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MUTE">mute</a>, &c. For flight, also, on an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACCUSATION">accusation</a> of treason, felony, or even petit larceny, whether the party be found guilty or acquitted, if the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JURY">jury</a> find the flight, the party shall forfeit his goods and chattels: for the very flight is an offence, carrying with it a strong presumption of guilt, and is at least an endeavour to elude and to stifle the course of justice prescribed by the law. But the jury very seldom find the flight: forfeiture being looked upon, since the vast increase of personal property of late years, as too <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> a penalty for an offence to which a man is prompted by the natural <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> of liberty. There is a remarkable <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> between the forfeiture of lands and of goods and chattels. (1.) Lands are forfeited upon attainder, and not before; goods and chattels are forfeited by conviction. Because in many of the cases where goods are forfeited, there is never any attainder; which happens only where judgment of death or outlawry is given; therefore, in those cases, the forfeiture must be upon conviction or not at all; and, being necessarily upon conviction in those, it is so ordered in all other cases, for the law loves uniformity. (2.) The forfeiture of lands has relation to the time the fact was committed, so as to avoid all subsequent sales and encumbrances: but the forfeiture of goods and chattels has no relation backwards; so that those only which a man has at the time of conviction shall be forfeited. Therefore a traitor or felon may <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BONA">bona</a> fide sell any of his chattels, real or personal, for the sustenance of himself and family between the fact and conviction; for personal property is of so fluctuating a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, that it passes through many <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> in a short time; and no buyer could be safe, if he were liable to return the goods which he had fairly bought, provided any of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIOR">prior</a> vendors had committed a treason or felony. Yet if they be collusively and not bona fide parted with, merely to defraud the crown, the law (and particularly the statute 13 Eliz. c. 5.) will reach them; for they are all the while truly and substantially the goods of the offender; and as he, if acquitted, might recover them himself, as not parted with for a good consideration; so, in case he happens to be convicted, the law will recover them for the king.

FORFEX

Pages 19-19

in Roman antiquity, was a way of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> up an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> in the form of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a> of sheers. It was intended to receive the cuneus <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> wedge, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the enemy should make <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of that <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>. For when the forfex opened to admit the wedge, they had an opportunity of defeating their <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> them in pieces.

FORFICULA

Pages 19-19

the Earwig, a genus of insects belonging to the order of coleoptera. See Entomology <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

FORGE

Pages 19-19

properly signifies a little <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FURNACE">furnace</a>, wherein smiths and other artificers of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-STEEL">steel</a>, &c. <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> their <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-METALS">metals</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> hot, in order to soften them and render them more malleable and manageable on the anvil. An ordinary forge is nothing but a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a> of bellows, the nozzle of which is directed upon a smooth <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AREA">area</a>, on which coals are placed. The nozzle of a pair of bellows may be also directed to the bottom of any furnace, to excite the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMBUSTION">combustion</a> of the coals placed there, by which a kind of forge is formed. In laboratories, there is generally a small furnace consisting of one cylindrical piece, open at top, which has at its lower side a hole for receiving the nozzle of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> bellows. This kind of forge furnace is very convenient for fusions, as the operation is quickly performed, and with few coals. In its lower <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a>, two inches above the hole for receiving the nozzle of the bellows, may be placed an iron plate of the same diameter, supported upon two <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HORIZONTAL">horizontal</a> bars, and pierced near its circumference with four holes diametrically opposite to each other. By this disposition, the <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> of the bellows, pushed forcibly under this plate, enters at these four holes; and thus the heat of the fire is equally distributed, and the crucible in the furnace is equally surrounded by it. This contrivance is used in the forge-furnaces for melting <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>, with this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> only, that these furnaces are <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>, which is a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> of no <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a>. As the wind of bellows strongly and rapidly excites the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTION">action</a> of the fire, a forge is very convenient when a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> heat is to be applied quickly; but it is not suitable when the heat is to be gradually increased. The forge, or blast of bellows, is used in several operations in small; as to <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol4.html#article-FUSE">fuse</a> salts, metals, ores, &c. It is also much used in works in the great, which require strong heat, without much management; and chiefly in the smelting of ores, and fusion of metallic matters. Forge is also used for a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> furnace, wherein iron ore, taken out of the mine, is melted <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a>: or it is more properly applied to another kind of furnace, wherein the iron-ore, melted down and separated in a former furnace, and then <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> into sows and pigs, is heated and fused over again, and beaten afterwards with large <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-HAMMERS">hammers</a>, and thus rendered more soft, pure, ductile, and fit for <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>. Forge, in the train of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTILLERY">artillery</a>, is generally called a travelling forge, and may not be improperly called a portable smith's shop: at this forge all manner of smith's <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> is made, and it can be used upon a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">march</a> as well as in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMP">camp</a>. Formerly they were very ill contrived, with two <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHEELS">wheels</a> only, and wooden supporters to prop the forge for working when in the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARK">park</a>. Of late years they are made with four wheels, which answers the purpose much better. Forge for red-hot Balls, is a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where the balls are made red hot before they are fired off: it is built about five or six feet below the surface of the ground, of strong brick-work, and an iron grate, upon which the balls are laid, with a large fire under them.

FORGERY

Pages 19-21

(from the French forger, i.e. accudare, fabricare, "to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEAT">beat</a> on an anvil, forge, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> form") may be defined at <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a>, to be "the fraudulent making or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALTERATION">alteration</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>, to the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PREJUDICE">prejudice</a> of another <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a>:" for which the offender may suffer fine, imprisonment, and pillory. And also, by a variety of statutes, a more severe <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> is inflicted on the offender in many particular <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a>, which are so multiplied of late as almost to become general. We shall mention the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> instance. By statute 5 Eliz. c. 14. to forge or make, or knowingly Forgery. ingly to publish or give in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a>, any forged <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DEED">deed</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>-roll, or <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a>, with intent to affect the right of real <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a>, either freehold or copyhold, is punished by a forfeiture to the party grieved of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> costs and damages; by standing in the pillory, and having both his ears cut off, and his nostrils slit and seared; by forfeiture to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> of the profits of his lands, and by perpetual imprisonment. For any forgery relating to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> of years or annuity, bond, obligation, acquittance, release, or discharge of any debt or demand of any personal chattels, the same forfeiture is given to the party grieved; and on the offender is inflicted the pillory, loss of one of his ears, and half a year's imprisonment: the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> offence, in both cases, being felony without benefit of clergy. Besides this general <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a>, a multitude of others, since the Revolution (when <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> was first established), have inflicted <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> punishment on the forging, altering, or uttering as true when forged, of any <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANK">bank</a> bills or notes, or other securities; of bills of credit issued from the exchequer; of South <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">Sea</a> bonds, &c.; of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOTTERY">lottery</a> tickets or orders: of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVY">navy</a> debentures; of East <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a> bonds; of writings under <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEAL">seal</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXCHANGE">exchange</a> assurance; of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> of the receiver of the pre-sines, or of the accountant-general and certain other officers of the court of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CHANCERY">chancery</a>; of a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> of attorney or other power to receive or transfer stock or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANNUITIES">annuities</a>; and on the personating a proprietor thereof, to receive or transfer such annuities, stock or dividends: also on the personating, or procuring to be personated, any seaman or other person, entitled to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WAGES">wages</a> or other naval emoluments, or any of his personal representatives; and the taking, or procuring to be taken, any false oath in order to obtain a probate or letters of administration, in order to receive such payments; and the forging or procuring to be forged, and likewise the uttering or publishing, as true, of any counterfeited seaman's will or power; to which may be added, though not strictly reducible to this head, the counterfeiting of Mediterranean passes under the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the lords of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ADMIRALTY">admiralty</a>, to protect one from the piratical states of Barbary; the forging or imitating of any stamps to defraud the public revenue; and the forging of any <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REGISTER">register</a> or license: all which are, by distinct acts of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, made felonies without benefit of clergy. By statutes 13 Geo. III. c. 52. and 59. forging or counterfeiting any stamp or mark to denote the standard of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> and silver plate, and certain other offences of the like tendency, are punished with transportation for 14 years. By statute 12 Geo. III. c. 48. certain frauds on the stamp-duties, therein described, principally by using the same stamps more than once, are made single felony, and liable to transportation for <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> years. And the same punishment is inflicted by statute 13 Geo. III. c. 38. on such as counterfeit the common seal of the corporation for manufacturing plate glass (thereby erected), or knowingly demand <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> by virtue of any writing under such counterfeit seal. There are also two other general laws with regard to forgery; the one 2 Geo. II. c. 25. whereby the first offence in forging or procuring to be forged, acting or assisting therein, or uttering or publishing as true, any forged deed, will, bond, writing obligatory, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BILL">bill</a> of exchange, promissory <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOTE">note</a>, indorsement or assignment thereof, or any acquittance or receipt for money or goods, with intention to defraud any person (or corporation), is made felony without benefit of clergy. And by statute 7 Geo. II. c. 22. it is equally penal to forge, or cause to be forged, or utter as true, a counterfeit <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACCEPTANCE">acceptance</a> of a bill of exchange, or the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of any accountable receipt for any note, bill, or any other security for money, or any warrant or order for the payment of money or delivery of goods. So that, through the number of these general and special <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a>, there is now hardly a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> possible to be conceived, wherein forgery, that tends to defraud, whether in the name of a real or fictitious person, is not made a capital crime. Forging, in Law, the act of Forgery. Forging, in smithery, the heating or hammering <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> on an anvil, after having first made it <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> hot in the forge, in order to extend it into various forms, and fashion it into various works. There are two ways of forging and hammering iron. One is by the force of the hand, in which there are usually several persons employed, one of them <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> the iron and hammering likewise, and the rest only hammering. The other way is by the force of a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>-mill, which raises and works several huge <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-HAMMERS">hammers</a> beyond the force of man; under the strokes whereof the workmen present <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> lumps or pieces of iron, which are sustained at one end by the anvils, and at the other by iron chains fastened to the ceiling of the forge. See Mill. This last way of forging is only used in the largest works, as anchors for ships, &c. which usually weigh several thousand pounds. For the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIGHTER">lighter</a> works, a single man serves to hold, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>, and turn with one hand, while he hammers with the other. Each purpose the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> is designed for requires its proper heat; for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> it be too <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLD">cold</a>, it will not feel the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of the hammer, as the smiths call it when it will not batter under the hammer; and if it be too hot, it will red sear, that is, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> or crack under the hammer. The several degrees of heat the smiths give their iron, are, first, a blood-red heat; secondly, a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAME">flame</a> heat; and thirdly, a sparkling or welding heat. Forisfamiliation, in Law, When a child, upon receiving a portion from his father, or otherwise, renounces his legal <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> to any further share of his father's succession, he is said to be forisfamiliated. Fork, a well known <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a>, consisting of a handle and blade, divided at the end into two or more <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">points</a> or prongs. The pitch-fork is a large utensil of this <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a> employed in hay-making, &c. The <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a>-fork, an instrument now so indispensable, did not come into <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> in England till the reign of James I., as we learn from a remarkable passage in Coryat. The reader will probably smile at the solemn manner in which this important discovery or innovation is related: "Here I will mention a thing that might have been spoken of before in discourse of the first Italian townes. I observed a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> in all those Italian cities and townes through the which I passed, that is not used in any other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> that I <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> in my travels, neither do I thinke that any other <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> of Christendom..." <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DOME">dome</a> doth use it, but only <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>. The Italians and also most strangers that are commorant in Italy, doe always at their meals use a little forke when they eat their meate; for while with their <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KNIFE">knife</a> which they hold in one hand they cut the meate out of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DISH">dish</a>, they fasten the forke which they hold in the other hand upon the same dish, so that whatsoever he be that sitting in the company of any others at meale shall unadvisedly touch the dish of meat with his fingers from which all the table doe cut, he will give occasion of offence unto the company as having transgressed the lawes of good manners, insomuch that for his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ERROR">error</a> he shall be at least brow-beaten if not reprehended in wordes. This form of feeding I understand is generally used in all parts of Italy, their forkes for the most <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> being made of yronn, steele, and some of silver, but those are used only by gentlemen. The reason of this their curiosity is, because the Italian cannot by any means indure to have his dish touched with fingers, seeing all men's fingers are not alike cleane. Hereupon I myself thought good to imitate the Italian fashion by this forked <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> of meate, not only while I was in Italy, but also in Germany, and often times in England since I came home: being once quipped for that frequently using my forke, by a certain learned <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a>, a familiar friend of mine, Mr Lawrence Whitaker; who in his merry humour doubted not to call me a table furcifer, only for using a forke at feeding, but for no other cause."

FORLI

Pages 21-21

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> and considerable town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a territory of the same name, in Romagna, with a bishop's see. The public structures are very handsome; and it is seated in a fertile, healthy, and pleasant <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, 10 miles south-east of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FAENZA">Faenza</a>, and 45 <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-east of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLORENCE">Florence</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 12. I. N. Lat. 44. 28.

FORLORN-HOPE

Pages 21-21

in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> art, signifies men detached from several regiments, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> otherwise appointed, to make the first attack in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>; or at a siege, to storm the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTERSCARP">counterscarp</a>, mount the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREACH">breach</a>, or the like. They are so called from the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> danger they are unavoidably exposed to; but the word is old, and begins to be obsolete.

FORM

Pages 21-22

in Physics, denotes the manner of being peculiar to each body; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> that which constitutes it such a particular body, and distinguishes it from every other. Mr Harris uses the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> form likewise in another <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, as an efficient animating principle; to which he supposes Ovid to refer in the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> of his Metamorphoses. In nova fert animus mutatas dicere formas, Corpora. These animating forms are of themselves no objects either of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-EAR">ear</a> or of the eye; but their <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> or character is understood in this, that were they never to exert their proper energies on their proper subjects, the marble on which the sculptor exercises his art would remain for ever shapeless, and the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-HARP">harp</a> from which the harper calls forth sounds would remain for ever silent. Thus also, the animating form of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> body is neither its organization nor its <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, nor any other of those inferior forms which make up the system of its visible qualities: but it is the power, which is yet able to produce, preserve, and employ these. It is the power, which first moves, and then conducts that latent <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROCESS">process</a>, by which the acorn becomes an oak, and the embryo becomes a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>; by which digestion is performed in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> and animals, and, which departing, the body ceases to live, and its members putrefy: and by which every being produces another like itself, and every <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> is <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a>. In animals, it is that higher <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FACULTY">faculty</a>, which, by employing the organs of sense, peculiar to them as animals, distinguishes them as sensitive beings from vegetables; and it is also that more noble faculty, which by its own divine vigour, unassisted perhaps with organs, makes and denominates him a being intellective and rational. So that Mr Harris reckons two sorts of forms, those which are <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PASSIVE">passive</a> elements, and those which are efficient causes. And all of them agree in this, that they give to every being its peculiar and distinctive character: and on the whole he concludes, that form appears in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> to be an element, and in part an efficient cause, i.e. a cause which associates the constituent elements of natural substances, and which employs them, when associated, according to their various and peculiar <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a>. The philosophers generally allow two principles of bodies: <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>, as the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> basis or substratum of all; and form, as that which specifies and distinguishes each; and which added to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of common matter, determines or denominates it this or that; wood, or fire, or ashes, &c. Substantial forms seem to have been first broached by the followers of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a>, who thought matter, under different modes or modifications, not sufficient to constitute different bodies; but that something substantial was necessary to set them at a greater distance: and thus introduced substantial forms, on the footing of souls, which specify and distinguish animals. What led to this erroneous notion were the circumstances of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>: For observing, that, as soon as the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUL">soul</a> was departed out of a man, all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>, respiration, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NUTRITION">nutrition</a>, &c. immediately ceased, they concluded, that all these functions depended on the soul, and consequently that the soul was the form of the animal body, or that which constituted it such: that the soul was a substance, independent of matter, nobody doubted; and hence the forms of other bodies were concluded equally substantial. But to this it is answered, that though the soul be that by which a man is man, and consequently is the form of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> body, as human; yet it does not follow, that it is properly the form of this body of ours, as it is a body; nor of the several parts thereof, considered as distinct from each other: For those several parts have their proper forms so closely connected with their matter, that it remains inseparable therefrom <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> after the soul has quitted the body; thus <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> has the form of flesh, bone of bone, &c. long after the soul is removed as well as before. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> is, the body does not become incapable of performing its accustomed functions because the soul has deserted it; but the soul takes its leave, because the body is not in a condition to perform its functions. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> corpuscular philosophers, therefore, with the Cartesians, exclude the notion of substantial forms; and show, by many arguments, that the form is only the modus or manner of the body it is inherent in. And as there are only three primary modes of matter, viz. figure, rest, or motion, with two others arising therefrom, viz. magnitude and situation, the form of all bodies they hold to consist therein; and suppose the variations these modes are capable of, sufficient to present all the variety observable in bodies. Forms are usually distinguished into essential and accidental. Essential. Though the five modes above mentioned, generally taken, be adventitious; yet to this or that body, e.g., to fire or <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, they are essential; thus it is accidental to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, to have this or that magnitude, figure, or situation, since it might exist in different ones; yet to a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KNIFE">knife</a> or hammer, the figure, magnitude, and position of parts, which constitute it a hammer or knife, are essential; and they cannot exist or be conceived without them. Hence it is inferred, that though there be no substantial, there are essential forms, whereby the several species of bodies become what they are, and are distinguished from all others. Accidental forms, are those really inherent in bodies, but in such manner as that the body may exist in all its perfection without them. Such as whiteness in a wall, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> in water, a figure of a man in wax, &c. Form is also used, in a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MORAL_SENSE">moral sense</a>, for the manner of being or doing a thing according to rules: thus we say, a form of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, a form of argument, &c. Form, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, the rules established and requisite to be observed in legal proceedings. The formal part of the law, or method of proceeding, cannot be altered but by <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>; for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> once these outworks were demolished, there would be an inlet to all manner of innovation in the body of the law itself. Form, in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARPENTRY">carpentry</a>, is used to denote the long seats or benches in the choirs of churches or in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a>, for the priests, prebends, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a>, or scholars, to sit on. Du Cange takes the name to be derived from hence, that the backs of the seats were anciently enriched with figures of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SCULPTURE">sculpture</a>, called in Latin formæ et typi. In the life of St William of Roschild, we meet with forma as signifying a seat for an ecclesiastic, or religious, in a choir; and in that of St Lupicin, we have formula in the same sense. In the rule of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a> of St Cesarea, the man who presides over the choir is called primiceria, vel formari. At schools, the word form is frequently applied to what is otherwise termed a class. See Class.

FORM ALSO

Pages 22-22

m also denotes the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> appearance <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> surface of a body, or the disposition of its parts as to the length, breadth and thickness. Form is also used among <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MECHANICS">mechanics</a>, for a sort of mould wherein any thing is fashioned or wrought. Printer's Form, an assemblage of letters, words, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a>, ranged in order, and so disposed into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAGES">pages</a> by the compositor; from which, by means of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INK">ink</a> and a press, the printed sheets are drawn. Every form is enclosed in an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHEST">chest</a>, wherein it is firmly locked by a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of pieces of wood; some <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> and narrow, and others of the form of wedges. There are two forms required for every sheet, one for each side; and each form consists of more or fewer pages according to the size of the book. Hatter's Form, is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLOCK">block</a> or piece of wood, of a cylindrical <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>; the top thereof rounded, and the bottom quite flat. Its <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> is, to mould or fashion the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> of the hat, after the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> thereof has been beaten and fulled. Papermaker's Form, is the frame or mould wherein the sheets are fashioned. See <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PAPER">Paper</a>.

FORMA PAUPERIS

Pages 22-22

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, is when a person has <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> cause of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUIT">suit</a>, but is so <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a> that he cannot defray the usual charges of suing at law <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EQUITY">equity</a>; in which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>, on making oath that he is not worth 5l. in the world, on all his debts being paid, and producing a certificate from some lawyer that he has good cause of suit, the judge <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> admit him to sue in forma pauperis; that is, without paying any fee to counsellors, attorneys, or clerk: the statute 11 Hen. VII. c. 12, having enacted, that counsel and attorneys, &c. shall be assigned to such poor persons gratis. Where it appears that any pauper has sold or contracted for the benefit of his suit whilst it is depending in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>, such cause shall be thenceforth totally dismissed; and a person suing in forma pauperis shall not have a new <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a> granted him, but is to acquiesce in the judgment of the court.

FORMAL

Pages 22-22

something belonging to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> constituting the form of a thing. See Form.

FORMALITY

Pages 22-22

the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of a form, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> formula; or that which constitutes and denominates them such. Formality, as defined in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a>, is any manner wherein a thing is conceived; or a manner in any object, importing a relation for the understanding whereby it may be distinguished from another object. Thus animality and rationality are formalities. The Scottists made <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of formalities, in opposition to the virtualities of the Thomists. Formalities, in matters of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a>, are frequently used for the formulas themselves, or the rules prescribed for judiciary proceedings. In contracts of strict law, all the formalities must be strictly observed: an omission of the least formality may ruin the whole convention. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> is also used for a certain order or <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECORUM">decorum</a> to be observed.

FORMAN

Pages 22-23

ANDREW, archbishop of St Andrew's, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of Pittenweem, and of Cottingham in England, one of the lords of the regency appointed by the states during the minority of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> James V. of Scotland, legate a latere, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIMATE">primate</a> of all the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of Scotland, and archbishop of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOURGES">Bourges</a> in France, was descended from the family of the Formans of Hutton in the shire of Berwick, and is considered to have been one of the best statesmen of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> in which he lived. He was employed in 1501, along with Robert Blackader, archbishop of Glasgow, and Patrick earl of Bothwell to negotiate a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MATCH">match</a> between Ja. IV. of Scotland and Margaret eldest <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Hen. VII. of England, which next year was ratified by the Scottish ambassadors. He was afterwards frequently employed as Scots <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBASSADOR">ambassador</a> to Rome, England, and France, upon the most important occasions. In 1514, he was translated from the see of Moray, to which he had been appointed in 1502, to that of St Andrews. During the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of his possessing the former, he was employed as mediator betwixt Pope Julius II. and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> XII. of France, who were at that time at variance; and he happily succeeded in conciliating the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a>. Having taken leave of the Pope, he passed through France on his return home, where he was kindly received by the king and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a>, who bestowed upon him the bishopric of Bourges in France, which annually brought him in 400 tons of wine, 10,000 francs of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, and other smaller <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a>. Besides all this, he was most liberally rewarded by Pope Julius, who promoted him to the archbishopric of St Andrew's, as has been already mentioned; conferred on him the two rich abbeys of Dunfermline and Aberbrothick; and made him his legate à latere. At that time, however, there were two other candidates for the archiepiscopal see. The learned Gavin Douglas, bishop of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DUNKELD">Dunkeld</a>, having been nominated by the queen, had actually taken possession of it; but John Hepburn, a bold and factious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, having been preferred by the monks, drove out the officers of Gavin Douglas, and placed a strong garrison in the castle. So <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> was the power of this man, that when Forman was nominated by the Pope, no person could be found who durst proclaim the bulls for his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTION">election</a>. At last <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Home, at that time the most powerful nobleman in Scotland, was induced, by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> promises, besides some gifts of great <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a>, among which was the donation of the abbacy of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLDINGHAM">Coldingham</a> to his youngest <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAVID">David</a>, to undertake the task. It was executed at <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a> and St Andrew's; to which places Lord Home's brother went with 10,000 men; though the doing of it, contrary to Forman's inclination, proved a source of much trouble to that nobleman afterwards. The quarrel betwixt Hepburn and Forman, however, was at last terminated by the latter surrendering the bishopric of Moray, as well as some years revenue of the archbishopric itself; paying Hepburn also 3000 French crowns annually out of his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> revenues. On the appointment of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALBANY">Albany</a> to the regency, Hepburn endeavoured to undermine the primate's <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> with that nobleman, by representing him as one who had in a manner collected all the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, and who consequently might endanger the tranquillity of the kingdom. These insinuations, however, were but little regarded by the regent; and Forman had the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOOD_FORTUNE">good fortune</a> afterwards to make up a difference between him and the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a>, which was likely to be attended with much bloodshed. In 1517, the archbishop was appointed by the states one of the lords of the regency, on occasion of the duke of Albany's going to France. We have already mentioned his embassy to Pope Julius II. In M'Kenzie's Lives we are informed, that in the collection of the Letters of the Scottish Kings from the year 1505 till the year 1626, in the lawyers library, there is a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> from the pope to King James IV. wherein he not only highly commends Forman, but likewise promises that at the first <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREATION">creation</a> of cardinals he should be made one. This letter is dated the 6th of May, 1511: but the pope died before he had an opportunity of performing his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROMISE">promise</a>. In the same collection there is a letter from the duke of Albany to Leo X. Julius's successor, wherein he presses the pope to advance him to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDINAL">cardinal</a> promised him by his predecessor, and to continue him his legate à latere. Archbishop Forman died in 1521, and was buried at Dunfermline. Dempster says that he wrote a book against <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LUTHER">Luther</a>, a book concerning the Stoic <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">Philosophy</a>, and a Collection out of the Decretals.

FORMATION

Pages 23-23

in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAMMAR">Grammar</a>, signifies the manner of forming one word from another; thus accountantship is formed from accountant, and this last from account.

FORMEDON

Pages 23-23

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, (breve de forma donationis), a writ that lies for a person who has a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> to lands <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> tenements, by virtue of any entail, arising from the statute of Westm. 2. Ch. II. This writ is of three kinds, viz. a descender, remainder, and reverter. Formedon in descender, lies where a tenant in tail infeoffs a stranger, or is disseised and dies, and the heir may bring this writ to recover the lands. Formedon in remainder, lies where a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> gives lands, &c. to a person in tail, and for the default of issue of his body, the remainder to another in tail: here <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the tenant in tail die without issue, and a stranger abates and enters into the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a>, he in remainder shall have this writ. Formedon in reverter, lies where lands are entailed on certain persons and their issue, with remainder over for want of issue; and on that remainder failing, then to revert to the donor and his heirs; in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>, if the tenant in tail dies without issue, and also he in remainder, the donor and his heirs, to whom the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVERSION">reversion</a> returns, may have this writ for the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RECOVERY">recovery</a> of the estate, though the same be alienated, &c. FORMIÆ, or FORMIA, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARITIME">maritime</a> town of the Adjected or New Latiom, to the south-east of Cajeta; built by the Lacedæmonians, (Strabo); called originally Hormice, on account of its commodious harbour. An ancient municipium. Formiani, the people; who were admitted to the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> the very year in which <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALEXANDRIA">Alexandria</a> was built; but not to the right of suffrage till a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> after the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> Punic <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, (Livy). Formiae at this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> lies in ruins, near a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> now called <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOLA">Mola</a>.

FORMICA

Pages 23-24

the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANT">Ant</a>, a genus of insects belonging to the order of hymenoptera. See ENTOMOLOGY <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. The insects called <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> ants, which abound in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a> and the East Indies, belong to the genus termes, which see in ENTOMOLOGY Index. Formica Leo, the Ant lion, so called from its devouring <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> numbers of ants. It is the caterpillar <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> worm of a fly much resembling the libellæ or dragon flies; and feeds chiefly upon ants. FORMING is used for the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> of giving being or birth to any thing. The word is also simply used for giving the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> to any thing. The potter forms his vessels as he pleases. <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOMETRY">Geometry</a> teaches how to form all kinds of figures. It is likewise used for the producing of a thing: thus, the lineaments of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FACE">face</a> began to be formed. FORMING of a Siege, is the making <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> of circum- vallation to fortify the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMP">camp</a>, and disposing things for the attack of a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in form. They also say, to form a squadron or battalion; meaning to range the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> in form of a squadron, &c. FORMING the Line, is <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> up infantry, cavalry, and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTILLERY">artillery</a>, into line of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>. See LINE. FORMING is also used in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAMMAR">grammar</a>, in speaking of certain tenses of verbs, which are made from others by a change of certain letters. The present tense is formed from the infinitive. <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPOUND">Compound</a> and derivative words also, and even all that have any <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ETYMOLOGY">etymology</a>, are said to be formed.

FORMOSA

Pages 24-26

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PACIFIC_OCEAN">Pacific ocean</a>, be- tween 119° and 122° of E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>, and 22° and 25° N. Lat. about 100 miles east of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANTON">Canton</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHINA">China</a>. It is subject to the Chinese; who, however, notwithstanding its vicinity, did not know of its existence until the year 1430. It is about 85 leagues in length, and 25 in breadth. A long chain of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, which runs from <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> to south, divides it into two parts, the eastern and western. The Dutch formed an establish- ment in the western <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> in 1634, and built the fort of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZEALAND">Zealand</a>, which secured to them the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> port of the island; but they were driven from thence in 1659 <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> 1661 by a celebrated Chinese <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PIRATE">pirate</a>, who made himself <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of all the western part, which afterwards submitted in 1682 to the authority of Kang-he <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> of China. This western part of Formosa is divided into three distinct governments, all subordinate to the governor of Tai-ouan, the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the island, who is himself sub- ject to the viceroy of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of FoKien. This island presents extensive and fertile plains, wa- tered by a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of rivulets that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> from the eastern mountains. Its <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> is pure and wholesome; and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> produces in abundance, corn, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICE">rice</a>, and the greater part of other grains. Most of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> are found here, such as oranges, bananas, pine-apples, guavas, papaws, cocoa nuts; and part of those of Eu- rope, particularly peaches, apricots, figs, raisins, ches- nuts, pomegranates, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> melons, &c. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOBACCO">Tobacco</a>, su- gar, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEPPER">pepper</a>, camphire, and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CINNAMON">cinnamon</a>, are also <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a>. Horses, sheep, and goats, are very rare in this island; there are even few hogs, although these animals abound in China. <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOMESTIC">Domestic</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POULTRY">poultry</a>, such as fowls, geese, and ducks, are exceedingly plenty; pheasants also are sometimes seen; and monkeys and stage have multiplied so much, that they wander through the coun- try in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> flocks. The inhabitants of Formosa rear a great number of oxen, which they <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> for riding, from a want of horses and mules. They accustom them early to this kind of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>, and by daily <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> train them to go as well and as expeditiously as the best horses. These oxen were furnished with a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRIDLE">bridle</a>, saddle, and crupper. A Chinese looks as big and proud when mounted in this manner, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he were carried by the finest Barbary courser. Wholesome water fit for drinking is the only thing wanting in the island of Formosa. It is very extra- ordinary, that every kind of water in it is a deadly poi- son to strangers, for which no remedy has hitherto been found. "One of the governor's servants," says Father de Maille, "whom I had in my train (a strong and robust <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>), trusting too much to the force of his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a>, would not believe what had been told him concerning this water: he drank some of it; and died in less than five days, after every medicine and antidote had been administered without success. There is none but the water of the capital which can be drunk: the mandarins of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> therefore always took care to transport a sufficiency of it in carts for our use." Our author adds, that at the bottom of a mountain a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEAGUE">league</a> distant from Fong-kan-hien there is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> that produces a stream, the water of which is of a whitish blue <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, and so noxious, that no one can approach it. There are few mulberry trees in Formosa, conse- quently little <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a> is made in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. Numerous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a>, however, would soon be introduced in- to it, were the Chinese permitted indiscriminately to transport themselves thither, and to form establishments in the island. Those who go to it must be protected by passports from the Chinese mandarins, and these passports are sold at a dear rate; securities are besides required. This is not all: when they arrive, <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a> must be given to the mandarins who are appointed to examine those who enter or quit the island, and who generally discharge this duty with the most rigid seve- rity. If they give no present, or offer only a trifle, they meet with little mercy: and are sure to be sent back, whatever <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PASSPORT">passport</a> they may have. The Chinese, through policy, connive at these exactions, to prevent too great a number of people from emigrating to this island, which is rendered a place of great importance by its <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROXIMITY">proximity</a> to China. They fear, and with great reason (especially since Tartar emperors have been on the throne), that if any revolt should happen in For- mosa, its influence might spread and occasion great <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIS">dis</a>- turbance in the whole empire. On this account, the Tartars keep a garrison there of 10,000 men: which they take care to change every three years, or even oftener if they judge it necessary. Besides the capital, the Chinese have also two other cities, and some villages, where they inhabit alone; for they do not permit the Indians, who are their sub- jects, to live among them; they suffer none to remain but those who are either their slaves or domestics.— These Indians are united into 45 villages; 36 of which <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> to the north, and 9 towards the south. The nor- thern villages are very populous, and the houses are built almost after the Chinese manner. The habita- tions of the southern islanders are only heaps of huts or cottages of earth. In these huts they have neither chairs, benches, tables, beds, nor any piece of furni- ture; the middle part is occupied by a kind of hearth or chimney, raised two feet <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, and constructed of earth, upon which they dress their victuals. Their ordinary food is rice, other small grain, and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GAME">game</a> which they catch by coursing or kill with their arms. These islanders run with such surprising swiftness, that they can almost outstrip the fleetest greyhound. The Chinese <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-ATTRIBUTE">attribute</a> this agility to the precaution they take of confining their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KNEES">knees</a> and reins by a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> band- <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> until the age of 14 or 15. Their favourite arms are lances, which they dart to the distance of 60 or 80 feet with the greatest dexterity and precision. They use bows and arrows, and can kill a pheasant on wing with as much certainty as an European sportsman could with a fuser. These people are very dirty in their manner of eating. They have neither plates, dishes, nor spoons, nor even the small sticks used in China. Whatever they dress is placed on a plain board or mat, and they make use of their fingers for conveying it to their mouths. They eat <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> half raw; and provided it has been only presented to the fire, it appears to them excellent. Their beds are formed of fresh gathered leaves. They go almost naked, and wear only a piece of cloth which hangs from their girdle to their knees. Those among them, who, according to the judgment of the chiefs of the village, have borne away the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIZE">prize</a> for agility in running, or dexterity in the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHASE">chase</a>, obtain the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> privilege of making on their skin, by a very painful operation, several fantastical figures of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>, trees, and animals. All have the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> of blackening their <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a>, and of wearing ornaments of bracelets and crowns made of shells and crystal. The islanders who inhabit the northern part, where the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> is somewhat colder, clothe themselves with the skins of the stags which they kill in hunting. They make a kind of dress of them without sleeves, that pretty much resembles a dalmatic, or vestment worn at the altar by the Roman clergy. They wear on their heads caps in the form of a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CYLINDER">cylinder</a>, made of palm leaves, and ornamented with several crowns placed one above another, on the top of which they fix plumes composed of the feathers of a cock or pheasant. The <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> ceremonies of the inhabitants of Formosa approach near to the simple laws of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>. They neither purchase, as in China, the women whom they espouse, nor does <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> ever preside over their unions. Fathers and mothers are scarcely ever consulted. If a young man has a mind to marry, and has fixed his affection on a young girl, he appears for several days following near the place where she lives with a musical <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> in his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>. If the young woman is satisfied with the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of her gallant, she comes forth and joins him: they then agree and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> the marriage <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRACT">contract</a>. After this, they give notice to their parents who prepare a wedding dinner, which is always given in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> where the young woman resides, and where the bridegroom remains without returning again to his father. The young man afterwards considers the house of his father-in-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a> as his own. He becomes the whole support of it, and he has no farther connection with that of his father; like married women in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, who generally quit their paternal home in order to live with their husbands. These islanders therefore seldom offer up vows for obtaining <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MALE">male</a> children: they prefer daughters, because they procure them sons-in-law, who become their supports in old age. Although the Formosans are entirely subjected to the Chinese, they still preserve some remains of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>. Each village chooses three or four old men from among those who have the greatest reputation for probity. By this choice they become the rulers and judges of the rest of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAMLET">hamlet</a>. They have the power of finally determining all differences; and if any one should refuse to abide by their judgment, he would be immediately banished from the village, without hopes of ever being able to re-enter it, and none of the inhabitants would afterwards dare to receive him.
