From these different sentiments it may be inferred, that the ancients at one <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> took Fortune for a peremptory cause, bent upon doing good to some, some, and persecuting others; and sometimes for a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLIND">blind</a> inconstant cause, without any view or determination at all. If then the word fortune had no certain idea in the mouth of those who erected altars to her, much less can it be ascertained what it denotes in the minds of those who now <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> the word in their writings. They who would substitute the name <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVIDENCE">Providence</a> in lieu of that of Fortune, cannot give any tolerable sense to half the phrases wherein the word occurs. Horace paints the goddess, preceded by <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">Necessity</a>, holding nails and wedges in her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, with a cramp-<a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, and melted <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> to fasten it; rarely accompanied with Fidelity, unless when she abandons a family; for in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> Fidelity never fails to depart with her, as well as friends. She is disrespectfully spoken of by most of the Roman writers, and represented as blind, inconstant, unjust, and delighting in mischief, (Ovid, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AD">ad</a> Liv. ver. 52, ver. 374. (Hor. lib. i. od. 34. ver. 26. lib. iii. od. 29. ver. 15. Statius, Theb. xii. ver. 505.). However they had a good as well as a bad Fortune, a constant and inconstant Fortune; the latter of which was represented with wings, and a wheel by her, (Hor. lib. iii. od. 29. ver. 56.). Juvenal alludes to a statue of Fortune, which exhibited her under a very good character, as the patroness of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INFANTS">infants</a> that were exposed by their parents in the streets, (Sat. vi. ver. 605.). The painters represent her in a woman's <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HABIT">habit</a>, with a bandage before her eyes, to show that she acts without discernment; and standing on a wheel, to express her instability. The Romans, says Lactantius, represented her with a cornucopia, and the helm of a ship, to shew that she distributes <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RICHES">riches</a>, and directs the affairs of the world. In effect, it is with such <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> that we see her represented on so many medals, with the inscription, FORTUNA AVG. FORTUNA REDVX, FORTUNAE AVG. or REDVCIS, &c. Sometimes she is seen pointing at a globe before her feet, with a sceptre in one <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, and holding the cornucopia in the other. The Romans had a virile as well as a muliebrian Fortune, for the objects of their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ADORATION">adoration</a>: the Fortuna virilis was honoured by the men, and the Fortuna muliebris by the women. They honoured fortune also under a variety of other appellations. The Romans derived the worship of Fortune from the Greeks, under the reign of Servius Tullius, who dedicated the first temple to her in the public market. Nero also built a temple to Fortune. The Fortune worshipped at Antium was probably of the most exalted character of any among the Romans; if we may judge by the account which Horace gives us of the great solemn processions that were made to her, (Hor. lib. i. od. 35. ver. 22.). But the most celebrated temple of Fortune was at Praeneste. Statins speaks of several Fortunes there, and calls them the Praenestine sorores, (lib. i. Sylv. iii. ver. 80.). Fortune-Tellers. Persons pretending to tell fortunes are to be punished with a year's imprisonment, and standing four times on the pillory. Stat. ix. Geo. II. c. 5. FORTY days <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">Court</a>, the court of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a> or woodnote, held before the verderors of the forest once every forty days, to inquire concerning all offenders against vert and venison. See ATTACHMENT.

FORUM

Pages 51-52

in Roman antiquity, a public standing <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> within the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Rome, where causes were judicially tried, and orations delivered to the people. Forum was also used for a place of traffic, answering to our market-place. These were generally called fora venalia; in contradistinction to the former, which were called fora civilia. The fora civilia were public courts of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>, very magnificent in themselves, and surrounded with porticoes and stately edifices; of these there were six very remarkable: 1. Forum Romanum. 2. Julianum. 3. Augustum. 4. <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALLADIUM">Palladium</a>. 5. Forum Traiani. 6. Forum Salustii. The Forum Romanum was the most noted, and is often called simply Forum, by way of eminence. Here was the pleading place called Rostra, the Cenitium, the sanctuary of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SATURN">Saturn</a>, temple of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASTOR">Castor</a>, &c. See Rostra, Comitium, &c. The fora venalia, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> market-places, were very numerous. The <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> of them were the forum boarium for oxen or beef; suarium for swine; pistorium for <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a>; cupendarium for dainties; olitorium for garden stuff. The Grecian Αξεια, exactly correspond with the Roman fora, being places where courts and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MARKETS">markets</a> were held. At <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a> they had many fora, but the chief of them were the old and the new. Forum Indicere, was the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> of the praetor appointing the place in Rome where causes were to be tried. Agere forum denoted the bringing on causes out of Rome, in a Roman <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> (Cicero, Suetonius); the same with agere conventum (Florus). The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> forum added to a proper name, denoted some town or market borough; as, Forum Allieni, a place mentioned only by Tacitus; and, from what he says of it, thought to be <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FERRARA">Ferrara</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of that name in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 12. 5. N. Lat. 44. 46. Forum Appii (Cicero, Luke); a town of the Volsci, in Latium, on the Via Appia; a little beyond the Tres Taberne; set <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a> Itinerary as situated near the river Nymphacus: now entirely extinct. Forum Cornelii, a town of the Cispadana, built by Sylla: Now <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMOLA">Imola</a>, a city in Romagna, and territory of the Pope. E. Long. 12. 12. N. Lat. 44. 30. Forum Domitii, a town of Gallia Narbonensis; probably built by Domitius Ahenobarbus, who commanded in those parts: Now <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-FRONTIGNAN">Frontignan</a>, or Frontigniac, in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANGUEDOC">Languedoc</a>, near the Mediterranean. E. Long. 3. 30. N. Lat. 43. 30. Forum Fulii, a town of Liguria, surnamed Valentimum: from which it is conjectured that it is now Valenza, in the duchy of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILAN">Milan</a>; which is confirmed by Peutinger's distances. E. Long. 9°. N. Lat. 45°. Forum Gallorum, a small town of the Cispadana, on the Via Æmilia, eight miles from Mutina, beyond the river Scultenna. Here Antony defeated Pansa, and was in his turn defeated by Hirtius: Now Castelfranco, in the territory of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOLOGNA">Bologna</a>.—Another Forum Gallorum, a town of the Vascones in the Hither <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>: Now Gurrea, a small town of Arragon. Forum Julium. There are several <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> of this name; as a Forum Julium of Gallia Narbonensis; or Forojulium: Now Frejus, or Frejules, in Provence, at the mouth of the Argens. Forum Julium Carnorum, to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of Aquileia, in the Transpadana: Now Cividal di Friuli; formerly Cividal d’ <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AUSTRIA">Austria</a>, in the territory of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>. Forum Jutuntorum, a town of the Insubres, in the Transpadana: Now <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREMA">Crema</a>, capital of the Cremasco, in the territory of Venice. E. Long. 10. 15. N. Lat. 45. 20. Forum Livii, a town of the Sennones, in the Cispadana: Now Forlì, in Romagna. E. Long. 12. 45. N. Lat. 44. 25. Forum Segusianorum, situated on the east side of the Liger, in Gallia Celtica: now Feurs, on the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LOIRE">Loire</a>, in the Lyonnais, capital of the territory of Forez. E. Long. 4. 15. N. Lat. 45. 44. Forum Tiberii, a town of the Pagus Tigurinus, in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BELGICA">Belgica</a>, on the left or south side of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHINE">Rhine</a>: Now Kayserstull; literally the tribunal of Tiberius, which he held there when commander in the Rhetian <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>. Forum Volcani (Strabo); the Campi Phlegrei of Pliny; a place in Campania encompassed with rocky eminences, near Puteoli, and distant from it two miles towards <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>, emitting <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SMOKE">smoke</a>, and in some places <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAME">flame</a>, like a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> extensive <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FURNACE">furnace</a>, and yielding sulphur: Now called <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOLFATARA">Solfatara</a>, in the Terra di Lavoro. Forum is also used, among casuists, &c. for jurisdiction; thus they say, In foro legis, &c.

FOSSA MAGNA

Pages 52-52
or NAVICULARIS, is an oblong cavity, forming the inside of the pudendum muliebre, and which presents itself upon opening the labia; and in the middle whereof are the carunculae myrtiformes. See ANATOMY. Fossa, in our ancient customs, was a ditch full of water, where women committing felony were drowned; as men were hanged: Nam et ipsi in omnibus tenementis suis omnem ab antiquo legalem habuerent justitiam, videlicet ferrum, fossam, furcas, et similia. In another sense it is taken for a grave, as appears by these old verses: Hic jacent in fossa Bedae venerabilis ossa: Hic est fossatus, qui bis erat hic cathedratus. Foss Way was anciently one of the four great Roman highways of England: so called, according to Camden, because it was ditched on both sides, which was the Roman method of making highways.

FOSSARI

Pages 52-52

in antiquity, a kind of officers in the eastern <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, whose business was to inter the dead. Ciaconius relates, that Constantine created 950 fossaries, whom he took out of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> colleges <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> companies of tradesmen: he adds, that they were exempted from taxes, services, burdensome offices, &c. F. Goar, in his notes on the Greek Euchologion, insinuates that the fossarii were established in the times of the apostles; and that the young men, who carried off the body of Ananias, and those persons full of the fear of God who interred St Stephen, were of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>. St Jerome assures us, that the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> of fossarii held the first <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> among the clerks; but he is to be understood of those clerks only who had the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> and intendance of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTERMENT">interment</a> of the devout.

FOSSE

Pages 52-52

the Roman <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> way in South <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, begins at Totness, and passes through <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXETER">Exeter</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IVELCHESTER">Ivelchester</a>, Shepton <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALLET">Mallet</a>, Bath, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CIRENCESTER">Cirencester</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEICESTER">Leicester</a>, the Vale of Belvoir, Newark, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LINCOLN">Lincoln</a>, to Barton upon the Humber, being still visible in several parts, though of 1400 years standing. It had the name from the fosses <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> ditches made by the sides of it.

FOSSIL

Pages 52-53

in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, denotes, in general, every thing dug out of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, whether it be a native thereof, as <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-METALS">metals</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, salts, earths, and other minerals; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> extraneous, reposed in the bowels of the earth by some extraordinary means, as earthquakes, the deluge, &c. Native fossils are substances found in the earth, or on its surface, of a simple structure, exhibiting no appearances of organization; and these are included under the general names of simple and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPOUND">compound</a>, earthly or metallic minerals. See <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINERALOGY">MINERALOGY</a>. Extraneous fossils are bodies of the vegetable or animal kingdoms accidentally buried in the earth. Of the vegetable <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, there are principally three kinds; trees or parts of them, herbaceous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, and corals: and of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ANIMAL_KINGDOM">animal kingdom</a> there are four kinds; <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> shells, the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a> or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BONY">bony</a> palates and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONES">bones</a> of fishes, complete fishes, and the bones of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> animals. See <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOLOGY">GEOLOGY</a>. These adventitious or extraneous fossils, thus found buried in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> abundance in <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> parts of the earth, have employed the curiosity of several of our latest naturalists, who have each their several system to account for the surprising appearances of petrified sea fishes, in places far remote from the sea, and on the tops of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>; shells in the middle of quarries of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>; and of elephants teeth, and bones of divers animals, peculiar to the southern climates, and plants only growing in the east, found fossil in our northern and western parts. Some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> have these shells, &c. to be real stones, and stone plants, formed after the usual manner of other figured stones; of which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> is the learned Dr Lister. Another opinion is, that these fossil shells, with all the foreign bodies found within the earth, as bones, trees, plants, &c. were buried therein at the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of the universal deluge; and that, having been penetrated either by the bituminous <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> abounding chiefly in watery places, or by the salts of the earth, they have been preserved entire, and sometimes petrified. Others think, that those shells, found at the tops of the highest mountains, could never have been carried thither by the waters, even of the deluge; inasmuch as most of these aquatic animals, on account of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of their shells, always remain at the bottom of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, and never move but <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> along the ground. They imagine, that a year’s continuance of the waters of the deluge, intermixed with the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> waters of the sea, upon the surface of the earth, might well give occasion to the production of shells of divers kinds in different climates; climates; and that the universal saltiness of the water was the real cause of their resemblance to the sea shells, as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a> formed daily by the retention of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">rain</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> water produce different kinds. Others think, that the waters of the sea, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, with those which fell from heaven, turned the whole surface of the earth upside <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a>; after the same manner as the waters of the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LOIRE">Loire</a>, and other rivers, which roll on a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SANDY">sandy</a> bottom, overturn all their sands, and even the earth itself, in their swellings and inundations; and that in this general subversion, the shells came to be interred here, fishes there, trees there, &c. See Deluge. Dr. Woodward, in his Natural History of the Earth, pursuing and improving the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HYPOTHESIS">hypothesis</a> of Dr Burnet, maintains the whole <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MASS">mass</a> of earth, with every thing belonging thereto, to have been so broken and dissolved at the time of the deluge, that a new earth was then formed on the bosom of the water, consisting of different <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STRATA">strata</a> or beds of terrestrial matter, ranged over each other usually according to the order of their specific gravities. By this means, plants, animals, and especially fishes and shells, not yet dissolved among the rest, remained mixed and blended among the mineral and fossil matters; which preserved them, or at least assumed and retained their figures and impressions either indentedly or in relievo. See Geology. Fossil Pitch. See <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PETROLEUM">Petroleum</a>, Mineralogy <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

FOSTER

Pages 53-55

James, a nonconformist divine, very highly celebrated for his pulpit eloquence and erudition, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXETER">Exeter</a> in the year 1697. At the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> of five years he was put to the free school of that <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>, where his progress in the acquisition of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAMMAR">grammar</a> was so rapid, that his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> boasted of him as the most eminent genius in his school. From this seminary he went to the academy where young men designed for clergymen in the dissenting <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> were educated, where his progress and applause were equally <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a>. His <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPREHENSION">apprehension</a> was remarkably quick, his judgment <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOLID">solid</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> retentive, eloquence commanding, and his talents for argumentation were truly admirable; but above all, his piety was genuine, and few men possessed candour, <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODESTY">modesty</a>, liberality, integrity, tenderness and benevolence, in such a remarkable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>. He commenced preacher at the age of 21, and was much admired where he occasionally officiated. About this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> the doctrine of the Trinity was much agitated in the west of England, which was not consonant to the notions of Mr Foster, and the honesty and openness of his heart would not allow him to conceal these, which brought so much odium upon him from the orthodox party, that he retired to another <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCENE">scene</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTION">action</a>. He became pastor of a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONGREGATION">congregation</a> at Milborne-port, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOMERSETSHIRE">Somersetshire</a>; but as soon as his hearers became zealously attached to what was deemed the orthodox <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, he retired to Ashwick under the hills of Mendip, in the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a>. In this <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASYLUM">asylum</a> he preached to two congregations at a little distance from each other, as <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a> as they were plain, the united contributions of which did not amount to £5 per annum. In this humble poverty and obscurity he lived for some years, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a>, however, as it was occasioned by his determined uprightness and sincerity. In the year 1720, he gave the world his "<a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ESSAY">Essay</a> on Fundamentals, with a particular regard to the doctrine of the ever-blessed Trinity," &c. The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> was to check an uncharitable and intolerant spirit, at that time extremely prevalent, by shewing that the trinitarian notion is not a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FUNDAMENTAL">fundamental</a> article of Christianity, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> made an express condition of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALVATION">salvation</a> in the sacred scriptures. A sermon accompanied this essay, entitled "The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESURRECTION">resurrection</a> of Christ proved, and vindicated against the most important objections of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Jews, or <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> Deists, and his disciples shown to be sufficient witnesses of the fact." From Ashwick he removed to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TROWBRIDGE">Trowbridge</a> in Wiltshire, where his congregation did not usually exceed 20 or 30 people. By <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">reading</a> Dr <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-GALE">Gale</a>'s treatise on infant <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BAPTISM">baptism</a>, he became a convert to the doctrine, that immersion is the true scriptural rite, and was accordingly soon after baptised in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a> in conformity to that <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODE">mode</a>. This unreserved manner of adopting whatever his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSCIENCE">conscience</a> believed to be <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>, excluded him from almost every <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> party among whom he might otherwise have expected preferment. But while he deliberated with himself whether he should abandon the ministry, and acquire the knowledge of some <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MECHANICAL">mechanical</a> employment, Robert Houlston, Esq. took him to his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> in the capacity of chaplain, where his circle of acquaintances became wider and more respectable. In 1724, he was appointed to succeed Dr Gale in the baptist congregation in Barbican, London. In the year 1728 he commenced a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUNDAY">Sunday</a> evening lecture in the Old Jewry, which he <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> till within a short time of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, with such a degree of popularity as few dissenters at that time experienced. In 1732 appeared his valuable work, entitled "The usefulness, truth, and excellency of the Christian <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVELATION">revelation</a>, defended against the objections contained in a late book, called Christianity as old as the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREATION">Creation</a>," &c. In this reply Mr Foster exhibited no ordinary share of talents and ingenuity, and it was admired by the candid and judicious of every <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a>. Dr Tindal, against whom it was written, is said to have spoken of it always with great respect. He published a volume of sermons in the year 1734, followed by other three volumes, the last of which appeared in 1744. At this time he was appointed successor to Dr Jeremiah Hunt, in the protestant congregation at Pinner's-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HALL">hall</a>. In 1746, he attended the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KILMARNOCK">Kilmarnock</a> when under <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a> of death for <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a>-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TREASON">treason</a>, after which he published an octavo pamphlet, with the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of "An account of the behaviour of the late earl of Kilmarnock after his sentence, and on the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> of his execution." He received from the Marischal <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> of Aberdeen the degree of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a> in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a>, accompanied with handsome letters from the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> and Professor Fordyce, the latter of whom thus addressed him. "We beg that you <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be so good as to accept of the diploma, as a small mark of the sincere veneration we have for you, and of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> we entertain of the eminent services you have done to the cause of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, and virtue, by your writings as well as public instructions." The first volume in quarto of his 'Discourses on all the Principal Branches of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> Religion and Social Virtue,' was published in the year 1749, and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> appeared in 1752. They were published by subscription; and to evince the high estimation in which his talents and virtues were held, 2000 names were contained in the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIST">list</a>, many of them distinguished by their dignified <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> and literary abilities. In the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of April 1750, he was seized with a violent distemper, from the effects of which he never thoroughly recovered; yet while at all able to officiate, he continued to preach till the beginning of 1752, when he had another attack, which seems to have been of a paralytic <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>. After declining for some time, he expired like a genuine Christian on the 5th of November, in the 53rd year of his age. His private and public <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> were alike irreproachable. Such was the wonderful <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of his beneficence, that he must have died in indigent circumstances, had it not been for the numerous subscriptions to his discourses on natural religion. Mr Rider gives him the following eulogium: "His <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> was naturally sweet, strong, distinct, harmonious, always adapted to his <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>, always varied as his method changed; as expressive of the sense as the most judicious recitative. <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONOTONY">Monotony</a> was a fault he was never guilty of. His action, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUL">soul</a> of eloquence, was <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAVE">grave</a>, expressive, free from distortions, animated without being theatrical; in short, such as became the pulpit. He reminded us of Paul at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>, arresting the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> of his auditors." It was no doubt such rare accomplishments which induced Mr Pope to be an occasional hearer, and to pay him the following compliment: Let modest Foster, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he will, excel Ten metropolitans in preaching well. In a poem describing the respective merits of dissenting ministers at that <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>, and supposed to have been the work of Mr <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAVAGE">Savage</a>, we find the following <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> upon Dr Foster: But see th' accomplish'd orator appear, Refin'd his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, and his reasoning clear; Thou only, Foster, hast the pleasing art, At once to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARM">charm</a> the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-EAR">ear</a> and mend the heart. Besides the works formerly taken notice of, Dr Foster published three funeral sermons, one of which was intended for that celebrated confessor Mr Emlyn; together with a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of essays in the Old Whig. Foster, Samuel, an ingenious English mathematician of the last century, and astronomical professor in Gresham college, was one of that learned <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ASSOCIATION">association</a> which met for cultivating the new <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> during the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> confusions, and which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> II. established into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a>. Mr Foster, however, died in 1632, before this incorporation took <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>; but wrote a number of mathematical and astronomical treatises, too many to particularize. There were two other mathematical students of this name; William Foster, a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a> of Mr Oughtred, who taught in London, and Mark Foster, author of a treatise on <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIGONOMETRY">trigonometry</a>, who lived later than the former two. Fother, or Fodder, is a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, containing eight pigs, and every pig one and twenty <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a> and a half; so that it is about a ton or <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CART">cart</a> load. Among the plumbers in London, it is nineteen hundred and a half; and at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a> it is two and twenty hundred and a half. The word is of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TEUTONIC">Teutonic</a> origin, from fuder. Fothergill, Dr George, was born in Westmorland in 1705, where his family had been <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> seated on a competent estate that had descended regularly for several generations. After an academical <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a>'s college, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, of which he became a fellow, he was, in 1751, elected principal of St Edmund's hall, and presented to the vicarage of Brumley in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HAMPSHIRE">Hampshire</a>. Having been long afflicted with an asthma, he died in 1760. He was the author of a collection of much esteemed sermons, in 2 vols. 8vo. The first volume consists of occasional discourses, published by himself; the second printed from his MSS. Fothergill, Dr John, a late eminent physician, son of John and Margaret, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUAKERS">Quakers</a>, was born in 1712, at Carr End in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORKSHIRE">Yorkshire</a>, where his father, who had been a brewer at Knaresborough (after having travelled from one end of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a> to the other), lived retired on a small estate which he cultivated. The Doctor was the second of five children (four sons and a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a>), and received his education under the care of his grandfather Thomas Hough, a person of fortune in Cheshire, which gave him a predilection for that county, and at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEDBERGH">Sedbergh</a> in Yorkshire. He afterwards served his time to one Mr Bartlett an apothecary at <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRADFORD">Bradford</a>. From thence he removed to London, and became a pupil of Dr (afterwards Sir Edward) Wilmot, at St Thomas's <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOSPITAL">hospital</a>. He then went to the university of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a> to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> physic, and took his doctor's degree there. From Edinburgh he went to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEYDEN">Leyden</a>; whence, after a short stay, he returned to London, and began to practise about the year 1740, in a house in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">White</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HART">hart</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">Court</a>, Lombard-street, where he resided during the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of his life, and acquired most of his fortune. In 1746, he was admitted a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LICENTIATE">licentiate</a> of the College of Physicians in London; and in 1754 a fellow of that of Edinburgh, to which he was a considerable benefactor. He afterwards became a member of the Royal Medical Society at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, and a member both of the Royal and Antiquarian <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETIES">Societies</a>. He continued his practice with uninterrupted success till within the last two years of his life, when the illness which he had brought on himself by unremitting attention, obliged him to give up a considerable part of it. Besides his application to medical science, he had imbibed an early <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> for <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY">natural <a clas</a>s="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, improved by his friend <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> Collinson, and employed himself on <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONCHOLOGY">conchology</a> and smaller objects of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">botany</a>. He was for many years a valuable contributor to the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">Gentleman</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAGAZINE">Magazine</a>; where his observations on the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a> and diseases were begun in April 1751, and discontinued in the beginning of 1756, being disappointed in his views of exciting other experienced physicians in different parts to imitate the example. He had very extensive practice, but he did not add to his art any great or various improvements. His pamphlet on the ulcerous sore throat is, on every account, the best of his publications; but owes much of its merit to the information of the late Dr Letherland. It was printed in 1748, on the re-appearance of that fatal disorder which in 1739 had carried off the two only sons of Mr Pelham. In 1762 Dr Fothergill purchased an estate at Upton in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ESSEX">Essex</a>; and formed a botanic garden there, the second in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>; <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KEW">Kew</a> is the first. In 1766 he began regularly to withdraw, from Midsummer to Michaelmas, from the excessive fatigue of his profession, to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEE">Lee</a> Hall, near <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MIDDLEWICH">Middlewich</a>, in Cheshire; which, though he only rent- He took no fees during this recess, but attended to prescribe gratis at an inn in Middlewich once a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-WEEK">week</a>. In 1767, after he found himself obliged to relax his attention to business, he removed from his house in the city, to reside in Harpur-street, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">Red</a>-Lion <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">Square</a>. Some time before his death he had been industrious to contrive a method of generating and preserving <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ICE">ice</a> in the West Indies. He was the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATRON">patron</a> of Sidney Parkinson, and drew up the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREFACE">preface</a> prefixed to his account of the voyage to the South Seas. At his expense also was made and printed an entire new translation of the whole <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BIBLE">Bible</a>, from the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a> and Greek originals, by Anthony Purver, a Quaker, in two volumes, 1764, folio, and also, in 1780, an edition of Bishop Percy's "<a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KEY">Key</a> to the New <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a>," adapted to the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of a seminary of young Quakers, at Acworth, near <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEEDS">Leeds</a> in Yorkshire, founded in 1778 by the Society, who purchased, by a subscription in which Dr Fothergill stood foremost, the house and an estate of thirty acres which the Foundling Hospital held there, but which they found inconvenient for their purpose on account of distance. The Doctor himself first projected this on the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> of a smaller <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a> of the same kind at Gildersomes. He also endowed it handsomely by his will. It now contains above 300 children of both sexes, who are clothed and instructed. Among the other beneficent schemes suggested by Dr Fothergill were those of bringing fish to London by <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> carriage, which, though it did not in every respect succeed, tended to destroy a supposed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMBINATION">combination</a>; and of rendering <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a> much cheaper, though equally wholesome, to the poor, by making it with one part of potatoes and three parts of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSEHOLD">household</a> flour. But his public benefactions, his encouragements of science, the instances of his attention to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a>, the <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol18.html#article-POLICE">police</a>, the convenience of the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METROPOLIS">metropolis</a>, &c., we cannot pretend to specify. The fortune which Dr Fothergill had acquired was immense; and, taking all things together, the house and moveables in Harpur-street, the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> in Essex, and the estate in Cheshire (which he held on a lease), and his ready <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, amounted to 80,000l. His business, when he was in full practice, was calculated at near 7000l. per annum. In the influenza of 1775 and 1776, he is said to have had 60 patients on his list daily, and his profit was estimated at 8000l. per annum. The disorder which hastened his death was a scirrhus of the prostate, and an obstruction of the bladder (in which were found after his death two quarts of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>), which had been gradually coming on him for six years past, occasioned by a delicacy, which made him unwilling to alight from his carriage, and when, after his temporary <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RECOVERY">recovery</a> from it the year before he died, he submitted to use relief in his carriage, it was too late. He died at his house in Harpur-street, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a> 26, 1780; and his remains were interred, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 5, in the Quakers burying-ground at Winchmore-hill, whither they were accompanied by more than 70 coaches and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a>-chaises, notwithstanding the intention of the executors to have the funeral private. The Doctor by his will appointed, that his shells and other pieces of natural history should be offered to the late Dr Hunter at 500l. under the valuation he ordered to be taken of them. Accordingly Dr Hunter Fothergill bought them for 1200l. The drawings and collections in natural history were also to be offered to Mr (now Sir <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOSEPH">Joseph</a>) Bankes at a valuation. His English portraits and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINTS">prints</a>, which had been collected by Mr John Nickolls of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WARE">Ware</a>, and purchased by him for 80 guineas, were bought for 200 guineas by Mr <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THANE">Thane</a>. His books were sold by auction, April 30, 1781, and the eight following days. His house and garden at Upton, in which 15 men were constantly employed, were valued at 10,000l. He spared no expense to augment this as well as his other collections. He had an ingenious <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ARTIST">artist</a> qualified to collect for him at the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a> of Good Hope, and another on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALPS">Alps</a>, and employed for several years before his death a painter in natural history at Leeds. Dr Fothergill's character was excellent. A transaction, indeed, with regard to one Dr Leeds, gave occasion to some of his enemies to blame him; but how unjustly, has been abundantly shown by his biographers Dr Elliot and Dr Lettsome. Besides the pamphlet already mentioned, Dr Fothergill wrote a considerable number of Tracts, which are now collected into one volume 8vo, by Dr Elliot. He sometimes wrote in the newspapers, and is said to be the author of more than 100 letters in the Gazetteer, concerning the New Pavement.

FOTHERGILLA

Pages 55-55

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the polyandra class. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

FOTHERING

Pages 55-55

a peculiar method of endavouring to stop a leak in the bottom of a ship while she is afloat, either under sail <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANCHOR">anchor</a>. It is usually performed in the following manner: A <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BASKET">basket</a> is filled with ashes, cinders, and chopped rope yarns, and loosely covered with a piece of canvas; to this is fastened a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> pole, by which it is plunged repeatedly in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, as <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> as possible to the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where the leak is conjectured to <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a>. The oakum or chopped rope yarns being thus gradually shaken through the twigs, or over the top of the basket, are frequently sucked into the hole along with the water, so that the leak becomes immediately choked; and the future entrance of the water is thereby prevented.

FOTHERINGAY

Pages 55-56

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTHAMPTONSHIRE">Northamptonshire</a>, about four miles from Staneford, situated on the river Avon, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Nen, and consisting of one street. Edward <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORK">York</a>, in the reign of Henry V, founded and endowed a fine collegiate <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> here, in which he was interred. At the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISSOLUTION">dissolution</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> and the choir were pulled <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a>, and the bodies of the founder and his family left exposed till <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, who ordered them to be interred, and the present monuments to be erected. On the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> side of the church is a free school, founded by Henry VII, or Edward VI, endowed with 20l. per annum for a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>, payable out of the exchequer by the receiver of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> over the river here was first built by Queen Elizabeth, 1573, of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a>, with three pillars upon the foundation. Daniel, first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NOTTINGHAM">Nottingham</a>, and the other <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-TRUSTEES">trustees</a> for William Saville, marquis of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HALIFAX">Halifax</a>, rebuilt it in 1722, of freestone from <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a>'s Cliffe. On the south-east side of the cliff stood the castle; which was of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> antiquity and considerable strength. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a> queen of Scots, who had been in the custody of Sir Amias. Amias Powlet here, was tried and beheaded in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HALL">hall</a>; and her son afterwards, forgiving and even taking into favour her greatest enemy Cecil, only took the childish <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVENGE">revenge</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEATING">beating</a> down the castle; which he so completely demolished, that no more than the earthworks now remain. Within the first <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> is a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FARM">farm</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, with some carved <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONES">stones</a> wrought into it, and at the south-west corner of the inner trench are some masses of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a> walls. Sir Robert Cotton carried the wainscot of the hall to Connington.

FOU-TCHEOU

Pages 56-56

a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHINA">China</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Fo-kien. It carries on a considerable trade; but is chiefly remarkable for the magnificence of its <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a>, which has more than 100 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARCHES">arches</a> constructed of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, and ornamented with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> balustrade throughout. This city is the residence of a viceroy, and has under its jurisdiction <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> cities of the third class.

FOUGADE

Pages 56-56
or Fougasse, in the art of war, a little mine, about 8 or 10 feet wide, and 10 or 12 deep, dug under some work or post, which is in danger of falling into the enemy's hands; and charged with sacks of powder, covered with stones, earth, and whatever else can make great destruction. It is set on fire like other mines, with a saucisse. See mine.

FOUL

Pages 56-56
or Foule, in the sea language, is used when a ship has been long untrimmed, so that the grass weeds, or barnacles, grow on her sides under water. A rope is also foul when it is either tangled in itself, or hindered by another, so that it cannot run or be overhauled. Foul imports, also, the running of one ship against another. This happens sometimes by the violence of the wind, and sometimes by the carelessness of the people on board, to ships in the same convoy, and to ships in port by means of others coming in. The damages occasioned by running foul, are of the nature of those in which both parties must bear a share. They are usually made half to fall upon the sufferer, and half upon the vessel which did the injury; but in cases where it is evidently the fault of the master of the vessel, he is alone to bear the damage. Foul-Water. A ship is said to make foul water, when, being under sail, she comes into such shoal water, that though her keel do not touch the ground, yet it comes so near it, that the motion of the water under her raises the mud from the bottom. Foul is also a disease in cattle, proceeding from blood, and a waterish rheum that falls down into the legs, and makes them swell. Foul or Pimpled Face. See Gutta Rosacea.

FOULA

Pages 56-56
or Foul Island, one of the Shetland isles, lying between six and seven leagues west from the main land. It is about three miles long, narrow, and full of rough, steep, and bare rocks; one of which is so large, and runs up to such a height, that it may be clearly seen from Orkney. This, it is probable, is the Thole of Tacitus. It has scarcely any pasturage, and but little arable land. The only commodities exported are stock fish, train oil, and feathers.

FOULAHS

Pages 56-56

a people of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, which inhabit the confines of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DESERT">desert</a> Sahara. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> of the Foulah states is that within <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SIERRA_LEONE">Sierra Leone</a>, and of which Teembo is the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>. See SIERRA LEONA.

FOUNDATION

Pages 56-56

denotes also a donation <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> legacy, either in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a> or lands, for the maintenance and support of some <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMUNITY">community</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOSPITAL">hospital</a>, school, &c. The <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> only can found a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>, but there may <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JACOB">Jacob</a>'s be a college in reputation founded by others. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> it cannot appear by <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INQUISITION">inquisition</a> who it was that founded a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> or college, it shall be intended that it was the king, who has power to found a new church, &c. The king may found and erect an hospital, and give a name to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> upon the inheritance of another, or license another person to do it upon his own lands; and the words fundo, creo, &c. are not necessary in every foundation, either of a college or hospital, made by the king; but it is sufficient if there be words <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EQUIVALENT">equivalent</a>: the incorporation of a college or hospital is the very foundation; but he who endows it with lands is the founder; and to the erection of an hospital, nothing more is requisite but the incorporation and foundation. Persons seised of estates in fee simple, may erect and found <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-HOSPITALS">hospitals</a> for the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a> by <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DEED">deed</a> enrolled in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CHANCERY">chancery</a>, &c. which shall be incorporated, and subject to such visitors as the founder shall appoint, &c. stat. 39 Eliz. c. 5.

FOUNDER

Pages 56-56

in a general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, the person who lays a foundation, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> endows a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, school, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, or other charitable <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a>. See FOUNDATION. Founder, also implies an <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ARTIST">artist</a> who casts <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-METALS">metals</a>, in various forms, for different uses, as guns, bells, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINTING">printing</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a>, candlesticks, buckles, &c. whence they are denominated <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUN">gun</a>-founders, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BELL">bell</a>-founders, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>-founders, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a>-founders, founders of small works, &c. See FOUNDRY. Founder, in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>: A ship is said to founder, when by an extraordinary leak, or by a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> sea breaking in upon her, she is so filled with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, that she cannot be freed of it; so that she can neither veer nor steer, but <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> like a log; and not being able to swim <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> at last sink.

FOUNDRY

Pages 56-65
or FOUNDRY, the art of casting all sorts of metals into different forms. It likewise signifies the workhouse or smelting hut wherein these operations are performed. FOUNDRY of Small Works, or casting in Sand. The sand used for casting small works is at first of a pretty soft, yellowish, and clammy nature; but it being necessary to strew charcoal dust in the mould, it at length becomes of a quite black colour. The sand is worked over and over, on a board, with a roller, and a sort of knife; being placed over a trough to receive it, after it is by these means sufficiently prepared. This done, they take a wooden board of a length, and breadth proportional to the things to be cast, and putting a ledge round it they fill it with sand, a little moistened, moistened, to make it duly cohere. Then they take either wood or metal models of what they intend to cast, and apply them so to the mould, and press them into the sand, as to leave their impression there. Along the middle of the mould is laid half a small brass cylinder, as the chief canal for the metal to run through, when melted, into the models or patterns; and from this chief canal are placed several others, which extend to each model or pattern placed in the frame. After this frame is finished, they take out the patterns, by first loosening them all around, that the sand may not give way. Then they proceed to work the other half of the mould with the same patterns in just such another frame; only that it has pins, which, entering into holes that correspond to it in the other, make the two cavities of the pattern fall exactly on each other. The frame, thus moulded, is carried to the melter; who, after extending the chief canal of the counterpart, and adding the cross canals to the several models in both, and strewing mill dust over them, dries them in a kind of oven for that purpose. Both parts of the mould being dry, they are joined together by means of the pins: and to prevent them giving way, by reason of the melted metal passing through the chief cylindrical canal, they are screwed or wedged up like a kind of press. While the moulds are thus preparing, the metal is fusing in a crucible of a size proportionate to the quantity of metal intended to be cast. When the moulds are coolish, the frames are unscrewed or unwedged, and the cast work taken out of the sand, which sand is worked over again for other casting. **Foundery of Statues.** The casting of statues depends on the due preparation of the pit, the core, the wax, the outer mould, the inferior furnace to melt off the wax, and the upper to fuse the metal. The pit is a hole dug in a dry place something deeper than the intended figure, and made according to the prominence of certain parts thereof. The inside of the pit is commonly lined with stone or brick; or when the figure is very large, they sometimes work on the ground, and raise a proper fence to resist the impulsion of the melted metal. The inner mould, or core, is a rude mass to which is given the intended attitude and contours. It is raised on an iron grate, strong enough to sustain it, and is strengthened within by several bars of iron. It is generally made either of potters clay, mixed with hair and horse dung; or of plaster of Paris mixed with brick dust. The use of the core is to support the wax, the shell, and lessen the weight of the metal. The iron bars and the core are taken out of the brass figure through an aperture left in it for that purpose, which is soldered up afterwards. It is necessary to leave some of the iron bars of the core, that contribute to the steadiness of the projecting part, within the brass figure. The wax is a representation of the intended statue. If it be a piece of sculpture, the wax should be all of the sculptor's own hand, who usually forms it on the core: Though it may be wrought separately in cavities, moulded on a model, and afterwards arranged on the ribs of iron over the grate; filling the vacant space in the middle with liquid plaster and brick dust, whereby the inner core is proportioned as the sculptor carries on the wax. When the wax, which is the intended thickness of the metal, is finished, they fill small waxen tubes perpendicular to it from top to bottom, to serve both as canals for the conveyance of the metal to all parts of the work; and as vent holes, to give passage to the air, which would otherwise occasion great disorder when the hot metal came to encompass it. The work being brought thus far, must be covered with its shell, which is a kind of crust laid over the wax, and which being of a soft matter, easily receives the impression of every part, which is afterwards communicated to the metal upon its taking the place of the wax, between the shell and the mould. The matter of this outer mould is varied according as different layers are applied. The first is generally a composition of clay, and old white crucibles well ground and sifted, and mixed up with water to the consistence of a colour fit for painting: accordingly they apply it with a pencil, laying it seven or eight times over, and letting it dry between whiles. For the second impression they add horse dung and natural earth to the former composition. The third impression is only horse dung and earth. Lastly, The shell is finished by laying on several more impressions of this last matter, made very thick with the hand. The shell, thus finished, is secured by several iron girths, bound round it, at about half a foot distance from each other, and fastened at the bottom to the grate under the statue, and at top to a circle of iron where they all terminate. If the statue be so big that it would not be easy to move the moulds with safety, they must be wrought on the spot where it is to be cast. This is performed two ways: in the first, a square hole is dug underground, much bigger than the mould to be made therein, and its inside lined with walls of free-stone or brick. At the bottom is made a hole of the same materials, with a kind of furnace, having its aperture outwards: in this is a fire made to dry the mould, and afterwards melt the wax. Over this furnace is placed the grate, and upon this the mould, &c. formed as above. Lastly, At one of the edges of the square pit, is made another large furnace to melt the metal. In the other way, it is sufficient to work the mould above ground, but with the like precaution of a furnace and grate underneath. When finished, four walls are to be run around it, and by the side thereof a massive made for a melting furnace. For the rest, the method is the same in both. The mould being finished, and enclosed as described, whether under ground or above it, a moderate fire is lighted in the furnace under it, and the whole covered with planks, that the wax may melt gently down, and run out at pipes contrived for that purpose, at the foot of the mould, which are afterwards exactly closed with earth, so soon as the wax is carried off. This done, the hole is filled up with bricks thrown in at random, and the fire in the furnace augmented, till such time as both the bricks and mould become red hot. After this, the fire being extinguished, and everything cold again, they take out the bricks, and fill up their place with earth moistened, and a little beaten at the top of the mould, in order to make it more firm and steady. These preparatory measures being duly taken, there remains nothing but to melt the metal, and run it into the mould. This is the office of the furnace above described, which is commonly made in the form of an oven with three apertures, one to put in the wood, another for a vent, and a third to run the metal out at. From this last aperture, which is kept very close while the metal is in fusion, a small tube is laid, whereby the melted metal is conveyed into a large earthen bason, over the mould, into the bottom of which all the big branches of the jets, or casts, which are to convey the metal into all the parts of the mould, are inserted. These casts or jets are all terminated with a kind of plugs, which are kept close, that, upon opening the furnace, the brass, which gushes out with violence, may not enter any of them, till the basin be full enough of matter to run into them all at once. Upon which occasion they pull out the plugs, which are long iron rods with a head at one end, capable of filling the whole diameter of each tube. The whole of the furnace is opened with a long piece of iron fitted at the end of each pole, and the mould filled in an instant. This completes the work in relation to the casting part; the rest being the sculptor's or carver's business, who, taking the figure out of the mould and earth wherewith it is encompassed, saws off the jets with which it appears covered over, and repairs it with chisels, gravers, puncheons, &c. Foundery of Bells. The metal, it is to be observed, is different for bells from what it is for statues; there being no tin in the statue metal; but there is a fifth, and sometimes more, in the bell metal. The dimensions of the core and the wax, for bells, if a chime of bells especially, are not left to chance, but must be measured on a scale, or diapason, which gives the height, aperture, and thickness, necessary for the several tones required. It is on the wax that the several mouldings and other ornaments and inscriptions, to be represented in relief on the outside of the bell, are formed. The clapper or tongue is not properly part of the bell, but is furnished from other hands. In Europe, it is usually of iron, with a large knob at the extreme; and is suspended in the middle of the bell. In China, it is only a huge wooden mallet, struck by force of arm against the bell; whence they can have but little of that consonancy so much admired in some of our chimes of bells. The Chinese have an extraordinary way of increasing the sound of their bells, viz. by leaving a hole under the cannon; which our bell-founders would reckon a defect. The proportions of our bells differ very much from those of the Chinese. In ours, the modern proportions are, to make the diameter 15 times the thickness of the brim, and the height 12 times. The parts of a bell are, 1. The sounding bow, terminated by an inferior circle, which grows thinner and thinner. 2. The brim or that part of a bell whereon the clapper strikes, and which is thicker than the rest. 3. The outward sinking of the middle of the bell, or the point under which it grows wider to the brim. 4. The waist or furniture, and the part that grows wider and thicker quite to the brim. 5. The upper vase, or that part which is above the waist. 6. The pallet which supports the staple of the clapper within. 7. The bent and hollowed branches of metal uniting with the cannons, to receive the iron keys, whereby the bell is hung up to the beam, which is its support and counterpoise when rung out. The business of bell foundery is reducible to three particulars. 1. The proportion of a bell. 2. The forming of the mould. And, 3. The melting of the metal. There are two kinds of proportions, viz. the simple and the relative; the former are those proportions only that are between the several parts of a bell to render it sonorous; the relative proportions establish a requisite harmony between several bells. The method of forming the profile of a bell, previous to its being cast, in which the proportion of the several parts may be seen, is as follows: the thickness of the brim, C r (Plate CCXXXIII.) is the foundation of every other measure, and is divided into three equal parts. First, draw the line HD, which represents the diameter of the bell; bisect it in F, and erect the perpendicular EF; let DF and HF be also bisected in E and G, and two other perpendiculars E e, G g, be erected at E and G: GE will be the diameter of the top or upper vase, i.e. the diameter of the top will be half that of the bell; and it will, therefore, be the diameter of a bell which will sound an octave to the other. Divide the diameter of the bell or the line HD into 15 equal parts, and one of these will give C r the thickness of the brim; divide again each of these 15 equal parts into three other equal parts, and then form a scale. From this scale take 12 of the larger divisions or \( \frac{1}{15} \) of the whole scale in the compass, and setting one leg in D describe an arc to cut the line E e in N; draw ND, and divide this line into 12 equal parts; at the point 1 erect the perpendicular \( \frac{1}{15} \) C = 10, and C r will be the thickness of the brim \( = \frac{1}{15} \) of the diameter: draw the line CD; bisect DN; and at the point of bisection erect the perpendicular 6 K \( = \frac{1}{15} \) of the larger divisions on the scale. With an opening of the compass equal to twice the length of the scale or 30 brims, setting one leg in N, describe an arc of a circle, and with the same leg in K and the same opening describe another arc to intersect the former: on this point of intersection as a centre, and with a radius equal to 30 brims, describe the arc NK; in 6 K produced take KB \( = \frac{1}{15} \) of the larger measure of the scale or \( \frac{1}{15} \) of the brim, and on the same centre with the radius 30 brims describe an arc AB parallel to NK. For the arc BC, take 12 divisions of the scale or 12 brims in the compass; find a centre, and from that centre, with this opening, describe the arc BC, in the same manner as NK or AB were described. There are various ways of describing the arc KP; some describe it on a centre at the distance of nine brims from the points p and K; others, as it is done in the figure, on a centre at the distance only of seven brims from those points. But it is necessary first to find the point p, and to determine the rounding of the For this purpose, on the point C as a centre, and with the radius C r, describe the arc r p n; bisect the part r, 2 of the line D n, and erecting the perpendicular p m, this perpendicular will cut the arc r p n in m, which terminates the rounding r p. Some founders make the bendings K a third of a brim lower than the middle of the line DN; others make the part C r D more acute, and instead of making C r perpendicular to DN at r, draw it 3/8th of a brim higher, making it still equal to one brim; so that the line r D is longer than the brim C r. In order to trace out the top part N a, take in the compass eight divisions of the scale or eight brims, and on the points N and D as centres, describe arcs to intersect each other in 8: on this point 8, with a radius of eight brims, describe the arc N b; this arc will be the exterior curve of the top or crown: on the same point 8 as a centre, and with a radius equal to 7/8 brims, describe the arc A e, and this will be the interior curve of the crown, and its whole thickness will be one-third of the brim. As the point 8 does not fall in the axis of the bell, a centre M may be found in the axis, by describing, with the interval of eight brims on the centres D and H, arcs which will intersect in M; and this point may be made the centre of the inner and outer curves of the crown as before. The thickness of the cap which strengthens the crown at Q is about one-third of the thickness of the brim; and the hollow branches or ears about one-sixth of the diameter of the bell. The height of the bell in proportion to its diameter as 12 to 15, or in the proportion of the fundamental sound to its third major: whence it follows, that the sound of a bell is principally composed of the sound of its extremity or brim as a fundamental, of the sound of the crown which is an octave to it, and of that of the height which is a third. The particulars necessary for making the mould of a bell are, 1. The earth: the most cohesive is the best; it must be well ground and sifted, to prevent any chinks. 2. Brick stone; which must be used for the mine, mould, or core, and for the furnace. 3. Horse dung, hair, and hemp, mixed with the earth, to render the cement more binding. 4. The wax for inscriptions, coats of arms, &c. 5. The tallow equally mixed with the wax, in order to put a slight lay of it upon the outer mould, before any letters are applied to it. 6. The coals to dry the mould. For making the mould, they have a scaffold consisting of four boards ranged upon trestles. Upon this they carry the earth, grossly diluted, to mix it with horse dung, beating the whole with a large spatula. The compasses of construction is the chief instrument for making the mould, which consist of two different legs joined by a third piece. And last of all the founders shelves, on which are the engravings of the letters, cartridges, coats of arms, &c. They first dig a hole of a sufficient depth to contain the mould of the bell, together with the case or cannon, under ground; and about six inches lower than the terrepian, where the work is performed. The hole must be wide enough for a free passage between the mould and walls of the hole, or between one mould and another, when several bells are to be cast. At the centre of the hole is a stake erected, that is strongly fastened in the ground. This supports an iron peg, on which the pivot of the second branch of the compasses turns. The stake is encompassed with a solid brick-work, perfectly round, about half a foot high, and of the proposed bell's diameter. This they call a millstone. The parts of the moulds are, the core, the model of the bell, and the shell. When the outer surface of the core is formed, they begin to raise the core, which is made of bricks that are laid in courses of equal height upon a lay of plain earth. At the laying of each brick, they bring near it the branch of the compasses on which the curve of the core is shaped, so as that there may remain between it and the curve the distance of a line, to be afterwards filled up with layers of cement. The work is continued to the top, only leaving an opening for the coals to bake the core. This work is covered with a layer of cement, made of earth and horse dung; on which they move the compasses of construction, to make it of an even smoothness everywhere. The first layer being finished, they put the fire to the core, by filling it half with coals, through an opening that is kept shut, during the baking, with a cake of earth that has been separately baked. The first fire consumes the stake, and the fire is left in the core half, or sometimes a whole day: the first layer being thoroughly dry, they cover it with a second, third, and fourth; each being smoothed by the board of the compasses, and thoroughly dried before they proceed to another. The core being completed, they take the compasses to pieces, with intent to cut off the thickness of the model, and the compasses are immediately put in their place to begin a second piece of the mould. It consists of a mixture of earth and hair, applied with the hand on the core, in several cakes that close together. This work is finished by several layers of a thinner cement of the same matter, smoothed by the compasses, and thoroughly dried before another is laid on. The first layer of the model is a mixture of wax and grease spread over the whole. After which are applied the inscriptions, coats of arms, &c. besmeared with a pencil dipped in a vessel of wax in a chafing dish: this is done for every letter. Before the shell is begun, the compasses are taken to pieces, to cut off all the wood that fills the place of the thickness to be given to the shell. The first layer is the same earth with the rest, sifted very fine: while it is tempering in water, it is mixed with cows hair to make it cohere. The whole being a thin cullis, is gently poured on the model, that fills exactly all the sinuosities of the figures, &c. and this is repeated till the whole is two lines thick over the model. When this layer is thoroughly dried, they cover it with a second of the same matter, but somewhat thicker; when this second layer becomes of some consistence, they apply the compasses again, and light a fire in the core, so as to melt off the wax of the inscriptions, &c. After this, they go on with other layers of the shell, by means of the compasses. Here they add to the cows hair a quantity of hemp, spread upon the layers, and afterwards smoothed by the board of the compasses. The thickness of the shell comes to four or five inches lower than the millstone before observed, and surrounds it quite close, which prevents the extravasation of the metal. The wax should be taken out before the melting of the metal. The ear of the bell requires a separate work, which is done during the drying of the several incrustations of the cement. It has seven rings: the seventh is called the bridge, and unites the others, being a perpendicular support to strengthen the curves. It has an aperture at the top, to admit a large iron peg, bent at the bottom; and this is introduced into two holes in the beam, fastened with two strong iron keys. There are models made of the rings, with masses of beaten earth, that are dried in the fire in order to have the hollow of them. Those rings are gently pressed upon a layer of earth and cows hair, one half of its depth; and then taken out, without breaking the mould. This operation is repeated 12 times for 12 half moulds, that two and two united may make the hollows of the six rings: the same they do for the hollow of the bridge, and bake them all to unite them together. Upon the open place left for the coals to be put in are placed the rings that constitute the ear.
