STEPHEN, professor of the Arabic and Chinese languages, and one of the most learned men of his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, was born at Herbelaï, a village four leagues from <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, in 1683. He studied in Mazarine <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>, and afterwards in the Seminary of Thirty-three. He was at length professor of Arabic in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> College, and was made a member of the Academy of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INSCRIPTIONS">Inscriptions</a>. In 1738, he was chosen a member of the Royal <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, and of that of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BERLIN">Berlin</a> in 1741. He was often consulted by the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORLEANS">Orleans</a>, first <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of the blood; who had a particular esteem for him, and made him one of his secretaries. He wrote a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of books; the most considerable of those which have been printed are, 1. The Roots of the Latin Tongue, in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a>. 2. Critical Reflections on the Histories of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Nations, 2 vols. 4to. 3. Meditationes Sinice, folio. 4. A Chinese <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAMMAR">Grammar</a>, in Latin, folio. 5. Several dissertations printed in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEMOIRS">Memoirs</a> of the Academy of Inscriptions, &c. He died at Paris in 1744. He ought not to be confounded with Michael Fourmont, his youngest <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a>; who took orders, was professor of the Syriac <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> in the Royal College, and a member of the Academy of Inscriptions. He died in 1746.

FOURNESS

Pages 65-66

in Loynsdale, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANCASHIRE">Lancashire</a>, is a tract, between the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KENT">Kent</a>, Leven, and Dudden sands, which runs <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> with the west sides of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUMBERLAND">Cumberland</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WESTMORELAND">Westmoreland</a>; and on the south runs out into the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> as a promontory. Here, as Mr Camden expresses it, "the sea, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> enraged at it, lashes it more furiously, and in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIDES">tides</a> has even devoured the shore, and made three <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> bays; viz. Kentsand, into which the river Ken empties itself; Levensand and Duddensand, between which the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> projects in such a manner that it has its name hence; Foreness and Foreland, signifying the same with us as promontorium anterius in Latin." Bishop Gibson, however, derives the name of Fourness <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Furness, from the numerous furnaces that were there anciently, the rents and services of which (called Bloomsmithy rents) are still paid. This whole tract, except on the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a>, rises in high hills and vast piles of rocks called Fourness-Fells; among which the Britons found a secure retreat, trusting to these <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> fortresses, though nothing was inaccessible to the victorious Saxons; for we find the Britons settled here 228 years after the arrival of the Saxons: because at that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> Egfrid <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTHUMBERLAND">Northumberland</a> gave St Cuthbert the land called Carthmell, and all the Britons in it, as is related in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. In these mountainous parts are found quarries of a fine durable blue slate to cover buildings with, which are made <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of in many other parts of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>. Here are several cotton <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MILLS">mills</a> lately erected; and if <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-FUEL">fuel</a> for fire were more plentiful, the trade of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> would much increase: but there being no coals nearer than <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WIGAN">Wigan</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITEHAVEN">Whitehaven</a>, and the coast duties high, firing is rather scarce, the country people using only turf or <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEAT">peat</a>, and that begins to be more scarce than formerly. In the mosses of Fourness much fir is found, but more oak: the trunks in general <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> with their heads to the east, the high winds having been from the west. High Furness has ever had <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> quantities of sheep, which browse upon the hollies left in great numbers for them; and produces <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARCOAL">charcoal</a> for melting <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> ore, and oak bark for tanners use, in great abundance. The forests abound with deer and wild boars, and the legh or scofe, or large stags, whose horns are frequently found under ground here. The low or plain <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of Fourness, which is so called to distinguish it from the woody or mountainous part, produces all sorts of grain, but principally oats, whereof the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a> eaten in this country is generally made; and there are found here veins of a very rich iron ore, which is not only melted and wrought here, but great quantities are exported to other parts to mix with poorer ores. The three sands above mentioned are very dangerous to travellers, by the tides and the many quicksands. There is a guide on horseback appointed to Kent or <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANCASTER">Lancaster</a> sands at 10l. per ann. to Leven at 6l. per ann. out of the public revenue; but to Dudden, which are most dangerous, none; and it is no uncommon thing for persons to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> over in parties of 100 at a time like <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARAVANS">caravans</a>, under the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of the carriers, who go to or fro every <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>. The sands are less dangerous than formerly, being more used and better known, and travellers never going without the carriers or guides. "Furnis <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">abbey</a> up in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>," was begun at Tulket in Announderness 1124, by Stephen <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOULOGNE">Boulogne</a>, afterwards king of England, for the monks of Savigni in France, and three years after removed to this valley, then called Bekengesgill, or, "the vale of nightshade." It was of the Cistercian order, endowed with FOURNESS above 800l. per ann. Out of the monks of this abbey, Mr Camden informs us, the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">Isle</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">Man</a>, which lies opposite to it, used to be chosen by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a>; it being as it were the mother of many monasteries in Man and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>. Some ruins, and part of the fosse which surrounded the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a>, are still to be seen at Tulket. The remains at Fourness breathe that plain simplicity of the Cisterian abbeys; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAPTER">chapter</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> was the only piece of elegant Gothic about it, and its <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROOF">roof</a> has lately fallen in. Part of the painted glass from the east window, representing the crucifixion, &c., is preserved at Windermere <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> in Bowlness, Westmoreland. The church (except the north side of the nave), the chapter-house, refectory, &c., remain, only unroofed. FOURTH redundant, in Music. See <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTERVAL">INTERVAL</a>.

FOWEY

Pages 66-66
or Foy, a town of Cornwall in England, 240 miles from London, with a commodious haven on the Channel. It contained 1319 inhabitants in 1811, and extends above one mile on the east side of a river of its own name; and has a great share in the fishing trade. It rose so much formerly by naval wars and piracies, that in the reign of Edward III. its ships refusing to strike when required as they sailed by Rye and Winchelsea, were attacked by the ships of those ports, but defeated them; whereupon they bore their arms mixed with the arms of those two cinque-ports, which gave rise to the name of the "Gallants of Fowey." And we learn from Camden, that this town quartered a part of the arms of every one of the cinque-ports with their own; intimating, that they had at times triumphed over them all; and indeed once they were so powerful, that they took several of the French men of war. In the reign of Edward III. they rescued certain ships of Rye from distress, for which this town was made a member of the cinque-ports. Edward IV. favoured Fowey so much, that when the French threatened to come up the river to burn it, he caused two towers, the ruins of which are yet visible, to be built at the public charge for its security; but he was afterwards so disgusted with the inhabitants for attacking the French after a truce proclaimed with Louis XI., that he took away all their ships and naval stores, together with a chain drawn across the river between the two forts above mentioned, which was carried to Dartmouth. It is said they were so insolent, that they cut off the ears of the king's pursuivants; for which some lives were forfeited as well as estates. The corporation consists of a mayor, recorder, 8 aldermen, a town clerk, and 2 assistants. The market is on Saturday, the fairs May-day and Sept. 10. Here are a fine old church, a free school, and an hospital. The toll of the market and fairs, and keyage of the harbour, were vested in the corporation on the payment of a fee-farm rent of about 40s. It does not appear to have sent members to parliament before the 13th of Queen Elizabeth. Here is a coinage for the tin; of which a great quantity is dug in the country to the north and west of it. The river Foy, or Foath, is very broad and deep here, and was formerly navigable as high as Lestwithiel. W. Long. 5. N. Lat. 50. 27.

FOWL

Pages 66-66

among zoologists, denotes the larger sorts of birds, whether <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> wild: such as geese, pheasants, partridges, turkeys, ducks, &c. Tame fowl make a necessary <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the stock of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FARM">farm</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POULTRY">POULTRY</a>. Fowls are again distinguished into two kinds, viz. <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> fowl, these last being so called from their living much in and about water; also into those which are accounted <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GAME">game</a>, and those which are not. See GAME.

FOWLING

Pages 66-66

is also used for the pursuing and taking birds with hawks, more properly called <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FALCONRY">FALCONRY</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAWKING">HAWKING</a>. See these <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a>.

FOWLING PIECE

Pages 66-66

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUN">gun</a> for <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SHOOTING">shooting</a> birds. That piece is always reckoned best which has the longest <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BARREL">barrel</a>, from 5½ to 6 feet, with a moderate bore; though every fowler should have them of different sizes, suitable to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GAME">game</a> he designs to kill. The barrel should be well polished and smooth within, and the bore of an equal bigness from one end to the other; which may be proved, by putting in a piece of pasteboard, cut of the exact roundness of the top: for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> this goes <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> without stops <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> slipping, you may conclude the bore good. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAN">pan</a> must be somewhat above the touch-hole, and ought to have a notch to let down a little powder: this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> prevent the piece from recoiling, which it would otherwise be apt to do. As to the locks, choose such as are well filled with true <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, whose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a> must be neither too strong nor too weak. The hammer ought to be well hardened, and pliable to go down to the pan with a quick <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>.

FOX

Pages 66-67

John, the martyrologist, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOSTON">Boston</a> in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LINCOLNSHIRE">Lincolnshire</a>, in the year 1517. At the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> of 16 he was entered a student of Brazen-Nose <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>; and in 1543 he proceeded <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of arts, and was chosen fellow of Magdalen college. He discovered an early genius for <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, and wrote several Latin comedies, the subjects taken from Scripture, which his son assures us were written in an elegant style. Forsaking the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUSES">muses</a>, he now applied himself with uncommon assiduity to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a>, particularly <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>; and, discovering a premature propensity to the doctrine of reformation, he was expelled the college as a heretic. His distress on this occasion was very <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a>; but it was not <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> before he found an <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASYLUM">asylum</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of Sir Thomas Lucy of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WARWICKSHIRE">Warwickshire</a>, who employed him as a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TUTOR">tutor</a> to his children. Here he married the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of a citizen of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COVENTRY">Coventry</a>. Sir Thomas's children being now grown up, after residing a short <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> with his wife's father, he came to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>; where finding no immediate means of subsistence, he was reduced to the utmost <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of want; but was at length length (as his son relates) miraculously relieved in the following manner: As he was one <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> sitting in St Paul's church, emaciated with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HUNGER">hunger</a>, a stranger accosted him familiarly, and, bidding him to be of good cheer, put a sum of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a> into his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>; telling him, at the same time, that in a few days new hopes were at hand. He was soon after taken into the family of the duchess of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RICHMOND">Richmond</a>, as tutor to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SURREY">Surrey</a>'s children, who, when their father was sent to the Tower, were committed to her care. In this family he lived at Ryegate in Surrey, during the latter <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the reign of Henry VIII., the entire reign of Edward VI., and part of that of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a>: but at length, persecuted by his implacable enemy Bishop Gardiner, he was obliged to seek refuge abroad. <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BASIL">Basil</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWITZERLAND">Switzerland</a> was the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of his retreat, where he subsisted by correcting for the press. On the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Queen Mary he returned to England; where he was graciously received by his former pupil the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORFOLK">Norfolk</a>, who retained him in his family as long as he lived, and bequeathed him a pension at his death. Mr Secretary Cecil also obtained for him the rectory of Shipton near <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALISBURY">Salisbury</a>; and we are assured that he might have had considerable church preferment, had it not been for his unwillingness to subscribe to the canons. He died in the year 1587, in the 70th year of his age; and was buried in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHANCEL">chancel</a> of St Giles's, Cripplegate. He was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of great industry, and considerable learning; a zealous, but not a violent reformer; a nonconformist, but not an enemy to the church of England. He left two sons; one of whom was bred a divine, the other a physician. He wrote many pieces; but his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> is, the Acts and Monuments of the Church, &c., <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called Fox's Book of Martyrs. His facts are not always to be depended on, and he often loses his temper; which, considering the subject, is not much to be wondered at. Fox, George, the founder of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECT">sect</a> of English <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUAKERS">Quakers</a>, was a shoemaker in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NOTTINGHAM">Nottingham</a>. The accounts of those times tell us, that as he wrought at his trade, he used to meditate much on the Scriptures; which, with his solitary course of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, improving his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> melancholy, he began at length to fancy himself inspired; and in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> thereof set up for a preacher. He proposed but few <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>, insisting chiefly on moral virtue, mutual <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARITY">charity</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> of God, and a deep <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> to the inward motions and secret operations of the Spirit; he required a plain simple worship, and a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> without ceremonies, making it a principal point to wait in profound silence the directions of the Holy Spirit. Fox met with much rough treatment for his zeal, was often imprisoned, and several times in danger of being knocked on the head. But all discouragements notwithstanding, his sect prevailed much, and many considerable men were drawn over to them; among whom were Barclay and Penn. He died in 1681. His followers were called Quakers. See Quakers. Fox, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">Right</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONOURABLE">Honourable</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> James, a late distinguished British statesman and orator. See Supplement. Fox-Glove. See Digitalis, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MATERIA_MEDICA">Materia Medica</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Fox <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">Islands</a>, the name of a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GROUP">group</a> of islands, 16 in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>, situated between the eastern <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KAMTSCHATKA">Kamtschatka</a> and the western coast of the continent of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>. Each <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> has a particular name; but the general name Fox Islands is given to the whole group, on account of the great number of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a>, gray, and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> foxes with which they abound. The dress of the inhabitants consist of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a>, and a fur coat which reaches <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to the knee. Some of them wear <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> caps of a party-coloured <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BIRD">bird</a> skin, upon which they leave part of the wings and tail. On the fore part of their hunting and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FISHING">fishing</a> caps, they place a small board like a skreen, adorned with the jaw <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONES">bones</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> bears, and ornamented with glass beads, which they receive in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BARTER">barter</a> from the Russians. At their festivals and <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-DANCING">dancing</a> parties they <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> a much more showy sort of caps. They feed upon the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> of all sorts of sea animals, and generally eat it raw. But <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> at any time they choose to dress their victuals, they make use of a hollow <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>; having placed the fish <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> flesh therein, they cover it with another, and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> the interstices with lime or clay. They then lay it horizontally upon two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> a fire under it. The provision intended for keeping is dried without <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> in the open <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a>. Their weapons consist of bows, arrows, and darts; and for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> they use wooden shields. The most perfect equality reigns among these islanders. They have neither chiefs nor superiors, neither laws nor punishments. They live together in families, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETIES">societies</a> of several families united, which form what they call a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a>, who, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> of an attack or defence, mutually help and support each other. The inhabitants of the same island always pretend to be of the same race; and every person looks upon his island as a possession, the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of which is common to all the individuals of the same <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>. Feasts are very common among them, and more particularly when the inhabitants of one island are visited by those of the others. The men of the village meet their guests <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEATING">beating</a> drums, and preceded by the women, who sing and dance. At the conclusion of the dance, the hosts serve up their best <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a>, and invite their guests to partake of the feast. They feed their children when very young with the coarsest flesh, and for the most part raw. If an infant cries, the mother immediately carries it to the seaside, and whether it be <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> or winter, holds it naked in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, until it is quiet. This <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> is so far from doing the children any harm, that it hardens them against the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLD">cold</a>, and they accordingly go barefooted through the winter without the least inconvenience. They seldom <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> their dwellings; but when they are desirous of warming themselves, they light a bundle of hay, and stand over it; or else they set fire to train-<a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, which they pour into a hollow stone. They have a good share of plain natural <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, but are rather slow of understanding. They seem cold and indifferent in most of their actions; but let an injury, or even a suspicion only, rouse them from this phlegmatic state, and they become inflexible and furious, taking the most violent <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVENGE">revenge</a> without any regard to the consequences. The least affliction prompts them to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SUICIDE">suicide</a>; the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPREHENSION">apprehension</a> of even an uncertain evil often leads them to despair; and

FRACASTOR

Pages 67-68

Jerome, an eminent Italian poet and physician, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERONA">Verona</a> in the year 1482. Two singularities are related of him in his infancy: one is, that his lips adhered so closely to each other when he came into the world, that a surgeon was obliged to divide them with his incision <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KNIFE">knife</a>; the other, that his mother was killed with <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIGHTNING">lightning</a>, while he, though in her arms at the very moment, escaped unhurt. Fracastor was of parts so exquisite, and made such progress in every thing he undertook, that he became eminently skilled not only in the belles lettres, but in all arts and sciences. He was a poet, a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, a physician, an astronomer, and a mathematician. He was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of vast <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> in his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>; as appears from Pope Paul III.'s making <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of his authority to remove the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRENT">Trent</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOLOGNA">Bologna</a>, under the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRETEXT">pretext</a> of a contagious distemper, which, as Fracastor deposed, made it no longer safe to continue at Trent. He was intimately acquainted with <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDINAL">Cardinal</a> Bembus, Julius Scaliger, and all the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> men of his time. He died of an apoplexy at Casi near Verona, in 1553; and in 1559, the town of Verona erected a statue in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of him. He was the author of many performances, both as a poet and a physician: yet never man was more disinterested in both these capacities than he: evidently so as a physician, for he practised without fees; and as a poet, whose usual reward is <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a>, nothing could be more indifferent. It is owing to this indifference, that we have so little of his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPARISON">comparison</a> of what he wrote; and that, among other compositions, his Odes and Epigrams, which were read in manuscript with infinite admiration, yet, never passing the press, were lost. What we have now of his, are the three books of "Siphilis, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> of the French <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a>;" a book of Miscellaneous Poems; and two books of his poem, entitled <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOSEPH">Joseph</a>, which he began at the latter end of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, but did not live to finish. And these works, it is said, would have perished with the rest, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> his friends had not taken care to preserve and communicate copies of them: For Fracastor, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> merely for amusement, never troubled himself in the least about what became of his works after they once got out of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>. Fracastor composed also a poem, called Alcon, sive de cura canum venaticorum. His poems as well as his other works are all written in Latin. His medical pieces are, De Sympathia et Antipathia,—De contagione et contagiosis morbis,—De causis criticorum dierum,—De vini temperatura, &c. His works have been printed separately and collectively. The best edition of them is that of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PADUA">Padua</a> 1234, in 4 vols. 4to.

FRACHES

Pages 68-68

in the glass trade, are the flat <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> pans into which the glass vessels already formed are put when in the tower over the working <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FURNACE">furnace</a>, and by means of which they are drawn out through the leers, that they may be taken gradually from the fire, and cool by degrees.

FRACTION

Pages 68-68

in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARITHMETIC">Arithmetic</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALGEBRA">Algebra</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of an unit or integer; or a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> which stands to an unit in the relation of a part to its whole. The word literally imports a broken number. Fractions are usually divided into decimal, sexagesimal, and vulgar. See ALGEBRA and ARITHMETIC.

FRACTURE

Pages 68-68

in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SURGERY">Surgery</a>, a rupture of a bone <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> a solution of continuity in a bone when it is crushed or broken by some <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> cause. See SURGERY <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. FRÆNUM, or Frenum, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRIDLE">Bridle</a>, in Anatomy, a name given to <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> ligaments, from their office in retaining and curbing the motions of the parts they are fitted to. FRÆNUM Linguae, or Bridle of the Tongue; a membranous ligament, which ties the tongue to the os hyoides, larynx, fauces, and lower parts of the mouth. In some subjects the frenum runs the whole length of the tongue to the very tip; in which <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> it were not cut, it would take away all possibility of speech. See TONGUE-Tied. FRÆNUM <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENIS">Penis</a>, a slender ligament, whereby the prepuce is tied to the lower parts of the glans of the penis. <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">Nature</a> varies in the make of this <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a>; it being so short in some, that unless divided it would not admit of perfect erection. There is also a kind of little frenum, fastened to the lower part of the clitoris.

FRAGA

Pages 68-68

a strong town with a handsome castle, in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of Arragon in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>. It is strong by situation among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>; having the river Cinca before it, whose <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> banks are difficult of access; and at its back a hill, which cannot easily be approached with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> cannon. Alphonso VII, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of Arragon, and the first of that name of Castile, was killed by the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOTHS">Goths</a> in 1134, when he besieged this town. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. o. 23. N. Lat. 41. 28.

FRAGARIA

Pages 68-68

the STRAWBERRY, a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ICOSANDRIA">icosandria</a> class; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 37th order, Senticose. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>; and for an account of the varieties and culture, see <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GARDENING">GARDENING</a> Index.

FRAIL

Pages 68-68

a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BASKET">basket</a> made of rushes <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the like, in which are packed up figs, raisins, &c. It signifies also a certain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of raisins, about 75 pounds.

FRAISE

Pages 68-68

in Fortification, a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> consisting of pointed stakes, six <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> feet <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a>, driven <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> to the horizon into the retrenchments of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMP">camp</a>, a half <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOON">moon</a>, or the like, to prevent any approach or scalade. Fraises differ from pallisades chiefly in this, that the latter stand perpendicular to the horizon, and the former jet out parallel to the horizon, or nearly so, being usually made a little sloping, or with the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">points</a> hanging <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a>. Fraises are chiefly used in retrenchments and other works thrown up of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>; sometimes they are found under the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PARAPET">parapet</a> of a rampart, serving instead of the cordon of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a> used in stone works. To FRAISE a Battalion, is to line the musqueteers round with pikes, that in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> they should be <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> with a body of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>, the pikes being presented, may cover the musqueteers from the shock, and serve as a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BARRICADE">barricade</a>.

FRAME

Pages 68-69

in Joinery, a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>, wherein a thing is set <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> inclosed, or even supported; as a window frame, a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a> frame, &c. Frame is also a machine used in <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> arts; as, Frame, among printers, is the stand which supports the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a>. See CASE. Frame, among founders, a kind of ledge enclosing a board; which, being filled with wetted sand, serves as a mould to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> their works in. See Foundery. Frame is more particularly used for a sort of loom, whereon artificers stretch their linens, silks, stuffs, &c., to be embroidered, quilted, or the like. Frame, among painters, a kind of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>, consisting of four <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> slips of wood joined together, whose intermediate space is divided by threads into several little squares like a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NET">net</a>; and hence sometimes called <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RETICULA">reticula</a>. It serves to reduce figures from <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> to small; or, to augment their size from small to great.

FRAMLINGHAM

Pages 69-69

a town in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUSSEX">Sussex</a>, 88 miles from <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. It is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> old <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, with a castle, supposed to have been built by some of the first kings of the East <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANGLES">Angles</a>; the walls yet standing, are 44 feet <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, 8 thick, with 13 towers 14 feet above them, two of which are watch-towers. <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPULATION">Population</a> 1965 in 1811. FRANC. See Frank.

FRANCE

Pages 227-228
Isle of France, a late province of France, but now divided into five departments, and so called, because it was formerly bounded by the rivers Seine, Marne, Oise, Aisne, and Ourque. It comprehends, besides Paris, the Beauvoisis, the Valois, the county of Senlis, the Vexin, and Hurepoix, the Gatinois, the Multien, the Goele, and the Mantois. Paris is the capital. FRANCFORF on the MAINE, an imperial and han- Vol. IX. Part I. FRANCFORT Since 1815 it has been the permanent seat of the German diet. The number of inhabitants is 41,000; and it is one of the four towns which still retain their privileges. It was taken in October 1792, by the French, who were dispossessed of it by the Prussians in December following; it was again taken by the French in July 1796, but they evacuated it to the Austrians in September following. The suburb is called Saxonia, and joined to the town by a stone bridge built over the Maine. E. Long. 8. 37. N. Lat. 50. 7. FRANCFORT on the Oder, a rich and handsome town of Germany, in the middle marche of Brandenburgh, formerly imperial, but now subject to the king of Prussia. It is remarkable for three great fairs, and a celebrated university; and was taken by the French in 1806. It lies about 45 miles south-east of Berlin, and 72 south of Stetin. E. Long. 14. 45. N. Lat. 52. 22.

FRANCHE-COMTE

Pages 228-228

a late <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of France, bounded on the south and west by Champagne and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BURGUNDY">Burgundy</a>; on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by Lorrain; and to the east by the earldom of Mumplegard, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWITZERLAND">Switzerland</a>. It is in length from north to south about 30 leagues; in breadth about 20. It is partly flat and partly hilly. The flat <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> is fruitful in grain, wine, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEMP">hemp</a>, and pasture; and the hilly country abounds in cattle, producing also some wine and corn, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, and silver ores, mineral waters, and quarries of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, marble, and alabaster. It now forms the three departments of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DOUBS">Doubs</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JURA">Jura</a>, and Upper Saone.

FRANCHISE

Pages 228-228

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">Law</a>. Franchise and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> are used as <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYNONYMOUS">synonymous</a> terms; and their <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-DEFINITION">definition</a> is, "a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> privilege, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> branch of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PREROGATIVE">prerogative</a>, subsisting in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of a subject." Being therefore derived from the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>, they must arise from the king's <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRANT">grant</a>; or in some <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> may be held by <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRESCRIPTION">prescription</a>, which, as has been frequently said, presupposes a grant. The kinds of them are various, and almost infinite. We shall here briefly touch upon some of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a>, premising only, that they may be vested in either <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> persons or bodies politic; in one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, or in many: but the same identical franchise, that has before been granted to one, cannot be bestowed on another, for that would <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PREJUDICE">prejudice</a> the former grant. To be a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> palatine, is a franchise vested in a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of persons. It is likewise a franchise for a number of persons to be incorporated and subsist as a body politic; with a power to maintain perpetual succession, and do other corporate acts: and each individual member of such corporation is also said to have a franchise or freedom. Other franchises are, to hold a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> leet; to have a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANOR">manor</a> or lordship; or, at least, to have a lordship paramount; to have waifs, wrecks, estrays, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TREASURE_TROVE"><a class="xref</a>" href="vol20.html#article-TREASURE">treasure</a>-trove, royal fish, forfeitures, and deodands; to have a court of one's own, or liberty of holding pleas and trying causes; to have the cognizance of pleas; which is still a greater liberty, being an exclusive <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a>, so that no other court shall try causes arising within that jurisdiction; to have a bailiwick, or liberty exempt from the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SHERIFF">sheriff</a> of the county; wherein the grantee only, and his officers, are to execute all <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROCESS">process</a>: to have a fair or market; with the right of taking toll, either there or at any other public places, as at bridges, wharfs, or the like: which tolls must have a reasonable cause of commencement (as in consideration of repairs, or the like), else the franchise is illegal and void: or lastly, to have a forest, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHASE">chase</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARK">park</a>, warren, or fishery, endowed with privileges of royalty. See Chase, Forest, &c. Franchise is also used for an <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASYLUM">asylum</a> or sanctuary, where people are secure of their persons, &c. Churches and monasteries in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a> are franchises for criminals; so were they anciently in England, till they were abused to such a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> that there was a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> for abolishing the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a>. One of the most remarkable capitulars made by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLEMAGNE">Charlemagne</a> in his <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> of Heristal, in 779, was that relating to the franchises of churches. The right of franchise was held so sacred, that even the less <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> kings observed it to a degree of scrupulousness; but to such excess in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> was it carried, that Charlemagne resolved to reduce it. Accordingly he forbade any provision being carried to criminals retired into churches for refuge. FRANCHISE of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">Quarters</a>, is a certain space or district at Rome, wherein are the houses of the ambassadors of the princes of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>; and where such as retire cannot be arrested or seized by the sibiri or sergeants, nor prosecuted at law. The people of Rome look on this as an old usurpation and a scandalous privilege, which ambassadors, out of a jealousy of their power, carried to a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> length in the 15th century, by enlarging insensibly the dependencies of their palaces or houses, within which the right of franchise was anciently confined. Several of the popes, Julius III. Pius XIV. Gregory XIII. and Sixtus V. published bulls and ordinances against this abuse; which had rescued so considerable a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> from their authority, and rendered it a retreat for the most abandoned persons. At length Innocent XI. expressly refused to receive any more ambassadors but such as would make a formal renunciation of the franchise of quarters. FRANCIS I. king of France, the rival of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> V. and the restorer of learning and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLITENESS">politeness</a> in France. See (<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of) France.

FRANCIS

Pages 228-228
Philip, a very ingenious writer, of Irish extraction, if not born in that kingdom. His father was a dignified clergyman in Ireland, being dean of some cathedral; and our author, his son, was also bred to the church, and had a doctor's degree conferred on him. He was more distinguished as a translator than as an original writer. His versions of Horace and Demosthenes have been justly valued: the former is accompanied with notes, and is perhaps as complete and useful a work of its kind as hath yet appeared. He was also a considerable political writer; and in the beginning of the present reign is supposed to have been employed by the government: for which service he was promoted to the rectory of Barrow in Suffolk, and to the chaplainship of Chelsea hospital. He was also the author of two tragedies, Eugenia and Constantia; but as a dramatic writer, not very successful. He died at Bath in March 1773; leaving a son, who was then one of the supreme council at Bengal.

FRANCOIS

Pages 229-230

FRANCOIS, or FRANCAIS, Port Des, the name of a bay or harbour discovered by Peyrouse on the north-west coast of America, is situated in N. Lat. 58° 37' and in Long. 139° 50' W. from Paris. This harbour was from three to four leagues deep; he entered it with his two frigates in July 1786, and came to an anchor in an island near the middle of it, in 20 fathoms water, with a muddy bottom. The bottom of the bay, he observes, is one of the most extraordinary places in the world; the water is so deep that it could not be fathom'd, and surrounded by peaked mountains of a great height, covered with snow, without vegetation, and seemingly condemned by nature to perpetual sterility. He never saw the surface of the water ruffled with the smallest breath of air, or in the least disturbed but by the falling of enormous pieces of ice, which continually detach themselves from five different glaciers. The air was so calm, and the silence so profound, that the voice of a man might be heard at the distance of half a league, as well as the noise of sea-birds which hatch their eggs in the cavities of the rocks. He found the variation of the compass to be 28° E. and the dip of the needle 74°. At full and change of the moon, when it is high water at one o'clock, the sea rose seven feet and a half. The current of the channel at the entrance of the harbour, during the sea breeze, came in like a rapid river, so that it must be impracticable to take the channel when the winds blow violently from the southward; and indeed the currents at all times render the entrance difficult. This harbour possesses many advantages, but it is also subject to several inconveniences. It seems not to be convenient for ships to anchor, which are employed in trafficking in skins, because such ships ought to enter many bays, making in each a short stay, since the whole stock of the Indians is very soon disposed of; but it seems to be a very commodious place for the establishment of a factory, and this commercial settlement, it is suggested, should be made on Cenotaph island, a name given to an island in the middle of the harbour, from the monument erected on it to the memory of some of the crew of Peyrouse's ships, which were lost in the channel. This island is about a league in circumference, abounds with wood and water, and seems capable of cultivation. The quan- The climate of this coast, according to Peyrouse, seemed much milder than that of Hudson's Bay. For three or four months of the year vegetation was very vigorous; there was found abundance of celery, endive, lupin, and yarrow, with most of the plants which are common in the meadows and mountains of France. Gooseberries, raspberries, and strawberries, were also common in the woods; poplars, willows, hornbeam, and pines, some of which measured six feet in diameter, and 140 feet high, fit for masts of the largest ships. The river seemed to be filled with trout and salmon, and different kinds of fish were found in the bay itself. The variety of birds was not great; but bears, martens, and squirrels, were frequent in the woods. The inhabitants are said to be considerably different from the Californians, being taller, stouter, of a more agreeable figure, having greater vivacity of expression, and a greater share of courage and sense. Their colour is olive, and the hair in general is neither so coarse nor black as that of the South Americans. It is supposed that they are worshippers of the sun, for they were frequently observed addressing themselves in their prayers to this planet; but neither temple nor priest, nor trace of public worship, was seen. It is said that they burn their dead.

FRANCONIA

Pages 230-230

FRANCONIA, a circle of Germany, bounded on the north by the circle of Upper Saxony, on the east by that of Bavaria, on the south by that of Swabia, and on the west by the circles of the Rhine. The middle is fertile in corn, wine, and fruits, but the borders are full of woods and barren mountains. This country was overrun by the French republicans in the summer of 1796; but in September the Austrians compelled them to retreat. The Franks, who conquered France, came from this province, and gave their name to this kingdom.

FRANK

Pages 230-230

FRANK LANGUAGE, Lingua Franca, a kind of jargon spoken on the Mediterranean, and particularly throughout the coasts of and ports of the Levant, composed of Italian, Spanish, French, vulgar Greek, and other languages. FRANK, or Franc, an ancient coin, either of gold or silver, struck and current in France. The value of the gold frank was something more than that of the gold crown: this coin has been long out of use, though the name is still retained as the name of a money of account: in which sense it is equivalent to the livre, or 20 sols. FRANK, or Franc, meaning literally free from charges and impositions, or exempt from public taxes, has various significations in the ancient English customs. FRANK-Almoigne, (libera eleemosyna), or "free alms;" a tenure of a spiritual nature, whereby a religious corporation, aggregate or sole, holdeth lands of the donor to them and their successors for ever. The service which they were bound to render for these lands was not certainly defined: but only in general to pray for the souls of the donor and his heirs, dead or alive; and therefore they did no fealty (which is incident to all other services but this), because this divine service was of a higher and more exalted nature. This is the tenure by which almost all the ancient monasteries and religious houses held their lands; and by which the parochial clergy, and very many ecclesiastical and eleemosynary foundations, hold them at this day; the nature of the service being upon the Reformation altered, and made conformable to the purer doctrines of the church of England. It was an old Saxon tenure; and continued under the Norman revolution, through the great respect that was shown to religion and religious men in ancient times. This is also the reason that tenants in frank almoigne were discharged of all other services except the trinoda necessitas, of repairing the highways, building castles, and repelling invasions; just as the Druids, among the ancient Britons, had omnium rerum immunitatem. And even at present, this is a tenure of a very different nature from all others; being not in the least feudal, but merely spiritual. For, if the service be neglected, the law gives no remedy by distress, or otherwise, to the lord of whom the lands are holden; but merely a complaint to the ordinary or visitor to correct it. FRANK-Chase is defined to be a liberty of free chase, whereby persons that have lands within the compass of the same, are prohibited to cut down any wood, &c. out of the view of the forester. FRANK-Fee, signifies the same thing as holding lands and tenements in fee-simple; that is, to any person and his heirs, and not by such service as is required by ancient demesne, but is pleaded at common law. See Fee. FRANK-Law, a word applied to the free and common law of the land, or the benefit a person has by it. He that for any offence loseth this frank-law incurs these inconveniences, viz. He may not be permitted to serve on juries, nor used as an evidence to the truth; and if he has any thing to do in the king's court, he must not approach it in person, but appoint his attorney; his lands, goods, and chattels, shall be seized into the king's hands; and his lands be estreated, his trees rooted up, and his body committed to custody. FRANK-Marriage, in Law, is where tenements are given by one man to another, together with a wife, who is the daughter or cousin to the donor, to hold in frank-marriage. By such gift, though nothing but the word frank-marriage is expressed, the donees shall have the tenements to them, and the heirs of their two bodies begotten; that is, they are tenants in special tail. For this one word, frank marriage, denotes ex vi termini, not only an inheritance, like the word frank-almoigne, but likewise limits that inheritance; supplying, not only words of descent, but of procreation also. Such donees in frank-marriage are liable to no service but fealty: for a rent reserved therein is void until the fourth degree of consanguinity be past between the issues of the donor and donee. FRANK-Pledge, in Law, signifies a pledge or surety for the behaviour of freemen. According to the ancient custom of England, for the preservation of the public peace, every freeborn man, at the age of fourteen, except religious persons, clerks, knights, and their eldest sons, was obliged to give security for his truth and behaviour towards the king and his subjects, or else be imprisoned. Accordingly, a certain number of neighbours became interchangeably bound bound for each other, to see each person of their pledge forthcoming at all times, or to answer for the offence of any one gone away; so that whenever any person offended, it was presently inquired in what pledge he was, and there the persons bound either produced the offender in 31 days, or made satisfaction for his offence. FRANK-Tenement. See Tenure. FRANKED LETTERS. The privilege of letters coming free of postage to and from members of parliament was claimed by the house of commons in 1660, when the first legal settlement of the present post office was made; but afterwards dropped, upon a private assurance from the crown, that this privilege should be allowed the members. And accordingly a warrant was constantly issued to the postmaster general, directing the allowance thereof to the extent of two ounces in weight: till at length it was expressly confirmed by Geo. III. c. 24, which adds many new regulations, rendered necessary by the great abuses which had crept into the practice of franking; whereby the annual amount of franked letters had increased from £2,652l. in the year 1715, to £70,700l. in the year 1763. Further regulations have since taken place; in particular, franks must be dated (the month written at length), and put into the office the same day; notwithstanding which, the revenue still loses by this privilege a very considerable annual sum. FRANKEN, Franciscus, commonly called Old Frank, a famous Flemish painter, supposed to have been born about the year 1544; but though his works are well known, very few of the circumstances of his life have been transmitted to posterity. This master painted historical subjects from the Old and New Testaments; and was remarkable for introducing a great number of figures into his compositions, which he had the address to group very distinctly. Vandyck often commended his works, and thought them worthy of a place in any collection. FRANKEN, Franciscus, distinguished by the name of Young Frank, was the son of the former, born in the year 1580. He was instructed by his father; whose style he adopted so closely, that their works are frequently mistaken. When he found himself sufficiently skilled at home, he travelled into Italy for improvement in colouring; and, on his return, his works were much coveted. The most capital performances of this painter are, a scriptural performance in the church of Notre Dame at Antwerp; and an excellent picture, in a small size, of Solomon's idolatry. Young Frank died in 1642. FRANKENDAL, a strong town of Germany, in the dominions of the Elector Palatine, situated near the Rhine, about seven miles south of Worms. It was taken by the Spaniards in 1623, by the Swedes in 1632; burnt by the French in 1688, and finally taken by the allies in the year 1794. E. Long. 8. 29. N. Lat. 49. 25. FRANKENIA, a genus of plants belonging to the hexandria class; and in the natural method ranking under the 17th order, Calycanthemæ. See Botany Index. FRANKFORT, the name of several townships in different places of North America; such as Frankfort, a township in Hancock, and district of Maine, with a few houses regularly built. It contains 891 inhabitants, Frankfort and lies about 238 miles north-east of Boston. Frankfort, a thriving village in Philadelphia; the name of another in Hampshire, of one in Virginia, and the name of the metropolis of Kentucky. FRANKINCENSE. See Incense. FRANKLIN, Thomas, D.D. chaplain in ordinary to his majesty, was born in London about the year 1720, and was the son of Richard Franklin, well known as the printer of an anti-ministerial paper called The Craftsman; in conducting which he received great assistance from Lord Bolingbroke, Mr Pulteney, and other excellent writers, who then opposed Sir Robert Walpole's measures. By the advice of the second of these gentlemen, young Franklin was devoted to the church, with a promise of being provided for by the patriot; who afterwards forgot his undertaking, and then entirely neglected him. He was educated at Westminster school; from whence he went to the university of Cambridge, where he became fellow of Trinity college, and was some time Greek professor. In December 1758, he was instituted vicar of Ware and Thundridge; which, with the lectureship of St Paul, Covent Garden, and a chapel in Queen street, were all the preferments he held till he obtained the rectory of Brasted in Kent. This gentleman was possessed of no inconsiderable share of learning and poetical abilities, and was long a favourite in the literary world. His translations of Phalarus, Sophocles, and Lucian, equally evince his learning and his genius, as they are not more distinguished for fidelity in the version, than congeniality with the spirit of the admirable originals. Dr Franklin, like Mr Foote, suffered a translation from the French to be printed in his name; but the Orestes and Electra are supposed to be all that were really by him. It was a translation of Voltaire's works, to which also Dr Smollett's name appears. His own dramatic compositions, of which the principal are the tragedies of The Earl of Warwick and Matilda, are universally known, and deservedly esteemed by the public. He died in March 1784. FRANKLIN, Benjamin, a philosopher and a statesman of considerable eminence, was born in the year 1706, at Boston in New England. His family derived their origin from Ecton in Northamptonshire, where his ancestors had an inconsiderable freehold for many generations. The persecution of the non-conformists in the reign of Charles II. induced his father to take refuge in New England; and in the city of Boston he followed the occupation of a soap-boiler and tallow-chandler. Franklin drew up a history of his own life from his nativity to the 25th year of his age; but as at that period he had made no very conspicuous figure in the world, it is to be lamented that we have not the assistance of his own pen to the meridian of his career. This defect we have endeavoured to supply in the subsequent narrative from the most authentic materials, avoiding as much as possible the exaggerated panegyric of friends, and the unmerited detraction of enemies. Our author, from his very infancy, discovered the strongest propensity towards literary pursuits, which determined his father to qualify him for the ministry; but he was thwarted in his designs by a numerous and increasing family.

FRANKLIN

Pages 234-234

Franklin and his copartner began a newspaper, which the labours and talents of the former brought into repute, and by them the votes and laws of the assembly came afterwards to be printed. The partnership being dissolved by the departure of Meredith, Franklin, by the generous aid of friends, was enabled to take the whole business upon himself, to which he added the business of a stationer. When the increase of paper money engaged the attention of the American government, Franklin wrote an anonymous pamphlet in defence of the measure, by which he acquired considerable reputation, the countenance of men in power, and it placed his prosperity on a permanent basis. About this time he kept up a criminal correspondence with different females, chiefly owing, perhaps, to the disappointment he met with in the first object of his love, Miss Read, who by this time was married to another in consequence of his neglect. But we forget the faults of the man in the ingenuous confession of the penitent. A report prevailing that Miss Read's husband was married to another woman, he retired to the West Indies, where he died, and Franklin married the object of his first love in the month of September 1736, being then about 24 years of age. She proved a valuable wife, and in every sense of the word, an "help meet for him." To him we are to ascribe the establishment of a public library at Philadelphia, which he accomplished in the year 1731, and had the satisfaction of seeing it arrive at that flourishing condition which it has long since attained. His "Poor Richard's Almanac," was begun in 1732, and became remarkable for the many prudential maxims with which it abounded; and the proverbial manner in which they were expressed made them take fast hold of the memory. His political career commenced in 1736, when he was chosen clerk to the general assembly of Pennsylvania, to which he was re-elected for several years, and at last became a representative. In 1737, he was made postmaster of Philadelphia, and in the subsequent year he greatly improved the police of the city, by the formation of a fire-company, and afterwards an insurance-company against losses by fire. In the war with France, which broke out in 1744, when the best means of defending the province against the inroads of the enemy, and when the militia bill was thrown aside from its being obnoxious to the people, Franklin suggested the idea of a voluntary association for their mutual defence, which was instantly signed by 1200 persons, and 10,000 subscriptions were obtained in a short time by circulating it through the province. By this and similar means America had an opportunity of ascertaining her own strength, and how to make use of it with advantage in cases of emergency. About this time he began his interesting experiments on electricity, by the result of which he justly acquired a distinguished reputation. The library society of Philadelphia having received from Mr Peter Collinson in the year 1745, an account of the facts respecting electricity which at that time engrossed the attention of philosophers in Europe, Franklin set about studying the subject with the greatest assiduity. He gave the account of his researches, the title of "New experiments and observations on electricity, made at Philadelphia in America," and addressed to Mr Collinson in the form of letters, bearing date from 1747 to 1754. They were everywhere read with avidity, and universally admired; Dr Priestley speaks of them in the following terms. "It is not easy to say whether we are most pleased with the simplicity and perspicuity with which the author proposes every hypothesis of his own, or the noble frankness with which he relates his mistakes, when they were corrected by subsequent experiments." Not to swell this article with a detailed account of all his discoveries on this subject, we shall content ourselves with mentioning that most interesting of the whole, his grand discovery that lightning and electric fire are identically the same. This identity had begun to be suspected, and experiments had been made in France to ascertain the fact; but it was reserved to Franklin to demonstrate this fact by his own experiments. He obtained his first decisive proof of this in the month of June 1752, by setting up a silken kite into the air with a point of iron, and a key fastened to the end of the hempen string by which he held it. In this manner he drew down from a thunder cloud a sufficient quantity of electric fire to emit sensible sparks from the key. By means of an insulated iron rod which he fixed upon his house, he drew down the lightning, and was thus furnished with an opportunity of discovering whether it was positive or negative. As he firmly believed that philosophical discoveries were only valuable in so far as they could be productive of benefit to man, he made them subservient to the protection of buildings from the effects. Franklin effects of lightning, which are truly alarming in North America. He applied physics to the purposes of common life, and in 1745 invented his Pennsylvania fireplaces, in which the qualities of an open grate were combined with that of a stove. He turned his attention very much to the subject of politics, which was extremely natural for a man of a public spirit living under a popular government. He was chosen a representative of the city of Philadelphia for the provincial assembly in 1747. At this time a contest subsisted between the assembly and the proprietaries, as to the claim of the latter to be exempted from public burdens. Franklin took the popular side of the question, by which he acquired great influence, and was regarded as the head of the opposition. This was not the offspring of eloquence, for he seldom spoke, and never in the form of an harangue; but his pointed observations, his unadorned good sense, frequently destroyed the effect of the most elaborate orations. He drew up the plan of an academy to be founded at Philadelphia, from a conviction that education in a free state is of the utmost importance. It was carried into effect in the year 1750, by virtue of a subscription, to which the proprietors afterwards liberally contributed. He discharged the duties of his office as postmaster of Philadelphia with so much punctuality, that he was appointed deputy postmaster general for the British colonies in 1753, and the revenue was soon bettered by his unrevealed exertions. A plan for conciliating the Indians, and forming an alliance with them, was drawn up by Franklin in 1754, to which the commissioners at Albany agreed, and a copy of it was transmitted to the British privy council. It is a singular circumstance, that this plan was rejected by the assemblies as giving too much power to the crown, while the British ministry declared that it gave too much influence to the representatives of the people. In the year 1757, Franklin set sail for London, as agent for Pennsylvania, the assembly of that province being involved in disputes with the proprietary. It was agreed on by the privy council, that landholders should pay their share of the public burdens, on condition Franklin would engage that they should be fairly proportioned. He continued at the British court as agent for his province, and acquired so great reputation, that the same trust was imposed on him for Massachusetts, Maryland, and Georgia. His merit as a philosopher was now justly appreciated in Europe, and he was made a fellow of the Royal Society of London. The degree of L.L.D. was also conferred upon him at St Andrew's, Edinburgh, and Oxford. In the year 1762 he returned to America, where he received the thanks of the assembly of Pennsylvania, and a handsome recompense in money for his important services. When the stamp act occasioned so much disturbance in America, Dr Franklin was summoned to the bar of the house of commons, to give evidence respecting the dispositions of the people, whether he thought they could be induced to submit to it; and the energy and clearness of his representations were instrumental in procuring the repeal of that obnoxious measure. On the commencement of hostilities between Great Britain and the colonies in 1775, he returned to America, and was chosen a delegate to congress by the legislature of Pennsylvania. In 1776 he treated with Lord Howe on the subject of a reconciliation, and in one of his letters expressed in strong terms the temper of the British nation, to which he imputed the fatal extremity then arrived. When the question of independence came to be discussed, he was decidedly in favour of the measure, and was highly instrumental in bringing over the public mind to the same opinion. When a negotiation with France was opened, Dr Franklin was chosen one of the personages to reside at that court. His political abilities eminently qualified him for such a station, and his character as a philosopher gained him great esteem in a country where knowledge is revered. He brought about a treaty with France of an offensive and defensive nature in 1778, the immediate consequence of which was a war with Britain. He was one of those who signed the provisional treaty the year following. Prior to his leaving Europe he concluded a treaty with Sweden and Prussia. He was recalled from that active station in 1785, which he had filled with so much ability, and chosen president of the supreme executive council. He was chosen president of a society for alleviating the miseries of prisons, and abolishing slavery. His increasing infirmities made him withdraw from all public business in 1788; and on April the 17th 1790, he terminated his active and useful life, in the 85th year of his age. Perhaps no man ever exceeded Dr Franklin in that solid practical wisdom which consists in pursuing valuable ends by the most appropriate means. His cool temper and sound judgment secured him from erroneous expectations. He saw things in their true light, and predicted consequences with nearly a prophetic spirit. He said of himself "I have always set a greater value on the character of a doer of good," than any other kind of reputation." In 1779, his "Political, Miscellaneous, and Philosophical pieces," were published in 4to and 8vo. His essays, humorous, moral, and literary, were published after his death, in two small volumes. He was by no means inattentive to his own interest, of which his rapid advancement in life furnishes an ample proof; yet he never neglected the interest of society, or the good of mankind in general. The delicate situations in which he frequently stood, unavoidably exposed him to the censure of his enemies; yet his general conduct has long ago received the approbation of his countrymen, by whom he was considered as the best and most valuable of citizens. When we view him as a philosopher, we must ascribe his chief merit to his electrical discoveries, yet on many other topics, such as meteorology and mechanics, he evinced himself a man of considerable penetration. As a political writer, his great merit is clearness, energy, and simplicity; and as a miscellaneous author he possesses a fund of humour which cannot fail to be at once both entertaining and impressive.
