In 1705 he attended the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of Peterborough to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, as physician to the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> there; and, upon his return in 1707, published an account of the earl's expedition and conduct. In 1709 he published his Chemical Lectures. In 1712 he attended the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORMOND">Ormond</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLANDERS">Flanders</a>, as his physician. In 1716 he was admitted a fellow of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLLEGE">College</a> of Physicians in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. This year he published the first and third books of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HIPPOCRATES">Hippocrates</a> De morbis popularibus, with a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMENTARY">Commentary</a> on Fevers, written by himself. He sat member for the borough of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAUNCESTON">Launceston</a> in Cornwall in 1722, where he distinguished himself by his opposition to the administration. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a> 1722, he was committed to the Tower on a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TREASON">treason</a>; and while he was under confinement, he wrote a Latin epistle to Dr <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAD">Mead</a>, de quibusdam variolarum generibus; and began his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of Physic, the first <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of which was published in 1725, and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> in 1726. Upon the accession of George II. to the throne, he was appointed physician in ordinary to the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a>, who showed the utmost regard and esteem for him. He died at London in 1728. His works were published together in Latin at London, 1733, in folio, and dedicated to the queen. FREITS. See Freats.

FRENCH

Pages 244-245

in general, something belonging to France: thus we say, the French <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, French <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a>, polity, &c. The French language, as it now stands, is no original <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> mother language, but a medley of several. Those that prevail most, and which are, as it were, the basis thereof are, 1. The Celtic; whether that were a particular language itself, or whether it were only a dialect of the Gothic, as spoke in the west and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>. 2. The Latin, which the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> carried with them into <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAUL">Gaul</a>, when they made the conquest thereof. And, 3. The <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TEUTONIC">Teutonic</a>, or that dialect of the Teutonic spoke by the Franks, when they passed the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHINE">Rhine</a>, and established themselves in Gaul. Of these three languages, in the space of about thirteen hundred years, was the present French formed, such as it is now found. Its progress was very slow; and both the Italian and Spanish were regular languages <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> before the French. Pasquier observes, it was under <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a> de Valois that the French tongue first began to be polished; and that, in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REGISTER">register</a> of the chamber of accounts of that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, there is a purity seen almost equal to that of the present <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>. However, the French was still a very imperfect language till the reign of Francis I.; the custom of speaking Latin at the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAR">bar</a>, and of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> the public acts and instruments of the courts of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> in that language, had made them overlook the French, their own language. Add that the preceding ages had been remarkable for their <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a>, which was owing, in a good <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a>, to the long and calamitous wars which France had been engaged in; whence the French noblesse deemed it a kind of merit not to know anything; and the generals regarded little whether or not they wrote and talked politely, provided they could but fight well. But Francis I. who was the restorer of learning, and the father of the learned, changed the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FACE">face</a> of things; and after his time, Henry Stevens printed his book, De la Precellence du Langage Francais. The change had become very conspicuous at the end of the 16th century; and under Henry IV. Amyot, Cocteau, and Malherbe, contributed towards bringing it to its perfection; which the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDINAL">Cardinal</a> de Richelieu completed, by the establishment of the French academy; an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a>, wherein the most distinguished persons of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOWN">gown</a>, have been members. Nor did the long reign of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> XIV. contribute a little to the improvement of the language; the personal qualities of that <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>, and his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> for the fine arts, and that of the princes of the blood, rendered his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> the politest in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WIT">Wit</a> and magnificence seemed to vie; and his generals might have disputed with the Greeks, Romans, &c. the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> of writing well, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they could not that of fighting. From court, the elegance and purity of the language soon spread itself into the provinces; and now there is scarce anybody there who does not write and speak good French. One of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> of the French language is, to be <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> and easy. The words are ranged in it much in the same order as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> in our minds; in which it differs exceedingly from the Greek and Latin, where the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVERSION">inversion</a> of the natural order of words is reputed a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>. Indeed the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a> surpasses even the French in this point; but then it comes short of it in copiousness and variety. It must be added, however, that as to the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANALOGY">analogy</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAMMAR">grammar</a>, and the simplicity wherewith the moods of verbs are formed, the English has the advantage not only over the French, but over all the known languages in in the world; but then the turns, the expressions, and the idioms of the English, are sometimes so quaint and extraordinary, that it loses a good <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of the advantage which its grammatical simplicity gives it over the rest. The French has but few <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPOUND">compound</a> words; wherein it differs widely from the Greek, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">High</a> Dutch, and English. This the French authors own a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> disadvantage in their language; the Greek and Dutch deriving a great <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of their force and energy from the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> of words, and frequently expressing that in one sounding word, which the French cannot express but by a periphrasis. The diminutives in the French are as few as the compounds; the greatest part of those remaining in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> having lost their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DIMINUTIVE">diminutive</a> signification; but what distinguish the French most, are its justness, purity, accuracy, and flexibility. French is the most universal and extensive language in Europe. The policy of states and courts has rendered it necessary for the ministers of princes, and their officers, &c., and the taste of arts and sciences has had the same effect with regard to the learned. In Germany, and elsewhere, the princesses and persons of distinction value themselves on understanding French; and in several courts of Europe, French is almost as much known as the language of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>.

FRESCATI

Pages 245-245
or Frascati, a small town, situated on the brow of a hill, about twelve miles to the eastward of Rome. It derives its name from the coolness of the air, and fresh verdure of the fields around. It is built of the ruins of the ancient Tusculum; and the Tuscan villa where Cicero wrote his famous questions is at a place now called Grotta Ferrata, about two miles distant. E. Long, ii. 43. N. Lat. 41. 48. There is a very fine prospect from this town into the neighbouring country, which abounds with the seats of cardinals and other nobility. It is the see of a bishop, who is one of the six senior cardinals, and is surrounded by some of the most beautiful villas in Italy; the principal of which are the villa Aldobrandini, belonging to Prince Pamfili; the villa Taberna, belonging to Prince Borghese; and villa Ludovisi, to the family of Colonna. The villa Aldobrandini, called also Belvedere from its beautiful prospect, is the most remarkable, on account of its fine situation, extensive gardens, airy terraces, its grottoes, cascades, and water-works. Over a saloon, near the grand cascade, is the following inscription: Huc ego migravi musis comitatus Apollo; Hic Delphi, hic Helicon, hic mihi Delos erit. The walls are adorned with a representation of Apollo and the Muses; and some of that god's adventures are painted in fresco by Domenichino. The villa Taberna is one of the finest and best furnished of any in the neighbourhood of Rome. From this you ascend through gardens to Monte Dracone, another palace on a more lofty situation, belonging also to that prince, and deriving its name from the arms of his family. From hence you may see Rome, and the whole extent of the plain; it has a noble ascent, with a broad paved walk; and among other curiosities there is a hall adorned with the pictures of a vast number of men eminent for learning and arms. The gardens, laid out by Vignola, contain three miles in compass; and have many delightful walks and curious water-works. Near this place are the monks of Camaldoli and the capuchins; and higher up are ruins of the ancient Tusculum. Ascending towards the plain, two miles on the right hand, you find the famous abbey of Grotta Ferrata, belonging to the monks of St Basil, and situated on the ruins of Cicero's house. The Virgin Mary of the great altar is an ancient Greek picture; in the chapel the pictures of St Nilus and St Bartholomew the abbot, are by Annibal Caracci; and all the paintings in fresco of this chapel are by Domenichino. Villa Ludovisi has a charming walk going up to it, where you see the ruins of Lucullus's palace. The house is small; but the gardens are large, embellished with a great variety of walks and fountains, and a beautiful cascade.

FRESCO

Pages 245-246

a method of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a> in relievo on walls, so as to endure the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>. It is performed with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>-colours on fresh <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLASTER">plaster</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> on a wall laid with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MORTAR">mortar</a> not yet dry. This sort of painting has a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> advantage by its incorporating with the mortar; and drying along with it, becomes very durable. The Italians, from whom we borrow the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a>, call it fresco; because it is frequently used for walls, alcoves, and other buildings in the open <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a>. Vitruvius, lib. vii. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a>. 4. calls it udo tectorio. Painting in fresco is very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a>, having been practised in the earliest ages of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a> and Rome. It is chiefly performed on walls and vaults, newly plastered with lime and sand; but the plaster is only to be laid, in proportion as the painting goes on; no more being to be done at once than the painter can despatch in a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>, while it dries. Before he begins to paint, a cartoon or <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> is usually made on <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>, to be chalked, and transferred to the wall, about half an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> after the plaster is applied. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> painted on stucco; and we may remark in Vitruvius what infinite care they took in making the incrustation or plastering of their buildings to render them beautiful and lasting; though the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> painters find a plaster of lime and sand preferable to it; both as it does not dry so hastily, and as being a little brownish, it is fitter to lay colours on, than a ground so <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> as stucco. In this kind of painting all the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPOUND">compound</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> colours, and almost all the minerals, are set aside, and scarce anything is used but earths; which are capable of preserving their <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, defending it from the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> of the lime, and resisting its <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a>, which Vitruvius calls its bitterness. For the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> to come out in all its <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>, the colours must be laid on quick, while the plaster is yet moist; nor should they ever be retouched dry, with colours mixed up with the white of an <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGG">egg</a>, or size, or <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUM">gum</a>, as some workmen do; because such colours grow blackish; nor do any preserve themselves, but only such as were laid on hastily at first. The colours used are white made of lime slaked <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> before, and white marble dust; ochre, both <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a>; verditer; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAPIS">lapis</a> lazuli; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SMALT">smalt</a>; <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> chalk, &c. All which are only ground, and worked up with water; and most of them grow brighter and brighter as the fresco dries. The brushes and pencils for this work ought to be long and soft, otherwise they <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RAKE">rake</a> and raise the painting. The colours should be full, and flowing from the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRUSH">brush</a>; and the design perfect; for in this work you cannot alter or add upon any colour.

FRESH WATER

Pages 246-246

is that not tinctured <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> impregnated with <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> or saline particles enough to be discovered by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>. Such generally is that of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a>, rains, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WELLS">wells</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a>, &c. The dulcifying or making of salt <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> fresh is a secret that has been <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> sought with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>. For an account of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> attempts that have been made with this view, see <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">Sea</a> Water.

FRESH WIND

Pages 246-246

h <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">Wind</a> signifies strong, but not violent; hence when the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-GALE">gale</a> increases, it is said to freshen.

FRESHES

Pages 246-246

a local <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> signifying annual inundations, from the river being swollen by the melted snows and other fresh waters from the uplands, as is the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NILE">Nile</a>, &c. from periodical <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> tropical rains. As a sailor's term, it is opposed to marine or <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> floodings, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIDES">tides</a>, &c. The word is of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, where the inundations so called are of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>. They bring <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> to the intervals below, and form a fine mould, producing corn, grain, and herbage, in the most luxuriant plenty. They also afford another benefit, in regard to many <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> in America, viz. in equalizing the surface of the stream (where rapid falls, or cascades, obstruct the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a>), so that rafts of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a> and other <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GROSS">gross</a> produce are then floated down to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> ports in great quantities.

FRESNOY

Pages 246-246
CHARLES ALPHONSE DU, an excellent poet and painter, was born at Paris in 1611. He was instructed there by Perrier and Simon Vouet in painting; but he did not long adhere to Vouet's manner of colouring; for as soon as he fixed himself at Rome, he made the works of Titian the models for his imitation. He was, however, more celebrated as a poet than as a painter; and gave more attention to the theory than to the practice of the pencil. Accordingly he is better known by his incomparable poem De arte graphicca, than by his performances on the canvas: and on this poem he bestowed so much pains, that he died in 1665, before it was published. It was printed afterwards with a French prose translation and notes by M. de Piles; and was translated into English by Mr Dryden, who prefixed to it an original preface containing a parallel between painting and poetry.

FRET-WORK

Pages 246-246

that adorned with frets. It is sometimes used to fill up and enrich flat empty spaces; but it is mostly practised in roofs, which are fretted over with <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLASTER">plaster</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>.

FRETTES

Pages 246-246

in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINERALOGY">Mineralogy</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> used by our miners to express the worn side of the banks of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> in mine countries, where they search for the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SHOAD">shoad</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONES">stones</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> grewts washed <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> from the hills, in order from thence to trace out the running of the shoad up to the mine.

FREYBERG

Pages 246-246
or Friedberg, a town in the circle of Upper Saxony, containing upwards of 9000 people. There are mines of copper, tin, lead, and silver, in its vicinity, which afford employment to a considerable number of workmen, and produce an annual revenue of more than 10,000 rix-dollars. The princes of the house of Saxony are usually buried here, where there is also an academy for the study of mineralogy, instituted in the year 1765, and reckoned the most famous for that science of any in Germany. It is situated on a branch of the Muldau, 19 miles south-west of Dresden, in N. Lat. 51. and E. Long. 13. 18.

FRIABLE

Pages 246-246

among naturalists, an appellation given to bodies that are easily crumbled to pieces: such are pumice and all calcined <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONES">stones</a>.

FRIAR

Pages 246-246
or Friar, by the Latins called frater, the Italians fra, and the French frere, that is, brother: a term common to the monks of all orders; founded on this, that there is a kind of fraternity or brotherhood presumed between the several religious persons of the same convent or monastery. Friars are generally distinguished into these four principal branches, viz. 1. Minors, Gray friars, or Franciscans. 2. Augustines. 3. Dominicans, or Black friars. 4. White friars or Carmelites. From these four the rest of the orders descend. See Franciscans, Augustines, &c. Friar, in a more peculiar sense, is restrained to such monks as are not priests; for those in orders are usually dignified with the appellation of father. FRIARS OBSERVANT (fratres observantes) were a branch of the Franciscans; thus called, because not combined together in any cloister, convent, or corporation, as the conventuals are; but only agreed among themselves to observe the rules of their order, and that more strictly than the conventuals did, from whom they separated themselves out of a singularity of zeal, living in certain places of their own choosing.

FRIBURG

Pages 247-247

the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANTON">Canton</a> of, one of the 13 republics of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWITZERLAND">Switzerland</a>. It is surrounded on all sides by the canton of Bern. The <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> is fertile in corn, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>, and pastures; and it is said the canton can send 18,000 men into the field. This canton is entirely Catholic.

FRICASSEE

Pages 247-247

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DISH">dish</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> mess hastily dressed in a frying <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAN">pan</a>, and seasoned with <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUTTER">butter</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, or the like. The word is French, formed of the Latin frictura, "frying." Others <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> have fricassee formed in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a> of the noise made by butter, or other fat, when melted in the pan. We say a fricassee of pullets, of rabbits, of tench, of tripe, of frogs, of eggs, of peas, Fricassee &c.

FRICENTI

Pages 247-247

an episcopal town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>, and in the farther principality, near the river Tripalito, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 15. 2. N. Lat. 40. 59.

FRICTION

Pages 247-248

the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> of rubbing <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> grating the surface of one body against that of another, called also attrition. The phenomena arising upon the friction of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> bodies, under different circumstances, are very numerous and considerable. Mr Hawksbee gives us a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of experiments of this kind; particularly of the attrition or friction of glass, under various circumstances, the result of which was, that it yielded <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> and became electrical. All bodies by friction produce <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>; many of them emit light; particularly a cat's back, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>, beaten sulphur, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERCURY">mercury</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>, &c. but, above all, diamonds, which, when briskly rubbed against glass, gold, or the like, yield a light equal to that of a live coal when blowed by the bellows. See ELECTRICS and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTRICITY">ELECTRICITY</a>. Friction, in <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MECHANICS">Mechanics</a>, denotes the resistance a moving body meets with from the surface on which it moves. Friction arises from the roughness or asperity of the surface of the body moved on, and that of the body moving: for such surfaces consisting alternately of eminences and cavities, either the eminences of the one must be raised over those of the other, or they must be both broke and worn off: but neither can happen without <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>, nor can motion be produced without a force impressed. Hence, the force applied to move the body is either wholly or partly spent on this effect: and consequently there arises a resistance or friction, which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be greater, ceteris paribus, as the eminences are the greater and the substance the harder: and as the body, by continual friction, becomes more and more polished, the friction diminishes. See MECHANICS. Friction, in Medicine and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SURGERY">Surgery</a>, denotes the act of rubbing a diseased <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> with oils, unguents, or other matters, in order to ease, relieve, and cure it. Frictions are much used of late in venereal <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a>. They prefer the applying of mercury externally by way of friction, to that of giving it internally, to raise a salivation. There are also frictions with the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRUSH">brush</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> cloth, or the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> only. These frictions are a sort of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> which contributes greatly to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a>; as they excite and stir up the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> warmth, divert defluxions, promote perspiration, open the pores of the skin, and carry off stagnant humours. The flesh brush (Dr Cheyne observes) is an exercise extremely useful for promoting a full and free perspiration and circulation. Every body knows the effect of currying horses; that it makes them sleek, gay, lively, and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a>; so as even to be judged <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EQUIVALENT">equivalent</a> to half the feeding. This it can no otherwise effect, but by assisting <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> to throw off the recrements of the juices, which stop the free circulation, and, by constant friction, irritation, and stimulation, to bring the blood and spirits to the parts most distant from the seat of heat and motion; and so plump up the superficial muscles. And the same effect it would have in other creatures, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> himself, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> managed in the same manner, and with the same care and regularity. Persons, therefore, of weak nerves and sedentary lives, would do well to supply the want of other exercise with spending half an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a>, morning and night, in curving and rubbing their whole body, especially their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIMBS">limbs</a>, with a flesh brush. But this means of health is most advantageously used when the prime via are most empty.

FRIDAY

Pages 248-248

the sixth <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-WEEK">week</a>; so named of Freya, a Saxon deity. By the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> it was called dies Veneris. See FREA. Good-Friday. See Good-Friday.

FRIDSTOL

Pages 248-248

mentioned, in our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> writers, among the immunities granted to churches, signifies a seat, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of peace and security, where criminals might find safety and protection: of these there were many in England: but the most famous were that at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEVERLEY">Beverley</a>, and that in St <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PETER">Peter</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORK">York</a>, granted by <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARTER">charter</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> Henry I.

FRIEDENSHUETTEN

Pages 248-248

a Moravian settlement, whose name signifies tents of peace, situated on the Susquehannah river in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENNSYLVANIA">Pennsylvania</a>, about 24 miles below Tioga point, which owed its origin to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-UNITED_BRETHREN">united brethren</a>, in the year 1765. At that <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> it contained 13 huts belonging to the Indians, besides 40 houses constructed after the European manner, and a very neat chapel.

FRIENDLY ISLANDS

Pages 248-258

a cluster of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PACIFIC_OCEAN">Pacific ocean</a>, so named by <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPTAIN">Captain</a> Cook in the year 1773, on account of the friendship which appeared to subsist among the inhabitants, and from their courteous behaviour to strangers. <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABEL">Abel</a> Jansen Tasman, an eminent Dutch navigator, first touched here in 1643, and gave names to the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> islands. Captain Cook laboriously explored the whole cluster, which he found to consist of more than 60. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-THREE_ISLANDS">three islands</a> which Tasman <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> he named New <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMSTERDAM">Amsterdam</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROTTERDAM">Rotterdam</a>, and Middleburgh. The first is the largest, and extends about 21 miles from east to west, and about 13 from <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> to south. These islands are inhabited by a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a> of Indians, who cultivate the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> industry. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of Amsterdam is intersected by a straight and pleasant <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a> with fruit trees on each side, which provide <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SHADE">shade</a> from the scorching <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> islands are Annamooka, Tongataboo (the residence of the sovereign and the chiefs), Lefooga, and Eooa. Lefooga is about <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> miles <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a>, and in some places not above two <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> three <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>. It is in many respects superior to Annamooka. The plantations are both more numerous and more extensive; and enclosed by fences which, running <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> to each other, form fine spacious public <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROADS">roads</a>, which would appear beautiful in countries where rural conveniences have been carried to the highest perfection. They are, in general, highly cultivated, and well stocked with the several roots and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> which these islands produce; and Captain Cook endeavoured to add to their <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>, by <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTING">planting</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> corn, and the seeds of melons, pumpkins, and the like. Eooa, when viewed from the ship at <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANCHOR">anchor</a>, formed one of the most beautiful prospects in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, and very different from the others of the Friendly Isles; which being low, and perfectly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a>, exhibit nothing to the eye but the trees which cover them: whereas here, the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> rising gently to a considerable height, presents us with an extensive prospect, where groves of trees are only interspersed at <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a> distances, in beautiful disorder, and all the rest is covered with grass, except near the shores, where it is entirely covered with fruit and other trees; amongst which are the habitations of the natives. In order to have a view of as great a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the island as possible, Captain Cook and some of his officers walked up to the highest point of the island. From this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> they had a view of almost the whole island, which consisted of beautiful meadows of prodigious <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>, adorned with tufts of trees, and intermixed with plantations. 'While I was surveying this delightful prospect (says Captain Cook), I could not help flattering myself with the pleasing idea that some future navigator may, from the same station, behold these meadows stocked with cattle, brought to these islands by the ships of England; and that the completion of this single benevolent purpose, independent of all other considerations, would sufficiently mark to posterity, that our voyages had not been useless to the general interests of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a>.' 'The next morning,' says our benevolent commander, 'I planted a pine apple, and sowed the seeds of melons and other vegetables in Taoofa's plantation. I had indeed some encouragement to flatter myself that my endeavours of this kind also would not be fruitless: as I had this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DISH">dish</a> of turnips served up at my dinner, which was the produce of seeds I left here in my former voyage.' The natives of these islands seldom exceed the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> stature; but are very strong and well made, especially as to their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIMBS">limbs</a>. They are generally broad about the shoulders; and though the muscular disposition of the men, which seems a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of much <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTION">action</a>, rather conveys the appearance of strength than of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>, there are several to be seen who are really handsome. The women are not so much distinguished from the men by their features as by their general form, which is for the most part destitute of that strong fleshy firmness that appears in the latter. The features of some are so delicate, as not only to be a true <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">index</a> of their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEX">sex</a>, but to lay claim to a considerable share of beauty and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a>: for the bodies and limbs of most of the females are well proportioned; and some absolutely perfect models of a beautiful <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>. But the most remarkable distinction in the women is the uncommon smallness and delicacy of their fingers, which may be put in competition with the finest in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. The general <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> is a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> deeper than the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROWN">brown</a>; but several of the men and women have a true olive <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPLEXION">complexion</a>: and some of the last are even a great <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> fairer. Their countenances very remarkably express the abundant mildness or good nature which they possess; and are entirely free from that <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAVAGE">savage</a> keenness which marks nations in a barbarous state. They are frank, cheerful, and good-natured. There are, upon the whole, few <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> defects or deformities to be found among these people. The most common is the tetter or <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RING">ring</a> worm, that seems to affect almost one half of them, and leaves whitish serpentine marks everywhere behind it; but this is of less consequence than another which is very frequent, and appears on every part of the body. Captain Cook had the mortification to learn that all the care he took when he first visited these islands, to prevent the venereal <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a> from being communicated to the inhabi- friendly tenants, had proved ineffectual. What is extraordinary, they do not seem to regard it much; and as there appeared few signs of its destroying effects, probably the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a>, and the way of living of these people, greatly abated its virulence. There are two other complaints frequent amongst them; one of which is an indolent firm swelling, that affects the legs and arms, and increases them to an extraordinary size in their whole length. The other is a tumor of the same sort in the testicles, which sometimes exceeds the size of the two fists. But in other respects they may be considered as uncommonly healthy. Their <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> is in general straight, thick, and strong, though a few have it bushy or frizzled. The natural colour is <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a>; but the greatest part of the men, and some of the women, have it stained of a brown or purple colour, and a few of an <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORANGE">orange</a> cast. They wear it variously cut. Some have it cut off on one side of the head only; others have it entirely cut off except a single lock; the women in general wear it short. The men have their beards cut short; and both men and women strip the hair from the armpits. The men are stained from about the middle of the belly to about half way <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> the thighs with a deep blue colour. The women have only a few small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> or spots thus imprinted on the inside of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>. Their kings, as a mark of distinction, are exempted from this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a>. The men are all circumcised, or rather supercircised, as the operation consists in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> off only a small piece of the foreskin at the upper part: which by that means is rendered incapable ever after of covering the glans. This is all they aim at, as they say the operation is practised from a notion of cleanliness. The dress of both men and women is the same: and consists of a piece of cloth or matting (but mostly the former) about two yards wide and two and a half long: at least so long as to go once and a half round the waist, to which it is confined by a girdle or <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CORD">cord</a>. It is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> before, and hangs down like a petticoat, as low as the middle of the leg. The upper part of the garment above the girdle is plaited into several folds; so that, when unfolded, there is cloth sufficient to draw up and wrap round the shoulders; which is very seldom done. The inferior sort are satisfied with small pieces; and very often wear nothing but a covering made of leaves of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, or the maro, which is a narrow piece of cloth or matting like a sash. This they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> between the thighs and wrap round the waist; but the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of it is chiefly confined to the men. The ornaments worn by both sexes are necklaces made of the fruit of the pandanus, and various sweet smelling <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>, which go under the general name of kahulla. Others are composed of small shells, the wing and leg-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONES">bones</a> of birds, sharks <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a> and other things; all which hang loose upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a>; rings of tortoise shell on the fingers; and a number of these joined together as bracelets on the wrists. The lobes of the ears (though most frequently only one), are sometimes perforated with two holes, in which they wear cylindrical bits of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-IVORY">ivory</a> about three inches long. Cleanliness induces them to bathe in the ponds, which seem to serve for no other purpose. They are sensible that <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> hurts their skin; and when <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> obliges them to bathe in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> have some cocoa <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUT">nut</a> shells filled with fresh water poured over them to wash it off. People of superior <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> use cocoa nut <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, which improves the appearance of the skin very much. The employment of the women is of the easy kind, and, for the most part, such as may be executed in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>. The manufacturing their cloth is wholly consigned to their care; as is also that of their mats, which are esteemed both for their texture and their beauty. There are many other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> of less <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOTE">note</a> that employ the spare <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of their females; as combs, of which they make vast numbers, and little baskets with small beads; but all finished with such neatness and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> in the disposition of the various parts, that a stranger cannot help admiring their assiduity and dexterity. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> allotted to the men, as might be expected, is far more laborious and extensive than that of the women. <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRICULTURE">Agriculture</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOAT">boat</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FISHING">fishing</a>, and other things that relate to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a>, are the objects of their care. Cultivated roots and fruits being their principal support, this requires their constant <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> to agriculture, which they pursue very diligently, and seem to have brought almost to as great perfection as circumstances <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> permit. In planting the plantains and yams, they observe so much exactness, that, which ever way you look, the rows present themselves regular and complete. The cocoa nut and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a> fruit trees are scattered about without any order, and seem to give them no trouble after they have attained a certain height. The houses of the lower people are <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a> huts, and very small; those of the better sort are larger and more moderate. The dimensions of one of a middling size are about 30 feet long, 20 broad, and 12 <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a>. Their house is, properly speaking, a thatched <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROOF">roof</a> or shed, supported by posts and rafters, disposed in a very judicious manner. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOR">floor</a> is raised with earth smoothed, and covered with thick strong matting, and kept very clean. A thick strong mat, about two and a half or three feet broad, bent into the form of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEMICIRCLE">semicircle</a>, and set upon its edge, with the ends touching the side of the house, in shape resembling the fender of a fire heath, encloses a space for the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> and mistress of the family to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SLEEP">sleep</a> in. The rest of the family sleep upon the floor, wherever they please to <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> down; the unmarried men and women apart from each other: Or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the family be <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, there are small huts adjoining, to which the servants retire in the night; so that privacy is as much observed here as one could expect. The clothes that they wear in the day serve for their covering in the night. Their whole furniture consists of a bowl or two, in which they make kava; a few gourds; cocoa nut shells; and some small wooden stools, which serve them for pillows. They display much ingenuity in the building of their canoes, as well as in the navigating them. The only tools which they use to construct them, which are very dexterously made, are hatchets, or rather thick adzes, of a smooth black <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a> that abounds at Toofoa; augres, made of sharks teeth, fixed on small handles, and rasps of a rough skin of a fish, fastened on flat pieces of wood, thinner on one side, which also have handles. The cordage is made from the fibres of the cocoa nut husk, which, though not more than <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> or ten inches long, they plait, about the size of a quill, or less, to any length that they please, and roll it up in balls, from which the larger <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROPES">ropes</a> are made by twisting several of these together. The lines that they fish with are as strong and even as the best cord we make, resembling it almost in every respect. Their other fishing implements are large and small hooks made of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEARL">pearl</a> shell. Their weapons are clubs of different sorts, (in the ornamenting of which they spend much time,) spears and darts. They have also bows and arrows; but these seemed to be designed only for amusement, such as <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SHOOTING">shooting</a> at birds, and not for <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> purposes. The stools are about two feet long, but only four or five inches high, and near four broad, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BENDING">bending</a> downward in the middle, with four strong legs, and circular feet; the whole made of one piece of black or brown wood, neatly polished, and sometimes inlaid with bits of ivory. Yams, plantains, and cocoa nuts, composed the greatest part of their vegetable diet. Of their animal food, the chief articles are, hogs, fowls, fish, and all sorts of shell fish; but the lower people eat rats. The two first vegetable articles, with bread fruit, are what may be called the basis of their food, at different times of the year, with fish and shell fish; for hogs, fowls, and turtle, seem only to be occasional dainties, reserved for their chiefs. Their food is generally dressed by <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAKING">baking</a>, and they have the art of making, from different kinds of fruit, several dishes which most of us esteemed very good. The generality of them lay their victuals upon the first <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAF">leaf</a> they meet with, however dirty it may be; but when food is served up to the chiefs, it is commonly laid upon green plantain leaves. The women are not excluded from eating with the men; but there are certain ranks or orders amongst them that can neither eat nor drink together. This distinction begins with the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>; but where it ends could not be learnt. They seem to have no set time for meals. They go to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BED">bed</a> as soon as it is dark, and rise with the dawn in the morning. Their private diversions are chiefly singing, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-DANCING">dancing</a>, and music performed by the women. The dancing of the men has a thousand different motions with the hands, to which we are entire strangers; and they are performed with an ease and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRACE">grace</a> which are not to be described but by those who have seen them. Whether their marriages be made lasting by any kind of solemn <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRACT">contract</a>, our voyagers could not determine with precision; but it appeared that the bulk of the people satisfied themselves with one wife. The chiefs, however, have commonly several women, though it appeared as if one only was looked upon as the mistress of the family. When any person of consequence dies, his body is washed and decorated by some woman or women, who are appointed on the occasion; and these women are not, by their customs, to touch any food with their hands for many months afterwards; and it is remarkable, that the length of the time they are thus proscribed, is the greater in proportion to the rank of the chief whom they had washed. The concern of these people for the dead is most extraordinary. They <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEAT">beat</a> their teeth with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, strike a shark's tooth into the head until the blood flows in streams, and thrust spears into the inner part of the thigh, into their sides below the armpits, and through the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHEEKS">cheeks</a> into the mouth. All these operations convey an idea of such rigorous <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a>, as must require either an uncommon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of affection, or the grossest <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a>, to exact. It should be observed, however, that the more painful operations are only practised on account of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of those most nearly connected. Their long and general <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOURNING">mourning</a> proves, that they consider death as a very great evil. And this is confirmed by a very odd custom which they practise to avert it. They suppose that the Deity will accept of the little finger, as a sort of sacrifice efficacious enough to procure the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RECOVERY">recovery</a> of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a>. They cut it off with one of their stone hatchets. There appeared scarcely one in ten of them who was not thus mutilated in one or both hands. According to Captain King, it is common also for the inferior people to cut off a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOINT">joint</a> of their little finger on account of the sickness of the chiefs to whom they belong. They seem to have little <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONCEPTION">conception</a> of future <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a>. They believe, however, that they are justly punished upon earth; and consequently use every method to render their divinities propitious. The Supreme Author of all things they call Kallafootonga; who, they say, is a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> residing in the sky, and directing the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THUNDER">thunder</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">rain</a>, and in general all the changes of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>. They believe that when she is angry with them, the productions of the earth are blasted; that many things are destroyed by <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIGHTNING">lightning</a>; and that they themselves are afflicted with sickness and death as well as their hogs and other animals. When this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGER">anger</a> abates, they suppose that everything is restored to its natural order. They also admit a plurality of deities, though all inferior to Kallafootonga. They have less absurd sentiments about the immateriality and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IMMORTALITY">immortality</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUL">soul</a>. They call it <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, the living principle; or, what is more agreeable to their notions of it, Otooa; that is, a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a> or invisible being. Of the nature of their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> no more is known than the general outline. According to the information received, the power of the king is unlimited, and the life and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of the subject are at his disposal; and instances enough were seen to prove that the lower order of people have no property, nor safety for their persons, but at the will of the chiefs to whom they respectively belong. When any one wants to speak with the king or chief, he advances and sits down before him with his legs across; which is a posture to which they are so much accustomed, that any other <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of sitting is disagreeable to them. To speak to the king standing would be accounted here a striking mark of rudeness. Though some of the more potent chiefs may vie with the king in point of actual possessions, they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> very short in rank and in certain marks of respect, which the collective body have agreed to pay the monarch. It is a particular privilege annexed to his sovereignty, not to be punctured nor circumcised, as all his subjects are. Whenever he walks out, every one whom he meets must sit down till he has passed. No one is allowed to be over his head; on the contrary all must come under his feet; for there cannot be a greater outward mark of submission than that which is paid to the sovereign and other great people of these islands. FRIENDSHIP may be defined, a mutual <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a> subsisting between two persons: and arising, not merely from the general principle of benevolence, from emotions of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRATITUDE">gratitude</a> for favours received, from views of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a>, or from instinctive affection or animal <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PASSION">passion</a>; but from an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> entertained by each of them, that the other is adorned with some amiable or respectable qualities. The object of the general principle of benevolence is mankind, not any particular individual. Gratitude regards the person from whom he feels its emotions has received a favour, whether that person be a virtuous or vicious, a respectable or a contemptible character: it prompts the person obliged to make a suitable return to his benefactor, but not to enter into any particular intimacy with him, merely on account of the favours which he has received. Many connections are formed, and dignified with the name of friendship, upon no other principle but the sordid hope which one or perhaps each of the parties entertains of accomplishing some selfish purpose through the assistance of the other: but such a connexion is so base in its nature, and so transitory in its <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DURATION">duration</a>, as to render it unnecessary for us to spend time in demonstrating it to be unworthy of the name of friendship. The instinctive affection which a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARENT">parent</a> entertains for his child, as well as that which the child feels for his parent, seems intended by nature to form an union between the persons thus related to each other: but the union between parents and children, when supported by no other principle but <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTINCT">instinct</a>, is different from friendship: it extends no farther than to cause the parent to provide for his child during his helpless years, and the child to look up to his parent for protection and support. We need not mention that appetite which is the foundation of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a>, and is the provision which nature has made for the continuation of our <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>. This appetite alone, and unassisted by some nobler principle, cannot give rise to any connexion worthy of an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> name. After excluding these principles, we can refer the origin of friendship only to "an opinion entertained by each of the parties between whom it subsists, that the other is adorned with some amiable or respectable qualities." A connexion founded on different principles we cannot <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> with the name of friendship; but that which flows from this pure source must be noble and virtuous. When two persons of virtue and abilities contemplate each the other's character and conduct, they cannot but view them with complacency and esteem. Habits and actions displaying <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRUDENCE">prudence</a>, fortitude, moderation, integrity, benevolence, and piety, naturally command the approbation of the impartial spectator, and even affect him with delight. But as we are disposed to revisit a landscape the beauties of which we have contemplated with rapture, and read with frequent delight a poem in which genius has faithfully delineated some of the most enchanting scenes or the most interesting events in nature; so we also become desirous to enjoy frequent opportunities of contemplating a character distinguished for eminent abilities and illustrious virtues. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> of such a person is preferred to his who is disgraced by the opposite qualities. Hence, whenever men of truly respectable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> enjoy opportunities of mutual intercourse, an attachment naturally takes place between them; entirely disinterested, and founded solely on the approbation with which the one cannot avoid regarding the conduct of the other. The esteem which the one is thus induced to entertain for the other will <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> them to seek frequent opportunities of enjoying each other's society, mutually to ask and listen to advice, to trust their most secret and important purposes to each other's confidence, and to be no less concerned each of them for the other's interest and honour than for his own. This, and this alone, is genuine friendship; founded on virtue, and on that approbation which virtue never fails to command: it is a natural consequence of intercourse between virtuous men.—Where it is once established, it cannot die, while those virtues to which it owes its origin continue to adorn the persons between whom it subsists. But, perhaps, such a pure and sublime attachment can scarce be expected to exist among beings of substances so mixed and imperfect a character as mankind. The wise <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Stoics, or the Christian who fully obeys the precepts, and follows the steps of his Saviour, might be capable of it; but, unfortunately, humanity never reaches such perfection. Virtue and vice are so blended together in every <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> character, that while none is so worthless as to excite no other sentiment but abhorrence, there is scarcely any so uniformly virtuous as to command unvaried esteem or admiration. Even the purest and most disinterested of those friendships which prevail among men, owe their origin to other meaner principles, as well as to that which has been mentioned as the principle of genuine friendship. There are certain circumstances favourable, and others adverse, to the formation and continuance of friendship. These, making amends, as it were, for the imperfection of human virtue and human knowledge, lead men to overlook each other's faults and follies, and to unite in the bonds of friendship; a friendship which, though less <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOLID">solid</a>, less generous, and less lasting, than that which we have above described, is yet attended with effects favourable to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a> of individuals, and to the interests of society in general. Equality of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> is favourable to friendship. Infancy, manhood, and old age, differ so considerably from each other in their views, passions, and pursuits, that the man will seldom be disposed to associate with the boy Friendship, or the youth, in preference to one who has had equal <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> in the world with himself; and the old man will generally wish for the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> of some ancient friend, with whom he may speak of "the days of former years." They who cultivate the same trade or profession, enjoy opportunities favourable to the formation of friendship. Being engaged among the same objects, and acquiring skill in the same arts, their knowledge, their sentiments, and habits, are nearly the same; they cannot avoid frequent intercourse with each other; they naturally enter into each other's prejudices and views, and therefore cannot but take <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> in each other's conversation and society. Physicians, lawyers, and divines, form each of them a distinct body; and the members of each of those bodies associate with one another more readily than with men of a different profession. It is related by Swift or Addison, that, in the beginning of the last century, there was a particular coffeehouse in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a> which clergymen used to frequent, and that a son of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> scarcely ever ventured to show his head in any other. In the days of Dryden, poets, and all who pretended to poetical genius or taste, resorted to Will's, as to another <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PARNASSUS">Parnassus</a>, to sip cups of coffee, and now and then perhaps to drink of some more inspiring liquor, instead of the waters of the fountain Hippocrene. Equality of rank and fortune is also favourable to friendship. Seldom will a man of fortune be able to <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAIN">gain</a> the sincere friendship of any of his dependents. Though he treat them with the most obliging condescension, and load them with favours; yet still, either the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> of dependence, or resentment for imaginary injuries, or impatience of the debt of gratitude, or some other similar reason, will be likely to prevent them from regarding him with cordial affection. Servants are but rarely faithful even to the most indulgent master: Shakespeare's old <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADAM">Adam</a> is a very amiable but a very uncommon character. Indeed you may as soon expect to find the virtues and the generous courage of the chevalier Bayard among our military men of the present age, as to find an old Adam among the present race of servants. It is no less vain for the poor man to hope to acquire a sincere friend among his superiors in rank and fortune. The superior is generally disposed to exact such profound deference, such gratitude, such respect, even from the inferior whom he admits into his intimacy, that the equal <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMICABLE">amicable</a> intercourse of friendship can scarce ever take place between them. Among the letters of the younger Pliny, we are pleased to find many monuments of the goodness of his heart. A number of his epistles addressed to friends in meaner circumstances appear to have been accompanied with very considerable presents, which by his opulence he was well enabled to bestow. But he takes care to let those humble friends know the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of the obligations which he conferred, and the vastness of the debt of gratitude which they owed to him, in such plain, nay even indelicate terms, that though they might receive his favours with gratitude, and regard him as their benefactor, yet they could never regard him as a man with whom they might cultivate the free easy intercourse of friendship. Some one or other of the Greek writers mentions a singular instance of cordial friendship subsisting between two persons in unequal circumstances. One of them dying before the other, and leaving a wife and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> to whom he had no fortune nor even means of subsistence to bequeath, enjoined his rich friend, in his will, to take the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> of them on himself, and to support them in a liberal manner: nor did he entreat this from his humanity, but demanded it from his friendship. He had made a sure provision for his family. His rich friend delayed not to comply with his dying <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INJUNCTION">injunction</a>. He readily took upon himself the charge of the wife and daughter of his deceased friend, treated them with kindness, and at last divided his whole fortune equally between his own only daughter and the child of his friend. This is an agreeable instance of the power of friendship: but such instances are not to be expected to occur frequently in ordinary life, any more than the Stoic virtue of Cato, or the modest piety of a Nelson. Similarity of taste and temper will generally be found favourable to friendship. Two peevish men, indeed, will not long endure each other's company with much satisfaction; but two persons of mild, humane dispositions will naturally take delight in each other's society and conversation. They who are charmed with the bustle of a gay and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> life, avoid the haunts of the indolent and contemplative, and join <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> in hand to climb the heights of ambition, or <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-TREAD">tread</a> the round of amusement and dissipation. Those whom taste leads to cultivate the elegant objects of literature amid the sweets of a rural retirement, to wander through the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GROVE">grove</a>, or recline on the brink of some romantic rill, and peruse the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAGES">pages</a> of one of those geniuses who have shown themselves able to enlighten the understanding, and to kindle the glow of generous sentiment in the breast—those children of taste frequently associate in their elegant pursuits. We are pleased to read the correspondence of Pliny and Tacitus, of Locke and Molineaux, of Swift and Pope. We rejoice to find, that notwithstanding the rivalry of learning and genius, taste and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> have a natural tendency to promote benevolence and friendship among their votaries. The bustle of the world must be acknowledged to be generally unfavourable to friendship. When the heart is occupied with the sordid objects of ambition, or avarice, or gay dissipation, there is no room left for the pure and generous sentiments of friendship. Interests often interfere, competitions and jealousies arise, fatal to all the sweets of social intercourse. It is in active life that virtue shines with the most brilliant lustre; but seldom, alas! does pure virtue appear in the scenes of active life. How beautifully does the character of Atticus shine amid the characters of his illustrious cotemporaries! ut <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LUNA">Luna</a> inter minores ignes! Sylla, Caesar, Cicero, Brutus, Antony, and Augustus, were eminent for their abilities and virtues; but being engaged in the bustling pursuits of ambition, they seem to have been strangers to the calm and elegant happiness which Atticus enjoyed. Though those of them who were cotemporaries could not avoid perceiving and admiring each other's merits, yet never did cordial friendship subsist between them. Even Cicero, who could so well define the duties and describe the happiness of friendship, yet appears to have but seldom enjoyed its delights. But Atticus, who constantly declined entering the scenes of public life, friendship, life, experienced such happiness in a private condition, as must have been more than an ample reward to him for shunning all the splendid pursuits of ambition. He was the disinterested friend of all those eminent men, and enjoyed their esteem and friendship. So upright was his character, so amiable his manners, that they who were mortal enemies to each other, yet agreed in cultivating at the same time the friendship of Atticus. None of them appear to have hated him on account of his attachment to their enemies; and while he was the friend of Cicero and Octavius, he was at the same time the protector of the wife of Antony. Perhaps the virtue of such a character may be regarded as problematical. It may be alleged, that while such inveterate dissensions arose among his friends, the neutrality which he preserved was inconsistent with integrity. He has indeed been rashly branded by some writers as an avaricious time-serving man. But no <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a> appears to justify their assertions; on the contrary, the most respectable testimony, the nicest <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SCRUTINY">scrutiny</a>, exhibit his character in those amiable colours in which we have chosen to view it. Atticus is indeed no ordinary character. The general principles of human nature, and the examples which most frequently occur in the world, naturally suggest a suspicion, that had he been a man of genuine integrity, he must have observed a different tenor of conduct. But there is one circumstance which tends to strengthen considerably the respectable testimony of his contemporaries in his behalf. In Cato, in Epictetus, in the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, who, while suffering under all the violence of an acute distemper, maintained to Pompey that pain was no evil, we have instances of the tenets of philosophy opposing and repressing the principles of nature. We know how often <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> enthusiasm has produced the same effects. But Atticus was the votary of the mild and elegant philosophy of Epicurus; which, though there appears to have been a palpable inconsistency between its principles and the superstructure raised upon them, was yet in its general tendency not unfriendly to virtue, and recommended to its votaries that calm and innocent mode of life which Atticus cultivated. There is no small resemblance between the character of Atticus and that of Epicurus, the founder of this philosophy. The same tenets seem to have produced the same effects on both; and we will venture to pronounce so high an encomium on the Epicurean philosophy, as to assert, that it chiefly contributed to form the character of this amiable Roman. We know not if we may venture to affirm, that friendships are most naturally contracted among persons of the same sex. We believe they often are. If similarity of taste, of sentiments, of manners, be favourable to friendship, this cannot but happen. The distinction which nature has established between the two sexes, the new distinctions which are introduced by the different views with which their <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> is conducted, and the different duties which they are called to perform in life, have all a tendency to dispose men and women to enter into habits of intimacy with persons of their own sex rather than with the other. Young girls have their peculiar amusements, as boys have theirs: they knit and sew together, consult each other concerning their dress, and associate at their idle hours. Young men, in the same manner, prefer the society of their equals of the same sex till such time as their hearts begin to feel the impulse of a new passion. This soft passion, indeed, causes the youth to prefer the company of his favourite maid to that of his dearest <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPANION">companion</a>; and it perhaps causes the virgin to view her female companions with a jealous eye, while she fears that their charms may win the heart of the youth, whose fond regard she herself wishes to engage. But the fears, the jealousies, the timidity, nay even the fondness of love, are incompatible with friendship. Though the lover and his mistress be dear to each other, yet the free confidence of friendship cannot take place between them. They dare not yet venture to trust to each other all the secrets of their hearts. But if their mutual wishes be crowned by <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a>; then, indeed, as their interests become the same, if the transports of love are not succeeded by the calm delights and the free confidence of friendship, they must be unhappy. The marriage state is peculiarly favourable to friendship. Persons whose relations to each other are the more remote, will often find circumstances concurring to induce them to cultivate a friendly intercourse with each other. But here indifference is almost impossible. It is absolutely requisite, in order that they may not render each other miserable, that the husband and the wife be united in the bonds of friendship. This seems even to be one of the great laws of nature, by means of which provision is made for the happiness and the preservation of society.
