a fortress in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANADA">Canada</a>, situated at the head of a fine harbour, on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-west side of the outlet of Lake <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ONTARIO">Ontario</a>, where vessels of every <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> may ride in perfect safety. It is 300 miles from Quebec, and in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPARISON">comparison</a> of that <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> has a very short winter.

FRONTINUS

Pages 264-264

Sextus Julius, an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Roman writer, was of consular <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a>, and flourished under the emperors Vespasian, Titus, Domitian, Nerva, and Trajan. He commanded the Roman armies in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>; was made <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> praetor when Vespasian and Titus were consuls; and Nerva made him curator of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AQUEDUCTS">aqueducts</a>, which occasioned his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> De Aqueductibus urbis Romae. He wrote four books upon the Greek and Roman art of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>; a piece De Re Agraria, and another De Limitibus. These have been often separately reprinted; but were all collected together in a neat edition at <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMSTERDAM">Amsterdam</a> in 1661, with notes by Robertus Keuchenius. He died under Trajan.

FRONTISPIECE

Pages 264-264

in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">Architecture</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FACE">face</a> of a fine <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>. The word is formed of the Latin frontispicium, q.d. frontis hominis inspectio. Hence also, by a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, we say, the frontispiece of a book; meaning an ornament with an engraven <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> on the first page. FRONTLET. See Frontal.

FRONTO

Pages 264-264

Marcus Cornelius, was chosen for his eloquence to instruct the emperors Marcus Aurelius and Lucius Verus in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHETORIC">rhetoric</a>; in recompense of which he was promoted to the consulate, and a statue was erected to his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a>. He taught Marcus Aurelius not only eloquence, but the duty of kings, and excellent morals. Some say he wrote against the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>. A <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECT">sect</a> was formed of those who looked upon him as a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODEL">model</a> of perfect eloquence, and those were called Fronto-niani. The Civilians, whose names were Fronto, mentioned in the Pandects, were probably descended from him.

FROST

Pages 264-268

in Physiology, such a state of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ATMOSPHERE">atmosphere</a> as occasions the congelation <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> freezing of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> and other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLUIDS">fluids</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLD">Cold</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METEOROLOGY">Meteorology</a> Index. Water and other fluids are capable of containing the element of fire or <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> in two very different states. In the one, they seem to imbibe the fire in such a manner, that it eludes all the methods by which we are accustomed to observe it, either by our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSATION">sensation</a> of feeling, or the thermometer; in the other, it manifests itself obviously to our senses, either by the touch, the thermometer, or the emission of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>. In the first of these states, we call the body cold; and are apt to say that this coldness is occasioned by the absence of heat. But this manner of expressing ourselves, excepting in a relative <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>, is certainly improper; for even those fluids which are coldest to the touch contain a vast <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of heat. Thus vapour, which is colder to the touch than the water from which it was raised, contains an immense <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of fire, even more than sufficient to heat it <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> hot. The like may be said of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> and snow, or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ICE">ice</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> a quantity of each of these substances is separately reduced to the degree of 28 or 30 of Fahrenheit's thermometer, upon mixing them together, the heat which would have raised the thermometer to the degree above mentioned, now enters into the substance of them in such a manner that the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERCURY">mercury</a> falls <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to 0.—Here an excessive degree of cold is produced, and yet we are sure that the substances contain the very same quantity of heat that they formerly did: nay, they <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> even seem exceedingly cold, when they must certainly contain a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> deal more heat than they originally did; for they absorb it from all bodies around them; and if a small vessel full of water is put into the middle of such a mixture, it will in a short <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> be full of ice. It appears, therefore, that our senses, even when assisted by thermometers, can only judge of the state in which the element of fire is with relation to the bo- dies around us, without regard to the quantity contained in them. Thus, if heat flows from any <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of our body into any substance actually in contact with it, the sensation of cold is excited, and we call that substance cold; but if it flows from any substance into our body, the sensation of heat is excited, and we call that substance hot, without regard to the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> quantity contained in either <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>. Of all known substances, the atmosphere either absorbs or throws out heat with the most remarkable facility; and in one or other of these states it always is with respect to the surface of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, and such bodies as are placed on or near it; for these, properly speaking, have no temperature of their own, but are entirely regulated by that of the atmosphere.—When the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> has been for some time absorbing the heat from terrestrial bodies, a frost must be the undoubted <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a>, for the same reason that water freezes in a vessel put into a freezing mixture; and were this <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABSORPTION">absorption</a> to continue for a length of time, the whole earth would be converted into a frozen <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MASS">mass</a>. There are, however, certain powers in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, by which this effect is always prevented; and the most violent frost we can imagine, must always as it were defeat its own purposes, and end in a thaw. To understand this subject, we must observe, 1. In that state of the atmosphere which we denominate frost, there is a most intimate union between the air and the water it contains; and therefore frosty <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>, except in very <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> latitudes, is generally clear. 2. When such a union takes <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, either in winter or <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>, we observe the atmosphere also inclined to absorb heat, and consequently to frost. Thus in clear settled weather, even in summer, though the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> may be excessively hot by reason of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> sunshine, yet the mornings and evenings are remarkably cold, and sometimes even disagreeably so. 3. The air being therefore always ready in the time of frost or in clear weather, to absorb heat from every substance which comes into contact with it, it follows that it must also absorb part of that which belongs to the vapours contained in it. 4. Though vapour is capable of becoming much colder than water without being frozen, yet by a continued absorption it must at last part with its latent heat, i.e. that which essentially constitutes its vapour, and without which it is no longer vapour, but water or ice. No sooner, therefore, does the frost arrive at a certain pitch, than the vapours, everywhere dispersed through the air, give out their latent heat: the atmosphere then becomes clouded; the frost either totally goes off, or becomes milder by reason of the great quantity of heat discharged into the air; and the vapours descend in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">rain</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIL">hail</a>, or snow, according to the particular disposition of the atmosphere at the time. 5. Even in the polar regions, where it may be thought that the frost must increase beyond <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a>, there are also <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> means for preventing its running to extremes. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> cause here is, the mixture of a great quantity of vapours from the more temperate regions of the globe with the air in those dreary climates. It is well known, that aqueous vapour always flies from a warm to a colder place. For this reason, the vapours raised by the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> in the more temperate regions of the earth, must continually travel northward and southward in great quantities. Thus they furnish materials for those immense quantities of snow and ice which are to be found in the neighbourhood of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLES">poles</a>, and which we cannot imagine the weak influence of the sun in these parts capable of raising. It is impossible that a quantity of vapour can be mixed with frosty air, without communicating a great deal of heat to it; and thus there are often thaws of considerable <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DURATION">duration</a> even in those climates where, from the little influence of the sun, we should suppose the frost would be perpetual. 6. We may now account with some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a> for the uncertain duration of frosts. In this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> they are seldom of a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> continuance; because the vapours raised from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> with which our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> is surrounded, perpetually mix with the air over the island, and prevent a long duration of the frost. For the same reason, frosts are never of such long duration in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARITIME">maritime</a> places on the continent, as in the inland ones. There is nothing, however, more uncertain than the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> of the vapours with which the air is constantly filled; and therefore it is impossible to prognosticate the duration of a frost with any degree of certainty. In general, we may always be certain, that if a quantity of vapour is accumulated in any place, no intense frost can subsist in that place for any length of time; and by whatever causes the vapours are driven from place to place, by the same causes the frosts are regulated throughout the whole world. The effects of frost in different countries are enumerated under the article Congellation. In the northern parts of the world even <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> bodies are liable to be affected by frost. <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIMBER">Timber</a> is often apparently frozen, and rendered exceedingly difficult to <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARL">Marl</a>, chalk, and other less solid terrestrial concretions will be shattered by strong and durable frosts. <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-METALS">Metals</a> are contracted by frost: thus, an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> tube, 12 feet long, upon being exposed to the air in a frosty night, lost two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> of its length. On the contrary, frost swells or dilates water near one-tenth of its bulk. Mr Boyle made several experiments with metallic vessels, exceedingly thick and strong; which being filled with water, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> stopped, and exposed to the cold, burst by the expansion of the frozen fluid within them. Trees are frequently destroyed by frost, as if burnt up by the most excessive heat; and in very strong frosts, walnut trees, ashes, and even oaks, are sometimes split and cleft, so as to be seen through, and this with a terrible noise, like the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPLOSION">explosion</a> of firearms. Frost naturally proceeds from the upper parts of bodies downwards: but how deep it will reach in earth or water, is not easily known; because this depth may vary with the degree of coldness in the air, by a longer or shorter duration of the frost, the texture of the earth, the nature of the juices wherewith it is impregnated, the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> of its more internal parts as to heat and cold, the nature of its effluvia, &c. Mr Boyle, in order to ascertain this depth, after four nights of hard frost, dug in an orchard, where the ground was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> and bare, and found the frost had scarce reached three inches and a half, and in a garden nearer the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> only two inches below the surface. Frost. <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">Nine</a> or ten successive frosty nights froze the bare ground in the garden six inches and a half deep; and in the orchard, where a wall sheltered it from the south sun, to the depth of eight inches and a half. He also dug in an orchard, near a wall, about a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-WEEK">week</a> afterwards, and found the frost to have penetrated to the depth of 14 inches. In a garden at <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOSCOW">Moscow</a>, the frost in a hard season only penetrates to two feet: and the utmost effect that <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPTAIN">Captain</a> James mentions the cold to have had upon the ground of Charlton island, was to freeze it to 10 feet deep: whence may appear the different degrees of cold of that island and Russia. And as to the freezing of water at the above-mentioned island, the Captain tells us it does not naturally congeal above the depth of six feet, the rest being by accident. Water also, exposed to the cold air in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> vessels, always freezes first at the upper surface, the ice gradually increasing and thickening downwards; for which reason, frogs retire in frosty weather to the bottom of ditches; and it is said, that shoals of fish retire in winter to those depths of the sea and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> where they are not to be found in summer. Water, like the earth, seems not disposed to receive any very intense degree of cold at a considerable depth or distance from the air. The vast masses of ice found in the northern seas being only many flakes and fragments, which, sliding under each other, are, by the congelation of the intercepted water, cemented together. In cold countries, the frost often proves fatal to mankind; not only producing gangrenes, but even <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> itself. Those who die of it have their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> and feet first seized, till they grow past feeling it; after which the rest of their bodies is so invaded, that they are taken with a drowsiness, which, if indulged, they awake no more, but die insensibly. But there is another way whereby it proves mortal, viz. by freezing the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABDOMEN">abdomen</a> and viscera, which on dissection are found to be mortified and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a>. The great power of frost on vegetables is a thing sufficiently known; but the differences between the frosts of a severe winter, and those which happen in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> mornings, in their effects on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> and trees, were never perfectly explained, till by Mess. Du Hamel and Buffon in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEMOIRS">Memoirs</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> Academy. The frosts of severe winters are much more terrible than those of the spring, as they bring on a privation of all the products of the tenderer part of the vegetable world; but then they are not frequent, such winters happening perhaps but once in an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>; and the frosts of the spring are in reality greater injuries to us than these, as they are every year repeated. In regard to trees, the great <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> is this, that the frosts of severe winters affect even their wood, their trunks and large branches; whereas those of the spring have only power to hurt the buds. The winter frosts happening at a time when most of the trees in our woods and gardens have neither leaves, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>, nor <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> upon them, and have their buds so hard as to be <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> against slight injuries of weather, especially if the preceding summer has not been too wet; in this state, if there are no unlucky circumstances attending, the generality of trees bear moderate winters very well; but hard frosts, which happen late in the winter, cause very great injuries even to those trees which they do not utterly destroy. These are, 1. Long cracks following the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of the fibres. 2. Parcels of dead wood enclosed round with wood yet in a living state. 3. That distemperature which the foresters call the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> blea, which is a perfect circle of blea, or soft <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> wood, which when the tree is afterwards felled, is found covered by a circle of hard and solid wood. The opinions of authors about the exposition of trees to the different <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a>, have been very different, and most of them grounded on no rational foundation. Many are of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> that the effects of frost are most violently felt on those trees which are exposed to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>; and others think the south or the west the most strongly affected by them. There is no doubt but the north exposure is subject to the greatest cold. It does not, however, follow from this, that the injury must be always greatest on the trees exposed to the north in frosts: on the contrary, there are abundant proofs that it is on the south side that trees are generally more injured by frost: and it is plain from repeated experiments, that there are particular accidents, under which a more moderate frost may do more injury to vegetables, than the most severe one which happens to them under more favourable circumstances. It is plain from the accounts of the injuries trees received by the frosts in 1799, that the greatest of all were owing to repeated false thaws, succeeded by repeated new frosts. But the frosts of the spring season furnish abundantly more numerous examples of this <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>; and some experiments made by the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNT">Count</a> de Buffon at large in his own woods, prove incontestably, that it is not the severest cold or most fixed frost that does the greatest injury to vegetables. This is an observation directly opposite to the common opinion; yet is not the less true, nor is it in any way discordant to reason. We find by a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of experiments, that humidity is the thing that makes frost fatal to vegetables; and therefore every thing that can occasion humidity in them, exposes them to these injuries, and every thing that can prevent or take off an over proportion of humidity in them, every thing that can dry them though with ever so increased a cold, must prevent or preserve them from those injuries. Numerous experiments and observations tend to prove this. It is well known that vegetables always feel the frost very severely in low places where there are fogs. The plants which stand by a river side are frequently found destroyed by the spring and autumnal frosts, while those of the same <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> which stand in a drier place, suffer little or perhaps none at all by them; and the low and wet parts of forests are well known to produce worse wood than the high and drier. The coppice wood in wet and low parts of common woods, though it push out more vigorously at first than that of other places, yet never comes to so good a growth; for the frost of the spring killing these early top shoots, obliges the lower part of the trees to throw out lateral branches; and the same thing happens in a greater or lesser degree to the coppice wood that grows under cover of larger trees in great forests; for here the vapours not being carried off either by the sun or <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>, stagnate and freeze, and in the same manner destroy the young shoots, as the fogs of marshy places. It is a general observation also, that the frost is never hurtful to the late shoots of the vine, or to the flower-buds of trees, except when it follows heavy dews, or a long rainy season, and then it never fails to do great mischief, though it be ever so slight. The frost is always observed to be more mischievous in its consequences on newly cultivated ground than in other places; and this is because the vapours which continually arise from the earth, find an easier passage from those places than from others. Trees also which have been newly cut, suffer more than others by the spring frosts, which is owing to their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SHOOTING">shooting</a> out more vigorously. Frosts also do more damage on light and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SANDY">sandy</a> grounds, than on the tougher and firmer soils, supposing both equally dry; and this seems partly owing to their being more early in their productions, and partly to their lax texture suffering a greater quantity of vapours to transpire. It also has been frequently observed, that the side-shoots of trees are more subject to perish by the spring frosts than those from the top; and M. Buffon, who examined into this with great accuracy, always found the effects of the spring frosts much greater near the ground than elsewhere. The shoots within a foot of the ground quickly perished by them; those which stood at two or three feet high, bore them much better; and those at four feet and upwards frequently remained wholly unhurt; while the lower ones were entirely destroyed. There is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of observations, which have proved beyond all doubt, that it is not the hard frosts which so much hurt plants, as those frosts, though less severe, which happen when they are full of moisture; and this clearly explains the account of all the great damages done by the severe frosts being on the south side of the trees which are affected by them, though that side has been plainly all the while less cold than the north. Great damage is also done to the western sides of trees and plantations, when after a rain with a west wind the wind shifts to the north at sunset, as is frequently the case in spring, or when an east wind blows upon a thick fog before sunrise. Frost, it is well known, is particularly destructive to the blossom of fruit trees. The following method of securing such trees from being damaged by early frosts may be acceptable to many of our readers. A rope is to be interwoven among the branches of the tree, and one end of it brought down so as to be immersed in a bucket of water. The rope, it is said, will <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> as a conductor, and convey the effects of the frost from the tree to the water. This idea is not new, for the following passage may be found in Colerus, "If you dig a trench around the root of a tree, and fill it with water, or keep the roots moist till it has bloomed, it will not be injured by the frost. Or, in spring, suspend a vessel filled with water from the tree. If you wish to preserve the blossom from being hurt by the frost, place a vessel of water below it, and the frost will <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> into it." Hoar Frost, a cold moist vapour, that is drawn up a little way into the air, and in the night falls again on the earth, when it is congealed into icy crystals of various figures. Hoar frost, therefore, is nothing but <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-DEW">dew</a> turned into ice by the coldness of the air. Vol. IX. Part I. Melioration of Aromatic Spirits by Frost. Mr Beaume observes, that aromatic spirituous waters have less scent when newly distilled than after they have been kept about six months; and he found that the good effect of age was produced in a short time by means of cold; and that, by plunging <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUART">quart</a> bottles of the liquor into a mixture of pounded ice and sea salt, the spirit, after having suffered for six or eight hours the cold hence resulting, proves as grateful as that which hath been kept many years. Simple waters also, after having been frozen, prove far more agreeable than they were before. Geoffroy takes notice of this melioration by frost. Hist. Acad. 1713. Melioration of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">Land</a> by Frost. See <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRICULTURE">Agriculture</a> Index. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-FROTH">Froth</a>, a white light substance, formed on the surface of fluids by vehement agitation, consisting of air included in the films of water. <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-FROTH_SPIT">Froth Spit</a>, or Cuckoo Spit, a name given to a white froth, or spume, very common in the spring and first months of summer, on the leaves of certain plants, particularly on those of the common white field lychnis, or catchfly, thence called by some spitting poppy. All writers on vegetables have taken notice of this froth, though few have understood the cause or origin of it till of late. It is formed by a little <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAPING">leaping</a> animal, called by some the fleas grasshopper, by applying its anus close to the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAF">leaf</a>, and discharging thereon a small drop of a white viscous fluid, which, containing some air in it, is soon elevated into a small bubble; before this is well formed, it deposits such another drop; and so on, till it is every way overwhelmed with a quantity of these bubbles, which form the white froth which we see. Within this spume it is seen to acquire four <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TUBERCLES">tubercles</a> on its back, wherein the wings are enclosed: these bursting, from a reptile it becomes a winged animal: and thus, rendered perfect, it flies to meet its mate, and propagate its kind. It has an <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a>, obtuse body, and a large head with small eyes. The <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> wings (for it has four) are of a dusky <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROWN">brown</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, marked with two white spots: the head is black. It is a species of Cicada. Frowde, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a>, an English poet, was the son of a <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> who had been postmaster in the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a>. He was sent to the university of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, where he had the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of being distinguished by Addison, who took him under his protection. While he remained there, he became the author of several pieces of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, some of which in Latin were pure and elegant enough to entitle them to a place in the Muse Anglicana. He likewise wrote two tragedies: The Fall of Saguntum, dedicated to Sir Robert Walpole; and Philotas, addressed to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of Chesterfield. He died at his lodgings at Cecil Street in the Strand, in 1738; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a> Daily <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">Post</a> had the following character given him: "Though the elegance of Mr Frowde's writings has recommended him to the general public esteem, the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLITENESS">politeness</a> of his genius is the least amiable part of his character; for he esteemed the talents of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WIT">wit</a> and learning only as they were conducive to the excitement and practice of honour and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a>. Therefore, with a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUL">soul</a> cheerful, benevolent, and virtuous, he was in conversation genteelly delightful, in friendship punctually sincere, in death Christianly resigned. No <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> could live more beloved, no private man man could die more lamented." A fine eloge! and we have no reason to doubt the truth of it.

FRUCTESCENTIA

Pages 268-268

(from fructus, "fruit,") comprehends the precise <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> in which, after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> arrive at maturity, and disperse their seeds. In general, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> which flower in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIPEN">ripen</a> their fruits in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>, as rye; those which flower in summer have their fruits ripe in autumn, as the vine; the fruit of autumnal flowers ripens in winter, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the following spring, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> kept in a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STOVE">stove</a> or otherwise defended from excessive frosts. These frosts, says M. Adanson, are frequently so pernicious and violent as to destroy the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the perennial plants of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VIRGINIA">Virginia</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MISSISSIPPI">Mississippi</a>, that are cultivated in France, even before they have exhibited their fruit. The plants which flower during our winter, such as those of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a> of Good Hope, ripen their fruit in spring in our stoves.

FRUCTIFICATION OF PLANTS

Pages 268-268

is defined by Linnæus to be the temporary <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of a vegetable appropriated to <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENERATION">generation</a>, terminating the old vegetable and beginning the new. It consists of the following <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> parts; viz. the calyx, corolla, stamen, pistillum, pericarpium, semen <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> seed, and receptaculum. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a>.

FRUIT

Pages 268-268

in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a>, is properly that <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of a plant wherein the seed is contained; called by the Latins fructus; and by the Greeks μήκος. The fruit in the Linnean system is one of the parts of fructification, and is distinguished into three parts, viz. the pericarpium, seed, and receptacle, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> receptaculum seminum. See BOTANY. Colours extracted from <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRUITS">FRUITS</a>. See the article <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">COLOUR</a>-Making. <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">Bread</a>-FRUIT. See ARTOCARPUS, BOTANY <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

FRUIT-FLIES

Pages 268-269

a name given by gardeners and others to a sort of small <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> flies found in vast numbers among fruit trees, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> season, and supposed to do <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> injury to them. Mr Leeuwenhoeck preserved some of these flies for his microscopical observations. He found that they did not live longer than a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> two, but that the females during this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> laid a great <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of longish eggs. The gardeners, who suppose that these flies wound the leaves of the trees, are mistaken: it is true that they feed on their juices; but they have no instruments wherewith they can extract these for themselves: they feed on such as are naturally extravasated; and when there is not a sufficient <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of these for their purpose, they haunt the places to which the pucerons <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESORT">resort</a>, and feed on the juices which these little creatures extravasate by means of the holes they bore in the leaves with their trunks. FRUIT-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONES">Stones</a>. The mischiefs arising from the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> which many people have of swallowing the stones of plums and other fruit are very great. The Philosophical Transactions give an account of a woman who suffered violent pains in her bowels for 30 years, returning once in a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">month</a> or less. At length a strong purge being given her, the occasion of all these complaints was driven <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> from the bowels to the anus; where it gave a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSATION">sensation</a> of distension and stoppage, producing a continual desire of going to stool, but without voiding any thing. On the assistance of a careful <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>, there was taken out with a forceps a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALL">ball</a> of an oval <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, of about ten drachms in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>, and measuring five inches in circumference. This had caused all the violent fits of pain which she had suffered for so many years; and, after voiding it, she became perfectly well. The ball extracted looked like a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, and felt very hard, but it swam in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>. On <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> it through with a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KNIFE">knife</a>, there was found in the centre of it a plum stone; round which several coats of this hard and tough <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> had gathered. Another instance given in the same papers is of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, who, dying of an incurable colic, which had tormented him many years, and baffled the effects of medicines, was opened after <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>; and in his bowels was found a ball similar to that above mentioned; but somewhat larger, being six inches in circumference, and weighing an ounce and a half. In the centre of this, as of the other, there was found the stone of a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> plum, and the coats were of the same <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> with those of the former. These and several other instances mentioned in the same <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, sufficiently show the folly of that common <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> that the stones of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> are wholesome. For though by nature the guts are so defended by their proper mucus, that people very seldom suffer by things of this kind; yet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> we consider the various circumvolutions of the guts, their valves and cells, and at the same time consider the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> of the skins of animals we feed on, the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a> or down on herbs and fruit, and the fibres, vessels, and nerves of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, which are not altered by the stomach; it <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> appear a wonder that instances of this sort of mischief are not much more common. Cherry stones, swallowed in great quantities, have occasioned the death of many people; and there have been instances even of the seeds of strawberries collecting into a lump in the guts, and causing violent disorders, which could not be cured without great difficulty. FRUIT Trees. With regard to these it may be observed, 1. That the cutting and pruning them when young hurt their <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a>, though it contributes to the richness and flavour of the fruit, as well as to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> of the tree. 2. That kernel fruit trees come later to bear than stone fruit trees: the time required by the first, before they come to any fit <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> for bearing, being one with another five years; but when they do begin, they bear in greater plenty than stone fruit. 3. That stone fruit, figs, and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAPES">grapes</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> bear considerably in three or four years, and bear full crops the fifth and sixth year; and hold it for many years, if well ordered. 4. That fruit trees in the same neighbourhood will <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIPEN">ripen</a> a fortnight sooner in some grounds than in others of a different temperature. 5. That in the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, hot or <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLD">cold</a> summers set considerably forwards, or put backwards, the same fruit. 6. That the fruit on wall trees generally ripen before those on standards, and those on standards before those on dwarfs. 7. That the fruit of all wall trees planted in the south and east <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> commonly ripen about the same time, only those in the south rather earlier than those in the east; those in the west are later by eight or ten days; and those in the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by 15 or 20. For the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTING">planting</a>, pruning, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAFTING">grafting</a>, &c. of fruit trees, see <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GARDENING">Gardening</a>.

FRUITERY

Pages 269-269

a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> for the keeping of fruit, a fruit <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> fruit loft. A fruitery should be inaccessible to any thing of moisture; and should be as much as possible so, even to <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FROST">frost</a>.

FRUITS

Pages 268-268

with regard to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, are distinguished into recent, fresh, and dry. Recent FRUITS are those sold <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> as they are gathered from the tree, without any farther <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PREPARATION">preparation</a>; as are most of the productions of our gardens and orchards, sold by the fruiterers. Dry FRUITS are those dried in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> by the fire, with other ingredients sometimes added to them to make them keep; imported chiefly from beyond <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, and sold by the grocers. Such are raisins, currants, figs, capers, olives, cloves, nutmegs, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEPPER">pepper</a>, and other spices; which see under their respective <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a>. Under the denomination of dry fruits are also frequently included apples, pears, almonds, filberts, &c.

FRUMENTACEOUS

Pages 269-269

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> applied by botanists to all such <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> as have a conformity with wheat, in respect of their <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>, leaves, ears, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the like.

FRUMENTARI

Pages 269-269

a kind of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> archers under the western empire. The first <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> we read of these officers is in the reign of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Adrian, who made <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of them to inform himself of whatever passed. They did not make any particular corps distinct from the rest of the forces, but there was a certain <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of them in each legion. It is supposed, that they were at first a number of young persons, disposed by Augustus throughout the provinces, particularly on all the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROADS">roads</a>, to acquaint the emperor, with all expedition, of every thing that happened. Afterwards they were incorporated into the troops themselves, where they still retained their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> name. As their <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> office was the giving intelligence, they were often joined with the curiosi, with whom they agreed in that <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of their office. Their name of frumentarii is derived from their being also a sort of purveyors to the armies, cities, &c., collecting all the corn from the several provinces to furnish the commonwealth.

FRUMENTATION

Pages 269-269

in Roman antiquity, a largess of corn bestowed on the people. This practice of giving corn to the people was very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> among the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, and frequently used to soothe the turbulent humour of the populace. At first the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of those to whom this largess was given was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDETERMINATE">indeterminate</a>, till Augustus fixed it at 200,000.

FRUSTUM

Pages 269-269

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">Mathematics</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of some <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> body separated from the rest. The frustum of a cone is the part that remains, when the top is cut off by a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANE">plane</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> to the base; and is otherwise called a truncated cone. See <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONIC_SECTIONS">Conic Sections</a>. The frustum of a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PYRAMID">pyramid</a> is also what remains after the top is cut off by a plane parallel to its base. The frustum of a globe <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> sphere is any part thereof cut off by a plane, the solid contents of which may be found by this rule: To three times the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> of the semidiameter of the base add the square of its height; then multiply that sum by the height, and this product multiplied by .5236 gives the solidity of the frustum.

FRUTEX

Pages 269-269

a SHRUB. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHRUBS">Shrubs</a>, according to Linnaeus, make a branch of the seventh family in the vegetable <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>; and are distinguished from trees, in that they come up without buds. But this distinction is not universal, though it be generally <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> with regard to those of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">Nature</a> hath made no <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> distinction between trees and shrubs. Frutex, in its general acceptation, is a plant whose <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUNK">trunk</a> is perennial, gemmiparous, woody, dividing and subdividing into a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of branches. In short, it is the epitome of a tree, exemplified in the rose bush.

FRYING-PAN

Pages 269-269

a dangerous shoal, which has received this appellation from its <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>. It is situated at the entrance of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a> Fear river, in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> Carolina, the southern <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of which is in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a>. 75° W. and 33° 22' N. Lat. 24 miles south-east by south of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> on Bald Head.

FRYTH

Pages 269-269

JOHN, a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARTYR">martyr</a> to the Protestant <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> in the reign of Henry VIII. He was the son of an innkeeper at <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">Seven</a> Oaks in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KENT">Kent</a>; and educated in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLLEGE">College</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>, where he took the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of bachelor of arts. Thence he removed to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, and was made a junior canon of Wolsey's college. He had not been <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> in that university before he became acquainted with William Tyndale, a zealous Lutheran, with whom he conversed frequently on the abuses in religion. Fryth became a convert to Lutheranism, and publicly avowed his opinions. He was apprehended, examined by the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMISSARY">commissary</a>, and confined to his college. At length having obtained his <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>, in 1528 he went over to Germany, where he <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> about two years; and then returned to England, more than ever determined in his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> sentiments. Finding at that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> but few associates, he wandered about from <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> to place, till at last he was taken up at <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">Reading</a> as a vagrant, and set in the stocks, where he remained till he was near expiring for want of sustenance. He was at length relieved by the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a> of Leonard Cox, a schoolmaster; who finding him a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of letters, procured his enlargement, and administered to his necessities. Fryth now set out for <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, where with more zeal than <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRUDENCE">prudence</a>, he began to make proselytes; but was soon apprehended by order of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a> Sir Thomas More, and sent prisoner to the Tower. Refusing to recant his opinions, he was condemned to the flames, and accordingly burnt in Smithfield, on the 4th of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> 1533. He left several works behind him, which were printed in folio in 1573.

FUAGE

Pages 269-269

in old English writers, a tax of 12d. for every fire, levied in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of Edward III.

FUCINUS LACUS

Pages 269-270

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a lake of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>. Italy in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of the Marsi. Now Lago di Celano, from a cognominal citadel, lying on the south of the Abruzzo Ultra, in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>, near the Apennines. This lake was under the protection of a god of the same denomination, whose temple stood on its banks. According to the testimony of ancient authors, it was subject to extraordinary risings and decreasings. The actual circumference is 47 miles; the breadth in the widest <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> is 10, in the narrowest 4; its depth 12 feet upon an <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AVERAGE">average</a>. But all these have varied prodigiously. Two miles up the plain, behind <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-AVEZZANO">Avezzano</a>, the fragments of boats, shells, and other marks of its ancient <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>, have been casually discovered; and, on the contrary, there are people who remember when it did not flow nearer than within two miles of Avezzano. An immense tract of excellent lands is lost at every increase of its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a>. All round this noble piece of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> rises a circle of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, some of them the highest in Italy, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> we except the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALPS">Alps</a>, and many of them covered with snow; and at the foot of them are numerous villages, with rich and well cultivated farms. The environs of the lake, Mr Swinburne describes as all well enclosed, and the sides of the hills as covered with fine woods; its waters abound with fish of various kinds, and thither repair at stated seasons innumerable flights of wild fowl. As the swelling of the lake was attended with incredible damage, the Marsi had often petitioned the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENATE">senate</a> to drain it: Julius Caesar would have attempted it, had he lived longer. His successors were averse to the project; till Claudius, who delighted in expensive difficult enterprises, undertook it. During the space of 11 years he employed 30,000 men in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGGING">digging</a> a passage through the mountain; and when every thing was ready for letting off the water, exhibited a superb naval spectacle on the lake. A <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of condemned criminals were obliged to <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> the parts of Rhodians and Sicilians in separate fleets, to engage in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARNEST">earnest</a>, and to destroy one another for the entertainment of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> and the multitude of spectators that covered the hills: A line of well armed vessels and rafts loaded with <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> surrounded the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCENE">scene</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTION">action</a>, in order to prevent any of the wretches from escaping; but it was with great difficulty and many threats that they could be brought to an engagement. When this <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAVAGE">savage</a> diversion was ended, the operations for opening the passage commenced, and the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> was very near being swept away and drowned by the sudden rushing of the waters towards it. However, either through the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> negligence of the engineers, the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> did not answer as was expected, and Claudius did not live <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> enough to have the faults amended: Nero abandoned the scheme through envy. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HADRIAN">Hadrian</a> is said to have let off the water of the Fucinus; but none now escapes except through hidden channels formed by <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, which are probably subject to be obstructed, and thus occasion a superabundance of water in the lake, till some unknown cause removes the obstructions and again gives free passage. Sir William <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAMILTON">Hamilton</a>, who visited the Fucinus in 1785, says, "it is the most beautiful lake he ever <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a>, and would be complete if the neighbouring mountains were better wooded." It furnishes abundance of fish, though not of the best <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>. There are a few <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TROUT">trout</a>, but mostly tench, barbel, and dace. In the shallow water on the borders of the lake, he saw thousands of water snakes pursuing and preying upon a little kind of fish like our thornbacks, but much better armed; though their defensive weapons seemed to avail them but little against such ravenous foes. The opening made by Claudius he describes as still entire, though in many parts filled with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> and rubbish. He went into it with torches as far as he could. It is a covered underground canal three miles long, and part of it cut through a hard rock, and other parts supported by mason work, with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WELLS">wells</a> to give <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>. Hadrian is said to have let off the waters of the lake: and our author is of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, that if the canal were cleared and repaired it would still answer that purpose, and thereby restore a great <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of rich <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> fit for cultivation.

FUCUS

Pages 270-270

a name given by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> to certain dyes and paints. By this name they called a purple <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> plant used by them to dye woollen and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> things of that <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>. The dye was very beautiful, but not lasting; for it soon began to change, and in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> went wholly off. This is the account <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEOPHRASTUS">Theophrastus</a> gives of it. The women of those times also used something called fucus, to stain their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHEEKS">cheeks</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a>; and many have supposed, from the same word expressing both, that the same substance was used on both occasions. But this, on a strict inquiry, proves not to be the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>. The Greeks called every thing fucus that would stain <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> paint the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a>. But this peculiar substance used by the women to paint their cheeks was distinguished from the others by the name of rizion among the more correct writers, and was indeed a root brought from <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a> into <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>. The Latins, in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a> of the Greek name, called this root radicula; and Pliny very erroneously confounds the plant with the radix lunaria, or struthion of the Greeks. The word fucus was in those times become such an universal name for paint, that the Greeks and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> had a fucus metallicus, which was the ceruse used for <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a> the neck and arms <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a>; after which they used the purpurissum, or red fucus of the rizium, to give the colour to the cheeks. In after-times they also used a peculiar fucus or paint for the purpose, prepared of the creta argentaria, or silver-chalk, and some of the rich purple dyes that were in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> at that time: and this seems to have been very little different from our rose-pink; a colour <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> sold at the colour shops, and used on like occasions. Fucus, in the Linnæan system of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">botany</a>, is a genus of the order of algae, belonging to the cryptogamia class of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>.

FUEGO

Pages 270-270
or Fogo, one of the Cape de Verd islands, in the Atlantic ocean. It is much higher than any of the rest; and seems at sea to be one single mountain, though on the sides there are deep valleys. There is a volcano at the top which burns continually, and may be seen a great way off at sea. It vomits a great deal of fire and smoke, and throws out huge pieces of rock to a vast height; and sometimes torrents of melted matter run down the sides. The Portuguese, who first inhabited it, brought negro slaves with them, and a stock of cows, horses, and hogs; but the chief inhabitants now are blacks of the Romish religion. W. Long. 24° 29', Lat. 15°.

FUEN-HOA

Pages 271-271

a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHINA">China</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Petcheli, celebrated for its <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> and the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of its inhabitants, as well as for the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> of its streets and triumphal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARCHES">arches</a>. It is situated near the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> wall, amidst <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>; and has under its jurisdiction, besides two cities of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a>, and eight of the third class, a great number of fortresses, which <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAR">bar</a> the entrance of China against the Tartars.

FUGALIA

Pages 271-271

in Roman antiquity, a feast supposed by some to be the same with the refugium, held on the 24th of February, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of the expulsion of the kings and the abolishing of monarchical <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>. Others again distinguish the fugalia from the refugium. And others think that the fugalia was the same with the poplifugia, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the feast of Fugia, the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GODDESS">goddess</a> of joy, occasioned by the rout of an enemy, which was the reason the people abandoned themselves to riot and debauchery.

FUGITIVE

Pages 271-271

a person obliged to fly his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> remove from a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where he had some abode or establishment, on account of his crimes, debts, or other occasions. FUGITIVE Pieces, among the learned, denote those little compositions which are printed on loose sheets or half sheets; thus called, because easily lost and soon forgotten.

FUGUE

Pages 271-272

in Music, (from the Latin fuga, "a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHASE">chase</a>"), a piece of music sometimes longer and sometimes shorter, in which, agreeable to the rules of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HARMONY">harmony</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODULATION">modulation</a>, the composer treats a subject; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a>, in other words, what expresses the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> thought or sentiment of the piece, in causing it to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> successively and alternately from one <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> to another. These are the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> rules of the fugue; of which some are peculiar to itself, and others <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> to it with what the French call <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a>. 1. The subject proceeds from the tonic to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOMINANT">dominant</a>, or from the dominant to the tonic, in rising or descending. 2. Every fugue finds its response in the part immediately following that which commenced. 3. That response ought to resume the subject in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTERVAL">interval</a> of a fourth or fifth above or below the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KEY">key</a>, and to pursue it as exactly as the laws of harmony <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> admit; proceeding from the dominant to the tonic when the subject is introduced from the tonic to the dominant, and moving in a contrary <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> when the subject is introduced from the dominant to the tonic. One part may likewise resume the same subject in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OCTAVE">octave</a> or unison of the preceding; but in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>, it is a repetition rather than a real response. 4. As the octave is divided into two unequal parts, of which the one contains four gradations descending from the tonic to the dominant, and the other only three in continuing the ascent from the dominant to the tonic; this renders it necessary to have some regard to this change in the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a> of the subject, and to make some alterations in the response, that we may not quit the cords that are essential to the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODE">mode</a>. It is a different case when the composer intends to alter the modulation; for there the exactness of the response itself, when taken in a different tone, produces the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALTERATION">alteration</a> proper for this change. 5. It is necessary that the fugue should be planned in such a manner, that the response may commence before the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> of the first <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a>, so that both the one and the other may be in part heard at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>: that, by this anticipation, the subject may be as it were connected with itself, and that the art of the composer may discover itself in this concourse. It is <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> mockery, instead of a fugue, to impose upon the hearers the same air, merely transposed from one key to another, without any other restraint than an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACCOMPANIMENT">accompaniment</a> afterwards formed at <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>. This deserves at best no better name than what the French call imitation. See Imitation. Besides these rules, which are <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FUNDAMENTAL">fundamental</a>, there are others which, though prescribed by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> alone, are not less essential. Fugues, in general, render music more noisy than agreeable; it is for this reason that they are more agreeable in the chorus than anywhere else. Now, as their <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> merit consists in fixing the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-EAR">ear</a> on the principal air or subject, which for this reason is made to pass incessantly from part to part, and from mode to mode, the composer ought to exert his care in preserving that air always distinct; or to prevent it from being absorbed in, or confounded with, the other parts. To produce this effect, there are two different ways; one in the movement, which must be incessantly contrasted with itself; so that, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the procedure of the fugue be accelerated, the other parts move gravely and with protracted notes; or, on the contrary, if the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> of the fugue be slow and solemn, the accompaniments must have more and quicker business. The other method is to extend the harmony, by removing the parts at a greater distance one from the other; lest the others, too nearly approximated to that which contains the subject, should be confounded with it, and prevent it from being distinguished with sufficient clearness; so that what would be an imperfection anywhere else, becomes here a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>. The unity of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MELODY">melody</a> should be preserved: this is the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> and general rule, which must frequently be practised by different means. The cords must be chosen, and the intervals, so that one particular <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> may produce the same effect; this can only result from the unity of the melody. It will sometimes be necessary to employ voices and instruments of different kinds, that the parts which ought to prevail may be most easily distinguished; this again shows the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of preserving the unity of the melody. Another object of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>, no less necessary, is, in the different connections of modulation which are introduced by the procedure and progress of the fugues, to cause all these modulations to correspond at the same time in all the parts, to connect the whole in its progress by an exact conformity of modes: lest, if one part be in one mode, and another in another, the general harmony should be in none at all, and for that reason should no longer be able to produce simple effects upon the ear, nor simple <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> in the mind; which is another reason for preserving unity of melody. In a word, in every fugue the confusion of melodies and modulations is at once what a composer has most to fear, and will find the greatest difficulty in avoiding; and as this kind of music never produces a pleasure above mediocrity, one may say that a fine fugue is, though the masterpiece of an excellent harmonist, ungrateful to his toil. There are still several other kinds of fugues; such as the perpetual fugue*, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> fugue, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INVERTED">inverted</a> fugue. The inverted fugue is a manner of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a>, in which the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLYING">flying</a> part proceeds in a contrary direction to the other fugue, which had been formerly fixed in the same piece of music. Thus, when the first fugitive part is heard in ascending from the tonic to the dominant, or from the dominant to the tonic, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTER">counter</a> fugue ought to be heard in descending from the dominant to the tonic, or from the tonic to the dominant, and vice versa. Its other rules are exactly like those of the common fugue.

FULCRUM

Pages 272-272

in <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MECHANICS">Mechanics</a>, the prop <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> support by which a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEVER">lever</a> is sustained.

FULDA

Pages 272-272

a considerable town of Germany, in the circle of the Upper <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHINE">Rhine</a>, and in the Buchow, with a celebrated <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">abbey</a>; whose <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABBOT">abbot</a> was <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIMATE">primate</a> of the abbeys of the empire, perpetual <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a>, and sovereign of this small territory, which is now chiefly included in the dominions of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HESSE">Hesse</a> Cassel. It is seated on the river Fulda, 55 miles south of Cassel. F. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 9. 33. N. Lat. 50. 32.

FULGORA

Pages 272-272

a genus of insects belonging to the order of hemiptera. See ENTOMOLOGY <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

FULHAM

Pages 272-272

a village of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MIDDLESEX">Middlesex</a>, four miles from <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, with 5903 inhabitants in 1811. The Danes in 869 wintered at this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> till they retired to the continent. It was in the Conqueror's <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> held of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> by the canons of St Paul's; and there is an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> here, which is moated about, and belongs to the see of London, whose bishop has a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> here, and the demesne has belonged to that <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a> from 1067. From this place to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PUTNEY">Putney</a> there is a wooden <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> over the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THAMES">Thames</a>, where not only horses, coaches, and all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARRIAGES">carriages</a>, but even foot passengers, pay toll. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> here is both a rectory and a vicarage.

FULICA

Pages 272-272

the Gallinule and Coot, a genus of birds belonging to the order of grallae. See <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">ORNITHOLOGY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

FULIGINOUS

Pages 272-272

whatever proceeds from a thick <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOOTY">sooty</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SMOKE">smoke</a>, such as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAMP">lamp</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a>.

FULIGNO

Pages 272-272

a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, in the pope's territories, 10 miles <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of Spoleto.

FULLER

Pages 272-277

a workman employed in the woollen manufactories to mill <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> scour cloths, serges, and other stuffs, in order to render them more thick, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPACT">compact</a>, and durable. See FULLING. Fuller's <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">Earth</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of clay, of a grayish ash-coloured <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROWN">brown</a>, in all degrees from very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a> to almost <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a>, and it has generally something of a greenish <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a>. It is very hard and firm, of a compact texture, of a tough and somewhat dusty surface that adheres slightly to the tongue. It is very soft to the touch, not staining the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, nor breaking easily between the fingers. It has a little harshness between the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a>, and melts freely in the mouth. Thrown into <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, it makes no ebullition or hissing; but swells gradually in bulk, and falls into a fine soft powder. It makes no effervescence with aquafortis. The greatest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> and the finest earth of this kind in the world, is dug in the pits at Wavendon, near <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WOBURN">Woburn</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEDFORDSHIRE">Bedfordshire</a>. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STRATA">strata</a> in these pits <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> thus: From the surface to the depth of six feet, there are several layers or beds of sand, all reddish, but some <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIGHTER">lighter</a> coloured than others. Under these there is a thin stratum of a <a class="xref" href="../1823/vol0.html#article-SAND_STONE">sand-<a cl</a>ass="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, which they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> through, and then there is the fuller's earth. The upper stratum of this is about a foot thick: the workmen call it cledge, and throw it aside as useless; being <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> fouled with the sand which originally covered it, and which insinuates itself a good way into it. After this, they come to the fine fuller's earth for <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALE">sale</a>, which lies to the depth of eight feet more.
