The <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> of this is divided into several layers, there being commonly about a foot and a half between one <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HORIZONTAL">horizontal</a> fissure and another. Of these several layers, the upper half, where the earth breaks itself, is tinged <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a>; which seems to be owing to the running of the water upon it from among the sands above; some of which are probably of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FERRUGINOUS">ferruginous</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, or have ferruginous matter among them. This reddish fuller's earth the workmen call crop; and between the cledge and this there is a thin stratum of matter, of less than an inch, which in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> appearance, resembles the terra Japonica of the shops. The lower half of the strata of fuller's earth they call wall-earth. This is untigned with the red colour of the other, and seems the most proper for fulling. Under the fuller's earth there is a stratum of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> and coarse stone about two feet thick. They seldom dig through this; but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they do, they find more strata of sand. This earth is of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> in scouring cloths, stuffs, &c. imbibing all the grease and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a> used in preparing, dressing, The fulling of cloths and other stuffs is performed by a kind of water-mill, thence called a fulling or scouring mill. These <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MILLS">mills</a>, excepting in what relates to the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MILLSTONES">millstones</a> and hopper, are much the same with corn-mills; and there are even some which serve indifferently for either use: corn being ground, and cloths fulled, by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> of the same wheel. Whence, in some places, particularly in France, the fullers are called millers; as <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRINDING">grinding</a> corn and milling stuffs at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> parts of the fulling-mill are, The wheel, with its <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUNDLE">trundle</a>; which gives motion to the tree or spindle, whose teeth communicate it to the pestles or stampers, which are hereby raised and made to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> alternately, according as its teeth catch on or quit a kind of latch in the middle of each pestle. The pestles and troughs are of wood; each trough having at least two, sometimes three pestles, at the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-DISCRETION">discretion</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>, or according to the force of the stream of water. In those troughs are laid the cloths, stuffs, &c., intended to be fulled: then, letting the current of water fall on the wheel, the pestles are successively let fall thereon, and by their <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> and velocity stamp and press the stuffs very strongly, which by this means become thickened and condensed. In the course of the operation, they sometimes make use of urine, sometimes of fuller's earth, and sometimes of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOAP">soap</a>. To prepare the stuffs to receive the first impressions of the pestle, they are usually laid in urine; then in fuller's earth and water; and, lastly, in soap dissolved in hot water. Soap alone would do very well; but this is expensive: though fuller's earth, in the way of our dressing, is scarce inferior thereto; but then it must be well cleared of all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONES">stones</a> and grittinesses, which are apt to make holes in the stuff. As to urine, it is certainly prejudicial, and ought to be entirely discarded; not so much on account of its ill smell, as of its sharpness and saltiness, which qualities are apt to render the stuffs dry and harsh. The true method of fulling with soap is delivered by Mons. Colinet, in an authentic memoir on that subject, supported by experiments made by order of the marquis de Louvois, then superintendant of the arts and manufactories of France; the substance of which we shall here subjoin. Method of Fulling Cloths and Woollen Stuff with Soap.—A coloured cloth, of about 45 ells, is to be laid in the usual manner in the trough of a fulling-mill; without first soaking it in water, as is commonly practised in many places. To full this trough of cloth, 15 pounds of soap are required; one-half of which is to be melted in two pails of river or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> water, made as hot as the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> can well bear it. This solution is to be poured by little and little upon the cloth, in proportion as it is laid in the trough: and thus it is to be fulled for at least two hours; after which it is to be taken out and stretched. This done, the cloth is immediately returned into the same trough, without any new soap, and there fulled two hours more. Then taking it out, they wring it well, to express all the grease and filth. After the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> fulling, the remainder of the soap is dissolved as in the former, and cast four different times on the cloth; remembering to take out the cloth every two hours, to stretch it, and undo the plaits and wrinkles it has acquired in the trough. When they perceive it sufficiently fulled, and brought to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> and thickness required, they scour it for good in hot water, keeping it in the trough till it be quite clean. As to white cloths; in regard these full more easy and in less time than coloured ones, a third <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the soap may be spared. **Fulling of Stockings, Caps, &c.** should be performed somewhat differently; viz. either with the feet or the hands; or a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACK">rack</a>, or wooden machine, either armed with teeth of the same matter, or else horses or bullocks teeth. The ingredients made use of herein are, urine, green soap, white soap, and fuller's earth. But the urine also is reckoned prejudicial here. Woven stockings, &c. should be fulled with soap alone: for those that are knit, earth may be used with the soap. Indeed it is frequent to full these kinds of works with the mill, after the usual manner of cloth, &c. But that is too coarse and violent a manner, and apt to damage the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> unless it be very strong. **FULMAR,** in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">Ornithology</a>. See Procellaria, Ornithology <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. **Fulmar,** or **Foumart.** See Mustela, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAMMALIA">Mammalia</a> Index. **Fulminating,** something that thunders or resembles <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THUNDER">thunder</a>. **Fulminating <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">Gold</a>, Silver, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">Copper</a>, Quicksilver, &c.** See <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a> Index. **<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-FULMINATION">Fulmination</a>,** in Chemistry, the same with detonation. **Fulmination,** in the Romish canon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a>, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a> of a bishop, official, or other ecclesiastic appointed by the pope, by which it is decreed that some bull sent from the pope shall be executed. **Fumaria,** Fumitory, a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the diadelphia class, and in the natural method ranking under the 24th order, Corydales. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> Index. **<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-FUMIGATION">Fumigation</a>,** in Chemistry, a kind of calcination, when <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-METALS">metals</a> or other hard bodies are corroded or softened by receiving certain fumes for that purpose. **Fumigation,** in Medicine. By the subtle fumes that are inspired as well as inhaled into our bodies, much benefit or <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PREJUDICE">prejudice</a> is produced, according to the nature of the matter, and the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> into which it is received; as is evident from the palsies produced among workers in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a>, &c., and the benefits received in many <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> when the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> is impregnated with salutary materials. Catarrhs and catarrhous coughs are relieved by fumes received with the breath; and, by the same method, expectoration is assisted in humoral asthmas; and even ulcers in the lungs are said to have been healed by this method. The advantage of mercurial fumigations in the cure of venereal ulcers is known to every practitioner. **Fumitory.** See Fumaria, Botany Index. **Funambulus,** among the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, was what we call a rope-dancer, and the Greeks schenobates. See Rope-Dancer. There was a funambulus, it seems, who performed at the time when the Hecyra of Terence was acted; and the poet complains, that the spectacle prevented the people from attending to his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMEDY">comedy</a>. *Ita populus studio stupidus in funambulo, animum occuparat.* At Rome, the funambuli first appeared under the consulate of Sulpicius Paetius and Licinius Stolo, who were the first introducers of the scenic representations. It is added, that they were first exhibited in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of the Tyber, and that the censors Messala and Cassius afterwards promoted them to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a>. In the Floralia, or ludi Florales, held under Galba, there were funambulatory elephants, as we are informed by Suetonius. Nero also showed the like, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of his mother <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRIPPINA">Agrippina</a>. Vopiscus relates the same of the time of Carinus and Numerianus. **<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-FUNCHAL">Funchal</a>,** the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MADEIRA">Madeira</a>, situated round a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a>, on a gentle ascent, and containing about 15,000 inhabitants. It is watered by several streams from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>; and is defended by a castle on a steep rock, which is surrounded by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> water. The houses are built of brick or free-stone; but the streets are narrow, dark, and dirty. W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 16. 49. N. Lat. 32. 38. **<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-FUNCTION">Function</a>,** the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> of fulfilling the duties of any employment. **Function,** being also applied to the actions of the body, is by physicians divided into vital, animal, and natural. The vital functions are those necessary to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, and without which the individual cannot subsist; as the motion of the heart, lungs, &c. The natural functions are such as it cannot subsist any considerable time without; as the digestion of the aliment, and its conversion into blood. Under animal functions are included the senses of touching, tasting, &c., <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a>, judgment, and voluntary motion; without any or all of which an animal may live, but not very comfortably. The animal functions perform the motion of the body by the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTION">action</a> of the muscles; and this action consists chiefly in the shortening the fleshy fibres, which is called <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRACTION">contraction</a>, the principal agents of which are the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTERIES">arteries</a> and nerves distributed in the fleshy fibres. All parts of the body have their own functions, or actions, peculiar to themselves. Life consists in the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> of these functions, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> in the free and ready exercise of them. **Function,** a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> used in analytics for an algebraical <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a> any how compounded of a certain <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> or quantity with other quantities or numbers; and the expression is said to be a function of that letter or quantity. Thus $a - 4x$, or $ax + 3x^2$, or $2x - a\sqrt{a^2 - x^2}$, or $a^2$, or $e^x$, is each of them a function of the quantity $x$. **<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-FUND">Fund</a>,** in general, signifies any sum of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a> appropriated for a particular purpose. Thus, that part of the national revenue which is set apart for the payment of the national debt, is called the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SINKING_FUND">sinking fund</a>. But, when we speak of the funds, we generally <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> sums which have been <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LENT">lent</a> to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, and constitute the national debt; and for which the lenders, or their assignees, receive <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> from revenues allotted for that purpose. The term stock is used in the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, and is also applied to the sums which form the capital of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANK">bank</a> of England, the East <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a> and South Sea companies; the proprietors of which are entitled to a share of the profits of the respective companies. The practice of funding was introduced by the Venetians and Genoese in the 16th century, and has been adopted since by most of the nations in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. Princes had often borrowed money, in former times, to supply their exigencies, and sometimes mortgaged their territories in security; but these loans were generally extorted, and their payment was always precarious; for it depended on the good <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a> and success of the borrower, and never became a regular burden on posterity. The origin of funds is derived from the peculiar manners and circumstances of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> Europe. Since the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUNPOWDER">gunpowder</a>, and the progress of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> occupation has become a distinct employment in the hands of mercenaries; the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPARATUS">apparatus</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> is attended with more expense; and the decision of national quarrels has often been determined by command of money rather than by national bravery. Ambitious princes have therefore borrowed money, in order to carry on their projects with more vigour. Weaker states have been compelled, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SELF_DEFENCE">self-<a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a>, to apply to the same resource; the wealth introduced by commerce has afforded the means; the regularity of administration, established in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of the progress of civility, has increased the confidence of individuals in the public security; the complicated system of modern policy has extended the scenes of war, and prolonged their <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DURATION">duration</a>; and the colonies established by mercantile nations have rendered them vulnerable in more <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">points</a>, and increased the expense of defending them. When a greater sum has been required for the annual expense than could easily be supplied by annual taxes, the government have proposed terms to their own subjects, or foreigners, for obtaining an advance of money by mortgaging the revenue of future years for their indemnification. This mortgage may either be for a limited <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>, or perpetual. If the sum allotted annually for the benefit of those who advance the money, be considerably greater than the interests of the sums advanced, they may agree to accept of such allowance, for a limited time, as a full <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EQUIVALENT">equivalent</a>. Thus, they may either agree for the casual produce of the revenue assigned; or a fixed annuity for a greater or less <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of years; or a life annuity to themselves or nominees; or an annuity for two or more lives; or an annuity, with the benefit of survivorship, called a tontine, in which scheme, the whole sum to which the original annuitants were entitled continues to be distributed among the survivors. The establishment of the funds was introduced in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a> at the Revolution; and has since been gradually enlarged, and carried to an amazing <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>. The various methods above mentioned have been used in their turns, but perpetual <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANNUITIES">annuities</a> have been granted for the greatest part; and, even when the money was originally advanced on other conditions, the lenders have been sometimes induced, by subsequent offers, to accept of perpetual annuities, instead of the former terms. The debt for which perpetual annuities are granted, is called the redeemable debt, and the other is called the irredeemable debt. Although the debts thus contracted by government are seldom paid for a long term of years; yet any creditor of the public may obtain money for what is due him when he pleases, by transferring his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> in the funds to another; and regular methods are appointed for transacting these transfers in an easy manner. By means of this, the stocks become a kind of circulating capital; and have the same effect, in some respects, as the circulating money in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>. When a stockholder transfers his share, he may sometimes be able to obtain a greater price than the original value, and at other times be obliged to accept of a less one. The value of the funds depends on the proportion between the interest they bear, and the benefit which may be obtained by applying the money to other purposes. It is influenced by the plenty or scarcity of money, and by the quantity of the public debt; and it is impaired by any event which threatens the safety, or weakens the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a>, of the government. The business of stock-jobbing is founded on the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-VARIATION">variation</a> of the prices of stock. Persons possessed of real property may buy or sell stock, according to their notion that the value is likely to rise or fall, in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPECTATION">expectation</a> of making profit by the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> of price. And a practice has taken <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> among persons who often possess no property in the funds, to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRACT">contract</a> for the sale of stock, against a future <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>, at a price now agreed on. For instance: A agrees to sell B 100l. of bank stock, to be transferred, in 20 days, for 120l. A has, in fact, no such stock; but, if the price of bank stock, on the day appointed for the transfer, should be only 118 per cent. A may purchase as much as <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> enable him to fulfil his bargain for 118l., and thus gains 20l. by the transaction; on the contrary, if the price of bank stock be 125 per cent. he will lose 50l. The business is generally settled without any actual purchase or transfer of stock, by A paying to B, or receiving from him, the difference between the current price of the stock on the day appointed and the price bargained for. This practice, which is really nothing else than a wager concerning the price of stock, is contrary to law; yet it is carried on to a great extent. In the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXCHANGE">Exchange</a> Alley, where matters of this kind are transacted, the buyer is called a bull, and the seller a bear. As neither party can be compelled by law to implement these bargains, their sense of honour, and the disgrace and loss of future credit, which attend a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREACH">breach</a> of contract, are the principles by which the business is supported. When a person declines to pay his loss, he is called a lame duck, and dare never afterwards appear in the Alley. This opprobrious appellation, however, is not bestowed on those whose failure is owing to want of ability, providing they make the same surrender of their property voluntarily, which the law would have exacted if the debt had been entitled to its sanction. The interest or dividend on the stock is paid half-yearly; and the purchaser has the benefit of the interest due on the stock he buys, from the last term to the time of purchase. Therefore the prices of the stocks rise gradually, cæteris paribus, from term to term, and fall at the term when the interest is paid. In comparing the prices of the different stocks, it is necessary to advert to the term when the last interest was paid; and, allowance being made for this circumstance, the prices of all the government stocks, which bear interest at the same rate, must be nearly the same, as they all depend on the same security. When a loan is proposed, such terms must be offered to the lenders, as may render the transaction beneficial; and this is now regulated by the prices of the old stocks. If the stocks, which bear interest at 4 per cent, sell at par, or rather above, the government may expect to borrow money at that rate; but, if these stocks are under par, the government must either <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRANT">grant</a> a higher interest, or some other advantage to the lenders, in compensation for the difference. For this purpose, besides the perpetual annuity, another annuity has sometimes been granted for life, or for a term of years. Lotteries have frequently been employed to facilitate the loan, by entitling the subscribers to a certain number of tickets, for which no higher price is <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> than the exact value distributed in prizes, though their market price is generally 2l. or 3l. higher. Sometimes an abatement of a certain proportion of the capital has been granted, and a lender entitled to hold 100l. stock, though in reality he advanced no more perhaps than 95l. It belongs to the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a> of the exchequer to propose the terms of the loan in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>; and he generally makes a previous agreement with some wealthy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a>, who are willing to advance the money on the terms proposed. The subscribers to the loan deposit a certain part of the sum subscribed; and are bound to pay the rest by instalments, or stated proportions, on appointed days, under pain of forfeiting what they have deposited. For this they are entitled, perhaps, not only to hold their share in the capital, but to an annuity for 10 years, and to the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> of receiving a certain number of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOTTERY">lottery</a> tickets on advantageous terms. They may sell their capital to one person, their annuity to a second, and their right to the tickets to a third. The value of all these interests together is called omnium; and, in order to obtain a ready subscription, it ought to amount to 102l. or upwards, on 100l. of capital. This difference is called the bonus to the subscribers. The capital advanced to the public, in the form of transferable stocks, and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> interest from taxes appropriated for that purpose, is called the funded debt. Besides, there is generally a considerable sum due by government, which is not disposed of in that manner, and therefore is distinguished by the appellation of the unfunded debt. This may rise from any sort of national expence, for which no provision has been made, or for which provision has proved insufficient. The <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> branches are, 1st, Exchequer Bills. These are issued from the exchequer, generally by appointment of parliament, and sometimes without such appointment, when exigencies require. They bear interest from the time when issued, and are taken in by the Bank of England, which promotes their circulation. 2d, <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVY">Navy</a> Bills. The sums annually granted for the navy have always fallen short of what that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> required. To supply that deficiency, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ADMIRALTY">admiralty</a> issues bills in payment of victuals, stores, and the like, which bear interest six months after the time issued. The debt of the navy thus contracted is discharged, from time to time by parliament. In time of war, the public expences, since the Revolution, have always been much greater than the annual revenue; and large sums have consequently been borrowed. In time of peace, the revenue exceeds the expence, and part of the public debt has frequently been paid off. But, though there have been more years of peace than of war since the funds were established, the debts contracted during each war have much exceeded the payments during the subsequent peace. This will appear by the following <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABSTRACT">abstract</a> of the progress of the national debt. | Debt at peace of Ryswick, 1697 | L. 21,515,472 | | Debt at the to the finance book, was 900,212,132l.; and the annual interest at the same period was 30,947,150l. Of this debt 8,398,155l. consists of loans to Germany and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PORTUGAL">Portugal</a>. The above, however, is the nominal amount of the public debt; but its real amount, or the sum necessary to extinguish it, supposing the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AVERAGE">average</a> interest received to be 5 per cent, would be about 619,000,000l. The original provision of the sinking fund, of a million per annum, with the additions that have since been made to it; and the dividends on stock, bought up by the commissioners for managing that fund, amount at this time (1820) to fifteen millions per annum. It was calculated that the future rate of accumulation of the sinking fund, continuing the same as hitherto, namely, namely, at 5 per cent, the whole amount of the national debt would be extinguished in 45 years. But the abolition of the income tax in 1816, and the great distress felt by the agricultural, commercial, and manufacturing classes, has put an end to these expectations. Since the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> of the war, the real sinking fund, or the excess of the revenue over the expenditure, has not exceeded two millions per annum. The fruitless attempt to enlarge this fund, by imposing 3,000,000l. of new taxes in 1819, has only shewn, that <a class="xref" href="../1823/vol6.html#article-TAXATION">taxation</a> in the present state of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> has nearly reached its limit. See the nature and operation of the system fully explained in the article Funding System, in the Supplement.

FUNDAMENTAL

Pages 277-279

in Music. A fundamental <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> is that which forms the lowest <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOTE">note</a> of the CHORD, and from whence are deduced the harmonical relations of the rest; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a>, which serves for a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KEY">key</a> to the tone†. The fundamental <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BASS">bass</a> is that which serves for a foundation to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HARMONY">harmony</a>. A fundamental chord is that whose base is fundamental, and in which the sounds are ranged in the same order as when they are <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENERATED">generated</a>, according to the experiment so often repeated by M. d'Alembert in his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRELIMINARY">Preliminary</a> Discourse and Elements of Music†. But as this order removes the parts to an <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> distance one from the other, they must be approximated by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMBINATIONS">combinations</a> or inversions; but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the bass remains the same, the chord does not for this reason cease to bear the name of fundamental. Such an example is this chord, ut mi sol, included in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTERVAL">interval</a> of a fifth: whereas, in the order of its <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENERATION">generation</a>, ut sol mi, it includes a tenth, and even a seventeenth; since the fundamental ut is not the fifth of sol, but the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OCTAVE">octave</a> of that fifth. FUNDAMENTAL BASS. This <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> in music is, according to Rousseau, and indeed according to all authors who have proceeded upon M. Rameau's experiment, in its primary idea, that bass which is formed by the fundamental notes of every perfect chord that constitutes the harmony of the piece; so that under each chord it causes to be heard, or understood, the fundamental sound of that particular chord; that is to say, the sound from whence it is derived by the rules of harmony. From whence we may see, that the fundamental bass can have no other contexture than that of a regular and fundamental succession, without which the procedure of the upper parts would be illegitimate. To understand this well, it is necessary to be known, that, according to the system of Rameau, which Rousseau has followed in his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DICTIONARY">Dictionary</a>, every chord, though composed of several sounds, can only have one which is its fundamental, viz. that which produces this chord, and which is its bass according to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> order. Now, the bass which prevails under all the other parts, does not always express the fundamental sounds of the chords; for amongst all the sounds which form a chord, the composer is at <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> to transfer to the bass that which he thinks preferable; regard being had to the procedure of that bass, to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MELODY">melody</a>, and above all to the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a>, as may afterwards be explained. In this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> the real fundamental sound, instead of retaining its natural station, which is fundamental in the bass, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> either be transferred to some of the other parts, or perhaps even entirely suppressed, and such a chord is called an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INVERTED">inverted</a> chord. In reality, says Rameau, a chord inverted does not differ from the chord in its direct and natural order from which it was produced: but as these sounds form different combinations, these combinations have <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> been taken for fundamental chords; different names have been given them, (which may be seen at the word <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACCORD">Accord</a>, in Rousseau's Dictionary). These names, by the persons who bestowed them, were thought to create and sanctify their distinctions; as if a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> in names could really produce a difference in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>. M. Rameau in his Treatise of Harmony has shown, and M. d'Alembert in his Elements of Music has still more clearly evinced, that many of these pretendedly different chords were no more than inversions of one single chord. Thus the chord of the sixth is no more than the perfect chord of the third transferred to the bass; by adding a fifth, we shall have the chord of the sixth and fourth. Here there are three combinations of a chord, which only consists of three sounds; those which contain four sounds are susceptible of four combinations, since each of these sounds may be transferred to the bass. But in adding beneath this another bass which, under all the combinations of one and the same chord, always presents the fundamental sound; it is evident, that consonant chords are reduced to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> three, and the number of dissonant chords to four. Add to this all the chords by supposition, which may likewise be reduced to the same fundamentals, and you will find harmony brought to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of simplicity in which no person could ever hope to see it whilst its rules remained in that state of confusion where M. Rameau found them. It is certainly, as that author observes, an astonishing occurrence, that the practice of this art could be carried so far as it really was, without knowing its foundation; and that all the rules were so exactly found, without having discovered the principle on which they depended. After having shown what is the fundamental bass beneath the chords, let us now speak of its procedure, and of the manner in which it connects these chords among themselves. Upon this point the precept of the art may be reduced to the six following rules. 1. The fundamental bass ought never to sound any other notes than those of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERIES">series</a> or tone in which the composer finds himself, or at least those of the series or tone to which he chooses to make a transition. This of all the rules for the fundamental bass is the first and most indispensable. 2. By the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a>, its procedure ought to be so implicitly subjected to the laws of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODULATION">modulation</a>, as never to suffer the idea of a former <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODE">mode</a> to be lost till that of a subsequent one can be legitimately assumed; that is to say, that the fundamental bass ought never to be deviating, or suffer us to be one moment at a loss in what mode we are. 3. By the third, it is subjected to the connexion of chords and the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PREPARATION">preparation</a> of dissonances: a manoeuvre, which, as we shall afterwards see, is nothing else but a method of producing this connexion, and which of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> is only necessary when the connexion cannot subsist without it. See Connexion, Preparation. 4. By the fourth, it is necessitated, after every <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIS">dis</a>- Fundamental bass, to pursue that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAREER">career</a> which the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a> of the dissonance indispensably prescribes. See Resolution. 5. By the fifth, which is nothing else but a consequence of the former, the fundamental bass ought only to move by consonant intervals; except alone in the operation of a broken cadence, or after a chord of the seventh diminished, where it rises diatonically. Every other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> of the fundamental bass is illegitimate. 6. By the sixth, in short, the fundamental bass or harmony ought not to be syncopated; but to distinguish the bars and the times which they contain, by changes of chords properly marked with cadences; in such a manner, for instance, that the dissonances which ought to be prepared may find their preparation in the imperfect <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, but chiefly that all the repose may happen in the perfect time. This sixth rule admits of an infinite number of exceptions; but the composer ought however to be attentive to it, if he would form a music in which the movements are properly marked, and in which the bars may end gracefully. Wherever these rules are observed, the harmony shall be regular and without fault: this, however, will not hinder the music from being detestable. See <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPOSITION">Composition</a>. A word of illustration on the fifth rule may not be useless. Whatever turn may be given to a fundamental bass, if it is properly formed, one of these alternatives must always be found; either perfect chords moving by consonant intervals, without which these chords would have no connexion; or dissonant chords in operations of cadence: in every other case, the dissonance can neither be properly placed nor properly resolved. From thence it follows, that the fundamental bass cannot move regularly but in one of these three manners: 1st, To rise or descend by a third or by a sixth. 2dly, By a fourth or a fifth. 3dly, To rise diatonically by means of the dissonance which forms the connexion, or by a license upon a perfect chord. With respect to a diatonic <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a>, it is a motion absolutely prohibited to the fundamental bass; or, at most, merely tolerated in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> where two perfect chords are in succession, divided by a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> expressed or understood. This rule has no other exception: and it is from not discerning the foundation of certain transitions, that M. Rameau has caused the fundamental bass to descend diatonically under chords of the seventh; an operation which is impracticable in legitimate harmony. See Cadence, Dissonance. The fundamental bass, which they add for no other reason than to serve as a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of the harmony, must be retrenched in execution, and often in practice it would have a very bad effect; for it is, as M. Rameau very properly observes, intended for the judgment, and not for the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-EAR">ear</a>. It would at least produce a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONOTONY">monotony</a> extremely nauseous by frequent returns of the same chord, which they <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DISGUISE">disguise</a> and vary more agreeably by combining it in different manners upon the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> bass, without reckoning upon the different inversions of harmony, which furnish a thousand means of adding new beauties to the music and new energy to the expression. See Chord, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVERSION">Inversion</a>. But it will be objected, If the fundamental bass is not useful in composing good music, if it must even be retrenched in practice, what good purpose, then, can it serve? We answer, that, in the first <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, It serves for a rule to scholars, upon which they may learn to form a regular harmony, and to give to all the parts such a diatonic and elementary procedure as is prescribed them by that fundamental bass. It does more, as we have already said: it proves whether a harmony already formed be <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> and regular; for all harmony which cannot be subjected to the test of a fundamental bass, must according to all rules be bad. Finally, It serves for the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVESTIGATION">investigation</a> of a continued bass under a given <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a>: though, in reality, he who cannot directly form a continued bass will scarcely be able to form a fundamental bass, which is better; and much less still will he be able to transform that fundamental bass into a legitimate continued bass. These which follow are, however, the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> rules which M. Rameau prescribes for finding the fundamental bass of a given air. 1. To ascertain with precision the mode in which the composer begins, and those through which he passes. There are also rules for investigating the modes; but so long, so vague, so incomplete, that with respect to this, the ear may be formed long before the rules are acquired; and the dunce who should try to <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> them would <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAIN">gain</a> no improvement but the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HABIT">habit</a> of proceeding always note by note, without even knowing where he is. 2. To try in succession under each note the principal chords of the mode, beginning by those which are most analogous, and passing even to the most remote, when the composer sees himself under a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of doing so. 3. To consider whether the chord chosen can <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUIT">suit</a> the upper part in what precedes and in what follows, by a just fundamental succession; and when this is impracticable, to return the way he came. 4. Not to change the note of the fundamental bass till after having exhausted all the notes which are allowed in succession in the upper part, and which can enter into its chord; or till some syncopated note in the air may be susceptible of two or a greater number of notes in the bass, to prepare the dissonance which may be afterwards resolved according to rule. 5. To <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> the intertexture of the phrases; the possible succession of cadences, whether full or avoided; and above all, the pauses which for ordinary return at the end of every four, or of every two bars, so that they may always <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> upon perfect and regular cadences. 6. In short, to observe all the rules formerly given for the composition of the fundamental bass.—These are the principal observations to be made for finding one under any given air; for there are sometimes several different ones which may be investigated. But, whatever may be said to the contrary, if the air has <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACCENT">accent</a> and character, there is only one just fundamental bass which can be adapted to it. After having given a summary explication of the manner in which a fundamental bass should be composed, it should remain to suggest the means of transforming it into a continued bass; and this would be easy, if it were only necessary to regard the diatonic procedure and the agreeable air of this bass. But let us not imagine that the bass, which is the guide and support of the harmony, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUL">soul</a>, and as it were the interpreter of the air, should be limited to rules so simple: there are others which depend upon principles more certain and more radical; fruitful, but latent principles, which have been felt by every <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ARTIST">artist</a> of genius, without having been detected by any one. Rousseau hopes, that in his <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> upon French music he insinuated this principle. For those who understand him, he imagines he has said enough concerning it, and can never say enough of it for those who do not. He does not here mention the ingenious system by M. Serre of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENEVA">Geneva</a>, nor his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> fundamental bass; because the principles which, with a sagacity meritorious of praise, he had half detected, have afterwards been unfolded by M. Tartini, in a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> of which Rousseau has given an account in his article System.

FUNDI

Pages 279-279

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a town of Latium, on the Via Appia, near Cajeta; enjoying all the privileges of Roman citizens, except the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> of suffrage and of magistracy. Now Fondi; a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>, on the confines of the pope's dominions. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 14. 20. N. Lat. 1°. 35'.

FUNDY

Pages 279-279

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> of considerable <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, opening between the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> of Penobscot bay, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LINCOLN">Lincoln</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a> Sable, the south-west point of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NOVA_SCOTIA">Nova Scotia</a>. It reaches about 200 miles in a north-east <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a>, and forms a very narrow isthmus with Verte bay, which reaches into the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> in a south-west direction from the straits of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTHUMBERLAND">Northumberland</a>. It is 12 leagues from St John's in New <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRUNSWICK">Brunswick</a>, to the Gut of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANNAPOLIS">Annapolis</a> in Nova Scotia, where the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIDES">tides</a> are remarkably rapid, and rise to the height of 30 feet. The tides in this bay are so rapid, that it is said, they <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> overtake animals feeding on the shore.

FUNEN

Pages 279-279
or FIONIA, a considerable island in Denmark, seated in the Baltic sea, and separated from Jutland by a strait called the Lesser Belt, and from the island of Zealand by another called the Great Belt. It is fertile in wheat and barley; and abounds in cattle, horses, game of all sorts, and fish. Odensee is the capital town.

FUNERAL RITES

Pages 279-282

ceremonies accompanying the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTERMENT">interment</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BURIAL">burial</a> of any person. The word is formed of the Latin funus; and that of funalia, on account of the torches (which were fumus cera circumdata) used in the funerals of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>; though others derive funus from the Greek, φοινις, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> or slaughter. These <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RITES">rites</a> differed among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> according to the different genius and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> of each <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. The first people who seem to have paid any particular respect to their dead, were the Egyptians, the posterity of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAM">Ham</a>, the first cultivators of idolatrous worship and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a> after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOD">flood</a>: they were also the first who asserted the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IMMORTALITY">immortality</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUL">soul</a>, its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIGRATION">migration</a> into all kinds of animals in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a>, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, and its return to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> body; which they supposed to be within the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> of 3000 years: Hence proceeded their very <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> care in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMBALMING">embalming</a> of their dead bodies, and their being at such vast expences, as they were, in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> proper repositories for them; for they were more solicitous about their graves than their houses: This gave birth to those wonders of the world, the pyramids, which were built for the burial of their kings, with such vast charges, and almost incredible magnificence. See <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PYRAMID">PYRAMID</a>. Whenever a person died among the Egyptians, his parents and friends put on mournful habits, and abstained from all banquets and entertainments. This <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOURNING">mourning</a> lasted from 40 to 70 days, during which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> they embalmed the body. See EMBALMING. When this <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a> was finished, the embalmed body was restored to the friends, who placed it in a kind of open <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHEST">chest</a>, which was preserved either in their houses, or in the sepulchres of their <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a>. But before the dead were allowed to be deposited in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOMB">tomb</a>, they underwent a solemn judgment, which extended even to their kings. Of this remarkable <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> we have a particular account in the first book of Diodorus Siculus. "Those who prepare to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURY">bury</a> a relation, give notice of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> intended for the ceremony to the judges, and to all the friends of the deceased; informing them, that the body <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> over the lake of that district to which the dead belonged: when, on the judges assembling, to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of more than 40, and ranging themselves in a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEMICIRCLE">semicircle</a> on the farther side of the lake, the vessel is set afloat, which those who superintend the funeral have prepared for this purpose. This vessel is managed by a pilot, called in the Egyptian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARON">Charon</a>; and hence they say, that <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORPHEUS">Orpheus</a>, travelling in old times into <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, and seeing this ceremony, formed his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FABLE">fable</a> of the infernal regions, partly from what he <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a>, and partly from <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a>. The vessel being launched on the lake, before the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COFFIN">coffin</a> which contains the body is put on board, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a> permits all, who are so inclined, to produce an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACCUSATION">accusation</a> against it. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> any one steps forth, and proves that the deceased has led an evil <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, the judges pronounce <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a>, and the body is precluded from burial; but if the accuser is convicted of injustice in his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a>, he falls himself under a considerable penalty. When no accuser appears, or when the accusation is proved to be an unfair one, the relations, who are assembled, change their expressions of sorrow into encomiums on the dead; yet do not, like the Greeks, speak in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of his family, because they consider all Egyptians as equally well born; but they set forth the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> and manners of his youth, his piety and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> in maturer life, his moderation, and every virtue by which he was distinguished; and they supplicate the infernal deities to receive him as an associate among the blest. The multitude join their acclamations of applause in this celebration of the dead, whom they consider as going to pass an eternity among the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> below." Such is the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> which Diodorus gives of this funeral judicature, to which even the kings of Egypt were subject. The same author asserts, that many sovereigns had been thus judicially deprived of the honours of burial by the indignation of their people: and that the terrors of such a fate had the most salutary influence on the virtue of their kings. The funeral rites among the Hebrews were solemn and magnificent. When any person was dead, his relations and friends rent their clothes; which custom is but faintly imitated by the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> Jews, who only cut off a bit of their garment, in token of affliction. It was usual to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEND">bend</a> the dead person's thumb into the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, and fasten it in that posture with a string; be- cause the thumb then having the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of the name of God, they thought the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVIL">devil</a> would not dare to approach it. When they came to the burying <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, they made a speech to the dead in the following terms: "Blessed be God, who has formed thee, fed thee, maintained thee, and taken away thy life. O dead! he knows your numbers, and shall one day restore your life," &c. Then they spoke the elegium, or funeral <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORATION">oration</a>, of the deceased; after which they said a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRAYER">prayer</a>, called the righteousness of judgment; then <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FACE">face</a> of the deceased towards heaven, they called out, "Go in peace." Among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Greeks it was usual sometimes before the interment, to put a piece of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a> into the mouth of the deceased, which was thought to be Charon's fare for wafting the departed soul over the infernal river. This ceremony was not used in those countries which were supposed to be situated in the neighbourhood of the infernal regions, and to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> thither by a ready and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a>. The corpse was likewise furnished with a cake, composed of flour, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONEY">honey</a>, &c. which was designed to appease the fury of Cerberus the door-keeper of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HELL">hell</a>, and to procure the ghost a safe and quiet entrance. During the time the corpse <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, there stood before the door a vessel of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>: the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of which was, that those concerned about the body might purify themselves by washing; it being the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of the Greeks, as well as of the Jews, that pollution was contracted by touching a dead body. The ceremonies by which they expressed their sorrow for the death of their friends were various; but it seems to have been a constant rule to recede as much as possible in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HABIT">habit</a> and behaviour from their ordinary customs. For this reason they abstained from banquets and entertainments; they divested themselves of all ornaments; they tore, cut off, or shaved their <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>, which they <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> into the funeral pile, to be consumed with the body of their deceased friend. Sometimes they threw themselves on the ground and rolled in the dust, or covered their heads with ashes; they <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEAT">beat</a> their breasts, and even tore their <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> with their nails, upon the loss of a person they much lamented. When persons of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a>, such as public magistrates or great generals, died, the whole <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> put on a face of mourning: all public meetings were intermitted; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATHS">baths</a>, shops, <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a>, and all places of concourse, were shut up. After interment followed the epulæ or feasts, at which the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> used to appear crowned; when they spoke in praise of the dead, so far as they could go with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>, it being esteemed a notorious wickedness to <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> upon such an occasion. And not only at those feasts, but even before the company departed from the sepulchre, they were sometimes entertained with a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PANEGYRIC">panegyric</a> upon the dead person. The Grecian <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a>, who died in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, had not only their tombs adorned with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INSCRIPTIONS">inscriptions</a> showing their names, parentage, and exploits, but were also honoured with an oration in their praise. Particularly the custom among the Athenians in the interment of their soldiers was as follows, namely, "They used to place the bodies of their dead in tents three days before the funeral, that all persons might have opportunity to find out their relations, and pay their last respects to them. Upon the fourth day, a coffin of cypress was sent from every tribe, to convey the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONES">bones</a> of their own relations; after which went a covered <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HERSE">herse</a>, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of those whose bodies could not be found. All these, accompanied by the whole body of the people, were carried to the public burying place, called Ceramicus, and there interred. One oration was spoken in commendation of them all, and their monuments were adorned with pillars, inscriptions, and all other ornaments usual about the tombs of the most <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> persons. The oration was pronounced by the fathers of the deceased persons who had behaved themselves most valiantly. Thus after the famous <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARATHON">Marathon</a>, the fathers of Callimachus and Cynægirus were appointed to make the funeral oration. And upon the return of the day upon which the solemnity was first held, the same oration was constantly repeated every year." Interring or laying the dead in the ground seems to have been the most ancient practice among the Greeks; though <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> came afterwards to be generally used among them. It was customary to throw into the funeral pile those garments the deceased usually wore. The pile was lighted by one of the deceased's nearest relations or friends, who made prayers and vows to the <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> to assist the flames, that the body might quickly be reduced to ashes; and during the time the pile was burning, the dead person's friends stood by it, pouring libations of wine, and calling upon the deceased. The funeral rites among the ancient Romans were very numerous. The deceased was kept <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> days; and every day washed with hot water, and sometimes with <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, that, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> he was only in a slumber, he might be thus waked; and every now and then his friends meeting, made a horrible outcry or shout, with the same view; which last <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTION">action</a> they called conclamatione. The third conclamation was on the seventh day; when, if no signs of life appeared, the defunct was dressed and embalmed by the pollinctores; placed in a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BED">bed</a> near the door, with his face and heels towards the street; and the outside of the gate, if the deceased were of condition, was garnished with cypress boughs. In the course of these seven days, an altar was raised near his bed side, called <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACERRA">acerra</a>; on which his friends every day offered incense: and the libitinarii provided things for the funeral. On the seventh day a crier was sent about the city, to invite the people to the solemnization of the funeral in these words: Exequias L. Tit. filii, quibus est commodum ire, jam tempus est. Olius (i.e. ille) ex adibus effertur. The people being assembled, the last conclamation ended, and the bed was covered with purple: a trumpeter marched forth, followed by old women called praefice, singing songs in praise of the deceased: lastly, the bed followed, borne by the next relations; and if the person were of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> and office, the waxen images of all his predecessors were carried before him on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLES">poles</a>. The bed was followed by his children, kindred, &c. atrati, or in mourning: from which <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> of following the corpse, these funeral rites were called exequiae. The body thus brought to the restra, the next of kin laudabat defunctum pro rostris, made a funeral oration in his praise and that of his ancestors. This done, the body was carried to the pyra, or funeral pile, and there burnt: his friends first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> off a finger, to be bury... ried with a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> solemnity. The body consumed, the ashes were gathered; and the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> sprinkling the company thrice with clean water, the eldest of the preside crying aloud, *Ilicet*, dismissed the people, who took their leave of the deceased in this form, *Vale, vale, vale*: *nos te ordine quo natura permiscit sequer-mur.*—The ashes, enclosed in an urn, were laid in the sepulchre or tomb. The ancient <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> testified their abhorrence of the Pagan custom of burning their dead; and always deposited the body entire in the ground; and it was usual to bestow the honour of embalming upon the martyrs at least, if not upon others. They prepared the body for burial by washing it with water, and dressing it in a funeral attire. The <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPORTATION">exportation</a> or carrying forth of the body was performed by near relations, or persons of such <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> as the circumstances of the deceased required. Psalmody, or singing of psalms, was the great ceremony used in all funeral processions among the ancient Christians. In the Romish <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, when a person is dead, they wash the body, and put a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CRUCIFIX">crucifix</a> in its hand. At its feet stands a vessel full of holy water, and a sprinkler, that they who come in may sprinkle both themselves and the deceased. In the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> time some priest stands by the corpse, and prays for the deceased till it is laid in the earth. In the funeral <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESSION">procession</a>, the exorcist walks first, carrying the holy water; next the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a>-bearer, afterwards the rest of the clergy, and last of all the officiating priest. They all sing the *misere*, and some other psalms; and at the end of each psalm a *requiem*. We learn from <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALET">Alet</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RITUAL">ritual</a>, that the faces of deceased laymen must be turned towards the altar, when they are placed in the church; and those of the clergy towards the people. The corpse is placed in the church surrounded with lighted tapers; after the office for the dead, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MASS">mass</a> is said; then the officiating priest sprinkles the corpse thrice with holy water, and as often throws incense on it. The body being laid in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAVE">grave</a>, the friends and relations of the deceased sprinkle the grave with holy water. The funeral ceremonies of the Greek church are much the same with those of the Latin. It needs only be observed, that, after the funeral <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>, they kiss the crucifix, and salute the mouth and forehead of the deceased; after which each of the company eats a bit of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a> and drinks a glass of wine in the church, wishing the soul a good repose, and the afflicted family all consolation. Funeral Games, a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the ceremony of the ancient funerals. It was customary for persons of quality among the ancient Greeks and Romans, to institute games with all sorts of exercises, to render the death of their friends more remarkable. This practice was generally received, and is frequently mentioned by ancient writers. Patoclus's funeral games take up the greatest part of one of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a>'s Iliads; and Agamemnon's ghost is introduced by the same poet, telling the ghost of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACHILLES">Achilles</a>, that he had been a spectator at a great number of such solemnities. The celebration of these games among the Greeks mostly consisted of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> races; the prizes were of different sorts and value, according to the quality and magnificence of the person that celebrated them. The garlands given to victors on this occasion were usually of parsley, which was thought to have some relation to the dead. Those games, among the Romans, consisted chiefly of processions; and sometimes of mortal combats of gladiators around the funeral pile. They, as well as the Greeks, had also a custom, though very ancient, of cutting the throats of a number of captives before the pile, as victims to appease the manes of the deceased. Caesar relates, that the Gauls had this custom. The funeral games were abolished by the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Claudius. Funeral Oration, a discourse pronounced in praise of a person deceased, at the ceremony of his funeral. This custom is very ancient. In the latter part of the account above given of the Egyptian ceremonies of interment, may be perceived the first <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RUDIMENTS">rudiments</a> of funeral orations, and what was the subject of them, which were afterwards moulded into a more polite and regular form by other nations, who adopted this custom. Nor can we omit remarking, that those funeral solemnities were attended not only with orations in praise of the deceased, but with prayers for him: which prayers, it seems, were made by one who personated the deceased: an entire form of one of them is preserved by Porphyry, and perhaps it may in some <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> gratify the reader's curiosity to recite it from him. "When (says he) they (the Egyptians) embalm their deceased <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBLES">nobles</a>, they privately take out the entrails, and lay them up in an ark or chest: moreover, among other things which they do in favour of the deceased, lifting up the ark or chest to the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, they invoke him; one of the *libitinarii* making a prayer for the deceased, which Euphantes has translated out of the Egyptian language, and is as follows:—O <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a>, the sun, and all the gods who give life to men, receive me and admit me into the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> of the immortal ones; for, as <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> as I lived in this world, I religiously worshipped the gods whom my parents showed me, and have always honoured those who begat my body; nor have I killed any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, nor have I defrauded any of what has been committed to my trust, nor have I done any thing which is inexpiable. Indeed, whilst I was alive, if I have sinned either by eating or drinking any thing which was not lawful; not through myself have I sinned, but through these, showing the ark and chest where the entrails were. And having thus spoke, he casts it into the river, but the rest of the body he embalms as pure." The Grecians received the seeds of superstition and idolatrous worship from the Egyptians, through the coming of Cecrops, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CADMUS">Cadmus</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DANAUS">Danaus</a>, and Erechtheus, into <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>; and among other customs transplanted from Egypt, were the solemnities used at the burial of the dead. Of these, an encomium on the deceased always formed a part, as particularly noticed under the preceding article. From the Egyptians and Grecians, especially from the latter, the Romans received many of their laws and customs, as well as much of their polytheism and idolatrous worship. It is well known, that the custom of making funeral orations in praise of the dead obtained among them; and the manner in which their funeral services were performed has been already described. The corpse being brought into their great oratory, Funeral oratory, called the rostra, the next of the kin laudabat defunctum pro rostris, that is, made a funeral oration, in the commendation principally of the party deceased, but touching the worthy acts also of those his predecessors whose images were there present. The account given by Dr Kennet is in these words: "In all the funerals of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOTE">note</a>, especially in the public or indicative, the corpse was first brought with a vast train of followers into the forum; here one of the nearest relations ascended the rostra, and obliged the audience with an oration in praise of the deceased. If none of the kindred undertook the office, it was discharged by some of the most eminent persons in the city for learning and eloquence, as Appian reports of the funeral of Sylla. And Pliny the younger reckons it as the last addition to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a> of a very great man, that he had the honour to be praised at his funeral by the most eloquent Tacitus, then <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSUL">consul</a>; which is agreeable to Quintilian's account of this <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>, Nam et funebres, &c. For the funeral orations (says he) depend very often on some public office, and by order of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENATE">senate</a> are many times given in charge to the magistrates to be performed by themselves in person. The invention of this custom is generally attributed to Valerius Poplicola, soon after the expulsion of the regal family. Plutarch tells us, that honouring his colleague's obsequies with a funeral oration, it so pleased the Romans, that it became customary for the best men to celebrate the funerals of great persons with speeches in their commendations." Thus Julius Caesar, according to custom, made an oration in the rostra, in praise of his wife Cornelia, and his aunt Julia, when dead; wherein he showed, that his aunt's <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a>, by her mother's side, was from kings, and by her father's from the gods. Plutarch says, that "he approved of the law of the Romans, which ordered suitable praises to be given to women as well as to men after death."—Though by what he says in another place, it seems that the old Roman law was, that funeral orations should be made only for the elder women; and therefore he says, that Caesar was the first that made one upon his own wife, it not being then usual to take notice of younger women in that way: but by that action he gained much favour from the populace, who afterwards looked upon him, and loved him, as a very mild and good man. The reason why such a law was made in favour of the women, Livy tells us was this, That when there was such a scarcity of money in the public <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURY">treasury</a>, that the sum agreed upon to give the Gauls to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> up the siege of the city and capitol could not be raised, the women collected among themselves and made it up; who hereupon had not only thanks given them, but this additional honour, that after death, they should be solemnly praised as well as the men: which looks as if, before this time, only the men had those funeral orations made for them. This custom of the Romans very early obtained among the Christians. Some of their funeral sermons or orations are now extant, as that of Eusebius on Constantine; and those of Nazianzen on <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BASIL">Basil</a> and Cesarius; and of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBROSE">Ambrose</a> on <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-VALENTINIAN">Valentinian</a>, Theodosius, and others. Gregory, the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> of Basil, made εἰκονιστής λόγος, a funeral oration, for Melitus bishop of Antioch: in which orations, they not only praised the dead, but addressed themselves to them, which seems to have introduced the custom of praying to departed saints. Now these orations were usually made before the bodies of the deceased were committed to the ground; which custom has been more or less continued ever since, to this day. Thus it appears, that those rites and ceremonies among the heathens, which have been delivered from one people to another, are what have given birth to Funeral Sermons and Orations, among Christians.
