We learn from the Old <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a> that Gad was an author, who wrote a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of his own times, of which much <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> appears to have been made by the compilers of the books of Samuel and Chronicles. Gad was also the name of one of the twelve patriarchs, or sons of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JACOB">Jacob</a>.

GADARA

Pages 340-340

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a town of the Persea, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Transjordan, in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECAPOLIS">Decapolis</a>, a very strong <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>. Restored by Pompey after its demolition by the Jews (Josephus). After Herod's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, it was joined to the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a> by Augustus.

GADARENORUM AGER

Pages 340-340

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of the Gadarenes, called by Matthew the country of the Gergesenes, because it was a district that lay between Gadara and Gergesa, otherwise called Gerasa, both which lay within the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECAPOLIS">Decapolis</a> on the other side Jordan.

GADES

Pages 340-340
or GADIRA, in Ancient Geography, a small island in the Atlantic, on the Spanish coast, 25 miles from the Columns of Hercules. It was sometimes called Tartessus and Erythia according to Pliny. Geeryon, whom Hercules killed, fixed his residence there. Hercules, surnamed Gaditanus, had there a celebrated temple, in which all his labours were engraved with excellent workmanship. The inhabitants are called Gaditani.

GADUS

Pages 340-340

a genus of fishes belonging to the order of jugulares. This genus includes the cod, the whiting, the torsk, &c. See <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ICHTHYOLOGY">Ichthyology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. GAELIC <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">LANGUAGE</a>. See Highlands. GÆTULIA, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, lying to the south of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MAURITANIA">Mauritania</a>, called Gætulia Propria, and Vetus. Gætuli, the people, were distinguished by different epithets; as Nigri, Autoloes, Darce and Baniura, (Pliny. The Gætuli were among the first inhabitants of Africa; a rough, unpolished people, living on venison and the spontaneous productions of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>; a roving, wandering people, who took up with the first <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in which night surprised them, (Sallust).

GAFFAREL

Pages 340-341

JAMES, a French divine, and very learned writer, born about 1601. He acquired <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> skill in the oriental and several other languages; and was particularly versant in the cabbalistic and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OCCULT">occult</a> sciences, which he learned, exposed, and refuted. <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDINAL">Cardinal</a> Richelieu made choice of him for his library keeper, and sent him into <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> to collect the best <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUSCRIPTS">manuscripts</a> and books. He published a book entitled Curiositez Innouyes, i.e. Unheard-of Curiosities. It is said the cardinal designed to employ him in his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> project for the reunion of religions. He died in 1681, aged 80. He had been labouring for many years, and had almost finished a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of the subterranean world; containing an account of the caves, grottoes, vaults, catacombs, catacombs, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a>, he had met with in 30 years' travels.

GAGE

Pages 341-344

in joinery, is an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> made to strike a line truly <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> to the straight side of any board <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> piece of stuff. Its <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> is for gaging of tenons true, to fit into mortises; and for gaging stuff of an equal thickness. It is made of an oval piece of wood, fitted upon a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> stick, to slide up and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> stiffly thereon, and with a tooth at the end of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STAFF">staff</a>, to score, to strike a line upon the staff at any distance, according to the distance of the oval from it. **Sliding GAGE**, a tool used by the mathematical instrument makers for measuring and setting off the distances. **<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">Sea</a> GAGE**, an instrument invented by Dr Hales and Dr Desaguliers for finding the depth of the sea; the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> whereof is this. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AB">AB</a> (fig. 1.) is the gage bottle, in which is cemented the gage tube EF in the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> at G. The upper end of tube F is hermetically sealed, and the open lower end f is immersed in <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERCURY">mercury</a>, marked C, on which swims a small thickness or surface of treacle. On the top of the bottle is screwed a tube of brass HG, pierced with several holes to admit the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> into the bottle AB. The body K is a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> hanging by its shank L, in a socket N, with a notch on one side at m, in which is fixed the catch l of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> S, and passing through the hole, L, in the shank of the weight K, prevents its falling out when once hung on. On the top, in the upper <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the brass tube at H, is fixed a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> empty <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALL">ball</a>, or full blown bladder I, which must not be so large, but that the weight K may be able to sink the whole under water. The instrument thus constructed is used in the following manner. The weight K being hung on, the gage is let <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> into deep water, and sinks to the bottom: the socket N is somewhat longer than the shank L; and therefore, after the weight K comes to the bottom, the gage <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> continue to descend till the lower part of the socket strikes against the weight; this gives <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> to the catch to fly out of the hole l, and let go the weight K: when this is done, the ball or bladder I instantly buoys up the gage to the top of the water. While the gage is under water, the water having free access to the treacle and mercury in the bottle, will by its pressure force it up into the tube Ff, and the height to which it has been forced by the greatest pressure, viz. that at the bottom, will be shown by the mark in the tube which the treacle leaves behind it, and which is the only use of the treacle. This shows into what space the whole <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> in the tube Ff is compressed; and consequently the height or depth of the water which by its weight produced that compression, which is the thing required. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> the gage tube Ff be of glass, a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCALE">scale</a> might be drawn on it with the point of a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIAMOND">diamond</a>, showing, by inspection, what height the water stands above the bottom. But the length of 10 inches is not sufficient for fathoming depths at sea, since that, when all the air in such a length of tube is compressed into half an inch, the depth of water is more than 634 feet, which is not half a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILE">mile</a>. If, to remedy this, we make use of a tube 50 inches <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a>, which for strength may be a musket <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BARREL">barrel</a>, and suppose the air compressed into the hundredth part of half an inch; then by saying, as 1 : 99 :: 400 : 39600 inches, or 3300 feet; even this is but little more than half a mile, or 2640 feet. But since it is reasonable to suppose the cavities of the sea bear some proportion to the mountainous parts of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a>, some of which are more than three miles above the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-EARTH_S"><a clas</a>s="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>'s surface; therefore, to explore such <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> depths, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DOCTOR">Doctor</a> contrived a new form for the sea gage, or rather for the gage tube in it, as follows. BCDF (fig. 2.) is a hollow metallic globe, communicating on the top with a long tube AB, whose capacity is a ninth part of that globe. On the lower part at D, it has also a short tube DE, to stand in the mercury and treacle. The air contained in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPOUND">compound</a> gage tube is compressed by the water as before; but the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of compression, or height to which the treacle has been forced, cannot there be seen through the tube: therefore, to answer that end, a slender rod of metal or wood, with a knob on the top of the tube AB, will receive the mark of the treacle, and show it when taken out. If the tube AB be 50 inches long, and of such a bore... Gage. bore that every inch in length should be a cubic inch of air, and the contents of the globe and tube together 500 cubic inches; then when the air is compressed within an hundredth part of the whole, it is evident the treacle will not approach nearer than five inches of the top of the tube, which will agree to the depth of 3300 feet of water as above. Twice this depth will compress the air into half that space nearly, viz. 2½ inches, which correspond to 6600, which is a mile and a quarter. Again, half that space, or 1¼ inch, will show <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> the former depth, viz. 13200 feet, or 2½ miles; which is probably very nearly the greatest depth of the sea. Bucket Sea Gage, an instrument contrived by Dr Hales to find the different degrees of coolness and saltiness of the sea, at different depths: it consists of a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSEHOLD">household</a> pail or bucket, with two heads: These heads have each a round hole in the middle, about four inches in diameter, covered with square valves opening upward; and that they may both open and shut together, there is a small <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> rod fixed to the upper part of the lower <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VALVE">valve</a>, and the other end to the lower side of the upper valve. So that as the bucket descends with its sinking weight into the sea, both the valves may open by the force of the water, which by that means has a free passage through the bucket. But when the bucket is drawn up, then both the valves shut by the force of the water at the upper part of the bucket; so that the bucket is drawn up full of the lowest sea water to which it has descended. When the bucket is drawn up, the mercurial thermometer fixed in it is examined; but great care must be taken to observe the degree at which the mercury stands, before the lower part of the thermometer is taken out of the water in the bucket, lest it be affected by the different temperature of the air. In order to keep the bucket in a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> position, there are four cords fixed to it, reaching about three feet below it; to which the sinking weight is fixed. The result of several trials with this gage was, that when it was let down to different depths, from 360 feet to 5346 feet, in lat. 25° 13' N. and long. 25° 12' W. it was discovered by the thermometer, that the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLD">cold</a> increased gradually in proportion to the depths, till it descended to 3900 feet, viz. near ¼ths of a mile, whence the mercury in the thermometer came up at 53°; and though it was afterwards sunk to 5346 feet, i.e. a mile and 66 feet, it came up no lower: the warmth of the water upon the surface, and that of the air, was all that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> 84°. When the water in the bucket was become of the same temperature with that on the surface of the sea, equal quantities of both were weighed and tried by the hydrometer; that from below was found to be the heaviest, and consequently the saltiest. Dr Hales was probably led to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a> of this sea gage from an instrument invented by Dr Hook, and designed for the same purpose. This consists of a square wooden bucket C, (fig. 3.) whose bottoms are so contrived, that as the weight of A sinks the iron B, to which the bucket C is fastened by two handles D, D, on the end of which are the moveable bottoms or valves EE, and thereby draws down the bucket, the resistance of the water keeps up the bucket in the posture C, whereby the water, whilst the bucket was descending, hath a free passage through it; whereas, as soon as the bucket is pulled upwards by the line F, the resistance of the water to that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> beats the bucket downwards, and keeps it in the posture G; whereby the included water is kept from getting out, and the ambient water kept from getting in. Phil. Trans. No. ix. p. 149. and No. xxiv. p. 447. or Abr. vol. ii. p. 262. Aquæo-mercurial Gage, is the name of an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPARATUS">apparatus</a> contrived by Dr Hales, and applied in various forms to the branches of trees, in order to determine the force with which they imbibe moisture. Let e r, (fig. Fig. 4.) be a cylindric glass, e.g. of an inch diameter within, and eight inches long. Into this glass is introduced the branch of a young thriving apple tree b, about three feet long, with lateral branches; the diameter of the transverse cut i being ¼ths of an inch. Having fitted the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOINT">joint</a> r to the tube at r, by folding a piece of sheep's skin round the stem, it is cemented with a mixture of bees wax and turpentine melted together, in such proportion as to make a very stiff clammy paste when cold, and over the cement folds of wet bladders are bound firmly with pack thread. To the lower end c of the large tube, a smaller tube z e is cemented, being about ⅝ of an inch diameter, and 18 inches long, and in substance full ⅝ of an inch thick. These tubes are cemented together at e with common hard brick dust or powdered chalk cement, and the joint is farther secured with the cement of bees wax and turpentine, over which a wet bladder is bound. The apparatus being thus prepared, the branch is turned downwards, and the glass tube upwards, and then both tubes are filled with water; with the finger applied to the open end of the small tube, it is <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INVERTED">inverted</a> and immersed in the glass cistern x, full of mercury and water. In this situation the lower end of the branch was immersed six inches in water, viz. from r to i; the water was imbibed by the branch at its transverse cut i; and during its ascent into the sap vessels of the branch, the mercury rose in the tube z e from the cistern x, so that in half an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> it was risen 5¼ inches <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, as far as z. The height of the mercury indicated, in some <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a>, the force with which the sap was imbibed, though not the whole force; because while the water was imbibed by the branch, its transverse cut was covered with innumerable little hemispheres of air, and many air bubbles issued out of the sap vessels, which partly filled the tube e r, as the water was drawn out of it; and therefore the height of the mercury could only be <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROPORTIONAL">proportional</a> to the excess of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of water drawn off above the quantity of the air which issued out of the wood. If the quantity of air issuing from the wood had been equal to the quantity of water imbibed, it is plain that the mercury could not rise at all, because there would be no room for it in the tube: but if <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> parts in twelve of the water be imbibed by the branch, and only three such parts of air issue into the tube in the same time the mercury must rise near six inches, and so proportionally in other <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a>. Dr Hales observed, that the mercury rose highest, in most cases, when the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> was clear and warm, and that it subsided three or four inches towards evening, but rose again the next <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> as it grew warm, though seldom so high as at first. Dr Hales adapted the size and shape of the glass apparatus to a great variety of branches of several sizes and of different kinds of trees, and repeated the experiment above above described, mutatis mutandis, in a variety of instances. See his Vegetable <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STATICS">Statics</a>, vol. i. chap. ii. p. 84, &c. Tide Gage, the name of an instrument used for determining the height of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIDES">tides</a> by Mr Bayly, in the course of a voyage towards the south pole, &c. in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESOLUTION">Resolution</a> and Adventure, in 1772, 1773, 1774, and 1775. This instrument consists of a glass tube, whose internal diameter was <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a>-tenths of an inch, lashed fast to a ten-feet fir rod, divided into feet, inches, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a>: this rod was fastened to a strong <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a> fixed upright and firm in the water. At the lower end of the tube was an exceeding small aperture, through which the water was admitted. In <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of this construction, the surface of the water in the tube was so little affected by the agitation of the sea, that its height was not altered one-tenth of an inch, when the swell of the sea was two feet; and Mr Bayly was certain, that with this instrument he could discern a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> of one-tenth of an inch in the height of the tide. <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">Wind</a> Gage, an instrument for measuring the force of the wind upon any given surface. It was invented by Dr Lind, who gives the following description of it, Phil. Trans. vol. lxv. This instrument consists of two glass tubes AB, CD, (fig. 5.) of five or six inches in length. Their bores, which are so much the better for being equal, are about four-tenths of an inch in diameter. They are connected together like a siphon, by a small bent glass tube ab, the bore of which is about one-tenth of an inch in diameter. On the upper part of the leg AB there is a tube of latten brass, which is kneed, or bent perpendicularly outwards, and has its mouth open towards F. On the other leg CD, is a cover with a round hole G in the upper part of it two-tenths of an inch in diameter. This cover and the kneed tube are connected together by a slip of brass ed, which not only gives strength to the whole instrument, but also serves to hold the scale HI. The kneed tube and cover are fixed on with hard cement or sealing wax. To the same tube is soldered a piece of brass e, with a round hole in it to receive the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-STEEL">steel</a> spindle KL; and at f there is <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> such another piece of brass soldered to the brass hoop gh, which surrounds both legs of the instrument. There is a small shoulder on the spindle at f, upon which the instrument rests, and a small <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUT">nut</a> at i, to prevent it from being blown off the spindle by the wind. The whole instrument is easily turned round upon the spindle by the wind, so as always to present the mouth of the kneed tube towards it. The end of the spindle has a screw on it; by which it may be screwed into the top of a post or a stand made on purpose. It has also a hole at L, to admit a small <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEVER">lever</a> for screwing it into wood with more readiness and facility. A thin plate of brass k is soldered to the kneed tube about half an inch above the round hole G, so as to prevent <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">rain</a> from falling into it. There is likewise a crooked tube AB (fig. 6.) to be put occasionally upon the mouth of the kneed tube F, in order to prevent rain from being blown into the mouth of the wind gage when it is left out all night, or exposed in the time of rain. The force or momentum of the wind may be ascertained by the assistance of this instrument, by filling the tubes half full of water, and pushing the scale a little up or down till the o of the scale, when the instrument is held up perpendicularly, be on the line with the surface of the water in both legs of the wind-gage. The instrument being thus adjusted, hold it up perpendicularly, and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> the mouth of the kneed tube towards the wind, observe how much the water is depressed by it in the one leg, and raised in the other. The sum of the two is the height of a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLUMN">column</a> of water which the wind is capable of sustaining at that time; and every body that is opposed to that wind will be pressed upon by a force equal to the weight of a column of water, having its base equal to the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ALTITUDE">altitude</a> of the column of water sustained by the wind in the wind gage. Hence the force of the wind upon any body where the surface opposed to it is known may be easily found; and a ready <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPARISON">comparison</a> may be made betwixt the strength of one <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-GALE">gale</a> of wind and that of another. The force of the wind may be likewise measured with this instrument, by filling it until the water runs out of the hole G. For if we then hold it up to the wind as before, a quantity of water will be blown out; and if both legs of the instrument are of the same bore, the height of the column sustained will be equal to double the column of water in either leg, or the sum of what is wanting in both legs. But if the legs are of unequal bores, neither of these will give the true height of the column of water which the wind sustained. But the true height may be obtained by the following formulæ. Suppose that after a gale of wind which had blown the water from A to B (fig. 7.) forcing it at the same time through the other tube out at E, the surface of the water should be found standing at some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> DG, and it were required to know what was the height of the column EF or AB, which the wind sustained. In order to obtain this, it is only necessary to find the height of the columns DB or GF, which are constantly equal to one another; for either of these added to one of the equal columns <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AD">AD</a>, EG, will give the true height of the column of water which the wind sustained. 1. Let the diameters AC, EH, of the tubes be respectively represented by cd; and let a=AD, or EG, and x=DB, or FG: Then it is evident, that the column DB is to the column EG as c^2x to d^2a. But these columns are equal. Therefore c^2x=d^2a; and consequently x=\frac{d^2a}{c^2}. 2. But if at any instant of time whilst the wind was blowing, it was observed, that, when the water stood at E, the top of the tube out of which it is forced, it was depressed in the other to some given level BF, the altitude at which it would have stood in each, had it immediately subsided, may be found in the following manner: Let b=AB or EF.—Then it is evident that the column DB is equal to the difference of columns EF, FG. But the difference of these columns is as d^2b-d^2x; and consequently x=\frac{d^2b}{c^2+d^2}. For the cases when the wind blows in at the narrow leg of the instrument: Let AB=EF=b, EG or AD=a, GF=DB=x, and the diameters EH, GA, respectively Gage <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAINAGE">Gainage</a>. respectively \(=d, c\), as before. Then it is evident, that the column AD is to the column GF as \(a^c\) to \(d^x\). But these columns are equal; therefore \(d^x = a^c\); and consequently \(x = \frac{a^c}{d^x}\). It is also evident that the column AD is equal to the difference of the columns AB, DB; but the difference of these columns is as \(b^c - c^x\). Therefore \(d^x = b^c - c^x\). Whence we get \(x = \frac{b^c}{d^x + c}\). The use of the small tube of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> \(ab\) (fig. 5.) is to check the undulation of the water, so that the height of it may be read off from the scale with ease and certainty. But it is particularly designed to prevent the water from being thrown up to a much greater or less altitude than the true height of the column which the wind is able at that time to sustain, from its receiving a sudden impulse whilst it is vibrating either in its ascent or <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a>. As in some cases the water in this instrument might be liable to freeze, and thus <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> the tubes, Dr Lind recommends a saturated solution of sea <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> to be used instead of it, which does not freeze till Fahrenheit's thermometer falls to 0.

GAHNIA

Pages 344-344

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the hexandria class. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

GAIETA

Pages 344-344

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a>, handsome, and strong town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>, and in the Terra di Lavoro, with a fort, citadel, harbour, and bishop's see. It was taken by the Austrians in 1707, and by the Spaniards in 1734. It is seated at the foot of a mountain near the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 13° 37'. N. Lat. 41° 30'.

GAIN

Pages 344-344

in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">Architecture</a>, is the workman's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> for the bevelling shoulder of a joist <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> other <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a>. It is used also for the lapping of the end of the joist, &c. upon a trimmer or girder; and then the thickness of the shoulder is cut into the trimmer; also bevelling upwards, that it may <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> receive the gain; and so the joist and trimmer <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> even and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> with the surface. This way of working is used in floors and hearths. To GAIN the <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">Wind</a>, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, is to arrive on the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a> side or to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WINDWARD">windward</a> of some other vessel in sight, when both are plying to windward, or sailing as near the wind as possible.

GAINAGE

Pages 344-344

Gainagium, in our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> writers, signifies the draught oxen, horses, wain, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLOUGH">plough</a>, and furniture, for carrying on the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> of tillage by the baser sort of sokemen and villains. Gainage is the same with what is otherwise called wainage. Bracton, lib. i. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a>. 9. speaking of lords and servants, says, Ut si eos destruunt, quod saluum non possit eis esse wainagium suum. And again, lib. iii. tract. 2. cap. 1. Villanus non amerciabitur, nisi salvo wainagio suo: For ancientsly, as it appears both by <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MAGNA_CHARTA">Magna <a cla</a>ss="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CHARTA">Charta</a>, and other books, the villain, when amerced, had his gainage <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> wainage free, to the end his plough might not stand still; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a>, for the same reason, does still allow a like privilege to the husbandman; that is, his draught horses are not in many <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> distrainable. Gainage is also used for the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> itself, or the profit raised by cultivating it.

GAINSBOROUGH

Pages 344-344

a town of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LINCOLNSHIRE">Lincolnshire</a> in England, 148 miles from <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, seated on the east <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANK">bank</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRENT">Trent</a>, which brings tolerably sized vessels with the tide up to the town, about 40 miles from the Humber. It is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> well built town, with a pretty good trade, is noted for its ale, and has the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of an earldom. W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. i. 45. N. Lat 53° 26'. The <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> marsh in its neighbourhood is noted for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> races. The Danes who invaded the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> brought their ships up to this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>; and it was here that Sweno the Dane was murdered by one of the English, while revelling with his companions. In the year 1643 a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> was fought here between the royalists and the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> forces under Cromwell. The <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of inhabitants in 1811 amounted to 5172, of whom nearly 600 were employed in trade and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a>.

GALACTOPHAGI

Pages 344-344

and Galactopoe, in antiquity, persons who lived wholly on <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILK">milk</a>, without corn <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of any other food. The words are compounded of γάλα, γαλακτός, milk; φαίνω, to eat; and ποτεῖν, I drink. Certain nations in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SCYTHIA">Scythia</a> Asiatica, as the Getæ, Nomades, &c. are famous, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of galactophagi, or milk-eaters. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a> makes their eloge, Iliad, lib. iii. <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>, in his <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">geography</a>, places the Galactophagi between the Riphean <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> on one side, and the Hyrcanian <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> on the other.

GALANTHUS

Pages 344-344

the Snow-Drop, a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the hexandria class, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the ninth order, Spathaceæ. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

GALASHIELS

Pages 344-344

a small town in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SELKIRKSHIRE">Selkirkshire</a> in Scotland, situated on the stream called Gala <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">Water</a>, at the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where it joins the Tweed. Galashiels and its neighbourhood have been <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> famous for the manufacture of coarse woollen cloth, known by the name of Galashiels grey. The improved state of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRICULTURE">agriculture</a> of this vicinity is much commended. Galashiels is 30 miles S. E. from <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a>, and had 986 inhabitants in 1811.

GALATA

Pages 344-344

a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> suburb belonging to Constantinople, opposite to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERAGLIO">seraglio</a>, on the other side of the harbour. It is here the Greeks, Armenians, Franks, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>, and Jews inhabit, and are allowed the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> of their respective worships. GALATÆA, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Galatha, in fabulous <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NYMPH">nymph</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEREUS">Nereus</a> and Doris. She was passionately loved by the Cyclops <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLYPHEMUS">Polyphemus</a>, whom she treated with coldness and disdain; while Acis, a shepherd of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a>, enjoyed her unbounded affection. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a> of these two lovers was disturbed by the jealousy of the Cyclops, who crushed his rival to pieces with a piece of a broken rock while he reposed on the bosom of Galatæa. The nymph was inconsolable for the loss of Acis; and as she could not restore him to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, she changed him into a fountain.

GALATIA

Pages 344-347

the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> name of a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASIA_MINOR"><a class="</a>xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINOR">Minor</a>, now called <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMASIA">Amasia</a>. It was bounded on the east by Cappadocia, on the west by Bithynia, on the south by Pamphylia, and on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by the Euxine <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. It was the north <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHRYGIA">Phrygia</a> Magna; but upon being occupied by the Gauls was called Galatia; and because situated amidst Greek colonies, and itself mixed with Greeks, Gallogrecia; Strabo calls it Galatia and Gallogrecia; hence a twofold name of the people; Galates and Gallogreci. The Greeks called it Gallia Parva; to distinguish it from the Transalpina, both which they called Galatia. It was reduced under the subjection of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of Augustus, and is now in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the Turks. Here St Paul founded a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, to which he directed that epistle which is still known by the name of the Epistle to the Galatians, and was written to reclaim them from the observation of Jewish ordinances, into which they had been seduced by some false teachers.

GALAX

Pages 347-347

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the pentandria class, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking with those of which the order is doubtful. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a>.

GALAXY

Pages 347-347

in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a>, that <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LUMINOUS">luminous</a> track, which seems to encompass the heavens like a swath, scarf, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> girdle; and which is easily perceivable in a clear night, especially when the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOON">moon</a> does not appear. The Greeks call it Γαλαξίας, Galaxy, of Γάλα, γαλακτός, <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILK">Milk</a>; on account of its <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> and appearance; the Latins, for the same reason, call it via lactea; or milky way. It passes between Sagittarius and Gemini, and divides the sphere into two parts; it is unequally <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>; and in some parts is single, in others <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> poets, and even philosophers, speak of the Galaxy as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a> or way by which the heroes went to heaven. <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a> makes it a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-METEOR">meteor</a>, formed of a crowd of vapours, drawn into that <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> by certain <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> stars disposed in the regions of the heavens answering hereto. Others, finding that the Galaxy was seen all over the globe, that it always corresponded to the same fixed stars, and that it transcended the height of the highest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANETS">planets</a>, set aside Aristotle's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, and placed the Galaxy in the firmament, or region of the fixed stars, and concluded it to be nothing but an assemblage of an infinite <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of minute stars. Since the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TELESCOPE">telescope</a>, this opinion has been abundantly confirmed. By directing a good telescope to any part of the milky way; where before we only <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> a confused whiteness, we now descry an innumerable multitude of little stars, so remote, that a naked eye confounds them. See ASTRONOMY, No. 211.

GALBA

Pages 347-347

Sergius Sulpicius, a Roman <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a>, born the 24th of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a>, five years before the Christian era. He was gradually raised to the greatest offices of the state, and exercised his power in the provinces with the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EQUITY">equity</a> and unremitting diligence. He dedicated the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> to solitary pursuits, chiefly to avoid the suspicions of Nero. His disapprobation of the emperor's oppressive command in the provinces was the cause of new disturbances. Nero ordered him to be put to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>; but he escaped from the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> of the executioner, and was publicly saluted emperor. When he was seated on the throne, he suffered himself to be governed by favourites, who exposed the goods of the citizens to <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALE">sale</a> to gratify their avarice. Exemptions were sold at a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> price; and the crime of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDER">murder</a> was blotted out, and impunity purchased, with a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> sum of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a>. Such irregularities in the emperor's ministers greatly displeased the people; and when Galba refused to pay the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> the money which he had promised them when he was raised to the throne, they assassinated him in the 73rd year of his <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, and the eighth <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of his reign. The virtues which had shone so bright in Galba when a private <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, totally disappeared when he ascended the throne; and he who showed himself the most impartial judge, forgot the duties of an emperor and of a father of his people.

GALBANUM

Pages 347-347

in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHARMACY">Pharmacy</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUM">gum</a> issuing from the stem of an umbelliferous plant growing in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a> and many parts of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>. See BUBON, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. The juice, as brought to us, is semipellucid, soft, tenacious; of a strong, and to some unpleasant, smell; and a bitterish warm <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>: the better sort is in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a> coloured masses, which, on being opened, appear composed of clear <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> tears. Geoffroy relates, that a dark greenish <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a> is to be obtained from this simple by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DISTILLATION">distillation</a>, which, upon repeated rectifications, becomes of an elegant sky blue <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>. The purer sorts of galbanum are said by some to dissolve entirely in wine, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VINEGAR">vinegar</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>; but these liquors are only partial menstrua with regard to this drug; nor do spirit of wine or oils prove more effectual in this respect: the best <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISSOLVENT">dissolvent</a> is a mixture of two parts spirit of wine and one of water. Galbanum agrees in virtue with gum ammoniacum; but is generally accounted less efficacious in asthmas, and more so in hysterical complaints. It is an ingredient in various officinal compositions. See <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MATERIA_MEDICA">Materia Medica</a> Index.

GALEA

Pages 348-348

in antiquity, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASQUE">casque</a>, head piece, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> morion, coming <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to the shoulders, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a>; though Camillus, according to Plutarch, ordered those of his <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> to be of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, as being the stronger metal. The lower <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of it was called buccula, and on the top was a crest. The velites wore a light galea, made of the skin of some wild beast to make it more terrible.

GALEASSE

Pages 348-348

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> low-built vessel, in which both sails and oars are used, and the largest of all the vessels that make <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the latter. It may carry twenty guns, and has a stern capable of lodging a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARINES">marines</a>. It has three <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MASTS">masts</a>, which are never to be lowered <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> taken <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a>. It has also thirty-two benches of rowers; and to each <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BENCH">bench</a> six or <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> slaves, who sit under cover. This vessel is at present used only by the Venetians.

GALEGIA

Pages 348-348

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the dadelphia class; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 32d order, Papilionaceae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

GALEN

Pages 348-348

a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> township in the state of New-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORK">York</a>, situated on the creek of Canadaque, about 12 miles <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-west of Cayuga lake, and 13 south by east of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> Sodus.

GALENA

Pages 348-348

a name given by mineralogists to a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> ore. See Lead-Mine, and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINERALOGY">Mineralogy</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. It was also the original name given by Andromachus to the theriaca, from its effect in bringing on a pleasing calm over the blood and spirits on taking it.

GALENIA

Pages 348-348

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the ocandria class; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 13th order, Succulentae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

GALENIC

Pages 348-349
or Galenical, in Medicine, is that manner of considering and treating diseases, founded on the principle of Galen, or introduced by Galen. This author, collecting and digesting what the physicians before him had done, and explaining every thing according to the strictest doctrine of the Peripatetics, set physic on a new footing: he introduced the doctrine of the four elements; the cardinal qualities and their degrees; and the four humours or temperaments. Galenic is more frequently used as contradistinguished from chemical. The distinction of galenical and chemical was occasioned sioned by a division of the practitioners of medicine into two sects, which happened on the introduction of chemistry into medicine. Then the chemists, arrogating to themselves every kind of merit and ability, stirred up an opposition to their pretensions, founded on the invariable adherence of the other party to the ancient practice. And though this division into the two sects of galenists and chemists has long since ceased, yet the distinction of medicines which resulted from it is still sometimes observed. Galenical medicines are those which are formed by the easier preparations of herbs, roots, &c. by infusion, decoction, &c. and by combining and multiplying ingredients; while those of chemistry draw their more intimate and remote virtues by means of fire and elaborate preparations, as calcination, digestion, fermentation, &c.

GALENISTS

Pages 349-349
or Galenites, in church history, a branch of Mennonites or Anabaptists, who take in several of the opinions of the Socinians, or rather Arians, touching the divinity of our Saviour. In 1664 the Waterlandians were divided into two parties, of which the one were called Galenists, and the other Apostolians. They are thus called from their leader Abr. Galenus, a learned and eloquent physician of Amsterdam, who considered the Christian religion as a system that laid much less stress on faith than practice; and who was for taking into the communion of the Mennonites all those who acknowledged the divine origin of the books of the Old and New Testament, and led holy and virtuous lives. GALEON. See Galleon.

GALEOPSIS

Pages 349-349

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the didynamia class; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 42d order, Verticillatae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

GALIANI

Pages 349-349

FERDINAND, an eminent Italian writer. See Supplement. GALIC <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> GAELIC <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">Language</a>. See Highlands.

GALICIA

Pages 349-349

a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, bounded on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> and west by the ocean, on the south by <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PORTUGAL">Portugal</a>, and on the east by <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTURIAS">Asturias</a> and the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of Leon. The <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> is temperate along the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a>; but, in other places, it is <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLD">cold</a> and moist. It is but thinly peopled; and the produce is wine, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAX">flax</a>, and citrons: the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> is unequal, but affords good pasture. St Jago di <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPOSTELLA">Compostella</a> is the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> town.

GALILEANS

Pages 349-349

a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECT">sect</a> of the Jews. Their founder was one Judas a native of Galilee, from which <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> they derived their name. Their <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a>, esteeming it an indignity for the Jews to pay tribute to strangers, raised up his countrymen against the edict of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Augustus, which had ordered a <a class="xref" href="../1823/vol6.html#article-TAXATION">taxation</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> enrolment of all the subjects of the Roman empire. They pretended that God alone should be owned as <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">Master</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a>, and in other respects were of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHARISEES">Pharisees</a>; but, as they judged it unlawful to pray for <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INFIDEL">infidel</a> princes, they separated themselves from the rest of the Jews, and performed their sacrifices apart. As our Saviour and his apostles were of Galilee, they were suspected to be of the sect of Galileans; and it was on this principle, as St Jerome observes, that the Pharisees laid a snare for him; asking, Whether it was lawful to give tribute to Cassar; that in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> he denied it, they might have an occasion of accusing him.

GALILEE

Pages 349-349

once a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Judea, now of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, was bounded by Mount Lebanon on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, by the river Jordan and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> of Galilee on the east, by the Chison on the south, and by the Mediterranean on the west. It was the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCENE">scene</a> of many of our Saviour's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIRACLES">miracles</a>; but the bounds of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> are not now well known, nor yet the places where many of the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> stood.

GALILEO GALILEI

Pages 349-350

the famous mathematician and astronomer, was the son of a Florentine nobleman, and born in the year 1564. He had from his infancy a strong inclination to <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a>; and made prodigious progress in these sciences. In 1592, he was chosen professor of mathematics at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PADUA">Padua</a>; and during his abode there he invented, it is said, the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TELESCOPE">telescope</a>; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a>, according to others, improved that <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a>, so as to make it fit for astronomical observations: (See <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a>, No. 27.) In 1611, Cosmo II. <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TUSCANY">Tuscany</a>, sent for him to <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PISA">Pisa</a>, where he made him professor of mathematics with a handsome salary, and soon after inviting him to <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLORENCE">Florence</a>, gave him the office and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a> and mathematician to his highness. He had been but a few years at Florence, before he was convinced by sad <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a>, that <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a>'s doctrine, however ill grounded, was held too sacred to be called in question. Having observed some solar spots in 1612, he printed that discovery the following year at Rome; in which, and in some other pieces, he ventured to assert the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> of the Copernican system, and brought several new arguments to confirm it. For these he was cited before the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INQUISITION">inquisition</a>; and after some months imprisonment, was released upon a simple <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROMISE">promise</a>, that he would renounce his heretical opinions, and not defend them by word or <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>. But having afterwards, in 1632, published at Florence his "Dialogues of the two greatest systems of the world, the Ptolemaic and Copernican," he was again cited before the inquisition, and committed to the prison of that <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> at Rome. In <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 22nd N. S. that year, the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONGREGATION">congregation</a> convened; and in his presence pronounced <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a> against him and his books, obliging him to abjure his errors in the most solemn manner; committed him to the prison of their office during <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>; and enjoined him, as a saving <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PENANCE">penance</a>, for three years to come, to repeat once a-<a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-WEEK">week</a> the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PENITENTIAL">penitential</a> psalms: reserving to themselves, however, the power of moderating, changing, or taking away altogether or in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a>, the above-mentioned punish- ment and penance. On this sentence, he was detained a prisoner till 1634; and his "Dialogues of the system of the World" were burnt at Rome. He lived ten years after this, seven of which were employed in making still further discoveries with his telescope. But by the continual application to that instrument, added to the damage he received in his sight from the nocturnal <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a>, his eyes grew gradually weaker, till he became totally <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLIND">blind</a> in 1639. He bore this calamity with <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATIENCE">patience</a> and resignation, worthy of a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> philosopher. The loss neither broke his spirit, nor hindered the course of his studies. He supplied the defect by constant meditation: whereby he prepared a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of materials, and began to dictate his own conceptions; when, by a distemper of three months continuance, wasting away by degrees, he expired at Arcetri near Florence, in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 1642, N. S. in the 78th year of his <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>. Among various useful inventions of which Galileo was the author, is that of the simple <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PENDULUM">pendulum</a>, which he had made <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of in his astronomical experiments. He had thought of applying it to clocks; but did not execute it: the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> of that <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> was reserved for Vicenzo his son, who made the experiment at <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a> in 1649; and M. Huygens afterwards carried this invention to perfection. He wrote a great <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of treatises, several of which were published in a collection by Signior Mendessi, under the title of L'<a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OPERA">opera</a> di Galileo Galilei Lynceo. Some of these, with others of his pieces, were translated into English and published by Thomas <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALISBURY">Salisbury</a>, Esq. in his mathematical collections, &c. in two volumes folio. A volume also of his letters to several learned men, and solutions of several problems, were printed at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOLOGNA">Bologna</a> in quarto. Besides these, he wrote many others, which were unfortunately lost through his wife's <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a>; who, solicited by her confessor, gave him leave to peruse her husband's <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUSCRIPTS">manuscripts</a>; of which he tore and took away as many as he said were not fit to be published. GALINACEUS <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAPIS">LAPIS</a>. See GALLINACEUS.

GALIUM

Pages 350-350

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the te-trandria class; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 47th order, Stellatae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

GALL

Pages 350-352

in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, denotes any protuberance <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> tumour produced by the puncture of insects on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> and trees of different kinds. These <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GALLS">galls</a> are of various forms and sizes, and no less different with regard to their internal structure. Some have only one cavity, and others a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of small cells communicating with each other. Some of them are as hard as the wood of the tree they grow on, whilst others are soft and spongy; the first being termed gall nuts, and the latter berry galls, or apple galls. The general history of the gall is this. An insect of the fly kind (the cynips) is instructed by <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> to take care for the safety of her young, by lodging her eggs in a woody substance, where they <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be defended from all injuries: she for this purpose wounds the leaves or tender branches of a tree; and the lacerated vessels, discharging their contents, soon form tumours about the holes thus made. The <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> coat of this excrecence is dried by the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a>; and grows into a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> which bears some resemblance to the bow of an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCH">arch</a>, or the roundness of a kernel. This little <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALL">ball</a> receives its nutriment, growth, and vegetation, as the other parts of the tree, by slow degrees, and is what we call the gall <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUT">nut</a>. The worm that is hatched under this spacious vault, finds in the substance of the ball, which is as yet very tender, a subsistence suitable to its nature; gnaws and digests it till the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> comes for its transformation to a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NYMPH">nymph</a>, and from that state of existence changes into a fly. After this, the insect, perceiving itself duly provided with all things requisite, disengages itself soon from its confinement, and takes its flight into the open air. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>, however, is not similar with respect to the gall nut that grows in autumn. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLD">cold</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a> frequently comes on before the worm is transformed into a fly, or before the fly can pierce through its enclosure. The nut falls with the leaves; and although you may imagine that the fly which lies within is lost, yet in reality it is not so; on the contrary, its being covered up so <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">close</a>, is the means of its preservation. Thus it spends the winter in a warm <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, where every crack and cranny of the nut is well stopped up; and lies buried as it were under a heap of leaves, which preserves it from the injuries of the weather. This apartment, however, though so commodious a retreat in the winter, is a perfect prison in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>. The fly, roused from its <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETHARGY">lethargy</a> by the first heats, breaks its way through, and ranges where it pleases. A very small aperture is sufficient, since at this time the fly is but a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DIMINUTIVE">diminutive</a> creature. Besides, the ringlets whereof its body is composed dilate and become pliant in the passage. Oak galls put, in a very small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a>, into a solution of vitriol in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, though but a very weak one, give it a purple or violet <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>: which, as it grows stronger, becomes <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a>; and on this <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> depends the art of making our <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INK">ink</a>, as also the arts of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DYEING">dyeing</a> and dressing <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>, and other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a>. See Ink, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. The best galls come from <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALEPPO">Aleppo</a>: these are not quite round and smooth like the other sorts, but have several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TUBERCLES">tubercles</a> on the surface. Galls have a very austere styptic <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>, without any smell: they are very strong astringents, and as such have been sometimes made <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of both internally and externally, but are not much taken notice of by the present practice. Some recommend an ointment of powdered galls and hogs <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-LARD">lard</a> as very effectual in certain painful states of haemorrhoids; and it is alleged, that the internal use of galls has cured intermittents after the Peruvian bark has failed. A mixture of galls with a bitter and aromatic has been proposed as a substitute for the bark. Gall, St., a considerable town in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWITZERLAND">Switzerland</a>, and in the Upper Thurgow, with a rich and celebrated <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">abbey</a>, whose <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABBOT">abbot</a> is a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of the empire. This <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> has for some time been a republic, in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLIANCE">alliance</a> with the cantons. It is not very <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>; but well built, neat, and populous. It contains about 10,000 inhabitants, who are chiefly employed in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> manufacture; and make annually, it is said, 40,000 pieces of linen, of 200 ells each; which renders it one of the richest <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> in Switzerland. The inhabitants are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a>; for which reason there are often <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> contests between them and the abbey about <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> affairs. It is seated in a narrow barren valley, between two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, and upon two small streams. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 2° 59'. N. Lat. 47° 38'. Gall-Fly. See Cynips, Entomology Index. Galla, an Abyssinian <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>, originally dwelling, as Mr Bruce supposes, under the line, and exercising the profession of shepherds, which they still continue to do. For a number of years, our author tells us, they have been constantly migrating northwards, though the cause of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIGRATION">migration</a> is not known. At first they had no horses; the reason of which was, that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> they came from did not allow these animals to breed: but as they proceeded northward and conquered some of the Abyssinian provinces, they soon furnished themselves with such numbers, that they are now almost entirely cavalry, making little account of infantry in their armies. On advancing to the frontiers of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABYSSINIA">Abyssinia</a>, the multitude divided, and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> directed their course towards the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> ocean; after which, having made a settlement in the eastern part of the continent, they turned southward into the countries of Bali and Dawaw, which they entirely conquered, and settled there in the year 1537. Another <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> having taken a westerly course, spread themselves in a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEMICIRCLE">semicircle</a> along the banks of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NILE">Nile</a>; surrounding the country of Gojam, and passing eastward behind the country of the Agows, extended their possessions as far as the territories of the Gongas and Gafats. Since that time the Nile has been the boundary of their possessions; though they have very frequently plundered, and sometimes conquered, the Abyssinian provinces on the other side of the river, but have never made any permanent settlement in these parts. A third division has settled to the southward of the low country of Shoa, which the governor of that <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> has permitted, in order to form a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BARRIER">barrier</a> betwixt him and the territories of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a>, on whom he scarcely acknowledges any dependence. The Galla are of a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROWN">brown</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPLEXION">complexion</a>, and have long black <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>; but some of them who live in the valleys are entirely black. At first their <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> food was <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILK">milk</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUTTER">butter</a>; but since their intercourse with the Abyssinians, they have learned to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLOUGH">plough</a> and sow their <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a>, and to make <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a>. They seem to have predilection for the number <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a>, and each of the three divisions already mentioned is subdivided into seven tribes. In behaviour they are extremely barbarous; and live in continual <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> with the Abyssinians, whom they <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDER">murder</a> without mercy as often as they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> into their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>. They cut off the privities of the men, and hang them up in their houses by way of trophies; and are so cruel as to rip up women with child, in hopes of thus destroying a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MALE">male</a>. Yet notwithstanding their excessive cruelty abroad, they live under the strictest <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a> at home; and every broil or quarrel is instantly punished according to the nature of the offence. Each of the three divisions of the Galla above mentioned has a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of its own; and they also have a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a>, from among whom the sovereign can only be chosen: however, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONALTY">commonalty</a> are not excluded from rising to the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBLES">nobles</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they distinguish themselves very much in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>. None of the nobility can be elected till upwards of 40 years of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, unless he has with his own <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> killed a number of enemies which added to his own age makes up 40. There is a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of each of the seven tribes, which meets separately in its own district, to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> how many are to be left behind for the governing and cultivating of the territory, and other matters of importance. These nations have all a great veneration for a tree which grows plentifully in their country, called wanszy, and which these superstitious people are even said to adore as a god. Their assemblies for the choice of a king are all held under one of these trees; and when the sovereign is chosen, they put a bludgeon of this wood in his hand by way of sceptre, and a garland of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> upon his head. The Galla are reported to be very good <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a>, especially in case of surprise; but, like most other barbarians, have no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSTANCY">constancy</a> nor perseverance after the first attack. They will, however, perform extraordinary marches, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWIMMING">swimming</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> holding by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>'s tail, and thus being enabled to do very great mischief by reason of the rapidity of their movements. They are excellent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> horse for a regular <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> in a hostile country; but are very indifferently armed, on account of the scarcity of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> among them. Their <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> arms are lances made of wood sharpened at the end, and hardened in the fire; and their shields are composed only of one single fold of bull's hide; so that they are extremely apt to warp by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>, or become too soft. soft in wet weather. They are exceedingly cruel; and make a shrill horrid noise at the beginning of every engagement, which greatly terrifies the horses, and very often the barbarous riders which oppose them. The Galla, according to Mr Bruce's account, are somewhat below the middle size, but extremely light and nimble. The women are fruitful; and suffer so little in childbearing, that they do not even confine themselves for a single <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> after delivery. They plough, sow, and reap the corn, which is trodden out by the cattle; but the men have all the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> of the cattle in the fields. In their customs they are filthy to the last <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>; plaiting their hair with the guts of oxen, which they likewise twist round their middle, and which by the quick <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUTREFACTION">putrefaction</a> occasion an abominable stench. They anoint their heads and whole bodies with butter or grease; in which, as well as in other respects, they greatly resemble the Hottentots. It has been supposed that they have no <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> whatever; but Mr Bruce is of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> that this is a mistake.
