Suppose \( p \) the number of cases in which an event may happen, and \( q \) the number of cases wherein it may not happen, both sides have the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of probability, which is to each other as \( p \) to \( q \). If two gamesters, A and B, engage on this footing, that, if the cases \( p \) happen, A shall win; but if \( q \) happen, B shall win, and the stake be \( a \); the chance of A will be \( \frac{p}{q+p} \), and that of B \( \frac{q}{p+q} \); consequently, if they sell the expectancies, they should have that for them respectively. If A and B play with a single dice, on this condition, that, if A throw two or more aces at eight throws, he shall win; otherwise B shall win; What is the ratio of their chances? Since there is but one case wherein an ace may turn up, and five wherein it may not, let \( a = 1 \), and \( b = 5 \). And again, since there are eight throws of the die, let \( n = 8 \); and you will have \( a + b^n - b^n - n a b^n - 1 \), to \( b^n + n a b^n - 1 \); that is, the chance of A will be to that of B as 665997 to 10156525, or nearly as 2 to 3. A and B are engaged at single quoits; and, after playing some time, A wants 4 of being up, and B 6; but B is so much the better gamester, that his chance against A upon a single throw would be as 3 to 2; What is the ratio of their chances? Since A wants 4, and B 6, the game will be ended at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> throws; therefore, raise \( a + b \) to the ninth power, and it will be \( a^9 + 9 a^8 b + 36 a^7 b^2 + 84 a^6 b^3 + 126 a^5 b^4 + 126 a^4 b^5 + 84 a^3 b^6 + 36 a^2 b^7 + 6 a b^8 + b^9 \): call \( a = 3 \), and \( b = 2 \), and you will have the ratio of chances in numbers, viz. 1759077 to 194048. A and B play at single quoits, and A is the best gamester, so that he can give B 2 in 3: What is the ratio of their chances at a single throw? Suppose the chances as \( z \) to 1, and raise \( z^2 + 1 \) to its <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUBE">cube</a>, which will be \( z^3 + 3z^2 + 3z + 1 \). Now since A could give B 2 out of 3, A might undertake to win three throws running; and consequently the chances in this case will be as \( z^3 \) to \( 3z^2 + 3z + 1 \); hence \( z^3 = 3z^2 + 3z + 1 \); or \( 2z^3 = 3z^2 + 3z + 1 \). And therefore \( z = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2} - 1} \). The chances, therefore, are \( \frac{1}{\sqrt{2} - 1} \), and 1, respectively. Again, suppose I have two wagers depending, in the first of which I have 3 to 2 the best of the lay, and in the second 7 to 4; What is the probability I win both wagers? 1. The probability of winning the first is \( \frac{3}{5} \), that is, the number of chances I have to win, divided by the number of all the chances; the probability of winning the second is \( \frac{7}{11} \): therefore, multiplying these two fractions together, the product will be \( \frac{21}{55} \), which is the probability of winning both wagers. Now, this fraction being subtracted from 1, the remainder is \( \frac{34}{55} \), which is the probability I do not win both wagers: therefore the odds against me are 34 to 21. 2. If I would know what the probability is of winning the first, and losing the second, I argue thus; the probability of winning the first is \( \frac{3}{5} \), the probability of losing the second is \( \frac{4}{11} \): therefore multiplying \( \frac{3}{5} \) by \( \frac{4}{11} \), the product \( \frac{12}{55} \) will be the probability of my winning the first and losing the second; which being subtracted from 1, there will remain \( \frac{43}{55} \), which is the probability I do not win the first, and at the same time lose the second. 3. If I would know what the probability is of winning the second, and at the same time losing the first, I say thus: The probability of winning the second is \( \frac{7}{11} \); the probability of losing the first is \( \frac{4}{5} \): therefore, multiplying these two fractions together, the product \( \frac{28}{55} \) is the probability I win the second, and also lose the first. 4. If I would know what the probability is of losing both wagers, I say, the probability of losing the first is \( \frac{2}{5} \), and the probability of losing the second \( \frac{4}{11} \): therefore the probability of losing them both is \( \frac{8}{55} \); which, being subtracted from 1, there remains \( \frac{47}{55} \): therefore, the odds of losing both wagers is 47 to 8. This way of reasoning is applicable to the happening or failing of any events that may fall under consideration. Thus if I would know what the probability is of missing an ace four times together with a die, this I consider as the failing of four different events. Now the probability of missing the first is \( \frac{5}{6} \), the second is also \( \frac{5}{6} \), the third \( \frac{5}{6} \), and the fourth \( \frac{5}{6} \); therefore the probability of missing it four times together is \( \frac{5}{6} \times \frac{5}{6} \times \frac{5}{6} \times \frac{5}{6} = \frac{625}{1296} \); which being subtracted from 1, there will remain \( \frac{671}{1296} \) for the probability of throwing it once or oftener in three times: therefore the odds against throwing it in three times are 125 to 91. Again, suppose we would know the probability of throwing an ace once in four times, and no more; since the probability of throwing it the first time is \( \frac{1}{6} \), and of missing it the other three times, is \( \frac{5}{6} \times \frac{5}{6} \times \frac{5}{6} \), it follows, that the probability of throwing it the first time, and missing it the other three successive times, is \( \frac{1}{6} \times \frac{5}{6} \times \frac{5}{6} \times \frac{5}{6} = \frac{125}{1296} \); but because it is possible to <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol11.html#article-HIT">hit</a> every throw as well as the first, it follows, that the probability of throwing it once in four throws, and missing it the other three, is \( \frac{4 \times 125}{1296} = \frac{500}{1296} \); which being subtracted from 1, there will remain \( \frac{796}{1296} \) for the probability of throwing it once, and no more, in four times. Therefore, if one undertake to throw an ace once, and no more, in four times, he has 500 to 796 the worst of the lay, or 5 to 8 very near. Suppose two events are such, that one of them has twice as many chances to come up as the other; what is the probability that the event which has the greater number of chances to come up, does not happen twice before the other happens once, which is the case of flinging 7 with two dice before 4 once? Since the number of chances is as 2 to 1, the probability of the first happening before the second is \( \frac{2}{3} \), but the probability of its happening twice before it is \( \frac{2}{3} \times \frac{2}{3} \) or \( \frac{4}{9} \); therefore it is 5 to 4, seven does not come up twice before four once. But, if it were demanded, what must be the proportion of the facilities of the coming up of two events, to make that which has the most chances come up twice, before the other comes up once? The answer is, 12 to 5 very nearly: whence it follows, that the probability of throwing the first before the second is \( \frac{12}{17} \), and the probability of throwing it twice is \( \frac{12}{17} \times \frac{12}{17} \), or \( \frac{144}{289} \); therefore the probability of not doing it is \( \frac{145}{289} \); therefore the odds against it are as 145 to 144, which comes very near an equality. Suppose there is a heap of thirteen cards of one colour, and another heap of thirteen cards of another colour; What is the probability, that, taking one card at a venture out of each head, I shall take out the two aces? The probability of taking the ace out of the first heap is \( \frac{1}{13} \); the probability of taking the ace out of the second heap is \( \frac{1}{13} \); therefore the probability of taking out both aces is \( \frac{1}{13} \times \frac{1}{13} = \frac{1}{169} \), which being subtracted from 1, there will remain \( \frac{168}{169} \): therefore the odds against me are 168 to 1. In cases where the events depend on one another, the manner of arguing is somewhat altered. Thus, suppose that out of one single heap of thirteen cards of one colour I should undertake to take out first the ace; and, secondly, the two: though the probability of taking out the ace be \( \frac{1}{13} \), and the probability of taking out the two be likewise \( \frac{1}{13} \); yet, the ace being supposed as taken out already, there will remain only twelve cards in the heap, which will make the probability of taking out the two to be \( \frac{1}{12} \); therefore the probability of taking out the ace, and then the two, will be \( \frac{1}{13} \times \frac{1}{12} \). In this last question the two events have a dependence on each other; which consists in this, that one of the events events being supposed as having happened, the probability of the other's happening is thereby altered. But the case is not so in the two heaps of cards. If the events in question be \( n \) in number, and be such as have the same number \( a \) of chances by which they may happen, and likewise the same number \( b \) of chances by which they may fail, raise \( a + b \) to the power \( n \). And if A and B play together, on condition that if either one or more of the events in question happen, A shall win, and B lose, the probability of A's winning will be \( \frac{a + b}{a + b}^n - b^n \), and that of B's winning will be \( \frac{b^n}{a + b} \); for when \( a + b \) is actually raised to the power \( n \), the only <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> in which \( a \) does not occur is the last \( b^n \); therefore all the terms but the last are favourable to A. Thus if \( n = 3 \), raising \( a + b \) to the cube \( a^3 + 3a^2b + 3ab^2 + b^3 \), all the terms but \( b^3 \) will be favourable to A; and therefore the probability of A's winning will be \( \frac{a^3 + 3a^2b + 3ab^2 + b^3}{a + b} \), or \( \frac{a + b}{a + b}^3 - b^3 \); and the probability of B's winning will be \( \frac{b^3}{a + b}^3 \). But if A and B play on condition, that if either two or more of the events in question happen, A shall win; the probability of A's winning will be \( \frac{a + b}{a + b}^n - n a b^{n-1} \); for the only two terms in which \( a \) does not occur are the two last, viz. \( n a b^{n-1} \) and \( b^n \).

GAMMONING

Pages 403-403

among seamen, denotes several turns of a rope taken round the bowsprit, and reeved through holes in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KNEES">knees</a> of the head, for the greater security of the bowsprit.

GAMMUT

Pages 403-403

GAMUT, GAM-ut, in Music, a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCALE">scale</a> whereon we may learn to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> the musical notes, ut, re, mi, fa, sol, la, in their several orders and dispositions. See Music. The <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> of this scale is owing to Guido Are-tin, a monk of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AREZZO">Arezzo</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TUSCANY">Tuscany</a>, about the year 1009; though it is not so properly an invention, as an improvement on the diagram <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> scale of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>. See ARETIN. Several alterations have been made in the gammut. M. Le Maire, particularly, has added a seventh <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOTE">note</a>; viz. si; and the English usually throw out both ut and si, and make the other five serve for all.

GANDER

Pages 403-403

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">Ornithology</a>, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MALE">male</a> of the goose kind. See <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANAS">ANAS</a>, Ornithology <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

GANG-WAY

Pages 403-403

is the several <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> ways from one <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the ship to the other; and whatsoever is laid in any of those passages is said to <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> in the gang-way. GAN-GANELLI. See Clement XIV.

GANGES

Pages 403-403

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> and celebrated river of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a>. It has its source in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> which border on Little Thibet, in 78 degrees of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONGITUDE">longitude</a>, and 32 of latitude. It crosses several kingdoms, running from <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-west to south-east; and falls into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BENGAL">Bengal</a> by several mouths. The waters are lowest in April and May, and highest before the end of September. It overflows yearly like the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NILE">Nile</a>; and renders the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of Bengal as fruitful as that of the Delta in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>. The people in these parts hold the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> of this river in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> veneration; and it is visited annually by a prodigious <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of pilgrims from all parts of India. The greatest <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a> that many of the Indians wish for, is to die in this river. The English have several settlements on this river, which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be taken notice of in their proper places.

GANGLION

Pages 403-403

in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SURGERY">Surgery</a>, a hard tubercle, generally moveable, in the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> internal <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the carpus, upon the tendons or ligaments in that part; usually without pain to the patient.

GANGRENE

Pages 403-403

a very <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> and dangerous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of inflammation, wherein the parts affected begin to corrupt, and put on a state of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUTREFACTION">putrefaction</a>. See Medicine, and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SURGERY">Surgery</a>.

GANTLET

Pages 403-403
or Gauntlet, a large kind of glove made of iron, and the fingers covered with small plates. It was formerly worn by the cavaliers, when armed at all points. The word is derived of the French gantlet; and that from gant, or ganti, "glove." The casque and gauntlets were always borne in the ancient marches in ceremony. Gauntlets were not introduced till about the 13th century. The gauntlet was frequently thrown like the glove, by way of challenge. GANTLOPE. See Gauntlope.

GANYMEDE

Pages 403-403

in <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MYTHOLOGY">mythology</a>, a beautiful youth of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHRYGIA">Phrygia</a>, son of Tros and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> to Ilus; according to Lucian, he was the son of Dardanus. <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a> was charmed with him; and carrying him away, made him his cupbearer in the room of Hebe. Some say that he caused him to be carried away by an eagle, and others affirm he was himself the ravisher under the form of that <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BIRD">bird</a>. He deified this youth; and to comfort his father made a present to him of some of those very swift horses upon which the gods rode.

GAOL

Pages 403-404

is used metaphorically for a prison. It is a strong <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> for keeping of debtors, &c., and wherein a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> is restrained of his <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> to answer an offence done against the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a>: and every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> hath two gaols, one for debtors, which may be any house where the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SHERIFF">sheriff</a> pleases; the other for the peace and matters of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>, which is the county gaol. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> a gaol be out of repair, or insufficient, &c., justices of peace, in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> sessions, may <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRACT">contract</a> with workmen for the rebuilding or repairing it; and by their warrant order the sum agreed on for that purpose to be levied on the several <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-HUNDREDS">hundreds</a>, and other divisions in the county, by a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> rate, 11 and 12 <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">Will</a>. III. c. 19. See Prison. GAOL Delivery. The administration of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> being originally in the crown, in former times our kings Gaol in person rode through the realm once in <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> years, to judge of and determine crimes and offences; afterwards justices in eyre were appointed; and since, justices of assize and gaol delivery, &c. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a> of gaol delivery, is a patent in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> from the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> to certain persons, appointing them his justices, or two or three of them, and authorizing them to deliver his gaol, at such a place, of the prisoners in it: for which purpose it commands them to meet at such a place, at the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> they themselves shall appoint; and informs them, that, for the same purpose, the king hath commanded his sheriff of the same county to bring all the prisoners of the gaol, and their attachments, before them at the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> appointed. The justices of gaol delivery are empowered by the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> law to proceed upon indictments of felony, trespass, &c. and to order to execution or reprieve: they may likewise discharge such prisoners, as on their trials are acquitted, and those against whom, on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCLAMATION">proclamation</a> being made, no <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a> has appeared: they have authority to try offenders for <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TREASON">treason</a>, and to punish many particular offences, by statute, 2 Hawk. 24. 2. Hale's Hist. Placit. Cor. 35.

GAOLER

Pages 404-404

the keeper of a gaol <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> prison. Sheriffs are to make such gaolers for whom they <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be answerable: but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> there be any default in the gaoler, an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTION">action</a> lies against him for an escape, &c. yet the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SHERIFF">sheriff</a> is most usually <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a>; 2d Inst. 592. Where a gaoler kills a prisoner by hard usage, it is felony; 3d Inst. 52. No fee shall be taken by gaolers, but what is allowed by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a>, and settled by the judges, who may determine petitions against their extortions, &c. Geo. II. c. 22.

GAONS

Pages 404-404

a certain order of Jewish doctors, who appeared in the East, after the closing of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TALMUD">Talmud</a>. The word Gaons signifies "excellent, sublime;" as in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a> we formerly had Irrefragable, Sublime, Resolute, Angelic, and Subtile doctors. The Gaons succeeded the Seburaans <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Opiners about the beginning of the sixth century. Chanan Meischtia was the head and first of the excellents. He restored the academy of Pandebita, which had been shut up for 30 years.

GARAMA

Pages 404-404

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the Garaniantes in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBYA">Libya</a> Interior; near the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a> of the Cinyphus, now in ruins. Garamantes the people. It lay to the south of Gætulia, extending from the springs of the Cinyphus, and the adjacency of the river Gir, to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> which form at the Vallis Garamantica (Pliny): <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> from the springs of the Bagrades to the lake Nuba (<a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>).

GARAMOND

Pages 404-404
Claude, a very ingenious letter-founder, was born at Paris; where he began, in the year 1519, to found his printing types free from all the remains of the Gothic, or (as it is generally called) the black letter, and brought them to such perfection, that he had the glory of surpassing all who went before him, and of being scarcely ever excelled by his successors in that useful art. His types were prodigiously multiplied: both by the great number of matrices he struck, and the types formed in resemblance of his in all parts of Europe. Thus in Italy, Germany, England, and Holland, the booksellers, by way of recommending their books, distinguished the type by Garamond's name; and in particular the small Roman was by way of excellence known among the printers of these nations by the name of Garamond's small Roman. By the special command of King Francis I. he founded three sizes of Greek types for the use of Robert Stephens, who with them printed all his beautiful editions of the New Testament, and other Greek authors. He died at Paris in 1561.

GARASSE

Pages 404-404

Francis, a remarkable Jesuitical writer, the first author of that irreconcilable enmity that still subsists between the Jesuits and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JANSENISTS">Jansenists</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of Rome, was born at Angoulesme in 1585, and entered the Jesuits <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> in 1600. As he had a quick imagination, a strong <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VOICE">voice</a>, and a peculiar turn to <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WIT">wit</a>, he became a popular preacher in the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> cities of France; but not content with this <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a>, he distinguished himself still more by his writings, which were bold, licentious, and produced much controversy. The most considerable in its consequences was entitled La <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOMME">somme</a> theologique des veritez capitales de la <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> Creienne; which was first attacked by the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABBOT">abbot</a> of St Cyran, who observing in it a prodigious <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of falsifications of the Scriptures and of the fathers, besides many heretical and impious opinions, conceived the honour of the church required him to undertake a refutation. Accordingly he published a full answer to it; while Garasse's book was also under <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXAMINATION">examination</a> of the doctors of the Sorbonne, by whom it was afterwards condemned. Garasse replied to St Cyran; but the two parties of Jesuits and Jansenists, of whom these were respectively the champions, grew to an implacable animosity against each other, that is not even now likely to subside. The Jesuits were forced to remove their <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> to a distance from <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>; where, probably weary of his inactive obscurity, when the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAGUE">plague</a> raged at Poictiers in 1631, he begged leave of his superior to attend the sick, in which charitable office he caught the disorder, and died.

GARBE

Pages 404-404

in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERALDRY">Heraldry</a>, a sheaf of any kind of grain, borne in several coats of arms, and said to represent <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>, as a bunch of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAPES">grapes</a> does autumn.

GARBLE

Pages 404-404

a word used to signify the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTION">action</a> of separating the dross and dust from spice, drugs, &c. Garbling is the cleansing and purifying the good from the bad; and may come from the Italian garbo; i.e. finery <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> neatness: and hence, probably, we say, when we see a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> in a neat <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HABIT">habit</a>, that he is in handsome garb.

GARCILASSO DE LA VEGA

Pages 404-405

an eminent Spanish poet, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOLEDO">Toledo</a>, in 1503. He was the younger son of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a>, who had been employed in negotiating business of importance. Garcilasso was distinguished for his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WIT">wit</a> and bravery, and in a particular manner for his poetical talents. He was chiefly instrumental in giving popularity to an innovation of his friend Boscan, who introduced <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> borrowed from the Italians. His works consist chiefly of pastorals, which have a tedious prolixity. He is chiefly noted for tenderness, which is remarkably conspicuous in some of his sonnets. He is freer of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOMBAST">bombast</a> than the generality of his countrymen, owing to his familiar acquaintance with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>; and it is said that his learning and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> were superior to his genius. He followed the profession of arms, and attended <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> V. in a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of his expeditions. He lost his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> at the attack of a fortress in Provence, when only 33 years of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>. Garcilasso is also the name of an author, a native of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSCO">Cusco</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERU">Peru</a>, who composed a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLORIDA">Florida</a> in Spanish, and another of Peru and its Incas.

GARCINIA

Pages 405-405

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the dodecandra class; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 18th order, Bicornes. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

GARCON

Pages 405-405
or GARSON, a French term, literally signifying a boy, but also applied to divers inferior officers, amongst us called groom, garçônes.

GARD

Pages 405-405

a department in the south of France. The <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> which lies among the Cevennes is rugged and barren; but the south part is fertile and populous. It contains <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, and pit coal. The whole <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of inhabitants in 1815 was 322,000, of whom about one half were <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NISMES">Nismes</a> is the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> town.

GARDANT

Pages 405-405
or GUARDANT, in Heraldry, denotes any beast full faced, and looking right forward.

GARDEN

Pages 406-415

a piece of ground properly laid out, cultivated and ornamented with a variety of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>, &c. See <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GARDENING">GARDENING</a>. Gardens are usually distinguished into flower garden, fruit garden, and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KITCHEN">kitchen</a> garden: the first of which, being designed for <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> and ornament, is to be placed in the most conspicuous <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a>, that is, next to the back <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRONT">front</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>; and the two latter, being designed for <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>, should be placed less in sight. But though the fruit and kitchen gardens are here mentioned as two distinct gardens, yet they are now usually in one; and that with good reason, since they both require a good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> and exposure, and equally require to be placed out of the view of the house. In the choice of a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> proper for a garden, the most essential <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">points</a> to be considered are, the situation, the soil, the exposure, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, and prospect. 1st. As to the situation, it ought to be such a one as is wholesome, and in a place neither too <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> nor too low; for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> a garden be too high, it <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be exposed to the winds, which are very prejudicial to trees; and if it be too low, the dampness, the vermine, and the venomous creatures that breed in ponds and marshy places, add much to their insalubrity. The most happy situation is on the side of a hill, especially if the slope be easy, and in a manner imperceptible; if a good <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> ground be near the house; and if it abounds with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a> of water: for, being sheltered from the fury of the winds and the violent <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, a temperate <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> will be there enjoyed; and the water that descends from the top of the hill, either from springs <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">rain</a>, will not only supply fountains, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CANALS">canals</a>, and cascades for ornament, but, when it has performed its office, will water the adjacent valleys, and, if it be not suffered to stagnate, will render them fertile and wholesome. 2dly, A good <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> or soil is next to be considered; for it is scarce possible to make a fine garden in a bad soil. There are indeed ways to meliorate ground, but they are very expensive; and sometimes, when the expense has been bestowed of laying good earth three feet deep over the whole surface, a whole garden has been ruined, when the roots of the trees have come to reach the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> bottom. To judge of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of the soil, observe whether there be any heath, thistles, or such like weeds, growing spontaneously in it; for they are certain signs that the ground is <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a>. Or if there be <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> trees growing thereabouts, observe whether they grow crooked, ill-shaped, and grubby; and whether they are of a faded green, and full of moss, or infested with vermine: if this be the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>, the place is to be rejected. But, on the contrary, if it be covered with good grass fit for pasture, you may then be encouraged to try the depth of the soil. To know this, dig holes in several places, six feet wide and four deep; and if you find three feet of good earth it will do very well, but less than two will not be sufficient. The quality of good ground, is neither to be stony nor too hard to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>; neither too dry, too moist, nor too <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SANDY">sandy</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>; nor too strong and clayey, which is the worst of all for gardens. 3dly, The next requisite is water; the want of which is one of the greatest inconveniences that can attend a garden, and will bring a certain mortality upon whatever is planted in it, especially in the greater droughts that often happen in a hot and dry situation in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>; besides its usefulness in fine gardens for making fountains, canals, cascades, &c. which are the greatest ornaments of a garden. 4thly, The last thing to be considered is the prospect of a fine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>; and though this is not so absolutely necessary as water, yet it is one of the most agreeable beauties of a fine garden: besides, if a garden be planted in a low place that has no kind of prospect, it will not only be disagreeable but unwholesome. In the laying out and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTING">planting</a> of gardens, the beauties of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> should always be studied; for the nearer a garden approaches to nature, the longer it will please. According to Mr Miller, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AREA">area</a> of a handsome garden may take up 30 or 40 acres, but not more; and the following rules should be observed in the disposition of it. There ought always to be a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a> of at least three steps from the house to the gardens; this will render the house more dry and wholesome, and the prospect on entering the garden more extensive.—The first thing that ought to present itself to view should be an open <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAWN">lawn</a> of grass, which ought to be considerably broader than the front of the buildings; and if the depth be one half more than the width, it will have a better effect: if on the sides of the lawn there are trees planted irregularly, by way of open groves, the regularity of the lawn will be broken, and the whole rendered more like nature. For the convenience of walking in damp <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>, this lawn should be surrounded with a gravel walk, on the outside of which should be borders three or four feet wide for flowers: and from the back of these the prospect will be agreeably terminated by a slope of evergreen <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHRUBS">shrubs</a>; which, however, should never be suffered to exclude agreeable prospects, or the view of handsome buildings. These walks may <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> through the different plantations, gently winding about in an easy natural manner; which will be more agreeable than either those <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> straight walks, too frequently seen in gardens, or those serpentine windings that are twisted about into so many short turns as to render it difficult to walk in them; and as no garden can be pleasing where there is a want of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SHADE">shade</a> and shelter, these walks should lead as soon as possible into plantations, where persons may walk in private, and be sheltered from the <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>. Narrow rivulets, if they have a constant stream, and are judiciously led about a garden, have a better effect than many of the large stagnating ponds or canals so frequently made in large gardens. When wildernesses are intended, they should not be cut into stars and other ridiculous figures, nor formed into mazes of labyrinths, which in a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> appear trifling. In short, the several parts of a garden should be diversified; but in places where the eye takes in the whole at once, the two sides should be always the same. In the business of designs, the aim should be always at what is natural, great, and noble. The general disposition of a garden and of its parts ought to be accommodated to the different situations of the ground, to humour its inequalities, to proportion the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> and sorts of trees and shrubs to each part, and to shut out from the view of the garden no objects that may become ornamental. But for a more extended view of this subject, see the article Gardening. A practical <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> to a garden, is by some esteemed a degrading employment. It is true, indeed, that pastoral and agricultural manners, if we may form a judgment from the dignified descriptions of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>, are greatly degenerated. The employments of shepherds and husbandmen are now become <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> and sordid. The work of the garden is usually left to a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEASANT">peasant</a>. Nor is it unreasonable to assign the labour, which wearies without amusement, to those who are sufficiently amused by the prospect of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WAGES">wages</a>. But the operations of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAFTING">grafting</a>, of inoculating, of pruning, of transplanting, are curious experiments in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL_PHILOSOPHY">natural <a class="</a>xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>; and that they are pleasing as well as curious, those can testify who remember what they felt on seeing their attempts in the amusement of practical gardening attended with success. Among the employments suitable to old <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, Cicero has enumerated the superintendence of a garden. It requires no great exertion of mind or body; and its satisfactions are of that kind which please without violent agitation. Its beneficial influence on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> is an additional reason for an attention to it at an age when infirmities abound. In almost every <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of the seats of the blessed, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> of a garden seem to have predominated. The word Paradise itself is <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYNONYMOUS">synonymous</a> with garden. The fields of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELYSIUM">Elysium</a>, that sweet region of poesy, are adorned with all that imagination can conceive to be delightful. Some of the most pleasing <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILTON">Milton</a>, are those in which he represents the happy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a> engaged in cultivating their blissful abode. Poets have always been delighted with the beauties of a garden. Lucan is represented by Juvenal as reposing in his garden. Virgil's Georgics prove him to have been captivated with rural scenes; though, to the surprise of his readers, he has not assigned a book to the subject of a garden. Our Shenstone made it his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a>; but, with all his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> and fondness for it, he was not happy in it. The captivating scenes which he created at the Leasowes, afforded him, it is said, little pleasure in the absence of spectators. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> is, he made the embellishment of his grounds, which should have been the amusement of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, the business of it; and involved himself in such troubles, by the expences it occasioned, as necessarily excluded tranquil enjoyment. It is the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOT">lot</a> of few, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPARISON">comparison</a>, to possess territories like his, extensive, and sufficiently well adapted to constitute an ornamented <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FARM">farm</a>. Still fewer are capable of supporting the expense of preserving it in good condition. But let not the rich suppose they have appropriated the pleasures of a garden. The possessor of an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACRE">acre</a>, or a smaller portion, may receive a real pleasure, from observing the progress of vegetation, even in a plantation of culinary plants. A very limited tract, properly attended to, will furnish ample employment for an individual. Nor let it be thought a mean care; for the same <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> that raised the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CEDAR">cedar</a>, formed the hyssop on the wall. Even the orchard, cultivated solely for advantage, exhibits beauties unequalled in the shrubbery; nor can the greenhouse produce an appearance to exceed the blossom of the apple and the almond. Hanging Gardens, in antiquity, gardens raised on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARCHES">arches</a> by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEBUCHADNEZZAR">Nebuchadnezzar</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BABYLON">Babylon</a>, in order to gratify his wife Amyctis, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTYAGES">Astyages</a> king of Media. Quintus Curtius makes them equal in height to the walls of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>, viz. 50 feet. They contained a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> of 400 feet on every side, and were carried up into the air in several terraces laid above one another, and the ascent from terrace to terrace was by stairs 10 feet wide. The arches sustaining the whole pile were raised above one another, and it was strengthened by a wall, surrounding it on every side, of 22 feet in thickness. The floors of each of the terraces were laid in the following manner: on the top of the arches were first laid large flat <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONES">stones</a> 16 feet long and 4 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, and over them was a layer of reeds mixed with a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of bitumen, over which were two rows of bricks closely cemented together by <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLASTER">plaster</a>, and over all were laid thick sheets of lead; and lastly, upon the lead was laid the mould of the garden. The mould or earth was of such a depth as to admit the largest trees to take root and grow; and it was covered with various kinds of trees, plants, and flowers. In the upper terrace there was an aqueduct or engine, whereby water was drawn up out of the river for watering the whole garden. Floating Gardens. We are informed by the able Clavigero in his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEXICO">Mexico</a>, that when the Mexicans were brought under subjection to the Colhuans and Tepanecan nations, and confined to the miserable little <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> in the lake of Mexico, they ceased for some years to cultivate the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a>, because they had none, until <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> and industry together taught them to form moveable fields and gardens, which floated on the waters of the lake. The method which they pursued to make these, and which they still practise, is extremely simple. They plait and twist willows and roots of marsh plants or other materials together, which are light, but capable of supporting the earth of the garden firmly united. Upon this foundation they lay the light bushes which float on the lake; and over all, the mud and dirt which they draw up from the bottom of the same lake. Their regular <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> is quadrangular; their length and breadth various: but generally they are about eight perches long, and not more than three in breadth, and have less than a foot of elevation above the surface of the water. These were the first fields which the Mexicans owned after the foundation of Mexico; there they first cultivated the maize, great <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEPPER">pepper</a>, and other plants necessary for their support. In progress of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, as those fields grew numerous from the industry of the people, there were among them gardens of flowers and odoriferous plants, which were employed in the worship of their gods, and served for the recreation of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBLES">nobles</a>. At present they cultivate flowers and every sort of garden herbs upon them. Every <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> of the year, at sunrise, innumerable vessels loaded with various kinds of flowers and herbs, which are cultivated in those gardens, are seen arriving by the canals, at the great market place of that <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>. All plants thrive there surprisingly; the mud of the lake is an extremely fertile soil, and requires no water from the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CLOUDS">clouds</a>. In the largest gardens there is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> a little tree, and even a little hut to shelter the cultivator and defend him from rain or the sun. When the owner of a garden, or the Chinampa as he is usually called, wishes to change his situation, to remove from a disagreeable neighbour, or to come nearer to his own family, he gets into his little vessel, and by his own strength alone, if the garden is small, or with the assistance of others if it is large, he tows it after him, and conducts it wherever he pleases with the little tree and hut upon it. That part of the lake where those floating gardens are, is a place of infinite recreation, where the senses receive the highest possible gratification. GARDENING; The art of planning and cultivating gardens. In its utmost <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>, whatever contributes to render the scenes of nature delightful, is among the subjects of gardening; and animate as well as inanimate objects are circumstances of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> or character. The whole range of nature is open to the gardener, from the parterre to the forest; and whatever is agreeable to the senses or the imagination, he may appropriate to the spot he is to improve: it is a part of his business to collect into one place the delights which are generally dispersed through different <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of country. History of Gardening. Gardening, Mr Walpole† observes, was probably one of the first arts that succeeded to that of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> houses, and naturally attended <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> and individual possession. Culinary, and afterwards medicinal herbs, were the objects of every head of a family: it became convenient to have them within reach, without seeking them at random in woods, in meadows, and on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, as often as they were wanted. When the earth ceased to furnish spontaneously all those primitive luxuries, and culture became requisite, separate enclosures for rearing herbs grew expedient. Fruits were in the same predicament; and those most in use, or that demand attention, must have entered into and extended the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> enclosure. The good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOAH">Noah</a>, we are told, planted a vineyard, drank of the wine, and was drunken; and everybody knows the consequences. Thus we acquired kitchen gardens, orchards, and vineyards. No doubt the prototype of all these sorts was the garden of Eden; but as that Paradise was a good deal larger than any we read of afterwards, being enclosed by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> Pison, Gihon, Hiddekel, and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUPHRATES">Euphrates</a>; as every tree that was pleasant to the sight and good for food grew in it; and as two other trees were likewise found there, of which not a slip or sucker remains; it does not belong to the present discussion. After the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> no man living was suffered to enter into the garden; and the poverty and necessities of our first <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a> hardly allowed them time to make improvements in their estates in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a> of it, supposing any <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> had been preserved. A cottage and a slip of ground for a cabbage and a gooseberry bush, such as we see by the side of a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a>, were in all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a> the earliest seats and gardens: a well and bucket succeeded to the Pison and Euphrates. As settlements increased, the orchard and the vineyard followed; and the earliest princes of tribes possessed <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> the necessaries of a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FARMER">farmer</a>. Matters, we may well believe, remained long in this situation; and we have reason to think that for many centuries the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> garden implied no more than a kitchen garden or orchard. The garden of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALCINOUS">Alcinous</a>, in the Odyssey, is the most renowned in the heroic times. Is there an admirer of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a> who can read his description without rapture? or who does not form to his imagination a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCENE">scene</a> of delights more picturesque than the landscapes of Tinian or Juan Fernandez? "Yet (continues our author) what was that boasted Paradise with which the gods ordain'd To <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRACE">grace</a> Alcinous and his happy land? Why, divested of harmonious Greek and bewitching <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, it was a small orchard and vineyard, with some beds of herbs and two fountains that watered them, enclosed within a quickset hedge. The whole compass of this pompous garden enclosed—four acres: Four acres was th' allotted space of ground, Fenc'd with a green enclosure all around. The trees were apples, figs, pomegranates, pears, olives, and vines. Tall thriving trees confess'd the fruitful <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOLD">mold</a>; The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a>'ning apple ripens into <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>. Here the blue fig with luscious juice o'erflows, With deeper red the full pomegranate glows; The branch here <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BENDS">bends</a> beneath the weighty <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEAR">pear</a>, And verdant olives flourish round the year. Beds of all various herbs, for ever green, In beauteous order terminate the scene. Alcinous's garden was planted by the poet, enriched by him with the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAIRY">fairy</a> gift of eternal summer, and no doubt an effort of imagination surpassing anything he had ever seen. As he has bestowed on the same happy <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> with brazen walls and columns of silver, he certainly intended that the garden should be proportionably magnificent. We are sure, therefore, that, as late as Homer's age, an enclosure of four acres, comprehending orchard, vineyard, and kitchen garden, was a stretch of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LUXURY">luxury</a> the world at that time had never beheld." Previous to this, however, we have in the sacred writings hints of a garden still more luxuriously furnished. We allude to the Song of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLOMON">Solomon</a>, part of the scene of which is undoubtedly laid in a garden Chap. ii. Flowers and fruits are particularly spoken of as the ornaments and the produce of it; and besides these, aromatic vegetables formed a considerable part of the gratification it afforded. The camphor and the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CINNAMON">cinnamon</a> tree, with all trees of frankincense, and all the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> spices, flourished there†. Solomon tells us in another place†, That he made him great works;—gardens and orchards, and planted in them trees of every kind. Indeed we must suppose his gardens to have been both amply and curiously furnished, seeing the kinds, nature, and properties of the vegetable tribes, seem to have been a favourite study with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, and to have been deemed a subject worthy of his <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEN">pen</a>: for we are told, that he wrote of plants, from the great cedar of Lebanon <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to the hyssop of the wall §. § Kings iv. Fountains and streams of water appear also to have had a share in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a>, and probably for ornament as well as use. The hanging gardens of Babylon, mentioned in a preceding preceding article, were a still greater prodigy. But as they are supposed to have been formed on terraces and the walls of the palace, whither soil was conveyed on purpose, Mr Walpole concludes, "they were what sumptuous gardens have been in all ages till the present, unnatural, enriched by art, possibly with fountains, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a>, balustrades, and summer houses, and were any thing but verdant and rural." Others, however, have allowed them greater praise. They seem, in many respects, to have been laid out with good taste. Their elevation not only produced a variety and extent of view, but was also useful in moderating the heat. Such a situation would likewise <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUIT">suit</a> a greater variety of trees and plants than a plain surface, and would contain a larger as well as a more diversified extent. The suiting of the situation to the nature of the tree seems, from the account given by Josephus, to have been one view in the erecting the building in such a manner. And the success seems to have been answerable, as the trees are said to have flourished extremely well, and to have grown as tall as in their native situations. On the whole, then, however different these may appear from modern gardens, they seem to have been formed with judgment and taste, and well adapted to the situation and circumstances. It seems probable, from several circumstances, that the eastern gardens were adjoining to the house or palace to which they belonged. Thus, King Ahasuerus goes immediately from the banquet of wine to walk in the garden of the palace. The garden of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CYRUS">Cyrus</a>, at <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SARDIS">Sardis</a>, mentioned by Xenophon *, was probably contiguous to the palace; as was that of Attalus, mentioned by Justin. The hanging gardens at Babylon were not so much adjacent to the palace, as a part of the palace itself, since several of the royal apartments were beneath them. It is not clear what the taste for gardening was among the Greeks. The Academus, we know, was a wooded shady place; and the trees appear to have been of the olive species. It was situated beyond the limits of the walls, and adjacent to the tombs of the heroes; and though we are nowhere informed of the particular manner in which this <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GROVE">grove</a> was disposed or laid out, it may be gathered from Pausanias, in his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTICA">Attica</a>, that it was an elegant ornamented place. At the entrance was an altar dedicated to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">Love</a>, which was said to be the first erected to that deity. Within the Academus, were the altars of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROMETHEUS">Prometheus</a>, of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUSES">Muses</a>, of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERCURY">Mercury</a>, of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINERVA">Minerva</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERCULES">Hercules</a>; and at a small distance was the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOMB">tomb</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLATO">Plato</a>. So that in all probability, it was highly adapted by art, as well as nature, to philosophic reflection and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTEMPLATION">contemplation</a>. We are told by Plutarch, that before the time of Cimon, the Academus was a rude and uncultivated spot: but that it was planted by that general, and had water conveyed to it; whether this water was brought merely for use to refresh the trees, or for ornament, does not appear. It was divided into gymnasia, or places of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a>, and philosophic walks shaded with trees. These are said to have flourished very well, until destroyed by Sylla (when he besieged <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>), as well as those in the Lyceum. Near the academy were the gardens of the philosophers, of Plato and of Epicurus; which, however, were probably but small. The scene of Plato's <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIALOGUE">Dialogue</a> concerning Beauty is elegantly described as being on the banks of the river Ilissus, and under the shade of the plantain; but no <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> arrangement of objects is mentioned, nor anything which will lead us to imagine the prospect to be any other than merely natural. Among the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, a taste of gardening, any otherwise than as a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> of utility, seems not to have prevailed till a very late <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>; at least the writers on husbandry, Cato, Varro, Columella, and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALLADIUS">Palladius</a>, make not the least mention of a garden as an object of pleasure, but solely with respect to its productions of herbs and fruits. The Lucullan gardens are the first we find mentioned of remarkable magnificence; though probably from the extravagance to which these were arrived, they were not the first. Plutarch speaks of them as incredibly expensive, and equal to the magnificence of kings. They contained artificial elevations of ground to a surprising height, of buildings projected into the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, and vast pieces of water made upon land. In short, his extravagance and expense were so great, that he acquired thence the appellation of the Roman <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-XERXES">Xerxes</a>. It is not improbable, from the above account, and from the consideration of Lucullus having spent much time in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, in a situation wherein he had an opportunity of observing the most splendid constructions of this kind, that these gardens might be laid out in the Asiatic style. The vast masses of building said to have been erected, might have borne some resemblance, in the arrangement and style, to the Babylonian gardens; and the epithet of the Roman Xerxes might be applicable to the taste, as well as to the size and expense of his works. The Tuscan villa of Cicero, though often mentioned, is not anywhere described in his works, so as to give an adequate idea of the style in which his gardens or grounds were disposed. There is but little to be traced in Virgil relative to this subject. Pines, it seems probable, were a favourite ornament in gardens; and flowers, especially, were much esteemed, perfumes indeed having been always highly valued in warm climates. Virgil places <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANCHISES">Anchises</a> in Elysium, in a grove of bays: and is careful to remark, that they were of the sweet-scented kind. The Persian roses were chiefly valued for their excellent odour; and the same quality appears to be the cause why they were placed by Tibulus as ornaments to the Elysian fields. There appears also to have prevailed among the Romans a piece of luxury relative to gardens, which is equally prevalent at present among us, namely the forcing of flowers at seasons of the year not suited to their natural blooming: and roses were then, as at present, the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> flowers upon which these experiments were tried, as appears from Martial and others. When Roman authors (Mr Walpole remarks), whose <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> instilled a wish for cool retreats, speak of their enjoyments in that kind, they sigh for grottoes, caves, and the refreshing hollows of mountains, near irriguous and shady founts; or boast of their porticoes, walks of planes, canals, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATHS">baths</a>, and breezes from the sea. Their gardens are never mentioned as affording shade and shelter from the rage of the dog <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STAR">star</a>. Pliny has left us descriptions of two of his villas. As he used his Laurentine villa for his winter retreat, it is not surprising surprising that the garden makes no considerable part of the account. All he says of it is, that the gestatio or place of exercise, which surrounded the garden (the latter consequently not being very large), was bounded by a hedge of box, and, where that was perished, with rosemary; that there was a walk of vines; and that most of the trees were fig and mulberry, the soil not being proper for any other sorts. On his Tuscan villa he is more diffuse; the garden makes a considerable part of the description:—and what was the principal beauty of that pleasure ground? Exactly what was the admiration of this country about three score years ago; box trees cut into monsters, animals, letters, and the names of the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> and the artifice. In an age when <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a> displayed all its <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-GRANDEUR">grandeur</a>, all its purity, and all its taste; when arose Vespasian's <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMPHITHEATRE">amphitheatre</a>, the temple of Peace, Trajan's forum, Domitian's baths, and Adrian's villa, the ruins and vestiges of which still excite our astonishment and curiosity; a Roman <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSUL">consul</a>, a polished <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a>'s friend, and a man of elegant literature and taste, delighted in what the mob now scarce admire in a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> garden. All the ingredients of Pliny's corresponded exactly with those laid out by <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a> and Wise on Dutch principles. He talks of slopes, terraces, a wilderness, shrubs methodically trimmed, a marble <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BASON">bason</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PIPES">pipes</a> spouting water, a cascade falling into the bason, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> trees alternately planted with planes, and a straight walk from whence issued others parted off by hedges of box and apple trees, with <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-OBELISKS">obelisks</a> placed between every two. There wants nothing but the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMBROIDERY">embroidery</a> of a parterre, to make a garden in the time of Trajan serve for a description of one in that of King William. In one passage above, Pliny seems to have conceived that natural irregularity might be a beauty; in operae urbanissimo, says he, subita velut illiuri ruris initio. Something like a rural view was contrived amidst so much polished composition. But the idea soon vanished, lineal walks immediately enveloped the slight scene, and names and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INSCRIPTIONS">inscriptions</a> in box again succeeded to compensate for the daring introduction of nature. In the paintings found at Herculaneum are a few traces of gardens, as may be seen in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> volume of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINTS">prints</a>. They are small square enclosures, formed by trellis-work and espaliers, and regularly ornamented with vases, fountains, and caretides, elegantly symmetrical, and proper for the narrow spaces allotted to the garden of a house in a capital city. From what has been said, it appears how naturally and insensibly the idea of a kitchen garden slid into that which has for so many ages been peculiarly termed a garden, and by our ancestors in this country distinguished by the name of a pleasure garden. A square piece of ground was originally parted off in early ages for the use of the family:—to exclude cattle, and ascertain the property, it was separated from the fields by a hedge. As <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIDE">pride</a> and desire of privacy increased, the enclosure was dignified by walls; and in climes where fruits were not lavished by the ripening glow of nature and soil, fruit trees were assisted and sheltered from surrounding winds by the like expedient: for the inundation of luxuries, which have swelled into general necessities, have almost all taken their source from the simple fountain of reason. When the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> of making square gardens enclosed with walls was thus established to the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXCLUSION">exclusion</a> of nature and prospect, pomp and solitude combined to call for something that might enrich and enliven the insipid and unanimated partition. Fountains, first invented for use, which grandeur loves to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DISGUISE">disguise</a> and throw out of the question, received embellishments from costly marbles, and at last, to contradict utility, tossed their waste of waters into the air in spouting columns. Art, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of rude man, had at first been made a succedanum to nature; in the hands of ostentatious wealth, it became the means of opposing nature; and the more it traversed the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">march</a> of the latter, the more <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a> thought its power was demonstrated. Canals measured by the line were introduced in lieu of meandering streams, and terraces were hoisted aloft in opposition to the facile slopes that imperceptibly unite the valley to the hill. Balustrades defended these precipitate and dangerous elevations, and flights of steps rejoined them to the subjacent flat from which the terrace had been dug. Vases and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SCULPTURE">sculpture</a> were added to these unnecessary balconies, and statues furnished the lifeless spot with mimic representations of the excluded sons of men. Thus difficulty and expense were the constituent parts of those sumptuous and selfish solitudes; and every improvement that was made, was but a step farther from nature. The tricks of waterworks to wet the unwary, not to refresh the panting spectator; and parterres embroidered in patterns like a petticoat, were but the childish endeavours of fashion and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOVELTY">novelty</a> to reconcile greatness to what it had forfeited on. To <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> these impotent displays of false taste, the sheers were applied to the lovely wildness of form with which nature has distinguished each various species of tree and shrub. The venerable oak, the romantic beech, the useful elm, even the aspiring circuit of the lime, the regular round of the chestnut, and the almost moulded <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORANGE">orange</a> tree, were corrected by such fantastic admirers of symmetry. The compass and square were of more use in plantations than the nurseryman. The measured walk, the quincunx, and the etoile, imposed their unsatisfying sameness on every royal and noble garden. Trees were headed, and their sides pared away; many French groves seem green chests set upon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLES">poles</a>. Seats of marble, arbours, and summer houses, terminate every vista; and symmetry, even where the space was too large to permit its being remarked at one view, was so essential that, as Pope observed, each alley has a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a>, And half the garden just reflects the other. Knots of flowers were more defensibly subjected to the same regularity. Leisure, as Milton expressed it, in <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-TRIM">trim</a> gardens took his pleasure. In the garden of Marshal de Biron at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, consisting of 14 acres, every walk is buttressed on each side by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> of flower pots, which succeed in their seasons. It does not precisely appear what our ancestors meant by a bower: it was probably an arbour; sometimes it meant the whole frittered enclosure, and in one instance it certainly included a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LABYRINTH">labyrinth</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROSAMOND">Rosamond</a>'s bower was indisputably of that kind; though whether composed of walls or hedges, we cannot determine. A square and a round labyrinth were so capital ingredients of a garden formerly, that in Du Cercean's architecture, who lived in the time of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> IX. and Henry III. there is scarce a ground plot without one of each. In Kip's Views of the Seats of our Nobility and Gentry, we see the same tiresome and returning uniformity. Every house is approached by two or three gardens, consisting perhaps of a gravel walk and two grass plots or borders of flowers. Each rises above the other by two or three steps, and as many walls and terraces, and so many <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> gates, that we recollect those <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> romances in which every entrance was guarded by nymphs or dragons. Yet though these and such preposterous inconveniences prevailed from age to age, good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> in this country had perceived the want of something at once more <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> and more natural. These reflections, and the bounds set to the waste made by royal spoilers, gave origin to Parks. They were contracted forests, and extended gardens. Hentzner says, that, according to Rous of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WARWICK">Warwick</a>, the first <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARK">park</a> was that at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOODSTOCK">Woodstock</a>. If so, it might be the foundation of a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEGEND">legend</a> that Henry II. secured his mistress in a labyrinth: it was no doubt more difficult to find her in a park than in a palace, where the intricacy of the woods and various lodges buried in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COVERT">covert</a> might conceal her actual habitation. It is more extraordinary that, having so long ago stumbled on the principle of modern gardening, we should have persisted in retaining its reverse, symmetrical and unnatural gardens. That parks were rare in other countries, Hentzner, who travelled over great part of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, leads us to suppose, by observing that they were common in England. In France they retain the name, but nothing is more different both in compass and disposition. Their parks are usually square or <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a> enclosures, regularly planted with walks of chesnuts or limes, and generally every large town has one for its public recreation. "One man, one great man, we had (continues Mr Walpole), on whom nor <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> nor custom could impose their prejudices; who, 'on evil days though fallen, and with darkness and solitude compassed round,' judged that the mistaken and fantastic ornaments he had seen in gardens, were unworthy of the Almighty hand that planted the delights of Paradise. He seems with the prophetic eye of taste to have conceived, to have foreseen modern gardening; as <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BACON">Bacon</a> announced the discoveries since made by <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPERIMENTAL_PHILOSOPHY">experimental philosophy</a>. The description of Eden is a warmer and more just <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a> of the present style than Claud Lorraine could have painted from Hagley or Stourhead. The first lines we shall quote exhibit Stourhead on a more magnificent <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCALE">scale</a>: Thro' Eden went a river large, Nor chang'd his course, but thro' the shaggy hill, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">Pass</a>'d underneath ingulph'd: for God had thrown That mountain as his garden mound, high rais'd Upon the rapid current— Hagley seems pictured in what follows: Which thro' veins Of porous earth with kindly thirst updrawn, Rose a fresh fountain, and with many a rill Watered the garden— What colouring, what freedom of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PENCIL">pencil</a>, what landscape in these lines! —from that sapphire fount the crisped brooks, Rolling on orient <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEARL">pearl</a> and sands of gold, With mazy <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ERROR">error</a> under pendant shades, Ran <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NECTAR">nectar</a>, visiting each plant, and fed Flow'r's worthy of Paradise, which not nice art In beds and curious knots, but nature boon, Pour'd forth profuse on hill, and dale, and plain, Both where the morning sun first warmly smote The open field, and where the unpiec'd shade Imbrow'n'd the noontide bow'r—Thus was this place: A happy rural seat of various view.
