Read this transporting description, paint to your mind the scenes that follow, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRAST">contrast</a> them with the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAVAGE">savage</a> but respectable terror with which the poet guards the bounds of his paradise, fenced —with the champaign head Of a steep wilderness, whose hairy sides With thicket overgrown, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GROTESQUE">grotesque</a> and wild, Access denied; and over head up grew Insuperable height of loftiest shade, Cedar and pine, and fir, and branching palm, A sylvan scene, and, as the ranks ascend, Shade above shade, a woody <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a>, Of stateliest view— and then recollect, that the author of this sublime vision had never seen a glimpse of any thing like what he has imagined; that his favourite <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> had dropped not a hint of such divine scenery; and that the conceits in Italian gardens, and Theobalds and Nonsuch, were the brightest originals that his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> could furnish. His intellectual eye <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> a nobler plan, so little did he suffer by the loss of sight. It sufficed him to have seen the materials with which he could work. The vigour of a boundless imagination told him how a plan might be disposed, that would embellish nature, and restore art to its proper office, the just improvement or imitation of it. "Now let us return to an admired writer, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POSTERIOR">posterior</a> to Milton, and see how <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLD">cold</a>, how insipid, how tasteless, is his account of what he pronounced a perfect garden. We speak not of his style, which it was not necessary for him to animate with the colouring and glow of poetry. It is his want of ideas, of imagination, of taste, that deserve censure, when he dictated on a subject which is capable of all the graces that a knowledge of beautiful nature can bestow. Sir William Temple was an excellent man; Milton, a genius of the first order. "We cannot wonder that Sir William declares in favour of parterres, fountains, and statues, as necessary to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> the sameness of large grass plots, which he thinks have an ill effect upon the eye, when he acknowledges that he discovers fancy in the gardens of Alcinous. Milton studied the ancients with equal enthusiasm, but no bigotry; and had judgment to distinguish between the want of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> and the beauties of poetry. Compare his paradise with Homer's garden, both ascribed to a celestial design. For Sir William, it is just to observe, that his ideas centered in a fruit garden. He had the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of giving to his country many delicate fruits," fruits, and he thought of little else than disposing them to the best advantage. "The best figure of a garden (says he) is either a square or an oblong, and either upon a flat or a descent: they have all their beauties, but the best I esteem an oblong upon a descent. The beauty, the air, the view, make amends for the expence, which is very great in finishing and supporting the terrace walks, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVELLING">levelling</a> the parterres, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a> stairs that are necessary from one to the other. The perfectest figure of a garden I ever saw, either at home or abroad, was that of Moor Park in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HERTFORDSHIRE">Hertfordshire</a>, when I knew it about 30 years ago. It was made by the countess of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEDFORD">Bedford</a>, esteemed among the greatest wits of her time, and celebrated by Dr Donne; and with very great care, excellent contrivance, and much cost; but greater sums may be thrown away without effect or honour, if there want sense in proportion to <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, or 'if nature be not followed;' which I take to be the great rule in this, and perhaps in every thing else, as far as the conduct not only of our lives but our governments. [We shall see how natural that admired garden was]. Because I take the garden I have named to have been in all kinds the most beautiful and perfect, at least in the figure and disposition, that I ever have seen, I will describe it for a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODEL">model</a> to those that meet with such a situation, and are above the regards of common expence. It lies on the side of a hill, upon which the house stands, but not very steep. The length of the house, where the best rooms and of most use or pleasure are, lies upon the breadth of the garden; the great parlour opens into the middle of a terrace gravel walk that lies even with it, and which may be, as I remember, about 300 paces long, and broad in proportion; the border set with standard laurels and at large distances, which have the beauty of orange trees out of flower and fruit. From this walk are three descents by many stone steps, in the middle and at each end, into a very large parterre. This is divided into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> by gravel walks, and adorned with two fountains and eight statues in the several quarters. At the end of the terrace walk are two summer houses, and the sides of the parterre are ranged with two large cloisters open to the garden, upon arches of stone, and ending with two other summer houses even with the cloisters, which are paved with stone, and designed for walks of shade, there being none other in the whole parterre. Over these two cloisters are two terraces covered with lead and fenced with balusters; and the passage into these <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIRY">airy</a> walks is out of the two summer houses at the end of the first terrace walk. The cloister facing the south is covered with vines, and would have been proper for an orange house, and the other for myrtles or other more common greens, and had, I doubt not, been <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> for that purpose, if this piece of gardening had been then in as much vogue as it is now. From the middle of this parterre is a descent by many steps <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLYING">flying</a> on each side of a grotto, that lies between them, covered with lead and flat, into the lower garden, which is all fruit trees ranged about the several quarters of a wilderness, which is very shady; the walks here are all green, the grotto embellished with figures of shell rock-work, fountains, and water works. If the hill had not ended with the lower garden, and the wall were not bounded by a common way that goes through the park, they might have added a third <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of all greens; but this want is supplied by a garden on the other side the house, which is all of that sort, very wild, shady, and adorned with rough rock-work and fountains. This was Moor Park when I was acquainted with it, and the sweetest place, I think, that I have seen in my life, either before or since, at home or abroad." "It is unnecessary to add any remarks on this description. Any man might design and build as sweet a garden, who had been born in and never stirred out of Holborn. It was not, however, peculiar to Sir William Temple to think in that manner. How many Frenchmen are there who have seen our gardens, and still prefer natural flights of steps and shady cloisters covered with lead! Le Nautre, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ARCHITECT">architect</a> of the groves and grottoes at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSAILLES">Versailles</a>, came hither on a mission to improve our taste. He planted St James's and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREENWICH">Greenwich</a> Parks—no great monuments of his invention. "To do farther <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> to Sir William Temple, we must not omit what he adds. 'What I have said of the best forms of gardens is meant only of such as are in some sort regular; for there may be other forms wholly <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a>, that may, for ought I know, have more beauty than any of the others: but they must owe it to some extraordinary dispositions of nature in the seat, or some great <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a> of fancy or judgment in the contrivance, which may reduce many disagreeing parts into some figure, which shall yet, upon the whole, be very agreeable. Something of this I have seen in some places, but heard more of it from others who have lived much among the Chinese, a people whose way of thinking seems to <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> as wide of ours in Europe as their country does. Their greatest reach of imagination is employed in contriving figures, where the beauty shall be great and strike the eye, but without any order or disposition of parts, that shall be commonly or easily observed. And though we have hardly any notion of this sort of beauty, yet they have a particular word to express it: and when they find it <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol11.html#article-HIT">hit</a> their eye at first sight, they say the Sharawadgi is fine or is admirable, or any such <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a> of esteem: but I should hardly advise any of these attempts in the figure of gardens among us; they are adventures of too hard achievement for any common hands; and though there may be more honour if they succeed well, yet there is more dishonour if they fail, and it is twenty to one they will; whereas in regular figures it is hard to make any great and remarkable faults.' "Fortunately <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KENT">Kent</a> and a few others were not quite so timid, or we might still be going up and down stairs in the open air. It is true, we have heard much lately, as Sir William Temple did, of irregularity and imitations of nature in the gardens or grounds of the Chinese. The former is certainly true: they are as whimsically irregular, as European gardens are formally uniform and unvaried—but with regard to nature, it seems as much avoided, as in the squares and oblongs and straight lines of our ancestors. An artificial perpendicular rock starting out of a flat plain, and connected with nothing, often pierced through in various places with oval hollows, has no more pretension to be deemed natural than a lineal terrace or a parterre. The late Mr <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOSEPH">Joseph</a> Spence, who had both taste and zeal for for the present style, was so persuaded of the Chinese emperor's pleasure ground being laid out on principles resembling ours, that he translated and published, under the name of Sir Harry Beaumont, a particular account of that enclosure, from the collection of the letters of the Jesuits. But except a determined irregularity, one can find nothing in it that gives any idea of attention being paid to nature. It is of vast circumference, and contains 200 palaces, besides as many contiguous for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUNUCHS">eunuchs</a>, all gilt, painted, and varnished. There are raised hills from 20 to 60 feet high, streams and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a>, and one of the latter five miles round. These waters are passed by bridges: but even their bridges must not be straight—they serpentine as much as the rivulets, and are sometimes so long as to be furnished with resting places, and begin and end with triumphal arches. The colonnades undulate in the same manner. In short, this pretty gaudy scene is the work of caprice and whim, and, when we reflect on their buildings, presents no image but that of unsubstantial tawdriness. Nor is this all. Within this fantastic paradise is a square town, each side a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILE">mile</a> long. Here the eunuchs of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>, to entertain his imperial majesty with the bustle and business of the capital in which he resides, but which it is not of his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> ever to see, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a> and all sorts of trades, and even designedly exercise for his royal amusement every art of knavery that is practised under his auspicious <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>. Methinks this is the childish solace and repose of grandeur, not a retirement from affairs to the delights of rural life. Here too his majesty plays at <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRICULTURE">agriculture</a>: there is a quarter set apart for that purpose; the eunuchs sow, reap and carry in their <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HARVEST">harvest</a>, in the imperial presence; and his majesty returns to Pekin, persuaded that he has been in the country. Having thus cleared our way by ascertaining what have been the ideas on gardening in all ages as far as we have materials to judge by, it remains to show to what <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> Mr Kent invented the new style, and what hints he had received to suggest and conduct his undertaking. We have seen what Moor Park was, when pronounced a standard. But as no succeeding <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENERATION">generation</a> in an opulent and luxurious country contents itself with the perfection established by its ancestors, more perfect perfection was still sought; and improvements had gone on, till London and Wise had stocked all our gardens with giants, animals, monsters, coats of arms, and mottoes, in yew, box, and holly. Absurdity could go no farther, and the tide turned. Bridgman, the next fashionable designer of gardens, was far more chaste; and whether from good sense, or that the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> had been struck and reformed by the admirable <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-GUARDIAN">Guardian</a>, No 173, he banished verdant sculpture, and did not even revert to the square precision of the foregoing age. He enlarged his plans, disdained to make every <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> tally to its opposite; and though he still adhered much to straight walks with high clipped hedges, they were only his great lines; the rest he diversified by wilderness, and with loose groves of oak, though still within surrounding hedges. As his reformation gained footing, he ventured, in the royal garden at <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RICHMOND">Richmond</a>, to introduce cultivated fields, and even morsels of a forest appearance, by the sides of those endless and tiresome walks that stretched out of one into another without intermission. But this was not till other innovators had broke loose too from rigid symmetry. But the capital stroke, the leading step to all that has followed, was the destruction of walls for boundaries, and the invention of fosses—an attempt then deemed so astonishing, that the common people called them Ha! Ha's! to express their surprise at finding a sudden and unperceived check to their walk. A sunk <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FENCE">fence</a> may be called the leading step, for these reasons. No sooner was this simple enchantment made, than levelling, mowing, and rolling, followed. The contiguous ground of the park without the sunk fence was to be harmonized with the lawn within; and the garden in its turn was to be set free from its prime regularity, that it might assort with the wilder country without. The sunk fence ascertained the specific garden; but that it might not draw too obvious a line of distinction between the neat and the rude, the contiguous out-lying parts came to be included in a kind of general design; and when nature was taken into the plan, under improvements, every step that was made pointed out new beauties, and inspired new ideas. At that moment appeared Kent, painter enough to taste the charms of landscape, bold, and opinionative enough to dare and to dictate, and born with a genius to strike out a great system from the twilight of imperfect essays. He leaped the fence, and saw that all nature was a garden. He felt the delicious contrast of hill and valley changing imperceptibly into each other, tasted the beauty of the gentle swell or concave scoop, and remarked how loose grooves crowned an easy eminence with happy ornament; and while they called in the distant view between their graceful stems, removed and extended the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol8.html#article-PERSPECTIVE">perspective</a> by delusive comparison. Thus the pencil of his imagination bestowed all the arts of landscape on the scenes he handled. The great principles on which he worked were perspective, and light and shade. Groups of trees broke too uniform or too extensive a lawn; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EVERGREENS">evergreens</a> and woods were opposed to the glare of the champaign; and where the view was less fortunate, or so much exposed as to be beheld at once, he blotted out some parts by thick shades, to divide it into variety, or to make the richest scene more enchanting by reserving it to a farther advance of the spectator's step. Thus, selecting favourite objects, and veiling deformities by screens of plantation; sometimes allowing the rudest waste to add its foil to the richest theatre; he realized the compositions of the greatest masters in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a>. Where objects were wanting to animate his horizon, his taste as an architect could bestow immediate termination. His buildings, his seats, his <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a>, were more the works of his pencil than of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPASSES">compasses</a>. We owe the restoration of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a> and the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFUSION">diffusion</a> of architecture to his skill in landscape. But of all the beauties he added to the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FACE">face</a> of this beautiful country, none surpassed his management of water. Adieu to canals, circular basons and cascades tumbling down marble steps, that last absurd magnificence of Italian and French villas. The forced elevation of cataracts was no more. The gentle stream was taught to serpentine seemingly at its pleasure; and where discontinued by different levels, its course appeared to be concealed by thickets properly interspersed, and glittered again at a distance, where it might be supposed naturally to arrive. Its borders were smoothed, but preserved their waving irregularity. A few trees scattered here and there on its edges sprinkled the tame <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANK">bank</a> that accompanied its meanders; and when it disappeared among the hills, shades descending from the heights leaned towards its progress, and framed the distant point of light under which it was lost, as it turned aside to either hand of the blue horizon. "Thus, dealing in none but the colours of nature, and catching its most favourable features, men saw a new <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREATION">creation</a> opening before their eyes. The living landscape was chastened or polished, not transformed. Freedom was given to the forms of trees; they extended their branches unrestricted; and where any eminent oak, or master beech, had escaped maiming and survived the forest, bush and bramble was removed, and all its honours were restored to distinguish and shade the plain. Where the united plumage of an ancient wood extended wide its undulating canopy, and stood venerable in its darkness, Kent thinned the foremost ranks, and left but so many detached and scattered trees, as softened the approach of gloom, and blended a chequered light with the thus lengthened shadows of the remaining columns. "Succeeding artists have added new master strokes to these touches; perhaps improved or brought to perfection some that have been named. The introduction of foreign trees and plants, which we owe principally to Archibald <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Argyle, contributed essentially to the richness of colouring so peculiar to our modern landscape. The mixture of various greens, the contrast of forms between our forest trees and the northern and West <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> firs and pines, are improvements more recent than Kent, or but little known to him. The weeping willow, and every florid shrub, each tree of delicate or bold <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAF">leaf</a>, are new tints in the composition of our gardens. "But just as the encomiums are that have been bestowed on Kent's discoveries, he was neither without assistance or faults. Mr Pope undoubtedly contributed to form his taste. The design of the prince of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>'s garden at Carlton house was evidently borrowed from the poet's at Twickenham. There was a little of affected <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODESTY">modesty</a> in the latter, when he said, of all his works he was most proud of his garden. And yet it was a singular effort of art and taste to impress so much variety and scenery on a spot of five acres. The passing through the gloom from the grotto to the opening day, the retiring and again assembling shades, the dusky groves, the larger lawn, and the solemnity of the termination at the cypresses that lead up to his mother's tomb, are managed with exquisite judgment; and though Lord Peterborough assisted him To form his quincunx and to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> his vines, those were not the most pleasing ingredients of his little perspective. "Having routed professed art (for the modern gardener exerts his talents to conceal his art), Kent, like other reformers, knew not how to stop at the just limits. He had followed Nature, and imitated her so happily, that he began to think all her works were equally proper for imitation. In <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KENSINGTON">Kensington</a> garden he planted dead trees to give a greater air of truth to the scene—but he was soon laughed out of this excess. His ruling principle was, that nature abhors a straight line. His mimics (for every genius has his apes), seemed to think that she could love nothing but what was crooked. Yet so many men of taste of all ranks devoted themselves to the new improvements, that it is surprising how much beauty has been struck out, with how few absurdities. Still in some lights the reformation seems to have been pushed too far. Though an avenue crossing a park or separating a lawn, and intercepting views from the seat to which it leads, are capital faults; yet a great avenue cut through woods, perhaps before entering a park, has a noble air, and, Like footmen running before coaches To tell the inn what lord approaches, announces the habitation of some man of distinction. In other places the total banishment of all particular neatness immediately about a house, which is frequently left gazing by itself in the middle of a park, is a defect. Sheltered and even <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> walks, in so very uncertain a climate as ours, are comforts ill exchanged for the few picturesque days that we enjoy; and whenever a family can purloin a warm and even something of an old-fashioned garden from the landscape designed for them by the undertaker in fashion, without interfering with the picture, they will find satisfactions in those days that do not invite strangers to come and see their improvements." GARDINER

Pages 478-478

STEPHEN, bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WINCHESTER">Winchester</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a> of England, born at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BURY_ST_EDMUNDS"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol5.html#article-BURY">Bury</a> St Edmunds in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SUFFOLK">Suffolk</a>, was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> son to Richard Woodville, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a> wife to Edward IV. was learned in the canon and civil laws, and in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a>. He signed the divorce of Henry VIII. from Katharine of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>; abjured the pope's supremacy; and wrote De vera et falsa obedientia, in behalf of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>; yet in Edward's reign he opposed the reformation, and was punished with imprisonment; but Queen <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a> coming to the throne, she enlarged him. He drew up the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> between the queen and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a> of Spain, which were very advantageous to England. He was violent against the reformers; but on his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BED">bed</a> was dissatisfied with his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, and often repeated these words: Erravi cum Petro, sed non flevi cum Petro. He died in 1555. GARGARISM (from γαργαρίζω, "to wash the mouth") a gargle. Its <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> is for washing the mouth and throat with, when inflammations, ulcerations, &c. are there. A small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> may be taken into the mouth, and moved briskly about, and then spit out; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the patient cannot do this to any advantage, the liquor may be injected by a syringe. When gargles are required, their use should be more frequently repeated than is done in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> practice.

GARGETT

Pages 478-478

a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a> of cattle, consisting in a swelling of the throat and the neighbouring parts; to prevent which bleeding in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> is recommended.

GARGILL

Pages 478-478

a distemper in geese, which by stopping the head frequently proves mortal. Three <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> four cloves of garlic, beaten in a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MORTAR">mortar</a> with sweet <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUTTER">butter</a>, and made into little balls, and given the creature fasting, are the ordinary cure.

GARIDELLA

Pages 478-478

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the decandria class, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 26th order, Multisiliqua. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

GARIZIM

Pages 478-478

Gerizim, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Gerisim, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a mountain of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAMARIA">Samaria</a>, at the foot of which stood Sichem; so near, that Jotham could be heard by the Sichemites from its top, (Judges, ix. 7.). Famous for the temple built on it by Sanballet, in favour of his son-in-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANASSEH">Manasseh</a>, by the permission of Alexander the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">Great</a>, and 200 years after destroyed by John Hyrcanus, son of Simon, the fourth in succession of the Asmonaeans (Josephus).

GARLAND

Pages 478-478

a sort of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHAPLET">chaplet</a> made of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>, feathers, and sometimes precious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, worn on the head in manner of a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>.—The word is formed of the French guirlande, and that of the barbarous Latin garlanda, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Italian ghirlanda. Menage traces its origin from gyrus through gyrolus, to gyrolare, gyrolandum, ghirlandum; and at length ghirlanda and guirlande; so that guirlande and garland are descended in the sixth or seventh <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> from gyrus.—Hick rejects this derivation, and brings the word from gardel handa, which in the northern languages signify a nosegay artfully wrought with the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>.

GARLAND ALSO

Pages 478-478

d also denotes ornaments of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>, and leaves, intermixed; anciently much used at the gates of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a>, where feasts and solemn rejoicings were held; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> at any other <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where marks of public joy or gaiety were required, as at triumphal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARCHES">arches</a>, tournaments, &c. GARLIC. See Allium, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

GARMENT

Pages 478-478

that wherewith any person is clothed. See Dress and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HABIT">Habit</a>.

GARNET

Pages 478-480

in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, a very beautiful gem, of a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, with an admixture of blue. See <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINERALOGY">Mineralogy</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. When pure and free from blemishes, it is little inferior in appearance to the oriental <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RUBY">ruby</a>, though only of a middle <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HARDNESS">hardness</a> between the sapphire and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> crystal. It is found of various sizes, from that of a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PIN">pin</a>'s head to an inch in diameter. Among lapidaries and jewellers, genuine garnets are known by different names according to their different degrees of colour. 1. The garnet, simply so called, is the finest and most valuable kind, being of a very deep blood-red with a faint admixture of blue. 2. The rock-ruby; a name very improperly given to the garnet when it is of a very strong but not deep red, and has a fairer <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> of the blue; this is a very beautiful gem. 3. The sorane <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> serain garnet; that of a yet brighter red, approaching to the colour of native cinnabar. cinnabar, with a faint blue tinge. 4. The almandine, a garnet only a little paler than that called the rock-ruby. **Garnet-Colour.** See Colouring of Glass. To imitate Garnets. The making the counterfeit garnet in paste is done as follows.—Take prepared crystal two ounces, common red-<a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> six ounces, manganese 16 grains, zaffre three grains; mix all well, put them into a crucible, cover it with lute, and set it in a potter's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KILN">kiln</a> for 24 hours. Or take crystal two ounces, minium five ounces and a half, manganese 15 grains, zaffre four grains: mix them well together; and let all be baked, in a pot well luted, in a kiln, 24 hours. **Garonne,** a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> river of France, which has its source in the Pyrenean <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, and falls into the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> 60 miles below Bordeaux. **Garonne, Upper,** a department in the south of France. The south <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> extends to the Pyrenees, and is rugged and mountainous: the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> part has a hilly or undulating surface. It produces corn, wine, olives, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a>, figs, almonds, and abounds in pasturage. The mountains contain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>, lead, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, and coal. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> in 1815 was 367,000. <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOULOUSE">Toulouse</a> is the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> town. **Garrick, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAVID">David</a>,** Esq. the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> Roscius of his <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, who for nearly 40 years shone the brightest luminary in the hemisphere of the stage, was born at the Angel Inn at <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEREFORD">Hereford</a>, in the year 1716. His father, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPTAIN">Captain</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> Garrick, was a French refugee, and had a troop of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> which were then quartered in that <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>. This <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> he maintained in the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> for several years, and had a majority at the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>; that event, however, prevented him from ever enjoying it. Mr Garrick received the first <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RUDIMENTS">rudiments</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> at the free-school at <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LITCHFIELD">Litchfield</a>; which he afterwards completed at <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROCHESTER">Rochester</a>, under the celebrated Mr Colson, since mathematical professor at <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>. Dr Johnson and he were fellow-students at the same school; and it is a curious fact, that these two celebrated geniuses came up to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a> in the same <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COACH">coach</a>, with the intention of pushing themselves into <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. On the 9th of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a> 1736, he was entered at the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LINCOLN">Lincoln</a>'s Inn. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a>, however, he soon quitted; and followed for some time the employment of a wine merchant: but that too disgusting him, he gave way at last to the irresistible bias of his mind, and joined a traveling <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> of comedians at <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IPSWICH">Ipswich</a> in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SUFFOLK">Suffolk</a>, where he went by the name of Lydall. Having in this <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a> school of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOLLO">Apollo</a> got some acquaintance with the tragic art, he burst at once upon the world, in the year 1740-1, in all the lustre of perfection, at the little <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a> in Goodman's Fields, then under the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of Henry Gilfard. The character he first performed was Richard III., in which, like the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> bursting from behind a cloud, he displayed in the earliest dawn even more than meridian brightness. His excellence dazzled and astonished every one; and the seeing a young <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, in no more than his 24th year, and a novice in reality to the stage, reaching at one single step to that height of perfection which maturity of years and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> practical <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> had not been able to bestow on the most <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> performers of the English stage, was a phenomenon that could not but become the object of universal speculation and of as universal admiration. The Garrick <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-THEATRES">theatres</a> at the west end of the town were deserted; Goodman's Fields, from being the rendezvous of citizens and citizens wives alone, became the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESORT">resort</a> of all ranks of men; and Mr Garrick <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> till the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> of the season. Having very advantageous terms offered him for the performing in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUBLIN">Dublin</a> during some part of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> (1741), he went over thither, where he found the same <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> homage paid to his merit which he had received from his own countrymen. To the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of the latter, however, he esteemed himself more immediately bound; and therefore in the ensuing winter, engaged himself to Mr Fleetwood, then manager of Drury Lane; in which theatre he continued till the year 1745, when he again went over to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, and continued there the whole season, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOINT">joint</a> manager with Mr Sheridan in the direction and profits of the theatre <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> in Smock Alley. From thence he returned to England, and was engaged for the season of 1746 with Mr Rich at Covent Garden. This was his last performance as a hired <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTOR">actor</a>: for in the close of that season, Mr Fleetwood's patent for the management of Drury Lane being expired, and that <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> having no inclination further to pursue a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> by which, from his want of acquaintance with the proper conduct of it, or some other cause, he had considerably impaired his fortune; Mr Garrick, in conjunction with Mr Lacy, purchased the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of that theatre, together with the renovation of the patent; and in the winter of 1747, opened it with the greatest part of Mr Fleetwood's company, and with the great additional strength of Mr <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BARRY">Barry</a>, Mrs Pritchard, and Mrs Cibber, from Covent Garden. Were we to trace Mr Garrick through the several occurrences of his life,—a life so active, so busy, and so full of occurrences as his, we should swell this account to many <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAGES">pages</a>. Suffice it to say, he continued in the unmolested enjoyment of his fame and unrivalled excellence to the moment of his retirement. His universality of excellence was never once attacked by competition. Tragedy, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMEDY">comedy</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FARCE">farce</a>, the lover and the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERO">hero</a>, the jealous husband who suspects his wife without cause, and the thoughtless lively <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RAKE">rake</a> who attacks her without design, were all alike his own. Rage and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIDICULE">ridicule</a>, doubt and despair, transport and tenderness, compassion and contempt; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a>, jealousy, fear, fury, and simplicity; all took in turn possession of his features, while each of them in turn appeared to be the sole possessor of his heart. In the several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAR">Lear</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAMLET">Hamlet</a>, Richard, Dorilas, Romeo, and Lusignane; in his Ranger, Bayes, Drugger, Kitley, Brute, and Benedict, you <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> the muscular conformations that your <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> attached to them all. In short, <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">Nature</a>, the mistress from whom alone this great performer borrowed all his <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LESSONS">lessons</a>, being in herself inexhaustible, this her darling son, marked out for her truest representative, found an unlimited scope for change and diversity in his manner of copying from her various productions. There is one part of theatrical conduct which ought unquestionably to be recorded to Mr Garrick's <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a>, since the cause of virtue and morality, and the formation of public manners, are considerably dependent upon it; and that is, the zeal with which he aimed to banish from the stage all those plays which carry with them an immoral tendency, and to prune from those which do not absolutely, on the whole, promote the interests of vice, such scenes of licentiousness and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>, as a redundancy of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WIT">wit</a> and too great liveliness of imagination have induced some of our comic writers to indulge themselves in, and to which the sympathetic disposition of our age of gallantry and intrigue has given sanction. The purity of the English stage has certainly been much more fully established during the administration of this theatrical minister, than it had ever been during preceding managements. He seems to have carried his modest, moral, chaste, and pious principles with him into the very management of the theatre itself, and rescued performers from that obloquy which had attached to the profession. Of those who were accounted blackguards, unworthy the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ASSOCIATION">association</a> of the world, he made gentlemen, united them with society, and introduced them to all the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> comforts of life. The theatre was no longer esteemed the receptacle of all vice; and the moral, the serious, the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> part of mankind, did not hesitate to partake of the rational entertainment of a play, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> a cheerful evening undisgusted with the licentiousness, and uncorrupted by the immorality, of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXHIBITION">exhibition</a>. Notwithstanding the numberless and laborious avocations attendant on his profession as an actor, and his station as a manager; yet still his active genius was perpetually bursting forth in various little productions in the dramatic and poetical way, whose merit cannot but make us regret his want of time for the pursuance of more extensive and important works. It is certain that his merit as an author is not of the first magnitude: but his great knowledge of men and manners, of stage effect, and his happy turn for lively and striking satire, made him generally successful; and his prologues and epilogues in particular, which are almost innumerable, possess such a degree of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a>, both in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONCEPTION">conception</a> and execution, as to stand unequalled. His ode on the death of Mr Pelham ran through four editions in less than six weeks. His Ode on Shakespeare is a masterly piece of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>; and when delivered by himself, was a most capital exhibition. His alterations of Shakespeare and other authors have been at times successful, and at times exploded. The <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXCLUSION">exclusion</a> of the gravediggers <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCENE">scene</a> from Hamlet <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> never be forgotten by him by the inhabitants of the gallery at Drury. Though necessary to the chasteness of the scene, they cannot bear to lose so much true <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-STERLING">sterling</a> wit and humour; and it must be owned, that exuberances of that kind, though they hurt the uniformity, yet increase the luxuriance of the tree. Among his alterations the following are part; Every Man in his Humour, altered from Ben Johnson; Romeo and Juliet, Winter's Tale, Catherine and Petruchio, Cymbeline, Hamlet, &c. altered and made up from Shakespeare; Gamesters, a comedy, from Shirley; Isabella, from Southerne. To these we add, as original productions, The <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FARMER">Farmer</a>'s Return, and Linco's Travels, interludes; <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-GUARDIAN">Guardian</a>, Lethe, Lying <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VALET">Valet</a>, Miss in her Teens, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MALE">Male</a> Coquet, Irish Widow, and other comedies in two acts; Enchanter, a musical entertainment; Lilliput: the Christmas Tale is ascribed to him, and many others. We now bring him to the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> of his retirement in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> of 1776; when, full of fame, with the acquirement of a splendid fortune, and growing into years, he thought proper to seek the vale of life, to enjoy that dignified and honourable ease which was compatible with his public situation, and which he had so well earned by the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTIVITY">activity</a> and the merits of his dramatic reign. But very short indeed was the period allotted to him for this precious enjoyment: for on the 20th of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 1779, he departed this life; leaving no one rival in excellence upon <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> to compensate for his loss, or a hope of our ever meeting with his like again.

GARRISON

Pages 480-480

in the art of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, a body of forces, disposed in a fortress, to defend it against the enemy, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> to keep the inhabitants in subjection: or even to be subsisted during the winter season: hence garrison and winter <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> are sometimes used indifferently for the same thing; and sometimes they denote different things. In the latter <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>, a garrison is a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> wherein forces are maintained to secure it, and where they keep regular <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUARD">guard</a>, as a frontier town, a citadel, castle, tower, &c. The garrison should be always stronger than the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>-men. Du Cange derives the word from the corrupt Latin garnitio, which the latter writers <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> to signify all manner of munition, arms, victuals, &c. necessary for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of a place, and sustaining of a siege. Winter quarters signify a place where a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of forces are laid up in the winter season, without keeping the regular guard.

GARSTANG

Pages 480-480

a town in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANCASHIRE">Lancashire</a>, 227 miles from <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. It is near a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILE">mile</a> in length, but built in a very <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a> manner, with dirty streets, and very indifferent houses. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> amounts to 790 persons. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> is a stately Gothic structure. By the late inland <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a>, it has <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERSEY">Mersey</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEE">Dee</a>, Ribble, Ouse, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRENT">Trent</a>, Darwent, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEVERN">Severn</a>, Humber, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THAMES">Thames</a>, Avon, &c. which navigation, including its windings, extends above 500 miles, in the counties of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LINCOLN">Lincoln</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NOTTINGHAM">Nottingham</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORK">York</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WESTMORELAND">Westmoreland</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHESTER">Chester</a>, &c. W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 42. N. Lat. 53. 52.

GARTER

Pages 480-482

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LIGATURE">ligature</a> for tying up the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STOCKING">stocking</a>; but particularly used for the badge of a noble order of knights, hence denominated the Order of the Garter, a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> order of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KNIGHTHOOD">knighthood</a>, the most noble and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> of any lay order in the world, instituted by Edward III. The knights companions are generally princes and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEERS">peers</a>; and the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of England is the sovereign <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> of the order. The <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of knights was originally 26: but six were added in 1786, on account of the increase of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> family. They are a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> or corporation, having a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> and little <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEAL">seal</a>. Their officers are a prelate, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REGISTER">register</a>, king-at-arms, and usher of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> rod. They have also a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAN">dean</a>, and 12 canons and petty canons, vergers, and 26 pensioners or <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a> knights. The prelate is the head. This office is vested in the bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WINCHESTER">Winchester</a>, and has ever been so. Next to the prelate is the chancellor; which office is vested in the bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALISBURY">Salisbury</a>, who keeps the seals, &c. The next is the register, who by his oath is to enter upon the registry, the scrutinies, elections, penalties, and other acts of the order, with all fidelity: The dean of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WINDSOR">Windsor</a> is always register ex officio. The fourth officer is Garter and king-at-arms, being two distinct offices united in one person. Garter carries the rod and sceptre at the feast of St George, the protector of this order, when the sovereign is present. He notifies the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTION">election</a> of new knights, attends the solemnity of their installation, carries the garter to foreign princes, &c. He is the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> officer within the college of arms, and chief of the heralds. See King-at-Arms. All these officers except the prelate have fees and pensions. The college of the order is seated in the castle of Windsor, within the chapel of St George, and the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARTER">charter</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, erected by the founder for that purpose. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HABIT">habit</a> and ensign of the order, are, a garter, mantle, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPE">cape</a>, george, and collar. The three first were assigned the knights companions by the founder; and the george and collar by Henry VIII. The garter challenges pre-eminence over all the other parts of the dress, by reason that from it the noble order is denominated; that it is the first <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the habit presented to foreign princes and absent knights, who, and all other knights-elect, are therewith first adorned; and it is of so great <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-GRANDEUR">grandeur</a>, that by the bare <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVESTITURE">investiture</a> with this noble ensign, the knights are esteemed companions of the greatest military order in the world. It is worn on the left leg between the knee and calf; and is enamelled with this motto, Honi soit qui mal y pense; i.e. Shame to him that thinks evil thereof. The meaning of which is, that King Edward having laid claim to the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of France, retorted shame and defiance upon him that should dare to think amiss of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> enterprise he had undertaken, for recovering his lawful <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> to that <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>; and that the bravery of those knights whom he had elected into this order, was such as would enable him to maintain the quarrel against those that thought ill of it. The mantle is the chief of these vestments made <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of upon all solemn occasions. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> of the mantle is by the statutes appointed to be blue. The length of the train of the mantle only distinguishes the sovereign from the knights companions. To the collar of the mantle is fixed a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> strings, anciently woven with blue <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a> only, but now twisted round, and made of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> and silk, of the colour of the robes, with knobs or buttons, and tassels at the end. The left shoulder of the mantle has from the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a> been adorned with a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> garter, with the device Honi soit, &c. Within this is the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> of the order, which was ordained to be worn at all times by King <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> I. At length the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STAR">star</a> was introduced, being a sort of cross irradiated with beams of silver. The collar is appointed to be composed of pieces of gold in fashion of garters, the ground enamelled blue, and the motto gold. When the knights wear not their robes, they are to have a silver star on the left side; and they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> bear the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a> of St George, enamelled on gold, and beset with diamonds, at the end of a blue ribbon, crossing the body from the left shoulder. They are not to appear abroad without the garter, on penalty of 6s. 8d. paid to the register. The manner of electing a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KNIGHT">knight</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPANION">companion</a> into this most noble order, and the ceremonies of investiture, are as follow. When the sovereign designs to elect a companion of the Garter, the chancellor belonging to this order draws up the letters, which, passing both under the sovereign's sign <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MANUAL">manual</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SIGNET">signet</a> of the order, are sent to the person by Garter principal king at arms; and are in this manner, or to the same effect: "We, with the companions of our most noble order of the Garter, assembled in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAPTER">chapter</a>, holden this present <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> at our castle at Windsor, considering the virtuous fidelity you have shown, and the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> exploits you have done in our <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>, by vindicating and maintaining our right, &c. have elected or chosen you one of the companions of our order. Therefore, we require you to make your speedy repair unto us, to receive the ensigns thereof, and be ready for your installation upon the — day of this present <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">month</a>, &c." The garter, which is of blue velvet bordered with fine gold wire, having commonly the letters of the motto of the same, is, at the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of election, buckled upon the left leg, by two of the senior companions, who receive it from the sovereign, to whom it was presented upon a velvet cushion, by Garter king at arms, with the usual reverence, whilst the chancellor reads the following admonition, enjoined by the statutes: "To the honour of God omnipotent, and in memorial of the blessed <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARTYR">martyr</a> St George, tie about thy leg, for thy renown, this noble garter; wear it as the symbol of the most illustrious order, never to be forgotten or laid aside; that thereby thou mayest be admonished to be courageous; and having undertaken a just <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, in which thou shalt be engaged, thou mayest stand firm, valiantly fight, and successfully conquer." The princely garter being then buckled on, and the word of its signification pronounced, the knight elect is brought before the sovereign, who puts about his neck, kneeling, a dark blue ribbon, whereunto is appendant, wrought in gold within the garter, the image of St George on horseback, with his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWORD">sword</a> drawn, encountering with the dragon. In the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> time, the chancellor reads the following admonition: "Wear this ribbon about thy neck, adorned with the image of the blessed martyr and soldier of Christ, St George, by whose <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a> provoked, thou mayest so overpass both prosperous and adverse adventures, that having stoutly vanquished thy enemies both of body and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUL">soul</a>, thou mayest not only receive the praise of this transient <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMBAT">combat</a>, but be crowned with the palm of eternal victory." Then the knight elected kisses the sovereign's <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>; thanks his majesty for the great honour done him; rises up and salutes all the companions severally, who return their congratulations. See a representation of the above insignia, among others, on the plate belonging to Orders of Knighthood. Since the institution of this order, there have been eight emperors and twenty-eight kings, besides numerous sovereign princes, enrolled as companions thereof. Its origin is somewhat differently related. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> account is, that the countess of Salisbury at a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALL">ball</a> happening to drop her garter, the king took it up and presented it to her with these words, "Honi soit qui mal y pense; i.e. Evil to him that evil thinks. This accident, it is said, gave rise to the order and the motto; it being the spirit of the times to mix <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> and war together: but as in the original statutes of this order there is not the least conjecture to countenance such a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FEMININE">feminine</a> institution, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> cannot be given to this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRADITION">tradition</a>. Camden, Fern, &c. take it to have been instituted on occasion of the victory obtained by Edward over the French at the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CRESSY">Cressy</a>; that <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>, say some historians, ordered his garter to be displayed, as a signal of battle: in commemoration whereof, he made a garter the principal ornament of the order, erected in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of this signal victory, and a symbol of the indissoluble union of the knights. It appears from Rastel's <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHRONICLE">Chronicle</a>, lib. vi. quoted by Granger in the supplement to his Biographical <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, that this order was devised by Richard I. at the siege of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACRE">Acre</a>, when he caused twenty-six knights, who firmly stood by him, to wear thongs of blue <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a> about their legs, and that it was perfected in the nineteenth year of Edward III. In 1557, Edward VI. made some alterations in the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RITUAL">ritual</a> of this order: that prince composed it in Latin, the original whereof is still extant in his own handwriting. He there ordained, that the order should no longer be called the order of St George, but that of the Garter; and, instead of the george, hung at the collar, he substituted a cavalier, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> a book on the point of his sword, with the word protectio graven on the sword, and verbum Dei on the book: with a buckle in the left hand, and the word fides thereon. Garter, principal King at Arms. This office was instituted by Henry V. Garter, and principal king at arms, are two distinct offices united in one person: Garter's employment is to attend the service of the order of the Garter; for which he is allowed a mantle and badge, a house in Windsor castle, and pensions both from the sovereign and knights, and lastly, fees. He also carries the rod and sceptre at every feast of St George, when the sovereign is present, and notifies the election of such as are new chosen; attends the solemnity of their installations, takes care of placing their arms over their seats; and carries the garter to foreign kings and princes, for which services it has been usual to join him in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a> with some peer, or other person of distinction. Garter's oath relates only to services being performed within the order, and is taken in chapter before the sovereign knights. His oath, as king at arms, is taken before the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARL">earl</a> marshal. Garter is also a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERALDRY">heraldry</a>, signifying the moiety or half of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEND">bend</a>. Garth is used in some parts of England for a little backside or <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">close</a>. It is an ancient British word. Gardd, in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, signifies garden, and is pronounced and written garth. This word is also used for a <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-DAM">dam</a> or weir, &c. Garth Men, is used in our statutes for those who catch fish by means of fish garths, or wears. By statute it is ordained, that no fisher, nor garth men, shall use any nets or engines to destroy the fry of fish, &c. The word is supposed by some to be derived from the Scotch word gart, which signifies forced or compelled; because fish are forced by the wear to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> in a loop, where they are taken. Garth, Sir Samuel, an excellent English poet and physician, was descended from a good family in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORKSHIRE">Yorkshire</a>. He was admitted into the college of physicians at <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a> in 1663. He at that time zealously promoted and encouraged the erecting of the dispensary for the relief of the sick poor, by giving them advice gratis, and medicines at low <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RATES">rates</a>. This <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARITY">charity</a> having exposed him and many other physicians to the envy and resentment of several persons of the same <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FACULTY">faculty</a> as well as apothecaries, he ridiculed them, with a peculiar spirit and vivacity, in a poem called the Dispensary, in six cantos, highly esteemed. He was one of the most eminent members of the famous <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> called the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KIT">Kit</a> Kat Club, which consisted of noblemen and gentlemen distinguished by their excellent parts and affection to the house of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HANOVER">Hanover</a>. Upon the accession of George I. he was knighted, and made physician in ordinary to his majesty, and physician general to the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>. Nor were these more than just rewards even of his physical merit. He had gone through the office of censor of the college in 1702; and had practised always with great reputation, and a strict regard to the honour and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> of the faculty, never stooping to prostitute the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> of his profession, through mean and sordid views of self-interest, to any, even the most popular and wealthy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a>. In a steady adherence to this noble principle, he concurred with the much celebrated Dr Radcliffe, with whom he was also often joined in physical consultations. He had a very extensive practice, but was very moderate in his views of advancing his own fortune; his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a> and good <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> inclining him more to make use of the great interest he had with persons in power, for the support and encouragement of other men of letters. He chose to live with the great in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of independency and freedom which became a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> possessed of a superior genius, whereof he was daily giving fresh proofs to the public. One of his last performances in polite letters, was his translation of the whole fourteenth book, and the story of Cinnus in the fifteenth book, of Ovid's Metamorphoses. These, together with an English version of the rest, were published in 1717; and he has prefixed an excellent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREFACE">preface</a> to the whole, wherein he not only gives an idea of the work, and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">points</a> out its principal beauties, but shows the uses of the poem, and how it may be read to most profit. The distemper which seized him the ensuing year, and ended not but with his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, caused a general concern; which was particularly testified by <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Lansdowne, a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> poet. He died, after a short illness, which he bore with great <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATIENCE">patience</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 1719. Garve, Christian, an eminent German <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>. See Supplement. Garumna, or Garonne, a noble and navigable river of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAUL">Gaul</a>, which, rising from the Pyrenees, formerly bounded Aquitain on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> (Caesar); but by the new regulation of Augustus divided it in the middle, emptying itself to the north of Burdegala, in the Aquitanic ocean. Mela observes concerning it, that unless it is swelled by winter rains, or the melting of the snow, it is for a great part of the year shalby and scarcely navigable; but when increased by the meeting tide, whereby its waters are impelled, it is somewhat fuller; and the farther the river advances, it is broader, till at length it resembles a large frith or arm of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, not only bearing large vessels, but al-

GAS

Pages 482-484

in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a>, a general name for all permanently <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELASTIC">elastic</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLUIDS">fluids</a>, which are obtained by chemical processes, as azotic gas, muriatic acid gas, nitrous gas. See Chemistry <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. It is derived from the German gascht <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> gast, signifying the ebullition attending the expulsion of elastic fluids from substances in a state of effervescence. It was first employed by Van Helmont. Gas Lights. See Supplement. Gascoigne, Sir William, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BENCH">bench</a> under Henry IV. A most learned and upright judge; who being insulted on the bench by the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>, afterwards Henry V., with equal intrepidity and coolness committed the prince to prison; and by this seasonable fortitude laid the foundation of the future <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> of that <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> monarch, who from this event dated his reformation from the licentiousness of his youth. It is not well authenticated that the prince struck Sir William, as recorded by Shakespeare; but all authors agree, that he interrupted the course of justice to screen a lewd <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SERVANT">servant</a>. Sir William died in 1413. Gascoigne, George, an English poet of some fame in the early <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a>, was born at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WALTHAMSTOW">Walthamstow</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ESSEX">Essex</a>, of an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> family, and educated at both <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-UNIVERSITIES">universities</a>, but principally at <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>. From thence he removed to Gray's Inn, and commenced student of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a>; but having a genius too volatile for that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a>, he travelled abroad, and for some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> served in the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> in the Low Countries. He afterwards went to France; where he became enamoured of a Scottish lady, and married her. Being at length, says Wood, weary of those vanities, he returned to England; and settled once more in Gray's Inn, where he wrote most of his dramatic and other poems. The latter part of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> he spent in his native village of Walthamstow, where he died in the year 1578. He had the character of a polite <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a>, an eloquent and witty <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPANION">companion</a>, et vir inter poetas sui seculi praestantissimus. His plays, first printed separately, were afterwards, with several other poems, &c., reprinted into two volumes 4to; the first volume in 1577, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> in 1587. Gascoin, or Gascoign, denotes the hinder thigh of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>, which begins at the stifle, and reaches to the ply or <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BENDING">bending</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAM">ham</a>. Gasconade, a boast or vaunt of something very improbable. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> has its rise from the Gascons, or people of Gascony in France, who it seems have been distinguished for bragging and rhodomontade. Gascony, the most south-west <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of France, is bounded by Guienne on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, by <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANGUEDOC">Languedoc</a> on the east, by the Pyrenees which separate it from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a> on the south, and by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-BISCAY">Biscay</a> on the west. It had its name from the ancient inhabitants, called Gascones or Vascones; by the moderns Basques, or Vasques. After these were subdued by the Franks, they had for some time dukes of their own, who were subject to the dukes of Aquitaine; but both were at last dispossessed by the kings of France. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> produces corn, wine, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>, &c. The inhabitants are noted for a corrupt <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRONUNCIATION">pronunciation</a>; and their tendency to exaggerate their own exploits, has rendered Gasconade a proverbial <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a>. Gassendi, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PETER">Peter</a>, one of the most celebrated philosophers France has produced, was born at Chantiersier, about three miles from Digne in Provence, in 1592. When a child, he took particular delight in gazing at the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOON">moon</a> and stars as often as they appeared in clear unclouded <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>. This <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> frequently drew him into bye places, in order to feast his eye freely and undisturbed; by which means his parents had him often to seek, not without many anxious fears and apprehensions. They therefore put him to school at Digne; where, in a short time, he made such an extraordinary progress in learning, that some persons, who had seen specimens of his genius, resolved to have him removed to <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIX">Aix</a>, in order to study <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> under Fesay, a learned <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINOR">minor</a> friar.
