This proposal was so disagreeable to his father, who intended to breed him up in his own way to country business, as being more profitable than that of a scholar, that he would consent to it only upon condition that he should return home in two years at farthest. Accordingly young Gassendi, at the end of the appointed time, repaired to Chantiersier; but he had not been <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> there when he was invited to be professor of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHETORIC">rhetoric</a> at Digne, before he was quite 16 years of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>; and he had been engaged in that office but three years, when his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> Fesay dying, he was made professor in his room at Aix. When he had been there a few years, he composed his Paradoxical Exercitations; which, coming to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of Nicholas Peiresc, that great <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATRON">patron</a> of learning joined with <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOSEPH">Joseph</a> Walter <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIOR">prior</a> of Valette in promoting him; and he having entered into holy orders, was first made canon of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of Digne and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a>, and then obtained the wardenship or rectorship of that church. Gassendi's fondness for <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">astronomy</a> grew up with his years; and his reputation daily increasing, he was in 1645 appointed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> professor of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>. This <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a> being chiefly designed for astronomy, our author read lectures on that science to a crowded audience. However, he did not hold this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> long; for a dangerous cough and inflammation of the lungs obliged him, in 1647, to return to Digne for the benefit of his native <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a>.—Gassendi wrote against the metaphysical meditations of Descartes; and divided with that great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> the philosophers of his time, almost all of whom were Cartesians or Gassendians. He joined to his knowledge of philosophy and the mathematics an acquaintance with the languages and a profound erudition. He wrote, 1. Three volumes on Epicurus's Philosophy; and six others, which contain his own philosophy. 2. Astronomical Works. 3. The Lives of Nicholas de Peiresc, Epicurus, Copernicus, Tycho Brahe, Puerbachius, and Regiomontanus. 4. Epistles, and other treatises. All his works were collected together, and printed at Lyons in 1658, in six volumes folio. He died at Paris in 1658, aged 63. Gasterosteus, the Stickleback, a genus of fishes belonging to the order of thoracici. See <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ICHTHYOLOGY">Ichthyology</a> Index. Gast-<a class="xref" href="../1860/vol11.html#article-HOUND">hound</a>. See Gaze Hound. Gastric, in general, something belonging to the stomach. Gastric Juice, a thin pellucid liquor, which distils from certain glands in the stomach, for the dilution, &c. of the food. See ANATOMY.

GASTROMANCY

Pages 484-484
or GASTROMANTIA, a kind of divination practised among the ancients by means of words coming or seeming to come out of the belly. The word is Greek, γαστρομαντική, composed of γαστήρ, belly, and μαντεία, divination. There is another kind of divination, called by the same name gastromancy, which is performed by means of glasses or other round transparent vessels, within which certain figures appear by magic art. It is thus called, because the figures appear as in the belly of the vessels.

GASTRORAPHY

Pages 484-484

in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SURGERY">Surgery</a>, the operation of sewing up wounds of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABDOMEN">abdomen</a>. See SURGERY.

GASTROTOMY

Pages 484-484

the operation of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> open the belly; otherwise called the Cesarean <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECTION">section</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MIDWIFERY">MIDWIFERY</a>.

GATAKER

Pages 484-484

Thomas, a learned critic and divine, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a> in 1574, and studied at St John's <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>. He was afterwards chosen preacher at <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LINCOLN">Lincoln</a>'s Inn; which he quitted in 1611, for the rectory of Rotherhithe in Surry. In 1620, he made a tour through the Low Countries; and in 1624, published at London a book, entitled, Transubstantiation declared by the confession of the Popish Writers to have no necessary foundation in God's Word: he wrote likewise a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of this discourse. In 1642, he was appointed one of the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a> of divines, and was engaged with them in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> annotations upon the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BIBLE">Bible</a>. He died in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> 1654, in the 80th year of his <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>. Besides the above works, he published, 1. A Dissertation upon the Style of the New <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a>. 2. De Nomine Tetragrammata. 3. De Diphthongis, sive Bivocalibus. 4. An Edition and Translation of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">Emperor</a> Marcus Antoninus's Meditations. 5. A Collection of Sermons, in folio; and many other works. His piety and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARITY">charity</a> were very exemplary; and his <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODESTY">modesty</a> so <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a>, that he declined all <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> preferments. His extensive learning was admired by Salmasius and other great men abroad; his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> was a private seminary for young gentlemen of this <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>, and many foreigners resorted to him to receive advice in their studies.

GATE

Pages 484-484

in a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, is made of strong planks, with <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> bars, to oppose an enemy. They are generally made in the middle of the curtain, from whence they are seen, and defended by the two flanks of the bastions. They should be covered with a good ravelin, that they may not be seen <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> enfiladed by the enemy. These gates, belonging to a fortified <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, are <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> through the rampart, which may be shut and opened by means of doors and a portcullis. They are either private or public. Private gates are those passages by which the troops can go out of the town unseen by the enemy, when they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> to and from the relief of the duty in the outworks, or from any other occasion which is to be concealed from the besiegers. Public gates are those passages through the middle of such curtains, to which the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROADS">roads</a> of public ways <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>. The dimensions of these are usually about 13 or 14 feet <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, and 9 or 10 feet wide, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> through the rampart, with proper recesses for foot passengers to stand in out of the way of wheel <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARRIAGES">carriages</a>. GATES OF <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HELL">HELL</a>. This <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a> is used in Scripture, to denote figuratively either the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAVE">grave</a> or the powers of darkness, i.e. the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVIL">devil</a> and his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGELS">angels</a>. The Mahometans <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> the expression literally, and suppose that hell has <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> gates. The first is that where Mussulmans, who incur the guilt of sin, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be tormented. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> is for the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>. The third is for the Jews. The fourth is for the Sabians. The fifth for the Magians or worshippers of fire. The sixth for Pagans and idolaters. And the seventh for hypocrites, who make an outward show of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, but have none.

GATESHEAD

Pages 484-484

in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DURHAM">Durham</a>, is as it were the suburbs of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEWCASTLE">Newcastle</a>, though it lies in another county, being divided by the river Tyne; over which there is a fine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a>, with an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> gate in the middle, having the arms of Durham on one side, and those of Newcastle on the other, which is the boundary between the bishopric and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTHUMBERLAND">Northumberland</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> is a fine <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, with a very <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> tower, which is seen at a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> distance; and in the church-yard are several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> monuments. Few traces of its ancient <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a> remain, except a stone gateway. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> in 1811 amounted to 8782.

GATH

Pages 484-485
or GETH, in Ancient Geography, a celebrated city of the Philistines, and one of their five principalities. It is famous for having given birth to Goliath. David made a conquest of it in the beginning of his reign over all Israel; and it continued subject to the kings his successors till the declension and decay of the kingdom of Judah. Rehoboam rebuilt or fortified it; King Uzziah retook it, and Hezekiah once more reduced it under his subjection. Gath stood about five or six miles from Jamnia, about 14 south of Joppa, and 32 west of Jerusalem. Hence some authors (among whom is F. Calmet) have committed an egregious mistake in making Gath the most southern, and Ekron the most northern, of the Philistine cities; as if these two had been the two boundaries of their dominions, whereas these two cities are not above five miles asunder; and Gaza is the last of the five satrapies south. And Josephus (in the place already quoted) expresses himself plainly enough, when he says, that Hezekiah took all the Philistine cities cities from Gaza to Gath; there being many more cities of that name, which signifies in the Hebrew a wine press. Several other cities of the name of Geth or Gath are mentioned in Eusebius and St Jerome, whose situation, according to those authors, plainly shows them to have been different places from this, and from each other; besides those which had an adjunct to distinguish them. This city recovered its liberty and lustre in the time of the prophets Amos and Micah; but was afterwards demolished by Hazael king of Syria, after which it became of but little consideration till the time of the holy war, when Fulk king of Jerusalem built a castle on its ruins. Gath Opher, Gath Epher, or Gath, in the canton of Opher, in Galilee, was the birth-place of the prophet Jonah. Joshua makes this city to be part of the tribe of Zebulun; and St Jerome, in his preface upon Jonah, says, that it was two miles from Sephoris, otherwise called Diocesarea. Gath Rimmon, a city belonging to the tribe of Dan. St Jerome places it ten miles from Diospolis on the way from Eleutheropolis. It was given to the Levites of Kohath's family. Gath Rimmon, was also a city in the half tribe of Manasseh, on this side Jordan, and was also given for a place of abode to the Levites of Kohath's family. Gath Rimmon, was likewise a city in the tribe of Ephraim, given to the Kohathites.

GATTON

Pages 485-485

a village in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Surry, 19 miles south from <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. It lies under the side of a hill going to Reygate; and is supposed to have been known to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, by reason of their coins and other antiquities that have been found here. It is a borough by <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRESCRIPTION">prescription</a>; and has sent members to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> ever since the 29th of Henry VI. It was formerly a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> town; but is now a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> village, with a small <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, and without either fair <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> market. It sends two members to parliament. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> in 1801 amounted to 112.

GAUANITIS

Pages 490-491
or GAULONITIS (Josephus); in Ancient Geography, according to the different manner of writing the capital, Gaulan or Gaulon; the extreme part of Bashan to the south, and bordering on the tribe of Gad. It was divided into the Superior, which to the east extended to Arabia; and into the Inferior, which lay on the lake of Genesareth, (Josephus).

GAUBIUS

Pages 485-485

JEROME-<a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAVID">DAVID</a>, M.D. professor of medicine at <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEYDEN">Leyden</a>, and afterwards fellow of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEIDELBERG">Heidelberg</a> in the year 1705. From the Jesuits he received the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RUDIMENTS">rudiments</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>, and was much esteemed by them on account of his abilities; but his father afterwards sent him to the orphan <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HALLE">Halle</a>, lest he should be obliged to abjure his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a>, however, he here found to be much too severe, which induced him to request his father to remove him from it, which was accordingly complied with. His teacher at this <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOSPITAL">hospital</a> attributing the dislike of young Gaubius to the want of genius, urged him to give his son some <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MECHANICAL">mechanical</a> employment; but the father thought proper to indulge his ardent desire after knowledge, and accordingly sent him to <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMSTERDAM">Amsterdam</a> to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> under his uncle John, who was an eminent physician. After prosecuting his medical studies for some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> at Hordwyk, he resolved to visit Leyden, where the immortal Boerhaave was an eminent professor, and whose penetrating eye soon discovered that Gaubius was possessed of talents above mediocrity. He honoured him with unlimited access to his house, delighted in imparting instruction to him, and gradually forwarded the cultivation of his mind. He took the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a> at the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> of 20, after a disputation on the nature of solids, containing an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABSTRACT">abstract</a> of the system which he himself followed through <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. He travelled through various parts of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, and when he returned to Heidelberg by the way of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-STRASBOURG">Strasbourg</a>, he was appointed <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>-physician at <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVENTER">Deventer</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Overyssel; but he soon after removed to Amsterdam. Boerhaave never lost sight of his favourite pupil; for when the infirmities of old age and indefatigable labour made him anxious to resign his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a>, Gaubius on his recommendation was appointed to succeed him. He published his Instructions for <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> Recipes in the year 1738, by which he acquired <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> and justly merited approbation, as he reduced the art from a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> mechanical to a scientific form. His Principles of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOSOLOGY">Nosology</a> is perhaps his most masterly performance, as it evinced that he was highly worthy of such a preceptor. His next publication, which appeared in 1771, was his "Adversaria varii Argumenti," a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> which was particularly interesting to chemists; and his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORATION">oration</a> on the 200th anniversary of the academy of Leyden attracted considerable notice, as in it he traced out, with his accustomed acumen, the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> epochs of the arts and sciences in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>. He was likewise the author of numerous and valuable papers in the Transactions of the Society of Haerlem, and was editor of many excellent performances, among which we may <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> Cramer's Elementa artis docimastice; Albinius de presagienda vita et morte, and Swammerdam's Book of Nature, which he partly translated. His literary merit spread his fame so far beyond the bounds of his native <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, that pupils repaired to Leyden from every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of Europe. In addition to his widely extended reputation, he was blessed with the enjoyment of good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> till he was 70 years of age, and died on the 29th of November 1780, in his seventy-fifth year. One work of his, entitled "Institutiones Pathologiae Medicinalis," was deemed so valuable by Professor Ackerman, and of such singular advantage in academical lectures, that he gave the world a fourth edition of it, published at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUREMBERG">Nuremberg</a> in 1787.

GAUDEN

Pages 485-487

DR <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOSEPH">JOSEPH</a>, son of John Gauden <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VICAR">vicar</a> of Mayfield in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ESSEX">Essex</a>, was born there in 1605. At the commencement of the civil <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, he was chaplain to Robert <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WARWICK">Warwick</a>; who taking <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> with the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> against the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>, was followed by his chaplain. Upon the establishment of the Presbyterian <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODEL">model</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, he complied with the ruling powers, and was nominated one of the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a> of divines who met at Westminster in 1643, and took the covenant; yet having offered some scruples and objections to it, his name was afterwards struck out of the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIST">list</a>. Nor did he espouse the parliament cause any longer than they adhered to their first avowed principles of reforming only, instead of destroying, <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONARCHY">monarchy</a> and episcopacy. In this spirit he was one of those divines who signed a protestation to the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> against the violent proceedings that affected the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> of the king; and a few days after his execution published the famous Exornatus, A Portraiture of his Sacred Majesty in his Solitude and Sufferings; which ran through 50 editions in the course of a year. Upon the return of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> II. he was promoted to the see of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXETER">Exeter</a>; and in 1662 was removed to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORCESTER">Worcester</a>, much to his regret. regret, having flattered himself with the hopes of a translation to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WINCHESTER">Winchester</a>; and his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> happened the same year. He wrote many controversial pieces suited to the circumstances of the times, and to his own views from them. The *Eikon Basileike* above mentioned he published as the king's private meditations: though on this point there has been a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> controversy. After the bishop's death, his widow, in a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> to one of her sons, calls it *The <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JEWEL">Jewel</a>*; and said, her husband had hoped to make a fortune by it; and that she had a letter of a very <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>'s, which would clear up that he writ it. This assertion, as the earl of Clarendon had predicted, was eagerly espoused by the anti-royalists, in the view of disparaging Charles I. But it has been observed, that Gauden had too luxuriant an imagination, which betrayed him into a rankness of style in the Asiatic way; and from thence, as Bishop Burnet argues with others, it may be certainly concluded, that not he, but the king himself, was the true author of the *Eikon Basileike*; in which there is a nobleness and justness of thought, with a greatness of style, that made it be looked on as the best written book in the English <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>. **Gavel <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GABEL">Gabel</a>**, among builders. See **Gabel**. **Gavel**, in *<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">Law</a>*, tribute, toll, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a>, or yearly revenue; of which we had in old <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> several kinds. See **Gabel**. **Gavel Kind**, a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TENURE">tenure</a> or custom belonging to lands in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KENT">Kent</a>. The word is said by Leland to be compounded of three Saxon words, *gyfe*, *cal*, *kyn*, "omnibus cognatione proximis <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DATA">data</a>." Verstegan calls it *gavelkind*, quasi "give all kind," that is, to each child his part: and Taylor, in his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of *gavelkind*, derives it from the British *gavel*, that is, a hold or tenure, and *cenned*, "generatio aut familia;" and so *gavel cenned* might signify *tenura generationis*. It is universally known what struggles the Kentish men made to preserve their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> liberties, and with how much success those struggles were attended. And as it is principally here that we meet with the custom of gavelkind (though it was and is to be found in some other parts of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>), we may fairly conclude, that this was a part of these liberties: agreeable to Mr Selden's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, that gavelkind, before the Norman conquest, was the general custom of the realm. The distinguished properties of this tenure are various: some of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> are these: 1. The tenant is of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> sufficient to alienate his estate by feoffment, at the age of 15. 2. The estate does not <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ESCHEAT">escheat</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> of an attainder and execution for felony; their maxim being, "the father to the bough, the son to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLOUGH">plough</a>." 3. In most places he had the power of devising lands by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a>, before the statute for that purpose was made. 4. The lands descend, not to the eldest, youngest, or any one son only, but to all the sons together; which was indeed anciently the most usual course of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a>, all over England, though in particular places particular customs prevailed. **Gavellet**, in *Law*, an ancient and special cessavit used in Kent, where the custom of gavelkind continues, by which the tenant, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he withdraws his rent and services due to the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a>, forfeits his <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> and tenements. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> of the gavellet is thus. The lord is first to seek by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STEWARD">steward</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>, from three weeks to three weeks, to find some distress upon the tenement, till the fourth court; and if at that time he find none, at this fourth court it is awarded, that he take the tenement in his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> in name of a distress, and keep it a year and a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> without manuring; within which time, if the tenant pay his arrears, and make reasonable amends for the withholding, he shall have and enjoy his tenement as before: if he come not before the year and day be past, the lord is to go to the next county court with witnesses of what had passed at his own court, and pronounce there his process, to have further witnesses; and then by the award of his own court, he shall enter and manure the tenement as his own: so that if the tenant desired afterwards to have and hold it as before, he must agree with the lord; according to this old saying: "Has he not since anything given, or anything paid, then let him pay five <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POUND">pound</a> for his were, e'er he become healer again." Other copies have the first part with some <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-VARIATION">variation</a>; "Let him <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> times pay, and nine times repay." **Gavellet**, in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, is a writ used in the hustings, given to lords of rents in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of London. Here the parties, tenant and demandant, appear by *scire facias*, to show cause why the one should not have his tenement again on payment of his rent, of the other recover the lands on default thereof. **Gaugamelia**, in *Ancient <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>*, a village of Aturia, lying between the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> Lycus and Tigris; famous for Alexander's victory over <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DARIUS">Darius</a>. It is said to have been allowed to Darius Hystaspes for the maintenance of a camel; and hence the name. It was not far from a more considerable <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> called *Arbela*; whence the latter gave the name to the victory. See *Arbela*. **Gauge**, point of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a>, the diameter of a circle whose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AREA">area</a> is equal to the solid content of the same measure. **Gauger**, a king's officer, who is appointed to examine all tons, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PIPES">pipes</a>, hogsheads, and barrels, of wine, beer, ale, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONEY">honey</a>, &c. and give them a mark of allowance, before they are sold in any place within the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of his office. **Gauging**. See *<a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOMETRY">Geometry</a>*. **Gauging-Rod**, an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> used in gauging or measuring the contents of any vessel. That usually employed is the four-foot gauging rod. It is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> made of box, and consists of four rules, each a foot long and about three-eighths of an inch <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>, joined together by three <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JOINTS">joints</a>; by which means the rod is rendered four feet long when the four rules are quite opened, and but one foot when they are all folded together. On the first <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FACE">face</a> of this rod, marked ed 4, are placed two diagonal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a>: one for beer and the other for wine: by means of which the content of any <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> vessel in beer or wine gallons may be readily found, by putting the rod in at the bung hole of the vessel till it meets the intersection of the head of the vessel with the staves opposite to the bung hole. For distinction of this line, there is written thereon, *beer and wine gallons*. On the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> face, 5, are a line of inches and the gauge-line; which is a line expressing the areas of circles, whose diameters are the correspondent inches in ale gallons. At the beginning is written, *ale area*. On the third face, 6, are three scales of lines; the first, at the end of which is written *hogshead*, is for finding how many gallons there are in GAU A hogshead when it is not full, lying with its axis <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> to the horizon. The second line, at the end of which is written B. L., signifying a butt lying is for the same <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> as that for the hogshead. The third line is to find how much liquor is wanting to fill up a butt when it is standing: at the end of it is written B. S., signifying a butt standing. In the half of the fourth face of the gauging rod, there are the three scales of lines; to find the wants in a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIRKIN">firkin</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KILDERKIN">kilderkin</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BARREL">barrel</a>, lying with their areas parallel to the horizon. They are distinguished by letters F. K. B. signifying a firkin, kilderkin, and barrel. Use of the diagonal lines on this rod. To find the content of a vessel in beer or wine gallons, put the brased end of the gauging rod into the bung hole of the cask, with the diagonal lines upwards, and thrust this brased end to the meeting of the head and staves; then with chalk make a mark at the middle of the bung hole of the vessel, and also on the diagonal lines of the rod, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> against, over one another, when the brased end is thrust home to the head and staves: then turn the gauging rod to the other end of the vessel, and thrust the brased end home to the end, as before. Lastly, See if the mark made on the gauging rod come even with the mark made on the bung hole, when the rod was thrust to the other end; which if it be, the mark made on the diagonal lines will, on the same lines, show the whole content of the cask in beer or wine gallons. If the mark made on the bung hole be not right against that made on the rod when you put it the other way, then right against the mark made on the bung hole make another on the diagonal line; and the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> on the diagonal line between the two chalks will show the vessel's whole contents in beer or wine gallons. Thus, e. gr. if the diagonal line of the vessel be 28 inches four-tenths, its contents in beer gallons will be near 51, and in wine gallons 62. If a vessel be open, as a half barrel, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-TUN">tun</a>, or <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>, and the measure from the middle of one side to the head and staves be 38 inches, the diagonal line gives 122 beer gallons; half of which, viz. 61, is the content of the open half tub. If you have a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> vessel, as a tun or copper, and the diagonal line taken by a long rule proves 70 inches; the content of that vessel may be found thus: Every inch at the beginning end of the diagonal line call ten inches. Thus ten inches becomes 100 inches; and every tenth of a gallon call 100 gallons; and every whole gallon call 1000 gallons. Example. At 44.8 inches on the diagonal beer line is 200 gallons; so that 4 inches 48 parts, now called 44 inches 8-tenths, is <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> two-tenths of a gallon, now called 200 gallons; so also if the diagonal line be 76 inches and 7-tenths, a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> cask of such diagonal will hold 1000 beer gallons: but an open cask but half so much, viz. 500 beer gallons. Use of the Gauge Line. To find the content of any cylindrical vessel in ale gallons; seek the diameter of the vessel in inches, and just against it on the gauge line is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of ale gallons contained in one inch deep: this multiplied by the length of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CYLINDER">cylinder</a> will give its content in ale gallons. For example, suppose the length of the vessel 32.06, and the diameter of its base 25 inches; to find what is the content in ale gallons? Right against 25 inches on the gauge line is one gallon and .745 of a gallon; which multiplied by 32.06, the length, gives 55.9447 gallons for the content of the vessel. The bung diameter of a hogshead being 25 inches, the head diameter 22 inches, and the length 32.06 inches; to find the quantity of ale gallons contained in it?—Seek 25, the bung diameter, on the line of inches, and right against it on the gauge line you will find 1.745: take one-third of it which is .580, and set it <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> twice; seek 22 inches in the head diameter, and against it you will find on the gauge line 1.356; one-third of which added to twice .580 gives 1.6066; which multiplied by the length 32.06, the product will be 51.603776, the content in ale gallons. <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOTE">Note</a>, this operation supposes, that the aforesaid hogshead is in the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of the middle frustum of a spheroid. The use of the lines on the two other faces of the rod is very easy; you need only put it downright into the bung hole (if the vessel you desire to know the quantity of ale gallons contained therein be lying) to the opposite staves; and then where the surface of the liquor cuts any one of the lines appropriated to that vessel, will be the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of gallons contained in that vessel.

GAUL

Pages 487-490

the name given by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> that now forms the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of France.—The original inhabitants were descended from the Celtes <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Gomerians, by whom the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> was peopled; the name of Galli, or Gauls, being probably given them <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> after their settlement in that country. See Gallia. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of the Gauls is entirely wrapped up in obscurity and darkness; all we know concerning them for a long <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> is, that they multiplied so fast, that their country being unable to contain them, they poured forth in vast multitudes into other countries, which they generally subdued, and settled themselves in. It often happened, however, that these colonies were so molested by their neighbours, that they were obliged to send for assistance to their native country. This was always very easily obtained. The Gauls were upon every occasion, ready to send forth <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> numbers of new adventurers; and as these spread desolation wherever they came, the very name of Gauls proved terrible to most of the neighbouring nations.—The Account of earliest excursion of these people, of which we have any Gaulish distinct account, was into <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, under a famed leader incursions named Bellovesus, about 622 years before Christ. He into Italy, crossed the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RHONE">Rhone</a> and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALPS">Alps</a>, till then unattempted; defeated the Heturians; and seized upon that part of their country, since known by the names of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LOMBARDY">Lombardy</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PIEDMONT">Piedmont</a>.—The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> expedition was made by the Cenomani, a people dwelling between the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEINE">Seine</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LOIRE">Loire</a>, under a general named Elitonis. They settled in those parts of Italy, now known by the names of Bresciano, the Cremonese, the Mantuan, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARNIOLA">Carniola</a>, and the Venetian.—In a third excursion, two other Gaulish nations settled on both sides of the river Po; and in a fourth, the Boii and Lingones settled in the country between <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAVENNA">Ravenna</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOLOGNA">Bologna</a>. The time of these three last expeditions is uncertain. The third expedition of the Gauls was more remarkable than any of the former, and happened about 200 years after that of Bellovesus. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENONES">Senones</a> settled between <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEAUX">Meaux</a>, were invited into Italy by a Hetrurian <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a>, and settled themselves in Umbria. Brennus their <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> laid siege to Clusium, a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLIANCE">alliance</a> with Rome; and this produced a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> with the Romans, in which the latter were at first defeated, and their city taken and burnt; but at length the whole <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> was cut off by Camillus, insomuch, that not a single person escaped. Some other expeditions the Gauls undertook against the Romans: in which, though they always proved unsuccessful, by reason of their want of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a>; yet their fierceness and courage made them so formidable to the republic, that, on the first news of their <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">march</a>, extraordinary levies of troops were made, sacrifices and public supplications offered to the gods, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a> which granted an immunity from military <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> to priests and old men, was, for the time, abolished. Against the Greeks, the expeditions of the Gauls were very little more successful than against the Romans. The first of these we hear of was about 279 years before Christ, in the year after Pyrrhus had invaded Italy. At this time, the Gauls finding themselves greatly overstocked at home, sent out three great colonies to conquer new countries for themselves. One of these armies was commanded by Brennus, another by Cerethrius, and the third by Belgius. The first entered Panonia or <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUNGARY">Hungary</a>; the second Thrace; and the third marched into Illyricum and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-MACEDONIA">Macedonia</a>. Here Belgius at first met with great success; and enriched himself by plunder to such a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>, that Brennus envying him, resolved to enter the same countries, in order to share the spoil. In a short time, however, Belgius met with such a total defeat, that his army was almost entirely destroyed; upon which Brennus hastened to the same <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>. His army at first consisted of 150,000 foot and 15,000 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>: but two of his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> officers revolted, and carried off 20,000 men, with whom they marched into Thrace; where, having joined Cerethrius, they seized on Byzantium and the western <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of the Propontis, making the adjacent parts tributary to them.—To retrieve this loss, Brennus sent for fresh supplies from Gaul; and having increased his army to 150,000 foot, and upwards of 60,000 horse, he entered Macedonia, defeated the general who opposed him, and ravaged the whole country. He next marched towards the straits of Thermopylae, with a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> to invade <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>; but was stopped by the forces sent to defend that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> against him. He passed the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, however, as <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-XERXES">Xerxes</a> had formerly done; upon which the guards retired, to avoid being surrounded. Brennus then having ordered Acichorius, the next to him in command, to follow at a distance with part of his army, marched with the bulk of the forces to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DELPHI">Delphi</a>, in order to plunder the rich temple there. This enterprise proved exceedingly unfortunate: a great <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of his men were destroyed by a dreadful storm of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIL">hail</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THUNDER">thunder</a>, and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIGHTNING">lightning</a>; another part of his army was destroyed by an earthquake; and the remainder, somehow or other, imagining themselves attacked by the enemy, fought against each other the whole night, so that in the morning scarcely one half of them remained. The Greek forces then poured in upon them from all parts; and that in such numbers, that though Acichorius came up in due time with his forces, Brennus found himself unable to make head against the Greeks, and was defeated with great slaughter. He himself was desperately wounded; and so disheartened by his misfortune, that, having assembled all his chiefs, he advised them to kill all the wounded and disabled, and to make the best retreat they could: after which he put an end to his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. On this occasion, it is said that 20,000 of these unhappy people were executed by their own countrymen. Acichorius then set out with the remainder for Gaul; but, by being obliged to march through the country of their enemies, the calamities they met with by the way were so grievous, that not one of them reached their own country. A <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> judgment, say the Greek and Roman authors, for their sacrilegious intentions against Delphi. The Romans having often felt the effects of the Gaulish ferocity and courage, thought proper at last, in order to humble them, to invade their country. Their first successful attempt was about 118 years before Christ, under the command of Quintus Marcius, surnamed Rex. He opened a way betwixt the Alps and the Pyrenees, which laid the foundation for conquering the whole country. This was a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> of immense labour of itself, and rendered still more difficult by the opposition of the Gauls, especially those called the Steni, who lived at the foot of the Alps. These people, finding themselves overpowered by the consular army, set fire to their houses, killed their wives and children, and then threw themselves into the flames. After this Marcius built the city of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NARBONNE">Narbonne</a>, which became the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a>. His successor Scaurus also conquered some Gaulish nations; and in order to facilitate the sending troops from Italy into that country, he made several excellent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROADS">roads</a> between them, which before were almost impassable. These successes gave rise to the invasion of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CIMBRI">Cimbri</a> and Teutones; an account of whose unfortunate expedition is given under the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> CIMBRI, ROME, TEUTONES, &c. From this time, the Gauls seemed to be formidable to the Romans, and even seem to have been for some time on good terms with them. At last, however, the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HELVETII">Helvetii</a> kindled a war with the republic, which brought Caesar over the Alps, and ended in the total subjection of the country. Orgetorix was the first cause of it; who had engaged a vast number of his countrymen to burn their <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> and villages, and to go in search of new conquests. Julius Caesar, to whose <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOT">lot</a> the whole country of Gaul had fallen, made such haste to come and suppress them, that he was got to the Rhone in eight days; broke <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENEVA">Geneva</a>, and, in a few days more, finished the famed wall between that city and Monnt <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JURA">Jura</a>, now St <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLAUDE">Claude</a>, which extended seventeen miles in length, was sixteen feet <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, fortified with towers and castles at proper distances, and a ditch that ran the whole length of it. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> his own account of it may be relied upon, he did not set out till the beginning of April; and yet this huge work was finished by the ides or 13th of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">month</a>; so that, subtracting the eight days he was coming, it must have been all done in about five days; a prodigious work, considering he had but one legion there, or even though the whole country had given him assistance. Whilst this was doing, and the reinforcements he wanted were coming, he amused the Helvetii, Helvetii, who had sent to demand a passage through the country of the Allobroges, till he had got his reinforcements; and then flatly refused it to them: whereupon a dreadful <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> ensued; in which they lost one hundred and thirty thousand men, in spite of all their valour; besides a number of prisoners, among whom were the wife and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Orgetorix, the leader of this unfortunate expedition. The rest submitted, and begged they might be permitted to go and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> among the Edui, from whom they originally sprung; and at the request of these last, were permitted to go. The Gauls were constantly in a state of variance with one another; and Cæsar, who knew how to make the most of these intestine broils, soon became the protector of the oppressed, a terror to the oppressor, and the umpire of all their contentions. Among those who applied to him for help, were his allies the Edui; against whom Arioivistus, king of the Germans, had joined with the Arverni, who inhabited the banks of the Loire, had taken the country of the Sequani from them, and obliged them to send hostages to him. Cæsar forthwith sent to demand the restitution of both, and, in an interview which he soon after obtained of that haughty and treacherous <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>, was like to have fallen a sacrifice to his perfidy: upon which he bent his whole power against him, forced him out of his strong intrenchments, and gave him a total overthrow. Arioivistus escaped, with difficulty, over the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHINE">Rhine</a>; but his two wives, and a daughter, with a great number of Germans of distinction, fell into the conqueror's <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>. Cæsar, after this signal victory, put his army into winter <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a>, whilst he went over the Alps to make the necessary preparations for the next <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMPAIGN">campaign</a>. By this time all the Belgæ in general were so terrified at his success, that they entered into a confederacy against the Romans as their <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> enemy. Of this, Labienus, who had been left in Gaul, sent Caesar notice; upon which he immediately left Rome, and made such dispatch, that he arrived upon their confines in about fifteen days. On his arrival, the Rhemi submitted to him; but the rest appointing Galba king of the Suessiones general of all their forces, which amounted to one hundred and fifty thousand men, marched directly against him. Cæsar, who had seized on the bridge of the Axona, now Aisne, led his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> horse and infantry over it: and whilst the others were encumbered in crossing that river, made such a terrible slaughter of them, that the river was filled with their dead, insomuch that their bodies served for a bridge to those who escaped. This new victory struck such terror into the rest, that they dispersed themselves; immediately after which, the Suessiones, Bellovacii, Ambiones, and some others, submitted to him. The Nervii, indeed, joined with the Atrebates and Veromandui against them; and having first secured their wives and children, made a vigorous resistance for some time; but were at length defeated, and the greatest part of them slain. The rest, with their wives and old men, surrendered themselves, and were allowed to live in their own cities and towns as formerly. The Aduatichi were next subdued; and, for their treachery to the conqueror, were sold for slaves, to the number of 50,000. Young Crassus, the son of the triumvir, subdued likewise <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> other nations, and took possession of their cities; which not only completed the conquest of the Belgæ, but brought several nations from beyond the Rhine to submit to the conqueror. The Veneti, or ancient inhabitants of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-VANNES">Vannes</a> in Brittany, who had been likewise obliged to send hostages to the conqueror, were, in the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> time, making great preparations by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> to recover their <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>. Cæsar, then in Illyricum, was forced to equip a fleet on the Loire; and having given the command of it to Brutus, went and defeated them by land, as Brutus did by sea; and having put their <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> men to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, sold the rest for slaves. The Unelli, with Veridorix their chief, together with the Lexovii and Aulerci, were about the same time subdued by Sabinus, and the Aquitani by Crassus, with the loss of 30,000 men. There remained nothing but the countries of the Morini and Menapii to be conquered of all Gaul. Cæsar marched himself against them; but he found them so well intrenched in their inaccessible fortresses, that he contented himself with <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> and ravaging their country; and having put his troops into winter quarters, again passed over the Alps, to have a more watchful eye on some of his rivals there. He was, however, soon after obliged to come to defend his Gaulish conquests against some nations of the Germans, who were coming to settle there, to the number of 400,000. These he totally defeated, and then resolved to carry his conquering arms into Germany; but for an account of his exploits there, see the article Germany. Upon his return into Gaul, he found it labouring under a great famine, which had caused a kind of universal revolt. Cotta and Sabinus, who were left in the country of the Eburones, now <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIEGE">Liege</a>, were betrayed into an ambush by Ambiorix, one of the Gaulish chiefs, and had most of their men cut off. The Aduatichi had fallen upon Q. Cicero, who was left there with one legion, and had reduced him to great straits: at the same time Labienus, with his legion, was attacked by Indutiomarus, at the head of the Rhemi and Senones; but had better luck than the rest, and by one bold sally upon them, put them to flight, and killed their general. Cæsar acquired no small <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> by quelling all these revolts; but each victory cost the lives of so many of his troops, that he was forced to have recourse to Pompey for a fresh supply, who readily granted him two of his own legions to secure his Gaulish conquests. But it was not long before the Gauls, ever restless under a foreign yoke, raised up a new revolt, and revolted obliged him to return thither. His fear lest Pompey should <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAIN">gain</a> the affections of the Roman people, had obliged him to strip the Gauls of their <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> and silver, to bribe them over to his <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a>; and this gave no small handle to those frequent revolts which happened during his absence. He quickly, however, reduced the Nervii, Aduatichi, Menapii, and Treviri; the last of whom had raised the revolt, under the command of Ambiorix: but he found the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAME">flame</a> spread much farther, even to the greatest part of the Gauls, who had chosen Vercingetorix their <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENERALISSIMO">generalissimo</a>. Cæsar was forced to leave Insubria, whither he had retired to watch the motions of Pompey, and, in the midst of winter and snow, to repass the Alps into the province of Narbonne. Here he gathered his scattered troops with all possible speed; and, in spite of the hard <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>, besieged and took Noviodunum, now Noyons; and defeated Vercingetorix, who was come to the relief of that place. He next took the city of Avaricum, now <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOURGES">Bourges</a>, one of the strongest in Gaul, and which had a garrison of 40,000 men; of whom he made such a dreadful slaughter, that hardly 800 escaped. Whilst he was besieging Gergovia, the capital of the Arverni, he was informed that the Nitiobriges, or Agenois, were in arms; and that the Aedui were sending to Vercingetorix 10,000 men, which they were to have sent to reinforce Caesar. Upon this news, he left Fabius to carry on the siege, and marched against the Aedui. These, upon his approach, submitted, in appearance, and were pardoned; but soon after that whole <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> rose up in arms, and murdered all the Italian troops in their capital. Caesar, at this, was in great straits what <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> to take; but resolved at length to raise the siege of Gergovia, and at once attack the enemy's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMP">camp</a>, which he did with some success; but when he thought to have gone to Noviodunum, or Noyons, where his baggage, military <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHEST">chest</a>, &c., were left, he heard that the Aedui had carried it off, and burnt the place. Labienus, justly thinking that Caesar would want his assistance in the condition he now was, went to join him, and in his way defeated a Gaulish general named Camulogenus, who came to oppose his march; but this did not hinder the revolt from spreading itself all over Celtic Gaul, whither Vercingetorix had sent for fresh supplies, and, in the mean time, attacked Caesar; but was defeated, and forced to retire to Alesia, a strong place, now Alise in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BURGUNDY">Burgundy</a>, as is supposed. Hither Caesar hastened, and besieged him; and having drawn a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> circumvallation, with a design to starve him in it, as he was likely to have done, upon that account refused all offers of a surrender from him. At length, the long expected reinforcement came, consisting of 160,000 men, under four generals; these made several fruitless attacks on Caesar's trenches, but were defeated in three several battles, which at length obliged Vercingetorix to surrender at <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-DISCRETION">discretion</a>. Caesar used all his prisoners with great severity, except the Aedui and Arverni, by whose means he hoped to gain their nations, which were the most potent of Celtic Gaul; nor was he disappointed; for both of them submitted to him, and the former received him into the capital, where he spent the winter, after he put his army into winter quarters. This campaign, as it proved one of the hardest he ever had, so he gained more <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> by it than any Roman general had done before: yet could not at all by this procure from the servile <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENATE">senate</a>, now wholly dedicated to his rival, a prolongation of his proconsulship; upon which he is reported to have laid his hand upon his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>, and said, that that should do it. He was as good as his word; and the Gauls, upon their former ill success, resolving to have as many separate armies as provinces, in order to embarrass him the more, Caesar, and his generals Labienus and Fabius, were forced to fight them one after another; which they did, however, with such success, that, notwithstanding the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HARDNESS">hardness</a> of the season, they subdued the Bituriges, Carnutes, Rhemi, and Bellovaci, with their general Correus, by which he at once quieted all the Belgic provinces bordering on Celtic Gaul. The next who followed were the Treviri, the Eburones, and the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANDES">Andes</a>, under their general Dumnacus. The last place which held out against him was Uxellodunum; which was defended by the two last acting generals of the Gauls, Drapes the Senonian, and Luterius the Cadocean. The place being strong and well garrisoned, Caesar was obliged to march thither from the farthest part of Belgic Gaul; and soon after reduced it, for want of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>. Here again he caused the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of all that were fit to bear arms to be cut off, to deter the rest from revolting afresh. Thus was the conquest of Gaul finished from the Alps and Pyrenees to the Rhine, all which vast tract was now reduced to a Roman province under the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of a praetor. During his several expeditions into Gaul, Caesar is said to have taken 800 cities; to have subdued 300 different nations; and to have defeated, in several battles, three millions of men, of whom one million were killed, and another taken prisoners.—The history of the country, from the time of its conquest by the Romans to the present, is given under the articles Rome and France. The Gauls were anciently divided into a great number of different nations, which were continually at war with one another, and at variance among themselves. Caesar tells us, that not only all their cities, cantons, and districts, but even almost all families, were divided and torn by factions; and this undoubtedly facilitated the conquest of the whole. The general character of all these people was an excessive ferocity and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> of liberty. This last they carried to such an <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a>, that either on the appearance of servitude, or incapacity of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTION">action</a> through old <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, wounds, or chronic diseases, they put an end to their own lives, or prevailed upon their friends to kill them. In cities, when they found themselves so strictly besieged that they could hold out no longer, instead of thinking how to obtain <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> terms of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITULATION">capitulation</a>, their chief care very often was to put their wives and children to death, and then to kill one another, to avoid being led into <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SLAVERY">slavery</a>. Their excessive love of liberty and contempt of death, according to Strabo, very much facilitated their conquest by Caesar; for pouring their numerous forces upon such an experienced enemy as Caesar, their want of conduct very soon proved the ruin of the whole. The chief diversion of the Gauls was hunting; and indeed, considering the vast forests with which their country abounded, and the multitude of wild beasts which lodged in them, they were under an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> to hunt and destroy them, to prevent the country from being rendered totally uninhabitable. Besides this, however, they had also their hippodromes, horse and chariot races, tilts and tournaments; at all of which the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BARDS">bards</a> assisted with their poems, songs, and musical instruments.—For an account of their <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, see the article Druid. The Gauls were excessively fond of feasting, in which they were very profuse; as, like all other northern nations, they were great lovers of good eating and drinking. Their chief liquors were beer and wine. Their tables were very low. They ate but little <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a>, which was baked flat and hard, and easily broken in pieces; but devoured a great <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a>, boiled, roasted, or broiled; and this they did in a very slovenly manner, holding the piece in their hands, and tearing it with their <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a>. What they could not part by this way, they cut with a little <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KNIFE">knife</a> which hung at their girdle. When the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> was numerous, the Coryphe,

GAULON

Pages 491-491
or GOLEAN, the capital of the Gaulanitis Superior; a Levitical city and place of refuge, (Moses, Joshua).

GAULOS

Pages 491-491

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a>, in the African <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, adjoining to Melite <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALTA">Malta</a>; with commodious harbours; a colony of Phoenicians, with a cognominal town. Gaulonites, the people, (Inscription). Now called Gozo, five miles to the west of Malta.

GAULTHERIA

Pages 491-491

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the decandria class; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 18th order, Bicornes. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

GAUNT-BELLIED

Pages 491-491

in the manege, is said of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> whose belly shrinks up towards his flanks. GAUNTLET. See Gantlet.

GAUNTLOPE

Pages 491-491

pronounced Gauntlet, a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> for felony, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> some other heinous offence. In vessels of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, it is executed in the following manner. The whole ship's crew is disposed in two rows, standing <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FACE">face</a> to face on both sides of the deck, so as to form a line whereby to go forward on one side, and return aft on the other; each person being furnished with a small twisted <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CORD">cord</a>, called a knitlet, having two or three knots upon it. The delinquent is then stripped naked above the waist, and ordered to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> forward between the two rows of men, and aft on the other side, a certain <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of times, rarely exceeding three; during which every person gives him a stripe as he runs along. In his passage through this painful ordeal, he is sometimes tripped up, and very severely handled while incapable of proceeding. This punishment, which is called running the gauntlet, is seldom inflicted, except for such crimes as naturally excite a general antipathy among the seamen: as, on some occasions, the culprit would pass without receiving a single blow, particularly in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUTINY">mutiny</a> and sedition. But this <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of punishment is now, we believe, rarely or never reported to, either in the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVY">navy</a>. In the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>, when a soldier is sentenced to run the gauntlope, the regiment is drawn out in two ranks facing each other; each soldier, having a switch in his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, lashes the criminal as he runs along naked from the waist upwards. While he runs, the drums <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEAT">beat</a> at each end of the ranks. Sometimes he runs three, five, or <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> times, according to the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of the offence. The <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAJOR">major</a> is on horseback, and takes care that each soldier does his duty.

GAURA

Pages 491-491

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the octandra class; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 17th order, Calycanthemae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

GAUSE

Pages 491-491
or Gawse, in Commerce, a very thin, slight, transparent kind of stuff, woven sometimes of silk, and sometimes only of thread.—To warp the silk for making of gause, they use a peculiar kind of mill, upon which the silk is wound: this mill is a wooden machine, about six feet high, having an axis perpendicularly placed in the middle thereof, with six large wings, on which the silk is wound from off the bobbins by the axis turning round. When all the silk is on the mill, they use another instrument to wind it off again on two beams: this done, the silk is passed through as many little beads as there are threads of silk; and thus rolled on another beam to supply the loom. The ganse loom is much like that of the common weavers, though it has several appendages peculiar to itself. See Loom. There are figured gauses; some with flowers of gold and silver, on a silk ground: these last are chiefly brought from China.

GAVOTTA

Pages 491-491
or Gavotte, is a kind of dance, the air of which has two brisk and lively strains in common time, each of which strains is twice played over. The first has usually four or eight bars; and the second contains eight, twelve, or more. The first begins with a minim, or two crotchets, or notes of equal value, and the hand rising; and ends with the fall of the hand upon the dominant or mediant of the mode, but never upon the final, unless it be a rondeau: and the last begins with the rise of the hand, and ends with the fall upon the final of the mode. Tempi di Gavotta, is when only the time or movement of a gavotte is imitated, without any regard to the measures or number of bars or strains.—Little airs are often found in sonatas, which have this phrase to regulate their motions.

GAY

Pages 491-492

John, a celebrated English poet, descended from an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> family in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVONSHIRE">Devonshire</a>, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXETER">Exeter</a>, and received his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> at the free school of Barnstaple in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a>, under the care of Mr William Rayner.—He was bred a mercer in the Strand; but having a small fortune, independent of business, and considering the attendance on a shop as a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEGRADATION">degradation</a> of those talents which he found himself possessed of, he quitted that occupation, and applied himself to other views, and to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDULGENCE">indulgence</a> of his inclination for the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUSES">Muses</a>. In 1712 we find him secretary, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> rather <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STEWARD">steward</a>, to the duchess of Monmouth, in which station he <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> till the beginning of the year 1714; at which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> he accompanied the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of Clarendon to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HANOVER">Hanover</a>, whither that nobleman was despatched by <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a>. In the latter end of the same year, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of the queen's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, he returned to England, where he lived in the highest estimation and intimacy of friendship with many many persons of the first distinction both in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> and abilities.—He was even particularly taken notice of by Queen Caroline, then princess of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>, to whom he had the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">reading</a> in manuscript his tragedy of the Captives; and in 1726 dedicated his Fables, by permission, to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUMBERLAND">Cumberland</a>.—From this countenance shown to him, and numberless promises made him of preferment, it was reasonable to suppose, that he would have been genteelly provided for in some office suitable to his inclination and abilities. Instead of which, in 1727, he was offered the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> usher to one of the young princesses; an office which, as he looked on it as rather an indignity to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> whose talents might have been so much better employed, he thought proper to refuse; and some pretty warm remonstrances were made on the occasion by his sincere friends and zealous patrons the duke and duchess of Queensberry, which terminated in those two noble personages withdrawing from <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> in disgust. Mr Gay's dependencies on the promises of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a>, and the disappointments he met with, he has figuratively described in his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FABLE">fable</a> of the Hare with many friends. However, the very extraordinary success he met with from public encouragement made an ample amends, both with respect to satisfaction and emolument, for those private disappointments.—For, in the season of 1727-8, appeared his Beggar's <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OPERA">Opera</a>; the vast success of which was not only unprecedented, but almost incredible.—It had an uninterrupted run in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a> of 63 nights in the first season, and was renewed in the ensuing one with equal approbation. It spread into all the great <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> of England; was played in many places to the 30th and 40th time, and at Bath and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRISTOL">Bristol</a> 50; made its progress into Wales, Scotland, and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, in which last place it was acted for 24 successive nights; and last of all it was performed at <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINORCA">Minorca</a>.
