Nor was the same of it confined to the reading and representation alone, for the card <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> room shared with the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a> and closet in this respect; the ladies carried about the favourite songs of it engraven upon their fan mounts; and screens, and other pieces of furniture were decorated with the same. In short, the satire of this piece was so striking, so apparent, and so perfectly adapted to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> of all degrees of people, that it overthrew the Italian opera, that <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAGON">Dagon</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a> and gentry, which had so <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> seduced them to idolatry, and which Dennis, by the labours and outeries of a whole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, and many other writers by the force of reason and reflection, had in vain endeavoured to drive from the throne of public taste. The profits of this piece were so very great, both to the author and Mr Rich the manager, that it gave rise to a quibble, which became frequent in the mouths of many, viz. That it had made Rich gay, and Gay rich; and it has been asserted, that the author's own emoluments from it were not less than 2000l. In consequence of this success, Mr Gay was induced to write a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> to it, which he entitled Polly. But the disgust subsisting between him and the court, together with the misrepresentations made of him as having been the author of some disaffected libels and seditious pamphlets, occasioned a prohibition and suppression of it to be sent from the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a> chamberlain, at the very time when every thing was in readiness for the rehearsal of it. A very considerable sum, however, accrued to him from the publication of it afterwards in quarto.—Mr Gay wrote several other pieces in the dramatic way, and many very valuable ones in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a>. Among the latter, his Trivia, or the Art of Walking the Streets of London, though his first poetical attempt, is far from being the least considerable, and is what recommended him to the esteem and friendship of Mr Pope: but as, among his dramatic works, his Beggar's Opera did at first, and perhaps ever <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a>, stand as an univalled masterpiece, so, among his poetical works, his Fables hold the same rank of estimation; the latter having been almost as universally read as the former was represented, and both equally admired. Mr Gay's disposition was sweet and affable, his temper generous, and his conversation agreeable and entertaining. But he had one foible, too frequently incident to men of great literary abilities, and which subjected him at times to inconveniences which otherwise he needed not to have experienced, viz. an excess of indolence, without any knowledge of economy. So that, though his emoluments were, at some periods of his life, very considerable, he was at others greatly straitened in his circumstances; nor could he prevail on himself to follow the advice of his friend <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAN">Dean</a> Swift, whom we find in many of his letters endeavouring to persuade him to the purchasing of an annuity, as a reserve for the exigencies that might attend on old <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>.—Mr Gay chose rather to throw himself on <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATRONAGE">patronage</a>, than secure to himself an independent competency by the means pointed out to him; so that, after having undergone many vicissitudes of fortune, and being for some time chiefly supported by the liberality of the duke and duchess of Queensberry, he died at their <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURLINGTON">Burlington</a> gardens, in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a> 1732. He was interred in Westminster <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">Abbey</a>, and a monument erected to his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a>, at the expense of his aforementioned noble benefactors, with an inscription expressive of their regards and his own deserts, and an epitaph in verse by Mr Pope.

GAZA

Pages 492-493

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> and one of the five satrapies of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILISTINES">Philistines</a>. It was situated about 100 stadia from the Mediterranean, on an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> mount, and strongly walled round. It was destroyed by Alexander the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">Great</a>, and afterwards by Antiochus. In the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-MACCABEES">Maccabees</a> it was a strong and flourishing city; but was destroyed a third time by Alexander Jannaeus. At present it has a miserable appearance. The buildings are <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a>, both as to the form and <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>. Some remains of its ancient <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-GRANDEUR">grandeur</a> grandeur appear in the handsome pillars of Parian marble which support some of the roofs; while others are disposed of here and there, in different parts of almost every beggarly cottage. On the top of the hill, at the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-east corner of the town, are the ruins of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARCHES">arches</a> sunk low into the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, and other foundations of a stately <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, from whence some of the hashaws have carried off marble pillars of an incredible size. The castle is a contemptible structure, and the port is ruined. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>, 34° 55'. N. Lat. 31° 28'.

GAZE-HOUND

Pages 493-493
or Gast-hound, one that makes more use of his sight than of his nose. Such dogs are much used in the north of England: they are fitter in an open champaign country than in bushy and woody places. If at any time a well-taught gaze-hound takes a wrong way, he will return upon a signal, and begin the chase afresh. He is also excellent at spying out the fattest of a herd; and having separated it from the rest, will never give over the pursuit till he has worried it to death.

GAZETTE

Pages 493-493

a newspaper, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> printed account of the transactions of all the countries in the known world, in a loose sheet or half sheet. This name is with us confined to that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> of news published by authority. The word is derived from gazetta, a Venetian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COIN">coin</a>, which was the usual price of the first newspaper printed there, and which was afterwards given to the paper itself. The first gazette in England was published at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> being there, in a folio half sheet, November 7, 1665. On the removal of the court to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> was changed to the London Gazette. The Oxford gazette was published on Tuesdays; the London on Saturdays: and these have <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to be the days of publication ever since.

GAZNA

Pages 493-495

a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, once much celebrated, and the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a very extensive empire; but which is now either entirely ruined, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> become of so little consideration, that it is not taken notice of in our books of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">geography</a>. The city was anciently an emporium and fortress of Sablestan, not far from the confines of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a>. During the vast and rapid conquests of the Arabs, all this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> had been reduced under their subjection. On the decline of the power of the caliphs, however, the vast empire established by Mahomet and his successors was divided into a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of independent principalities, most of which were but of short <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DURATION">duration</a>. In the year of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HEGIRA">Hegira</a> 384, answering to the 994th of the Christian era, the city of Gazna, with some <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the adjacent country, was governed by Mahmud Gazni; who became a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> conqueror, and reduced under his subjection a considerable part of India and most of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>. This empire <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> in the family of Mahmud Gazni for upwards of 200 years. None of his successors, however, were possessed of his abilities; and therefore the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of the empire, instead of increasing, was very considerably diminished soon after Mahmud's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. The Seljuks made themselves masters of Khorasan, and could not be driven out; the greatest part of the Persian dominions also fell off; and in the 547th year of the Hegira, the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a> of Gazni sultans was entirely set aside by one Gauri, who conquered Khosru Shah the reigning <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>, and bestowed his dominions on his own nephew Gayathoddin Mohammed. These new sultans proved greater conquerors than the former, and extended their dominions farther than even Mahmud Gazni himself had done. They did not, however, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> enjoy the sovereignty of Gazna; for in 1218, Jenghiz Khan, having conquered the greatest part of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHINA">China</a> and almost all <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TARTARY">Tartary</a>, began to turn his arms westward; and set out against the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SULTAN">sultan</a> of Gazna at the head of 700,000 men. To oppose this formidable <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, Mohammed, the reigning sultan, could muster only 400,000 men; and, in the first <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>, 160,000 of his troops are said to have perished. After this victory, Jenghiz Khan advanced; Mohammed not daring to risk a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> battle, the loss of which would have been attended with the entire ruin of his <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>. He therefore distributed his army amongst the strongest fortified <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> he had in his dominions; all of which Jenghiz Khan took one after another. The rapid progress of his conquests, indeed, almost exceeds <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BELIEF">belief</a>. In 1219 and 1220, he had reduced Zarnuk, Nur, Bokhara, Otrar, Sagannak, Uzkant, Alhash, Jund, Tonkat, Khojend, and Samarcan. Mohammed, in the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, fled first to Bokhara; but on the approach of Jenghiz Khan's army, quitted that <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, and fled to Samarcan. When this last city was also in danger of being invested, the sultan did not think proper to trust himself in it more than in the other, though it was garrisoned by 110,000 of his bravest troops; and therefore fled through byways into the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Ghilan in Persia, where he took refuge in a strong fortress called Estabad. But being also found out in this retreat, he fled to an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> in the Caspian <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> called Abiskun; where he ended his days, leaving his empire, such as it was, to his son Jalaloddin. The new sultan was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of great bravery and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>; but nothing was able to stop the progress of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOGULS">Moguls</a>. In 1220 and 1221, they made themselves masters of all the kingdoms of Kârazim and Khorasan, committing everywhere such massacres as were never heard of before or since that time. In the mean time Jalaloddin assembled his forces with the utmost diligence, and defeated two detachments of the Mogul army. This happened while Jenghiz Khan was besieging Bamiyan; but answered little other purpose, than serving to bring upon that city the terrible destruction of which an account is given under the article BAMIAN. Immediately after the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REDUCTION">reduction</a> of that city, Jenghiz Khan marched towards Gazna; which was very strongly fortified, and where he expected to have found Jalaloddin. But he had left the place 15 days before; and, as Jenghiz Khan's army was much reduced, he might perhaps have stood his ground, had it not been for an accident. He had been lately joined by three Turkish commanders, each of whom had a body of 10,000 men under his command. After his victories over the Moguls, these officers demanded the greatest share of the spoils; which being refused, they separated themselves from the sultan. He used his utmost endeavours to make them hearken to reason; and sent several messages and letters to them, representing the inevitable ruin which must attend their separation, as Jenghiz Khan was advancing against them with his whole army. At last they were persuaded to lay aside their animosities; but it was now too late; for Jenghiz Khan, being informed of what passed, detached 60,000 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> to prevent their joining the sultan's army; who, finding himself deprived of this powerful aid, retired towards the river <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INDUS">Indus</a>. When he was arrived there, he stopped in a place where the stream was most rapid and the place confined, with a view both to prevent his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> from placing any hopes of safety in flight, and to hinder the whole Mogul army from attacking him at once. Ever since his departure from Gazna he had been tormented with a colic: yet, at a time when he suffered most, hearing that the enemy's vanguard was arrived at a place in that neighbourhood called Herder, he quitted his litter, and, mounting a horse, marched with some of his chosen soldiers in the night; surprised the Moguls in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMP">camp</a>; and having cut them almost all in pieces, without the loss of a single man on his side, returned with a considerable booty. Jenghiz Khan, finding by this that he had a vigilant enemy to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> with, proceeded with great circumspection. When he came near the Indus, he drew out his army in battalia: to Jagatay, one of his sons, he gave the command of the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> wing; to Otkay, another son, he gave the command of the left: and put himself in the centre, with 6000 of his guards. On the other side, Jaloloddin prepared for battle like one who had no resource but in victory. He first sent the boats on the Indus farther off; reserving only one to carry over his mother, wife, and children: but unluckily the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOAT">boat</a> split when they were going to embark, so that they were forced to remain in the camp. The sultan took to himself the command of the main body of the army. His left wing, drawn up under shelter of a mountain which hindered the whole right wing of the Moguls from engaging at once, was commanded by his vizir; and his right by a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a> named Amin Malek. This lord began the fight; and forced the enemy's left wing, notwithstanding the great disparity of numbers, to give ground. The right wing of the Moguls likewise wanting room to extend itself, the sultan made <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of his left as a body of reserve, detaching from thence some squadrons to the assistance of the troops who stood in need of them. He also took one part of them with him when he went at the head of his main body to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> that of Jenghiz Khan; which he did with so much <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a> and vigour, that he not only put it in disorder, but penetrated into the place where Jenghiz Khan had originally taken his station: but that prince having had a horse killed under him, was retired from thence, to give orders for all the troops to engage. This disadvantage had like to have lost the Moguls the battle; for a report being immediately spread that the enemy had broken through the main body, the troops were so much discouraged, that they would certainly have fled, had not Jenghiz Khan encouraged them by riding from place to place in order to show himself. At last, however, Jaloloddin's men, who were in all but 30,000, having fought a whole <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> with ten times their number, were seized with fear and fled. One part of them retired to the rocks which were on the shore of the Indus, where the enemy's horse could not follow them; others threw themselves into the river, where many were drowned, though some had the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOOD_FORTUNE">good fortune</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> over in safety; while the rest surrounding their prince, continued the fight through despair. The sultan, however, considering that he had scarce 7000 men left, began to think of providing for his own safety: therefore, having bidden a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FINAL">final</a> adieu to his mother, wife, and children, he mounted a fresh horse, and spurred him into the river, which he crossed in safety, and even stopped in the middle of it to insult Jenghiz Khan, who was now arrived at the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANK">bank</a>. His family fell into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the Moguls; who killed all the males, and carried the women into <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAPTIVITY">captivity</a>. Jaloloddin being now securely landed in India, got up into a tree in order to preserve himself from wild beasts. Next day, as he walked melancholy among the rocks, he perceived a troop of his soldiers, with some officers, three of whom proved to be his particular friends. These, at the beginning of the defeat, had found a boat in which they had sailed all night, with much danger from the rocks, shelves, and rapid current of the river. Soon after, he <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> 500 horse coming towards him; who informed him of 4000 more that had escaped by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWIMMING">swimming</a> over the river; and these also soon after joined the rest. In the mean time an officer of his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSEHOLD">household</a>, named Jamalurrazad, knowing that his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> and many of his people were escaped, ventured to load a very <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> boat with arms, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, and stuff to clothe the soldiers; with which he crossed the river. For this important <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> Jaloloddin made him <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STEWARD">steward</a> of his household, and surnamed him the Chosen or the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">Glory</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">Faith</a>. For some time after, the sultan's affairs seemed to go on prosperously: he gained some battles in India; but the princes of that country, envying his prosperity, conspired against him, and obliged him to repass the Indus. Here he again attempted to make head against the Moguls; but was at last defeated and killed by them, and a final end put to the once mighty empire of Gazna. The <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METROPOLIS">metropolis</a> was reduced by Otkay; who no sooner entered the country in which it was situated, than he committed the most horrid cruelties. The city was well provided with all things necessary for sustaining a siege; had a strong garrison, and a brave and resolute governor. The inhabitants, expecting no mercy from Jenghiz Khan, who they knew had sworn their ruin, were resolved to make a desperate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a>. They made frequent sallies on the besiegers, several times overthrew their works, and broke above 100 of their <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTERING">battering</a> rams. But one night, after an obstinate fight, part of the city walls fell <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a>; and a great number of Moguls having filled up the ditch, entered the city <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWORD">sword</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>. The governor perceiving all was lost, at the head of his bravest soldiers rushed into the thickest of his enemies, where he and his followers were all slain. However, Gazna was not entirely destroyed, nor were the people all killed; for after the massacre had continued for four or five hours, Otkay ordered it to cease, and taxed those who were left alive at a certain rate, in order to redeem themselves and the city. It does not, however, appear that after this time the city of Gazna ever made any considerable <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>.—It was taken by the Moguls in the year 1222. GEBRES. See <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GABRES">GABRES</a>.

GECCO

Pages 495-495

in *<a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>*, a name given by the Indians to their terrible <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POISON">poison</a>, which kills when mixed with the blood even in the smallest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a>. They say that this gecco is a venomous <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-FROTH">froth</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> humour vomited out of the mouths of their most poisonous <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERPENTS">serpents</a>; which they procure in this fatal strength, by hanging up the creatures by the tails, and whipping them to enrage them: they collect this in proper vessels as it falls; and when they <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> it, they either poison a weapon with it, or wounding any <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> introduce the smallest quantity imaginable into it; and this is said to be immediate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. GECKO. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LACERTA">LACERTA</a>, *Herpetology <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>*.

GED

Pages 495-495

WILLIAM, an ingenious though unsuccessful <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ARTIST">artist</a>, who was a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOLDSMITH">goldsmith</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a>, deserves to be recorded for his attempt to introduce an improvement in the art of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINTING">printing</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a>, first practised by Ged in 1725, was simply this. From any types of Greek <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Roman, or any other character, he formed a plate for every page, or sheet, of a book, from which he printed, instead of using a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TYPE">type</a> for every <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a>, as is done in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> way. This was first practised, but on blocks of wood, by the Chinese and Japanese, and pursued in the first essays of Coster the European inventor of the present art. "This improvement (says James Ged the inventor's son) is principally considerable in three most important <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a>, viz. expense, correctness, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> and uniformity." In <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> 1729, William Ged entered into <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PARTNERSHIP">partnership</a> with William Fenner, a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a> stationer, who was to have half the profits, in consideration of his advancing all the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a> requisite. To supply this, Mr John James, then an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ARCHITECT">architect</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREENWICH">Greenwich</a> (who built Sir Gregory Page's <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, Bloomsbury <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, &c.) was taken into the scheme, and afterwards his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> Mr Thomas James, a letter founder, and James Ged the inventor's son. In 1730, these partners applied to the university of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a> for printing Bibles and common <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRAYER">prayer</a> books by blocks instead of single types; and, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a>, a lease was sealed to them, April 23, 1731. In their attempt they sunk a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> sum of money, and finished only two prayer books; so that it was forced to be relinquished, and the lease was afterwards given up. Ged imputed his disappointment to the villany of the pressmen, and the ill treatment of his partners (which he specifies at large), particularly Fenner, whom John James and he were advised to prosecute, but declined it. He returned to Scotland in 1736, where he gave his friends a specimen of his performance, by an edition of Sallust. But being still unsuccessful, and having failed in obtaining redress from Fenner, who died insolvent, he was preparing again to set out for London, in order to join with his son James as a printer there, when he died October 19, 1749. Ged's son attempted unsuccessfully, in 1751, to revive this invention; Messrs Tiloch and Foulis about the year 1782 practised it on a small <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCALE">scale</a> at Glasgow; and of late years many beautiful editions of the classics have been printed in this way by Didot of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, and Wilson and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPANY">Company</a> of London.

GEDDES

Pages 495-497

ALEXANDER, a learned Scots Catholic divine and eminent <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BIBLE">bible</a> critic, was born in the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> of Ruthven in Banffshire, in the year 1737. His parents were respectable, although not opulent. His father was a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FARMER">farmer</a>, who deemed no trouble too <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a>, in order to procure for his children as liberal an <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> as possible. Both father and mother were of the Catholic persuasion, and the only book of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> which the former had in his library was an English translation of the bible, in which young Geddes was instructed with such care and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>, that he was able to give an account of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of it before he had reached the eleventh year of his <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>. The first instructions he received, after those of his parents, were communicated by a school-mistress in the vicinity, by whom he was so much distinguished, that it became the first mental gratification which, in his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, he ever felt. He was next put under the tuition of a young <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> from the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Aberdeen, who had been engaged by the laird for the education of his own children; and afterwards went to a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> called Scalarn, in the Highlands, where those were to be trained up who designed to devote themselves to the Catholic priesthood, and to finish their education at some foreign university. Here it was, in this obscure retreat, that Geddes laid the foundation of that intimate acquaintance with the learned languages, by which he was so eminently distinguished in the subsequent <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. He went to the Scots university at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> in the year 1758, and soon after began the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHETORIC">rhetoric</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> of Navarre. By the strength of his genius and his indefatigable attention, he was soon at the head of this class, although he had to contend with two veterans, and became the favourite of Vicaire the professor, whose friendship lasted to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> of life. Instead of entering into the philosophical class at the usual <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, he studied that subject at home, in order to facilitate his theological studies, on which he entered under M. M. Buré and de Sauvent, at the college of Navarre, and Lavocat at the Sorbonne was his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a> preceptor. So great, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> rather astonishing, was his progress, that Professor Lavocat urged him strongly to continue at Paris; but his friends prevailed with him to return to his native <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> in 1764. His first <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> as a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> was in a Catholic chapel in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANGUS">Angus</a>, from which he removed to Traquair in 1765, and became chaplain to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of that name, where he remained for about three years. This situation was most agreeable to his literary pursuits, as he had unlimited access to a very extensive library, which greatly assisted him in the prosecution of his darling studies. He left the earl's <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> in the year 1768, and returned to Paris, where he devoted his time during the following winter to the perusal of books and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUSCRIPTS">manuscripts</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>'s <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol13.html#article-LIBRARIES">libraries</a>, making <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> extracts from scarce copies, particularly such as were in the Hebrew tongue. In the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> of 1769, he returned to his native country, and became pastor of a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONGREGATION">congregation</a> at Auchinhallrig in Banffshire, where he was for some time involved in pecuniary difficulties, out of which he was extricated by the liberality of the then <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORFOLK">Norfolk</a>. These were occasioned by the debts he incurred in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> a new chapel for his flock, and in making the parson's house one of the neatest and most convenient in Scotland. With the view of bettering his circumstances he commenced farmer; but as he had to borrow <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a> to stock his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FARM">farm</a>, and as the crops failed for three successive seasons, he was under the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of abandoning this scheme in a much poorer state than when he first projected it. But his unwearied exertions, joined to the assistance of friends, again relieved him, and he was enabled to discharge every claim against him of a pecuniary <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> in an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> manner. In the year 1779 he resigned his pastoral charge at Auchinharig, which was a heavy stroke to the members of his congregation, as the zeal and diligence with which he discharged the duties of his ministerial <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-FUNCTION">function</a> had endeared him to all. He was also justly esteemed for his attention to the instruction of youth. Next year the university of Aberdeen conferred on him the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of LL.D., a literary <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> which was never bestowed on any Roman Catholic by that body since the Reformation. He afterwards went to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, that he might prosecute his favourite studies with greater facility, and give the world his English translation of the Old and New <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a>, to which he had turned his attention for a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of years. He officiated for some months after his arrival at the imperial <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBASSADOR">ambassador</a>'s chapel in Duke-street, till the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> of Easter 1782, at which time it was suppressed by order of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOSEPH">Joseph</a> II, after which Dr Geddes seems to have declined entirely the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> of his clerical functions. No sooner had the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of Mr Geddes, relative to a new translation of the Bible been made public, than he met with formidable opposition from his Catholic brethren; an event which the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a> with good reason seems to have anticipated. His own words on this occasion were: "I expect not excessive profits from excessive exertion. I trust I shall never want meat, and clothes, and fire; to a philosophical and contented mind, what more is necessary?" He was many years employed in preparing this important <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> for the press, before he had any prospect of adequate success. In addressing the English Catholics on the subject of his translation, he has these memorable words: "At any rate, I do what I think it my duty to do, and do it fairly and openly. In the following <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAGES">pages</a> ye <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> find neither palliation nor <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DISGUISE">disguise</a>. I pour out my sentiments with the same sincerity as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> I were before the tribunal of Him who is to judge the living and the dead. Mistake I may, but prevaricate I never will." He discovered this noble spirit in every <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTION">action</a> of his life, and in all his transactions and intercourse with mankind, although he did not conciliate the regard of those who could have bestowed upon him the most effectual assistance. After spending much of his life in biblical studies, he met with a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> and cruel interruption, of which he thus speaks: "I had but little hope of ever living in a situation to resume them, when <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVIDENCE">Providence</a> threw me into the arms of such a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATRON">patron</a> as <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORIGEN">Origen</a> himself might have been proud to boast of—a patron, who, for these ten years past, has, with a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> peculiar to himself, afforded me every convenience that my heart could desire towards the carrying on and completing of my arduous work." It is needless to inform the public, that the patron to whom the learned doctor here alludes was <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Petre. For this munificence, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> through the whole of his life, and even beyond it by his latter will, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> of every denomination will feel sentiments of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRATITUDE">gratitude</a>, when they are qualified to make a true estimate of the advantages of free and impartial enquiry. In the year 1792, the first volume of his translation was published, dedicated to his patron Lord Petre, containing the first six books of the Old Testament. Soon after this volume made its appearance, three apostolic vicars, calling themselves the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RAMA">Rama</a>, Acanthos, and Centuriae, issued a pastoral <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a>, addressed to their respective flocks over which they presided, warning them against the reception of Dr Geddes's translation. In his reply to the bishop of Centuriae we find these words: "Perhaps, my lord, you wish to have another occasion of exercising your episcopal authority, and of playing with censures as children do with a new <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALL">ball</a>.—I wish your lordship much joy of the bauble; but however, my lord, beware of playing too often with it. Read St Chrysostom on <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">Ecclesiastical</a> Censures, and learn from him a little more moderation. Permit an old priest to tell you, that it is a very great ornament in a young bishop. As to myself, my lord, I am not afraid of your threats, and shall laugh at your censures as long as I am conscious that I deserve them not.—You cannot hinder me from praying at home; and at home I will pray, in defiance of your censure, as often as I please. The <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> Bishop of our souls is always accessible; and through him I can, at all times, have free access to the Father, who will not reject me, but for voluntary, unrepented crimes. In the panoply of conscious innocence, the whole <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THUNDER">thunder</a> of the Vatican would in vain be levelled at my head." The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> volume of his translation, owing to a variety of interruptions, did not make its appearance till the year 1797, to which was prefixed a dedication to her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> highness the duchess of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GLOUCESTER">Gloucester</a>, as an "early, spontaneous, and liberal encourager of the work." In this volume the doctor gives up, and boldly combats, the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSPIRATION">inspiration</a> of scripture, believing that the Hebrew, like all other historians, wrote from such <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> documents as they could find, and were of consequence liable to similar mistakes. This latitude of thinking naturally led the doctor to give up as fabulous, and wholly unworthy of the divine philanthropy, every command, precept, and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INJUNCTION">injunction</a>, which appeared unworthy even of human authority. He denied of consequence, that the command given to destroy the Canaanites could have God for its author. This volume of Critical Remarks was published in 1800, in which he enters into an able vindication of his own <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEORY">theory</a>, which rather increased than diminished the number of enemies, for as he wrote to please no party, he foresaw that he would have enemies in every party, and so it happened. Dr Geddes was a man of extensive literature, uncommon liberality of thinking, the friend of all mankind; a man of integrity, honour, and benevolence; in the strictest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> of the word, a truly genuine Catholic, and whose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> was so invincible, that neither hopes nor fears could induce him to conceal it. His prospectus of a new translation of the Bible in 4to was published in 1786, and a letter to the bishop of London on the same subject in 1787. His proposals were printed in 1788. As a controversial writer, Dr Geddes was eminently distinguished by his letter to Dr Priestley, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> Christ, and by one to a member of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, on the expediency of a general repeal of the penal statutes. tutes which have a respect to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> opinions. In the spring of the year 1800, he published an apology for the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ROMAN_CATHOLICS">Roman Catholics</a> of Great <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, in which he zealously defended his peculiar tenets, but displayed a commendable moderation, when he mentioned the injuries to which he himself and brethren were subjected by the continuance of persecuting laws; and, when he argued in behalf of abolishing all legal disabilities, he discovered the soundest logical understanding. We shall close our short account of this great man in the words of one who was well acquainted with him, and fully qualified to appreciate his merits. "It must be lamented, that, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Dr Geddes, the world has lost the services of a man, who by his acute and penetrating genius—his various, profound, and extensive erudition—his deep research—his indefatigable application—and his independent, dignified, and unfettered spirit, rising superior to the prejudices of education; nobly disdaining the shackles of system; spurning the petty temporizing arts of unmanly accommodation; and setting at defiance all the terrors of malignity, bigotry, and intolerance, was supremely qualified for the great, laborious, and important work in which he had, for a long <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of years, been engaged, of giving an English version of the venerable literary remains of sacred antiquity, the scriptures of the Old and New Testament. During his life, this work did not meet with encouragement adequate to the magnitude of the design; or, it may be added, to the merit of the execution. In this last respect, it will be <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> of surprise to all who are competent to judge of the nature of such an enterprise, how much has been done, and with what uncommon ability and success. It everywhere displays the skilful <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>." He had corrected and prepared his translation for the press up to the hundredth and eighteenth psalm, when he was seized with a most painful and excruciating distemper, which put a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> to his inestimable life on the 26th of February 1802. The learned world will unquestionably have cause to lament, that Dr Geddes was arrested by the hand of death in the midst of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAREER">career</a>, unless that unexpected phenomenon, another Geddes, should make his appearance, and happily finish what his extraordinary predecessor conducted so far with such astonishing abilities; but rara <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-AVIS">avis</a> in terris.

GEHENNA

Pages 497-497

a scripture <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> which has given some pain to the critics. It occurs in St Matthew, v. 22. 29. 30. x. 28. xviii. 9. xxiii. 15. 33. Mark ix. 43. 45. 47. Luke xii. 5. James iii. 6. The authors of the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LOUVAIN">Louvain</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENEVA">Geneva</a> versions retain the word gehenna as it stands in the Greek; the like does M. Simon: the English translators render it by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HELL">hell</a> and hell fire, and so do the translators of Mons and Father Bohours. The word is formed from the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a> gehinnom, i.e. "valley of Hinnom." In that valley, which was near <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a>, there was a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> named Tophet, where some Jews sacrificed their children to Moloch, by making them <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> through the fire. <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> Josias, to render this place for ever abominable, made a cloaca <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEWER">sewer</a> thereof, where all the filth and carcasses in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> were <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a>. The Jews observed farther, that there was a continual fire kept up there, to burn and consume those carcases; for which reason, as they had no proper term in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> to signify hell, they made <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of that of gehenna or gehinnom, to denote a fire unextinguishable.

GELA

Pages 497-497

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> on the south of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a>, taking its name from the river Gelas, which washes it. It was built by colonists from <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RHODES">Rhodes</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CRETE">Crete</a>, 45 years after the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYRACUSE">Syracuse</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> in the third year of the 22d Olympiad, 690 before Christ; originally called Lindii, from the colonists of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINDUS">Lindus</a>, a city of Rhodes, who settled there first. Now Terra Nuova, and the river called <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FIUME">Fiume</a> di Terra Nuova. The people were called Geloi, Gelenes, and Gelani. The city of Gela, after having stood 408 years, was destroyed by Phintias, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TYRANT">tyrant</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRIGENTUM">Agrigentum</a>; and the inhabitants were removed to a new city, called Phintias after his name.

GELATINOUS

Pages 497-497

among the physicians, is applied to any thing approaching to the glutinous consistence of a jelly.

GELDENHAUR

Pages 497-497

GERARD, in Latin Goldenhaeus, an historian and Protestant divine in the 16th century. He was a native of Nimeguen, and studied classical learning at <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVENTER">Deventer</a>. He went through his course of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LOUVAIN">Louvain</a>, where he contracted a very strict friendship with several learned men, and particularly with Erasmus. He became reader and historian to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AUSTRIA">Austria</a>, and afterwards to Maximilian of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BURGUNDY">Burgundy</a>. At length he embraced the Protestant <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, taught <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARBURG">Marburg</a>, and afterwards <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a> till his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, in 1542. He wrote, 1. History of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>. 2. History of Low Countries. 3. History of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-UTRECHT">Utrecht</a>; and other works. GELDERLAND. See Guelderland. GELDERS. See Guelders.

GELDING

Pages 497-497

the operation of castrating any animal. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASTRATION">Castration</a>, Farriery <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

GELENHAUSEN

Pages 497-497

a small imperial town of Westphalia in Germany, with a castle built by the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Frederic I. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 8. 13. N. Lat. 50. 20.

GELLENIUS

Pages 497-497

SIGISMUND, a learned and excellent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, born of a good family at <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRAGUE">Prague</a>, about the year 1498. Erasmus conceiving an esteem for him at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BASIL">Basil</a>, recommended him to John Frobenius as a corrector for his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINTING">printing</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>; which laborious <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> he accepted, and had a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a>, Greek, and Latin books to correct: he also translated many works himself from the Greek and Latin; and published a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DICTIONARY">dictionary</a> in four languages, Greek, Latin, German, and Slavonian. Profitable and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> employments were offered him in other places; but nothing could tempt him to quit his peaceful situation at Basil. He died in 1555. All his translations are highly esteemed.

GELLERT

Pages 497-498

CHRISTIAN FURGHTEGOLT, was born at Haynichen, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> 1715, near Freyberg, where his father was a clergyman. He was extraordinary professor of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> at Leipsic, and a distinguished writer among the Germans. When but 13 years of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> he discovered a poetical genius; but having none to guide his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> for this kind of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a>, he was led to imitate Gunther, Neukerch, and Hanke, men of indifferent abilities. He studied <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEOLOGY">theology</a> at Leipsic in 1734, and returned home at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPIRATION">expiration</a> of four years, when he commenced public speaker; but his timid disposition prevented him from shining as an orator in the pulpit. The delicacy of his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> forbidding him to aspire after extensive learning, he confined himself to the acquisition of that which might render him useful. He was much respected for his first attempts in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, called Amusements of Reason and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WIT">Wit</a>, which appeared in 1742. The labour which he found requisite for the composition of sermons, inclined him to lay aside the clerical profession, and devote himself wholly to the instruction of youth, in which he not only diffused knowledge through the minds of his pupils, but also inspired them with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> and virtue. He was made A.M. in 1744, and published the first volume of his fables in the ensuing year. His "Swedish Countess" was the first German <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROMANCE">romance</a> deserving of notice. He gave the world the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of his fables in 1748, although two years before this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> he was much afflicted with hypochondriacal affections. In 1751, he was solicited to accept the office of extraordinary professor of philosophy, together with a decent salary, which was augmented on the termination of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>. Assailed by unconquerable lowness of spirits and confirmed melancholy, he still exhibited the same <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATIENCE">patience</a>, resignation, and universal philanthropy as he had ever shewn, and which excited the admiration of the enemy during the war. His sufferings <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to increase in severity, and at last terminated his existence on the 13th of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a> 1769. He contributed much to the improvement of the taste and morals of his countrymen, and their <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRATITUDE">gratitude</a> for his services made them deeply lament his loss. His praise was resounded by every <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VOICE">voice</a>, his likeness was <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> in gypsum, and moulded in wax; it was engraved on <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>, and represented in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SCULPTURE">sculpture</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a>. It is said of this amiable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> and captivating writer, by Kutner, who wrote the lives of German authors, that it <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> probably be a century before the appearance of another poet, so fully qualified to excite the love and admiration of his contemporaries, and obtain such a powerful influence over the taste and way of thinking of all descriptions of men. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> it would indicate too much partiality to call him a genius of the first class, he certainly was a most agreeable and fertile writer; the poet to whom religion and virtue are deeply indebted; an able reformer of public manners, and fonder of affording consolation, than of plunging into despondency. Kutner gives him a most excellent and enviable character, in these words: "As <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> as the Germans shall understand their present <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, will the works of Gellert be read; and his character will be honoured while virtue is known and respected."

GELLI

Pages 498-498

John Baptist, an eminent Italian writer, was born of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> parents at <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLORENCE">Florence</a>, in the year 1498. He was bred a taylor, some say a shoemaker; but had such an extraordinary genius, that he acquired several languages, and made an uncommon progress in the belles lettres; and though he <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> always to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> at his trade, became acquainted with all the wits and learned men at Florence, and his merit was universally known. He was chosen a member of the academy there, and the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> made him a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BURGESS">burgess</a>. He acquired the highest reputation by his works, which are, 1. I. Caprici del Bottaio, quarto; which contains ten dialogues. 2. La Circe, octavo. This, which also contains ten dialogues, and treats of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, has been translated into Latin, French, and English. 3. Dissertations in Italian on the poems of Dante and Petrarch. 4. The comedies of La Sporta and La Errore; and other works. He died in 1563.

GELLIBRAND

Pages 498-498

Henry, a laborious astronomer of the 17th century, was born in 1597. Though he was not without good views in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, yet he became so enamoured with mathematical studies, that on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of his father he became a student at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, contented himself with his private patrimony, and devoted himself solely to them. On the death of Mr Gunter, he was recommended by Mr <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRIGGS">Briggs</a> to the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-TRUSTEES">trustees</a> of Gresham <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>, for the astronomical professorship there; to which he was elected in 1627. His friend Mr Briggs dying in 1630, before he had finished his Trigonometria Britannica, it was finished by Gellibrand at his request. He wrote several other things, chiefly tending to the improvement of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a>; and died in 1636.

GELLIUS

Pages 498-498

Aulus, a celebrated grammarian who lived in the 2d century under Marcus Aurelius and some succeeding emperors. He wrote a collection of observations on authors, for the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of his children; and called it Noctes Atticae, because composed in the evenings of a winter he spent at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> value of it is for preserving many facts and monuments of antiquity not to be found elsewhere. Critics and grammarians have bestowed much pains on this writer. GELLY. See Jelly.

GELO

Pages 498-498
or Gelon, a son of Dinomenes who made himself absolute at Syracuse 484 years before the Christian era. He conquered the Carthaginians at Himera, and made his oppression popular by his great equity and moderation. He reigned seven years, and his death was universally lamented at Syracuse. He was called the father of his people, and the patron of liberty, and honoured as a demigod. His brother Hiero succeeded him. See Syracuse.

GEM

Pages 498-507

in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> name for all precious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONES">stones</a>; of which there are two classes, the pellucid and semipellucid. The bodies composing the class of pellucid gems are bright, elegant, and beautiful fossils, which are found in small detached masses, extremely hard, and of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> lustre. The bodies composing the class of semipellucid gems, are stones naturally <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPOUND">compound</a>, not inflammable <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> soluble in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, found in detached masses, and composed of crystalline <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> debased by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>; however, they are but slightly debased; and are of great <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> and brightness, of a moderate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of transparency, and are usually found in small masses. The knowledge of gems depends principally on observing their <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HARDNESS">hardness</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>. Their hardness is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> commonly allowed to stand in the following order: The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIAMOND">diamond</a> the hardest of all; then the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RUBY">ruby</a>, sapphire, jacinth, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMERALD">emerald</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMETHYST">amethyst</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GARNET">garnet</a>, carnel, chalcedony, onyx, jasper, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGATE">agate</a>, porphyry, and marble. This <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a>, however, is not regular and constant, but frequently varies. Good crystals may be allowed to succeed the onyx; but the whole family of metallic glassy flours seems to be still softer.—In point of colour, the diamond is valued for its transparency, the ruby for its purple, the sapphire for its blue, the emerald for its green, the jacinth for its <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORANGE">orange</a>, the amethyst carnel for its carnation, the onyx for its tawney, the jasper, agate, and porphyry, for their variegated colours, and the garnet for its transparent blood <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a>. All these gems are sometimes found coloured and spotted, and sometimes quite limpid and colourless. In this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> the diamond <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CUTTER">cutter</a> or polisher knows how to distinguish their different <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> by their different degrees of hardness upon the mill. For the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> or polishing of gems, the fine powder of the fragments of those that are next in degree of hardness is always required to grind away the softer; but as none of them are harder than the diamond, this can only be polished by its own powder. Cronstedt observes of gems in general, that the colour of the ruby and emerald are said to remain in the fire, while that of the topaz flies off: hence it is usual to burn the topaz, and thence substitute it for the diamond. "Their colours (says our author) are commonly supposed to depend upon metallic vapours; but may they not more justly be supposed to arise from a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHLOGISTON">phlogiston</a> united with a metallic or some other earth? because we find that metallic earths which are perfectly well calcined give no colour to any glass: and that the manganese, on the other <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, gives more colour than can be ascribed to the small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of metal which is to be extracted from it." M. Magellan is of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, that their colour is owing chiefly to the mixture of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> which enters their <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a>; but approves the sentiment of Cronstedt, that phlogiston has a share in their production, it being well known that the calces of iron when <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEPHLOGISTICATED">dephlogisticated</a> produce the red and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> colours of marble, and when phlogisticated to a certain degree produce the blue or green colours. With regard to the texture of gems, M. Magellan observes, that all of them are foliated or laminated, and of various degrees of hardness. Whenever the edges of these laminae are sensible to the eye, they have a <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-FIBROUS">fibrous</a> appearance, and reflect various shades of colour, which change successively according to their angular position to the eye. These are called by the French chatoyantes; and what is a blemish in their transparency, often enhances their value on account of their scarcity. But when the substance of a gem is composed of a broken texture, consisting of various sets of laminae differently inclined to each other, it emits at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> various irradiations of different colours, which succeed one another according to their <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a> of position. This kind of gems has obtained the name of opals, and are valued in proportion to the brilliancy, beauty, and variety of their colours. Their <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CRYSTALLIZATION">crystallization</a>, no doubt, depends on the same cause which produces that of salts, earths, and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-METALS">metals</a>, which is treated of under the article Crystallization. The following <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a> shows the component parts of gems according to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANALYSIS">analysis</a> of Bergman and M. Achard; the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> B prefixed to each denoting Bergman's analysis, and A that of Achard. | Gem | Argil. | Silic. Calc Iron. | |----------------------|-------|-------------------| | Red oriental ruby | B 40 | 39 9 10 | | <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DITTO">Ditto</a> | A 37.5| 42.5 9 11 | | Blue oriental sapphire| B 58 | 35 5 2 | | Ditto | A 58 | 33 6 3 | | Yellow topaz from <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAXONY">Saxony</a>| B 46 | 39 8 6 | | Green oriental emerald| B 60 | 24 8 6 | | Ditto | A 60 | 23 10 7 | | Yellow <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROWN">brown</a> orient. hyacinth| B 40 | 25 20 13 | | Ditto | A 42 | 22 20 16 | | Tourmalin from Ceylon| B 39 | 37 15 9 | | Ditto from Brasil | B 50 | 34 11 5 | | Ditto from Tyrol | B 42 | 40 12 6 | | Garnet from <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOHEMIA">Bohemia</a> | A 30 | 48 11 10 | But later analyses shew that the component parts are different from the above, particularly the colouring matters which are here ascribed to iron. See <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINERALOGY">Mineralogy</a>. The chrysoprase from Koseinitz in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SILESIA">Silesia</a> was likewise analyzed by M. Achard; who found that it contained 456 grains of siliceous earth, 13 of calcareous, six of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAGNESIA">magnesia</a>, three of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>, and two of iron. "This (says M. Magellan) seems to be the only gem that contains no argillaceous earth." <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMITATION">Imitation</a> or Counterfeiting of Gems in Glass. The art of imitating gems in glass is too considerable to be passed without notice: some of the leading compositions therein we shall mention upon the authority of Neri and others. These gems are made of pastes; and are noway inferior to the native stones, when carefully made and well polished, in brightness or transparence, but want their hardness. The general rules to be observed in making the pastes are these: 1. That all the vessels in which they are made be firmly luted, and the lute left to dry before they are put into the fire. 2. That such vessels be chosen for the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> as <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> bear the fire well. 3. That the powders be prepared on a porphyry <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>; not in a metal <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MORTAR">mortar</a>, which would communicate a tinge to them. 4. That the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> proportion in the quantity of the several ingredients be nicely observed. 5. That the materials be all well mixed; and, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> not sufficiently baked the first time, to be committed to the fire again, without breaking the pot; for if this be not observed, they will be full of blisters and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> bladders. 6. That a small vacuity be always left at the top of the pot, to give room to the swelling of the ingredients. To make paste of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> hardness, and capable of all the colours of the gems, with great lustre and beauty.—Take of prepared crystal, ten pounds; <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> of polverine, six pounds; sulphur of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, two pounds; mix all these well together into a fine powder; make the whole with common water into a hard paste; and make this paste into small cakes of about three ounces <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> each, with a hole made in their middle; dry them in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, and afterwards calcine them in the straitest <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of a potter's <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FURNACE">furnace</a>. After this, pow- der them, and levigate them to a perfect fineness on a porphyry stone, and set this powder in pots in a glass furnace to purify for three days; then <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> the whole into water, and afterwards return it into the furnace, where let it stand 15 days, in which time all foulness and blisters will disappear, and the paste will greatly resemble the natural jewels. To give this the colour of the emerald, add to it <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a> thrice calcined; for a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> green, brass simply calcined to a redness; for a sapphire, add zaffer, with manganese; and for a topaz, manganese and tartar. All the gems are thus imitated in this, by the same way of working as the making of coloured glasses; and this is so hard, that they very much approach the natural gems. The colour of all the counterfeit gems made of the several pastes, may be made deeper or <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIGHTER">lighter</a> according to the work for which the stones are designed; and it is a necessary general rule, that small stones for rings, &c. require a deeper colour, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> ones a paler. Besides the colours made from manganese, verdigris, and zaffer, which are the ingredients commonly used, there are other very fine ones which care and skill may prepare. Very fine red may be made from <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, and one not much inferior to that from iron; a very fine green from brass or copper; a sky colour from silver, and a much finer one from the granates of Bohemia. A very singular and excellent way of making the paste to imitate the coloured gems is this: Take a quantity of saccharum saturni, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a> of lead, made with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VINEGAR">vinegar</a> in the common way; set it in sand, in a glass body well luted from the neck downwards; leave the mouth of the glass open, and continue the fire 24 hours; then take out the salt, and if it be not red but yellowish, powder it fine, and return it into the vessel, and keep it in the sand <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> 24 hours more, till it becomes as red as cinnabar. The fire must not be made so strong as to melt it, for then all the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> is spoiled. Pour distilled vinegar on this calcined salt, and separate the solution from the dregs; let the decanted liquor stand six days in an earthen vessel, to give time for the finer sediment to subside; filter this liquor, and evaporate it in a glass body, and there will remain a most pure salt of lead; dry this well, then dissolve it in fair water; let the solution stand six days in a glazed <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAN">pan</a>; let it subside, then filter the clear solution, and evaporate it to a yet more pure <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> and sweet salt; repeat this operation three times; put the now perfectly pure salt into a glass vessel, set it in a sand heat for several days, and it will be calcined to a fine impalpable powder of a lively red. This is called the sulphur of lead. Take all the ingredients as in the common composition of the pastes of the several colours, only instead of red lead, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> this powder; and the produce will well reward the trouble of the operation, as <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> has often proved. A paste proper for receiving colours may be readily made by well pounding and mixing six pounds of white sand cleansed, three pounds of red lead, two pounds of purified <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEARL">pearl</a> ashes, and one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POUND">pound</a> of nitre. A softer paste may be made in the same manner, of six pounds of white sand cleansed; red lead, and purified pearl-ashes, of each three pounds; one pound of nitre, half a pound of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BORAX">borax</a>, and three ounces of arsenic. For common use a pound of common salt may be substituted for the borax. This glass will be very soft, and will not bear much wear if employed for rings, buckles, or such imitations of stones as are exposed to much rubbing; but for <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-EAR">ear</a>-rings, ornaments worn on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a>, and those little used, it may last a considerable time. In order to give paste different colours, the process is as follows: For Amethyst. Take ten pounds of either of the compositions described under Colouring of Glass, one ounce and a half of manganese, and one drachm of zaffer; powder and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol4.html#article-FUSE">fuse</a> them together. <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">Black</a>. Take ten pounds of either of the compositions just referred to, one ounce of zaffer, six drachms of manganese, and five drachms of iron, highly calcined; and proceed as before. Blue. Take of the same composition, ten pounds; of zaffer, six drachms; and of manganese, two drachms; and proceed as with the foregoing. Chrysolite. Take of either of the compositions for paste above described, prepared without <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALTPETRE">saltpetre</a>, ten pounds, and of calcined iron five drachms; and pursue the same process as with the rest. Red Cornelian. Take of the compositions mentioned under Colouring of Glass, two pounds; of glass of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANTIMONY">antimony</a>, one pound; of the calcined vitriol called scarlet ochre, two ounces; and of manganese, one drachm.
