An hospital, however, is now preparing at <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol6.html#article-CAROUGE">Carouge</a>, a village in Savoy, between Geneva and Grange Colonge, for Frenchmen, to which, it is expected, the soldiers will be removed in May or June. Here is also a general hospital, once the nunnery of St Clair; it was founded, together with many other useful institutions, by that celebrated reformer, John Calvin, who fled from the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERSECUTION">persecution</a> of Francis I, and found an <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASYLUM">asylum</a> in Geneva. The revenue arising from the estates of this hospital has, till within these last few years, been commensurate with its expenses: but, for some time back, it has been found necessary to collect almost an additional fourth, in order to supply its disbursements: twice in the year the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-TREASURER">treasurer</a> goes round to every house, and solicits the charitable contribution of its inmates. "<a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIOR">Prior</a> to the last revolution, I learn, that 600,000 French livres discharged all the public expenses: with this very trifling sum were paid the salaries of the magistrates, of the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of the town, of the master of the country, the expenses of the academy, of repairing the roads, of cleaning and lighting the town; in short, these 600,000 livres were sufficient to defray all the ordinary expenses of the government. Since that too memorable event, the citizens of Geneva have been assessed to the amount of 1,500,000 livres, the salaries of the inferior magistrates are in arrears, the roads are not kept in good repair, the town is very dimly lighted, and the streets, a few of the principal ones excepted, are left with all their dirty honours thick upon them! The inhabitants go so far as to assert, that, in consequence of the neglect which the public <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DRAINS">drains</a> have suffered, they have been affected with fevers and other illnesses to which they had hitherto been strangers. "I understand, that the revenue of Geneva, since it has been annexed to the republic of France, arises chiefly from the following sources.—An <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXCISE">excise</a> duty is laid on all <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a> (wheat excepted), on wine and merchandise of every <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a>, which is brought into Geneva: the annual produce of this tax is about 120,000 French livres; a land tax; a tax on doors and windows; a tax on the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALE">sale</a> of estates; a heavy tax on the collateral inheritance of an estate—where the inheritance is lineal and immediate, the tax is moderate. To these taxes or contributions, as they are called, must be added la contribution mobilière, which is a small tax on personal property, and produces annually about 75,000 livres. The collectors of these taxes are appointed by the First Consul, and are paid very highly for their trouble: the prefect, and all the principal public officers, are very regularly paid, but those in a subordinate situation seldom get above one-third of their stipends. "Divorces seem to be obtained here with too much facility. But, in the first place, as to marriages, they must be celebrated, according to the French law, before the municipality, at the maison de ville. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">Marriage</a> in France, you know, is merely a civil <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a>, the parties being obliged to swear before an appointed <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-MAGISTRATE">magistrate</a>, that they are of age, and that they have consented..." consented to become man and wife. The Genevans, however, do not consider this ceremony as sufficient; but, as our Gretna Green couples, on their return to <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, think it necessary, after the fervour of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PASSION">passion</a> is abated, and the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERCURY">mercury</a> is fallen, in the animal thermometer, something lower than blood <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>, to have the holy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RITES">rites</a> performed with the solemnity prescribed by law; so the Genevans, in addition to the civil ceremony prescribed by the laws of the republic of France, voluntarily conform to the religious ordinance of their own church. If a woman leaves her husband, and refuses to return to his habitation, after being summoned by him for that purpose, he can repudiate her for disobedience.* The inhabitants, though obliged to submit to superior force, were always averse to the French yoke; and when the French garrison capitulated to the Austrian general Bubna, in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a> 1813, the restoration of the republic was instantly decreed. On the 12th September 1814, Geneva was admitted a member of the Swiss confederation, and a new constitution was framed, in which it was declared, that "no patricians or privileged classes are acknowledged by the state, but that all the Genevese are equal before the law." Public affairs are managed by the great council of 250 members, and by the smaller council of 28, the latter being the executive. The territory of Geneva, which was originally very small, was augmented by late treaties, and now contains 120 square miles, and 25,000 inhabitants. GENEVA Lake. This lake is in the shape of a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CRESCENT">crescent</a>; along the concave side of which Mr Coxe travelled 54 miles. Switzerland forms the hollow, and Savoy the convex part; the greatest breadth being about 12 miles. The country on the side of Savoy is full of high and craggy mountains; but from Geneva to the environs of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAUSANNE">Lausanne</a> it slopes to the margin of the lake, and is very rich and fertile. The banks rise considerably in the neighbourhood of Lausanne, and form a most beautiful terrace, with a rapid <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a> a few miles beyond the town. A plain begins in the neighbourhood of Vevey, which continues for a great way beyond the end of the lake, but contracting towards the water by the approach of the mountains. The lake itself appears at a distance of a beautiful blue <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, and the water is very clear and transparent. Near Geneva the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of the lake abounds with pebbles; between that city and Lausanne it is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SANDY">sandy</a>; from thence to Chilon it is bounded by hard calcareous rocks; and the extremity of the shores is a marsh formed by mud collected from the river Rhone. The greatest depth of this lake found by M. de Luc is 160 fathoms. Here the birds called tippet grebes make their appearance in December, and retire in February to other places where they breed. They make floating nests of reeds; but as the lake of Geneva affords none of these, they are obliged to migrate to other places where they grow. Their skins are much esteemed, and sell for 12s. or 14s. each. The lake of Geneva, like all others situated between mountains, is subject to sudden storms.

GENEVA

Pages 521-521
or Gin, among distillers, an ordinary malt spirit, distilled a second time, with the addition of some juniper berries. Originally, the berries were added to the malt in the grinding; so that the spirit thus obtained was flavoured with the berries from the first, and exceeded all that could be made by any other method. At present, they leave out the berries entirely, and give their spirits a flavour by distilling them with a proper quantity of oil of turpentine; which though it nearly resembles the flavour of juniper berries, has none of their valuable virtues.

GENEVIEVE

Pages 521-521

fathers <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> of; the name of a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONGREGATION">congregation</a> of regular canons of the order of St Augustine, established in France. The congregation of St Genevieve is a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REFORM">reform</a> of the Augustine canons. It was begun by St <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> Faure, in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">abbey</a> of St Vincent de <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENLIS">Senlis</a>, of which he was a member, in the year 1618. In the year 1634, the abbey was made <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTIVE">elective</a>; and a general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAPTER">chapter</a>, composed of the superiors of 15 houses who had now received the reform, chose F. Faure coadjutor of the abbey of St Genevieve, and general of the whole congregation. Such were its beginnings. It has since increased very much, and it now consists of above a hundred monasteries; in some whereof the religious are employed in the administration of the parishes and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-HOSPITALS">hospitals</a>; and in others, in the celebration of divine <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>, and the instruction of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ECCLESIASTICS">ecclesiastics</a> in seminaries for the purpose. The congregation takes its name from the abbey of St Genevieve, which is the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> of the order, and whose <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABBOT">abbot</a> is the general thereof. The abbey itself took its name from St Genevieve, the patroness of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, who died in the year 512. Five years after her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, Clovis erected the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of St Genevieve, under the name and invocation of St <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PETER">Peter</a>, where her relics are still, or were till lately preserved, her shrine visited, and her image carried with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> processions and ceremonies upon extraordinary occasions, as when some great favour is to be entreated of heaven.

GENGIS KHAN

the renowned sovereign of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOGULS">Moguls</a>, a barbarous and bloody conqueror. See JENGHIZ KHAN, and (<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of the) MOGULS.

GENIAL

Pages 521-521

an epithet given by the Pagans to certain gods who were supposed to preside over <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENERATION">generation</a>. The genial gods, says Festus, were <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a>, fire, and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>. The twelve signs, together with the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOON">moon</a>, were sometimes also ranked in the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>.

GENII

Pages 521-522

a sort of intermediate beings, by the Mahometans believed to exist, between men and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGELS">angels</a>. They are of a grosser fabric than the latter, but much more <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> and powerful than the former. Some of them are good, others bad, and they are capable of future <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALVATION">salvation</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> damnation like men. The orientals pretend that these genii inhabited the world many thousand years before the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREATION">creation</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADAM">Adam</a>, under the reigns of several princes, who all bore the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> name of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLOMON">Solomon</a>; that falling at length into an almost general corruption, Eblis was sent to drive them into a remote <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, there to be confined; and that some of that <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENERATION">generation</a> still remaining were by Tahmurath, one of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> kings of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>, forced to retreat into the famous mountain of Kaf; of whose successions and wars they have many fabulous and romantic stories. They also made several ranks and degrees among this kind of beings (<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they are not rather different different <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>); some being absolutely called Jin; some Peri, or fairies; some Div, or giants; and others Taewins, or fates.

GENITES

Pages 522-522

among the Hebrews, those descended from <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABRAHAM">Abraham</a>, without any mixture of foreign blood. The Greeks distinguished by the name of genites such of the Jews as were issued from parents, who, during the Babylonish <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAPTIVITY">captivity</a>, had not allied with any <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENTILE">gentile</a> family.

GENITIVE

Pages 522-522

in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAMMAR">Grammar</a>, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> of the declension of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-NOUNS">nouns</a>. The relation of one thing considered as belonging in some manner to another, has occasioned a peculiar termination of nouns called the genitive case; but in the vulgar tongues they make <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of a sign to express the relation of this case. In English they prefix the particle of, in French de <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> du, &c. Though in strictness there are no <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> in either of these languages; insomuch as they do not express the different relations of things by different terminations, but by additional prepositions, which is otherwise in the Latin.

GENIUS

Pages 522-523

in matters of literature, &c. a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TALENT">talent</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> disposition to do one thing more than another; or the aptitude a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> has received from <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> to perform well and easily that which others can do but indifferently and with a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of pains. To know the bent of nature is the most important concern. Men come into the world with a genius determined not only to a certain art, but to certain parts of that art, in which alone they are capable of success. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> they quit their sphere, they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> even below mediocrity in their profession. Art and industry add much to natural endowments, but cannot supply them where they are wanting. Every thing depends on genius. A painter often pleases without observing rules; whilst another displeases though he observes them, because he has not the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a> of being born with a genius for <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a>. A man born with a genius for commanding an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, and capable of becoming a great general by the help of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a>, is one whose organical conformation is such, that his valour is no obstruction to his presence of mind, and his presence of mind makes no abatement of his valour. Such a disposition of mind cannot be acquired by art: it can be possessed only by a person who has brought it with him into the world. What has been said of these two arts may be equally applied to all other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROFESSIONS">professions</a>. The administration of great concerns, the art of putting people to those employments for which they are naturally formed, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of physic, and even <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-GAMING">gaming</a> itself, all require a genius. Nature has thought fit to make a distribution of her talents talents among men, in order to render them necessary to one another; the wants of men being the very first link of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>: she has therefore pitched upon particular persons, to give them aptitude to perform rightly some things which she has rendered impossible to others; and the latter have a greater facility granted them for other things, which facility has been refused to the former. Nature indeed has made an unequal distribution of her blessings among her children; yet she has disinheritied none; and a man divested of all kinds of abilities, is as great a phenomenon as an universal genius. From the diversity of genius the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> of inclination arises in men, whom nature has had the precaution of leading to the employments for which she designs them, with more or less impetuosity in proportion to the greater or lesser <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of obstacles they have to surmount in order to render themselves capable of answering this vocation. Thus the inclinations of men are so very different, because they follow the same mover, that is, the impulse of their genius. This, as with the painter, is what renders one poet pleasing, even when he trespasses against rules; while others are disagreeable, notwithstanding their strict regularity. The genius of these arts, according to the abbé du <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOS">Bos</a>, consists in a happy arrangement of the organs of the brain; in a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> conformation of each of these organs; as also in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of the blood, which disposes it to ferment, during <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a>, so as to furnish plenty of spirits to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a> employed in the functions of the imagination. Here he imagines that the composer's blood is heated; for that painters and poets cannot invent in cool blood; nay, that it is evident they must be rapt into a kind of enthusiasm when they produce their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a> mentions a poet who never wrote so well as when his poetic fury hurried him into a kind of frenzy. The admirable pictures we have in Tasso of Armida and Clorinda were drawn at the expense of a disposition he had to real madness, into which he fell before he died. "Do you imagine," (says Cicero), "that Pauvius wrote in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLD">cold</a> blood? No, it was impossible. He must have been inspired with a kind of fury, to be able to write such admirable verses."

GENOA

Pages 523-526

a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, and formerly <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a republic of the same name, situated in E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 8° 36' N. Lat. 44° 25'.—By the Latin authors it is very frequently, though corruptly called Janua; and its present territories made <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Liguria. The era of its foundation is not known. In the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> Punic <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> it was a celebrated emporium; and having declared for the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, was plundered and burnt by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGO">Mago</a> the Carthaginian. It was afterwards rebuilt by the Romans; and with the rest of Italy <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> under their dominion till the decline of the western empire in 476. Soon after, it fell under the power of Theodoric the Ostrogoth; who having defeated the usurper Odoacer, became <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of Italy. This happened in the year 498; and in a short time, the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOTHS">Goths</a> being almost entirely subdued by <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BELISARIUS">Belisarius</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTINIAN">Justinian</a>'s general, Genoa was reannexed to the Roman empire. In 628, it was plundered and burnt by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOMBARDS">Lombards</a>, whose king Protharis erected it into a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCIAL">provincial</a> dukedom. The Lombards continued masters of Genoa till the year 774, when they were conquered by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">Great</a>, son to Pepin king of France. He reduced Liguria to the ancient bounds settled by Augustus, and erected it into a marquisate: appointing his relation Audemarus the first <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNT">count</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MARGRAVE">margrave</a>. Genoa at this time being distinguished for its wealth and populousness, began to give its name to the whole <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a>; and continued under the dominion of these counts for about 100 years, till the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a> of the Pepins became entirely extinct in Italy, and the empire was transferred to the German princes.—In the year 935 or 936, while the Genoese forces were absent on some expedition, the Saracens surprised the city, which they plundered and burnt, putting to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> a great <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of the inhabitants, and carrying others into <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAPTIVITY">captivity</a>. Having embarked their captives, together with an immense booty, they set sail for <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>; but the Genoese immediately returning, pursued the invaders; and having entirely defeated them, recovered all the captives and booty, and took a great many of the enemy's ships. About the year 950, the Franks having lost all authority in Italy, the Genoese began to form themselves into a republic, and to be governed by their own magistrates, who were freely elected, and took the name of Consuls. In order to support their independence, they applied themselves with great assiduity to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a>; and being apprehensive that some of the German emperors, who frequently entered Italy as invaders, might renew their pretensions to their state, they consented to acknowledge Berengarius III., <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Friuli, who had been elected emperor by a party of Italian <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBLES">nobles</a>. Berengarius, who had much ado to maintain himself in his new <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a>, endeavoured by his concessions to enlarge the number of his friends and adherents; and accordingly made no difficulty to confirm the new republic in all its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a> and privileges. After this the Genoese began to extend their commerce from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a>, and from <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a> to Constantinople: their vessels, according to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> of these times, being fitted for fighting as well as merchandise. Having thus acquired great reputation, they were invited in 1017, by the Pisans, who had likewise formed themselves into a republic, to join with them in an expedition against <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SARDINIA">Sardinia</a>, which had been conquered by the Moors. In this expedition they were successful; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> was reduced; but from this time an enmity commenced between the two republics, which did not end but with the ruin of the Pisans. The first war with <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PISA">Pisa</a> commenced about 30 years after the Sardinian expedition, and lasted 18 years; when the two contending parties having concluded a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> of peace, jointly sent their forces against the Moors in Africa, of whom they are said to have killed 100,000. The Genoese were very <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> in the time of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CRUSADES">crusades</a>, and had a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> share in the taking of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a>. They also waged considerable wars with the Moors in Spain, of whom they generally got the better. They also prevailed against the neighbouring states; and, in 1220, had enlarged their territories beyond the skirts of the Apennines, so that the rest of Italy looked upon them with a jealous eye; but in 1311 the factions which had for a long time reigned in the city, notwithstanding all its wealth and power, induced... Genoa induced the inhabitants so submit themselves for 20 years to the dominion of Henry VII, emperor of Germany. That emperor, however, died in August 1312; and the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VICAR">vicar</a> he had left soon after went to Pisa, upon which the dissensions in Genoa revived with greater fury than ever. In 1317, a quarrel happened between the families of Spinola and Doria; which came to such a height, that both parties fought in the streets for 24 days without intermission, raised <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTERING">battering</a> engines against each other's houses, and filled the city with blood. At last the Spinolae quitted the city, and retired to their territories in the Apennine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>. The civil war continued till the year 1331; when, by the mediation of the king of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>, it was concluded, that all exiles should return to the city; that the republic should be governed by the king's vicar; and all the offices of the state be equally divided between the Guelfs and the Gibellines, the two contending parties. By this ruinous war, the coast of Genoa, formerly adorned with palaces and vineyards, was now reduced to the appearance of a barren waste. So great was the general desolation, that according to Petrarch, the spectators who sailed along were struck with astonishment and horror. Villani, a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTEMPORARY">contemporary</a> author, relates, that it was supposed by the learned, that greater exploits had not been performed at the siege of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TROY">Troy</a>; and that the losses each party had sustained would have been sufficient to have purchased a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, the Genoese republic being in his time the richest and most powerful state in Christendom. The annalist Stella informs us, that, before the war, the most extravagant profusion and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LUXURY">luxury</a> prevailed among the Genoese: but that, towards the end, many noble families were reduced to indigence and poverty; so that about 100 years after, it became fashionable for the nobles to live in a plain manner, without any show or magnificence. In 1336, both parties, suspending their mutual animosities, sent two fleets of 20 galleys each into the German ocean, to the assistance of the king of France, who was engaged in a war with Edward III, king of England. This naval expedition proved the cause of a most remarkable revolution in the Genoese <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>. The sailors of the fleet, thinking themselves injured by their officers, whom they accused of defrauding them of their pay, proceeded to an open <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUTINY">mutiny</a>; and having expelled the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADMIRAL">admiral</a>, and other commanders, seized the galleys. The king of France being chosen arbitrator, decided in favour of the officers, and imprisoned 16 of the chiefs of the mutineers. Upon this several of the sailors left the fleet, and returned to Genoa; where they went round the coasts, repeating their mutinous complaints, which were greatly hearkened to, upon a false report that the mutineers who had been imprisoned were broke upon the wheel. The factious spirit increased: and at last the Genoese insisted in a tumultuous manner for having an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABBOT">abbot</a> of their own choosing, and 20 of the people with the consent of the captains of the republic assembled for that purpose. While the mob were impatiently expecting their decision, a mechanic, generally accounted a fool, mounted a wooden <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BENCH">bench</a>, and called out that one Simon Bucanigree should be chosen abbot. This being instantly echoed by the populace, he was first declared abbot, then <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a>, and at last duke of Genoa. This new expedient did not at all answer the purpose. The dissensions continued as violent as ever, notwithstanding the power of the new magistrates, and by these perpetual divisions the republic was at last so much weakened, that in 1390 the king of France was declared lord of Genoa. Under the French government, however, they soon became exceedingly impatient; and, in 1422, the duke of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILAN">Milan</a> obtained the sovereignty. With this situation they were equally displeased, and therefore revolted in 1436. Twenty-two years after, finding themselves pressed by a powerful fleet and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> sent by Alphonso king of Naples, they again conferred the sovereignty of their state, upon the king of France. In 1460, they revolted from the French; and, four years after, put themselves again under the protection of the duke of Milan: from whom they revolted in 1478. He was again declared sovereign of the republic in 1488; and, 11 years after, the city and territories of Genoa were conquered by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> XII, of France. The almost unparalleled fickleness of the Genoese disposition was not to be corrected by this misfortune. They revolted in 1506; but next year were again subdued by Louis. Six years after, they again revolted; and in 1516, the city was taken and plundered by the Spaniards. In 1528, Andrew Doria, a Genoese admiral in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of the French, undertook to rescue his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> from the dominion of foreign princes, and restore it to its <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>. Knowing well the fickle disposition of his countrymen, he took all occasions of exciting discontent among them against the government. He persuaded them, that the French (who had again obtained the sovereignty) had left them only a shadow of liberty, while they pretended to protect them from their enemies. To the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a> he represented the disgrace of suffering the government to be vested in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of foreigners less worthy of authority than themselves. Thus he soon formed a strong <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACTION">faction</a>, and formed his <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a>; for the execution of which he took the most proper time, namely, when almost three-fourths of the French garrison had been carried off by the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAGUE">plague</a>. He advanced with 500 men; and his friends having opened the gates of the city to him, he seized the principal posts, and thus became <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of it without <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>. The garrison retired to the forts, where they soon after capitulated, and being driven out of the city, Doria re-established the ancient form of government. See DORIA. The republic hath since continued to preserve her liberty, though greatly fallen from her ancient splendour, and now become a very inconsiderable state. In 1684, the Genoese had the misfortune to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> under the resentment of Louis XIV, at which time the city was almost destroyed by a formidable bombardment. In the year 1688, it was bombarded by Admiral Byng, and forced to capitulate; but there were at that time no views of making a permanent conquest of the city. In 1730, the island of Corsica revolted from the Genoese, and could never afterwards be reduced by them; for which reason it was sold to the French, who in the year 1770 totally reduced it. The Genoese territories extend along that part of the Mediterranean <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GULF">Gulf</a> of Genoa, about 152 miles; but their breadth is very unequal, being from eight to about 20 miles. Where they are not bounded by the sea, the following states and countries, taking them from west to east, are their boundaries, viz. <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PIEDMONT">Piedmont</a>, Montferrat, Milan, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACENTIA">Placentia</a>, Parma, the dukedom of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TUSCANY">Tuscany</a>, and the republic of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-LUCCA">Lucca</a>. This tract, though a great part of it is mountainous, and some of that barren enough, yet produces plenty of excellent fruit, good pasture, wood, garden stuff, and mulberry trees, with some wine and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, but little corn. What they want of the last, they have either from <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LOMBARDY">Lombardy</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a>, or Naples. Genoa stands on the coast of the Mediterranean sea, at the bottom of a little gulf, partly on the flat, and partly on the declivity, of a pleasant hill; in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of which, it appears to great advantage from the sea. It is defended on the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> side by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> wall, which in circumference is about ten Italian miles. Two of the streets consist entirely of a double straight row of magnificent palaces. The others, though clean and well paved, are crooked and narrow. The palaces of the nobility are almost all of marble, and many of them are painted on the outside. That there should be such a profusion of marble here, is not to be wondered at, as the neighbouring hills abound with it. The city contains a vast number of palaces, churches, and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CONVENTS">convents</a>, and several <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-HOSPITALS">hospitals</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> where the doge resides, and where the great and little <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>, and the two colleges of the procuratori and governatori assemble, is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> in the centre of the city. It contains some fine paintings in fresco; two <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a> of Andrew and John Doria in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> marble; and an arsenal, in which are said to be arms for thirty-four thousand men, with a shield, containing one hundred and twenty pistol barrels, and thirty-three coats of mail, which, it is pretended, were worn by as many Genoese heroines in a crusade. Of the churches, the finest are those of the Annunciation, St <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a> Carignan, St Dominic, and St Martha. In the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DISH">dish</a> made of a single <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMERALD">emerald</a>. All the inhabitants here, except the principal ladies, who are carried in chairs, walk on foot, on account of the narrowness or steepness of the streets. The fortifications of the city, towards the sea, are remarkably strong. There are two fine stone bridges over the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> Bonzerra and Bisagno, the first whereof washes the west, and the other the east side of the city, within which there is also a surprising stone <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> joining two hills. The harbour, though large, is far from being safe; but no care or expense has been spared to render it as safe and commodious as possible. The <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> to which it is most exposed, is that called Labecchio, or the south-west. The <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where the republic's galleys <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a>, is called the Darsena, where are a great number of Turkish slaves. On a rock, on the west side of the harbour, is the fanal or <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-LIGHTHOUSE">lighthouse</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> tower on the top of which is a lanthorn, containing thirty-six lamps. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> of Genoa is estimated at 150,000, and the trade is chiefly in velvets, damasks, plush, and other silks, brocades, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LACE">lace</a>, gloves, sweetmeats, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>, oil, Parmesan cheese, anchovies, and medicinal drugs from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEVANT">Levant</a>; but the badness of the harbour, and the high price of commodities, greatly checks the commerce. In 1751, Genoa was declared a free port for ten years, under certain restrictions: in that called Porto Franco, any merchant may have a warehouse, and import or export goods duty free; but such as are disposed of in the city, or on the continent, are taxed pretty high. The nobility are allowed to trade in the wholesale way; to carry on velvet, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a>, and cloth <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a>; and to have shares in merchant ships: and some of them, as the Palavicini, are actually the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a> in Genoa. Another very profitable article of trade carried on by them is <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BANKING">banking</a>, and dealing in bills of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXCHANGE">exchange</a>. A new academy of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SCULPTURE">sculpture</a>, civil and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a>, was instituted here in 1751. One may walk the streets of Genoa in the night with the greatest safety, which is more than can be said of many cities in Italy. Excessive splendour and luxury are, in several respects, restrained by salutary laws. No beggars are permitted to ask alms in Genoa, and the inns are better than those at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURIN">Turin</a>. When a single person is buried, a kind of garland of all sorts of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> is placed on the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COFFIN">coffin</a>. The Genoese in general are esteemed crafty, industrious, and inured to hard labour above the other Italians. Amidst the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> convulsions which agitated <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, in consequence of the unexampled French revolution, it was scarcely to be expected that Genoa would escape the shock. Accordingly in the year 1798, by the force and intrigues of the French republicans, its political <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> was totally subverted, and changed into what was afterwards denominated the Ligurian Republic, which was to be governed in a manner similar to that of their own, and the country also was divided into departments. As the preceding <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMPAIGN">campaign</a> had terminated in favour of the combined powers, and left them in the possession of every important place in Italy, this only excepted, the capture of it became an object of the utmost consequence to the contending parties. To regain it was the highest ambition of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AUSTRIA">Austria</a>, while the retaining of it was <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> of solicitude to the French republic. The reason is obvious. The conquest of it restored to the emperor of Germany the possession of all Italy, gave him the means of resuming his former positions in the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARITIME">Maritime</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALPS">Alps</a>, and reinforcing his former position on the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHINE">Rhine</a>. To the French it was a place of the utmost consequence, because while they were enabled to retain it in their own hands, they could easily favour the operations of their army in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWITZERLAND">Switzerland</a>, or their entrance into Italy by the defiles of Piedmont. As the allies were fully determined on its conquest for the reasons already assigned, as well as for others of an inferior <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> and magnitude, it is but candid to admit that the general by whom it was defended had innumerable difficulties to struggle with, and obstacles to surmount. When Massena succeeded Championet, the army was reduced to the most melancholy situation. Confined during the winter season to the bleak summits of the Apennines, it was reduced in numbers more than one half, and a constant prey to famine and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a>. To add to the difficulties which everywhere presented themselves to Massena, the higher classes of the Genoese looked upon the French only as the destroyers of their <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a>, commerce, and political importance; in consequence of which they secretly aided every <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> by which they might be driven from the country. Instead of 60,000 men which he was promised, Massena had no more than 20,000 after all his unwearied exertions, and with these he had to defend an <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of country from Mount Cenis to the frontiers of Tuscany. He wisely dismissed all the former generals, independent of their merit, because the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> associated with them the idea of former misery and disgrace. In addition to the superior strength of the Austrian army, Massena found a formidable insurrection raised against him in the eastern territory of the Genoese republic. The passage by sea was obstructed by the British fleet, and his expected succours from <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARSEILLES">Marseilles</a> only reached him in part. As he could not meet the army in the field by which he was blockaded, his only alternative was to remain in Genoa, every moment in dread of perishing by famine, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> not speedily relieved. After enduring great hardships, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a> for the starving inhabitants induced him to surrender. The victory of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARENGO">Marengo</a> however restored it again to the French; and after being indulged with a nominal independence for some time, it was incorporated with France in 1805. When Bonaparte sustained his great reverses in 1814, Genoa surrendered to a British force, under a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROMISE">promise</a> of independence, which promise was however broken, and the city with its territory was annexed to Sardinia. When the insurrection took place in this kingdom in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a> 1821, Genoa gladly seized the opportunity to throw off the foreign yoke. But the failure of the revolution in Piedmont led to the suppression of the independence of Genoa. GENSING. See Panax, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

GENTIANA

Pages 526-526

Gentian, a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the pentandria class; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 20th order, Rotaceae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

GENTILE

Pages 526-526

in matters of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, a Pagan, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> worshipper of false gods. The origin of this word is deduced from the Jews, who called all those who were not of their name gojim, i.e. gentes, which in the Greek translations of the Old <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a> is rendered ἔθνη; in which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> it frequently occurs in the New Testament; as in Matth. vi. 32. "All these things the nations or Gentiles seek." Whence the Latin <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> also used gentes in the same sense as our Gentiles, especially in the New Testament. But the word gentes soon got another signification, and no longer meant all such as were not Jews; but those only who were neither Jews nor <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>, but followed the superstitions of the Greeks and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, &c. In this sense it <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> among the Christian writers, till their manner of speech, together with their religion, was publicly and by authority received in the empire; when gentiles, from gentes, came into <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>: and then both words had two significations, viz. in treatises or laws concerning religion, they signified Pagans, neither Jews nor Christians; and in civil affairs, they were used for all such as were not Romans. Gentile, in the Roman <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, a name which sometimes expresses what the Romans otherwise called barbarians, whether they were allies of Rome or not: but this word was used in a more particular sense for all strangers and foreigners not subject to the Roman empire.

GENTILESCHI

Pages 526-526

Horatio, an Italian painter, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PISA">Pisa</a> in 1563. After having made himself famous at <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLORENCE">Florence</a>, Rome, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENOA">Genoa</a>, and other parts of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, he removed to Savoy; from whence he went to France, and at last, upon the invitation of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> I., came over to England. He was well received by that <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>, who appointed him lodgings in his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>, together with a considerable salary; and employed him in his <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREENWICH">Greenwich</a>, and other public places. The most remarkable of his performances in England, were the ceilings of Greenwich, and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORK">York</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>. He did also a Madonna, a Magdalen, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOT">Lot</a> with his two daughters, for King Charles; all which he performed admirably well. After the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of the king, when his collection was exposed to <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALE">sale</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> pictures of Gentileschi were sold for 600l. and are now said to be the ornaments of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HALL">hall</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARLBOROUGH">Marlborough</a> house. His most esteemed piece abroad was the portico of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDINAL">Cardinal</a> Bentivoglio's palace at Rome. He made several attempts in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FACE">face</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a>, but with little success; his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TALENT">talent</a> lying altogether in histories, with figures as big as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. He was much in favour with the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUCKINGHAM">Buckingham</a>, and many others of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a>. After 12 years continuance in England, he died here at 84 years of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, and was buried in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a>'s chapel at Somerset-house. His print is among the heads of Vandyke, he having been drawn by that <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>. He left behind him a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTEMISIA">Artemisia</a> Gentileschi, who was but little inferior to her father in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> painting, and excelled him in portraits.

GENTILIS

Pages 526-527

Albericus, professor of civil <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>; an Italian by birth. He had quitted <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> with his father, on account of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>. He wrote several works; three books, in particular, De jure belli, which have not been unserviceable to Grotius. He died at <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a> in 1608. Gentilis, Scipio, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> to the former, and as celebrated a civilian as he, forsook his native <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> that he might openly profess the Protestant religion. He was counsellor of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUREMBERG">Nuremberg</a>, and professor of law with uncommon reputation. He was a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> humanist; and in his lectures, as well as books, mixed the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> of polite learning with the thorns of the law. He died in 1616. <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">GENTLEMAN</a>. Under this denomination are comprehended all above the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> of yeomen*, whereby noblemen are truly called gentlemen. A gentleman is usually defined to be one, who, without any <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a>, bears a coat of arms, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> whose <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a> have been freemen: and by the coat that a gentleman giveth, he is known to be, or not to be, descended from those of his name that lived many hundred years since. The word is formed of the French gentilhomme; or rather of gentil, "fine, fashionable, or becoming;" and the Saxon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, q.d. honestus, or honesto loco natus.—The same signification has the Italian gentiluomo, and the Spanish hidalgó, or hijo dalgo, that is, the son of somebody, or a person of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOTE">note</a>.—<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> we go farther back, we shall find gentleman originally derived from the Latin gentilis homo; which was used among the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> for a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a> of noble persons of the same name, born of free or ingenuous parents, and whose ancestors had never been slaves or put to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> by law. Thus Cicero in his Topics, "Gentiles sunt, qui inter se eodem sunt nomine, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AB">ab</a> ingenuis oriundi, quorum majorum nemo servitutem servivit, qui <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITE">capite</a> non sunt diminuti," Some hold that it was formed from <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENTILE">gentile</a>, i.e. pagan; and that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Franks, who conquered <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAUL">Gaul</a>, which was then converted to Christianity, were called gentiles by the natives, as being yet heathens. Others relate, that towards the declension of the Roman empire, as recorded by <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMMIANUS_MARCELLINUS">Ammianus Marcellinus</a>, there were two companies of brave <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a>, the one called gentiles, and the other scutarii; and that it was hence we derive the names gentleman and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ESQUIRE">esquire</a>. See ESQUIRE.—This sentiment is confirmed by Pasquier, who supposes the appellation gentiles and ecuyers to have been transmitted to us from the Roman soldiery; it being, to the gentiles and scutarii, who were the bravest of the soldiery, that the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> benefits and portions of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> were assigned. See BENEFICE. The Gauls observing, that during the empire of the Romans, the scutarii and gentiles had the best tenements or appointments of all the soldiers on the frontiers of the provinces, became insensibly accustomed to apply the same names, gentilhommes and ecuyers, to such as they found their kings gave the best <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a> or appointments to. Gentleman Usher of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">Black</a> Rod. See Rod. Gentlemen of the Chapel; officers whose duty and attendance is in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> chapel, being in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> 32. Twelve of them are priests; the other 20, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called clerks of the chapel, assist in the performance of divine <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>. One of the first 12 is chosen for confessor of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSEHOLD">household</a>; whose office is to read prayers every morning to the household servants, to visit the sick, examine and prepare communicants, and administer the sacrament. One of 20 clerks, well versed in music, is chosen first organist, who is <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of the children, to instruct them in music, and whatever else is necessary for the service of the chapel; a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> is likewise an organist; a third, a lutanist; and a fourth a violist. There are likewise three vergers, so called from the silver rods they carry in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>; being a serjeant, a yeoman, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GROOM">groom</a> of the vestry; the first attends the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAN">dean</a> and subdean, and finds surplices and other necessaries for the chapel; the second has the whole care of the chapel, keeps the pews, and seats of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a> and gentry; the groom has his attendance within the chapel door, and looks after it.

GENTOOS

Pages 527-527

in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, according to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> acceptation of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a>, denote the professors of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> of the bramins <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> brachmans, who inhabit the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> called Hindostan, in the East Indies, from the word stan, a "region," and hind or hindoo; which Ferishtah, as we learn from <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLONEL">Colonel</a> Dow's translation of his history, supposes to have been a son of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAM">Ham</a> the son of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOAH">Noah</a>. It is observed, however, that Hindoo is not the name by which the inhabitants originally styled themselves; but according to the idiom of the Shamscrit which they <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>, jumbodeep from jumbo, a "jackall," an animal common in their country; and deep, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> portion of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> surrounded by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>; or bhertekhunt, from khunt, i.e. "a continent," and bherrhut, the name of one of the first <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> rajahs. It is also to be observed, that they have assumed the name of Hindoos only since the era of the Tartar <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, to distinguish themselves from their conquerors the Mussulmans. The term Gentoo or Gent, in the Shanscrit dialect, denotes animal in general, and in its more confined <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> mankind, and is never appropriated particularly to such as follow the doctrines of Brama. These are divided into four <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> tribes, each of which has its own separate appellation; but they have no common or collective term that comprehends the whole <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> under the idea affixed by the Europeans to the word Gentoo. Mr Halhed, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREFACE">preface</a> to his translation of the Code of Gentoo Laws, conjectures that the Portuguese, on their first arrival in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a>, hearing the word frequently in the mouths of the natives, as applied to mankind in general, might adopt it for the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> appellation of the Indians themselves, or perhaps their bigotry might force from the word Gentoo a fanciful allusion to <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENTILE">gentile</a> or Pagan. The Hindoos, or Gentoos, vie with the Chinese as to the antiquity of their nation. They reckon the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DURATION">duration</a> of the world by four jogues, or distinct ages; the first the Suttee jogue, or <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> of purity, which is said to have lasted about 3,200,000 years; during which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> was 100,000 years, and his stature 21 cubits; the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a>, the Tirat jogue, or the age in which one-third of mankind were reprobate; which consisted of 2,400,000 years, when men lived to the age of 10,000 years; the third, the Dwapar jogue, in which half of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a> became depraved, which endured to 600,000 years, when men's lives were reduced to 1000 years; and fourthly, the Collee jogue, in which all mankind were corrupted, or rather diminished, which the word collee imports. This is the present era, which they suppose <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> subsist for 400,000 years, of which near 5000 are already past; and man's life in this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> is limited to 100 years. It is supposed by many authors, that most of the Gentoo shasters, or scriptures, were composed about the beginning of the Collee jogue: but an objection occurs against this supposition, viz. that the shasters take no notice of the deluge; to which the bramins reply, that all their scriptures were written before the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of Noah, and the deluge never extended to Hindostan. Nevertheless, it appears from the shasters themselves, that they claim a much higher antiquity than this; instances of which are recited by Mr Halhed. The doctrine of transmigration is one of the distinguishing tenets of the Gentoos. With regard to this subject, it is their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, according to Mr Holwell, that those souls which have attained to a certain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of purity, either by the innocence of their manners or the severity of their mortifications, are removed to regions of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a> proportioned to their respective merits: but that those who cannot so far surmount the prevalence of bad example, and the powerful degeneracy of the times, as to deserve such a promotion, are condemned to undergo continual <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANIMATION">animation</a> of successive animal forms, until, at the stated period, another renovation of the four jogues shall commence, upon the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISSOLUTION">dissolution</a> of the present. They imagine six different spheres above this <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>; the highest of which, called suttee, is the residence of Brama, and his particular favourites. This sphere is also the habitation of those men who never uttered a falsehood, and of those women who have voluntarily burned themselves with their husbands; the propriety of which practice is expressly enjoined in the code of the Gentoo laws. This code, printed by the East India <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPANY">Company</a> in 1776, is a very curious collection of Hindoo...

GENU FLEXION

Pages 527-528

(of genu, "knee," and flecto, "I <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEND">bend</a>,") the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> of bowing <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BENDING">bending</a> the knee; or rather of kneeling <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a>. The Jesuit Rosweyd, in his Onomasticon, shows, that genuflexion, or kneeling, has been a very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, and even under the Old <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a> dispensation; and that this practice was observed throughout all the year, excepting on Sundays, and during the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> from Easter to Whitsuntide, when kneeling was forbidden by the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of Nice. Others have shown, that the custom of not kneeling on <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUNDAY">Sunday</a> had obtained from the time of the apostles, as appears from St Irenæus, and Tertullian; and the Ethiopic church, scrupulously attached to the ancient ceremonies, still retain that of not kneeling at divine <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>. The Russians esteem it an indecent posture to worship God on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KNEES">knees</a>. Add, that the Jews usually prayed standing. Rosweyd gives the reasons of the prohibition of genuflexion on Sundays, &c., from St <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BASIL">Basil</a>, Anastasius, St Justin, &c. Baronius is of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, that genuflexion was not established in the year of Christ 58, from that passage in Acts xx. 36, where St Paul is expressly mentioned to kneel down at <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRAYER">prayer</a>; but Saurin shows, that nothing can be thence concluded. The same author remarks, also, that the primitive <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> carried the practice of genuflexion so far, that some of them had worn cavities in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOR">floor</a> where they prayed: and St Jerome relates of St James, that he had contracted a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HARDNESS">hardness</a> on his knees equal to that of camels.

GENUS

Pages 528-529

among metaphysicians and logicians, denotes a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of beings which agree in certain general properties <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> to them all: so that a genus is nothing else but an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABSTRACT">abstract</a> idea, expressed by some general name <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a>. See LOGIC and <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METAPHYSICS">METAPHYSICS</a>. Genus, is also used for a character or manner applicable to every thing of a certain <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> or condition; in which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> it serves to make <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> divisions in <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> sciences, as medicine, <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, &c. Genus, in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHETORIC">Rhetoric</a>. Authors distinguish the art of rhetoric, as also orations or discourses produced thereby, into three genera or kinds, demonstrative, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DELIBERATIVE">deliberative</a>, and judiciary. To the demonstrative kind belong panegyrics, genethliacoms, epithalamiums, funeral harangues, &c. To the deliberative belong persuasions, dissuasions, commendations, &c. To the judiciary kind belong defences and accusations. Genus, in Medicine. See MEDICINE, under the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOSOLOGY">Nosology</a>. Genus, in Natural History, a subdivision of any class or order of natural beings, whether of the animal, vegetable, or mineral kingdoms, which agree in certain common <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a>. See NATURAL HISTORY. Genus, in Music, by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> called genus melodia, is a certain manner of dividing and subdividing the principles of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MELODY">melody</a>; that is, the consonant and dissonant intervals, into their concinnous parts. The moderns considering the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OCTAVE">octave</a> as the most perfect of intervals, and that whereon all the concords depend, in the present <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEORY">theory</a> of music, the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of that <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTERVAL">interval</a> is considered as containing the true division of the whole <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCALE">scale</a>. But the ancients went to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> somewhat differently: the diatessaron, or fourth, was the least interval which they admitted as concord; and therefore they sought first how that might be most conveniently divided; from whence they constituted the diapente and diapason. The diatessaron being thus, as it were, the root and foundation of the scale, what they called the genera, or kinds, arose from its various divisions; and hence they defined the genus modulandi to be the manner of dividing the tetrachord and disposing its four sounds as to succession. The genera of music were three, the enharmonic, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHROMATIC">chromatic</a>, and diatonic. The two first were variously subdivided; subdivided; and even the last, though that is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> reckoned to be without any <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, yet different authors have proposed different divisions under that name, without giving any particular names to the species as was done to the other two. For the characters, &c. of these several genera, see Enharmonic, Chromatic, and Diatonic.

GEOCENTRIC

Pages 529-529

in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a>, is applied to a planet, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> its orbit, to denote it concentric with the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, or as having the earth for its centre, or the same centre with the earth. GEOFFREÆA, a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the diadelphia class, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 32d order, Papilionaceæ. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MATERIA_MEDICA">Materia Medica</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

GEOFFREY OF MONMOUTH

Pages 529-529

bishop of St Asaph, called by our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> biographers Gallofridus Monimentensis. Leland conjectures that he was educated in a Benedictine convent at Monmouth, where he was born; and that he became a monk of that order. <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALE">Bale</a>, and after him Pits, call him archdeacon of Monmouth; and it is generally asserted that he was made bishop of St Asaph in the year 1151 <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> 1152, in the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> Stephen. His <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> was probably finished after the year 1138. It contains a fabulous account of British kings, from the Trojan Brutus to the reign of Cadwallader in the year 690. But Geoffrey, whatever censure he may deserve for his credulity, was not the inventor of the stories he relates. It is a translation from a manuscript written in the British <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, and brought to England from Armorica by his friend Gualter, archdeacon of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>. But the achievements of King <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTHUR">Arthur</a>, Merlin's prophecies, many speeches and letters, were chiefly his own addition. In excuse for this historian, Mr Wharton judiciously observes, that fabulous histories were then the fashion, and popular traditions a recommendation to his book.

GEOFFROY

Pages 529-529

STEPHEN-FRANCIS, a physician eminent for his chemical and botanical knowledge, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> in the year 1672, where his father kept an apothecary's shop, and had been several times in the magistracy. He received a liberal <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>; and, while prosecuting the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of medicine, he had conferences at his father's <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> with Cassini, du Verney, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOMBERG">Homberg</a>, and other men of distinguished eminence. At <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTPELLIER">Montpellier</a> he attended the lectures of the most able professors of physic, and afterwards visited the south of France, carefully viewing every object deserving of his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>. He accompanied <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNT">count</a> de Tallard to England in 1693, where he became acquainted with the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> men of science, and was made a member of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a>. He next went into <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, and in 1700 he attended the abbé de Louvois in a tour to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>. He was, on his return, made bachelor of medicine in 1702, and, in two years after, he was created M.D. One of his theses was on the question, "An hominis primordia vermis?" which was translated into French for the sake of some ladies of exalted <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a>, by whom it was deemed interesting. Geoffroy did not hastily commence the practice of medicine, continuing the prosecution of his studies in retirement for some years. He never appeared anxious to push himself forward, although his knowledge made him be often consulted by several gentlemen of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FACULTY">faculty</a>. He was so concerned for the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RECOVERY">recovery</a> of his patients, that it gave him an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> of melancholy, which at first alarmed them, till they became acquainted with the cause. He was, in 1709, made professor of physic by the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> to the Royal <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLLEGE">College</a>, vacant by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of the celebrated Tournefort. He began with lectures on <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MATERIA_MEDICA">materia medica</a>; and in 1712, M. Fagon resigned to him the chemical <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a>: on both which topics Geoffroy lectured with unwearied assiduity. He was twice chosen to the office of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAN">dean</a> by the faculty of Paris, and he filled a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in the Royal Academy of Sciences, from the year 1699. His <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> at last yielded to his toils, and he died in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JANUARY">January</a>, 1731. He is known to the chemical world by his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a> of affinities, far superior to any which had appeared before his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>.
