The streets are <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> and well paved, the market places spacious, and the houses built with brick. But the Friday's market place is the largest, and is remarkable for the statue of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> V., which stands upon a pedestal in the imperial <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HABIT">habit</a>. That of Cortere is remarkable for a fine walk under several rows of trees. In 1737 a fine <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OPERA">opera</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> was built here, and a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUARD">guard</a> house for the garrison. Near the town is a very <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> tower, with a handsome clock and chimes. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BELL">bell</a> weighs 11,000 pounds. This town is famous for the pacification signed here, in 1526, for settling the tranquillity of the Seventeen Provinces, which was afterwards confirmed by the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>. It was taken by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> XIV. in 1678, who who afterwards restored it. The French took possession of it again after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Charles II. of Spain. In 1706, it was taken by the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARLBOROUGH">Marlborough</a>; and by the French in 1708; but it was retaken the same year. Last of all, the French took it by surprise after the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of Fontenoy; but at the peace of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIX">Aix</a>-la-Chapelle, it was rendered back. It was also taken by the French in 1794; and was restored to the Netherlands in 1814. This is the birth-place of John of Gaunt. It is very well seated for trade, on account of its rivers and canals. It has <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a>, woollen, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of inhabitants is about 61,000. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 3° 50'. N. Lat. 51° 14'.

GHOST

Pages 763-765

an apparition, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> spirit of a person deceased. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> supposed every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> to be possessed of three different ghosts, which after the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISSOLUTION">dissolution</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> body were differently disposed of. These three ghosts were distinguished by the names of Manes, Spiritus, Umbra. The manes, they fancied, went <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> into the infernal region; the spiritus ascended to the skies; and the umbra hovered about the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOMB">tomb</a>, as being unwilling to quit its old connexions. Thus Dido (Virg. Æn. iv. 384.) threatens Æneas after <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> that she <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> haunt him with her umbra, whilst her manes rejoices in his torments below. This idea of a threefold <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUL">soul</a> is very clearly expressed in these <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a>, which have been attributed to Ovid. Bis duo sunt homini: Manes, Caro, Spiritus, Umbra: Quatuor ista loci bis duo suscipiunt. Terra tegit Carnem, tumulum circumvolat Umbra, Orcus habet Manes, Spiritus astra petit. The most striking outlines of the popular superstitions respecting ghosts among us, are thus humorously collected by <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPTAIN">Captain</a> Grose in his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCIAL">Provincial</a> Glossary: "A ghost is supposed to be the spirit of a person deceased, who is either commissioned to return for some special errand, such as the discovery of a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDER">murder</a>, to procure restitution of lands or <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a> unjustly withheld from an orphan or widow—or, having committed some injustice whilst living, cannot rest till that is redressed. Sometimes the occasion of spirits revisiting this world, is to inform their heir in what secret <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, or private drawer in an old <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUNK">trunk</a>, they had hidden the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> deeds of the estate; or where, in troublesome times, they buried their money or plate. Some ghosts of murdered persons, whose bodies have been secretly buried, cannot be at ease till their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONES">bones</a> have been taken up, and deposited in consecrated ground with all the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RITES">rites</a> of Christian <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BURIAL">burial</a>. "Sometimes ghosts appear in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of an agreement made, whilst living, with some particular friend, that he who first died should appear to the survivor. "Glanvil tells us of the ghost of a person who had lived but a disorderly kind of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, for which it was condemned to wander up and down the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> of evil spirits, till the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> of judgment. "In most of the relations of ghosts, they are supposed to be <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> aerial beings, without substance, and that they can <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> through walls and other <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> bodies at <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>. A particular instance of this is given, in relation the 27th, in Glanvil's collection, where one <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAVID">David</a> Hunter, neat-herd to the bishop of Down and Connor was for a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> haunted by the apparition of an old woman, whom he was by a secret impulse obliged to follow whenever she appeared, which he says he did for a considerable time, even <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BED">bed</a> with his wife: and because his wife could not hold him in his bed, she would go too, and walk after him till day, though she <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> nothing; but his little dog was so well acquainted with the apparition, that he would follow it as well as his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>. If a tree stood in her walk, he observed her always to go through it. Notwithstanding this seeming immateriality, this very ghost was not without some substance; for, having performed her errand, she desired Hunter to lift her from the ground; in the doing of which, he says, she felt <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> like a bag of feathers. We sometimes also read of ghosts striking violent blows; and that, if not made way for, they overturn all <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-IMPEDIMENTS">impediments</a>, like a furious whirlwind. Glanvil mentions an instance of this, in relation 17th, of a Dutch <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LIEUTENANT">lieutenant</a> who had the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FACULTY">faculty</a> of seeing ghosts; and who being prevented making way for one which he mentioned to some friends as coming towards them, was, with his companions, violently thrown down, and sorely bruised. We further learn, by relation 16th, that the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> of a ghost is 'as <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLD">cold</a> as a clod.' "The usual time at which ghosts make their appearance is midnight, and seldom before it is dark: though some audacious spirits have been said to appear even by day <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>: but of this there are few instances, and those mostly ghosts who have been laid, perhaps in the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-RED_SEA"><a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">Red</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> (of which more hereafter), and whose times of confinement were expired: these, like felons confined to the lighters, are said to return more troublesome and daring than before. No ghosts can appear on Christmas <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EVE">eve</a>; this Shakespeare has put into the mouth of one of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAMLET">Hamlet</a>. "Ghosts <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> appear in the same dress they usually wore whilst living, though they are sometimes clothed all in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a>; but that is chiefly the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCHYARD">churchyard</a> ghosts, who have no particular business, but seem to appear pro bono publico, or to scare drunken rustics from tumbling over their graves. "I cannot learn that ghosts carry tapers in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, as they are sometimes depicted, though the room in which they appear, if without fire or <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANDLE">candle</a>, is frequently said to be as light as day. Dragging chains is not the fashion of English ghosts; chains and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> vestments being chiefly the accoutrements of foreign spectres seen in arbitrary governments: dead or alive, English spirits are free. One instance, however, of an English ghost dressed in black is found in the celebrated ballad of William and Margaret, in the following lines: And clay cold was her lily hand That held her sable shroud. This, however, may be considered as a poetical license, used, in all likelihood, for the sake of the opposition of lily to sable. "If, during the time of an apparition, there is a lighted candle in the room, it will burn extremely blue: this is so universally acknowledged that many eminent philosophers have busied themselves in accounting for it, without once doubting the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> of the fact. Dogs, too, have the faculty of seeing spirits, as is instanced in..." David Hunter's relation above quoted; but in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> they usually show signs of terror, by whining and creeping to their master for protection; and it is generally supposed that they often see things of this <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> when their owner cannot; there being some persons, particularly those born on a Christmas eve, who cannot see spirits. "The coming of a spirit is announced some time before its appearance, by a variety of loud and dreadful noises; sometimes rattling in the old <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HALL">hall</a> like a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COACH">coach</a> and six, and rumbling up and down the staircase like the trundling of bowls or cannon balls. At length the door flies open, and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SPECTRE">spectre</a> stalks slowly up to the bed's foot, and opening the curtains, looks steadfastly at the person in bed by whom it is seen; a ghost being very rarely visible to more than one person, although there are several in company. It is here necessary to observe, that it has been universally found by <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a>, as well as affirmed by diverse <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-APPARITIONS">apparitions</a> themselves, that a ghost has not the power to speak till it has been first spoken to; so that notwithstanding the urgency of the business on which it may come, everything must stand still till the person visited can find sufficient courage to speak to it: an event that sometimes does not take place for many years. It has not been found that <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> ghosts are more loquacious than those of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MALE">male</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEX">sex</a>, both being equally restrained by this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a>. "The <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of addressing a ghost is by commanding it, in the name of the Three Persons of the Trinity, to tell you who it is, and what is its business; this it may be necessary to repeat three times; after which it will, in a low and hollow <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VOICE">voice</a>, declare its satisfaction at being spoken to, and desire the party addressing it not to be afraid, for it will do him no harm. This being premised, it commonly enters into its narrative; which being completed, and its request or commands given, with injunctions that they be immediately executed, it vanishes away, frequently in a flash of light; in which case, some ghosts have been so considerate as to desire the party to whom they appeared to shut their eyes: sometimes its departure is attended with delightful music. During the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NARRATION">narration</a> of its business, a ghost must by no means be interrupted by questions of any kind; so doing is extremely dangerous; if any doubts arise, they must be stated after the spirit has done its tale. Questions respecting its state, or the state of any of their former acquaintance, are offensive, and not often answered; spirits perhaps being restrained from divulging the secrets of their prison <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>. Occasionally spirits will even condescend to talk on <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> occurrences, as is instanced by Glanvil in the apparition of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAJOR">Major</a> George Sydenham to Captain William Dyke, relation 10th, wherein the major reproved the captain for suffering a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWORD">sword</a> he had given him to grow rusty: saying, 'Captain, captain, this sword did not <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> to be kept after this manner when it was mine.' This <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> to the state of arms, was a remnant of the major's professional duty when living. "It is somewhat remarkable that ghosts do not go about their business like the persons of this world. In <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> of murder, a ghost, instead of going to the next <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> of the peace, and laying its information, or to the nearest relation of the person murdered, appears to some <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a> labourer who knows none of the parties, draws the curtains of some decrepit nurse or old woman, or hovers about the place where his body is deposited. The same circuitous mode is pursued with respect to redressing injured orphans or widows; when it seems as if the shortest and most certain way would be, to go to the person guilty of the injustice, and haunt him continually till he be terrified into a restitution. Nor is the pointing out lost writings generally managed in a more summary way; the ghost commonly applying to a third person ignorant of the whole affair, and a stranger to all concerned. But it is presumptuous to scrutinize too far into these matters: ghosts have undoubtedly forms and customs peculiar to themselves. "If after the first appearance, the persons employed neglect, or are prevented from, performing the message or business committed to their management, the ghost appears continually to them, at first with a discontented, next an angry, and at length with a furious countenance, threatening to tear them in pieces if the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> is not forthwith executed; sometimes terrifying them, as in Glanvil's relation 26th, by appearing in many formidable shapes, and sometimes even striking them a violent blow. Of blows given by ghosts there are many instances, and some wherein they have been followed with an incurable lameness. "It should have been observed, that ghosts, in delivering their commissions, in order to ensure <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BELIEF">belief</a>, communicate to the persons employed some secret known only to the parties concerned and themselves, the relation of which always produces the effect intended. The business being completed, ghosts appear with a cheerful countenance, saying they shall now be at rest, and will never more disturb any one; and, thanking their agents, by way of reward communicate to them something relative to themselves, which they will never reveal. "Sometimes ghosts appear, and disturb a house, without deigning to give any reason for so doing: with these, the shortest and only way is to <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a>, and eject them; or, as the vulgar <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> is, lay them. For this purpose there must be two or three clergymen, and the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a> must be performed in Latin; a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> that strikes the most audacious ghost with terror. A ghost may be laid for any term less than 100 years, and in any place or body, full or empty; as, a solid oak—the pommel of a sword—a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BARREL">barrel</a> of beer, if a yeoman or simple <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a>—or a pipe of wine, if an <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ESQUIRE">esquire</a> or a justice. But of all places the most common, and what a ghost least likes, is the Red sea; it being related, in many instances, that ghosts have most earnestly besought the exorcists not to confine them in that place. It is nevertheless considered as an indisputable fact, that there are an infinite <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> laid there, perhaps from its being a safer prison than any other nearer at hand; though neither <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> nor <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRADITION">tradition</a> gives us any instance of ghosts escaping or returning from this kind of transportation before their time. "Another <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of human apparition may be here noticed, though it does not come under the strict <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of a ghost. These are the exact figures and resemblances of persons then living, often seen not only by their friends at a distance, but many times by themselves; selves; of which there are several instances in Aubery's Miscellanies; one of Sir Richard Napier, a physician of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, who being on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a> from <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEDFORDSHIRE">Bedfordshire</a> to visit a friend in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BERKSHIRE">Berkshire</a>, saw at an inn his own apparition lying on his bed as a dead corpse; he nevertheless went forward, and died in a short time: another of Lady <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DIANA">Diana</a> Rich, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, who met her own apparition walking in a garden at <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KENSINGTON">Kensington</a>, and died a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">month</a> after of the smallpox. These apparitions are called fetches; in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUMBERLAND">Cumberland</a>, swarts; and in Scotland, wraiths; they most commonly appear to distant friends and relations, at the very instant preceding the death of the person whose <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> they put on. Sometimes, as in the instances above mentioned, there is a greater <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTERVAL">interval</a> between the appearance and death." For a philosophical inquiry into the subject of apparitions in general, see the article SPECTRE.

GIAGH

Pages 765-765

in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHRONOLOGY">Chronology</a>, a cycle of 12 years; in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> among the Turks and Cathayans. Each year of a giagh bears the name of some animal: the first that of a mouse; the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> that of a bullock; the third of a lynx <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> leopard; the fourth of a hare; the fifth of a crocodile; the sixth of a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SERPENT">serpent</a>; the seventh of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>; the eighth of a sheep; the ninth of a monkey; the tenth of a hen; the eleventh of a dog; and the twelfth of a <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-HOG">hog</a>. They also divide the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> into 12 parts, which they call giaghs, and distinguish them by the name of some animals. Each giagh contains two of our hours, and is divided into eight kehs, as many as there are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> in our hours.

GIALLOLINO

Pages 765-765

in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, a fine <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> pigment, much used under the name of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a> Yellow.

GIANT

Pages 765-768

a person of extraordinary bulk and stature. The romances of all ages have furnished us with so many extravagant accounts of giants of incredible bulk and strength, that the existence of such people is now generally disbelieved. It is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> thought, that the stature of men hath been the same in all ages; and some have even pretended to demonstrate the impossibility of the existence of giants mathematically. Of these our countryman M'Laurin hath been the most explicit. "In general (says he) it <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> easily appear, that the efforts tending to destroy the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COHESION">cohesion</a> of beams arising from their own gravity only, increase in the quadruplicate ratio of their lengths: but that the opposite efforts tending to preserve their cohesion, increase only in the triplicate proportion of the same lengths. From which it follows, that the greater beams must be in greater danger of breaking than the lesser similar ones; and that though a lesser beam may be firm and secure, yet a greater similar one may be made so <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a>, that it will necessarily <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> by its own <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>. Hence Galileo justly concludes, that what appears very firm, and succeeds very well in models, may be very weak and infirm, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> even <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> to pieces by its own weight, when it comes to be executed in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> dimensions according to the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODEL">model</a>. From the same principle he argues, that there are necessary limits in the operations of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> and art, which they cannot surpass in magnitude. Were trees of a very enormous size, their branches would fall by their own weight. Large animals have not strength in proportion to their size; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> there were any <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> animals much larger than those we know, they could hardly move, and would be perpetually subject to the most dangerous accidents. As to the animals of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, indeed the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> is different; for the gravity of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> in a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> manner sustains those animals; and in fact these are known sometimes to be vastly larger than the greatest land animals. Nor does it avail against this doctrine to tell us, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONES">bones</a> have sometimes been found which were supposed to have belonged to giants of immense size; such as the skeletons mentioned by Strabo and Pliny, the former of which was 60 cubits <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, and the latter 46: for naturalists have concluded on <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> grounds, that in some <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> these bones had belonged to elephants; and that the larger ones were bones of whales, which had been brought to the places where they were found by the revolutions of nature that have happened in past times. Though it must be owned, that there appears no reason why there may not have been men who have exceeded by some feet in height the tallest we have seen." It will easily be seen, that arguments of this kind can never be conclusive; because, along with an increase of stature in any animal, we must always suppose a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROPORTIONAL">proportional</a> increase in the cohesion of the parts of its body. Large works sometimes fail when constructed on the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> of models, because the cohesion of the materials whereof the model is made, and of the large <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, are the same; but a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> in this respect will produce a very remarkable difference in the ultimate result. Thus, suppose a model is made of firwood, the model may be strong and firm enough; but a large work made also of fir, when executed according to the plan of the model, may be so weak that it will fall to pieces by its own weight. If, however, we make <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> for the large work instead of fir, the whole will be sufficiently strong, even though made exactly according to the plan of the model. The like may be said with regard to large and small animals. If we could find an animal whose bones exceeded in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HARDNESS">hardness</a> and strength the bones of other animals as much as iron exceeds fir, such an animal might be of a monstrous size, and yet be exceedingly strong. In like manner, if we suppose the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> and bones of a giant to be greatly superior in hardness and strength to the bones of other men, the great size of his body will be no objection at all to his strength. The whole of the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> therefore concerning the existence of giants must rest on the credibility of the accounts we have from those who pretend to have seen them, and not on any arguments drawn a priori. In the Scripture we are told of giants, who were produced from the marriages of the sons of God with the daughters of men. This passage indeed has been differently interpreted, so as to render it doubtful whether the word translated giants does there imply any extraordinary stature. In other parts of Scripture, however, giants, with their dimensions, are mentioned in such a manner that we cannot possibly doubt; as in the case of Og <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of Bashan, and Goliath. In a memoir read before the Academy of Sciences at <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROUEN">Rouen</a>, M. Le Cat gives the following account of giants that are said to have existed in different ages. "Profane historians have given <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> feet of height..." Giant. to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERCULES">Hercules</a> their first <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERO">hero</a>; and in our days we have seen men eight feet high. The giant who was shown in Rouen in 1735, measured eight feet some inches. The <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Maximian was of that size; Shenkius and Platerus, physicians of the last century, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> several of that stature; and Goropius saw a girl who was ten feet high.—The body of Orestes, according to the Greeks, was eleven feet and a half; the giant Galbarra, brought from <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARABIA">Arabia</a> to Rome under Claudius Caesar, was near ten feet; and the bones of Secondilla and Posio, keepers of the gardens of Sallust, were but six inches shorter. Funnarn, a Scotsman, who lived in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of Eugene II., king of Scotland, measured eleven feet and a half; and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JACOB">Jacob</a> le Maire, in his voyage to the Straits of Magellan, reports, that on the 17th of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a> 1615, they found at Port Desire several graves covered with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONES">stones</a>; and having the curiosity to remove the stones, they discovered <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> skeletons of ten and eleven feet long. The chevalier Scory, in his voyage to the peak of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TENERIFFE">Teneriffe</a>, says, that they found in one of the sepulchral caverns of that mountain the head of a Guanche which had 80 <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a>, and that the body was not less than 15 feet long. The giant Ferragus, slain by Orlando nephew of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLEMAGNE">Charlemagne</a>, was 13 feet high. Rioland, a celebrated anatomist, who wrote in 1614, says, that some years before there was to be seen in the suburbs of St Germain the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOMB">tomb</a> of the giant Isoret, who was 20 feet high. In Rouen, in 1509, in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGGING">digging</a> in the ditches near the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOMINICANS">Dominicans</a>, they found a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a> tomb containing a skeleton whose skull held a bushel of corn, and whose shin bone reached up to the girdle of the tallest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> there, being about four feet long, and consequently the body must have been 17 or 18 feet high. Upon the tomb was a plate of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>, whereon was engraved, “In this tomb lies the noble and puissant <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a> the chevalier Ricon de Vallmont, and his bones.” Platerus, a famous physician, declares, that he saw at Lucerne the true human bones of a subject which must have been at least 19 feet high. Valence in Dauphiné boasts of possessing the bones of the giant Bucart, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TYRANT">tyrant</a> of the Vivarais, who was slain with an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARROW">arrow</a> by the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNT">count</a> de Cabillon his vassal. The Dominicans had a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the shin bone, with the articulation of the knee, and his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> painted in fresco, with an inscription, showing that this giant was 22 feet and a half high, and that his bones were found in 1705, near the banks of the Morderi, a little river at the foot of the mountain of Crussol, upon which (<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRADITION">tradition</a> says) the giant dwelt. “<a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 11, 1613, some masons digging near the ruins of a castle in Dauphiné, in a field, which (by tradition) had long been called the giant’s field, at the depth of 18 feet discovered a brick tomb 30 feet long, 12 feet wide, and 8 feet high; on which was a gray stone, with the words Theotobochus Rex cut thereon. When the tomb was opened, they found a human skeleton entire, 25 feet and a half long, 10 feet wide across the shoulders, and five feet deep from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a> bone to the back. His teeth were about the size each of an ox’s foot, and his shin bone measured four feet.—Near Mazarino, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a>, in 1516, was found a giant 30 feet high; his head was the size of an hogshead, and each of his teeth weighed five ounces. Near Palermo, in the valley of Mazara, in Sicily, a skeleton of a giant 30 feet long was found, in the year 1548; and another of 33 feet high, in 1550; and many curious persons have preserved several of these gigantic bones. “The Athenians found near their <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> two famous skeletons, one of 34 and the other of 36 feet high. “At Totu, in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOHEMIA">Bohemia</a>, in 758, was found a skeleton, the head of which could scarce be encompassed by the arms of two men together, and whose legs, which they still keep in the castle of that city, were 26 feet long. The skull of the giant found in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-MACEDONIA">Macedonia</a>, September 1601, held 270 pounds of corn. “The celebrated Sir Hans Sloane, who treated this matter very learnedly, does not doubt these facts; but thinks the bones were those of elephants, whales, or other enormous animals. “Elephants bones may be shown for those of giants; but they can never impose on connoisseurs. Whales, which, by their immense bulk, are more proper to be substituted for the largest giants, have neither arms nor legs; and the head of that animal hath not the least resemblance to that of a man. If it be true, therefore, that a great <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of the gigantic bones which we have mentioned have been seen by anatomists, and by them have been reputed real human bones, the existence of giants is proved.” With regard to the credibility of all or any of these accounts, it is difficult to determine anything. If, in any castle of Bohemia, the bones of a man’s leg 26 feet in length are preserved, we have indeed a decisive <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of the existence of a giant in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPARISON">comparison</a> of whom most others would be but pigmies. Nor indeed could these bones be supposed to belong to an elephant: for an elephant itself would but be a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DWARF">dwarf</a> in comparison of such an enormous monster. But if these bones were really kept in any part of Bohemia, it seems strange that they have not been frequently visited, and particular descriptions of them given by the learned who have travelled into that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. It is certain, however, that there have been nations of men considerably exceeding the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> stature. Thus, all the Roman historians inform us, that the Gauls and Germans exceeded the Italians in size; and it appears that the Italians in those days were of much the same stature with the people of the present <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>. Among these northern nations, it is also probable, that there would be as great differences in stature as there are among the present <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a> of men. If that can be allowed, we may easily believe that some of the barbarians might be called giants, without any great impropriety. Of this superiority of size, indeed, the historian Florus gives a notable instance in Teutobochus, above mentioned, king of the Teutones: who being defeated and taken prisoner by Marius, was carried in triumph before him at Rome, when his head reached above the trophies that were carried in the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESSION">procession</a>. But whether these accounts are credited or not, we are very certain, that the stature of the human body is by no means absolutely fixed. We ourselves are a kind of giants in comparison of the Laplanders; nor are these the most <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DIMINUTIVE">diminutive</a> people to be found upon the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>. The Abbé la <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAPPE">Chappe</a>, in his journey into <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SIBERIA">Siberia</a> in order to observe the last transit of Venus, passed through a village inhabited by people called Wotiacks. Wottacks, neither men nor women of whom were above four feet high. The accounts of the Patagonians also, which cannot be entirely discredited, render it very probable, that somewhere in South <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a> there is a race of people very considerably exceeding the common size of mankind, and consequently that we cannot altogether discredit the relations of giants handed <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to us by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> authors; though what <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> we ought to give them is not easy to be determined. See <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATAGONIA">Patagonia</a>. Rebel Giants, in ancient <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MYTHOLOGY">mythology</a>, were the sons of Cælus and Terra. According to <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-HESIOD">Hesiod</a>, they sprang from the blood of the wound which Cælus received from his son <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SATURN">Saturn</a>, and Hyginus calls them sons of Tartarus and Terra. They are represented as men of uncommon stature, with strength proportioned to their gigantic size. Some of them, as Cottus, Briareus, and Gyges, had each 50 heads and 100 arms, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERPENTS">serpents</a> instead of legs. They were of a terrible aspect, their <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> hung loose about their shoulders, and their <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEARD">beard</a> was suffered to grow unmolested. Pallene and its neighbourhood was the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of their residence. The defeat of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TITANS">Titans</a>, to whom they were nearly related, incensed them against <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a>, and they all conspired to dethrone him. Accordingly they reared Mount Ossa upon Pelion, and Olympus upon Ossa; and from thence attacked the gods with huge rocks, some of which fell into the sea and became <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>, and others fell on the earth and formed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>. Jupiter summoned a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of the gods; when being informed that it was necessary to obtain the assistance of some mortal, he by the advice of Pallas called up his son Hercules; and with the aid of this hero he exterminated the giants Enceladus, Polybotes, Alcyon, Porphyron, the two sons of Alcæus, Epialtes, Othus, Eurytus, Clytius, Tithys, Pallas, Hippolitus, Agrius, Thoon, and Typhon; the last of whom it was more difficult to vanquish than all the others. Jupiter having thus gained a complete victory, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> the rebels down to Tartarus, where they were to receive the full <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> of their enormous crimes: according to the accounts of some of the poets, he buried them alive under Mount Ætna and different islands. Giants Causeway, a vast collection of basaltic pillars in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Antrim, on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>. See Basaltes. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> causeway consists of a most regular arrangement of many hundred thousands of columns of a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> kind of rock, very hard; almost all of them are of a pentagonal figure, but so closely and compactly situated on their sides, though perfectly distinct from top to bottom, that scarce any thing can be introduced between them. The columns are of an unequal height and breadth; some of the highest, visible above the surface of the strand, and at the foot of the impending angular precipice, may be about 20 feet; they do not exceed this height, at least none of the principal arrangement. How deep they are fixed in the strand, was never yet discovered. This grand arrangement extends nearly 200 yards, visible at low water; how far beyond is uncertain: from its declining appearance, however, at low water, it is probable it does not extend under water to a distance anything equal to what is seen above. The breadth of the principal causeway, which runs out in one <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> range of columns, is, in general, from 20 to 30 feet; at one place or two it may be nearly 40 for a few yards. In this account are excluded the broken and scattered pieces of the same kind of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a>, that are detached from the sides of the grand causeway, as they do not appear to have ever been contiguous to the principal arrangement, though they have frequently been taken into the width: which has been the cause of such wild and dissimilar representations of this causeway, which different accounts have exhibited. The highest part of this causeway is the narrowest, at the very foot of the impending cliff from whence the whole projects, where, for four or five yards, it is not above ten or fifteen feet wide. The columns of this narrow part incline from a perpendicular a little to the westward, and form a slope on their tops, by the very unequal height of the columns on the two sides, by which an ascent is made at the foot of the cliff, from the head of one <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLUMN">column</a> to the next above, gradually, to the top of the great causeway, which, at the distance of half a dozen yards from the cliff, obtains a perpendicular position, and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LOWERING">lowering</a> in its general height, widens to about 20 or between 20 and 30 feet, and for 100 yards nearly is always above water. The tops of the columns for this length being nearly of an equal height, they form a grand and singular parade, that may be easily walked on, rather inclining to the water's edge. But from high water mark, as it is perpetually washed by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEATING">beating</a> surges on every return of the tide, the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLATFORM">platform</a> lowers considerably, and becomes more and more uneven, so as not to be walked on but with the greatest care. At the distance of 150 yards from the cliff, it turns a little to the east for 20 or 30 yards, and then sinks into the sea. The figure of these columns is almost unexceptionally pentagonal, or composed of five sides; there are but very few of any other figure introduced: some few there are of three, four, and six sides, but the generality of them are five-sided, and the spectator must look very nicely to find any of a different construction: yet what is very extraordinary, and particularly curious, there are not two columns in ten thousand to be found, that either have their sides equal among themselves, or whose figures are alike. Nor is the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> of these columns or pillars less deserving the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> of the curious spectator. They are not of one <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> stone in an upright position; but composed of several short lengths, curiously joined, not with flat surfaces, but articulated into each other like <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALL">ball</a> and socket, or like the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JOINTS">joints</a> in the vertebrae of some of the larger kind of fish, the one end at the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOINT">joint</a> having a cavity, into which the convex end of the opposite is exactly fitted. This is not visible, but by disjoining the two stones. The depth of the concavity or convexity is generally about three or four inches. And what is still farther remarkable of the joint, the convexity, and the correspondent concavity, is not conformed to the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> angular figure of the column, but exactly round, and as large as the size or diameter of the column will admit; and consequently as the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a> of these columns are in general extremely unequal, the circular edges of the joint are seldom coincident with more than two or three sides of the pentagon, and from the edge of the circular part of the joint to the exterior sides and angles they are quite plain. It is still Giants still farther very remarkable, likewise, that the articulations of those joints are frequently <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INVERTED">inverted</a>; in some the concavity is upwards, in others the reverse. This occasions that variety and mixture of concavities and convexities on the tops of the columns, which is observable throughout the platform of this causeway, yet without any discoverable <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> or regularity with respect to the number of either. The length also of these particular stones, from joint to joint, is various: in general, they are from 18 to 24 inches long; and, for the most part, longer toward the bottom of the columns than nearer the top, and the articulation of the joints something deeper. The size or diameter likewise of the columns is as different as their length and figure; in general, they are from 15 to 20 inches in diameter. There are really no traces of uniformity or design discovered throughout the whole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMBINATION">combination</a>, except in the form of the joint, which is invariably by an articulation of the convex into the concave of the piece next above or below it; nor are there any traces of a finishing in any part, either in height, length, or breadth, of this curious causeway. If there is here and there a smooth top to any of the columns above water, there are others just by, of equal height, that are more or less convex or concave, which show them to have been joined to pieces that have been washed, or by other means taken off. And undoubtedly those parts that are always above water have, from time to time, been made as even as might be; and the remaining surfaces of the joints must naturally have been worn smoother by the constant friction of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a> and walking, than where the sea, at every tide, is beating upon it and continually removing some of the upper stones and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPOSING">exposing</a> fresh joints. And farther, as these columns preserve their diameters from top to bottom, in all the exterior ones, which have two or three sides exposed to view, the same may with reason be inferred of the interior columns whose tops only are visible. Yet what is very extraordinary, and equally curious, in this phenomenon, is, that notwithstanding the universal dissimilitude of the columns, both as to their figure and diameter, and though perfectly distinct from top to bottom, yet is the whole arrangement so closely combined at all <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">points</a>, that hardly a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KNIFE">knife</a> can be introduced between them either on the sides or angles. The cliffs at a great distance from the causeway, especially in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> to the eastward, exhibit at many places the same kind of columns, figured and jointed in all respects like those of the grand causeway: some of them are seen near to the top of the cliff, which in general, in these bays to the east and west of the causeway, is near 300 feet in height; others again are seen about midway, and at different elevations from the strand. A very considerable exposure of them is seen in the very bottom of the bay to the eastward, near a hundred rods from the causeway, where the earth has evidently fallen away from them upon the strand, and exhibits a most curious arrangement of many of these pentagonal columns, in a perpendicular position, supporting, in appearance, a cliff of different <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STRATA">strata</a> of earth, clay, rock, &c. to the height of 130 feet or more, above. Some of these columns are between 30 and 40 feet high, from the top of the sloping <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANK">bank</a> below them; and, being longest in the middle of the arrangement, shortening on either <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> in view, they have obtained the appellation of organs, from a rude likeness in this particular to the exterior or frontal tubes of that <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a>; and as there are few broken pieces on the strand near it, it is probable that the outside range of columns that now appears is really the original exterior line, to the seaward, of this collection. But how far they extend internally into the bowels of the incumbent cliff, is unknown. The very substance, indeed, of that part of the cliff which projects to a point, between the two bays on the east and west of the causeway, seems composed of this kind of materials; for besides the many pieces that are seen on the sides of the cliff that circulate to the bottom of the bays, particularly the eastern side, there is, at the very point of the cliff, and just above the narrow and highest part of the causeway, a long collection of them seen, whose heads or tops just appearing without the sloping bank, plainly show them to be in an oblique position, and about half way between the perpendicular and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HORIZONTAL">horizontal</a>. The heads of these, likewise, are of mixed surfaces, convex and concave, and the columns evidently appear to have been removed from their original upright, to their present inclining or oblique position, by the sinking or falling of the cliff.

GIBBET

Pages 768-768
or Gibbet, a machine in manner of a gallows, whereon notorious criminals, after execution, are hung in irons or chains, as spectacles in terrorem. See GALLOWS.—The word in French, gibet, properly denotes what we call gallows: it is supposed to come originally from the Arabic gibel, “mount or elevation of ground;” by reason gibets are usually placed on hills or eminences.

GIBBON

Pages 768-769

EDWARD, a historian of distinguished eminence, was born at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PUTNEY">Putney</a> in the year 1737. He was the son of a <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> of fortune and family distinction, who sat as a member in two separate parliaments. Edward when a boy, was of such an extremely delicate <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> that his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> was frequently despaired of. When at the school of Westminster, his progress was often retarded by repeated shocks of bad <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a>. After being for a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> under the management of the best medical practitioners, his constitution was radically changed for the better, which induced his father to <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> him in Magdalen <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> as a gentleman <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMONER">commoner</a>, that he might be pushed into manly acquisitions. This was <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIOR">prior</a> to the completing of his fifteenth year. Before this time his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">reading</a> had been of such a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> as to store his mind with much valuable historical knowledge, although his grammatical and philosophical knowledge at this time was not so extensive as that of some others at the same <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> of life. He says of himself; I arrived at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a> with a stock of erudition that might have puzzled a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a>, and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a> of which a school-boy would have been ashamed. Under such circumstances he was but ill prepared to receive the benefits of an university <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>, and this was no doubt the reason why he exclaimed so bitterly against the public and private instructions at Oxford. He was fond of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLEMICAL">polemical</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a> from his infancy, and during his leisure moments he turned his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>, when farther advanced, to the celebrated controversy between Papists and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a>; and as he had not then acquired talents sufficient to enable him to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMBAT">combat</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ERROR">error</a> and defend the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>, he fell a victim to the sophistry of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of Rome. His father, with a view to reclaim him from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> of what he considered as the most destructive of all errors, sent him to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAUSANNE">Lausanne</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWITZERLAND">Switzerland</a>, and put him under the care of Mr Pavilliard, a clergyman of the Calvinistic persuasion. This gentleman called his pupil Edward, "A little thin <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, with a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> head, disputing, and urging with the greatest ability, all the best arguments that had ever been used in favour of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPERY">Popery</a>." The masterly exertions of Mr Pavilliard, who had to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> with a young <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> reason and matured reflection, accomplished the recantation of Mr Gibbon, and he received the sacrament in the Protestant church on the 25th of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a> 1754. At Lausanne, too, he made <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> progress in many branches of knowledge which he had hitherto neglected, and acquired a regular <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HABIT">habit</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a>. He became <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of the French and Latin languages, and was a profound logician. He gave full scope to the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> of reading excellent authors, which was his ruling <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PASSION">passion</a>. He did not appear fond of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a>, and therefore soon relinquished the study of them. At Lausanne he fell in love with a young lady, the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of a village clergyman; but he was frustrated in his hopes, and the lady became afterwards the wife of the celebrated Necker. On his return home in April 1758, his father received him with every mark of tenderness and affection, and his mother-in-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a> found means to conciliate his good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> and his confidence. It is a singular circumstance that he should have taken a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, a profession, one would have imagined, for which he was very ill calculated. Indeed he soon evinced the truth of this, for his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TENT">tent</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> were frequently encumbered with the odd furniture of Greek and Latin authors. On the event of peace he resigned his commission, and paid a visit to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> in the year 1763, where he resided a few months, and afterwards went to Lausanne, where he remained about a year, in order to prepare for a journey into <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, which he accomplished in 1765. He thus speaks on the occasion of his entering Rome: "After a sleepless night, I trod, with a lofty step, the ruins of the forum; each memorable spot, where <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROMULUS">Romulus</a> stood, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Tully spoke, or Caesar fell, was at once present to my eye; and several days of intoxication were lost or enjoyed before I could descend to a cool and minute <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVESTIGATION">investigation</a>." On the 15th of October, he informs us, the idea of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> the decline and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> of Rome first came into his mind, when the bare-footed friars were singing vespers in the temple of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a>. In the year 1770 Mr Gibbon lost his father, and succeeded to an estate which was very much involved; yet he considered his circumstances as very well adapted to the great and extensive <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> he had undertaken to accomplish, which in his own opinion he had probably never finished, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he had been either poorer or richer than he was. He had an extensive circle of acquaintance in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, but the time necessarily devoted to their <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>, he made up by early rising and intense application. In the year 1774 he was chosen member of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> for the borough of Liskeard, by the influence of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Elliot, which threatened to give his studies a very serious interruption. He sat eight years in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of commons without having the courage so much as once to open his mouth, notwithstanding he was such an elegant writer. When the first volume of his "Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire," made its appearance in 1776, it met with a greater degree of applause than he expected; but by no praise was he so highly gratified as by that which the two great historians of Scotland, Hume and Robertson, bestowed upon him. For his two chapters which relate to the spread of Christianity he met with many antagonists, to whom he made no reply but to a Mr Davis, which was considered as a masterpiece. There can be no doubt that Gibbon was a real enemy to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVELATION">revelation</a> in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DISGUISE">disguise</a> of a believer, a conduct not so abominable as at first sight may appear, so long as penal laws exist against an open <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DECLARATION">declaration</a> of opinion. Soon after the publication of the first volume of his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, he paid another visit to Paris, and did not appear to be in much haste to complete his extensive work. In 1781, however, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> and third volumes of his history were given to the world; and although in the estimation of many competent judges they were inferior to the first, they still were allowed to possess sufficient merit to support his reputation. Having lost his seat for Liskeard, the influence of ministry brought him in as representative for Lymington, and on the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISSOLUTION">dissolution</a> of Lord <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a>'s ministry, he lost his office as one of the lords of trade, which was a serious diminution of his income. He again determined to visit his favourite Lausanne, where he completed the remaining volumes of his history; but when the revolutionary mania began to rage on the continent, he quitted Lausanne, and sought for an <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASYLUM">asylum</a> in England. He mortally hated innovations of every kind, whether necessary or not, as appears from the following exclamation: "I beg leave to subscribe my assent to Mr Burke's creed on the revolution of France. I admire his eloquence, I approve his politics, I adore his chivalry, and can almost excuse his reverence for church establishments." During his consoling visit to Lord <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SHEFFIELD">Sheffield</a>, who had met with a trying <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> loss, his attention was called to the rapid progress of a distemper which had subsisted for about 30 years. A mortification at last ensued, which terminated his existence on the 16th of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 1794, in the 67th year of his <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>. Mr Gibbon gives himself a character which is perhaps pretty near the truth. "I am endowed with a cheerful temper, a moderate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSIBILITY">sensibility</a>, and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> disposition to repose rather than to <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTIVITY">activity</a>: some mischievous appetites and habits have perhaps been corrected by <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> or time. The love of study supplies each <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>, each <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a>, with a perpetual source of independent and rational <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>." Mr Gibbon possessed the manners and sentiments of a gentleman in an eminent degree; he was easy in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>, of which he was extremely fond, and beloved by all who had the pleasure of intimately knowing him.

GIBBOS

Pages 770-770

in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> used in reference to the enlightened parts of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOON">moon</a>, whilst she is moving from the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> to the full, and from the full to the last quarter; for all that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> the dark <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> appears horned <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FALCATED">falcated</a>; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> one hunched out, convex, or gibbous.

GIBBOUS

Pages 769-770

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> in Medicine, denoting any protuberance <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> convexity of the body, as a person hunched or hump-backed. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INFANTS">Infants</a> are more subject to gibbosity than adults, and it oftener proceeds from <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> than internal causes. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a>, blow, or the like, frequently thus distorts the tender <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONES">bones</a> of infants. When it proceeds from an internal cause, it is generally from a relaxation of the ligaments that sustain the spine, or a caries of its vertebrae; though the spine may be infected forward, and the vertebrae thrown out by a too strong and repeated <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTION">action</a> of the abdominal muscles. This, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> not timely redressed, grows up and fixes as the bones harden, till in adults it is totally irretrievable: but when the disorder is recent, and the person young, there are hopes of a cure. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> method is by a machine of pasteboard, wood, or <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-STEEL">steel</a>, which is made to press principally on the gibbous <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a>; and this by <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> wearing may set all <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a>. The surgeons, however, have a different <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a>, which they call a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a>, much more efficacious, though not quite so convenient in the wearing. By the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of this, the parts are always prevented from growing any worse, and are often cured. During the application of these assistances, the parts should be at times rubbed with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUNGARY">Hungary</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, spirit of lavender, or the like, and defended with a strengthening <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLASTER">plaster</a>.

GIBEAH

Pages 770-770

a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> in the tribe of Benjamin, lying <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a> about 20 <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> 30 furlongs, and built upon a hill, as its name imports.—This city gave birth to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAUL">Saul</a>, the first <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of Israel, for which reason it is frequently called Gibeah of Saul, or Gibeah the native <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of Saul.

GIBELINS

Pages 770-770
or GIBELLINS, a famous faction in Italy, opposite to another called the Guelphs. Those two factions ravaged and laid waste Italy for a long series of years; so that the history of that country, for the space of two centuries, is no more than a detail of their mutual violences and slaughters. The Gibelins stood for the emperor against the pope: but concerning their origin and the reason of their names we have but a very obscure account. According to the generality of authors, they rose about the year 1240, upon the emperor Frederick II.'s being excommunicated by Pope Gregory IX. Other writers maintain, that the two factions arose ten years before, though still under the same pope and emperor. But the most probable opinion is that of Maimbourg, who says, that the two factions of Guelphs and Gibelins arose from a quarrel between two ancient and illustrious houses on the confines of Germany, that of the Henries of Gibeling, and that of the Guelphs of Adorf.

GIBEON

Pages 770-770

a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> seated on an eminence about 40 furlongs from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a> northward, and not far from the city of Gibeah. See GEBA. This was the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> city of the Gibeonites, who took the advantage of Joshua's oath, and of that which the elders of Israel likewise swore to them, upon an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> representation which they made of their belonging to a very remote <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, and their desire of making an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLIANCE">alliance</a> with the Hebrews. Joshua (ix. 3, 4, et seq.) and the elders inconsiderately entered into a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEAGUE">league</a> with these people; but soon discovered their mistake. Upon this, sending for the Gibeonites, they reproached them with their fraud; and without revoking the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROMISE">promise</a> which they had made to them, of giving them their lives, they condemned them to carry wood and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABERNACLE">tabernacle</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a>, as slaves and captives taken in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>; in which state of servitude they remained till the ruin and entire <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DISPERSION">dispersion</a> of the Jewish <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>. The Gibeonites were descended from the Hivites, the old inhabitants of that country, and possessed four cities, whereof Gibeon was the capital. The cities were Chephirath, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEEROTH">Beeroth</a>, Kirjathjearim, and Gibeon, Josh. ix. 17. These cities were afterwards given to the tribe of Benjamin, except Kirjathjearim, which fell to the tribe of Judah. The Gibeonites <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> ever after subject to those burdens which Joshua had imposed on them, and were very faithful to the Israelites.

GIBLETS

Pages 770-770

the offals <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> entrails of a goose; including the heart and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIVER">liver</a>, with the feet, gizzard, &c. The word is supposed to be formed of goblets, from the French godeau, "mouthful."—Giblets make a considerable article in cookery: they boil giblets, stew giblets, make ragouts of giblets, giblet pies, &c.

GIBRALTAR

Pages 770-782

a famous promontory, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> rather <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PENINSULA">peninsula</a>, of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, lying in N. Lat. 36. 6. W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 5. 17. To the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> it was known by the name of Calpe, and was also called one of the Pillars of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERCULES">Hercules</a>; by the Arabsians it is called Gebel Tarek, that is, "the mount of Tarek," from Tarek, the name of the Saracen general who conquered Spain in the beginning of the eighth century. The whole is an immense rock, rising perpendicularly about 440 yards, measuring from <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> to south about two English miles, but not above one in breadth from east to west. The town lies along the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> on the west side of the mountain on a declivity; by which, generally speaking, the rains <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> through it, and keep it clean. The old town was considerably larger than the new. Many of the streets are narrow and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a>: the buildings are of different materials; some of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a> out of the quarries, some of a factitious or <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> stone, and a few of brick. The people are supplied with fresh <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a> chiefly from the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of Barbary, with fruit, roots, and vegetables of all sorts from thence, or from their own gardens. Besides what is properly called the town, there are several spacious and commodious public edifices erected; such as <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BARRACKS">barracks</a> for the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a>, with apartments for their officers, magazines of different kinds, storehouses for provisions, &c. The inhabitants, exclusive of the British subjects dependent on the garrison, or who reside there from other motives, consist of some Spaniards, a few Portuguese, a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of Genoese, about as many Jews, and even some Moors; making in the whole a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> of twelve thousand persons, without reckoning the garrison; though some make them much fewer. This town may be said to have two ports; the first lying to the north, and is proper only for small vessels; the other is very commodious for <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> vessels, and has a fine stone quay. The bay is very beautiful and capacious, being in breadth about five miles, and in length eight or <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a>, with several small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> running into it. It is very advantageous to the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>. There is no ground to be found in the middle of it at one hundred fathoms depth, so that a squadron may <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> there in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> safety; the breezes from it are very refreshing; and it contributes likewise likewise to the subsistence of the inhabitants by supplying them with plenty of fish. The strait of Gibraltar, through which the ocean passes into the Mediterranean, thereby dividing <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> from <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, runs from west to east about 13 leagues. In this strait there are three remarkable promontories or capes on the Spanish side, and as many opposite to them on the Barbary side. The first of these, on the side of Spain, is <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a> Trafalgar, opposite to which is Cape Spartal; and in the neighbourhood of this stood the fortress of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TANGIER">Tangier</a>, once in the possession of the British. The next on the Spanish side is Tarifa; and opposite it lies Malabata, near the town of Alcassar, where the straits are about five leagues <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>. Lastly, Gibraltar facing the mountain of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABYLA">Abyla</a>, near the fortress and town of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CEUTA">Ceuta</a>, which make the eastern entry of the straits. This important fortress seems to have been first particularly noticed as a place of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> in the year 712. At that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> the general of the caliph Al Walid landed with an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> of 12,000 men on the isthmus between Mount Calpe and the continent; and that he might secure an intercourse with Africa, ordered a castle to be built on the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FACE">face</a> of that hill. <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">Part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> still remains; and, from an inscription discovered above the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> gate, appears to have been finished in 725.
