The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>, in general, upon the mountain of Gibraltar is but thinly sown; and in many parts that thin covering has been washed off by the heavy autumnal rains, which have left the superficies of the rock, for a considerable extent, bare and open to inspection. In those situations, an observing eye may trace the effects of the slow, but constant, decomposition of the rock, caused by its exposure to the air, and the corrosion of sea-salts, which, in the heavy gales of easterly winds, are deposited with the spray on every part of the mountain. Those uncovered parts of the mountain rock also expose to the eye a phenomenon worthy of some attention, as it tends clearly to demonstrate, that, however high the surface of this rock may now be elevated above the level of the sea, it has once been the bed of agitated waters. This phenomenon is to be observed in many parts of the rock, and is constantly found in the beds of torrents. It consists of pot-like holes, of various sizes, hollowed out of the solid rock, and formed apparently by the attrition of gravel or pebbles, set in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> by the rapidity of rivers or currents in the sea. "Upon the west side of the mountain, towards its base, some strata occur, which are <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HETEROGENEOUS">heterogeneous</a> to the mountain rock: the first, or highest, forms the segment of a circle; its convex side is towards the mountain, and it slopes also in that direction. This stratum consists of a number of thin beds; the outward one, being the thinnest, is in a state of decomposition, and is mouldering down into a blackish <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROWN">brown</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FERRUGINOUS">ferruginous</a> coloured earth. The beds, inferior to this, progressively increase in breadth to 17 inches, where the stratification rests upon a rock of an argillaceous nature. "This last bed, which is 17 inches thick, consists of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTZ">quartz</a> of a blackish blue <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, in the septa or cracks of which are found fine quartz crystals, colourless, and perfectly transparent. These crystals are composed of 18 planes, disposed in hexangular columns, terminated at both extremities by hexangular pyramids. The largest of those that Major Imrie saw did not exceed one-fourth of an inch in length: They, in general, adhere to the rock by the sides of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLUMN">column</a>, but are detached without difficulty. Their great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of transparency has obtained them the name of Gibraltar diamonds. "In the perpendicular fissures of the rock, and in some of the caverns of the mountain (all of which afford evident proofs of their former communication with the fissures of surface), a calcareous concretion is found, of a reddish-brown ferruginous colour, with an earthy fracture, and considerable induration, inclosing the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONES">bones</a> of various animals, some of which have the appearance of being human. These bones are of various sizes, and lie in all directions, intermixed with shells of snails, fragments of the calcareous rock, and particles of spar; all of which materials are still to be seen in their natural uncombined states, partially scattered over the surface of the mountain. These have been swept, by heavy rains at different periods, from the surface into the situations above described, and having remained for a long series of years in those places of rest, exposed to the permeating action of water, have become enveloped in, and cemented by, the calcareous matter which it deposits. "The bones, in this composition, have not the smallest appearance of being petrified; and if they have undergone any change, it is more like that of calcination than that of petrifaction, as the most solid parts of them generally admit of being cut and scraped down with the same ease as chalk. "Bones combined in such concretions are not peculiar to Gibraltar: they are found in such large quantities in the country of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DALMATIA">Dalmatia</a> and upon its coasts, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHERSO">Cherso</a> and Osero, that some naturalists have been induced to go so far as to assert, that there has been a regular stratum of such matter in that country, and that its present broken and interrupted appearance has been caused by earthquakes, or other convulsions, experienced in that part of the globe. But, of late years, a traveller (Abbé Alberto Fortis) has given a minute <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of the concretion in which the bones are found in that country: And by his account it appears, that with regard to situation, composition, and colour, Gibraltar, colour, it is perfectly similar to that found at Gibraltar. By his description, it also appears that the two mountain rocks of Gibraltar and Dalmatia consist of the same <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of calcareous stone; from which it is to be presumed, that the concretions in both have been formed in the same manner and about the same periods. "Perhaps if the fissures and caves of the rocks of Dalmatia were still more minutely examined, their former communications with the surface might yet be traced, as in those described above; and, in that case, there would be at least a strong <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a>, that the materials of the concretions of that country have been brought together by the same accidental cause which has probably collected those found in the caverns of Gibraltar. Major Imrie traced, in Gibraltar, this concretion, from the lowest part of a deep perpendicular fissure, up to the surface of the mountain. As it approached to the surface, the concretion became less firmly combined, and, when it had no covering of the calcareous rock, a small degree of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADHESION">adhesion</a> only remained, which was evidently produced by the argillaceous earth, in its composition, having been moistened by <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">rain</a> and baked by the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>. "The depth at which these materials had been penetrated by that proportion of stalactitical matter, capable of giving to the concretion its greatest adhesion and solidity, he found to vary according to its situation, and to the quantity of matter to be combined. In fissures, narrow and contracted, he found the concretion possessing a great degree of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HARDNESS">hardness</a> at six feet from the surface; but in other situations more extended, and where a larger quantity of the materials had been accumulated, he found it had not gained its greatest degree of adhesion at double that depth. In one of the caves, where the mass of concretion is of considerable size, he perceived it to be divided into different beds, each bed being covered with a crust of the stalactitical spar, from one inch to an inch and a half in thickness, which seems to indicate, that the materials have been carried in at various periods, and that those periods have been very remote from each other. "At Rosia bay, upon the west side of Gibraltar, this concretion is found in what has evidently been a cavern, originally formed by huge unshapely masses of the rock which have tumbled in together. The fissure, or cavern, formed by the disruption and subsidence of those masses, has been entirely filled up with the concretion, and is now exposed to full view by the outward mass having dropped down in consequence of the encroachments of the sea. It is to this spot that strangers are generally led to examine the phenomenon; and the composition having here attained to its greatest degree of hardness and solidity, the hasty observer, seeing the bones inclosed in what has so little the appearance of having been a vacuity, examines no further, but immediately adopts the idea of their being incased in the solid rock. The communication from this former chasm, to the surface from which it has received the materials of the concretion, is still to be traced in the face of the rock, but its opening is at present covered by the base of the line wall of the garrison. Here bones are found that are apparently human; and those of them that appear to be of the legs, arms, and vertebrae of the back, are scattered among others of various kinds and sizes, even down to the smallest bones of small birds. Major Imrie found here the complete jaw-bone of a sheep; it contained its full complement of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a>, the enamel of which was perfect, and its whiteness and lustre in no degree impaired. In the hollow parts of some of the large bones was contained a minute <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CRYSTALLIZATION">crystallization</a> of pure and colourless calcareous spar; but, in most, the interior part consisted of a sparry crust of a reddish colour, scarcely in any degree transparent. "At the northern extremity of the mountain, the concretion is generally found in perpendicular fissures. The miners there employed upon the fortifications, in excavating one of those fissures, found at a great depth from the surface, two skulls, which were supposed to be human; but, to the Major, one of them, if not both, appeared to be too small for the human species. The bone of each was perfectly firm and solid; from which it is to be presumed, that they were in a state of maturity before they were inclosed in the concretion. Had they appertained to very young children, perhaps the bone would have been more porous, and of a less firm texture. The probability is, that they belonged to a species of monkey, which still continues to inhabit, in considerable numbers, those parts of the rock which are to us inaccessible. "This concretion varies, in its composition, according to the situation in which it is found. At the extremity of Prince's Lines, high in the rock which looks towards Spain, it is found to consist only of a reddish calcareous earth, and the bones of small birds cemented thereby. The rock around this spot is inhabited by a number of hawks, that, in the breeding season, nestle here and rear their young; the bones in this concretion are probably the remains of the food of those birds. At the base of the rock, below King's Lines, the concretion consists of pebbles of the prevailing calcareous rock. In this concretion, at a very considerable depth under the surface, was found the under parts of a glass bottle, uncommonly shaped, and of great thickness; the colour of the glass of a dark green." The subterranean galleries are very extensive, and pierce the rock in several places and in various directions, and at various degrees of elevation; all of them have a communication with each other, either by flights of steps cut in the rock, or by wooden stairs where the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> are required to be very perpendicular. "The centinels may now be relieved during a siege from one post to another in perfect safety; whereas, previously to the constructing of these galleries a vast number of men were killed by the Spaniards while marching to their several stations. The width of these galleries is about twelve feet, their height about fourteen. The rock is broken through in various places, both for the purpose of giving <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> and for placing the guns to bear on the enemy. In different parts there are spacious recesses, capable of accommodating a considerable number of men. To these recesses they give names, such as St Patrick's Chamber, St George's Hall, &c. The whole of these singular structures have been formed out of the solid rock by <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLASTING">blasting</a> with gunpowder. Through the politeness of an officer on duty, a place called Smart's Reservoir was opened for our inspection, which is a great curiosity, and not generally permitted to be shewn. It is a spring at a considerable depth in the body of the rock, and is above 700 feet above the level of the sea; we descended into the cavern that contains

GIBSON

Pages 782-784

Richard, an English painter, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DWARF">Dwarf</a>, was originally page to a lady at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MORTLAKE">Mortlake</a>; who, observing that his genius led him to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a>, had the generosity to get him instructed in the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RUDIMENTS">rudiments</a> of that <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a>. He devoted himself to Sir <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> Lely's manner, and copied his pictures to admiration, especially his portraits: his paintings in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> colours were also esteemed. He was in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> favour with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> I. who made him his page of the back stairs; and he had the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> to instruct in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a> and Queen <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a> when they were princesses. He married one Mrs Anne Shepherd, who was also a dwarf; on which occasion <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> Charles I. honoured their <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> with his presence, and gave away the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRIDE">bride</a>. Mr Waller wrote a poem on this occasion, entitled "The Marriage of the Dwarfs;" in which are these <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a>: <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">Design</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> chance makes others wive, But <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> did this <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MATCH">match</a> contrive; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EVE">Eve</a> might as well have <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADAM">Adam</a> fled, As she deny'd her little <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BED">bed</a> To him for whom heav'n seem'd to frame And <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> out this only dame." Mr Fenton, in his notes on this poem, observes that he had seen this couple painted by Sir Peter Lely; and that they were of an equal stature, each being three feet ten inches <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a>. They had <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> children, five of whom arrived at maturity; these were well proportioned, and of the usual standard of mankind. But what nature denied this couple in stature, she gave them in length of days: for Mr Gibson died in the 75th year of his <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>; and his wife, having survived him almost 20 years, died in 1709, aged 89. Gibson, Dr Edmund, bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, was born in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WESTMORELAND">Westmoreland</a>, in 1699. He applied himself early and vigorously to learning, and displayed his knowledge in several writings and translations, which recommended him to the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATRONAGE">patronage</a> of Archbishop Tenison. He was appointed <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> chaplain to his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRACE">Grace</a>; and we soon after find him rector of Lambeth, and archdeacon of Surry. Becoming thus a member of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONVOCATION">convocation</a>, he engaged in a controversy, which was carried on with great warmth by the members of both houses, and defended his <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATRON">patron</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a>, as <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">president</a>, in eleven pamphlets; he then formed and completed his more comprehensive scheme of the legal duties and rights of the English clergy, which was at length published under the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Codex Juris Ecclesiastici Anglicani, in folio. Archbishop Tennison dying in 1715, and Dr Wake bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LINCOLN">Lincoln</a> being made archbishop of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANTERBURY">Canterbury</a>, Dr Gibson succeeded the latter in the see of Lincoln, and in 1720 was promoted to the bishopric of London. He now not only governed his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a> with the most exact regularity, but by his great care promoted the spiritual affairs of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of England colonies in the West Indies. He was extremely jealous of the least of the privileges belonging to the church; and therefore, though he approved of the toleration of the Protestant Dissenters, he continually guarded against all the attempts made to procure a repeal of the corporation and test acts; in particular, his opposition to those licentious assemblies called masquerades, gave great umbrage at <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>, and effectually excluded him from all further favours. He spent the latter part of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINTING">printing</a> pastoral letters, visitation-charges, occasional sermons, and tracts against the prevailing immoralities of the age. His pastoral letters are justly esteemed as the most masterly productions against <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INFIDELITY">infidelity</a> and enthusiasm. His most celebrated <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, the Codex, has been already mentioned. His other publications are, 1. An edition of Drummond's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLEMO">Polemo</a> Middinia, and James V. of Scotland's Cantilenae Rusticae, with notes. 2. The Chronicon Saxonicum, with a Latin translation, and notes. 3. Reliquiae Spelmannianae, the posthumous works of Sir Henry Spelman, relating to the laws and antiquities of England. 4. An edition of Quintilian de Arte Oratoria, with notes. 5. An English translation of Camden's Britannia, with additions, two volumes folio: and, 6. A <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of small pieces, that have been collected together and printed in three volumes folio.—His intense application to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> impaired his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a>; notwithstanding which, he attained the age of 79. He expired in September 1748, after an episcopate of near 33 years.—With regard to Bishop Gibson's private life and character, he was in every respect a perfect economist. His abilities were so well adapted to discharge the duties of his sacred <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-FUNCTION">function</a>, that during the incapacity of Archbishop Wake, the transaction of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> affairs was committed to the bishop of London. He was a true friend to the established church and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, and as great an enemy to <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERSECUTION">persecution</a>. He was usually consulted by the most learned and exalted personages in church and state, and the greatest deference was paid to his judgment. He possessed the social virtues in an eminent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>; his beneficence was very extensive; and he had such generosity, rosity, that he freely gave two thousand five hundred pounds, left him by Dr Crow, who was once his chaplain, to Crow's own relations, who were very <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a>.

GIDEON

Pages 784-784

the son of Joash, of the tribe of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANASSEH">Manasseh</a>. He dwelt in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Ophrah; and had a very extraordinary call to deliver the Israelites from the oppression of the Midianites, to which they had become subject after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Barak and Deborah. Having effected their deliverance by supernatural aid, he was chosen judge of Israel in the year of the world 2759, and died in 2768. (See Judges, chap. vii. and viii.).

GIFT

Pages 784-784

Donum, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, is a conveyance which passeth either lands <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> goods; and is of a larger <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> than a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRANT">grant</a>, being applied to things moveable and immoveable; yet as to things immoveable, when taken strictly, it is applicable only to lands and tenements given in tail; but gift and grant are too often confounded. New Year's GIFTS, presents made on new year's <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>, as a token of the giver's good <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a>, as well as by way of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRESAGE">presage</a> of a happy year. This practice is very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a>, the origin of it among the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> being referred to Tatus <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of the Sabines, who reigned at Rome conjointly with <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROMULUS">Romulus</a>, and who having considered as a good <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OMEN">omen</a> a present of some sprigs of vervain gathered in a wood consecrated to Strema the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GODDESS">goddess</a> of strength, which he received on the first day of the new year, authorized this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> afterwards, and gave to these presents the name of Strema. However this may be, the Romans on that day celebrated a festival in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JANUS">Janus</a>, and paid their respects at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> to Juno; but they did not <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> it in idleness, lest they should become indolent during the rest of the year. They sent presents to one another of figs, dates, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONEY">honey</a>, &c. to show their friends that they wished them a happy and agreeable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. Clients, that is to say, those who were under the protection of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a>, carried presents of this kind to their patrons, adding to them a small piece of silver. Under Augustus, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENATE">senate</a>, the knights, and the people, presented such gifts to him, and in his absence deposited them in the Capitol. Of the succeeding princes some adopted this custom, and others abolished it, but it always <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> among the people. The early <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> condemned it, because it appeared to be a relic of Paganism, and a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a>; but when it began to have no other object than that of being a mark of veneration and esteem, the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> ceased to disapprove of it.

GIGGLEWICK

Pages 784-784

a town in the west riding of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORKSHIRE">Yorkshire</a>, half a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILE">mile</a> from <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">Settle</a>, stands on the river Ribble; where, at the foot of a mountain, is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>, the most noted in England for ebbing and flowing sometimes thrice in an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> subsides three <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> of a yard at the reflux, though the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> is 30 miles off. At this town is an eminent free <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAMMAR">grammar</a> school; and in the neighbourhood are dug up flags, slate, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>.

GILAN

Pages 784-784
or GHILAN, a considerable province of Persia, on the side of the Caspian sea, to the southwest. It is supposed to be the Hyrcania of the ancients. It is very agreeably situated, having the sea on one side and high mountains on the other; and there is no entering in but through narrow passes, which may easily be defended. The sides of the mountains are covered with many sorts of fruit trees, and in the highest parts of them there are deer, bears, wolves, leopards, and tygers; which last the Persians have a method of taming, and hunt with them as we do with dogs. Gilan is one of the most fruitful provinces of Persia, and produces abundance of silk, oil, wine, rice, and tobacco, besides excellent fruits. The inhabitants are brave, and of a better complexion than the other Indians, and the women are accounted extremely handsome. Resht is the capital town.

GILBERT

Pages 784-785

Sir Humphrey, a brave officer and skilful navigator, was born about the year 1539, in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVONSHIRE">Devonshire</a>, of an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> family. Though a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> son, he inherited a considerable fortune from his father. He was educated at <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ETON">Eton</a>, and afterwards at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>; where probably he did not continue <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a>. It seems he was intended to finish his studies in the Temple; but being introduced at <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> by his aunt Mrs Catharine Ashley, then in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a>'s <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>, he was diverted from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a>, and commenced soldier. Having distinguished himself in several <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> expeditions, particularly that to Newhaven in 1563, he was sent over to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a> to assist in suppressing a rebellion; where, for his signal services, he was made commander in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> and gover- nor of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUNSTER">Munster</a>, and knighted by the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEPUTY">deputy</a>, Sir Henry Sidney, on the first <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> of the year 1570. He returned soon after to England, where he married a rich heiress. Nevertheless, in 1572, he sailed with a squadron of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> ships to reinforce <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLONEL">Colonel</a> Morgan, who at that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> meditated the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RECOVERY">recovery</a> of Flushing. Probably on his return to England he resumed his cosmographical studies, to which he was naturally inclined; for, in the year 1576, he published his book on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-west passage to the East Indies; and as Martin Frobisher sailed in the same year, probably it was in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of this treatise. In 1578, he obtained from the queen a very ample patent, empowering him to discover and possess in North <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a> any lands then unsettled. He sailed to Newfoundland, but soon returned to England without success; nevertheless, in 1583, he embarked a second time with five ships, the largest of which put back an account of a contagious distemper on board. Our general landed on Newfoundland on the third of August, and on the fifth took possession of the harbour of St John's. By virtue of his patent he granted <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEASES">leases</a> to several people; but though none of them remained there at that time, they settled afterwards in consequence of these leases; so that Sir Humphrey deserves to be remembered as the real founder of the vast American empire. On the 20th of August he put to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> again, on board a small sloop; which on the 29th foundered in a hard <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-GALE">gale</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>. Thus perished Sir Humphrey Gilbert; a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of quick parts, a brave soldier, a good mathematician, a skilful navigator, and of a very enterprising genius. We learn also, that he was remarkable for his eloquence, being much admired for his patriotic speeches both in the English and Irish parliaments. He wrote "A discourse to prove a passage by the north-west to Cathaia and the East Indies," printed <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a> 1576." This treatise, which is a masterly performance, is preserved in Hakluyt's Collection of Voyages, vol. iii. p. ii. The style is superior to most, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> not to all, the writers of that <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>; and shows the author to have been a man of considerable <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">reading</a>. He mentions, at the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> of this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, another treatise on <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a>, which he intended to publish: it is probably lost.

GILBERTINES

Pages 785-785

an order of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a>, thus called from St Gilbert of Sempringham, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LINCOLN">Lincoln</a>, who founded the same about the year 1148: the monks of which observed the rule of St Augustine; and were accounted canons; and the nuns that of St Benedict. The founder of this order erected a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> rather two different ones, contiguous to each other, the one for men, the other for women, but parted by a very <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> wall. St Gilbert himself founded 13 monasteries of this order, viz. four for men alone, and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> for men and women together, which had in them 700 brethren and 1500 <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SISTERS">sisters</a>. At the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISSOLUTION">dissolution</a> there were about 25 houses of this order in England and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>.

GILBOA

Pages 785-785

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAMARIA">Samaria</a>, stretching out from west to east, on the confines of the half tribe of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANASSEH">Manasseh</a>, and of the tribe of Issachar, and to the south <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the valley of Jezreel; beginning westward at the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Jezreel, situated at the foot of these mountains, reaching almost quite to the Jordan, lying at the distance of six miles from Scythopolis. Famous for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAUL">Saul</a> and his son <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JONATHAN">Jonathan</a>, and the defeat of the Israelites by the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILISTINES">Philistines</a>.

GILCHRIST

Pages 785-785

Dr EBENEZER, an eminent Scots physician, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUMFRIES">Dumfries</a> in 1707. He began the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of medicine at <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a>, which he afterwards prosecuted at <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>. He obtained the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a> of medicine from the university of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHEIMS">Rheims</a>; and in the year 1732 he returned to the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATIVITY">nativity</a>, where he afterwards constantly resided, and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> the practice of medicine till his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. It may with <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> be said, that few physicians of the present century have exercised their profession in a manner more respectable <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> successful than Dr Gilchrist; and few have contributed more to the improvement of the healing art. Having engaged in business at an early <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> was wholly devoted to observation. Endowed by <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> with a judgment acute and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOLID">solid</a>, and a genius <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> and inventive, he soon distinguished himself by departing, in various important particulars, from established but unsuccessful modes of practice. Several of the improvements which he introduced have procured him <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> and deserved reputation both at home and abroad. His practice, in ordinary <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a>, was allowed to be judicious, and placed him <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> in the confidence and esteem of the inhabitants of that <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> where he lived. But his usefulness was not confined to his own neighbourhood. On many occasions he was consulted by <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> from the most distant parts of the country. In different collections are to be found several of his performances, which prove that he had something new and useful to offer upon every subject to which he applied himself. But those writings which do him the greatest <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> are two <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> dissertations on Nervous Fevers, in the Medical Essays and Observations published by a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a> in Edinburgh; and a treatise on the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">Sea</a> Voyages in Medicine, which first made its appearance in the year 1757, and was afterwards reprinted in 1771. By means of the former, the attention of physicians was first turned to a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of fever which is now found to prevail universally in this country; and the liberal use of wine, which he was the first among the moderns to recommend, has since been adopted in these fevers by the most judicious physicians of the present <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, and has probably contributed not a little to the success of their practice. His treatise on Sea Voyages <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">points</a> out their utility in various distempers, and particularly in consumptions; but <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> by no means confirms the observation, that there is now a prospect of our being able to employ a remedy in this untractable <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a> much more efficacious than any hitherto in use. Dr Gilchrist died in 1774.

GILDAS

Pages 785-786

surnamed the Wise, was born in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WALES">Wales</a> in the year 511. Where he was educated is uncertain; but it appears from his own writings that he was a monk. Some writers say that he went over to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>; others, that he visited France and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>. They agree however in asserting, that after his return to England he became a celebrated and most assiduous preacher of the gospel. Du <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PIN">Pin</a> says he founded a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a> at Venetia in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>. Gildas is the only British author of the sixth century whose works are printed; Gilding; they are therefore valuable on account of their antiquity, and as containing the only information we have concerning the times of which he wrote. His <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of Britain is, however, a flimsy performance, and his style obscure and inelegant.

GILDING

Pages 786-789

the art of spreading <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> covering a thing over with <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, either in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAF">leaf</a> or liquid. The art of gilding was not unknown among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, though it never arrived among them at the perfection to which the moderns have carried it. Pliny assures us, that the first gilding seen at Rome was after the destruction of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARTHAGE">Carthage</a>, under the censorship of Lucius Mummius, when they began to gild the ceilings of their <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a> and palaces; the Capitol being the first <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> on which this enrichment was bestowed. But he adds, that <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LUXURY">luxury</a> advanced on them so hastily, that in a little <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> you might see all, even private and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a> persons, gild the very walls, vaults, &c. of their houses. We need not doubt but they had the same method with us, of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEATING">beating</a> gold, and reducing it into leaves; though it should seem they did not carry it to the same height, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> it be true which Pliny relates, that they only made 750 leaves of four fingers <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> out of a whole ounce. Indeed he adds, that they could make more; that the thickest were called bracteae Prænestinae, by reason of a statue of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GODDESS">goddess</a> Fortune at Præneste gilt with such leaves; and that the thinner sort was called bracteae questoriae. The <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> gilders do also make <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of gold leaves of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> thicknesses; but there are some so fine, that a thousand do not weigh above four or five drachms. The thickest are used for gilding on <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> and other <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-METALS">metals</a>; and the thinnest on wood. But we have another advantage over the ancients in the manner of using or applying the gold; the secret of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, discovered of late ages, furnishes us with means of gilding works that shall endure all the injuries of time and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>, which to the ancients was impracticable.—They had no way to lay the gold on bodies that would not endure the fire but with whites of eggs or size, neither of which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> endure the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>; so that they could only gild such places as were sheltered from the moisture of the weather. The Greek called the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> on which they applied their gilding on wood leucophorum or leucophorum; which is described as a sort of glutinous <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPOUND">compound</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, serving in all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a> to make the gold stick and bear polishing. But the particulars of this earth, its <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, ingredients, &c. the antiquaries and naturalists are not agreed upon. The lustre and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> of gold have occasioned several inquiries and discoveries concerning the different methods of applying it to different substances. Hence the art of gilding is very extensive, and contains many particular operations and various management. A colour of gold is given by painting and by varnishings, without employing gold; but this is a false kind of gilding. Thus a very fine <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> colour is given to <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a> and to silver, by applying upon these metals a gold-coloured <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VARNISH">varnish</a>, which, being transparent, shows all the brilliancy of the metals beneath. Many ornaments of brass were varnished in this manner, which is called gold lacquering, to distinguish them from those which are really gilt. Silver leaves thus varnished are put upon <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>, which is then called gilt leather. See LAQUER. Amongst the false gilding may also be reckoned those which are made with thin leaves of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a> or brass, called Dutch leaf. In this manner are made all the kinds of what is called gilt <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>. In the true gilding, gold is applied to the surface of bodies. The gold intended for this purpose ought in general to be <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEAT">beat</a> into thin leaves, or otherwise divided into very fine parts. As metals cannot adhere well merely by contact to any but to other metallic substances, when gold is to be applied to the surface of some unmetallic body, that surface must be previously covered with some gluey and tenacious substance by which the gold shall be made to adhere. These substances are in general called sizes. Some of these are made of vegetable and animal glues, and others of oily, gluey, and drying matters. Upon them the leaves of gold are applied, and pressed <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> with a little cotton or a hare's foot; and when the whole is dry, the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> is to be finished and polished with a hard <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a>, called a dog's tooth, to give lustre. When the work is required to be capable of resisting <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">rain</a> or moisture, it ought to be previously covered with a composition of drying oil and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> ochre ground together; otherwise a water size may be used, which is prepared by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BOILING">boiling</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTINGS">cuttings</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARCHMENT">parchment</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> leather in water, and by mixing with this some chalk or whiting: several layers of this size must be laid upon the wood, and over these a layer of the same size mixed with yellow ochre. Lastly, Another mixture, called gold size, is to be applied above these; upon which the gold leaves are to be fixed. This gold size, the use of which is to make the gold leaf capable of being burnished, is composed of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOBACCO">tobacco</a>-pipe clay, ground with some ruddle or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK_LEAD"><a class="</a>xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, and tempered with a little tallow or oil of olives. The edges of glasses may be gilt by applying first a very thin coat of varnish, upon which the gold leaf is to be fixed; and when the varnish is hardened, may be burnished. This varnish is prepared by boiling powdered <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBER">amber</a> with linseed oil in a brass vessel to which a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VALVE">valve</a> is fitted, and by diluting the above solution with four or five times its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of oil of turpentine; and that it may dry sooner, it may be ground with some white lead. The method of applying gold upon metals is entirely different. The surface of the metal to be gilt is first metal to be cleaned; and then leaves are to be applied to it, which, by means of rubbing with a polished bloodstone, and a certain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>, are made to adhere perfectly well. In this manner silver leaf is fixed and burnished upon brass in the making of what is called French plate, and sometimes also gold leaf is burnished upon copper and upon iron. Gold is applied to metals in several other ways. One of these is by previously forming the gold into a paste or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMALGAM">amalgam</a> with <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERCURY">mercury</a>. In order to obtain a small amalgam of gold and mercury, the gold is first to be reduced into thin plates or grains, which are heated <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> hot, and thrown into mercury previously heated, till it begins to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SMOKE">smoke</a>. Upon stirring the mercury with an iron rod, the gold totally disappears. The proportion of mercury to gold is generally as six or eight to one. With this amalgam the surface of the metal to be gilded is to be covered; then a sufficient heat is to be applied to evaporate the mercury: and the gold is lastly to be burnished with a blood-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>. This method of gilding by amalgamation is chiefly used for gilding copper, or an alloy of copper, with a small portion of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZINC">zinc</a>, which more readily receives the amalgam; and is also preferable for its colour, which more resembles that of gold than the colour of copper. When the metal to be gilt is wrought or chased, it ought to be previously covered with quicksilver before the amalgam is applied, that this may be easier spread: but when the surface of the metal is plain, the amalgam may be applied directly to it. The quicksilver or amalgam is made to adhere to the metal by means of a little aquafortis, which is rubbed on the metallic surface at the same time, by which this surface is cleansed from any rust or tarnish which might prevent the union or <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADHESION">adhesion</a> of the metals. But the use of the nitrous acid in this operation is not, as is generally supposed, confined merely to cleanse the surface of the metal to be gilt from any rust or tarnish it may have acquired; but it also greatly facilitates the application of the amalgam to the surface of that metal, probably in the following manner: It first dissolves <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the mercury of the amalgam; and when this solution is applied to the copper, this latter metal having a stronger <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFFINITY">affinity</a> for nitrous acid than the mercury has, precipitates the mercury upon its surface, in the same manner as a polished piece of iron precipitates copper upon its surface from a solution of blue vitriol. When the metal to be gilt is thus covered over with a thin precipitated coat of mercury, it readily receives the amalgam. In this solution and precipitation of mercury, the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> use of the nitrous acid in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> of gilding appears to consist. The amalgam being equally spread over the surface of the metal to be gilt by means of a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRUSH">brush</a>, the mercury is then to be evaporated by a heat <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> sufficient for that purpose; for if it be too <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a>, part of the gold may also be expelled, and part of it will run together, and leave some of the surface of the metal bare: while the mercury is evaporating, the piece is to be from time to time taken from the fire, that it may be examined, that the amalgam may be spread more equally by means of a brush, that any defective parts of it may be again covered, and that the heat may not be too suddenly applied to it: when the mercury is evaporated, which is known by the surface being entirely become of a dull yellow colour, the metal must then undergo other operations, by which the fine gold colour is given to it. First, The gilded piece of metal is rubbed with a scratch brush (which is a brush composed of brass wire) till its surface is made smooth; then it is covered over with a composition called gilding wax, and is again exposed to the fire till the wax be burnt off. This wax is composed of bees wax, sometimes mixed with some of the following substances; red ochre, verdigrise, copper scales, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALUM">alum</a>, vitriol, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BORAX">borax</a>: but according to Dr <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEWIS">Lewis</a>, the saline substances alone are sufficient, without any wax. By this operation the colour of the gilding is heightened; and this effect seems to be produced by a perfect dissipation of some mercury remaining after the former operation. This dissipation is well effected by this equable application of heat. The gilt surface is then covered over with a saline composition, consisting of nitre, alum, or other vitriolic <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a>, ground together, and mixed up into a paste with water or urine. The piece of metal thus covered is exposed to a certain degree of heat, and then quenched in water. By this method its colour is further improved, and brought nearer to that of gold. This effect seems to be produced by the acid of nitre (which is disengaged by the vitriolic acid of the alum, or other vitriolic salt, during the exposure to heat) acting upon any particles of copper which may happen to <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> on the gilded surface. Lastly, Some artists think that they give an additional lustre to their gilt work by <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIPPING">dipping</a> it in a liquor prepared by boiling some yellow materials, as sulphur, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORPIMENT">orpiment</a>, or turmeric. The only advantage of this operation is, that a part of the yellow <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>, as the sulphur or turmeric, remains in some of the hollows of the carved work, in which the gilding is apt to be more imperfect, and to which it gives a rich and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> appearance. Iron cannot be gilt by amalgamation, unless, as it is said, it be previously coated with copper by dipping in a solution of blue vitriol. Iron may also receive a golden coat from a saturated solution of gold in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AQUA">aqua</a>-regia, mixed with spirit of wine, the iron having a greater affinity with the acid, from which it therefore precipitates the gold. Whether any of these two methods be applicable to use, is uncertain: but the method <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> employed of fixing gold upon iron is that above mentioned, of burnishing gold leaf upon this metal when heated so as to become blue; and the operation will be more perfect if the surface has been previously scratched or graved. Another method is mentioned by authors of gilding upon metals, and also upon earthen <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WARE">ware</a>, and upon glass; which is, to <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol4.html#article-FUSE">fuse</a> gold with regulus of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANTIMONY">antimony</a>, to pulverize the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MASS">mass</a> which is sufficiently brittle to admit that operation, to spread this powder upon the piece to be gilt, and expose it to such a fire that the regulus may be evaporated, while the gold remains fixed. The inconveniences of this method, according to Dr Lewis, are, that the powder does not adhere to the piece, and cannot be equally spread; that part of the gold is dissipated along with the regulus; that glass is fusible with the heat necessary for the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EVAPORATION">evaporation</a> of regulus of antimony; and that copper is liable to be corroded by the regulus, and to have its surface rendered uneven. On this subject of gilding by amalgamation Dr Lewis improves the following remarks. "There are two principal inconveniences in this business: One, that the workmen are exposed to the fumes of the mercury, and generally, sooner or later, have their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> greatly impaired by them: the other, the loss of the mercury; for though part of it is said to be detained in cavities made in the chimney for that purpose, yet the greatest part of it is lost. From some trials I have made, it appeared that both these inconveniences, particularly the first and most considerable one, might in good <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> be avoided, by means of a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FURNACE">furnace</a> of a due <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a>. If the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> of a furnace with its chimney, instead of being over the fire, is made under the grate, the ash-pit door, or other apertures beneath the grate, closed, and the mouth of the furnace left open; the current of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a>, which otherwise would have entered be- Gilding enters now at the top, and passing down through the grate to the chimney, carries with it completely both the vapour of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-FUEL">fuel</a> and the fumes of such matters as are placed upon it: the back part of the furnace should be raised a little higher above the fire than the fore part, and an iron plate laid over it, that the air may enter only at the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRONT">front</a>, where the workman stands, who will be thus effectually secured from the fumes and from being incommoded with the heat, and at the same time have full <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> of introducing, inspecting, and removing the work. If such a furnace is made of strong forged (not milled) iron plate, it will be sufficiently durable: the upper end of the chimney may reach above a foot and a half higher than the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> of the fire: over this is to be placed a larger tube, leaving an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTERVAL">interval</a> of an inch or more all round between it and the chimney, and reaching to the height of 10 or 12 feet, the higher the better. The <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> air, passing up between the chimney and the outer pipe, prevents the latter from being much heated, so that the mercurial fumes will condense against its sides into running quicksilver, which, falling down to the bottom, is there catched in a hollow rim, formed by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> inwards a portion of the lower part, and conveyed, by a pipe at one side, into a proper receiver. Mr Hellot communicates, in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEMOIRS">Memoirs</a> of the French Academy for the year 1745, a method of making raised figures of gold on works of gold or silver, found among the papers of M. du Fay, and of which M. du Fay himself had seen several trials. Fine gold in powder, such as results from the parting of gold and silver by aquafortis, is directed to be laid in a heap on a levigating stone, a cavity made in the middle of the heap, and half its <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of pure mercury put into the cavity; some of the fetid spirit obtained from garlic root by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DISTILLATION">distillation</a> in a retort, is then to be added, and the whole immediately mingled and ground with a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MULLER">muller</a> till the mixture is reduced into an uniform gray powder. The powder is to be ground with lemon juice to the consistence of paint, and applied on the piece previously well cleaned and rubbed over with the same acid juice; the figures drawn with it may be raised to any degree by repeating the application. The piece is exposed to a gentle fire till the mercury is evaporated so as to leave the gold yellow, which is then to be pressed down, and rubbed with the finger and a little sand, which makes it appear solid and brilliant; after this it may be cut and embellished. The author observes, that being of a spongy texture, it is more advisable to cut it with a chissel than to raise it with a graver; that it has an imperfection of being always <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a>; and that it would be a desirable thing to find means of giving it colour, as by this method ornaments might be made of exquisite beauty, and with great facility. As the paleness appears to proceed from a part of the mercury retained by the gold, I apprehend it might be remedied by the prudent application of a little warm aquafortis, which dissolving the mercury from the exterior part, would give at least a superficial <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> colour: if the piece is silver, it must be defended from the aquafortis by covering it with wax. Instruments and ornaments of gold, stained by mercury where the gold is connected with substances incapable of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> fire, may be restored to their colour by the same means. The foregoing process is given entirely on the authority of the French writer. I have had no <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> of it myself, but have seen very elegant figures of gold raised upon silver, on the same principle, by another different procedure. Some cinnabar was ground, not with the distilled spirit, but with the expressed juice of garlic, a fluid remarkably tenacious. This mixture was spread all over the polished silver; and when the first layer is dry, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a>, and after this a third, was applied. Over these were spread as many layers of another mixture, composed chiefly of asphaltum and linseed oil boiled down to a due consistence. The whole being dried with a gentle heat on a kind of wire grate, the figures were traced and cut down to the silver so as to make its surface rough: the incisions were filled with an amalgam of gold, raised to different heights in different parts according to the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a>; after which a gentle fire, at the same time that it evaporated the mercury, destroyed the tenacity of the gummy juice, so that the coating, which served to confine the amalgam, and as a guide in the application of it, was now easily got off. The gold was then pressed down and embellished as in the former method; and had this advantage, that the surface of the silver under it having been made rough, it adhered more firmly, so as not to be in danger of coming off, as M. du Fay says the gold applied in his way sometimes did. The <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ARTIST">artist</a>, however, found the process so troublesome, that though he purchased the receipt for a considerable sum, he has laid the practice aside." Finally, Some metals, particularly silver, may be gilt in the following manner: Let gold be dissolved in aqua-regia. In this solution pieces of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> are to be dipt, and burnt to black thod of gilg ashes. These ashes being rubbed on the surface of the ing silver, silver by means of a wet linen rag, apply the particles of gold which they contain, and which by this method adhere very well. The remaining part of the ashes is to be washed off; and the surface of the silver, which in this state does not seem to be gilt, is to be burnished with a blood-stone, till it acquire a fine colour of gold. This method of gilding is very easy, and consumes a very small quantity of gold. Most gilt ornaments upon fans, snuff boxes, and other toys of much show and little value, are nothing but silver gilt in this manner. Gold may also be applied to glass, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PORCELAIN">porcelain</a>, and other vitrified matters. As the surface of these matters of gilding is very smooth, and consequently is capable of a very perfect contact with gold leaves, these leaves adhere to them with some force, although they are not of metallic nature. This gilding is so much more perfect, as the gold is more exactly applied to the surface of the glass. The pieces are then to be exposed to a certain degree of heat, and burnished slightly to give them lustre. A more substantial gilding is fixed upon glass, enamel, and porcelain, by applying to these substances powder of gold mixed with a solution of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUM">gum</a> arabic, or with some essential oil, and a small quantity of borax; after which a sufficient heat is to be applied to soften the glass and the gold, which is then to be burnished. With this mixture any figures may be drawn. The powders for this purpose may be made, i. By <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRINDING">grinding</a> gold leaf with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONEY">honey</a>, which is afterwards to be washed away with water. 2. By distilling to dryness a solution of gold in aqua-regia. 3. By evaporating the mercury from an amalgam of gold, taking care to stir well the mass near the end of the process. 4. By precipitating gold from its solution in aqua-regia, by applying to it a solution of green vitriol in water, or some copper, and perhaps some other metallic substances.

GILEAD

Pages 789-789

the son of Machir, and grandson of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANASSEH">Manasseh</a>, had his inheritance allotted him in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> of Gilead, from whence he took his name. The mountains of Gilead were <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of that ridge which runs from Mount Lebanon southward, on the east of the Holy <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">Land</a>; gave their name to the whole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> which lies on the east of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> of Galilee, and included the mountainous region called in the New <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a> Trachonitis. Jeremiah (xxii. 6.) seems to say, that Gilead begins from Mount Libanus. 'Thou art Gilead unto me, and the head of Lebanon.' <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JACOB">Jacob</a>, at his return from Mesopotamia, came in six days to the mountains of Gilead (Gen. xxxi. 21. &c.) where this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATRIARCH">patriarch</a>, with Laban his father-in-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a>, raised a heap of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of their agreement and covenant, and called it Galeed, i.e. "an heap of witnesses," and which Laban called Jegar-sahadutha. These mountains were covered with a sort of trees abounding with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUM">gum</a>, called the Balm of Gilead, which the Scripture commends much (Jer. viii. 21. xlvii. ii. li. 8.). The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a> who bought <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOSEPH">Joseph</a> came from Gilead, and were carrying balm into <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, (Gen. xxxvii. 25.). The Gileadites being invaded by the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMMONITES">Ammonites</a>, &c. chose Jephthah for their general, who vanquished all their enemies. Balm of GILEAD. See AMYRIS, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

GILGAL

Pages 789-789

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> between <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JERICHO">Jericho</a> and Jordan, noted for the first encampment of the Israelites on this side Jordan, about a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILE">mile</a> from Jericho. It sometimes also denotes Galilee, (Joshua xii. 23.).

GILL

Pages 789-790

JOHN, D.D. a Protestant dissenting minister of the Baptist denomination, and the son of Edward and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a> Gill, was born at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-KETTERING">Kettering</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTHAMPTONSHIRE">Northamptonshire</a>, November 23. 1697. At a very early <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, his father, who was a deacon of the Baptist <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> at Kettering, discovered in him an uncommon capacity for learning; and his ability for literary pursuits afterwards appeared by the rapid progress in whatever became the object of his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a>. He was sent to a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAMMAR">grammar</a> school in the neighbourhood; where he soon surpassed those boys who were much his seniors in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> and as pupils. At this school he <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> till he arrived at his 11th year; where he read most of the Latin classics, and made considerable proficiency in the Greek <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>. Mr Gill's celebrity as a scholar, and his strong <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a> to books, were soon observed by the neighbouring clergy, who frequently met and conversed with him at a bookseller's shop, to which he resorted for the purpose of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">reading</a>; and indeed such was his application to books, that it became a proverbial saying among the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> people, "Such a thing is as certain, as that John Gill is in the bookseller's shop." He left the grammar school, however, early in life. This was occasioned by the imperious conduct of his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>, who insisted that the children of dissenting parents should, with other scholars that belonged to the establishment, attend him to church on <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-WEEK">week</a> days during the performance of divine <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>. The dissenters considered this requisition as a stretch of power to which his engagements with them gave no claim; and as it was virtually making conformity a test by which his pupils were to expect the benefits of tuition, they resented his conduct; and the children of those parents that were in affluent circumstances were removed to seminaries where the same advantages might be obtained without being subject to the impositions of clerical bigotry. But as the parents of Mr Gill had it not in their power to confer on him the same privilege, the same steps could not be taken to facilitate his advancement in learning. To pave the way, however, for the completion of his studies, efforts were made by several ministers, of different denominations, to get him upon one <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> other of the funds in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. For this purpose specimens of his progress in the different branches of literature were transmitted to the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METROPOLIS">metropolis</a>: in answer to which it was objected, "that he was too young, and that should he continue, as it might be expected he would, to make such rapid advances in his studies, he would go through the common circle before he would be capable of taking care of himself, or of being employed in any public service." But these formidable objections were of no <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> with our young scholar; his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> of learning was unconquerable. Insuperable difficulties, it is true, obstructed the way in which literary eminence is usually acquired; but these difficulties could neither repress his ardent desire of knowledge, nor damp the zeal and application that had marked his former studies. For though his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> was daily devoted to the business of his father; yet he had so far improved the hours of leisure, as to be able, before he arrived at his 10th year, to read all the Greek and Latin authors that fell in his way. He studied logic, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHETORIC">rhetoric</a>, moral and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL_PHILOSOPHY"><a class="xref" hr</a>ef="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>; and learnt the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a> language so as to read it with ease, without any other assistance than Buxtorf's grammar and lexicon. Neither the pursuit of learning, however, nor the other necessary avocations incumbent on Mr Gill, could eradicate those <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> impressions received in early life. On November 1. 1716, he made a public profession of his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a> before the Baptist church at Kettering, and was baptized the same <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> by Mr Thomas Wallis. Of this church Mr Gill had not been <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> a member before he was called to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> of the ministry: soon after which, he removed to <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HIGHAM_FERRERS">Higham-Ferrers</a>, with a view to pursue his studies under the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of Mr Davis; but his stay at this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> was soon interrupted by an invitation from London in 1719, to preach to the Baptist church in Horslydown, over which he was the same year, being the 22d of his age, ordained pastor; which office he sustained upwards of 51 years. Mr Gill had not been long in London, before rabbinical learning, of which he had before considerable knowledge, became an object of pursuit. To facilitate his progress through the intricacies of this <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LABYRINTH">labyrinth</a>, he contracted an acquaintance with one of the most learned Jewish rabbies. He read the Targums, the Talmuds, the Rabbot, their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> commentaries, the book Zohar, and whatever else of this kind he was able to procure. Of the oriental languages he made himself himself a complete master: in short, there was no branch of knowledge that could either enlarge or enrich Biblical learning, which, however difficult, was not attempted and attained; and it may be truly asserted, that in this line he had but few equals, and that the annals of literature do not exhibit a character by whom he was excelled. In 1748, Mr Gill published a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMENTARY">commentary</a> on the New <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a>, in three volumes folio. The immense reading and learning discoverable in this arduous work, attracted the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> of the Marischal <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLLEGE">College</a> and University of Aberdeen; and procured for him, without either his solicitation or his knowledge, a diploma, creating him <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a> in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a>. This intelligence was communicated to the doctor in the most handsome terms by the professors Osborn and Pollock; who declared, "that on account of his knowledge of the Scriptures, of the Oriental languages, and of Jewish antiquities, of his learned <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of the Scriptures against Deists and Infidels, and the reputation gained by his other works; the university had, without his privity, unanimously agreed to confer on him the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of doctor in divinity." Dr Gill's sentiments, as a divine, were throughout Calvinistic: "And perhaps no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> (says the Rev. Mr Toplady, a minister in the church of England) since the days of Austin, has written so largely in defense of the system of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRACE">grace</a>; and certainly no man has treated that momentous subject in all its branches, more closely, judiciously, and successfully. What was said of Edward the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">Black</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">Prince</a>, that he never fought a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> which he did not win; what has been remarked of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARLBOROUGH">Marlborough</a>, that he never undertook a siege which he did not carry; may be justly accommodated to our great <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a> and divine; who, so far as the distinguishing doctrines of the gospel are concerned, never besieged an <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ERROR">error</a> which he did not force from its strong holds, nor ever encountered an adversary whom he did not baffle and subdue. His learning and labours, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> exceedable, were exceeded only by the invariable sanctity of his life and conversation. From his childhood to his entrance on the ministry, and from his entrance on the ministry to the moment of his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISSOLUTION">dissolution</a>, not one of his most inveterate opposers was ever able to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> him with the least shadow of immorality.
