Dacier takes to be a clenching of the fingers of both <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> between one another, and so holding the two thumbs upright <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> together; and, when they would have the combat finished and the vanquished slain, *verterunt policem,* they bent back the thumb; which we learn from Juvenal, Sat. iii. ver. 36. The gladiators challenged or defied each other, by showing the little finger; and, by extending this, or some other, during the combat, they owned themselves vanquished, and begged mercy from the people: *Victi ostensos digitii veniam a populo postulabant,* says the old scholiast on Persius. There were various kinds of gladiators, distinguished by their weapons, manner, and time of fighting, &c., as, The *andabate,* mentioned under ANDABATÆ. The *catervarii,* who always fought in troops or companies, number against number; or, according to others, who fought promiscuously, without any certain order. The *dimachae,* who fought armed with two poniards or swords, or with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWORD">sword</a> and dagger. The *esserarii,* who fought in cars. The *fiscales,* or *Caesariani,* who belonged to the emperor's <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>; and who, being more robust and dexterous than the rest, were frequently called for, and therefore named also *postulatitii.* Several other kinds are mentioned in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> authors. **GLADIATORS War** (*bellum Gladiatoriorum* or *Spartacum*), called also the *servile war,* was a war which the Romans sustained about the year of their city 680. Spartacus, Crinis, and Oenomaus, having escaped, with other gladiators to the number of seventy-four, out of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where they had been kept at <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPUA">Capua</a>, gathered together a body of slaves, put themselves at their head, rendered themselves masters of all Campania, and gained several victories over the Roman praetors. At length they were defeated in the year 862, at the extremity of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>; having, in vain, attempted to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> over into <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a>. This war proved very formidable to the Romans. Crassus was not able to finish it: the great Pompey was forced to be sent as general. The Dying GLADIATOR, a most valuable monument of ancient <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SCULPTURE">sculpture</a>, which is now preserved in the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> of Chighi. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, when he had received the mortal stroke, is particularly careful *ut procumbat honeste,* "that he might <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> honourably." He is seated in a reclining posture on the ground, and has <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> strength sufficient to support himself on his <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> arm; and in his expiring moments it is plainly seen, that he does not abandon himself to grief and dejection; but is solicitous to maintain that firmness of aspect which the gladiators valued themselves on preserving in this season of distress, and that attitude which they had learnt of the masters of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a>. He fears not death, nor seems to betray any tokens of fear by his countenance, nor to shed one tear: *quis mediocris gladiator ingemuit, quis vulturn mutavit unquam, quis non modo stetit, verum etiam decubit turpiter,* says Cicero, in that part of his Tusculan where he is describing the astonishing firmness of those persons. We see, in this instance, notwithstanding his remaining strength, that he has but a moment to live; and we view him with <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>, that we may see him expire and fall: thus the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> knew how to animate marble, and give it almost every <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a> of life.

GLADIOLUS

Pages 800-801

CORN <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAG">FLAG</a>, a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the triandra class, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the sixth order, Ensata. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. **GLAIR** of eggs, is the same as the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> of eggs, and is used as a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VARNISH">varnish</a> for preserving paintings. For this purpose it is <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEAT">beat</a> to an unctuous consistence, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> mixed with a little brandy <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> spirit of wine, to make it <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> more freely, and with a lump of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a> to give it body and prevent its cracking: and then spread over the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a> with a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRUSH">brush</a>. **GLAMORGANSHIRE,** a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of South <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>, said to have derived its name from a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRACTION">contraction</a> of the Welsh words *Gwlad Morgan,* or "the county of Morgan," and supposed to have been thus called from a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of this <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, said to have been killed 800 years before the birth of our Saviour: but some other writers derive the name from the word *Mor,* which in the British tongue signifies the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>; this being a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARITIME">maritime</a> county. It is bounded on the south and part of the west, by <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRISTOL">Bristol</a> channel; on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-west, by Caernarvonthshire; on the north by Brecknockshire; and on the east, by <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONMOUTHSHIRE">Monmouthshire</a>. It extends 48 miles in length from east to west, 27 in breadth from north to south, and is 116 in circumference. It is divided into 10 <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-HUNDREDS">hundreds</a>, in which are one <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>, 7 market <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, 118 parishes, 17,758 houses, and, in 1811, 85,067 inhabitants. It is in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LLANDAFF">Llandaff</a>. This county, in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, was part of the district inhabited by the Silures, and had several Roman stations. Thus Boverton, a few miles to the south of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COWBRIDGE">Cowbridge</a>, is supposed to be the Bovium of Antoninus: <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NEATH">Neath</a> to be his Nidum; and Loghor, to the west of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWANSEA">Swansea</a>, to be his Leucarum. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> of this county are the Rhymny, the Taff, the Ogmore, the Avon, the Cledaugh, and the Tave. The <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a>, in the south part, towards the sea, is temperate and healthful; but the northern part, which is mountainous, is <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLD">cold</a> and piercing, full of thick woods, extremely barren, and thin of inhabitants. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, however, serve to feed herds of cattle, and send forth streams which add greatly to the fertility of the other parts of the county: GLA county: they have likewise coal and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> ore. The south part is so remarkably fertile, pleasant, and populous, that it is generally styled the garden of Wales; but it has no manufacture. This county was formerly full of castles, most of which are now fallen to decay. It has many small harbours on the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a> for exporting coals and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a>. Of the former it sends <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> quantities both to England and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>; but of the latter, to England almost solely, especially <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUTTER">butter</a>. It sends two members to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, one for the shire, and one for the borough of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDIFF">Cardiff</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>. See Glamorganshire, Supplement.

GLAMOUR

Pages 801-801
or Glamer, an old term of popular superstition in Scotland, denoting a kind of magical mist believed to be raised by sorcerers, and which deluded their spectators with visions of things which had no real existence, altered the appearance of those which really did exist, &c.—The eastern nations have a similar superstition, as we may learn from the Arabian Nights Entertainments and other works of oriental fiction.

GLANDORE

Pages 801-801

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, situated in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Cork and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUNSTER">Munster</a>, near the harbour of that name. GLANDORE Harbour, situated two leagues west of the Galley-head in the county of Cork, province of Munster, N. Lat. 51° 22'. W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 8° 36'. Between this harbour and Ross the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a> continues <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> and bold, with only two small coves; that to the east called Millocove, and that to the west Coucove. This harbour lies three miles west of Ross; and though small, is an exceeding good one; near it is a castle of the same name, and on the upper end is a deep and dangerous glin, called the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAP">Leap</a>. Glandore gives <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARL">earl</a> to the family of Crosbie. GLANDULÆ RENALES. See Anatomy <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

GLANS

Pages 801-801

in Anatomy, the tip <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUTTON">button</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENIS">penis</a>, or that <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> covered with the prepuce, called also balanus. See Anatomy <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Glans is also used to denote the tip or extremity of the clitoris, from its resemblance, both in form and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>, to that of the penis. See Anatomy Index.

GLANVIL

Pages 801-801
JOSEPH, a learned and ingenious, but fanciful and credulous, writer in the 17th century, was born at Plymouth in 1636, and bred at Oxford. He became a great admirer of Mr Baxter, and a zealous person for a commonwealth. After the Restoration, he published The Vanity of Dogmatizing; was chosen a fellow of the Royal Society; and, taking orders in 1662, was presented to the vicarage of Frome-Selwood in Somersetshire. The same year he published his Lex Orientalis: in 1665, his Sceptis Scientifica; and in the year following, Some Philosophical Considerations touching the being of Witches and Witchcraft, and other pieces on the same subject. In 1669, he published Plus ultra; or, The Progress and Advancement of Knowledge since the Days of Aristotle. He likewise published A seasonable Recommendation and Defence of Reason; and Philosophia Pia, or A Discourse of the Religious Temper and Tendencies of the Experimental Philosophy. In 1678 he was made a prebendary of Worcester, and died in 1680.

GLARIS

Pages 801-801

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWITZERLAND">Switzerland</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANTON">canton</a> of the same name, is seated in a plain, at the foot of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> craggy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>. The streets are <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, and the houses kept in good repair. It has some public buildings; among which are two churches, one in the middle of the town, and the other without upon an eminence. In this eminence there is a cavern, with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GROTESQUE">grotesque</a> figures formed by the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> that drops therein. The general assemblies of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> were formerly held on the first Sundays in May, where all the males above the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> of sixteen were obliged to appear. Both the Calvinists and the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ROMAN_CATHOLICS">Roman Catholics</a> are tolerated in this town, and they have divine <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> by turns in the same <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>. It is seated on the river Lint, E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 9° 13'. N. Lat. 47° 6'. <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPULATION">Population</a> about 2500.

GLASGOW

Pages 801-811

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Lanerkshire <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Clydesdale in Scotland, situated in W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 4° 16'. N. Lat. 55° 52'. Concerning the foundation of this city we have no authentic records. The word in the Gaelic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> signifies a gray smith; from whence it has been inferred, that some spot in the most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the city was originally the residence of some blacksmith who had become eminent in his profession, so that the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> went by his name. In the year 560, a bishopric is said to have been founded here by Saint Mungo, or Kentigern, supposed to be the son of Thamates, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Loth <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of the Picts; but in what state the town at that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> was, is altogether uncertain. Most probably the priests and disciples who attended St Kentigern would contribute considerably towards its advancement; the aged and infirm, who were unfit for the purposes of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, or such as were religiously inclined, would come and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> round the habitation of the holy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, in order to have the benefit of his prayers; and as a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIRACLES">miracles</a> were said to have been wrought at his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOMB">tomb</a>, the same causes would still contribute to the increase of the town. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> has not informed us of the name of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> who founded and endowed the bishopric of Glasgow in favour of St Kentigern. But from an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABSTRACT">abstract</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> of Kentigern (contained in Mr Innes's Critical <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ESSAY">Essay</a> on the Ancient Inhabitants of Scotland), which was written in the 12th century, we learn, that the saint being ill used by Marken or Marcus, one of the kings of the Britons, retired into <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>. On the invitation of Roderic, however, one of Marken's successors, he returned to Glasgow, and enjoyed the see till 601, when he died. He was buried in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of Glasgow, where his monument is still to be seen; and we find him marked among the saints in the Roman <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CALENDAR">calendar</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 13: 577. The immediate successors of Kentigern were Baldrede and Conwal. The first established a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> at Inchinnan; the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> went into <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LOTHIAN">Lothian</a> to preach to the Saxons; and both of them are ranked as saints in the Roman calendar, Baldrede on the 6th of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a>. March 608, and Conwai on the 18th of May 612. From this time, however, till the 1115, we have no distinct accounts concerning the city or bishopric of Glasgow. We find then, that <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAVID">David</a> I., king of Scotland made an attempt to retrieve the people from a state of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GROSS">gross</a> barbarity into which they were fallen, and restored to the church those lands of which she had been robbed. The only account we have of the transactions with regard to Glasgow, during that <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>, is in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INQUISITION">inquisition</a> made by David concerning the church lands of Glasgow, and is as follows.—"This church, by the divine appointment, admitted St Kentigern into the bishopric, who furnished large draughts of knowledge to those thirsting after heavenly things, &c. But a fraudulent destroyer, employing his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> wiles, brought in, after a long <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of time, unaccountable scandals into the Cambrian church. For after St Kentigern and many of his successors were removed to heaven, various disturbances everywhere arising, not only destroyed the church and her possessions, but, wasting the whole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, drove the inhabitants into exile. These good men being destroyed, various tribes of different nations flocking in from several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a>, possessed the foresaid deserted country; but being of different origins, and varying from each other in their language and customs, and not easily agreeing among themselves, they followed the manners of the Gentiles, rather than those of the true <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>. The inhabitants of which unhappy and abandoned country, though living like <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRUTES">brutes</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a>, who chooses that none should perish, vouchsafed to visit in mercy," &c. From the year 1116 to the Reformation, the records of the bishopric are tolerably complete. The most remarkable particulars furnished by them are the following: In 1136, John Achaius, chosen bishop of Glasgow by David I., built and adorned a part of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a>, which he solemnly consecrated on the 9th of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a>. The king was present at the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a>; and bestowed on the church the lands of Perdeyk, now Patrick. This prelate also divided the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a> into the two archdeaconries of Glasgow and Teviotdale; and established the offices of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAN">dean</a>, subdean, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-TREASURER">treasurer</a>, sacrist, chanter, and successor; and settled a prebendary upon each of them, out of the donatives he received from the king. In 1174, Joceline, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABBOT">abbot</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MELROSE">Melrose</a>, was elected bishop, and consecrated by Eskilus, bishop of Lundin in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DENMARK">Denmark</a>, the pope's legate for that <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, on the 1st of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 1175. He rebuilt the cathedral, or rather made an addition to the church already built by John Achaius. He also procured a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARTER">charter</a> from William king of Scotland, erecting Glasgow into a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> borough, and likewise a charter for a fair to be held there annually for eight days. In 1335, John Lindsay, bishop of Glasgow, was killed in an engagement at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> with the English, as he was returning home from <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLANDERS">Flanders</a>. His successor, William Rae, built the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> over the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLYDE">Clyde</a>. In the time of Matthew Glendoning, who was elected bishop in 1387, the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> spire of the church, which had been built only of wood, was consumed by <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIGHTNING">lightning</a>. The bishop intended to have built another of stone; but was prevented by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, in 1408, from accomplishing his purpose. His successor, William <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LADDER">Ladder</a>, laid the foundation of the vestry of the cathedral, and built the great tower of stone as far as the first battlement. The great tower of the episcopal <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> was founded about the year 1437, on which Bishop Cameron expended a great <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a>. In 1447, William Turnbull, a son of the family of Bedrule in <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROXBURGHSHIRE">Roxburghshire</a>, was chosen bishop. He obtained from King James II., in 1450, a charter erecting the town and the patrimony of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a> into a regality. He also procured a bull from Pope Nicholas V., for erecting an university within the city, which he endowed, and on which he also bestowed many privileges. He died in 1454, leaving behind him a most excellent character. The establishment of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> contributed more than any thing that had been formerly done towards the enlargement of the town. Before this time the town seems to have been inconsiderable. Mr Gibson* is of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, that the number of its inhabitants did not exceed 1500. But though the establishment of the university greatly increased the number of inhabitants, it in fact destroyed the freedom of the town. Bishop Turnbull seems to have made a point of it with King James II., that the city of Glasgow, with the bishop's forest, should be erected into a regality in his favour; which was accordingly done at the time above mentioned; and this at once took away all power from the citizens, and transferred it to the bishop. As the powers of the bishop, however, were reckoned by Turnbull insufficient to convey to the members of the university all that freedom which he wished to bestow upon them, he therefore obtained from the king a great many privileges for them; and afterwards he himself, with the consent of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAPTER">chapter</a>, granted them many more. The good effects of the establishment of the college <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> were very soon obvious in Glasgow. The number of inhabitants increased exceedingly; the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> street, from the convent of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">Black</a> Friars, to where the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> is now placed, was very soon filled up; the ancient <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a> which led to the common being too far distant for the conveniency of the new inhabitants, the Gallows-gate began to be built. Soon after, the collegiate church of the blessed <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a> (now the Tron church) being founded by the citizens, occasioned the Trongate street to be carried to the westward as far as the church. The rest of the city increased gradually towards the bridge, by the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> of the Saltmarket street. The thorough <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROADS">roads</a>, and the cattle that grazed on the commons, were now found insufficient to maintain the increased number of inhabitants; for which reason a greater <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> than formerly was paid to the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FISHING">fishing</a> in the river. Many <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a> people subsisted themselves by this occupation; they were incorporated into a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>; and in order that they might be at <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> to prosecute their business, they built a considerable part of the street now called the Bridge-gate, but at that time Fishers-gate. Notwithstanding all this, however, the city of Glasgow did not for a long time attain the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> among the other <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> of Scotland which it holds at present. In 1556, it held only the 11th place among them, as appears by <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> Mary's <a class="xref" href="../1823/vol6.html#article-TAXATION">taxation</a>. The introduction of the reformed <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> proved for some time prejudicial to the opulence of the city. The money which had had formerly been expended among the citizens by the bishop and his clergy, was now diverted into other channels: the advantages resulting from the university were also for a time lost; for as the reformers generally despised <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> learning, the college was in a manner deserted. In the time of the civil wars, Glasgow suffered severely. To the mischief attending intestine <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCORD">discord</a>, were added a pestilence and famine; and to complete their misfortunes, a violent fire broke out in June 1652, which destroyed the greatest part of the Saltmarket, Trongate, and High street. The fronts of the houses at that time were mostly of wood, so that they became an easy prey to the flames. The fire <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> with great violence for the space of 18 hours; by which a great many of the inhabitants were ruined, the habitations of almost 1000 families being totally destroyed. On this account collections were made through different parts of the country; and to prevent such accidents for the future, the fronts were built with freestone, which abounds in the neighbourhood. By the charter given to Bishop Turnbull in 1450, the citizens had been deprived of the power of electing their own magistrates, which was thenceforth exercised by the bishop; which, however, was not done without some resistance on the part of the inhabitants. After the Reformation was introduced into Scotland, we find this power exercised by the citizens, the bishop, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of Lennox, and others. The idea that the town was a bishop's borough, and not a royal free borough, gave occasion to this unsettled manner of appointing the magistracy; and though, in 1633, they were declared to be a royal free borough by the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, yet their freedom of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTION">election</a> was afterwards disturbed by the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PRIVY_COUNCIL">privy <a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>, by Cromwell, and the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORK">York</a>. But on the 4th of June 1690, the town was declared free by a charter of William and Mary; and in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONFIRMATION">confirmation</a> of this charter it was inserted in the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> of parliament, dated June 14th the same year, that they should have power to elect their own magistrates as fully and freely, in all respects, as the city of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a> or any other royal borough within the kingdom; which freedom of election still continues. By the assessment of the boroughs in 1695, we find the city of Glasgow reckoned the second in Scotland in point of wealth, which place it still continues to hold. To account for this great increase of wealth, we must observe, that for a long time, even before the restoration of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> II., the inhabitants of Glasgow had been in possession of the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALE">sale</a> of both raw and refined sugars for the greatest part of Scotland; they had a privilege of distilling spirits from their molasses, free of all duty and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXCISE">excise</a>; the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERRING">herring</a> fishery was also carried on to what was at that time thought a very considerable <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>; they were the only people in Scotland who made <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOAP">soap</a>; and they sent annually some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIDES">hides</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a>, &c. to <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRISTOL">Bristol</a>, from whence they brought back in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXCHANGE">exchange</a>, a little <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOBACCO">tobacco</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>, and goods, of the manufacture of England, with which they supplied a considerable part of the kingdom. From the year 1707, however, in which the union betwixt Scotland and England took place, we may <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DATE">date</a> the prosperity of Glasgow. By the union, the American trade was laid open to the inhabitants: and so sensible were they of their advantageous situation, that they began almost instantly to prosecute that <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>; an assiduous application to Glasgow, which, ever since, hath greatly contributed to raise the city to the pitch of affluence and splendour which it at present enjoys. The city was now greatly enlarged; and as the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMUNITY">community</a> were sensible of the inconvenience that attended the want of a sufficient <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> in the river for carrying on their commerce, they resolved to have a port of their own nigher the mouth of the river. At first, they thought of making their harbour at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUMBARTON">Dumbarton</a>: but as this is a royal borough, the magistrates opposed it; because they thought that the influx of sailors and others, occasioned by the harbour, would be so great, that a scarcity of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a> would be occasioned. The magistrates and town council of Glasgow, therefore, purchased some lands on the south side of the river Clyde for this purpose; and so expeditious were they in making their harbour, and rearing their town, that in 1710 a bailie was appointed for the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PORT_GLASGOW">Port-Glasgow</a>. It is now a very considerable <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARISH">parish</a>, and lies 21 miles nigher the mouth of Clyde than Glasgow. In 1725, Mr Campbell, the member of parliament for Glasgow, having given his vote for having the malt tax extended over Scotland, a riot ensued among the lower class of people. In this disturbance, Mr Campbell's furniture was destroyed, and some excisemen were maltreated for attempting to take an account of the malt. General Wade, who commanded the forces in Scotland, had sent two companies of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a>, under the command of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPTAIN">Captain</a> Bushel, to prevent any disturbance of this kind. Captain Bushel drew up his men in the street, where the multitude pelted them with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONES">stones</a>. He first endeavoured to disperse the mob by firing with powder only: but this expedient failing, he ordered his men to load their pieces with <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALL">ball</a>; and, without the sanction of the civil authority, commanded them to fire four different ways at once. By this discharge about 20 persons were killed and wounded; which enraged the multitude to such a degree, that having procured some arms, they pursued Bushel and his men to the castle of Dumbarton, about 14 miles distant. General Wade being informed of this transaction, assembled a body of forces, and being accompanied by Duncan Forbes, lord advocate, took possession of the town: the magistrates were apprehended and carried prisoners to Edinburgh; but on an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXAMINATION">examination</a> before the lords, their innocence clearly appeared, upon which they were immediately dismissed. Bushel was tried for <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDER">murder</a>, convicted, and condemned; but, instead of suffering the penalties of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a>, he was indulged with a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARDON">pardon</a>, and promoted in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>. Mr Campbell petitioned the house of commons for an indemnification of his losses: a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BILL">bill</a> was passed in his favour; and this, together with some other expenses incurred in the affair, cost the town 9000l. <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-STERLING">sterling</a>. During the time of the rebellion 1745, the citizens of Glasgow gave <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a> to revolution principles, by raising two battalions of 600 men each, for the service of government. This piece of loyalty, however, had like to have cost them dear. The rebels, in their journey south, took a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a> to plunder and burn the city: which would probably have been done, had not Mr Cameron of Lochiel threatened, in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>, to withdraw his clan. A heavy contribution, however, was laid on. The city was compelled Glasgow. pelled to pay 500l. in money, and 500l. in goods; and on the return of the rebels from England, they were obliged to furnish them with 12,000 linen shirts, 6000 cloth coats, 6000 pairs of shoes, 6000 pairs of hose, and 6000 bonnets. These goods, with the money formerly paid them, the expense of raising and subsisting the two city battalions, and the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> of maintaining the rebel <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> in free quarters for ten days, cost the community about 14,000l. sterling; 10,000l. of which they recovered in 1749, by an application to parliament. About the year 1750, a very considerable change took place in the manner of living among the inhabitants of Glasgow. Till this time, an attentive industry, and a frugality bordering upon parsimony, had been their general characteristic; the severity of the ancient manners prevailed in its full vigour: But now, when an extensive commerce and increased <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> had produced wealth, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> of the people were enlarged, and bolder schemes of trade and improvement were adopted; a new style was introduced in living, dress, building, and furniture; wheel <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARRIAGES">carriages</a> were set up, public places of entertainment were frequented, and an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a>-room, ball-room, and <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-PLAYHOUSE">playhouse</a>, were built by subscription; and from this time we may date all the improvements that have taken place, not only in Glasgow, but all over the west of Scotland. In 1753, an act passed for repairing several roads leading into the city of Glasgow. In 1756, an act for erecting and supporting a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>-house in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of Little Cunray, at the mouth of the Clyde, and for rendering the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a> of the frith and river more safe and commodious.—In 1759, an act for improving the navigation of the river Clyde to the city of Glasgow, and for building a new bridge across the river.—In 1767, the people of Glasgow having proposed to make a small cut or canal from the frith of Forth to that of Clyde, for the conveniency of their trade to the eastern side of the island, several gentlemen at Edinburgh, and throughout different parts of the kingdom, proposed that this canal should be executed upon a much larger <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCALE">scale</a> than what had been originally projected. An act was accordingly obtained, and the canal executed in the manner described under the article Canal.—In 1770, another act was obtained for improving the navigation of the river, building the bridge, &c. being an amendment of the former act for these purposes. In 1771, an act for making and widening a passage from the Saltmarket to St Andrew's church; for enlarging and completing the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCHYARD">churchyard</a> of that church, and likewise for building a convenient exchange or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> in the city; also for amending and explaining the former act relative to the navigation of the Clyde. In 1783, the society known by the name of the chamber of commerce and manufactures was established. The object was to unite the influence of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a> and manufacturers, and to establish a public <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-FUND">fund</a> to give greater efficacy to plans in which these classes might be interested. A royal charter was obtained constituting them a body politic, under the management of 30 directors. This chamber has since been of essential service, in promoting objects and undertakings connected with the advancement of trade. But the introduction of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COTTON_MANUFACTURE">cotton manufacture</a> on a considerable scale, about 1786, made a greater change in the state of the trade of Glasgow than any event which had previously occurred, and formed indeed a new era in its history. From that time the progress of the town in commerce, population, and wealth, has been surprising. The most ancient part of the city stands on a rising ground. The foundation of the cathedral is 104 feet of the higher than the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BED">bed</a> of the river; and the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a> from the high ground reaches to about 100 yards below the college. The rest of the city is built chiefly upon a plain, bounded southward by the Clyde, and northward by a gentle ridge of hills lying in a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> with that river. These grounds, till lately, consisted of gardens and fields; but are now covered with buildings, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of the increasing wealth and population of the city. The streets are all clean and well paved; and several of them intersecting one another at <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a>, produce a very agreeable effect. The four <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> streets, crossing one another in that manner, divide the city nearly into four equal parts; and the different views of them from the cross, or centre of intersection, have an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> of great magnificence. The houses, consisting of four or five floors in height, are built of hewn stone, generally in very good <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>, and many of them elegant. The most remarkable public buildings are, 1. The Cathedral, or High Church, is a magnificent building, and its situation greatly to its advantage, as it stands higher than any part of the city. It has been intended to form a cross, though the transverse part has never been finished. The great tower is founded upon four large massy pillars, each of them about 30 feet in circumference. The tower itself is 25½ feet square within; and is surrounded by a balustrade, within which rises an octangular spire terminated by a vane. The tower upon the west end is upon the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a>, but appears not to have been finished, though it is covered over with <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>. In this tower is a very large <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BELL">bell</a> 11 feet four inches in diameter. The principal entry was from the west; the gate 11 feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> at the base, and 17 feet in height. The west end of the choir is now appropriated for a place of divine worship; and is divided from the remaining part by a stone partition, which is enclosed by another stone wall parting it from the nave. It is impossible to form an adequate idea of the awful solemnity of the place occasioned by the loftiness of the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROOF">roof</a> and the range of pillars by which the whole is supported. The nave of the church rises four steps higher than the choir; and on the west side stood the organ loft, formerly ornamented with a variety of figures, but now defaced. The pillars here are done in a better taste than those in the choir, and their capitals are ornamented with <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>. The arched roof of the altar is supported by five pillars, over which was a fine terrace walk, and above it a large window of curious workmanship, but now shut up. On the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> side of the altar is the vestry, being a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUBE">cube</a> of 28 feet, the roof arched and vaulted at top, and supported by one pillar in the centre of the house. Arched pillars from every <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a> terminate in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> pillar, which is 19 feet high. The lower part of the south cross is made <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of as a burying place for the clergy of the city; and is by much the finest piece of workmanship in the whole building. It is 55 feet long, 28 broad, and 15 high; arched and vaulted at top, and supported by a middle range of pillars, with their capitals highly ornamented; corresponding to which are columns adjoining to the walls, which, as they rise, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> into semi-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARCHES">arches</a>, and are everywhere met at acute angles by their opposites, and are ornamented with carvings at the closing and crossing of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a>. At the east end of the choir you descend by flights of steps upon each side into <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> which, in former times, were the principal entries to the burying vault, which is immediately under the nave. It is now made use of as a parish church for the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BARONY">barony</a> of Glasgow; and is full of pillars, some of them very massy, which support the arched roof: but it is a very uncomfortable place for <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a>. The space under the altar and vestry, though now made use of as a burying place by the heirs of the barony, was formerly, according to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRADITION">tradition</a>, employed for keeping of the relics; and indeed, from the beautiful manner in which this place is finished, one would imagine that it had not been destined for common use. Here is shown the monument of St Mungo, or Kentigern, with his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> lying in a cumbent posture. The whole length of the cathedral within the walls is 284 feet, its breadth 65; the height of the choir, from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOR">floor</a> to the canopy, 90 feet; the height of the nave, 85 feet; the height of the middle tower, 220 feet. This fabric was begun by John Achaimus in 1123, and consecrated in 1136; and continued by succeeding bishops till such time as it was finished in the manner in which it stands at present. The wealth of the see of Glasgow, however, was not sufficient for so great an undertaking, so that they were obliged to have recourse to all the churches of Scotland for assistance in it. This venerable edifice was in danger of falling a victim to the frenzy of fanaticism in 1579; and owed its preservation to the spirit and good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> of the tradesmen, who, upon hearing the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEAT">beat</a> of drum for collecting the workmen appointed to demolish it, flew to arms, and declared that the first man who pulled <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> a single stone should that moment be buried under it. Near the cathedral are the ruins of the bishop's palace or castle, enclosed with a wall of hewn stone by Archbishop James Beaton; the great tower built by Archbishop Cameron in 1426. 2. St Andrew's Church was begun by the community in 1739, and finished in 1756. It is the finest piece of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a> in the city; and is built after the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODEL">model</a> of St Martin's in the Fields, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, whose <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ARCHITECT">architect</a> was the famous Gibbs. The length of the church is 104 feet, and its breadth 66. It has a fine arched roof, well ornamented with figures in stucco, and sustained by stone columns of the Corinthian order. Correspondent to the model, it has a place for the altar on the east, in which is a very ancient Venetian window; but the altar place being seated, makes this end appear to no great advantage. The fronts of the galleries and the pulpit are done in mahogany in a very elegant manner. The spire by no means corresponds with the rest of the building; and, instead of being an ornament, disgraces this beautiful fabric. Its height is 170 feet. Besides the cathedral (which contains three congregations) and St Andrew's church, there is a number of others, as the College church, Ram's-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORN">horn</a>, Tron, St Enoch's and St George's; together with an English chapel, Highland church, several seceding meeting-houses, and others for sectaries of various denominations. 3. The College.—The <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRONT">front</a> of this building extends along the east side of the High street, and is upwards of legs. 330 feet long. The gate at the entrance is decorated with rustics, and over it are the king's arms. The building consists of two principal courts or squares. The first is 88 feet long and 44 broad. The west side is elevated upon stone pillars, on which are placed pilasters supporting the Doric entablature, and ornamented with arches forming a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PIAZZA">piazza</a>. Above these is the public <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HALL">hall</a>; the ascent to which is by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> flight of steps enclosed by a handsome stone balustrade, upon the right of which is placed a lion, and on the left an unicorn, cut in freestone. The spire stands on the east side, is 135 feet high, and has a very good clock. Under this is the gateway into the inner and largest <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>, which is 103 feet long and 70 broad. Over the entry, in a niche, is a statue of Mr Zacharias Boyd, who was a benefactor to the university. On the east side of the court is a narrow passage leading into a handsome terrace walk, gravelled, 122 feet long by 64 feet broad. This walk is enclosed to the east by an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> palisade, in the centre of which is a gate leading into the garden. This last consists of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> acres of ground, laid out in walks for the recreation of the students; and there is also a botanic garden. On the south side of the walk stands the library; a very neat edifice, well constructed for the purpose intended, and containing a very valuable collection of books. Underneath are preserved in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> all the Roman <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INSCRIPTIONS">inscriptions</a> found on Graham's Dike, together with altars and other antiquities collected from different parts of Scotland.—Adjoining there is an <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OBSERVATORY">observatory</a>, well furnished with astronomical instruments. The college also possesses, by bequest, the late Dr Hunter's famous anatomical preparations, library, and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUSEUM">museum</a>. A beautiful building was erected in 1806 for its reception. 4. New Jail.—The old jail having become much too small in consequence of the rapid growth of the town, a new one was projected in 1808. As the Glasgow jail receives prisoners from the neighbouring counties, application was made first to them, and afterwards to government for assistance in defraying the expence, but without effect. In consequence of this the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> was reduced, and the expence, amounting to 34,800l., was defrayed from the funds of the burgh. The new jail was opened in 1814, and is admitted to be one of the most commodious and best arranged in the country. It is situated at the west end of the Green, in a healthy and well aired position; and besides a court house capable of containing 500 persons, and several other public offices, it contains 122 apartments for prisoners, sixteen large galleries for air and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a>, and two paved court yards, 60 feet by 46. The jail is formed into sixteen distinct allotments—eight for debtors, and eight for criminals. The building is amply supplied with pure water, and is carefully cleaned. There are four well aired infirmary rooms, and a chapel which holds 200 persons. During the year ending 1st April 1819, no less than 1809 persons had been incarcerated;—683 debtors and 1126 delinquents. 5. <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRIDEWELL">Bridewell</a>.—Till the year 1798 there was no regular Bridewell in Glasgow. The present Bridewell which is in Duke street, is six stories high, and contains a chapel, a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>-room, and 105 cells, each eight feet by seven, with a public <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KITCHEN">kitchen</a>, apartments for the keeper, and several work-rooms. It has now, however, become too small for the city; and a scheme is at present in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTEMPLATION">contemplation</a> for erecting another on a more extensive scale, and a better plan. 6. The Guild Hall or Merchants House. This building is situated upon the south side of Bridgegate street; and is in length 82 feet, in breadth 31. The great hall, which is the whole length and breadth of the building, is so capacious, that it is better adapted for the reception of great and numerous assemblies than any other in the city. This house is adorned with a very elegant spire 200 feet high. 7. The Town's <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOSPITAL">Hospital</a> is a very neat building, consisting of two wings and a large front; the length 156 feet, the breadth of the centre 30 feet, and the depth of the wings 68 feet. Behind the building is an infirmary 127 feet long by 25 feet broad, the ascent to which is by a flight of steps. The lower part of this building is appointed for the reception of lunatics. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AREA">area</a> between the buildings is large, which, with the agreeable open situation of the hospital on the river, must conduce to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> of the inhabitants. 8. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAMMAR">Grammar</a> School is situated in the new part of the town, to the north-west, and was built in 1787. It is a very handsome building, containing a large hall, and six <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIRY">airy</a> commodious teaching rooms. In this school there are four classes, the course being four years: each class is carried on the whole five years by the same <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>; so that, there being no rector, each master is head of the school one year in <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROTATION">rotation</a>. It is under the direction of a committee of the town council; who, assisted by the professors, clergy, and other persons of learning, frequently visit it during the session; and at an annual examination, prizes are distributed to the scholars according to their respective merits. The number of scholars is about 540. It is found that there are 10,200 persons educated in Glasgow who pay fees, besides 1100 educated at free or <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARITY">charity</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a>. 9. Bridges.—There are at Glasgow two stone bridges over the Clyde, and a wooden one. The Old Bridge at the foot of Stockwell street, was built by Bishop Rae in 1345. Ten feet were added to its breadth in 1777, and its present dimensions are, 415 feet in length, and 22 in breadth. The New Bridge is built in an elegant manner. It is 32 feet wide, with a commodious footway for passengers, five feet broad on each side, raised above the road made for carriages, and paved with freestone. This bridge is about 500 feet in length, and consists of seven arches, the faces of which are wrought in rustic, with a strong <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLOCK">block</a> cornice above. The arches spring but a little way above low water mark; which, though it renders the bridge stronger than <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they sprung from taller piers, diminishes its <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>. This bridge was begun in 1768, and finished in 1772. 10. The <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MARKETS">Markets</a> in King's Street are justly admired, as being the completest of their kind in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>. They are placed on both sides of the street. That on the east side, appropriated entirely for <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUTCHER">butcher</a> meat, is 112 feet in length, and 67 in breadth. In the centre is a spacious gateway, decorated on each side with coupled Ionic columns, set upon their pedestals, and supporting an angular pediment. At the north end is a very neat hall belonging to the incorporation of butchers, the front ornamented with rustics and a pediment. The markets upon the west side of the street consist of three courts, set apart for fish, mutton, and cheese. The whole of the front is 173 feet, the breadth 46 feet; in the centre of which, as on the opposite side, is a very spacious gateway of the Doric order, supporting a pediment. This is the entry to the mutton market. Each of the other two has a well proportioned <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCH">arch</a> faced with rustics for the entrance. All these markets are well paved with freestone, have walks all round them, and are covered over for shelter by roofs standing upon stone piers, under which the different commodities are exposed to sale. They have likewise <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUMP">pump</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WELLS">wells</a> within, for cleansing away all the filth; which render the markets always sweet and agreeable. These markets were erected in 1754. 11. The Market for Vegetables is neat and commodious; and the principal entry is decorated with columns. It is situated in the Candleriggs, and is laid out in the same manner with the markets in King's street. 12. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUARD">Guard</a> House is a very handsome building, with a piazza formed by arches, and columns of the Ionic order set upon their pedestals. It was originally situated on the High street, at the corner of the Candleriggs street: but was afterwards carried near half way up the Candleriggs, where it occupies the ground on which the weigh-house formerly stood, and is made larger and more commodious than it was before. An excellent new weigh-house has been erected at the head of the Candleriggs: and at the foot of the Candleriggs, or corner next the High street, where the guardhouse was formerly situated, a superb new <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOTEL">hotel</a> has been built, containing 75 fire rooms. The most remarkable public charities in Glasgow are, 1. Muirhead's or St Nicholas's Hospital. This was originally appointed to subsist 12 old men and a chaplain; but its revenues have, from some unknown causes, been lost; so that no more of them now remains than the paltry sum of 139l. 2s. 5d. Scots money, 128l. of which is annually divided among four old men, at the rate of 2l. 13s. 4d. sterling each. 2. Hutcheson's Hospital, was founded and endowed in 1639 by George Hutcheson of Lamb-hill, notary public, and Mr Thomas Hutcheson his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a>, who was bred a preacher, for the maintenance of old men and orphans. The funds of this hospital were increased by James Blair, merchant in Glasgow in 1710, and by subsequent donations. The income, which is now large, is distributed in pensions to old people from 3l. to 2cl., and in educating about 70 children. The sum distributed in pensions in 1819 was 1790l. 7s. 3. The Merchants House likewise distributes in pensions and other charities about 800l. yearly. 4. The Town's Hospital, above described, was opened for the reception of the poor on the 15th of November 1733. The funds whence this hospital is subsisted are, the general session, the town council, the trades house, house, and merchants house, the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> of money belonging to their funds, which are sums that have been mortified for the use of the house. These supplies, however, are found insufficient to defray the expenses of the house; for which reason an assessment is annually made upon the inhabitants in the following manner. The magistrates nominate 12, 14, or sometimes more gentlemen of known integrity and character, who have a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIST">list</a> laid before them of all the inhabitants in town. This list they divide into 16 or 18 columns. Each of these columns contains the names of such inhabitants as carry on trade to a certain extent, or are supposed to be well able to pay the sum affixed to the particular <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLUMN">column</a> in which their names are inserted. If it is necessary to raise 500l. for instance, then each name, in every separate column, is valued at as much as the fortunes of the persons in each particular column are supposed to be. If 1000l. or more is to be raised, it is only continuing a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROPORTIONAL">proportional</a> increase through the whole of the columns. This assessment has been gradually increasing. In 1782 it was 10,571l.; in 1800 it was 4534l., and in 1819 it was 10,303l. The rate of assessment has also increased during the war from 1 to 3 shillings on 100l. of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a>. 5. Wilson's Charity for the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> of boys, was founded by George Wilson, who in 1778 left 3000l. for that purpose. This fund is now considerably increased, and gives education and clothing to 48 boys, who each continues four years, so that 12 are admitted annually. Besides these, there are many public schools for the education of children; as well as many institutions of private <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETIES">societies</a> for the purpose of relieving the indigent and instructing youth, such as Graham's Society, Buchanan's Society, the Highland Society, &c. These last put annually 20 boys apprentices to trades, and during the first three years give them clothing and education. The university of Glasgow owes its origin, as we have already observed, to Bishop Turnbull. The <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a> consisted at first of a rector, a dean of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FACULTY">faculty</a>, a principal who taught <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEOLOGY">theology</a>, and three professors of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>; and, soon after this, the civil and canon laws were taught by some clergymen. From the time of its establishment in 1450 to the Reformation in 1560, the college was chiefly frequented by those who were intended for the church; its members were all <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ECCLESIASTICS">ecclesiastics</a>, and its principal support was derived from the church. The Reformation brought the university to the verge of destruction: masters, students, and servants, all forsook it. The magistrates were so sensible of the loss which the community had sustained by this desertion, that they endeavoured to restore it in 1572, by bestowing upon it considerable funds, and prescribing a set of regulations for its management. These, however, proved insufficient; for which reason King James VI. erected it anew, by a charter called the Nova Erectio, 1577, and bestowed upon it the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-TEINDS">teinds</a> of the parish of Govan. The persons who were to compose the new university were, a principal, three professors of philosophy, four students bursars, one economus, a principal's <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SERVANT">servant</a>, a janitor, and cook. Since the year 1577, the funds of the university have been considerably increased by the bounty of kings and the donations of private persons. The professors have therefore also been increased: so that at present the university of Glasgow consists of a chancellor, rector, dean of faculty, principal, and 14 professors (six of them in the gift of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>), together with bursars, &c. The archbishop of Glasgow was formerly chancellor of the university ex officio; at present, the chancellor is chosen by the rector, dean of faculty, principal, and masters. The chancellor, as being the head of the university, is the fountain of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a>, and in his name are all academical degrees bestowed. The office of rector is to exercise that academical jurisdiction in disputes among the students themselves, or between the students and citizens, which is bestowed upon the greater part of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-UNIVERSITIES">universities</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. He is chosen annually in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMITIA">comitia</a>; that is, in a meeting in which all the students, as well as the other members of the university, have a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VOICE">voice</a>. Immediately after his admission, he has been in use to choose certain persons as his assessors; and counsellors in his capacity of judge; and, in former periods, it was customary to name the ministers of Glasgow, or any other gentlemen who had no connexion with the university; but, for a great while past, the rector has constantly named the dean of faculty, the principal, and masters, for his assessors; and he has always been, and still is, in the daily practice of judging in the causes belonging to him, with the advice of his assessors. Besides these powers as judge, the rector summons and presides in the meetings of the university for the election of his successor; and he is likewise in use to call meetings of the professors for <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> up addresses to the king, electing a member to the general assembly, and other business of the like kind. The dean of faculty has, for his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a>, the giving direction with regard to the course of studies; the judging, together with the rector, principal, and professors, of the qualifications of those who desire to be created masters of arts, doctors of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a>, &c.; and he presides in meetings which are called by him for these purposes. He is chosen annually by the rector, principal, and masters. The principal and masters, independent of the rector and dean, compose a meeting in which the principal presides; and as they are the persons for whose behoof chiefly the revenue of the college was established, the administration of that revenue is therefore committed to them. The revenue arises from the teinds of the parish of Govan, granted by King James VI. in 1557; from the teinds of the parishes of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-RENFREW">Renfrew</a> and Kilbride, granted by the same monarch in 1617, and confirmed by King Charles I. on the 28th of June 1630; from the teinds of the parishes of Calder, Old and New Monkland, conveyed to them by a charter from Charles II. in 1670; from a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TACK">tack</a> of the archbishopric; and from several donations conferred by private persons. The college of Glasgow, for a very considerable time after its erection, followed the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of public teaching which is common even to this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>, and in many other universities throughout Europe; that is, each professor gave a few lectures every year, gratis, upon the particular science which he professed: but in place of this, the professors have, for a great while past, adopted the mode of private teaching: that is, they lecture and examine two hours every every day during the session, viz. from the 10th of October to the 10th of June; a method which comes much cheaper to the student, as he has it in his power, if he is attentive, to acquire his education without being under the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of employing a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TUTOR">tutor</a>. They have also private classes, in which they teach one <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> per day. The number of students who attended this college at the various classes in the session 1819-1820, was no less than 1264. The trade of Glasgow is said to have been first promoted by one Mr William Elphinstone in 1420. This trade was most probably the curing and exporting of salmon; but the first authentic <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DOCUMENT">document</a> concerning Glasgow as a trading city is in 1546. Complaints having been made by Henry VIII, king of England, that several English ships had been taken and robbed by vessels belonging to Scotland, an order of council was issued, discharging such captures for the future; and among other places made mention of in this order is the city of Glasgow. The trade which at that time they carried on could not be great. It probably consisted of a few small vessels to France loaded with pickled salmon; as this fishery was, even then, carried on to a considerable extent, by Glasgow, Renfrew, and Dumbarton. Between the years 1630 and 1660, a very great degree of attention seems to have been paid to inland commerce by the inhabitants of Glasgow. Principal Baillie informs us, that the increase of Glasgow arising from this commerce was exceedingly great. The <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPORTATION">exportation</a> of salmon and of herrings was also continued and increased. In the war between Britain and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a> during the reign of Charles II, a privateer was fitted out in Clyde to cruise against the Dutch. She was called the Lion of Glasgow, Robert M'Allan commander; and carried five pieces of cannon, and 60 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>. A spirit of commerce appears to have arisen among the inhabitants of Glasgow between the years 1660 and 1707. The citizens who distinguished themselves most during this period were Walter Gibson and John Anderson. Gibson cured and packed in one year 300 lasts of herrings, which he sent to St Martin's in France on board of a Dutch vessel called the St <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGATE">Agate</a> of 450 tons burden; his returns were brandy and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a>. He was the first who imported iron from <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STOCKHOLM">Stockholm</a> into Clyde. Anderson is said to have been the first who imported <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> wines. Whatever their trade was at this time, it could not be considerable: the ports to which they were obliged to trade lay all to the eastward: the circumnavigation of the island would therefore prove an almost unsurmountable <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAR">bar</a> to the commerce of Glasgow; and of consequence the people on the east <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a> would be possessed of almost all the commerce of Scotland. The union with England opened a field for commerce for which the situation of Glasgow, so convenient in respect to the Atlantic, was highly advantageous. Since that time the commerce of the east coast was declined, and that of the west increased to an amazing degree. No sooner was the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> of union signed, than the inhabitants of Glasgow began to prosecute the trade to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VIRGINIA">Virginia</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARYLAND">Maryland</a>; they chartered vessels from <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITEHAVEN">Whitehaven</a>, sent out cargoes of goods, and brought back tobacco in return. The method in which they at first proceeded in this trade was certainly a very prudent one. A supercargo went out with every vessel. He bartered his goods for tobacco, until such time as he had either sold off his goods, or procured as much tobacco as was sufficient to load his vessel. He then immediately set out on his return; and if any of his goods remained unsold, he brought them home with him. While they continued to trade in this way, they were of great advantage to the country, by the quantity of manufactures which they exported; their own wealth began to increase; they purchased ships of their own; and, 1718, the first vessel of the property of Glasgow crossed the Atlantic. Their imports of tobacco were now considerable, and Glasgow began to be looked upon as a considerable port: the tobacco made at the ports of Bristol, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-LIVERPOOL">Liverpool</a>, and Whitehaven, was observed to dwindle away; the people of Glasgow began to send tobacco to these places, and to undersell the English even in their own ports. Thus the jealousy of the latter was soon excited, and they took every method in their power to destroy the trade of Glasgow. The people of Bristol presented remonstrances to the commissioners of the customs at London against the trade of Glasgow, in 1717. To these remonstrances the merchants of Glasgow sent such answers to the commissioners, as convinced them that the complaints of the Bristol merchants were without foundation. But in 1721, a most formidable confederacy was entered into by almost all the tobacco merchants in South Britain against the trade of Glasgow. Those of London, Liverpool, and Whitehaven, presented severally to the lords of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURY">treasury</a>, petitions, arraigning the Glasgow merchants of frauds in the tobacco trade. To these petitions the Glasgow people gave in replies; and the lords of the treasury, after a full and impartial hearing, were pleased to dismiss the cause with the following <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a>: "That the complaints of the merchants of London, Liverpool, and Whitehaven, were groundless; and that they proceeded from a spirit of envy, and not from a regard to the interest of trade, or of the king's revenue." But the efforts of these <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> did not stop here. They brought their complaints into the house of commons. Commissioners were sent to Glasgow in 1722, who gave in their reports to the house in 1723. The merchants sent up distinct and explicit answers to these reports; but such was the interest of their adversaries, that these answers were disregarded. New officers were appointed at the ports of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GREENOCK">Greenock</a> and Port Glasgow, whose private instructions seem to have been to ruin the trade if possible by putting all imaginable hardships upon it. Hence it languished till the year 1737; but after that time it began to revive, though even after its revival it was carried on but slowly for a considerable space of time. At last, however, the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> and enterprising spirit of the merchants, seconding the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> advantages of their situation, prevailed over all opposition; and the American trade continued to flourish and increase until the year 1775, insomuch that the importation of tobacco into Clyde that year from the provinces of Virginia, Maryland, and Carolina, amounted to 57,143 hogsheads. But since the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREACH">breach</a> with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, this trade has now greatly fallen off, and very large sums are are said to remain due to the merchants from that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of the world. With regard to the manufactures of Glasgow, Mr Gibson is of opinion that the commerce to America first suggested the idea of introducing them, in any considerable degree at least.
