It is reckoned incurable, when inveterate, and in aged persons: and even under other circumstances, is very difficult of cure, externals proving of little <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>. The internals best suited to it, are those used in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUTTA">gutta</a> serena. Jul. Cæsar Claudinus, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSUL">Consul</a>. 74. gives a remedy for the glaucoma. The glaucoma is usually distinguished from the cataract or suffusion, in this, that in the cataract the whiteness appears in the pupil, very near the corner; but it shows deeper in the glaucoma. See Surgery <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

GLAUCUS

Pages 833-833

a marine god, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> deity of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. There are a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> many fabulous accounts of this <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a>: but the poetical <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of him is, that before his deification, he was a fisherman of the town of Andethon, who having one <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> taken a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of fishes, which he laid upon the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANK">bank</a>, on a sudden perceived, that these fishes, having touched a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERB">herb</a> that grew on the shore, received new strength, and leaped again into the sea: upon the sight of which extraordinary accident, he was tempted to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> of the herb himself, and presently leaped into the sea after them, where he was metamorphosed into a Triton, and became one of the sea gods.

GLAUX

Pages 833-833

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the pentandria class, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 17th order, Calycanthemæ. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

GLAZIER

Pages 833-833

an artificer who works in glass.—The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of a glazier's business consists in fitting panes of glass to the sashes and window frames of houses, pictures, &c. and in cleaning the same.

GLAZING

Pages 833-836

the crusting over earthen <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WARE">ware</a> with a vitreous substance, the basis of which is <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>. See Glass of Lead. The workers of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> earthen ware, however, are not not at the trouble of thus previously making a pure glass of lead. Their usual <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> for glazing their ware is formed of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> sand 45 pounds, of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> lead 20 pounds, of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEARL">pearl</a> ashes 20 pounds, and of common <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> 12 pounds. Powder the sand by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRINDING">grinding</a> it, and then add it to the other ingredients and grind them together; after which calcine them for some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> with a moderate <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>, and when the mixture is <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLD">cold</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POUND">pound</a> it to powder; and when wanted for <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> temper it with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>. The proportion of these ingredients may be occasionally varied. The ware after being turned on the wheel and dried in the open <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a>, is covered over with the above composition by means of a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRUSH">brush</a>; and when set in the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FURNACE">furnace</a> the violent heat soon reduces it to a perfect glass, covering the whole internal and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> surface of the vessel. We may observe, however, in general, that lead ought to be excluded from the composition of glazings, and other fluxes substituted in its stead. A transparent glazing may be prepared without lead, by calcining 40 pounds of white sand, 25 pounds of pearl ashes, and 15 pounds of common salt; and proceeding as before; and a more perfect transparent glazing may be made of sand 40 pounds, of wood ashes perfectly burnt 50 pounds, of pearl ashes 10 pounds, and of common salt 12 pounds. The following receipts are taken for the most <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> from Kunckel, who says, that they are the true glazings used at Delft and other Dutch manufactories. <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">Black</a> is made of eight parts of red lead, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> filings three, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a> ashes three, and zaffer two <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a>. This when melted <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> make a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROWN">brown</a> black; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> you want it blacker, add more zaffer to it. Blue is thus prepared: Take lead ashes <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> red lead one pound, clear sand or powdered flints two pounds, common salt two pounds, white calcined tartar one pound, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a> or other glass half a pound, zaffer half a pound; mix them well together and melt them for several times, quenching them always in cold water. If you would have it fine and good, it will be proper to put the mixture into a glass furnace for a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> or two. Another blue glazing may be formed of one pound of tartar, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of a pound of red lead, half an ounce of zaffer, and a quarter of a pound of powdered flints, which are to be fused and managed as in the last receipt. Or, take two pounds of calcined lead and tin, add five pounds of common salt, five pounds of powdered flints, and of zaffer, tartar, and Venetian glass, each one pound. Calcine and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol4.html#article-FUSE">fuse</a> the mixture as before. Or, again, take of red lead one part, of sand three parts, and of zaffer one part. For a violet blue glazing, take four ounces of tartar, two ounces of red lead, five ounces of powdered flints, and half a drachm of manganese. Brown is made of red lead and flints of each 14 parts, and of manganese two parts fused; or of red lead 12 parts, and manganese one part fused. A brown glazing, to be laid on a white ground, may be made of manganese two parts, and of red lead and white glass of each one part, twice fused. <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLESH">Flesh</a> coloured is made of 12 parts of lead ashes, and one of white glass. <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">Gold</a> coloured. Take of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LITHARGE">litharge</a> three parts, of sand or calcined flint one part; pound and mix these very well together, then run them into a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> glass with Glazing. A strong fire. Pound this glass, and grind it into a subtle powder, which moisten with a well saturated solution of silver; make it into a paste, which put into a crucible, and cover it with a cover. Give at first a gentle <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of fire; then increase it, and continue it till you have a glass, which will be green. Pound this glass again, and grind it to a fine powder; moisten this powder with some beer, so that by means of a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PENCIL">pencil</a> you may apply it upon the vessels or any piece of earthen ware. The vessels that are painted or covered over with this glazing must be first well heated, then put under a muffle; and as soon as the glass runs, you must <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SMOKE">smoke</a> them, by holding them over <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> vegetables, and take out the vessels. Mr Heinsius of Petersburgh, who sent this receipt to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a>, uses the words afflare debes fumum, which is rendered smoke them, in the Transactions. Phil. Trans. No 465. § 6. Kunckel gives several preparations for a gold coloured yellow glazing. This may be produced by fusing a mixture of three parts of red lead, two parts of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANTIMONY">antimony</a>, and one part of saffron of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARS">Mars</a>; by again melting the powdered <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MASS">mass</a>, and repeating the operation four times, or by fusing four or five times a composition of red lead and antimony of each an ounce, and of scales of iron half an ounce: or by calcining and fusing together eight parts of red lead, six parts of flints, one part of yellow ochre, one part of antimony, and one part of white glass. A transparent gold coloured glazing may be obtained by twice fusing red lead and white flints, of each 12 parts, and of filings of iron one part. Green may be prepared of eight parts of litharge or red lead, eight parts of Venice glass, four parts of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a> dust or filings of copper; or of ten parts of litharge, twelve of flint or pebble, and one of aes ustum or copper ashes.—A fine green glazing may be produced by fusing one part of the Bohemian granate, one part of filings of copper, one part of red lead, and one part of Venetian glass; or by fusing one part of white glass, the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of red lead, and also of filings of copper; powdering the mass, and adding one part of Bohemian granate to two parts of this powder. A fine green may be obtained by mixing and grinding together any of the yellow glazings with equal quantities of the blue glazings; and all the shades and teints of green will be had by varying the proportion of the one to the other, and by the choice of the kind of yellow and blue. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">Sea</a> green is made of five pounds of lead ashes, one pound of tin ashes, three pounds of flint, three <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> of a pound of salt, half a pound of tartar, and half a pound of copper dust. Iron <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> is prepared of 15 parts of lead ashes or red lead, 15 of white sand or flints, and five of calcined copper. This mixture is to be calcined and fused. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIVER">Liver</a> colour is prepared of 12 parts of litharge, eight of salt, six of pebble or flint, and one of manganese. Purple brown consists of lead ashes 15 parts, clean sand or powdered flints 18 parts, manganese one part, and white glass 15 measures, to which some add one <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> of zaffer. Red is made of antimony three pounds, litharge or red lead three, and rust of iron one: grind them to a fine powder. Or, take two pounds of antimony, three of red lead, and one of calcined saffron of Mars, and proceed as before. White. The white glazing for common ware is made of 40 pounds of clear sand, 75 pounds of litharge or lead ashes, 26 of pot ashes, and ten pounds of salt: these are three times melted into a cake, quenching it each time in clear cold water. Or it may be made of 50 pounds of clean sand, 70 of lead ashes, 30 of wood ashes, and 12 of salt. For a fine white: Take two pounds of lead and one of tin; calcine them to ashes; of this take two parts, calcined flint, white sand, or broken white glass, one part, and salt one part; mix them well together and melt them into a cake for use. The trouble of calcining the tin and lead may be prevented by procuring them in a proper state. A very fine white glazing may be obtained by calcining two parts of lead and one part of tin; and taking one part of this mass, and of flints and common salt of each one part, and fusing the mixture. A white glazing may be also prepared by mixing 100 pounds of masticof, 60 pounds of red lead, 20 pounds of calcined tin or putty, and 10 pounds of common salt, and calcining and powdering the mixture several times. Yellow is prepared of red lead three pounds; calcined antimony and tin, of each two pounds; or, according to some, of equal quantities of the three ingredients. These must be melted into a cake, then ground fine; and this operation repeated several times; or it may be made of 15 parts of lead ore, three parts of litharge of silver, and 15 parts of sand.—A fine yellow glazing may be procured by mixing five parts of red lead, two parts of powdered brick, one part of sand, one part of the white glazings, and two parts of antimony, calcining the mixture and then fusing it. Or, take four parts of white glass, one part of antimony, three parts of red lead, and one part of iron scales, and fuse the mixture; or fuse 16 parts of flints, one part of iron filings, and 24 parts of litharge. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> yellow glazing may be produced with ten parts of red lead, three parts of antimony, and three of glass, and two parts of calcined tin. See Gold colour, above.—A <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-CITRON">citron</a> yellow is made of six parts of red lead, <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> parts of fine red brick dust, and two parts of antimony. This mixture must be calcined day and night for the space of four days, in the ash hole of a glass-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> furnace, and at last urged to fusion. For the glazing of Delft ware, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PORCELAIN">Porcelain</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">Stone</a>-ware, &c., see the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> Delft Ware, Porcelain, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POTTERY">Pottery</a>. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> had a method of glazing their earthen vessels, which in many respects appears to have been superior to ours. The common brown glazing easily scales off, cracks, and in a short time becomes disagreeable to the eye. Besides, it is very easily destroyed by <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACIDS">acids</a>; nor can vessels glazed in this manner be even employed to hold water, without part of it oozing through their pores. Lead is also very destructive to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> body; and if acids are unwarily put into vessels glazed with lead, the liquors will receive a very dangerous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IMPREGNATION">impregnation</a> from the metal. The Roman glazing, which is yet to be seen upon urns dug up in several places, appears to have been made of some kind of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VARNISH">varnish</a>; and Pliny gives us a hint that it was made of bitumen. He tells us that it never lost its <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>, and that at length it became customary to glaze over <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a> in this manner. As this varnish sunk deep into the substance of the ware, it was not subject to those cracks and flaws which disfigure our vessels; and as it was not liable to be corroded by acids, it could not be subject to any of the accidents which may ensue from the use of vessels glazed with lead. Glead, or Glade, a name used in the northern parts of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> for the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-KITE">kite</a>. See Falco, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">Ornithology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Gleam is popularly used for a ray or beam of light. Among falconers a hawk is said to gleam when she casts or throws up filth from the gorge. Gleaning, the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> of gathering or picking up the ears of corn left behind after the field has been reaped and the crop carried home. By the customs of some countries, particularly those of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MELUN">Melun</a> and Estampes, all farmers and others are forbid, either by themselves or servants, to put any cattle into the fields, or prevent the gleaning in any manner whatever for the space of 24 hours after the carrying off the corn, under the penalty of confiscation. Glebe, among miners, signifies a piece of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> in which is contained some mineral ore. Glebe, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> belonging to a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> besides the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITHES">tithes</a>. Glechoma, Ground Ivy, a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the didynamia class, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 42d order, Verticillate. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> Index. Gleditsia, Triple Thorned <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ACACIA">Acacia</a>, or <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONEY">Honey</a> Locust, a genus of plants belonging to the polygamia class, and in the natural method ranking under the 33d order, Lomentaceae. See Botany Index. Gleet, in Medicine, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLUX">flux</a> of a thin limpid humour from the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-URETHRA">urethra</a>. See Medicine Index. <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol7.html#article-GLENDALAGH">Glendalagh</a>, otherwise called the Seven Churches, anciently a celebrated town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, situated five miles <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-west of Rathdrum, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WICKLOW">Wicklow</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEINSTER">Leinster</a>. The name signifies "the valley of the two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a>." In this valley, surrounded by <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> and almost inaccessible <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, St Kevin or Cavan, called also St Coemgene, about the middle of the 6th century, founded a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a>, which in a short time from the sanctity of its founder was much resorted to, and at length became a bishoprick and a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>. St Kevin died 3d <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 618, aged 120; and on that day annually numbers of persons flock to the Seven Churches to celebrate the festival of that venerated saint. During the middle ages the city of Glendalagh, called by Hovedon, Episcopatus Bistigniensis, was held in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> esteem, and received several valuable donations and privileges, its episcopal jurisdiction extending to the walls of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUBLIN">Dublin</a>.—About the middle of the 12th century, on some account or other, it was much neglected by the clergy; and became, instead of a holy city, a den of thieves, wherefore <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDINAL">Cardinal</a> Papiro, in 1214, united it to the see of Dublin, which union was confirmed by <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> John. The O'Tools, chiefs Glendalagh of Firthual, however, by the assistance of the Pope, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> after this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> to elect <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a> and abbots to Glendalagh, though they had neither revenues or authority, beyond the district of Tuathal, which was the western part of the county of Wicklow; in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of which the city was suffered to decay, and had become nearly a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DESERT">desert</a>, in 1497, when Dennis White, the last <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TITULAR">titular</a> bishop, surrendered his <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> church of St Patrick, Dublin. From the ruins of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> city still remaining, it appears to have been a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of consequence, and to have contained seven churches and religious houses; small indeed, but built in a neat elegant stile, in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a> of the Greek <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a>: the cathedral, the walls of which are yet standing, was dedicated to St <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> and St Paul. South of the cathedral stands a small church roofed with stone, nearly entire; and in several parts of the valley are a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of stone crosses, some of which are curiously carved, but without any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INSCRIPTIONS">inscriptions</a>. In the north-west corner of the cemetery belonging to the cathedral stands a round tower, 95 feet high, and 15 in diameter; and in the cemetery of a small church, on the south side of the river, near the great lake, called the Rheedhart church, are some tombs, with Irish inscriptions, belonging to the O'Tools. In a perpendicular projecting rock on the south side of the great lake, 30 yards above the surface of the water, is the celebrated <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BED">bed</a> of St Kevin, hewn out of the rock, exceedingly difficult of access and terrible of prospect. Amongst the ruins have been discovered a number of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, curiously carved, and containing inscriptions in the Latin, Greek, and Irish languages. As this city was in a valley, surrounded on all sides, except the east, by high, barren, and inaccessible mountains, the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROADS">roads</a> leading thereto are by no means the least curious part of the remains; the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> is that leading into the county of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KILDARE">Kildare</a> through Glendason. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a> for near two miles is yet perfect, composed of stones placed on their edges, making a firm and durable pavement, about 10 feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>. At a small distance from St Kevin's bed, on the same side of the mountain, are to be seen the ruins of a small stone <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> called Saint Kevin's <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CELL">cell</a>.

GLENNOIDES

Pages 836-836

the name of two cavities, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> small depressions, in the inferior <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the first vertebra of the neck.

GLINUS

Pages 836-836

in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a>, a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the decandria class; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 22d order, Caryophyllae. See Botany <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

GLIRES

Pages 836-836

the name of Linnæus's fourth order of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAMMALIA">mammalia</a>. See MAMMALIA <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

GLISSON

Pages 836-836

Francis, a learned English physician in the 17th century, was educated at <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>, and was made regius professor of that university. In 1634 he was admitted a fellow of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLLEGE">College</a> of Physicians in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. During the civil wars, he practised physic at <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLCHESTER">Colchester</a>, and afterwards settled in London. He greatly improved physic by his anatomical dissections and observations, and made several new discoveries of singular <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> towards establishing a rational practice. He wrote, 1. De rachitide, &c. 2. De lymphaeductis nuper repertis: with the Anatomica prolegomena, et Glisson Anatomiæ hepatis. 3. De naturæ substantia energitica; seu de via vitæ naturæ, ejusque tribus primis facultatibus, &c. quarto. 4. Tractatus de ventriculo et intestinis, &c. The world is obliged to him for the capsula communis, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VAGINA">vagina</a> portæ.

GLOBBA

Pages 836-836

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the monandra class. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

GLOBE

Pages 836-836

in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOMETRY">Geometry</a>, a round <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> spherical body, more usually called a Sphere. See Sphere. Globe is more particularly used for an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> sphere of metal, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLASTER">plaster</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>, or other <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>; on whose convex surface is drawn a map, or representation either of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> or heavens, with the several circles conceived thereon. See <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>. Globes are of two kinds, terrestrial and celestial; each of very considerable <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>, the one in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">astronomy</a>, and the other in geography, for performing many of the operations thereof in an easy obvious manner, so as to be conceived without any knowledge of the mathematical grounds of those arts. The <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FUNDAMENTAL">fundamental</a> parts, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> to both globes, are an axis, representing that of the world; and a spherical shell, or cover, which makes the body of the globe, on the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> surface of which the representation is drawn. See Geography <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Globes, we have observed, are made of different materials, viz. silver, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a>, paper, plaster, &c. Those <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> used are of plaster and paper. For the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a> of globes, see Geography Index. For the uses, &c. of the globes, see Geography and Astronomy. Globe Animal. See Animalcule. Globe Fish. See Ostracion, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ICHTHYOLOGY">Ichthyology</a> Index.

GLOBULARIA

Pages 836-836

Globular Blue Daisy; a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, belonging to the tetrandria class; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 48th order, Aggregatae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

GLOBULE

Pages 836-836

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DIMINUTIVE">diminutive</a> of globe, frequently used by physicians in speaking of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> particles of the blood. See Blood.

GLOCESTER

Pages 836-837

the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GLOUCESTERSHIRE">Gloucestershire</a>, in England, 106 miles from <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. It is an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>; and by Antoninus is called Clevum, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Glevum, which Camden thinks was formed from the British Caer-Gloce, signifying "a fair city." It was one of the 28 cities built by the Britons before the arrival of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, who made it one of their colonies, and in the eighth century it was esteemed one of the noblest cities in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>. It has suffered considerably by fire at different periods. It stands upon a hill; and from the middle of the city, where the four <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> streets meet, there is a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a> every way, which makes it not only clean and healthy, but adds to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>. Forging of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> seems to have been its manufacture so early as the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of William the Conqueror. <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> Henry VIII. made it the see of a bishop with a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAN">dean</a> and six prebends. Its castle, which was erected in the time of William the Conqueror, is very much decayed; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of it is leased out by the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>; and the rest serves for a prison, one of the best in England. In its <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a>, which is an ancient but magnificent fabric, and has a tower reckoned one Glocester, one of the most curious pieces of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a> in England, are the tombs of Robert <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Normandy, son to William the Conqueror, and of Edward II., and there is a whispering place like to that of St Paul's at London. In the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAPTER">chapter</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> lies Strongbow who conquered <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>. There are 12 chapels in it, with the arms and monuments of many <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> persons. King John made it a borough to be governed by two bailiffs. Henry III. who was crowned here, made it a corporation. By its present <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARTER">charter</a> from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> I. it is governed by a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STEWARD">steward</a>, who is generally a nobleman; a mayor; a recorder; 12 aldermen, out of whom the mayor is chosen; a town clerk; two sheriffs, chosen yearly out of 26 <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> councilmen; a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>-bearer; and four sergeants at mace. Here are 12 incorporated trading companies, whose masters attend the mayor on all public occasions, &c. Besides the cathedral, there are five <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> churches in this city; which is likewise well provided with <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-HOSPITALS">hospitals</a>, particularly an infirmary upon the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> of those at London, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WINCHESTER">Winchester</a>, Bath, &c. Here is a good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> over the river <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEVERN">Severn</a>, with a quay, wharf, and customhouse; but most of its business is engrossed by <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRISTOL">Bristol</a>. King Edward I. held a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> here in 1272, wherein some good laws were made, now called the Statutes of Glocester; and he erected a gate on the south side of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">abbey</a>, still called by his name, though almost demolished in the civil wars. King Richard II. also held a parliament here: and King Richard III. in consideration of his having (before his accession to the crown) borne the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Duke of Glocester, added the two adjacent <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-HUNDREDS">hundreds</a> of Dudston and King's Barton to it, gave it his sword and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a> of maintenance, and made it a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of itself by the name of the county of the city of Glocester. But after the Restoration the hundreds were taken away by <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> of parliament, and the walls pulled <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a>; because the city shut the gates against Charles I. when he besieged it in 1643; by which, though the siege was raised by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ESSEX">Essex</a>, it had suffered 20,000l. damage, having 241 houses destroyed, which reduced it so much that it has scarce recovered its former size and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-GRANDEUR">grandeur</a>. Before that time it had 11 parish churches, but six of them were then demolished. Here are abundance of crosses, and <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a> of the English kings, some of whom kept their Christmas here; several market houses supported with pillars; and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> remains of monasteries, which were once so numerous, that it gave occasion to the monkish proverb, As sure as God is in Glocester. Here is a barley market; and a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HALL">hall</a> for the assizes, called the Booth Hall. Its <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> manufacture is pins. Under the bridge is a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> engine to supply the town, and it is served with it also from Robin Hood's well, to which is a fine walk from the city. Camden says, that the famous Roman way, called Ermin Street, which begins at St <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAVID">David</a>'s in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEMBROKESHIRE">Pembrokeshire</a>, and reaches to Southampton, passes through this city. Here is a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARITY">charity</a> school for above 80 children, of whom above 70 are also clothed; and a well endowed blue-coat school. <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPULATION">Population</a> 8280 in 1811. The city sends two members to parliament. W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 2. 13. N. Lat. 51° 48'. Glocester is also the name of two counties and of several <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>; such as the county of Glocester in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-NEW_JERSEY">New <a cla</a>ss="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JERSEY">Jersey</a>, bounded on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURLINGTON">Burlington</a>, on the south by Salem and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUMBERLAND">Cumberland</a>, on the east by the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATLANTIC_OCEAN">Atlantic ocean</a>, and on the west by the river <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DELAWARE">Delaware</a>. It contains 13,172 inhabitants, besides 191 slaves. Glocester in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VIRGINIA">Virginia</a> is a well cultivated and fruitful county, about 55 miles long and 30 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, with a population of 13,498 souls, among whom are included 7063 slaves.

GLOCESTERSHIRE

Pages 837-838

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of England, is bounded on the west by <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONMOUTHSHIRE">Monmouthshire</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEREFORDSHIRE">Herefordshire</a>, on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORCESTERSHIRE">Worcestershire</a>, on the east by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-OXFORDSHIRE">Oxfordshire</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WARWICKSHIRE">Warwickshire</a>, and on the south by Wiltshire, and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOMERSETSHIRE">Somersetshire</a>. It is sixty miles in length, twenty-six in breadth, and one hundred and sixty in circumference; containing 1,100,000 acres, 320 parishes, 1229 villages, 2 cities, and 28 market <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>. In 1811 it contained 54,040 houses, and 285,514 inhabitants. It sends only 8 members to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, 6 for three towns, viz. Glocester, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TEWKESBURY">Tewkesbury</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CIRENCESTER">Cirencester</a>; and two for the county. Its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> are woollen cloths of various kinds, men's <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-HATS">hats</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>, pens, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAR">bar</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, edge tools, nails, wire, tinned plates, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a>, &c.; and of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> of the county, it exports cheese 8000 tons; <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BACON">bacon</a>, grain, cider, 5000l. worth; perry, fish, 4000l. worth, &c. It lies in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a> that takes its name from the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a> circuit. The <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> of the county is very wholesome, but the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FACE">face</a> of it is very different in different parts: for the eastern part is hilly, and is called Cotteswold; the western woody, and called the Forest of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAN">Dean</a>; and the rest is a fruitful valley, through which runs the river <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEVERN">Severn</a>. This river is in some places between two and three miles <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>; and its course through the county, including its windings, is not less than seventy miles. The tide of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOD">flood</a>, called the Boar, rises very <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, and is very impetuous. It is remarkable, that the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIDES">tides</a> are one year at the full <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOON">moon</a>, and the other at the new; one year the night tides, and the next the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>. This river affords a noble conveyance for goods and merchandise of all sorts to and from the county; but it is watered by several others, as the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WYE">Wye</a>, the Avon, the Isis, the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEYDEN">Leyden</a>, the Frome, the Stroud, and Windrush, besides lesser streams, all abounding with fish, the Severn in particular with salmon, conger eels, and lampreys. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> is in general very fertile, though pretty much diversified, yielding plenty of corn, pasture, fruit, and wood. In the hilly part of the county, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Cotteswold, the air is sharper than in the lowlands; and the soil, though not so fit for grain, produces excellent pasture for sheep; so that of the four hundred thousand that are computed to be kept in the county, the greater part are fed here. Of these sheep the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a> is exceeding fine; and hence it is that this shire is so eminent for its manufacture of cloth, of which fifty thousand pieces are said to have been made yearly, before the practice of clandestinely exporting English wool became so <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a>. In the vale, or lower part of the county, through which the Severn passes, the air and soil are very different from those of the Cotteswold: for the former is much warmer, and the latter richer, yielding the most luxuriant pastures; in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of which, numerous herds of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> cattle are kept, and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> quantities of that excellent cheese, for which it is so much celebrated, made in it. The remaining part of the county, called the Forest of Dean, was formerly almost entirely overrun with wood, and extended 20 miles in length, and 10 in breadth. It was then a nest of robbers, especially towards the Severn; but now it contains many towns and villages, consisting chiefly of miners, employed in the coal pits, or in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGGING">digging</a> for or forging iron ore, with both which the forest abounds. These miners have their particular laws, customs, courts, and judges; and the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>, as in all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> forests, has a swain-mote for the preservation of the vert and venison. This forest was anciently, and is still noted for its oaks, which thrive here surprisingly; but as there is a prodigious consumption of wood in the forges, it is continually dwindling away. A navigable canal is made from Stroud to Framilode, forming a junction between the Severn and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THAMES">Thames</a>. Its chalybeate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a> are, St Anthony's well, in Abbenhall <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARISH">parish</a>; at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BARROW">Barrow</a> and Maredon, in Bodington parish; at Ash-<a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, near Tewkesbury; at Dumbleton, near Winchcomb; at Easington, near Dursley; and at <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHELTENHAM">Cheltenham</a>. Its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> fortifications, attributed to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, Saxons, or Danes, are Abston and Wick, and at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DOWNTON">Downton</a>, Dixton, Addlesthorp, Knole, Over Upton, and Hanham. See <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GLOUCESTERSHIRE">GLOUCESTERSHIRE</a>, Supplement.

GLOCHIDON

Pages 838-838

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, belonging to the monocotyledon class. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

GLOGAW

Pages 838-838

a strong town of Germany, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SILESIA">Silesia</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of the same name. It is not very <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, but is well fortified on the side of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLAND">Poland</a>. It has a handsome castle, with a tower, in which several counsellors were condemned by <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">Duke</a> John, in 1498, to perish with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HUNGER">hunger</a>. Besides the Papists, there are a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a> and Jews. It was taken by assault, by the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRUSSIA">Prussia</a>, in 1741, and the garrison made prisoners. After the peace in 1742, the king of Prussia settled the supreme <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> here, it being, next to <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRESLAU">Breslau</a>, the most populous <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in Silesia. It is seated on the river <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ODER">Oder</a>, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>., 16° 15', N. Lat. 51° 39'. GLOGAW the Less, a town of Silesia, in the duchy of Oppeln, now in the possession of the king of Prussia. It is 19 miles south of Oppeln, and 45 northwest of Breslau. E. Long. 16° 15', N. Lat. 51° 38'.

GLORIOSA

Pages 838-838

SUPERB LILY, a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, belonging to the hexandria class, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 11th order, Sarmentosae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

GLORY

Pages 838-839

renown <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> celebrity. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> of renown, or desire of fame and reputation, appears to be one of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTION">action</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>. Glory, therefore, is not to be contemned, as some of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> philosophers affected to teach; but it imports us to regulate our pursuit after it by the dictates of reason; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the public approbation <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> not follow us in that course, we must leave her behind.—We ought to have our judgments well instructed as to what actions are truly glorious; and to remember, that in every important enterprise, as Seneca observes, *Recte facti fecisse merces est; officii fructus, ipsum officium est:* "The reward of a thing well done, is to have done it; the fruit of a good office, is the office itself." Those who by other methods scatter their names into many mouths, show they rather hunt after a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> reputation than a good one, and their reward is oftener glory, infamy than fame. Men generally, and almost instinctively, affix glory only to such actions as have been produced by an innate desire for public good; and we <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> it by that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of influence which any thing done has upon the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a>. If the actions of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERO">hero</a> conduct soonest to glory and with the greatest splendour, and if the victorious general is so great after a signal engagement; it is because the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> he has done is for the moment, and for all; and because we think without reflecting, that he has saved our habitations, our wealth, and our children, and every thing that attaches us to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. If the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of science, who in his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> has discovered and calculated the motions of the heavenly bodies, who in his alembics has unveiled some of the secrets of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, or who has exhibited to mankind a new art, rises to fame with less noise; it is because the utility which he procures is more widely diffused, and is often of less service to the present than to succeeding generations. The consequences, therefore, of these two advantages are as opposite as the causes are different; and while the benefits procured by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WARRIOR">warrior</a> appear to have no more influence, and while his glory becomes obscure, that of a celebrated writer or inventor still increases, and is more and more enlarged. His works every <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> bring back his name to that <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> which uses them, and thus still add to his celebrity and fame. This posthumous fame indeed has been decried by some writers. In particular, the author of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">Religion</a> of Nature delineated has treated it as highly irrational and absurd. "In reality (says he) the man is not known even the more to posterity, because his name is transmitted to them: He doth not live, because his name does. When it is said Julius Caesar subdued <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAUL">Gaul</a>, conquered Pompey, &c. it is the same thing as to say, the conqueror of Pompey was Julius Caesar; i.e. Caesar and the conqueror of Pompey is the same thing; Caesar is as much known by one designation as by the other. The amount then is only this, that the conqueror of Pompey conquered Pompey; or somebody conquered Pompey; or rather, since Pompey is as little known now as Caesar, somebody conquered somebody. Such a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a> business is this boasted <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IMMORTALITY">immortality</a>! and such is the thing called glory among us! To discerning men this fame is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a>, and what they despise if not shun." But surely it were to consider too curiously (as Horatio says to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAMLET">Hamlet</a>) to consider thus. For (as the elegant author of Fitzosborne's Letters observes) although fame with posterity should be, in the strict <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANALYSIS">analysis</a> of it, no other than what is here described, a mere uninteresting proposition, amounting to nothing more than that somebody acted meritoriously; yet it would not necessarily follow, that true <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> would banish the desire of it from the human <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a>: for this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PASSION">passion</a> may be (as most certainly it is) wisely implanted in our <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, notwithstanding the corresponding object should in reality be very different from what it appears in imagination. Do not many of our most refined and even contemplative pleasures owe their existence to our mistakes? It is but extending some of our senses to to a higher degree of acuteness than we now possess them, to make the fairest views of nature, or the noblest productions of art, appear horrid and deformed. To see things as they truly and in themselves are, would not always, perhaps, be of advantage to us in the intellectual world, any more than in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a>. But, after all, who shall certainly assure us, that the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> of virtuous fame dies with its possessor, and reaches not to a farther <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCENE">scene</a> of existence? There is nothing, it should seem, either absurd or unphilosophical in supposing it possible at least, that the praises of the good and the judicious, the sweetest music to an honest <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-EAR">ear</a> in this world, may be echoed back to the mansions of the next; that the poet's <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of Fame may be literally true, and though she walks upon <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, she may yet lift her head into heaven. To be convinced of the great advantage of cherishing this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> regard to posterity, this noble desire of an after life in the breath of others, one need only look back upon the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of the ancient Greeks and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>. For what other principle was it which produced that exalted strain of virtue in those days, that may well serve, in too many respects, as a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODEL">model</a> to these? Was it not the consentiones lux bonorum, the incorrupta vox bene judicantium (as Tully calls it), "the concurrent approbation of the good, the uncorrupted applause of the wise," that animated their most generous pursuits? In short, can it be reasonable to extinguish a passion which nature has universally lighted up in the human breast, and which we constantly find to burn with most strength and brightness in the noblest and best formed bosoms? Accordingly <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVELATION">revelation</a> is so far from endeavouring to eradicate the seed which nature has thus deeply planted, that she rather seems, on the contrary, to cherish and forward its growth. To be exalted with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a>, and to be had in everlasting <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REMEMBRANCE">remembrance</a>, are in the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of those encouragements which the Jewish dispensation offered to the virtuous; and the person from whom the sacred Author of the Christian system received his birth, is herself represented as rejoicing that all generations should call her blessed.

GLOSS

Pages 839-839

a comment on the text of any author, to explain his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> more fully and at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, whether in the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> any other. See the article <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMENTARY">COMMENTARY</a>. The word, according to some, comes from the Greek γλῶσσα, "tongue;" the office of a gloss being to explain the text, as that of the tongue is to discover the mind. GLOSS is likewise used for a literal translation, or an interpretation of an author in another language word for word. GLOSS is also used in matters of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, &c. for the lustre of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a>, stuff, or the like.

GLOSSARY

Pages 839-839

a sort of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DICTIONARY">dictionary</a>, explaining the obscure and antiquated terms in some old author; such are Du Cange's Latin and Greek Glossaries, Spelman's Glossary, and Kennet's Glossary at the end of his Parochial Antiquities.

GLOSSOPETRA

Pages 839-839
or GLOTTOPETRA, in href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">Natural History, a kind of extraneous fossil, something in form of a serpent's tongue; frequently found in the island of Malta and other places. The vulgar notion is, that they are the tongues of serpents petrified; and hence their name, which is a compound of γλῶσσα, "tongue" and πέτρα, "stone." Hence also their traditionary virtue in curing the bites of serpents. The general opinion of naturalists is, that they are the teeth of fishes, left at hand by the waters of the deluge, since petrified. The several sizes of the teeth of the same species, and those of the several different species of sharks, afford a vast variety of these fossil substances. Their usual colours are black, bluish, whitish, yellowish, or brown; and in shape they usually approach to a triangular figure. Some of them are simple; others are tricuspidate, having a small point on each side of the large one: many of them are quite straight; but they are frequently found crooked, and bent in all directions; many of them are serrated on their edges, and others have them plain; some are undulated on their edges, and slightly serrated on these undulations. They differ also in size as much as in figure; the larger being four or five inches long, and the smaller less than a quarter of an inch. They are most usually found with us in the strata of blue clay, though sometimes also in other substances, and are frequent in the clay pits of Richmond and other places. They are very frequent also in Germany, but nowhere so plentiful as in the island of Malta. The Germans attribute many virtues to these fossil teeth; they call them cordials, sudorifics, and alexipharmics: and the people of Malta, where they are extremely plentiful, hang them about their children's necks to promote dentition. They may possibly be of as much service this way as an anodyne necklace; and if suspended in such a manner that the child can get them to its mouth, may, by their hardness and smoothness, be of the same use as a piece of coral.

GLOTTIS

Pages 839-839

in Anatomy, the narrow slit at the upper <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the aspera arteria, which is covered by the epiglottis when we hold our breath and when we swallow. The glottis, by its <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DILATATION">dilatation</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRACTION">contraction</a>, modulates the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VOICE">voice</a>. See ANATOMY, No 183.

GLOVE

Pages 839-840

a covering for the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WRIST">wrist</a>. Gloves, with respect to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, are distinguished into leathern gloves, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a> gloves, thread gloves, cotton gloves, worsted gloves, &c. Leathern gloves are made of chamois, kid, lamb, doe, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELK">elk</a>, buff, &c. Gloves now pay a duty to the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>, which increases according to their value. To throw the glove, was a practice <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a> very usual among our forefathers; being the challenge whereby another was defied to single <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMBAT">combat</a>. It is still retained at the coronation of our kings; when the king's champion casts his glove in Westminster <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HALL">hall</a>. See CHAMPION. Favyn supposes the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> to have arisen from the eastern nations, who in all their sales and deliveries of lands, goods, &c. used to give the purchaser their glove by way of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIVERY">livery</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVESTITURE">investiture</a>. To this effect he quotes Ruth iv. 7, where the Chaldee <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PARAPHRASE">paraphrase</a> calls glove what the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> version renders by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SHOE">shoe</a>. He adds, that the Rabbins interpret by glove that passage in the cviith Psalm, In Idumeam extendam calceamentum meum, "Over Edom <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> I <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> out my shoe." Accordingly, among us, he who took up the glove, declared thereby his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACCEPTANCE">acceptance</a> of the challenge; and as a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the ceremony, continues Favyn, took the glove off his own <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> hand, and cast it upon the ground, ground, to be taken up by the challenger. This had the force of a mutual engagement on each side, to meet at the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> which should be appointed by the king, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, or judges. The same author asserts, that the custom which still obtains of blessing gloves in the coronation of the kings of France, is a remain of the eastern practice of giving possession with the glove, lib. xvi. p. 1017, &c. Anciently it was prohibited the judges to wear gloves on the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BENCH">bench</a>. And at present in the stables of most princes, it is not safe going in without pulling off the gloves.

GLOVER

Pages 840-841

RICHARD, the author of Leonidas and several other esteemed works, was the son of Richard Glover, a Hamburgh merchant in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, and was born in St Martin's lane in the year 1712. He very early showed a strong propensity to and genius for <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>; and while at school, he wrote, amongst other pieces, a poem to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of Sir <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISAAC">Isaac</a> Newton, prefixed to the view of that incomparable author's <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, published in 4to, in 1728, by his intimate friend Dr <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PEMBERTON">Pemberton</a>. But though possessed of talents which were calculated to excel in the literary world, he was content to devote his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, and at a proper <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> commenced a Hamburgh merchant. He still, however, cultivated literature, and associated with those who were eminent in science. One of his earliest friends was Matthew Green, the ingenious but obscure author of some admirable poems, which in 1737, after his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, were collected and published by Mr Glover. In 1737, Mr Glover married Miss Nunn, with whom he received a handsome fortune; and in the same <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">month</a> published Leonidas, a poem in 4to, which in this and the next year passed through three editions. This poem was <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSCRIBED">inscribed</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Cobham; and on its first appearance was received by the world with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> approbation, though it has since been un- accountably neglected. Lord Lyttleton, in a popular publication called <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">Common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">Sense</a>, and in a poem <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AD">ad</a>- dressed to the author, praised it in the warmest terms; and Dr Pemberton published, Observations on Poetry, especially epic, occasioned by the late poem upon Leo- nidas, 1738, 12mo, merely with a view to point out its beauties. In 1739, Mr Glover published "London, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the Progress of Commerce," 4to; and a ballad en- titled, Hosier's Ghost. Both these pieces seem to have been written with a view to incite the public to resent the misbehaviour of the Spaniards; and the latter had a very considerable effect. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> dissensions at this period raged with great violence, and more espe- cially in the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METROPOLIS">metropolis</a>; and at different meetings of the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIVERY">livery</a> on those occasions, Mr Glover was always called to the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a>, and acquitted himself in a very able manner, his conduct being patriotic and his speeches masterly. His talents for public speaking, his know- ledge of political affairs, and his information concern- ing trade and commerce, soon afterwards pointed him out to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a> of London as a proper person to conduct their application to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> on the subject of the neglect of their trade. He accepted the office; and in summing up the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a> gave very striking proofs of his oratorical powers. This speech was pro- nounced Jan. 27, 1742. In the year 1744 died the duchess of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARLBOROUGH">Marlborough</a>, and by her <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> left to Mr Glover and Mr <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALLET">Mallet</a> 500l. each, to write the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">Duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARL">Marl</a>- borough's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">Life</a>. This bequest, however, never took <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>. It is supposed, that Mr Glover very early re- nounced his share of it; and Mallet, though he con- tinued to talk of performing the task almost as <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> as he lived, is now known never to have made the least progress in it. About this period Mr Glover withdrew a good <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> from public notice, and lived in retire- ment. He had been unsuccessful in his business; and with a very laudable delicacy had preferred an obscure retreat to popular observation, until his affairs should put on a more prosperous appearance. He had been honoured with the attention of Frederick <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>, who once presented him with a complete set of the classics, elegantly bound; and, on his absenting himself for some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> on account of the embarrassment in his circumstances, sent him, it is said, 500l. The prince died in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a> 1751; and in May following Mr Glover was once more drawn from his retreat by the importunity of his friends, and stood candidate for the place of chamberlain of London. It unfortunately happened that he did not declare himself until most of the livery had engaged their votes; by which means he lost his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTION">election</a>. In 1753, Mr Glover produced at Drury Lane his tragedy of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BOADICEA">Boadicea</a>; which was acted <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> nights, in the month of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a>. It had the advantage of the performance of Mr Garrick, Mr Mosso, Mrs Cibber, and Mrs Pritchard. From the prologue it seems to have been patronized by the author's friends in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>; and Dr Pemberton wrote a pamphlet to recom- mend it.—In 1761, Mr Glover published Medea, a tragedy written on the Greek <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODEL">model</a>; but it was not acted until 1767, when it appeared for the first time on the stage at Drury Lane for Mrs Yates's benefit. At the accession of his present majesty, he appears to have surmounted the difficulties of his situation. In the parliament which was then called, he was chosen member for Weymouth, and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to sit as such until the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISSOLUTION">dissolution</a> of it. He, about this time, in- terested himself about <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a> affairs, at one of Mr Sul- livan's elections; and in a speech introduced the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FABLE">fable</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>, and bear; and drew this conclusion, that, whenever merchants made <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of armed forces to maintain their trade, it would end in their destruction. In 1770, the poem of Leonidas requiring a new edition, it was republished in two volumes 12mo, cor- rected throughout, and extended from nine books to twelve. It had also several new <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> added, be- sides placing the old ones in new situations. The im- provements made in it were very considerable; but we believe the public curiosity, at this period, was not suf- ficiently alive to recompense the pains bestowed on this once popular performance. The calamities arising from the wounds given to public <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 1772, by the failure of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANK">bank</a> of Douglas, Heron, and Co. in Scotland, occasioned Mr Glover's taking a very <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> in the settling those complicated concerns, and in stopping the distress then so universally felt. In Fe- bruary 1774, he called the annuitants of that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BANKING">banking</a>- <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> together, at the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a>'s Arms tavern, and laid proposals before them for the security of their de- mands, with which they were fully satisfied. He also undertook to manage the interests of the merchants and traders of London concerned in the trade to Ger- many many and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, and of the dealers in foreign linens, in their application to parliament in May 1774. Both the speeches made on these occasions were published in a pamphlet in that year. In the succeeding year he engaged on behalf of the West India merchants in their application to parliament, and examined the witnesses and summoned up the evidence in the same masterly manner he had done on former occasions. For the assistance he afforded the merchants in this business, he was complimented by them with a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of plate, of the value of £300l. The speech which he delivered in the house was in the same year printed. This, we believe, was the last opportunity he had of displaying his oratorical talents in public. Having now arrived at a period of life which demanded a recess from business, Mr Glover retired to ease and independence, and spent the remainder of his days with <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> and with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a>. It is probable that he still continued his attention to his muse, as we are informed that, besides an epic poem of considerable length, he has left some tragedies and comedies behind him in manuscript. After experiencing for some time the infirmities of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, he departed this life 25th November 1785; leaving behind him a most estimable character as a man, a citizen, and a writer. GLOW-WORM. See Lampyris, Entomology <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

GLUCINA
