in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a>, an earthy substance which was discovered by Vauquelin in 1798, in analyzing the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMERALD">emerald</a>, of which it forms a component <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a>. For an account of its properties and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMBINATIONS">combinations</a>, see Chemistry, No 1165.

GLUCKSTADT

Pages 841-841

a strong and considerable town of Germany, in the circle of Upper <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAXONY">Saxony</a>, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLSTEIN">Holstein</a>, with a strong castle, and subject to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DENMARK">Denmark</a>. It is seated on the river <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-ELBE">Elbe</a>, near its mouth, and 28 miles from Hamburgh. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 9° 20'. N. Lat. 53° 31'.

GLUE

Pages 841-843

among artificers, a tenacious viscid <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>, which serves as a cement to bind <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> connect things together. Glues are of different kinds, according to the various uses they are designed for, as the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> glue, glove glue, and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARCHMENT">parchment</a> glue; whereof the two last are more properly called size. Hamel du Monceau has written one of the best works on the subject of glue. According to this author, glue was at first principally prepared from the membranous, tendinous, and cartilaginous parts of animals, and after being dried, they were melted into tablets. It is certain, however, that every animal substance containing jelly, may be used in the manufacture of glue; and, according to Du Hamel himself, a strong, but <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a>-coloured glue may be obtained from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONES">bones</a> and harts-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORN">horn</a>, after they are dissolved in Papin's digester. Of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> of this fact Papin himself likewise assures us, for he prepared a jelly from bones, and even from <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-IVORY">ivory</a>, by which he glued together some pieces of broken glass; and subsequent experiments made by other chemists have confirmed his assertion. To the information contained on this subject in the works of Papin, Spielman has added many valuable remarks. He not only extracted glue from bones, but also from all the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> parts of animals, by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BOILING">boiling</a> alone, as well as from the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>, the wild boar, the wood-louse, and the viper. The glue manufactured in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> is of different kinds; but that which is made in England is esteemed the best. Its <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> is of a brownish <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLANDERS">Flanders</a> glue is considered as of an inferior <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> to that made in England, while the glue manufactured in France is not so good as either. The reason assigned for this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> of quality is, that bones and sinews are made <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of by the Flemish and French in the manufacture of this article, while the English employ skins, which yield a much stronger glue. Dr <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEWIS">Lewis</a> informs us that the English steep and wash the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTINGS">cuttings</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIDES">hides</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, then boil them in fresh water till the liquor becomes of a proper consistence; after which they strain it through baskets, allow it to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a>, then expose it to further <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EVAPORATION">evaporation</a>, and pour it into flat <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOULDS">moulds</a>, where it unites. When thoroughly cooled, it is converted into solid cakes, which are cut into pieces, and dried on a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NET">net</a>. Grenet for many years turned his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> to the manufacturing of glue. Having made a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of experiments on every substance formerly employed for this purpose, he found that bones afford the most abundant <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of glue, and yield it with facility. Having deprived them of the fat they contain, he procured a jelly by simply boiling them, which, when dried, and thus changed into glue, he found superior to that which was prepared in France, and nearly equal to the best glue of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>. From the experiments of Parmentier, it appears that six pounds of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUTTON">button</a>-makers raspings yielded a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POUND">pound</a> of excellent glue, not inferior to that which is manufactured in England. The glue which he obtained from the filings of ivory was equally as good, but more highly coloured. The filings of horn yielded none of this substance. To obtain glue as colourless as possible, a very small quantity of water should be employed for extracting the jelly, by which means it may be concentrated without <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> evaporation, as exposure to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> has always a greater or less influence on the colour in proportion to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. The whiteness and transparency of the Flanders glue are said to originate from an adherence to this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a>. In their consistence, colour, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>, smell, and solubility, glues are found to differ from each other. Some glues <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> dissolve by agitation in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLD">cold</a> water, while others are only soluble at the point of ebullition. It is generally admitted that the best glue is transparent, of a brownish <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> colour, and having neither taste nor smell. It is perfectly soluble in water, forming a viscous fluid, which, when dry, preserves its tenacity and transparency in every <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a>, and has more solidity, colour and viscosity, in proportion to the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> and strength of the animal from which it is produced. For the following account of the manufacture of glue, we are indebted to Mr John Clennell of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEWCASTLE">Newcastle</a>. "The improvement (he observes) of any manufacture depends upon its easy access to men of science, and a prudential theorist can never be better employed than in attempting to reduce to regularity or system the manufacture that may <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> under his attention. In conformity to the first principle, I made some notes whilst visiting a glue manufactory a few years ago in Southwark, and those, interwoven with the remarks on that subject of some chemists of the first respectability, I take the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> of sending..." sending you: at the same time I must beg of you, or your correspondents, that where it may be corrected in any manner, it may be done, and I shall feel myself obliged by the attention. "Glue is an inspissated jelly, made of the parings of hides or horns of any kind, the pelts obtained from furriers, and the hoofs and ears of horses, oxen, calves, sheep, &c. quantities of all which are imported in addition to the home supply, by many of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> manufacturers of this article: these are first digested in lime water, to cleanse them as far as it can from the grease or dirt they may have contracted; they are then steeped in clean water, taking care to stir them well from time to time; afterwards they are laid in a heap, and the superabundant water pressed out; then they are boiled in a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CALDRON">caldron</a> with clean water, skimming off the dirt as it rises, and further cleansed by putting in, after the whole is dissolved, a little melted <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALUM">alum</a> or lime finely powdered, which, by their detergent properties, still further purge it: the skimming is <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> for some time, when the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MASS">mass</a> is strained through baskets, and suffered to settle, that the remaining impurities, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> any, may subside; it is then poured gently into the kettle again, and further evaporated by boiling a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> time, and skimming, until it becomes of a clear but darkish <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROWN">brown</a> colour: when it is thought to be strong enough (which is known either by the length of time a certain quantity of water and materials have boiled, or by its appearance during ebullition), it is poured into frames or moulds of about six feet long, one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, and two deep, where it hardens gradually as the heat decreases: out of these troughs or receivers it is cut, when cold, by a spade, into <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> pieces or cakes, and each of these placed within a sort of wooden box, open in three divisions to the back; in this the glue, as yet soft, is taken to a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a> by women, where they divide it into three pieces (A) with an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> not unlike a bow, having a brass wire for its string; with this they stand behind the box and cut by its openings, from <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRONT">front</a> to back; the pieces thus cut are taken out into the open <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a>, and dried on a kind of coarse net <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, fastened in moveable sheds of about four feet square, which are fastened in rows in the glue-maker's field (every one of which contains four or five rows of net work); when perfectly dry and hard, it is fit for <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALE">sale</a>. "That is thought the best glue which swells considerably without melting, by three or four days immersion in cold water, and recovers its former dimensions and properties by drying. Glue that has got <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FROST">frost</a>, or that looks thick and black, may be melted over again and refined, with a sufficient quantity added of fresh to overcome any injury it may have sustained; but it is generally put into the kettle after what is in it has been purged in the second boiling. To know good from bad glue, it is necessary for the purchaser to hold it between his eye and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>, and if it appears of a strong dark brown colour, and free from cloudy or black spots, the article is good." A glue that is colourless and of superior quality, is obtained from the skins of eels, and known by the name of size. It is even procured from <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VELLUM">vellum</a>, parchment, and some of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>; but for common purposes this is by far too expensive, and is only made use of in those <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> of delicate workmanship where glue would be too <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GROSS">gross</a>. The skins of the rabbit, hare, and cat, are made use of in the manufacturing of size, by those who are employed in gilding <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, polishing, and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a>, in various colours. From the experiments of Mr Hatchett it appears, that membrane yields different quantities of gelatine, the solutions of which evaporated to dryness, afforded him an opportunity of observing the different degrees of viscosity and tenacity of mucilage, size, and glue. He also found that the more viscid glues are obtained with greater difficulty than such as are less so. When a cake of glue has been steeped three or four days in cold water, it is considered of the best quality, if it swell much without being dissolved, and if, when taken out, it recovers its original <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HARDNESS">hardness</a> by drying. On comparing the skins of different animals, Mr Hatchett found, that such as were most <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLEXIBLE">flexible</a> more readily yielded their gelatine, and that produced from the skin of the rhinoceros was by far the most viscid of any. The true skin of any animal was most affected by long boiling; but the hide of the rhinoceros was the most insoluble. He found that <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> was not so much affected as skin; but the cartilages of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JOINTS">joints</a>, when boiled long in water, were as perfectly soluble as the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CUTIS">cutis</a>, which is not the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> with the other cartilages, as they afford little or no gelatine. The horns of the ox, ram, and goat, are very different from those of the stag; and the small quantity of gelatine they are found to contain, is produced more gradually, and with greater difficulty. According to Hatchett, the effects of diluted nitric acid on the substances <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> employed in the manufacturing of glue, were exactly analogous to those of boiling water, and were always most powerful on those substances which contained the greatest quantity of gelatine. Almost all animal substances are convertible either into glue or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOAP">soap</a>, with this additional advantage, that those parts of them which would not be employed in making the one, are the most proper in the manufacture of the other. Another fine species of glue, known by the name of isinglass, is the produce of certain fish, very common in the Russian seas, found on entering the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> Wolga, Lyak, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DON">Don</a>, and Danube. In Muscovy it is prepared of the sturgeon and the storied, which yield the most beautiful isinglass. The fish from fresh water are esteemed the best, as they afford an isinglass more flexible and transparent than any other. When the bladder is extracted, it is washed in water to free it from the blood, if any adheres to it, but, not otherwise. It is then cut longitudinally, and the outer membrane taken off, the colour of which is brown, while the other membrane is so fine and white as to be (A) When the women, by mistake, cut only two, that which is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> the size is called a bishop, and thrown into the kettle again. with difficulty separated from the fish. They are formed into rolls of the size of the finger, with the fine membrane in the middle, and hung in the air to dry by degrees. Good isinglass is white, perfectly dry, semitransparent, and without smell. It is soluble in water with a gentle heat, but is easily dissolved in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALCOHOL">alcohol</a>, in which it differs essentially from common glue. That which is made from different parts of sea wolves, sea cows, sharks, and whales, is employed in the clarifying of different wines and other liquors. Isinglass is of all shades of colour, from pure transparency to black; but such as are large and yellow are reckoned the worst. They are opaque, and their smell is disagreeable. From 500 grains of isinglass Mr Hatchett obtained 36 grains of coal, from which 1½ grain of earthy residuum were obtained by reducing it to ashes. Of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> there were only 54.5 grains of pure coal, and the remaining 1.5 he found to be phosphate of soda, with an extremely small proportion of phosphate of lime.

GLUME

Pages 843-843

among botanists, a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of calyx, consisting of two <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> three membranous valves, which are often pellucid at the edges. This kind of calyx belongs to the grasses.

GLUTA

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the gyandria class. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. GLUTÆUS, a name <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> to three muscles whose office it is to extend the thigh. See Anatomy, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">Table</a> of the Muscles. GLUTTON. See Mustela, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAMMALIA">Mammalia</a> Index.

GLUTTONY

Pages 843-843

a voracity of appetite, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> a propensity to gormandizing. There is a morbid sort of gluttony, called fames canina, "dog-like appetite," which sometimes occurs, and renders the person seized with it an object of pity and of cure as in other diseases: (see Bulimy).—But professed habitual gluttons may be reckoned amongst the monsters of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, and deemed in a manner punishable for endeavouring to bring a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> or famine into the places where they live. For which reason, people think <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> James I. was in the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a>, when a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> being presented to him who could eat a whole sheep at one <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAL">meal</a>, he asked "What he could do more than another man?" and being answered "He could not do so much, said "Hang him then; for it is not a man should live that eats so much as 20 men, and cannot do so much as one." The <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Clodius <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALBINUS">Albinus</a> would devour more apples at once than a bushel would hold. He would eat 500 figs to his breakfast, 100 peaches, 10 melons, 20 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POUND">pound</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAPES">grapes</a>, 100 gnat-snappers, and 400 oysters. "Fye upon him (saith Lipsius); God keep such a curse from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>." One of our Danish kings named Hardiknute was so <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> a glutton, that a historian calls him Baccus de Porco, "Swine's mouth." His tables were covered four times a-<a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> with the most costly viands that either the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, or <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a>, could furnish; and as he lived he died; for, revelling and carousing at a wedding banquet at Lambeth, he fell <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> dead. His death was so welcome to his subjects, that they celebrated the day with sports and pastimes, calling it Hock tide, which signifies scorn and contempt. With this king ended the reign of the Danes in England. One Phagon, under the reign of the emperor Aurelianus, at one meal, ate a whole boar, 100 loaves of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a>, a sheep, a pig, and drank above three gallons of wine. We are told by Fuller*, that one Nicholas Wood, *Worthies, of Harrison in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KENT">Kent</a>, ate a whole sheep of 16s. price at one meal, raw; at another <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> 30 dozen of pigeons. At Sir William Sidney's in the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a>, he ate as much victuals as would have sufficed 30 men. At <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Wotton's mansion <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> in Kent, he devoured at one dinner 84 rabbits; which, by computation, at half a rabbit a man, would have served 168 men. He ate to his breakfast 18 yards of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> pudding. He devoured a whole <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-HOG">hog</a> at one sitting down; and after it, being accommodated with fruit, he ate three pecks of damosins. A counsellor at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a>, whose name was <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALLET">Mallet</a>, well known in the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> I. ate at one time an ordinary provided in Westminster for 30 men at 12d. a-piece. His practice not being sufficient to supply him with better sort of meat, he fed generally on offals, ox livers, hearts, &c. He lived to almost 60 years of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, and for the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> last years of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> ate as moderately as other men. A narrative of his life was published.

GMELIN

Pages 843-844

John George, M. D. public lecturer on <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">botany</a> and physic at Tubingen, member of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOTTINGEN">Gottingen</a>, and of the Academy of Sciences at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STOCKHOLM">Stockholm</a>, was born on the 12th of August 1709, at Tubingen, where his father was an apothecary. Such was his diligence while at school, that he was qualified to attend the academical lectures at the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> of 14, and was created <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a> of medicine when only 19. He paid a visit about this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METROPOLIS">metropolis</a> of the Russian empire, that he might have the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> of seeing some of his former teachers. There he became acquainted with Blumentrost, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTOR">director</a> of the academy, who introduced him to the meetings of the members, and procured for him an annual pension. At Petersburgh he was so much esteemed, that when he intimated a wish in 1729 to return to Tubingen, he was honoured with a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> among the regular members of the academy, and chosen professor of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHEMISTRY">chemistry</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> in the year 1731. In order to carry into execution a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> which had been formed by <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">Great</a>, for exploring a passage to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHINA">China</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JAPAN">Japan</a> along the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of the Russian empire, Gmelin was selected along with two others, as properly qualified for that undertaking, and likewise to ascertain the boundaries of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SIBERIA">Siberia</a>. The department of natural history was assigned to our author. He had with him and his companions, six students, two craftsmen, two hunters, two miners, four <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a>-surveyors, and 12 <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a>, with a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERGEANT">sergeant</a> and drummer. They began their journey on the 19th of August 1733; and in 1736, Steller and a painter joined their society, in order to assist Gmelin in his arduous labours. By exploring <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KAMTSCHATKA">Kamtschatka</a>, they hoped to accomplish their mission in a satisfactory manner, for which purpose Steller proceeded to this place, and the rest of the society <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> their travels through Siberia. In February 1743 Gmelin returned to Petersburg in safety after a dangerous journey which lasted <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> years and a half, but proved of the utmost importance to various branches of science. He resumed the offices which he had filled before; and having paid a visit in 1747 to his native <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, he was chosen professor, while absent, in the room of Bachmeister deceased. He was seized with a violent fever in May 1755, which put a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> to his valuable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, in the 45th year of his age. He was undoubtedly one of the most eminent botanists of the last century, and has rendered his name immortal by his *Flora Sibirica, seu historia plantarum Siberiae*, in four parts, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> quarto. He determined the boundaries between <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, which every celebrated geographer has adopted since his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>. Through all his works the traces of great <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODESTY">modesty</a>, a sacred regard to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>, and the most extensive knowledge of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, are remarkably conspicuous. **Gmelin, Dr Samuel**, was born in 1743 at Tubingen, where he also studied, and became doctor in medicine in 1763. He was afterwards admitted a member of the Imperial Academy of Sciences at St Petersburg. He commenced his travels in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 1768; and having traversed the provinces of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOSCOW">Moscow</a>, Voronetz, New Russia, Azof, Casan, and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRACAN">Astracan</a>, he visited, in 1770 and 1771, the different harbours of the Caspian, and examined with peculiar <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> those parts of the Persian provinces which border upon that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, of which he has given a circumstantial account in the three volumes of his travels already published. Actuated by a zeal for extending his observations, he attempted to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> through the western provinces of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>, which are in a perpetual state of warfare, and infested by numerous banditti. Upon this expedition, he quitted, in April 1772, Einzillee, a small trading place in Ghilan, upon the southern shore of the Caspian; and, on account of many difficulties and dangers, did not, until <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a> 2, 1773, reach <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SALLIAN">Sallian</a>, a town situated upon the mouth of the river Koor. Thence he proceeded to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BAKU">Baku</a> and Kuba, in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Shirvan, where he met with a friendly reception from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALI">Ali</a> Feth Khan, the sovereign of that district. After he had been joined by 20 Uralian Cossacks, and when he was only four days journey from the Russian fortress Kislar, he and his companions were, on the 5th of February 1774, arrested by order of Usmei Khan, a petty Tartar <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>, through whose territories he was obliged to pass. Usmei urged as a pretence for this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARREST">arrest</a>, that 30 years ago several families had escaped from his dominions, and had found an <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASYLUM">asylum</a> in the Russian territories; adding, that Gmelin should not be released until these families were restored. The professor was removed from prison to prison; and at length, wearied out with continued persecutions, he expired, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> 27th, at Achmet-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KENT">Kent</a>, a village of Mount <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAUCASUS">Caucasus</a>. His <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> was occasioned partly by vexation for the loss of several papers and collections, and partly by disorders contracted from the fatigues of his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> journey. Some of his papers had been sent to Kislar during his imprisonment, and the others were not without great difficulty rescued from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the barbarian who had detained him in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAPTIVITY">captivity</a>. The arrangement of these papers, which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> form a fourth volume of his travels, was at first consigned to the care of Guildenstaedt, but upon his death has been transferred to the learned Pallas.

GNOMON

Pages 844-844

in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a>, a style erected perpendicular to the horizon, in order to find the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ALTITUDE">altitude</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>. See Astronomy. By means of a gnomon, the sun's meridian altitude, and consequently the latitude of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, may be found more exactly than with the smaller quadrants. See <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUADRANT">Quadrant</a>. By the same <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> the height of any object may be found: for as the distance of the observer's eye from the gnomon, is to the height of the style; so is the distance of the observer's eye from the object, to its height. For the uses and application of gnomons, see <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>. **GNOMON of a Globe**; the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">index</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> circle.

GNOSTICS

Pages 844-846
ancient heretics, famous from the first rise of Christianity, principally in the east. It appears from several passages of the sacred writings, particularly 1 John ii. 18. 1 Tim. vi. 20. and Col. ii. 8. that many persons were infected with the Gnostic heresy in the first century; though the sect did not render itself conspicuous, either for number or reputation, before the time of Adrian, when some writers erroneously date its rise. The name is formed of the Latin *gnosticus*, and that of the Greek *γνῶσις*, "knowing," of *γνωρίζω*, "I know;" and was adopted by those of this sect, as if they were the only persons who had the true knowledge of Christianity. Accordingly, they looked on all other Christians as simple, ignorant, and barbarous persons, who explained and interpreted the sacred writings, in a too low, literal, and unedifying signification. At first the Gnostics were only the philosophers and wits of those times, who formed for themselves a peculiar system of theology, agreeable to the philosophy of Pythagoras and Plato; to which they accommodated all their interpretations of Scripture. But Gnostics afterwards became a general name, comprehending divers sects and parties of heretics, who rose in the first centuries, and who, though they differed among themselves as to circumstances, yet all agreed in some common principles. They were such as corrupted the doctrine of the gospel by a profane mixture of the tenets of the oriental philosophy, concerning the origin of evil and the creation of the world, with its divine truths. Such were the Valentinians, Simonians, Carpocratians, Nicolaitans, &c. Gnostics was sometimes also more particularly attributed to the successors of the first Nicolaitans and Carpocratians, in the second century, upon their laying aside the names of the first authors. Such as would be thoroughly acquainted with all their doctrines, reveries, and visions, may consult St Irenaeus, Tertullian, Clemens Alexandrinus, Origen, and St Epiphanius; particularly the first of these writers, who relates their sentiments at large: and confutes them at the same time: indeed, he dwells more expressly on the Valentinians than any other sort of Gnostics; but he shows the general principles whereon all their mistaken opinions were founded, and the method they followed in explaining scripture. He accuses them of introducing into religion certain vain and ridiculous genealogies, i.e. a kind of divine processions or emanations which had no other foundation but in their own wild imaginations. In effect, the Gnostics confessed that these aeons or emanations were nowhere expressly delivered in the sacred writings; but insisted at the same time, that Jesus Christ had intimated them in parables to such as could understand him. They built their theology not only on the gospels and the epistles of St Paul, but also on the law of Moses and the prophets. These last laws were peculiarly serviceable to them, on account of the allegories and allusions with which they abound, which are capable of different interpretations: Though their doctrine, concerning the creation of the world by one or more inferior beings of an evil or imperfect nature, led them to deny the divine authority of the books of the Old Testament, which contradicted this idle fiction, and filled them with an abhorrence of Moses and the religion he taught; alleging, that he was actuated by the malignant author of this world, who consulted his own glory and authority, and not the real advantage of men. Their persuasion that evil resided in matter, as its centre and source, made them treat the body with contempt, discourage marriage, and reject the doctrine of the resurrection of the body and its re-union with the immortal spirit. Their notion, that malevolent genii presided in nature, and occasioned diseases and calamities, wars, and desolations, induced them to apply themselves to the study of magic, in order to weaken the powers or suspend the influence of their malignant agents. The Gnostics considered Jesus Christ as the Son of God, and consequently inferior to the Father, who came into the world for the rescue and happiness of miserable mortals, oppressed by matter and evil beings; but they rejected our Lord's humanity, on the principle that every thing corporeal is essentially and intrinsically evil; and therefore the greatest part of them denied the reality of his sufferings. They set a great value on the beginning of the gospel of St John, where they fancied they saw a great deal of their aeons, or emanations, under the Word, the Life, the Light, &c. They divided all nature into three kinds of beings, viz. hylic, or material; psychic, or animal; and pneumatic, or spiritual. On the like principle they also distinguished three sorts of men; material, animal, and spiritual. The first, who were material and incapable of knowledge, inevitably perished, both soul and body; the third, such as the Gnostics themselves pretended to be, were all certainly saved; the psychic, or animal, who were the middle between the other two were capable either of being saved or damned, according to their good or evil actions. With regard to their moral doctrines and conduct, they were much divided. The greatest part of the sect adopted very austere rules of life, recommended rigorous abstinence, and prescribed severe bodily mortifications, with a view of purifying and exalting the mind. However, some maintained, that there was no moral difference in human actions; and thus confounding right and wrong, they gave a loose rein to all the passions, and asserted the innocence of following blindly all their motions, and of living by their tumultuous dictates. They supported their opinions and practice by various authorities; some referred to fictitious and apocryphal writings of Adam, Abraham, Zoroaster, Christ, and his apostles; others boasted, that they had deduced their sentiments from secret doctrines of Christ, concealed from the vulgar; others affirmed, that they arrived at superior degrees of wisdom by an innate vigour of mind; and others asserted, that they were instructed in these mysterious parts of theological science by Theudas, a disciple of St Paul, and by Matthias, one of the friends of our Lord. The tenets of the ancient Gnostics were revived in Spain, in the fourth century, by a sect called the Priscillianists. The appellation Gnostic sometimes also occurs in a good sense, in the ancient ecclesiastical writers, and particularly Clemens Alexandrinus, who, in the person of his Gnostic, describes the characters and qualities of a perfect Christian. This point he labours in the seventh book of his Stromata, where he shows that none but the Gnostic or learned person, has any true religion. He affirms, that were it possible for the knowledge ledge of God to be separated from eternal salvation, the Gnostic would make no scruple to choose the knowledge; and that if God would promise him impunity in doing of any thing he has once spoken against, or offer him heaven on those terms, he would never alter a whit of his measures. In this sense the father uses Gnostics, in opposition to the heretics of the same name; affirming, that the true Gnostic is grown old in the study of the holy scriptures; and that he preserves the orthodox doctrine of the apostles and of the church; whereas the false Gnostic abandons all the apostolical traditions, as imagining himself wiser than the apostles. At length the name Gnostic, which originally was the most glorious, became infamous, by the idle opinions and dissolute lives of the persons who bore it.

GOA

Pages 846-846

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> and strong town of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PENINSULA">peninsula</a> on this side the Ganges, and on the Malabar <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a>. It was taken by the Portuguese in 1508, and is the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> town of all their settlements on this side the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a> of Good Hope. It stands in an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of the same name, about 12 miles in length, and six in breadth; and the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> is built on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> side of it, having the conveniency of a fine <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> river, capable of receiving ships of the greatest burden, where they <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> within a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILE">mile</a> of the town. The banks of the river are beautified with a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of handsome structures; such as churches, castles, and gentlemen's houses. The <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> within the town is unwholesome, for which reason it is not so well inhabited now as it was formerly. The viceroy's <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> is a handsome <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>; and stands at a small distance from the river, over one of the gates of the city, which leads to a spacious street, terminated by a beautiful <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>. This city contains a great number of handsome churches, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CONVENTS">convents</a>, and cloisters, with a stately large <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOSPITAL">hospital</a>; all well endowed, and kept in good repair. The market <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> occupies an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACRE">acre</a> of ground; and in the shops about it may be had the produce of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHINA">China</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BENGAL">Bengal</a>, and other countries of less <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOTE">note</a>. Every church has a set of bells, some of which are continually ringing. There are a great many <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> converts; but they generally retain some of their old customs, particularly they cannot be brought to eat beef. The clergy are very numerous and illiterate; but the churches are finely embellished, and have great numbers of images. In one of these churches, dedicated to Bon <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a>, is the chapel of St Francisco de Xavire, whose <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOMB">tomb</a> it contains: this chapel is a most superb and magnificent place; the tomb of the saint is entirely of fine <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> marble brought from <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LISBON">Lisbon</a>; on the four sides of it the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> actions of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> of the saint are most elegantly carved in basso relievo; these represent his converting the different nations to the Catholic <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>: the figures are done to the life, and most admirably executed: it extends to the top in a pyramidal form, which terminates with a coronet of mother-of-<a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEARL">pearl</a>. On the sides of this chapel are excellent paintings, done by Italian masters; the subjects chiefly from Scripture. This tomb and the chapel appertaining to it, must have cost an immense sum of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a>; the Portuguese justly esteem it the greatest rarity in the place. The houses are large, and make a fine show; but within they are but poorly furnished. The inhabitants are contented with greens, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>, and roots; which, with a little <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICE">rice</a>, and fish, is their principal diet, though they have hogs and fowls in plenty. The river's mouth is defended by several forts and batteries, well planted with large cannon on both sides; and there are several other forts in different places. Goa is the residence of a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a> general, who lived formerly in great splendour. He is also commander in chief of all the Portuguese forces in the East Indies. They kept here formerly two regiments of European infantry, three legions of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEPOYS">sepoys</a>, three troops of native <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>, and a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITIA">militia</a>; in all about 5000 men. But Goa is at present on the decline, and in little <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> no estimation with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> powers; indeed their bigotry and superstitious <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a> to their faith is so general, that the inhabitants of the city and island are now reduced to about 20,000; the chief <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of whom have been baptized; for they <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> not suffer any Mussulman or Gentoo to live within the precincts of the city; and these few are unable to carry on the husbandry or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> of the country. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PORTUGAL">Portugal</a> is obliged to send out annually a very large sum of money, to defray the current expenses of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>; which money is generally swallowed up by the convents and soldiery. There was formerly an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INQUISITION">inquisition</a> at this place, but it is now abolished; the building still remains, and by its black outside appears a fit <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMBLEM">emblem</a> of the cruel and bloody transactions that passed within its walls! <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVISIONS">Provisions</a> are to be had at this place in great plenty and perfection. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 73. 46. N. Lat. 15. 28. GOAL. See Gaol. GOAT. See Capra, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAMMALIA">Mammalia</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. GOAT'S <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEARD">Beard</a>. See Tragopogon, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> Index. GOAT-Sucker. See Caprimulgus, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">Ornithology</a> Index.

GOBELIN

Pages 846-846

Gilles, a celebrated French dyer, in the reign of Francis I. discovered a method of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DYEING">dyeing</a> a beautiful scarlet, and his name has been given ever since to the finest French scarlets. His <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, in the suburb of St Marcel at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, and the river he made <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of, are still called the Gobelins. An academy for <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a>, and a manufactory of fine tapestries, were erected in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> in 1666; for which reason the tapestries are called the Gobelins.

GOBIUS

Pages 846-846

a genus of fishes belonging to the order of thoracici. See <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ICHTHYOLOGY">Ichthyology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

GOBLET

Pages 846-846
or Gobelet, a kind of drinking cup, or bowl, ordinarily of a round figure, and without either foot or handle. The word is French, goblet; which Salmasius, and others, derive from the barbarous Latin cupa. Budeus deduces it from the Greek κύπαρισσος, a sort of cup.

GOD

Pages 846-847

one of the many names of the Supreme Being. See Christianity, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METAPHYSICS">Metaphysics</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MORAL_PHILOSOPHY">Moral <a class="</a>xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">Philosophy</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEOLOGY">Theology</a>. God is also used in speaking of the false deities of the heathens, many of which were only creatures to which divine honours and worship were superstitiously paid. The Greeks and Latins, it is observable, did not <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> by the name of God, an all-perfect being, whereof eternity, infinity, omnipresence, &c. were essential attributes; with them, the word only implied an excellent and superior <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>; and accordingly they gave the appellation gods to all beings of a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> class higher and more perfect than that of men; and especially to those who were inferior agents in the divine administration, all subject to the one Supreme. Thus men themselves, according to their system, might become gods after <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>; inasmuch as their souls might attain to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of excellence superior to what they were capable of in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. The first divines, Father Bossu observes, were the poets: the two functions, though now separated, were originally combined; or, rather, were one and the same thing. Now the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> variety of attributes in God, that is, the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of relations, capacities, and circumstances, wherein they had occasion to consider him, put these poets, &c., under a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of making a partition, and of separating the divine attributes into several persons; because the weakness of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> mind could not conceive so much power and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTION">action</a> in the simplicity of one single divine nature. Thus the omnipotence of God came to be represented under the person and appellation of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a>; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a> of God, under that of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINERVA">Minerva</a>; the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> of God, under that of Juno. The first idols or false gods that are said to have been adored, were the stars, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOON">moon</a>, &c., on account of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>, and other benefits, which we derive from them. Afterwards the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> came to be devised, for furnishing <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> necessary for the subsistence of men and animals; then fire and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> became objects of divine worship, for their usefulness to human life. In <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, and by degrees, gods became multiplied to infinity; and there was scarce anything but the weakness or caprice of some devotee or other elevated into the rank of deity; things useless or even destructive not excepted. See <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MYTHOLOGY">Mythology</a>.

GODALMING

Pages 847-847

a town of England, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SURREY">Surrey</a>, 35 miles from <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. It is situated on the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WYE">Wye</a>, which has been rendered navigable for barges from <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUILDFORD">Guildford</a>, whence the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> is open to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THAMES">Thames</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> is much admired for its neat and lofty spire. Here are manufactories of mixed and blue kerseys, of stockings, blankets, &c. <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPULATION">Population</a> 3,543 in 1811. W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. c. 31. N. Lat. 51. r. GODFREY of Bouillon, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of Lorrain, a most celebrated crusader, and victorious general. He was chosen general of the expedition which the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> undertook for the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RECOVERY">recovery</a> of the Holy <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">Land</a>, and sold his dukedom to prepare for the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>. He took <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a> from the Turks in 1099; but his piety, as historians relate, would not permit him to wear a diadem of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> where his Saviour had been crowned with thorns. The <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SULTAN">sultan</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a> afterwards sent a terrible <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> against him; which he defeated, with the slaughter of about 100,000 of the enemy. He died in 1160.

GODDESS

Pages 847-847

a heathen deity of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEX">sex</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> had almost as many goddesses as gods: such were, Juno the goddess of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DIANA">Diana</a> the goddess of woods, &c., and under this character were represented the virtues, graces, and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> advantages of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>; <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>, piety, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>, fortune, victory, &c. It was the peculiar privilege of the goddesses to be represented naked on medals; for it was supposed that the imagination must be awed and restrained by the consideration of the divine character. GODFATHERS and GODMOTHERS, persons who, at the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BAPTISM">baptism</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INFANTS">infants</a>, answer for their future conduct, and solemnly <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROMISE">promise</a> that they <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> renounce the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVIL">devil</a> and all his works, and follow a life of piety and virtue; and by this means lay themselves under an indispensable obligation to instruct them, and watch over their conduct. This <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> is of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> antiquity in the Christian <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>; and was probably instituted to prevent children being brought up in idolatry, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> their parents died before they arrived at years of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-DISCRETION">discretion</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of godfathers and godmothers is reduced to two, in the church of Rome; and three, in the church of England: but formerly they had as many as they pleased. GODFREY of Bouillon, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of Lorrain, a most celebrated crusader, and victorious general. He was chosen general of the expedition which the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> undertook for the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RECOVERY">recovery</a> of the Holy <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">Land</a>, and sold his dukedom to prepare for the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>. He took <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a> from the Turks in 1099; but his piety, as historians relate, would not permit him to wear a diadem of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> where his Saviour had been crowned with thorns. The <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SULTAN">sultan</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a> afterwards sent a terrible <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> against him; which he defeated, with the slaughter of about 100,000 of the enemy. He died in 1160.

GODMANCHESTER

Pages 847-847

a town of Huntingdonshire 16 miles from <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>, and 37 from <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. It has a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> on the Ouse, opposite to Huntingdon; was formerly a Roman <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>, by the name of Durostorpone, where many Roman coins have been often dug up; and according to old writers, in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of the Saxons it was the see of a bishop, and had a castle built by one Gorman a Danish <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>, from which the town was called Gormanchester. It is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> village, containing 1,779 inhabitants in 1811, and is seated in a fertile <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>, abounding with corn. It is said that no town in England kept more ploughs at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> than this has done. The inhabitants boast they formerly received our kings as they made a progress this way, with <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> score ploughs at a time, finely adorned with their trappings, &c. James I. made it a corporation by the name of two bailiffs, 12 assistants, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONALTY">commonalty</a> of the borough of Godmanchester. Here is a school, called the Free <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAMMAR">Grammar</a>-School of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a>. On the west side of the town is a noble though <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> seat otherwise called <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUTTA">Gutta</a> Anglica, the secret of which he sold to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> II. for £1000l. and which Dr. Lister assures us was only the volatile spirit of raw <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a> rectified with <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CINNAMON">cinnamon</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> some other essential oil. But he claims more particular regard, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> what Bishop Seth <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WARD">Ward</a> says be true, that he was the first Englishman who made that noble astronomical <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TELESCOPE">telescope</a>.

GODSTOW

Pages 847-848

a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-west of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, in a sort of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> formed by the divided streams of the Isis after being joined by the Evenlode. It is noted for catching of fish and dressing them; but more so for the ruins of that nunnery which fair <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROSAMOND">Rosamond</a> quitted for the embraces of Henry II. The people show a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> hole in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> here, where they say is a subterraneous passage, which goes under the river to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOODSTOCK">Woodstock</a>, by which she used to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> and repass. Little more remains at present than ragged walls, scattered over a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of ground. An arched gateway, and another venerable ruin, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the tower of the conventual <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, are still standing. Near the altar in this church fair Rosamond was buried, but the body was afterwards removed by order of a bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LINCOLN">Lincoln</a>, the visitor. The only entire part is small, formerly a private chapel. Not many years since a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COFFIN">coffin</a>, said to have been Rosamond's, who, perhaps, was removed from the church to this place, was to be seen here. The <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> has been put to various uses, and at present serves occasionally for a stable.

GODWIN

Pages 848-848

Francis, successively bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LLANDAFF">Llandaff</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEREFORD">Hereford</a>, was born in 1567. He was eminent for his learning and abilities; being a good mathematician, an excellent <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, a pure Latinist, and an accurate historian. He understood the true <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEORY">theory</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOON">moon</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> a century before it was generally known. He first started those hints afterwards pursued by Bishop Wilkins, in his "Secret and swift messenger;" and published "A catalogue of the lives of English <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a>." He has nevertheless been accused as a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> simoniac, for omitting no opportunity of disposing of preferments in order to provide for his children. He died in 1648. GODWIN <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Goodwin Sands. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KENT">KENT</a>. GODWIT. See SCOLOPAX, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">ORNITHOLOGY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

GOES

Pages 848-848
or Ter Goes, a strong and considerable town of the United Provinces, in Zealand, and capital of the island of South Beverland. It communicates with the sea by a canal; and is 10 miles east of Middleburgh, and 30 north of Ghent. Population 3700. E. Long. 3° 50'. N. Lat. 51° 33'. GOG and MAGOG, two names generally joined together in scripture, (Ezek. xxxviii. 2, 3, &c. xxxix. 1, 2, &c. Rev. xx. 8.). Moses speaks of Magog the son of Japhet, but says nothing of Gog, (Gen. x. 2. 1 Chr. i. 5.). Gog was prince of Magog, according to Ezekiel. Magog signifies the country or people, and Gog the king of that country. The generality of the ancients made Magog the father of the Scythians and Tartars; and several interpreters discovered many footsteps of their name in the provinces of Great Tartary. Others have been of opinion that the Persians were the descendants of Magog; and some have imagined that the Goths were descended from Gog and Magog; and that the wars described by Ezekiel, and undertaken by Gog against the saints, are no other than those which the Goths carried on in the fifth age against the Roman empire. Bochart has placed Gog in the neighbourhood of Caucasus. He derives the name of this celebrated mountain from the Hebrew Gog chasan "the fortress of Gog." He maintains that Prometheus, said to be chained to Caucasus by Jupiter, is Gog, and no other. There is a province in Iberia called the Gogarene. Lastly, the generality believe, that Gog and Magog, mentioned in Ezekiel and the Revelation, are to be taken in an allegorical sense, for such princes as were enemies to the church and saints. Thus many by Gog in Ezekiel understand Antiochus Epiphanes, the persecutor of the Jews who were firm to their religion; and by the person of the same name in the Revelations, they suppose Antichrist to be meant, the great enemy of the church and faithful. Some have endeavoured to prove that Gog, spoken of in Ezekiel, and Cambyses king of Persia, were one and the same person; and that Gog and Magog in the Revelation denote all the enemies of the church, who should be persecutors of it to the consummation of ages.

GOGMAGOG HILLS

Pages 848-848

are hills so called, three miles from <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>, remarkable for the intrenchments and other works <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> up here; whence some suppose it was a Roman <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMP">camp</a>; and others, that it was the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> of the Danes.

GOGUET

Pages 848-848

Antony Yves, a French writer, and author of a celebrated <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, intitled, L'Origine des Lois, des Arts, des Sciences, et de leur Progres chez les anciens Peuples, 1758, 3 vols 4to. His father was an advocate, and he was born at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> in 1716. He was very unpromising as to abilities, and reckoned even dull, in his early years; but his understanding developing itself, he applied to letters, and at length produced the above work. The reputation he gained by it was <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a>; but he enjoyed it a very short <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>; dying the same year of the smallpox, which disorder, it seems, he always dreaded. It is remarkable, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONRAD">Conrad</a> Fugere, to whom he left his library and his MSS. was so deeply affected with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of his friend, as to die himself three days after him. The above work has been translated into English, and published in 3 vols 8vo.

GOITO

Pages 848-848

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANTUA">Mantua</a>, taken by the Germans in 1701, and by the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HESSE">Hesse</a> in 1706. It is seated on the river Mincio, between the lake of Mantua and that of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GARDA">Garda</a>, 10 miles <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-west of Mantua. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 11° 0. N. Lat. 45° 16'.

GOLCONDA

Pages 848-849

a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Hindostan, now called <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HYDERABAD">Hyderabad</a>. It is bounded on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by that of Orixa, on the west by that of Balagate, on the south by Bisnagar, and on the east by the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BENGAL">Bengal</a>. It abounds in corn, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICE">rice</a>, and cattle; but that which renders it most remarkable are the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIAMOND">diamond</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a>, which were formerly the most considerable in the world: they were usually purchased of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a>, who bought parcels of ground to search for these precious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONES">stones</a> in. They have also mines of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a>, fine <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> for <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>-blades, and curious calicoes and chintzes. As this is one of the few of the old Mogul governments remaining, more of the old forms and ceremonies of that <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> dynasty are retained at the nizam's <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> than at any other in Hindostan. There is a town of the same name, seated at the foot of a mountain. It was formerly the residence of the kings, and is now much frequented by the European merchants. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 78° 42'. N. Lat. 17° 10'.

GOLD

Pages 849-849

the most valuable of all the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-METALS">metals</a>, is of a bright <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> when pure, but becomes more <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> less <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> in proportion as it is alloyed with other metals. It is the heaviest of all known bodies, platinum only excepted. See <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINERALOGY">Mineralogy</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Method of Recovering Gold from Gilt Works. The solubility of gold, and the indissolubility of silver, in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AQUA">aqua</a> regia, affords a principle on which gold may be separated from the surface of silver; and, on this foundation, different processes have been contrived, of which the two following appear to be the best.—Some powdered sal ammoniac, moistened with aquafortis into the consistence of a paste, is spread upon the gilt silver, and the piece heated till the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> smokes and becomes nearly dry: being then thrown into <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, it is rubbed with a scratch <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRUSH">brush</a> composed of fine <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a> wire bound together; by which the gold easily comes off. The other way is, by putting the gilt silver into <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> aqua regia, kept so hot as nearly to boil, and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> the metal frequently till it becomes all over <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a>; it is then to be washed with a little water, and rubbed with the scratch brush, to get off what gold the aqua regia may have left. This last method appears preferable to the other; as the same aqua regia may be made to serve repeatedly till it becomes saturated with the gold, after which the gold may be recovered pure by precipitation with sulphate of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>. For separating gold from gilt <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>, some <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> a solution of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BORAX">borax</a> to be applied on the gilt parts, but nowhere else, with a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PENCIL">pencil</a>, and a little powdered sulphur to be sprinkled on the places thus moistened; the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the solution of borax seems to be to make the sulphur adhere; the piece being then made <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> hot, and quenched in water, the gold is said to be so far loosened as to be wiped off with a brush. Others mix the sulphur with nitre and tartar, and form the mixture with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VINEGAR">vinegar</a> into a paste, which is spread upon the gilt parts.

GOLF

Pages 856-856

the name of a certain <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GAME">game</a> among the Scots, and said to be peculiar to their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>.—Among them it has been very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a>; for there are statutes prohibiting it as early as the year 1457, lest it should interfere with the sport of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHERY">archery</a>. It is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> played on rugged broken ground, covered with short grass, in the neighbourhood of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> shore. A field of this sort is in Scotland called links. The game is generally played in parties of one <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> two on each side. Each party has an exceeding hard <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALL">ball</a>, somewhat larger than a hen's <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGG">egg</a>. This they strike with a slender and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELASTIC">elastic</a> club, of about four feet <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a>, crooked in the head, and having <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> run into it, to make it heavy. The ball being struck with this club, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> fly to the distance of 200 yards, and the game is gained by the party who puts his ball into the hole with the fewest strokes. But the game does not depend solely upon the striking of the longest ball, but also upon measuring the strength of the stroke, and applying it in such <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> as to lay the ball in smooth ground, whence it may be easily moved at the next stroke. To encourage this amusement, the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a>, A.D. 1744, gave to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> of golfers a silver club, to be played for annually by the company, the victor to append a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> or silver piece to the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIZE">prize</a>. It has been played for every year since, except the years 1746 and 1747. For their better accommodation, 22 members of the company subscribed 30l. each in the year 1768, for <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, where their meetings might be held. The spot chosen for this purpose was the south-west corner of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-LEITH">Leith</a> Links, where an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AREA">area</a> was taken in feu from the magistrates of Edinburgh, and a commodious house and tavern built upon it.

GOLIUS

Pages 856-856

JAMES, a celebrated professor of Arabic and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEYDEN">Leyden</a>, was descended from a very <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> family, and born at the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAGUE">Hague</a> in the year 1596. He was put to the university of Leyden, where he studied under Erpinius; and having made himself <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of all the learned languages, applied himself to the mathematics, physic, and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a>. He afterwards travelled into <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>; and became greatly esteemed by the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOROCCO">Morocco</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SULTAN">sultan</a> of the Turks. He at length returned to Leyden, loaded with <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUSCRIPTS">manuscripts</a>; and in 1624, succeeded Erpinius in the Arabic <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a>.
