As he had been an eyewitness of the wretched state of Christianity in the Mahometan countries, he was filled with the compassion of a fellow-Christian; and none ever solicited for a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> and profit with greater eagerness, than he for procuring a new edition of the New <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a>, in the original <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, with a translation into the vulgar Greek, by an Archimandrite; and as there are some of these <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> who <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> the Arabic tongue in divine <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>, he also took care to have dispersed among them an Arabic translation of the confession of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a>, together with the Catechism and Liturgy. In 1626, he was also chosen professor of mathematics; and discharged the functions of both professorships with the greatest applause during 40 years. He was likewise appointed interpreter in ordinary to the states for the Arabic, Turkish, Persian, and other eastern languages, for which he had an annual pension, and a present of a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> chain, with a very beautiful medal, which he wore as a badge of his office. He published, 1. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TAMERLANE">Tamerlane</a>, written in Arabic. 2. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of the Saracens, written by Elmarin. 3. Alferganus's Elements of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a>, with a new version, and learned commentaries. 4. An excellent Arabic lexicon. 5. A Persian <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DICTIONARY">Dictionary</a>. He died in 1667.

GOLTZIUS

Pages 856-857

HENRY, a famous engraver and painter, born in 1558, at Mulbreck in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of Juliers. He was taught the art of engraving by Theodore Cuenenbert; and succeeded very wonderfully in it, notwithstanding the disadvantage of a lame <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, which was occasioned by his falling into the fire whilst young. He was first employed by his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>, and afterwards he worked for <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a> Galle. <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOMESTIC">Domestic</a> troubles and ill <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> occasioned him to travel. He went through Germany into <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>; and passed under a feigned name, that his studies might not be interrupted. He visited <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOLOGNA">Bologna</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLORENCE">Florence</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>, and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>, constantly applying himself to <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> from the antique <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a>; and the works of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> masters. At Rome he resided the longest; and there he produced several excellent engravings from Polidoro Raphael, and other eminent painters. On his return to his native <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> he established himself at Haerlem, where he engraved many of the drawings which he had made during his abode in Italy. He died at Haerlem in 1617, aged 59. He is said to have been 40 years old before he began to paint: yet his pictures are spoken of with great commendation; but as he did not produce any great <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of them, they are rarely to be met with. As an engraver, he deserves the highest commendation. No <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> ever surpassed, and few have equalled, him in the command of the graver and freedom of execution. He copied the style of Albert Durer, Lucas of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEYDEN">Leyden</a>, and other old masters, with astonishing exactness. Sometimes his engravings are neat in the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a>; at other times they are performed in a bold open manner, without the least restraint. He also engraved several of his own designs on wood, in that manner which is distinguished by the appellation of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CHIARO_SCURO">chiaro-scuro</a>. Of his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINTS">prints</a>, which are very numerous, it may here suffice to specify two <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> three of the most celebrated: 1. Six <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> upright plates, known by the name of his masterpieces. These, it is said, he engraved to convince the public that he was perfectly capable of imitating the styles of Albert Durer, Lucan Van Leyden, and other masters, whose works were then held in higher estimation than his own: for he had adopted a new manner, which he pursued because he thought it superior, and not because he was incapable of following the others. It is reported that with one of them, the Circumcision, which he smoked to give it the more plausible <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> of antiquity, he actually deceived some of the most <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> connoisseurs of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>; by one of whom it was bought for an original engraving of Albert Durer. The subjects of these plates are, The Annunciation of the Virgin; the Meeting of the Virgin with <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a>, called the Visitation; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATIVITY">Nativity</a> of Christ; the Circumcision of Christ; the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ADORATION">Adoration</a> of the Wise Men; the Holy Family. 2. The Judgment of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIDAS">Midas</a>, a large plate lengthwise. 3. The Venetian <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALL">Ball</a>, a large plate lengthwise, from Theodore Bernard. 4. The Boy and Dog. Dog, a middling-sized upright plate, from a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of his own; an admirable print. 5. The Necromancer, a middling-sized upright oval print, in chiaro-scuaro. 6. Night in her Chariot, the same.

GOMBAULD

Pages 857-857

JOHN OGIER DE, one of the best French poets in the 17th century, and one of the first members of the French academy, was born at St <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">Just</a> de Lussac. He acquired the esteem of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a> de Medicis, and of the wits of his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. He was a Protestant, and died in a very advanced <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>. He wrote many works in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a> and prose. His epigrams, and some of his sonnets, are particularly esteemed.

GOMBROON

Pages 857-857

by the natives called Bander Abassi, a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>, situated in N. Lat. 27° 20' E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 55° 40'. The name of Gombroon, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Comerong, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPTAIN">Captain</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAMILTON">Hamilton</a> tells us, it had from the Portuguese; because it was remarkable for the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of prawns and shrimps caught on its coasts, by them called come-rong. This city owes its wealth and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-GRANDEUR">grandeur</a> to the demolition of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-ORMUS">Ormus</a>, and the downfall of the Portuguese empire in the East Indies. It is now justly accounted one of the greatest marts in the East, was built by the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> Shah Abas, and from him, as some think, obtained the name of Bander Abassi, which signifies the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of Abas. It stands on a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> about <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> leagues to the northward of the east end of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of Kishmish, and three leagues from the famous Ormus. The English began to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> here about the year 1631, when, in consideration of their services against the Portuguese, Shah Abas granted them half the customs of that port. This was confirmed by a phirmaund, and duly regarded, till the English began to neglect the services they had stipulated. Whether the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> has any emolument from the customs at present, is what we cannot pretend to ascertain. The town is <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, but its situation bad; wanting almost every thing that contributes to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a> and even support of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. Towards the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> it is encompassed by a sort of wall; and towards the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> are several small forts with a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLATFORM">platform</a>, and a castle or citadel, mounted with cannon to secure it and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a> from the attempts of an enemy by sea. The houses in most of the streets are so out of repair, some half <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a>, others in a heap of rubbish, that a stranger would imagine the town had been sacked and ravaged by a barbarous people; not a vestige of the wealth really contained in the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> appearing in view. The bazars and shops round them are kept, for the most <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a>, by Banians, whose houses are generally in good order. Most of the houses are built with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> and lime, but some of the best with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>. Many of them have a sort of ventilators at top, which contributes greatly to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> of the inhabitants in the hot seasons of the year. The most sickly months here are April, May, September, and October. With fish and mutton the inhabitants are well supplied. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICE">Rice</a> is imported from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a>; and wheat is so plenty, that the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a> subsist chiefly on <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a> and dates. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> hereabouts abounds in the most delicious <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>, as apricots, peaches, pomegranates, pears, mangoes, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAPES">grapes</a>, quavas, plums, sweet quinces, and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> melons. The apricots, however, are small, and extremely dangerous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> eaten to excess. Those conveniences are more than overbalanced by the scarcity of fresh water, with which the inhabitants are supplied from Asseen, a place <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> miles distant, Gombroon; there not being a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> or well in the town. Persons of condition keep a camel constantly employed in bringing fresh and wholesome water. Captain Hamilton gives it as his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, that one cause of the unwholesomeness of this city is the reflection of the rays of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> from a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> mountain to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of it. He says, that when the beams are reflected from this mountain, they almost fire the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a>; and, for two or three months in the year, render the situation intolerable. For this reason the people of condition retire into the country, to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> the heats of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a>, and August. The very sea, during this season, is affected, insomuch that the stench is no less disagreeable than that of putrid carcases; and this is increased by the quantities of shell-fish left on the shore, from which an exhalation arises that tarnishes <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> and silver, and is less tolerable than the bilge-water of a tight ship. At Asseen the English <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACTORY">factory</a> have a country <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> and gardens, to which they retire occasionally. Here they have whole groves of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEVILLE">Seville</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORANGE">orange</a> trees, which, though not <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> to the country, thrive very well, and are always verdant, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> ripe and green fruit, with blossoms, all at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. They have likewise tanks and ponds of fine fresh water, with everything else that can moderate the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a>, and render life agreeable and elegant. About 10 miles from Asseen is a place called Minoa, where are <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLD">cold</a> and hot natural <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATHS">baths</a>, reckoned infallible in the cure of all scrophulous disorders, rheumatisms, and other diseases, by <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATHING">bathing</a>. Gombroon is extremely populous, on account of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> carried on by the Dutch and English factories, as well as the natives. The English factory is <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> by the sea, at some distance from the Dutch, which is a commodious and fine new <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>. A great part of the company's profits arises from freights. As the natives have not one good ship of their own, and are extremely ignorant of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a>, they freight their goods for <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SURAT">Surat</a>, and other <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> marts, in English and Dutch bottoms, at an exorbitant rate. The commodities of the Gombroon market are, fine wines of different kinds, raisins, almonds, kish-mishes, prunellas, dates, pistachio-nuts, ginger, silks, carpets, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>, tutti, galbanum, ammoniae, assafetida, tragacanth, with other <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUMS">gums</a>, and a variety of shop medicines. These are in a great <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> the produce of Carmania, which they bring to Gombroon in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARAVANS">caravans</a>. The English company had once a small factory in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Carmania, chiefly for the sake of a fine <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a> produced there, and used by the hatters. The said company had once a project of carrying a breed of the Persian goats to St Helena; but whether it was executed, or what success it met with, we cannot say. Although the company pay no customs, yet they usually make a present to the shabander, to avoid the trouble he has it in his power to give them. All private traders with the company's passes, enjoy the same privileges, on paying two per cent. to the company, one to the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGENT">agent</a>, and one to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROKER">broker</a>. All private trade, either by European or country ships, has long been engrossed by the company's servants.

GOMERA

Pages 857-857

one of the Canary <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>, lying between Ferro and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TENERIFFE">Teneriffe</a>. It has one good town of the same name, with an excellent harbour, where the Spanish...

GOMORRAH

Pages 857-858

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, one of the cities of the plain <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> of the vale of Siddim in Judea, destroyed together with Sodom by fire from heaven, on account of the wickedness of the people. To determine its particular situation at present is impossible.

GOMOZIA

Pages 858-858

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the tetrandria class. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

GOMPHOSIS

Pages 858-858

in Anatomy, that kind of articulation by which the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a> are fixed in the jaw-bone. See Anatomy, No. 2. GOMPHRÆNA, Globe Amaranth; a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the pentandra class; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 54th order, Miscellanea. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

GONAQUA

Pages 858-858

the name of a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> inhabiting about the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a>, and supposed by Dr Sparrman to be a mixture of Hottentots and Caïres. See Hottentots.

GONDAR

Pages 858-858

the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABYSSINIA">Abyssinia</a>; situated, according to Mr Bruce's observations, in latitude 12° 30' <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONGITUDE">longitude</a> 57° 40' east from <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREENWICH">Greenwich</a>. It lies upon the top of a hill of considerable height, and consists of about 10,000 families in times of peace. The houses are chiefly of clay, with roofs thatched in the form of cones. At the west end of the town is the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>; formerly, as Mr Bruce informs us, a structure of considerable <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a>, being a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> four stories <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, flanked with square towers, and affording from the top of it a magnificent view of all the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> southward to the lake Tzana. It was built in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of Facilidas, by masons from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a>, and by such Abyssinians as had been instructed in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a> by the Jesuits before their expulsion. <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of it is now in ruins, having been burnt at different times; but there is still ample lodging in the two lowest floors, the audience chamber being above 120 feet <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a>. By the side of this structure there have been built by different kings apartments of clay only, in the fashion of their own country. The palace, with all its contiguous buildings, is surrounded by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a> wall thirty feet high and a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILE">mile</a> and a half in circumference, with <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BATTLEMENTS">battlements</a> upon the outer wall, and a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PARAPET">parapet</a> <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROOF">roof</a> between the outer and inner, by which you can go along the whole and look into the street. The hill on which the town is built rises in the middle of a deep valley, through which run two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>: one of which, the Kakha, coming from the Mountain of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">Sun</a>, flanks all the south of the town; while the other, called the Angrab, falling from the mountain Woggora, encompasses it on the north and north-east; and both rivers unite at the bottom of the hill about a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of a mile south of the town. Upon the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANK">bank</a> opposite to Gondar, on the other side of the river, is a large town of Mahometans; a great part of whom are employed in taking care of the king's and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a>'s equipage, both when they take the field and when they return from it. They are formed into a body under proper officers; but never fight on either side, being entirely confined to the occupation <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> mentioned, in which by their care and dexterity in pitching and striking the tents, and in leading and conducting the baggage-waggons, they are of great <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>.—The valley of Gondar is described as having three outlets; one south, to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEMBEA">Dembea</a>, Maitsha, and the Agows; another on the north-west, towards Senmaar, from which it is distant 180 miles, over the Mountain of the Sun; and the third north, leading to Woggora, over the high mountain Lamalmon, and so on through Tigre to the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-RED_SEA"><a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">Red</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>.

GONDI

Pages 858-858

John Francis Paul, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDINAL">Cardinal</a> de Retz, was the son of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a> Emanuel de Condi, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNT">Count</a> de <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOIGNY">Joigny</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LIEUTENANT">lieutenant</a>-general, &c. and was born in 1613. From a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a> of the Sorbonne, he first became co-adjutor to his uncle John Francis de Condi, whom he succeeded in 1654 as archbishop of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>; and was finally made a cardinal. This extraordinary person has drawn his own character in his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEMOIRS">memoirs</a> with impartiality. He was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> who, from the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of debauchery, and still languishing under its consequences, made himself adored by the people as a preacher. At the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> of 23, he was at the head of a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSPIRACY">conspiracy</a> against the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> of Cardinal Richelieu; he precipitated the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> into cabals, and the people into sedition: he was (says M. Voltaire) the first bishop who carried on a civil <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> without the mask of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>. However, his intrigues and schemes turned out so ill, that he was obliged to quit France; and he lived the life of a vagrant exile for five <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> six years, till the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> enemy Cardinal Mazarin, when he returned on certain stipulated conditions. After assisting in the conclave at Rome, which chose Clement IX., he retired from the world, and ended his life like a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a> in 1679; which made Voltaire say, that in his youth he lived like Catiline, and like Atticus in his old age. He wrote his Memoirs in his retirement; the best edition of which is that of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMSTERDAM">Amsterdam</a>, 4 vols 12mo, 1719.

GONDOLA

Pages 858-858

a flat <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOAT">boat</a>, very <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> and narrow, chiefly used at <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a> to row on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CANALS">canals</a>. The word is Italian, gondola. Du Cange derives it from the vulgar Greek κοντάξ, "a bark," <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> "little ship;" Lancelot deduces it from γόνδολα, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> in Athenæus for a sort of vase. The middle-sized gondolas are upwards of thirty feet long and four <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>: they always terminate at each end in a very sharp point, which is raised perpendicularly to the full height of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a> of the Venetian gondoliers, in passing along their narrow canals, is very remarkable: there are usually two to each gondola, and they row by pushing before them. The fore-man rests his oar on the left side of the gondola: the hind man is placed on the stern, that he may see the head over the tilt or covering of the gondola, and rests his oar, which is very long, on the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> side of the gondola. Gondola is also the name of a passage-boat of six or eight oars, used in other parts of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>.

GONIOMETRY

Pages 858-859

a method of measuring <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a>, so called by M. de Lagny, who gave several papers, on this method, in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEMOIRS">Memoirs</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> Academy an. 1724, 1725, 1729. M. de Lagny's method of goniometry consists in measuring the angles with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPASSES">compasses</a>, and that without any <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCALE">scale</a> whatever, except an undivided <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEMICIRCLE">semicircle</a>. Thus, having any <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a> drawn... drawn upon <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>, to be measured; produce one of the sides of the angle backwards behind the angular point; then with a pair of fine compasses describe a pretty <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> semicircle from the angular point as a centre, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> the sides of the proposed angle, which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> intercept a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the semicircle. Take then this intercepted part very exactly between the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">points</a> of the compasses, and turn them successively over upon the arc of the semicircle, to find how often it is contained in it, after which there is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> some remainder: then take this remainder in the compasses, and in like manner find how often it is contained in the last of the integral parts of the first arc, with again some remainder: find in like manner how often this last remainder is contained in the former; and so on continually, till the remainder become too small to be taken and applied as a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a>. By this means he obtains a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of quotients, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> fractional parts, one of another, which being properly reduced into one fraction, give the ratio of the first arc to the semicircle, or of the proposed angle to two <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> angles, or 180 degrees, and consequently that angle itself in degrees and minutes. *Hutton's Math. Dict.*

GONORRHOEA

Pages 859-859

an efflux of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, greenish, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> differently-coloured <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>, from the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-URETHRA">urethra</a>; most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> owing to venereal infection. See **MEDICINE** and **<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SURGERY">SURGERY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>**.

GONZAGA

Pages 859-859

Lucretia**, was one of the most illustrious ladies of the 16th century; and much celebrated for her <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WIT">wit</a>, her learning, and her delicate style. Hortensio Landi wrote a beautiful <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PANEGYRIC">panegyric</a> upon her, and dedicated to her his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIALOGUE">dialogue</a> of moderating the passions. Her beautiful letters have been collected with the greatest care. We learn from these, that her <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> with John Paul Manfrone was unhappy.—She was married when she was not 14 years of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, and his conduct afterwards gave her infinite uneasiness. He engaged in a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSPIRACY">conspiracy</a> against the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FERRARA">Ferrara</a>; was detected and imprisoned by him; but, though condemned by the judges, not put to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. She did all in her power to obtain his enlargement, but in vain; for he died in prison, having shown such impatience under his misfortunes, as made it imagined he had lost his senses. She never would listen afterwards to any proposals of marriage, though several were made to her. All that came from her <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEN">pen</a> was so much esteemed, that a collection was made even of the notes she writ to her servants; several of which are to be met with in the edition of her letters.

GOOD

Pages 859-862

in general, whatever is apt to increase <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>, to diminish pain in us; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a>, which amounts to the same, whatever is able to procure or preserve to us the possession of agreeable sensations, and remove those of an opposite <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>. *Moral Good*, denotes the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> conduct of the several senses and passions, or their <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> proportion and accommodation to their respective objects and relations. See **MORALS**. **Good Abearing (bonus gestus)**, signifies an exact carriage or behaviour of a subject towards the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> and the people, whereunto some persons upon their misbehaviour are bound: and he that is bound to this, is said to be more strictly bound than to the peace: because where the peace is not broken, the surety de bono gestu may be forfeited by the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>, or by their weapons. **Good Behaviour**, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, an exact carriage and behaviour to the king and his people. A <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> of the peace may, at the request of another, or where he himself sees cause, demand surety for the good behaviour; and to that end the justice may issue out his warrant against any persons whatsoever, under the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a>; but when it is a nobleman, complaint is to be made in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CHANCERY">chancery</a>, or king's <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BENCH">bench</a>, where such nobleman may be bound to keep the peace. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INFANTS">Infants</a> and feme-coverts, who ought to find surety by their friends, may be bound over to their good behaviour; as also lunatics, that have sometimes lucid intervals, and all others who <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> the peace, or being suspected to do it by affrays, assaults, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTERY">battery</a>, wounding, fighting, quarrelling, threatening, &c. A person may be likewise bound to his good behaviour for a scandalous way of living, keeping bawdy-houses, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-GAMING">gaming</a>-houses, &c. and so may <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> drunkards, whoremongers, common whores, cheats, libellers, &c. He who demands surety for the peace, on any violence offered, must take an oath before the justice, that he goes in fear of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, or some bodily harm, &c. and that it is not out of malice, but from a regard to his own safety. **Good Breeding.** See **Good Manners**. **Good Friday**, a fast of the Christian <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of the sufferings and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> Christ. It is observed on the Friday in holy or <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PASSION">passion</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-WEEK">week</a>; and it is called, by way of eminence, good, because of the blessed effects of our Saviour's sufferings, which were a propitiatory or expiating sacrifice for the sins of the world. The commemoration of our Saviour's sufferings has been kept from the very first ages of Christianity, and was always observed as a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> of the strictest fasting and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HUMILIATION">humiliation</a>. Among the Saxons it was called <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>-Friday; but for what reason, except on account of the long fastings and offices then used, is uncertain. On Good Friday the pope sits on a plain form: and, after <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> is ended, when the cardinals wait on him back to his chamber, they are obliged to keep a deep silence, as a testimony of their sorrow. In the night of Good-Friday, the Greeks perform the obsequies of our Saviour round a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CRUCIFIX">crucifix</a> laid on a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BED">bed</a> of state, adorned with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>; these the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a> distribute among the assistants when the office is ended. The Armenians, on this day, set open a holy sepulchre, in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a> of that of Mount Calvary. **Good Hope**, or <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a> of Good Hope, a promontory of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, with a town and a considerable territory, now subject to <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>. It is situated in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of the Hottentots: for an account of whom, see the article **HOTTENTOTS**. The Cape of Good Hope has been generally esteemed the most southerly point of Africa, though it is not truly so. In Phillips's *Voyage to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOTANY_BAY"><a class="</a>xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">Bay</a>* we are told, that the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> which projects farthest to the south is a point to the east of it, called by the English Cape Lagullus; a name corrupted from the original Portuguese das Aguilhas which, as well as the French appellation des Aiguilles, is descriptive of its form, and would rightly be translated <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NEEDLE">Needle</a> cape. On approaching the cape, a very remarkable emi- Good Hope, nence may in clear <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a> be discovered at a considerable distance; and is called the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">Table</a>-mountain from its appearance, as it terminates in a flat <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HORIZONTAL">horizontal</a> surface, from which the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FACE">face</a> of the rock descends almost perpendicularly. In the mild or <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> season, which commences in September, and continues till <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a>, the Table Land or Mountain, is sometimes suddenly capped with a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> cloud, by some called the spreading of the Table-cloth. When this cloud seems to roll <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> the steep face of the mountain, it is a sure indication of an approaching <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-GALE">gale</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> from the south-east; which generally blows with great violence, and sometimes continues a day or more, but in common is of short <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DURATION">duration</a>. On the first appearance of this cloud, the ships in Table Bay begin to prepare for it, by striking yards and top-<a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MASTS">masts</a>, and making every thing as snug as possible.—A little to the westward of the Table Land, divided by a small valley, stands on the right-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> side of Table Bay a round hill, called the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUGAR">Sugar</a> Loaf; and by many the Lion's Head, as there is a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTIGUITY">contiguity</a> from it contiguous to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, called the Lion's Rump; and when you take a general view of the whole, it very much resembles that animal with his head erect. The Sugar Loaf or Lion's Head, and the Lion's Rump, have each a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAG">flag</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STAFF">staff</a> on them, by which the approach of ships is made known to the governor, particularizing their number, <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> from which they come. To the eastwards, separated by a small chasm from the Table Land, stands <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a>'s Mount, well known by the appellation of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVIL">Devil</a>'s Tower, or Devil's Head; and so called from the violent gusts of wind supposed to issue from it when it partakes of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a> that covers the Table Land, though these gusts are nothing more than a degree of force the wind acquires in coming through the chasm. When this phenomenon appears in the morning, which is by no means so frequent as in the evening, the sailors have a saying, as the Devil's Tower is almost contiguous to the Table Land, that the old <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> is going to breakfast; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> in the middle of the day, that he is going to dinner; and if in the evening, that the cloth is spread for <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUPPER">supper</a>. Table-mountain rises about 3567 feet above the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> of the sea; the Devil's Tower, about 3368; and the Lion's Head, 2764. In the neighbourhood of the latter lies Constantia, a district consisting of two farms, wherein the famous wines of that name are produced. The above-described <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> lands form a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMPHITHEATRE">amphitheatre</a> about the Table-valley, where the Cape-town stands. This is situated at the bottom of the middle height, or Table-mountain; and almost in the centre of the Table Bay, so called from that mountain.—This bay, it is observed in Phillips's Voyage, "cannot properly be called a port, being by no means a station of security; it is exposed to all the violence of the winds which set into it from the sea; and is far from sufficiently secured from those which blow from the land. The gusts which descend from the summit of Table-mountain are sufficient to force ships from their anchors, and even violently to annoy persons on the shore, by destroying any tents or other temporary edifices, which may be erected, and raising <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CLOUDS">clouds</a> of fine dust, which produce very troublesome effects. A gale of this kind, from the south-east, blew for three days successively when <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPTAIN">Captain</a> Cook lay here in his first voyage; at which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, he informs us, the Good Hope <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESOLUTION">Resolution</a> was the only ship in the harbour that had not dragged her <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANCHOR">anchor</a>. The storms from the sea are still more formidable; so much so, that ships have frequently been driven by them from their anchorage, and wrecked at the head of the bay. But these accidents happen chiefly in the quadrae mousson, or winter months, from May 14th to the same day of August; during which time few ships venture to anchor here. Our fleet arriving later, lay perfectly unmolested as long as it was necessary for it to remain in this station.—False Bay, on the south-east side of the Cape, is more secure than Table Bay during the prevalence of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-west winds, but still less so in strong gales from the south-east. It is, however, less frequented, being 24 miles of very heavy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a> distant from Cape Town, whence almost all necessaries must be procured. The most sheltered <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of False Bay is a recess on the west side, called Simon's Bay." Mr White, in his Journal of a Voyage to New South <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>, thus describes Cape Town. From the shipping, he observes *, the town appears pleasantly situated, * Page 87, but at the same time small; a deception that arises from its being built in a valley with such stupendous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> directly behind it. On landing, however, you are surprised, and agreeably disappointed, to find it not only extensive, but well built, and in a good style; the streets spacious, and intersecting each other at right <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a> with great precision. This exactness in the formation of the streets, when viewed from the Table Land, is observed to be very great. The houses in general are built of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, cemented together with a glutinous kind of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> which serves as <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MORTAR">mortar</a>, and afterwards neatly plastered and whitewashed with lime. As to their height they do not in common exceed two stories, on account of the violence of the wind, which at some seasons of the year blows with great strength and fury. For the same reason thatch has been usually preferred to tiles or shingles; but the bad effects that have proceeded from this <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODE">mode</a> when fires happen, has induced the inhabitants in all their new buildings to give the preference to slates and tiles. The lower parts of the houses, according to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> of the Dutch nation, are not only uncommonly neat and clean in appearance, but they are really so; and the furniture is rather rich than elegant. But this is by no means the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> with the bed-rooms or upper apartments; which are very barely and ill furnished. The streets are rough, uneven, and unpaved. But many of the houses have a space flagged before the door; and others have trees planted before them, which form a pleasant <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SHADE">shade</a>, and give an agreeable <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> to the streets. The only landing-<a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> is at the east end of the town, where there is a wooden quay running some paces into the sea, with several cranes on it for the convenience of loading and unloading the scouts that come alongside. To this place excellent <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> is conveyed by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PIPES">pipes</a>, which makes the watering of ships both easy and expeditious. <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">Close</a> to the quay, on the left hand, stands the castle and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> fortress; a strong extensive <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, having excellent accommodations for the troops, and for many of the civil officers belonging to the company. Within the gates, are the principal stores; which are spacious as well as convenient. This fort covers and defends the east part of the town and harbour. Good Hope, bour, as <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMSTERDAM">Amsterdam</a> fort does the west part. The latter, which has been built since Commodore Johnston's expedition, and whereon both French and Dutch judgment have been united to render it effectual and strong, is admirably planned and calculated to annoy and harass ships coming into the bay. Some smaller detached fortifications extend along the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a>, both to the east and west, and make landing, which was not the case before the late <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, hazardous and difficult. In a word, Cape Town is at this time fortified with strength, regularity, and judgment. It consists of 1145 houses, inhabited by about 5500 whites and people of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, and 10,000 blacks. There are two churches in the town; one <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, plain, and unadorned, for the Calvinists, the prevailing <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECT">sect</a>; and a smaller one for the Lutherans. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOSPITAL">hospital</a>, which is large and extensive, is situated at the upper end of the town, close to the company's garden; where the convalescents reap the benefit of a wholesome pure air, perfumed with the exhalations of a great variety of rich fruit trees, aromatic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHRUBS">shrubs</a>, and odorous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> and flowers; and likewise have the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of every production of it. The territory round the Cape is distinguished by three chains of mountains, running <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> to one another and to the coast. The first chain, called Lange Kloof, or Long <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">Pass</a>, runs parallel to the southern coast, at the distance of from 20 to 60 miles, widening towards the west. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> chain, called Zwarte <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BERG">Berg</a>, or <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">Black</a> Mountain, is considerably higher and more rugged than the first, and consists often of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> or triple ranges. The belt interposed between the Zwarte Berg and the Lange Kloof is nearly of the same breadth as that between the Lange Kloof and the sea, and is considerably more elevated. Beyond the Zwarte Berg, at an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTERVAL">interval</a> of 80 or 100 miles, rises the Nieuweldts Gebirg, the highest chain in southern Africa, and the summits of which are generally covered with snow. Its elevation is supposed to be 10,000 feet. The belt or plain interposed between the two last ridges is more elevated than any of the former, so that southern Africa forms as it were a succession of terraces rising above one another. The plain next the sea is covered with a deep and fertile <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>, watered by numerous rivulets, well clothed with grass and with a beautiful variety of trees and shrubs. Rains are frequent, and from its <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROXIMITY">proximity</a> to the sea, it enjoys a more mild and equable temperature than the interior and remoter parts of the colony. The second terrace contains a considerable proportion of well watered and fertile lands, but these are mixed with large tracts of the arid <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DESERT">desert</a> called Karroo. The third terrace, called the Great Karroo, is composed of a vast plain 300 miles in length, and nearly 100 in breadth, the soil of which is of a hard and impenetrable texture, and destitute almost of any trace of vegetation. It is obvious, from this outline, that a large portion of the settlement must be devoted to complete and hopeless sterility. The Karroo, of which the greatest part of the second, and the whole of the third and largest belt is composed, is quite unoccupied by man or animal. Only a few shrivelled and parched plants occasionally meet the eye, faintly extending their half withered fibres along the ground. The surface consists of clay, thinly sprinkled over with sand, and is scarcely ever moistened with a shower of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">rain</a>. The hills, which sometimes break the surface of these plains, are equally destitute of plants as the plain beneath. The upper regions of all the chains of mountains consist of masses of naked sandstone. Mr <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BARROW">Barrow</a>, in short, concludes, that <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a>-tenths of the settlement for a great part of the year, and a large proportion of it at all times, is destitute of the least appearance of verdure. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> of the Cape is besides subject to various disadvantages. It is deluged with rain during the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLD">cold</a> season; while, in the hot months, scarcely a shower falls to refresh the earth. During this season also a dry wind blows, having the pernicious effects of the African <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SIROCCO">sirocco</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLASTING">blasting</a> vegetation, and relaxing the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> frame. Tempestuous winds are besides extremely common, and often uproot trees and destroy the crops. There are, however, many spots about the Cape of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> fertility. But the want of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROADS">roads</a>, or other means of transporting commodities, renders the good soil often of no value. The Cape town is supplied with grain from places generally at more than one and less than three days' journey distant. Beyond that, ground can only be applied to the purpose of grazing with advantage. Wine and brandy are the staple produce of the Cape. The Constantia wine, raised only on two farms, is pretty much esteemed; but the mode of management is far too rude and slovenly to produce good wine generally; and notwithstanding the encouragement given to the Cape wines, by diminishing the duties, they are not relished in Britain. Some attempts, it is understood, are now making to improve the processes of manufacture. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOBACCO">Tobacco</a>, aloes, with almonds, and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> of almost all kinds, succeed extremely well, but are not much cultivated. Attempts are now making to colonize the country round the Cape with British settlers; time can only shew whether it <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> succeed. The inhabitants of the Cape, though in their persons large, stout, and athletic, have not all that phlegm about them which is the characteristic of Dutchmen in general. The physical influence of climate may in some degree account for this; for it is well known that in all southern latitudes the temper and disposition of the people are more gay, and that they are more inclined to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LUXURY">luxury</a> and amusements of every kind, than the inhabitants of the northern hemisphere. The ladies are lively, good natured, and familiar; and from a peculiar gay turn, they admit of liberties that would be thought reprehensible in England, though perhaps they as seldom overlap the bounds of virtue as the women of other countries. The heavy draft work about the Cape is mostly performed by oxen; which are here brought to an uncommon degree of usefulness and docility. It is not uncommon to see 14, 16, and sometimes 18, in one of their teams; when the roads are heavy, they sometimes, though rarely, yoke 20; all which the Hottentots, Malays, and Cape slaves, have in the most perfect subjection and obedience. One of these fellows places himself on the fore part of the waggon, or, when loaded, on the top of the load, and with a tremendous long whip, which from its size he is obliged to hold in both his Good Hope, his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, manages these creatures with inexpressible <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a>. When he finds expedition needful, he can make them keep whatever pace he chooses, either trot or gallop, (a gait performed or kept up with difficulty by European oxen), and that with as much ease as if he was driving horses. They likewise manage horses with the same dexterity; and to see one of them driving three, four, five, and sometimes six <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a>, in hand, with one of these long whips, would make the most complete <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of the whip in England cut a despicable <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARRIAGES">Carriages</a> are not very numerous at the Cape, as the inhabitants in general travel in covered waggons, which better <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUIT">suit</a> the roughness of the country. The governor and some few of the principal people keep coaches, which are a good <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> in the English style, and always drawn by six horses. Its geographical position on the globe is so commanding a feature, that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> looking at a map, independent of any other information, must shew its value and importance in various respects. Its distance from the coast of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRAZIL">Brazil</a> is a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">month</a>'s voyage; from the Dutch colonies of Surinam, Berbice, and Essequibo, it is a voyage of six weeks; it is about equally distant from the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-RED_SEA"><a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">Red</a> sea, and two months from Coromandel and Malabar. It is half way between Britain and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a>, in a temperate climate, and productive of every <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of refreshment in great abundance. Considered in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> of a naval station, the importance of the Cape is equally conspicuous. It may serve as a port for refreshing and refitting the ships of the East India Company; a station for ships of war keeping the entrance into the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> seas, and affording, by its geographical position, a ready <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> with every part of the globe. There is no place, in the homeward bound voyage from India, so proper or convenient for East India ships to assemble at for convoy, as the Cape of Good Hope. Their crews might be refreshed with fruits, vegetables, and fresh <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a>, at a very reasonable rate. <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">Salt</a> beef for the remainder of the voyage might there be laid in. An establishment for curing salt provisions, would be an incalculable saving, as well as a singular convenience. The moderate expense at which a fleet could here be maintained, is a circumstance that deserves <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>. At the Cape a sailor may be furnished his ration of fresh beef or mutton, biscuit and wine, for one-fourth of what the same ration of salt beef costs the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> when sent out from Britain. If a naval establishment was formed at Saldanha bay, many <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COASTING">coasting</a> vessels and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FISHING">fishing</a> ships would be constructed in it, as it abounds with every convenience that could be required for <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> ships, which would be the means of very much increasing the coasting trade. It is thought also, that were a depot for the southern whale fishery established at the Cape, it might be attended with beneficial consequences. By promoting <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a>, the strength and security of the British empire are also promoted, and its very existence as an independent nation is owing to the superiority of its <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVY">navy</a>. A nation of fishermen implies a nation of seamen, a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a> of bold and hardy warriors. The cultivation of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FISHERIES">fisheries</a> would afford a never-failing supply of men so instructed, increase our conveniency, and promote our <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>. The colony of the Cape comprehends at least 120,000 <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> miles; yet the whole <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> of whites, blacks, and Hottentots, does not exceed 60,000 souls, or a Gordianus single individual for every two square miles. The rural occupants may be divided into the wine-growers, the corn-farmers, and the graziers. The first, who reside in the immediate vicinity of the Cape, are the most civilized and comfortably situated of the peasantry. Their <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> is usually about 120 acres in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>, and held in freehold. The corn-boors or farmers, reside generally at the distance of two or three days journey from the Cape. The <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRICULTURE">agriculture</a> is extremely rude. Their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLOUGH">plough</a>, an unwieldy machine, drawn by 14 or 16 oxen, does little more than skim the surface. They use almost no manure, and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-TREAD">tread</a> out the corn by the feet of horses. The grazier is the least cultivated, and indeed is half a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAVAGE">savage</a>. All these classes employ Hottentots, who are not slaves, strictly speaking, but in a condition nearly as bad. **Good Manners.** See **Manners.** **GOOINGS,** in sea-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, are clamps of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> bolted on the stern-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a> of a ship, whereon to hang the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RUDDER">rudder</a> and keep it steady; for which purpose there is a hole in each of them, to receive a correspondent spindle bolted on the back of the rudder, which turns thereby as upon hinges. **GOOSE.** See **<a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANAS">ANAS</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">Ornithology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.** The goose was held in great esteem amongst the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> for having saved the Capitol from the invasion of the Gauls by cackling and clapping its wings. Geese were kept in the temple of Juno; and the censors, when they entered upon their office, provided meat for them. There was also an annual feast at Rome, at which they carried a silver image of a goose in state; and hanged a dog, to punish that animal because he did not bark at the arrival of the Gauls. **Goose-Ander.** See **MERGUS, Ornithology Index.** **Goose-Berry.** See **RIBES, Botany Index.** **Goose-Neck,** in a ship, a piece of iron fixed on the one end of the tiller, to which the laniard of the whip-staff or the wheel-rope comes, for steering the ship. **Goose-Wing,** in the sea language. When a ship sails before, or with a quarter-wind on a fresh gale, to make the more haste, they launch out a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOOM">boom</a> and sail on the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEE">lee</a>-side; and a sail so fitted is called a goose-wing. **GORCUM,** a town in South <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, which carries on a considerable trade in cheese and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUTTER">butter</a>. It is situated on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> Ligne and Maese, in E. Long. 4° 55'. N. Lat. 51° 49'. **GORDIANUS I.** a Roman general, was for his valour and virtues chosen <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> by the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> in the reign of Maximinus, A.D. 237; but his son, whom he had associated with himself in the throne, being slain by Capellian, the governor of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MAURITANIA">Mauritania</a> for Maximinus, Gordianus killed himself the same year. See **Rome.** **GORDIANUS III.** grandson of the former, a renowned <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WARRIOR">warrior</a>, and styled *The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-GUARDIAN">guardian</a> of the Roman commonwealth.* He was treacherously assassinated by Philippus, an Arabian, one of his generals; who, to the eternal disgrace of the Romans of that era, succeeded him in the empire, A.D. 244. See **Rome.** **GORDIAN-KNOT,**

GOOGLES

Pages 848-848

in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SURGERY">Surgery</a>, are instruments used for curing squinting, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> that <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISTORTION">distortion</a> of the eyes which occasions this disorder. They are short conical tubes, composed of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-IVORY">ivory</a> stained <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a>, with a thin plate of the same ivory fixed in the tubes near their anterior extremities. Through the centre of each of these plates is a small circular hole, about the size of the pupil of the eye, for the transmission of the rays of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>. These goggles must be continually worn in the daytime, till the muscles of the eye are brought to <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> regularly and uniformly, so as to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> the pupil straight forwards; and by these means the cure <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be sooner or later effected.

GORDIAN-KNOT

Pages 862-863

in antiquity, a knot made in the leathers <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> harness of the chariot of Gordius <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHRYGIA">Phrygia</a>, so very intricate, that there was no finding where it began or ended. The inhabitants had a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRADITION">tradition</a>, that the oracle had declared, that he who untied this knot should be <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>. Alexander having undertaken it, was unable to accomplish it; when fearing lest his not untying it should be deemed an ill augury, and prove a check in the way of his conquests, he cut it asunder with his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>, and thus either accomplished or eluded the oracle.

GORDIUS

Pages 863-863

the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIR">HAIR</a>-WORM, a genus of insects belonging to the class of vermes intestina. See <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HELMINTHOLOGY">HELMINTHOLOGY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Gordius, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHRYGIA">Phrygia</a>, and father of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIDAS">Midas</a>, was a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a> husbandman, with two yokes of oxen, wherewith he ploughed his <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> and drew his wain. An eagle sitting a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> while upon one of his oxen, he consulted the soothsayers; a virgin bid him sacrifice to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a> in the capacity of king. He married the virgin, who brought forth Midas. The Persians, instructed by the oracle to set the first person they met in a wain upon the throne, met Gordius, and made him king. Midas for this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOOD_FORTUNE">good fortune</a> dedicated to Jupiter his father's <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CART">cart</a>. The knot of the yoke, they say, was so well twisted, that he who could unloose it was promised the empire of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>; hence the proverb of the Gordian knot had its original. See GORDIAN KNOT.

GORDON

Pages 863-863

Thomas, noted for his translations and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> writings, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KIRKCUDBRIGHT">Kirkcudbright</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>. He came young to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>; where he supported himself by teaching languages, until he procured employment under the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, but in what capacity is not now known. He first distinguished himself in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of Dr Hoadley in the Bangorian controversy; which recommended him to Mr Trenchard, in conjunction with whom he wrote the well-known Cato's Letters, upon a variety of important public subjects. These were followed by another periodical <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>, under the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of the Independent Whig; which was <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> some years after Mr Trenchard's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, by Gordon alone, against the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HIERARCHY">hierarchy</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>; but with more acrimony than was shown in Cato's Letters. At length Sir Robert Walpole retained him to defend his administration, to which end he wrote several pamphlets. At the time of his death, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> 28th 1750, he was first <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMISSIONER">commissioner</a> of the wine licenses, an office which he had enjoyed many years. He was twice married. His <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> wife was the widow of his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> friend Trenchard, by whom he had children.—He published English translations of Sallust and Tacitus, with additional discourses to each author, which contain much good <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>. Also, two collections of his tracts have been preserved: the first entitled, A Cordial for Low-spirits, in three volumes: and the second, The Pillars of Priestcraft and Orthodoxy shaken, in two volumes. But these, like many other posthumous things, had better have been suppressed. In his translations as well as his other works he places his verbs at the ends of sentences, according to the Latin idiom, in a very stiff and affected manner.

GORDONIA

Pages 863-863

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, belonging to the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONADELPHIA">monadelphia</a> class. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

GOREE

Pages 863-863

the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> town of an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of the same name in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, eight miles south of Briell. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 3° 50'. N. Lat. 51° 55'.

GOREY

Pages 863-863

a borough, fair, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a>-town in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEXFORD">Wexford</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEINSTER">Leinster</a>, otherwise called Newborough. It stands about 18 miles <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of Wexford town, and 45 from <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUBLIN">Dublin</a>. N. Lat. 52° 40'. W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 6° 30'. It sent formerly two members to the Irish <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>.

GORGE

Pages 863-863

in Fortification, the entrance of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLATFORM">platform</a> of any <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>. See FORTIFICATION.

GORGED

Pages 863-864

in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERALDRY">Heraldry</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>, coronet, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the like, about the neck of a lion, a swan, &c. Gorged &c. and in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> it is said, the lion or cygnet is gorged with a ducal coronet, &c. Gorged is also used when the gorge or neck of a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PEACOCK">peacock</a>, swan, or the like <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BIRD">bird</a>, is of a different <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> or metal from the rest.

GORGET

Pages 864-864
or Gogeret, in Surgery, is the name which the French give to the concave or cannulated conductor, used in lithotomy. See Surgery Index.

GORGONA

Pages 864-864

a small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of the South <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, 12 miles west of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERU">Peru</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>. It is indifferent <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a>, very woody, and some of the trees are very tall and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, and proper for <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MASTS">masts</a>. It is about 10 miles in circumference, and has several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a> and rivulets of excellent <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, but is subject to constant rains. W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 73° 3'. S. Lat. 3°

GORGONIA

Pages 864-864

in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, a genus of zoophytes, which formerly were called ceratophytons, and are known in English by the names of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-fans, sea-feathers, and sea-whips. Linnaeus and Dr Pallas consider them as of a mixed <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> in their growth, between animals and vegetables; but Mr Ellis shows them to be true animals of the polype kind, growing up in a branched form resembling a shrub, and in no <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> vegetable. They differ from the fresh <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> polype in many of their qualities, and particularly in producing from their own substance a hard and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> support, serving many of the purposes of the bone in other animals. This is formed from a concreting juice thrown out from a peculiar set of longitudinal <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> tubes, running along the internal surface of the fleshy part: in the coats of these tubes are a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of small orifices, through which the osseous liquor exudes, and concreting, forms the layers of that hard part of the annular circles, which some, judging from the consistence rather than the texture, have erroneously denominated wood.
