As the cutting proceeds, they should be rolled up compactly with the grass side in. If they are not closely rolled up they will be apt to break in carrying. They must be laid on the walk or lawn close to one another after the surface has been rendered level and compact by proper treading, that it may not settle unequally. When they have been put on they must be beat down with a wooden rammer, and afterwards rolled with a large iron or wooden roller. Gravel walks should be cleared of weeds and all decayed leaves, and kept clean; and in dry weather they should be occasionally rolled. New walks may likewise be formed now. For the method, see March. Edgings of boxwood, thrift, &c., may be planted any time this month in open weather. See October. Hedges of hawthorn, barberry, privet, hazel, holm, yew, birch, elm, elder, &c., may be planted during this month. See November. Old hedges which have become open below should be plashed. See December. Forest trees for ornamental plantations, coppices, or woods, may be planted either now, or at any time from the fall of the leaf till the rise of the sap in spring. See October. Sect. IV. Nursery. Prune and transplant shrubs, fruit and forest trees. Trim the stems of forest trees, and cut off all irregular regular rambling shoots of shrubs, and reduce them to a regular neat form. This work may be executed any time this month, even during frost, when little else can be done. All kinds of hardy deciduous shrubs, fruit, and forest trees, may be transplanted during open weather. Dig ground in open weather, and wheel out dung in frost. Vacant compartments of ground may be dug any time during open weather; and likewise after the necessary pruning has been given to the trees and shrubs, the ground between the rows may be dug, and all weeds carefully buried. The young plants of many of the tenderer kinds of trees and shrubs, such as cedar of Lebanon, and some other species of pine, cypress, chinese arbor vitae, strawberry-tree, &c., require to be protected during frost. If they have been raised in boxes or pots, they may be placed in garden frames and occasionally covered with the glasses; but care must be taken always to remove the glasses in mild open weather. If the plants stand in beds in the open ground, they may be covered with mats supported on hoops, which must be removed during favourable weather, or a covering of pease straw, or something of that nature may answer the purpose. Layers of many kinds of trees and shrubs may be made any time this month during open weather; many of them which are laid now will be well rooted and fit for removing by October; for the method, see November. Put in cuttings of honeysuckles, gooseberries, currants, &c., indeed most kinds of trees and shrubs may be propagated by cuttings. For this purpose select the straight shoots of last year's growth; take them off by a clean cut with a sharp knife, and reduce them to the length of ten, twelve, or fifteen inches, by cutting off part of their smaller extremities. Plant them in rows a foot apart, and at the distance of four or five inches from one another in the rows, taking care to insert one-third or one half of their length into the ground. Though cuttings will grow when their smaller extremities are put into the ground, they never succeed so well in this inverted position, therefore in planting, attention should be paid to place them in their natural position. Older and longer branches of some trees and shrubs, viz. willow, elder, &c., may be employed as cuttings. Gooseberries, currants, roses, lilacs, and many other shrubs and trees, may be propagated by suckers or offsets from the roots; these may be taken off any time this month, and planted in rows. Previous to their being planted it would be proper to trim off part of their extremities. Sect. V. Green-House and Hot-House. During frost, keep the glasses shut; but whenever the weather is mild, give the green-house air by opening the glasses more or less according to the state of the weather; even in the brightest mild days during this month the glasses should not be opened until about ten o'clock in the morning, and ought to be shut again about three in the afternoon. In dull foggy days, even though the weather be mild, they should be opened but little, and that for a short time, and in very damp weather, not at all. When very severe frost prevails, fires must be put on, and the flues gently warmed; but the temperature of the air should not be raised higher than merely to keep off the effects of the external frost. A little fire should likewise be put on during very wet weather to banish the damps. Water should be given to such plants as require it, but sparingly. Succulent plants, such as aloe, &c., require little or no water at this season. All dead and decayed leaves should be carefully picked off, and the green-house kept clean. Particular attention must be paid to the pine apple plants which are to produce fruit the ensuing summer, plants re- as many of them in the course of this month begin to shew flowers. If due attention be not now paid to keep up a proper heat, both in the tanned bed and in the air of the hot-house, the plants may receive such a check as will considerably affect the size of the future fruit. The bark bed must be carefully examined; and if the bark be much decayed and the heat found on the decline, a quantity of fresh tanners bark should be prepared to be added as a refreshment to the old. The pots containing the pine apple plants should then be taken out of the tan pits, and a quantity of the decayed tan removed from the surface and sides of the pits, to make room for the fresh tan which is to be added. The old tan must likewise be turned up from the bottom, and well mixed with the new, after which the pots must be again plunged into the tan. But if, on examination, the heat of the tan pit be found good, and the tan not much decayed, it will be sufficient to turn the old tan, and to mix it well together without making any addition of new. This operation will revive the heat of the bed, and preserve it in good condition for some time to come. The heat of the air in the house must likewise be attended to, and regulated by the thermometer and by due attention to the fires. Moderate watering must be given once a week or ten days, according as the pine apple plants may seem to require it; and care must be taken not to pour any of the water into their hearts or among their leaves. The other plants in the hot-house must be regularly watered; but those of a succulent nature, such as the different species of aloe, euphorbia, mesembryanthemum, &c., require very little water at a time, and that but seldom. Kidney beans, sown in pots or in narrow boxes of about two or three feet long, may be reared in the hot-house. Those sown this month will produce fruit in April or March. When sown in pots, two or three may be put into each, and covered about an inch deep: When in boxes they may be planted to the depth of an inch along the middle, at the distance of two or three inches from one another. The pots or boxes may be placed on the crib of the bark bed, on shelves, or any convenient situation, within the house, where they may not encumber the other plants. After the plants have come up, they should be regularly and frequently watered. The kinds commonly used for this purpose are the early speckled dwarf, negro dwarf, and dun-coloured dwarf. Cucumbers may be raised with tolerable success in the hot-house, which will produce fruit early in spring. If the plants have been raised in small pots, plunged in the tan of the bark bed, or in hot-beds made of horse dung, they should be transplanted into larger pots or boxes, in which they may remain and produce fruit; or the seeds may be sown at once in the pots where they are to remain. In this case six or eight seeds may be sown in each pot, or patches containing that number may be sown at proper intervals in long narrow boxes. When the plants have come up, only two or three of the strongest should be left in each pot or patch. The pots or boxes may be placed in any convenient situation in the hot-house, but will succeed best on a shelf fixed near the top of the house, within a short distance of the glass. The plants must be frequently watered, and have some small rods fixed near them, to which the runners may be fastened.

PAINTING ON GLASS BY

Pages 830-831

g on Glass by means of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINTS">Prints</a>. See Back-<a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a>. Glass <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PORCELAIN">Porcelain</a>, the name given by many to a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> of imitating the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHINA">china</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WARE">ware</a> with glass. The method given by M. Reaumur, who was the first that carried the attempt to any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of perfection, is shortly this: The glass vessels to be converted into porcelain are to be put into a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> earthen vessel, such as the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> fine earthen dishes are baked in, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> into sufficiently large crucibles; the vessels are to be filled with a mixture of fine <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> sand, and of fine gypsum or <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLASTER">plaster</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a> burnt into what is called plaster of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, and all the interstices are to be filled up with the same powder, so that the glass vessels may nowhere touch either one another, or the sides of the vessel they are baked in. The vessel is to be then covered <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> and luted, and the fire does the rest of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>; for this is only to be put into a common potter's <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FURNACE">furnace</a>, and when it has stood there the usual <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAKING">baking</a> the other vessels, it is to be taken out, and the whole contents <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be found no longer glass, but converted into a white opaque substance, which is a very elegant porcelain, and has almost the properties of that of China. The powder which has served once will do again as well as fresh, and that for a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> many times: nay, it seems, ever so often. The cause of this transformation, says Macquer, is probably that the vitriolic acid of the gypsum quits its basis of calcareous <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, and unites with the alkaline <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> and saline earth of the glass, with which it forms a kind of salt, different from the calcareous selenite, by the interposition of which <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> the glass acquires the qualities of porcelain. Glass Pots, the vessels in the glass trade used for melting the glass. Those for the white glass works are made of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOBACCO">tobacco</a> pipe clay, brought from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">isle</a> of Wight, which is first well washed, then calcined, and afterwards ground to a fine powder in a mill; which being mixed with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, is then trod with the bare feet till it is of a proper consistence to mould with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> into the proper shape of the vessels. When these are thus made, they are afterwards annealed over the furnace. Those for the green glass works are made of the nonsuch, and another sort of clay from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STAFFORDSHIRE">Staffordshire</a>; they make these so large as to hold three or four hundred <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of metal. And besides these, they have a small sort called piling pots, which they set upon the larger, and which contain a finer and more nice metal fit for the nicest works. The clay that is used for this purpose should be of the purest and most refractory kind, and well cleansed from all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SANDY">sandy</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FERRUGINOUS">ferruginous</a>, and pyritous matters; and to this it will be proper to add ground crucibles, white sand, calcined flints duly levigated, or a certain proportion of the same clay baked, and pounded not very finely. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of baked clay that ought to be mixed with the crude clay, to prevent the pots from cracking when dried, or exposed to a great <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>, is not absolutely determined, but depends on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of the crude clay, which is more or less fat. M. D'Antic, in a memoir on this subject, proposes the following method of ascertaining it: The burnt and crude clay, being mixed in different proportions, should be formed into cakes, one inch thick, and four inches <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> and wide. Let these cakes be slowly dried, and exposed to a violent heat, till they become as hard and as much contracted as possible, and in this state be examined; and the cake, he says, which has suffered a diminution of its bulk equal only to an eighteenth <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a>, is made of the best proportions. He observes, in general, that most clays require that the proportion of the burnt should be to the fresh as four to five. Tin Glass, the same with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BISMUTH">Bismuth</a>. See Bismuth, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Glasses are distinguished, with regard to their form, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>, &c., into various kinds, as drinking glasses, optical glasses, looking glasses, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> glasses, &c. Drinking Glasses, are simple vessels of common glass or crystal, usually made in form of an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INVERTED">inverted</a> cone. Each glass consists of three parts, viz. the bowl, the bottom, and the foot; which are all wrought or blown separately. Nothing can be more dexterous and expeditious than the manner of blowing these parts: two of them opened, and all three joined together. An idea is only to be had thereof, by seeing it actually done. For the method of gilding the edges of drinking glasses, see Gilding on Enamel and Glass. Optical Glasses. See <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OPTICS">Optics</a>.

SCHLUTTER RECOMMENDS MECHANICAL

Pages 849-856

r recommends <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MECHANICAL">mechanical</a> means, as being generally the least expensive, for separating <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> from the surface both of silver and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> the gilt vessel is round, the gold is conveniently got off by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> it in a lathe, and applying a proper tool, a skin being placed underneath for receiving the shavings: he says it is easy to collect into two ounces of shavings all the gold of a gilt vessel weighing thrice as many pounds. Where the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of the piece does not admit of this method, it is to be properly fixed, and scrapers applied of different kinds according to its size and figure; some <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, and furnished with two handles, one at each end; others small and narrow, for penetrating into depressed parts. If the gold cannot be got off by either of these ways, the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FILE">file</a> must be had recourse to, which takes off more of the metal underneath than the turning tool <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the scraper, particularly than the former. The gold scrapings or filings may be purified from the silver or copper they contain, by the methods described under the article <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METALLURGY">Metallurgy</a>. The editors of the Encyclopédie give a method of recovering the gold from wood that has been gilded on a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> size: this account is extracted from a memoir of the same subject, presented to the Academy of Sciences by M. de Montamy. The gilt wood is steeped for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of water sufficient to cover it, made very hot: the size being thus softened, the wood is taken out, and scrubbed piece by piece, in a little warm water, with short stiff bristle brushes of different sizes, some small for penetrating into the carvings, and others large for the greater dispatch in flat pieces. The whole mixture of water, size, gold, &c., is to be boiled to dryness, the dry <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> made <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> hot in a crucible to burn off the size, and the remainder ground with <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERCURY">mercury</a>, either in a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MORTAR">mortar</a>, or, where the quantity is large, in a mill. Gold-<a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">Coast</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUINEA">Guinea</a>. Gold-Wire, a cylindrical ingot of silver, superficially gilt or covered with gold at the fire, and afterwards drawn successively through a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of little round holes, of a wire-<a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, each less than the other, till it be sometimes no bigger than a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> of the head. See Wire-Drawing. It may be observed that, before the wire be reduced to this excessive fineness, it is drawn through above 140 different holes; and that each <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> they draw it, it is rubbed afresh over with new wax, both to facilitate its passage, and to prevent the silver's appearing through it. Gold-Wire flatted, is the former wire flatted between two rollers of polished <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-STEEL">steel</a>, to fit it to be spun on a stick, or to be used flat, as it is, without <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SPINNING">spinning</a>, in certain stuffs, laces, embroideries, &c. See Stuff, &c. Gold-Thread, or Spun-gold, is flatted gold, wrapped or laid over a thread of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a>, by twisting it with wheel and iron bobbins. To dispose the wire to be spun on silk, they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> it between two rollers of a little mill: these rollers are of nicely polished steel, and about three inches in diameter. They are set very <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> to each other, and turned by means of a handle fastened to one of them, which gives <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> to the other. The gold wire in passing between the two is rendered quite flat, but without losing any thing of its gilding; and is rendered so exceedingly thin and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLEXIBLE">flexible</a>, that it is easily spun on silk-thread, by means of a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>-wheel, and so wound on a spool or bobbin. See Wire-Drawing. <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GOLD_LEAF">Gold-<a c</a>lass="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAF">Leaf</a> or Beaten Gold, is gold beaten with a hammer into exceeding thin leaves, so that it is computed, that an ounce may be beaten into 1600 leaves, each three inches <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>, in which state it takes up more than 159,052 times its former surface. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PREPARATION">preparation</a> of gold leaf, according to Dr <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEWIS">Lewis</a>, is as follows: "The gold is melted in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK_LEAD"><a class="</a>xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> crucible, with some..." some <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BORAX">borax</a>, in a <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FURNACE">furnace</a>, called by the workmen a wind hole: as soon as it appears in perfect fusion, it is poured out into an iron ingot mould, six or eight inches <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a>, and three <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> of an inch wide, previously greased, and heated, so as to make the tallow run and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SMOKE">smoke</a>, but not to take <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAME">flame</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAR">bar</a> of gold is made red hot, to burn off the unctuous matter, and forged on an anvil into a long plate, which is further extended by being passed repeatedly between polished steel rollers, till it becomes a ribbon as thin as <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>. Formerly the whole of this <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENSION">extension</a> was procured by means of the hammer, and some of the French workmen are still said to follow the same practice; but the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the flating mill both abridges the operation, and renders the plate of more uniform thickness. The ribbon is divided by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPASSES">compasses</a>, and cut with sheers into equal pieces, which consequently are of equal weights: these are forged on an anvil till they are an inch square; and afterwards well nealed, to correct the rigidity which the metal has contracted in the hammering and flating. Two ounces of gold, or 960 grains, the quantity which the workmen usually melt at a time, make 150 of these squares, whence each of them weighs six grains and two-fifths; and as 902 grains of gold make a cubic inch, the thickness of the square plates is about the 766th <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of an inch. "In order to the further extension of these pieces into fine leaves, it is necessary to interpose some smooth body between them and the hammer, for softening its blow, and defending them from the rudeness of its immediate <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTION">action</a>: as also to <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> between every two of the pieces some proper intermedium, which, while it prevents their uniting together, or injuring one another, may suffer them freely to extend. Both these ends are answered by certain animal membranes. "The goldbeaters use three kinds of membranes; for the outside cover, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARCHMENT">parchment</a> made of sheep skin; for interlaying with the gold, first the smoothest and closest <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VELLUM">vellum</a>, made of calf skin; and afterwards the much finer skins of ox gut, stript off from the large straight gut slipt open, curiously prepared on purpose for this use, and hence called goldbeater's skin. The preparation of these last is a distinct business, practised by only two or three persons in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, some of the particulars of which I have not satisfactorily learned. The general <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> is said to consist, in applying one upon another, by the smooth sides, in a moist state, in which they readily cohere and unite inseparably; stretching them on a frame, and carefully scraping off the fat and rough matter, so as to leave only the fine exterior membrane of the gut; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEATING">beating</a> them between <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> leaves of paper, to force out what unctuousness may remain in them; moistening them once or twice with an infusion of warm spices; and lastly, drying and pressing them. It is said, that some calcined gypsum, or <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLASTER">plaster</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, is rubbed with a hare's foot both on the vellum and the ox gut skins, which fills up such minute holes as may happen in them, and prevents the gold leaf from sticking, as it would do to the simple animal membrane. It is observable, that, notwithstanding the vast <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> to which the gold is beaten between these skins, and the great tenacity of the skins themselves, yet they sustain continual repetitions of the process for several months, without extending or throwing thinner. Our workmen find, that, after 70 or 80 repetitions, the skins, though they <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRACT">contract</a> no flaw, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> no longer permit the gold to extend between them; but that they may be again rendered fit for use by impregnating them with the virtue which they have lost, and that even holes in them may be repaired by the dexterous application of fresh pieces of skin: a microscopical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXAMINATION">examination</a> of some skins that had been long used plainly showed these repairs. The method of restoring their virtue is said in the Encyclopédie to be, by interlaying them with leaves of paper moistened with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> wine <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VINEGAR">vinegar</a>, beating them for a whole <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>, and afterwards rubbing them over as at first with plaster of Paris. The gold is said to extend between them more easily, after they have been used a little, than when they are new. "The beating of the gold is performed on a smooth <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLOCK">block</a> of black marble, weighing from 200 to 600 pounds, the heavier the better; about <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> inches square on the upper surface, and sometimes less, fitted into the middle of a wooden frame, about two feet square, so that the surface of the marble and the frame form one continuous <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANE">plane</a>. Three of the sides are furnished with a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> ledge; and the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRONT">front</a>, which is open, has a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a> flap fastened to it, which the gold-beater takes before him as an apron, for preserving the fragments of gold that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> off. Three <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-HAMMERS">hammers</a> are employed, all of them with two round and somewhat convex faces, though <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> the workman uses only one of the faces: the first, called the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CUTCH">cutch</a> hammer, is about four inches in diameter, and weighs 15 or 16 pounds, and sometimes 20, though few workmen can manage those of this last size: the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a>, called the shuddering hammer, weighs about 12 pounds, and is about the same diameter: the third, called the gold hammer, or finishing hammer, weighs 10 or 11 pounds, and is nearly of the same width. The French use four hammers, differing both in size and shape from those of our workmen: they have only one <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FACE">face</a>, being in figure truncated cones. The first has very little convexity, is near five inches in diameter, and weighs 14 or 15 pounds: the second is more convex than the first, about an inch narrower, and scarcely half its <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>: the third, still more convex, is only about two inches wide, and four or five pounds in weight: the fourth or finishing hammer is near as heavy as the first, but narrower by an inch, and the most convex of all. As these hammers differ so remarkably from ours, I thought proper to insert them, leaving the workmen to judge what advantage one set may have above the other. "A hundred and fifty of the pieces of gold are interlaid with leaves of vellum, three or four inches square, one vellum leaf being placed between every two of the pieces, and about 20 more of the vellum leaves on the outsides; over these is drawn a parchment <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>, open at both ends, and over this another in a contrary <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a>, so that the assemblage of gold and vellum leaves is kept tight and close on all sides. The whole is beaten with the heaviest hammer, and every now and then turned upside <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a>, till the gold is stretched to the extent of the vellum; the case being from time to time opened for discovering how the extension goes on, and the packet, at times, bent and rolled..." rolled as it were between the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, for procuring sufficient freedom to the gold, or, as the workmen say, to make the gold <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>. The pieces taken out from between the vellum leaves, are cut in four with a steel <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KNIFE">knife</a>; and the 600 divisions, hence resulting, are interlaid, in the same manner, with pieces of the ox-gut skins five inches square. The beating being repeated with a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIGHTER">lighter</a> hammer till the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> plates have again acquired the extent of the skins, they are a second time divided in four: the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> used for this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> is a piece of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANE">cane</a> cut to an edge, the leaves being now so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>, that the moisture of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> or breath condensing on a metalline knife would occasion them to stick to it. These last divisions being so numerous, that the skins necessary for interposing between them would make the packet too thick to be beaten at once, they are parted into three parcels, which are beaten separately, with the smallest hammer, till they are stretched for the third time to the size of the skins: they are now found to be reduced to the greatest thinness they will admit of; and indeed many of them, before this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> or fail. The French workmen, according to the minute detail of this process given in the Encyclopaedia, repeat the division and the beating once more; but as the squares of gold, taken for the first operation, have four times the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AREA">area</a> of those used among us, the number of leaves from an equal area is the same in both methods, viz. 16 from a square inch. In the beating, however simple the process appears to be, a good <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a> is requisite, for applying the hammers so as to extend the metal uniformly from the middle to the sides: one improper blow is apt not only to break the gold leaves, but to cut the skins. "After the last beating, the leaves are taken up by the end of a cane instrument, and, being blown flat on a leather cushion, are cut to a size, one by one, with a square frame of cane made of a proper sharpness, or with a frame of wood edged with cane: they are then fitted into books of 25 leaves each, the paper of which is well smoothed, and rubbed with red <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOLE">bole</a> to prevent their sticking to it. The French, for sizing the leaves, use only the cane knife; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> them first straight on one side, fitting them into the book by the straight side, and then paring off the superfluous parts of the gold about the edges of the book. The size of the French gold leaves is from somewhat less than three inches to three and three quarters square; that of ours, from three inches to three and three-eighths. "The process of gold-beating is considerably influenced by the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>. In wet weather, the skins grow somewhat damp, and in this state make the extension of the gold more tedious: the French are said to dry and press them at every time of using; with care not to overdry them, which would render them unfit for farther <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>. Our workmen complain more of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FROST">frost</a>, which appears to affect the metalline leaves themselves: in frost, a gold leaf cannot easily be blown flat, but breaks, wrinkles, or runs together. "Gold leaf ought to be prepared from the finest gold; as the admixture of other <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-METALS">metals</a>, though in too small a proportion to affect sensibly the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> of the leaf, would dispose it to lose of its <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> in the air. And indeed there is little temptation to the workman to use any other; the greater <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HARDNESS">hardness</a> of alloyed gold occasioning as much to be lost in point of time and labour, and in the greater number of leaves that break, as can be gained by any quantity of alloy that would not be at once discoverable by the eye. All metals render gold harder and more difficult of extension. Even silver, which in this respect seems to alter its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> less than any other metal, produces with gold a mixture sensibly harder than either of them separately, and this hardness is in no art more felt than in the goldbeater's. The French are said to prepare what is called the green gold leaf, from a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> of one part of copper and two of silver with eighty of gold. But this is probably a mistake: for such an admixture gives no greenness to gold: and I have been informed by our workmen, that this kind of leaf is made from the same fine gold as the highest gold-coloured sort, the greenish hue being only a superficial tint induced upon the gold in some part of the process: this greenish leaf is little otherwise used than for the gilding of certain books. "But though the goldbeater cannot advantageously diminish the quantity of gold in the leaf by the admixture of any other substance with the gold, yet means have been contrived for some particular purposes, of saving the precious metal, by producing a kind of leaf, called party-gold, whose basis is silver, and which has only a superficial coat of gold upon one side: a thick leaf of silver and a thinner one of gold, laid flat on one another, heated and pressed together, unite and cohere; and being then beaten into fine leaves, as in the foregoing process, the gold, though its quantity is only about one-fourth of that of the silver, continues everywhere to cover it, the extension of the former keeping pace with that of the latter." But it is to be observed by Mr Nicholson, that pure gold is too ductile to be worked between the goldbeater's skin. The newest skins will work the finest gold, and make the thinnest leaf, because they are the smoothest. Old skins, being rough or foul, require coarser gold. The finer the gold, the more ductile; insomuch, that pure gold, when driven out by the hammer, is too soft to force itself over the irregularities, but would pass round them, and by that means become divided into narrow slips. The finest gold for this purpose, has three grains of alloy in the ounce, and the coarsest twelve grains. In general the alloy is six grains, or one-eightieth part. That which is called <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a> gold contains three pennyweights of silver in the ounce. The alloy of gold leaf is silver, or copper, or both, and the colour is produced of various tints accordingly. Two ounces and two pennyweights of gold is delivered by the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> to the workman, who, if extraordinarily skilful, returns two thousand leaves, or eighty books of gold, together with one ounce and six pennyweights of waste <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTINGS">cuttings</a>. Hence one book weighs 4.8 grains; and as the leaves <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> 3.3 inches in the side, the thickness of the leaf is one two hundred and eighty-two thousandth part of an inch. The <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> metal called Dutch gold is fine <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a>. It is said to be made from copper plates, by cementation with calamine, without subsequent fusion. Its thickness, compared with that of leaf gold, proved as 19 to 4, and under equal surfaces it is considerably more than twice as heavy as the gold. Jour. vol. i. It must be observed, however, that gold is beaten more or less, according to the kind or quality of the work it is intended for; that for the gold-wire-drawers to gild their ingots withal, is left much thicker than that for gilding the frames of pictures, &c. See Gilding. **Gold <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROCADE">Brocade</a>.** See Brocade. **Fulminating Gold.** See <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. **Mosaic Gold,** is gold applied in panels on a proper ground, distributed into squares, lozenges, and other compartments; part of which is shadowed to raise or heighten the rest. See Mosaic. **Gold Plates for Enamelling** are generally made of ducat gold, whose fineness is from $23\frac{1}{2}$ to $23\frac{3}{4}$ carats; and the finest gold is the best for this purpose, unless where some parts of the gold are left bare and unpolished, as in watch-<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a>, snuff-boxes, &c., for which purpose a mixture of alloy is necessary, and silver is preferred to copper, because the latter disposes the plates to tarnish and turn green. See Enamelling. **Shell-Gold** is that used by the gilders and illuminers, and with which gold letters are written. It is made by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRINDING">grinding</a> gold leaves, or gold-beaters fragments, with a little <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONEY">honey</a>, and afterwards separating the honey from the powdered gold by means of water. When the honey is washed away, the gold may be put on paper or kept in shells; whence its name. When it is used, it is diluted with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUM">gum</a>-water or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOAP">soap</a>-suds. The German gold-powder, prepared from the Dutch gold leaf in the same manner, is generally used; and when it is well scoured with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VARNISH">varnish</a>, answers the end in japanners gilding as well as the genuine. **Gold Size** for burnished gilding is prepared of one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POUND">pound</a> and a half of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOBACCO">tobacco</a>-pipe clay, half an ounce of red chalk, a quarter of an ounce of black lead, forty drops of sweet <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, and three drams of pure tallow; grind the clay, chalk, and black lead, separately, very fine in water; then mix them together, add the oil and tallow, and grind the mixture to a due consistence. Gold size of japanners may be made by pulverizing gum animi and asphaltum, of each one ounce; red lead, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LITHARGE">litharge</a> of gold, and umber, of each one ounce and a half, mixing them with a pound of linseed oil, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BOILING">boiling</a> them, observing to stir them till the whole be incorporated, and appears on growing <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLD">cold</a> of the consistence of tar; strain the mixture through a <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-FLANNEL">flannel</a>, and keep it stopped up in a bottle for use. When it is used, it must be ground with as much <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERMILION">vermilion</a> as will give it an opaque body, and diluted with oil of turpentine, so that it may be worked freely with the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PENCIL">pencil</a>. A simple preparation consists of one pound of linseed oil and four ounces of gum animi; powder the guna, and mix it gradually with the boiling oil; let it continue to boil till it becomes of the consistence of tar; strain it through a coarse cloth; keep and use it as the other. **Gold-Finch.** See Fringilla, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">Ornithology</a> Index. **Gold Fish.** See Cyprinus, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ICHTHYOLOGY">Ichthyology</a> Index. **Golden,** something that has a relation to gold or consists of gold. **Golden Calf,** was a figure of a calf, which the Israelites <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> in that metal, and set up in the wilderness to worship during Moses's absence in the mount; and which that <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEGISLATOR">legislator</a> at his return burnt, grinded to powder, and mixed with the water the people were to drink off; as related in Exod. xxxii. The commentators have been divided on this article; the pulverizing of gold, and rendering it potable, is a very difficult operation in chemistry. Many, therefore, suppose it done by a miracle; and the rest, who allow of nothing supernatural in it, advance nothing but conjectures as to the manner of the process. Moses could not have done it by simple calcination, nor amalgamation, nor <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANTIMONY">antimony</a>, nor calcination; nor is there one of those operations that quadrates with the text. M. Stahl has endeavoured to remove this difficulty. The method Moses made use of, according to this author, was by dissolving the metal with hepar sulphuris; only, instead of the vegetable alkali, he made use of the Egyptian natron, which is common enough throughout the east. **Golden <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLEECE">Fleece</a>,** in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MYTHOLOGY">mythology</a>, was the skin or fleece of the ram upon which Phryxus and Hella are supposed to have swam over the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLCHIS">Colchis</a>; and which being sacrificed to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a>, was hung upon a tree in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GROVE">grove</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARS">Mars</a>, guarded by two brazen-hoofed bulls, and a monstrous dragon that never slept; but was taken and carried off by Jason and the Argonauts. Many authors have endeavoured to show that this <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FABLE">fable</a> is an allegorical representation of some real <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, particularly of the philosophers <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>. Others have explained it by the profit of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a> trade to Colchis, or the gold which they commonly gathered there with fleeces in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>. See Argonauts. Order of the Golden Fleece, is a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> order instituted by <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a> the Good, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BURGUNDY">Burgundy</a>, in 1429. It took its denomination from a representation of the golden fleece, borne by the knights on their collars, which consisted of flints and steels. The <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a> is now <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a>-master of the order, in quality of duke of Burgundy: the number of knights is fixed to thirty-one. It is usually said to have been instituted on occasion of an immense profit which that <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> made by wool; though others will have a chemical mystery couched under it, as under that famous one of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, which the adepts contend to be no other than the secret of the elixir, wrote on the fleece of a sheep. Oliver de la Marche writes, that he had suggested to Philip I. archduke of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AUSTRIA">Austria</a>, that the order was instituted by his grandfather Philip the Good duke of Burgundy, with a view to that of Jason; and that John Germain bishop of Chalons, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a> of the order, upon this occasion made him change his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, and assured the young prince that the order had been instituted with a view to the fleece of Gideon. William bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOURNAY">Tournay</a>, chancellor likewise of the order, pretends that the duke of Burgundy had in view both the golden fleece of Jason and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JACOB">Jacob</a>'s fleece; i.e. the speckled sheep belonging to this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATRIARCH">patriarch</a>, according to agreement made with his father-in-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a> Laban. Which sentiment gave birth to a great work of this prelate in two parts: in the first, under the symbol of the fleece of Jason, is represented the virtue of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAGNANIMITY">magnanimity</a>, which a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KNIGHT">knight</a> ought to possess; and under the symbol of the fleece of Jacob he represents the virtue of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>. Paradin is of the same mind; and tells us, that the duke designed to insinuate that the fabulous conquest which Jason is said to have made of the golden fleece in Colchis, was nothing else but the conquest of virtue, which gains a victory over those horrible monsters vice and our evil inclinations. Golden Number, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHRONOLOGY">Chronology</a>, a number showing what year of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOON">moon</a>'s cycle any given year is. See Chronology, No 27—30. Golden Rod, in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a>. See Solidago, Botany Index. Golden Rose. The pope annually consecrates a golden rose on the fourth <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUNDAY">Sunday</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LENT">Lent</a>, which is sent to princesses, or to some <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, as a mark of his peculiar affection. Golden Rule, in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARITHMETIC">Arithmetic</a>, a rule or praxis, of great use and extent in the art of numbers; whereby we find a fourth <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROPORTIONAL">proportional</a> to three quantities given. The golden rule is also called the Rule of Three, and Rule of Proportion. See its <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> and use under the article Arithmetic, No 13. Goldengen, a town of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLAND">Poland</a> in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURLAND">Courland</a>, with a handsome castle, seated on the river Weia, in E. Long. 21. 44. N. Lat. 56. 48. Goldoni, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a>, a comic writer of considerable eminence, was born at <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a> in the year 1707, in which <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> his father acted in the capacity of physician. His <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a> to the drama became conspicuous even in childhood, which his father was fond of countenancing, erecting a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a> in his own <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, where young Goldoni and some of his companions were the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTORS">actors</a>. It is said that he even drew the outlines of a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMEDY">comedy</a> of his own <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> when he was no more than eight years of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>—a most extraordinary indication of his future eminence. He studied <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHETORIC">rhetoric</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERUGIA">Perugia</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> of the Jesuits, and prosecuted his philosophical studies at <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIMINI">Rimini</a>. The stage, however, had too many charms to allow him to pay much <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a> or Quintilian, and he eloped from Rimini with a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> of comedians when they removed to Chioggia. In vain did his father attempt to make him fall in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> with physic, or the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of the law; yet his ardent imagination was so forcibly struck with a particular church-<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a>, that he formed the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a> of commencing capuchin, but the dissipation of Venice soon destroyed this resolution. After the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEMISE">demise</a> of his father, he was prevailed upon by his surviving <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARENT">parent</a> to take up the profession of the law for immediate support, but some unknown reasons induced him to quit the bar after which he went to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILAN">Milan</a>, where he was appointed secretary to the Venetian resident. At Milan he brought out his first performance, under the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Il Gondoliere Veneziano. He removed afterwards to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERONA">Verona</a>, where he joined himself to a company of players; and here too he entered into a state of wedlock. He composed a number of pieces for the players to whom he attached himself. While at Venice, he formed the laudable resolution of reforming the Italian stage, which at that time was disgraced by contemptible <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FARCE">farce</a> and low buffoonery. He made himself acquainted with the true nature of comedy, and kept within the limits of nature and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECORUM">decorum</a>. Such was the fertility of his genius, and such his indefatigable industry, that he produced no fewer than sixteen comedies and 42 other theatrical pieces in the course of Goldoni, twelve months! And what is most astonishing, some of Goldoni's these hasty performances are deemed his masterpieces. His works in 10 vols, 8vo. were first printed in 1753, and in 1761 his new pieces amounted to 59. About this time he was invited to Paris by the manager of the Italian theatre in that city, to compose pieces for the stage, of which invitation he accepted. His first attempt was unsuccessful, because he had to contend with the pantomime drollery, which was most agreeable to the depraved <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> of the times. When about to leave Paris on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPIRATION">expiration</a> of his engagement, he was introduced to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>, and appointed teacher of the Italian languages to the princesses. He had lodgings in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSAILLES">Versailles</a>, but his pension was not sufficient to keep him from <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> for the stage. When 62 years old, he ventured to compose in a foreign <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, his La Bourru Bieufaisant, which was received in the court theatre with extraordinary applause. He was deprived of his pension in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of the revolution, and reduced to indigence. It ought to be confessed, however, that this versatile <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> was <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> about to make him amends when he expired in 1792, and in the 85th year of his age. If the rapidity with which Goldoni composed was such as to prevent him from ranking with authors of the first class, it cannot be denied that his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TALENT">talent</a> for comedy was very great. Some have given him the appellation of the Molière of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, but this perhaps is too flattering a title. His whole works were printed at <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEGHORN">Leghorn</a> about the years 1788 and 1791, in 31 volumes 8vo. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOLDSMITH">Goldsmith</a>, or, as some choose to express it, silversmith, an <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ARTIST">artist</a> who makes vessels, utensils, and ornaments, in gold and silver. The goldsmith's work is either performed in the mould, or <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEAT">beat</a> out with the hammer or other engine. All works that have raised figures are cast in a mould, and afterwards polished and finished; plates or dishes, of silver or gold, are beat out from thin flat plates; and tankards, and other vessels of that kind, are formed of plates soldered together, and their <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOULDINGS">mouldings</a> are beat, not cast. The business of the goldsmiths formerly required much more labour than it does at present; for they were obliged to hammer the metal from the ingot to the thinness they wanted; but there are now invented flating-<a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MILLS">mills</a>, which reduce metals to the thinness that is required, at a very small expense. The goldsmith is to make his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOULDS">moulds</a>; and for that reason, ought to be a good designer, and have a taste in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SCULPTURE">sculpture</a>: he ought also to know enough of metallurgy to be able to <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASSAY">assay</a> mixed metals, and to mix the alloy. The goldsmiths in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a> employ several hands under them for the various <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> of their trade; such are the jeweller, the snuff-box and toy-maker, the silver-turner, the gilder, the burnisher, the chaser, the refiner, and the gold-beater. Goldsmiths are superior tradesmen; their wares must be assayed by the wardens of the company of this name in London, and marked; and gold is to be of a certain touch. No goldsmith may take above one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHILLING">shilling</a> the ounce of gold, besides what he has for the fashioning, more than the buyer may be allowed for it at the king's <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXCHANGE">exchange</a>; and here any false metal shall be seized and forfeited to the king. The cities Goldsmith, of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORK">York</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXETER">Exeter</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRISTOL">Bristol</a>, &c., are places appointed for the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ASSAYING">assaying</a> wrought plate of goldsmiths; also a duty is granted on silver-plate of sixpence an ounce, &c. Plate made by goldsmiths shall be of a particular fineness, on pain of forfeiting 10l. and if any parcel of plate sent to the assayers is discovered to be of a coarser alloy than the respective standards, it may be broken and defaced; and the fees for assaying are particularly limited. Goldsmith, Oliver, a celebrated English writer, was born at Roscommon in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a> in the year 1731. His father, who possessed a small estate in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a>, had nine sons, of whom Oliver was the third. He was originally intended for the church; and with that view, after being well instructed in the classics, was, with his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a>, the Rev. Henry Goldsmith, placed in Trinity College, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUBLIN">Dublin</a>, about the latter end of the year 1749. In this seminary of learning he <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> a few years, when he took a bachelor's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>; but his brother not being able to obtain any preferment after he left the college, Oliver, by the advice of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAN">Dean</a> Goldsmith of Cork, turned his thoughts to the study of physic; and, after attending some courses of anatomy in Dublin, proceeded to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a> in the year 1751, where he studied the several branches of medicine under the different professors in that university. His benevolent disposition soon involved him in unexpected difficulties; and he was obliged precipitately to leave Scotland, in consequence of engaging himself to pay a considerable sum of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a> for a fellow-student. A few days after, about the beginning of the year 1754, he arrived at Sunderland, near <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEWCASTLE">Newcastle</a>, where he was arrested at the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUIT">suit</a> of a taylor in Edinburgh, to whom he had given security for his friend. By the good offices of Laughlan Maclane, Esq., and Dr Sleigh, who were then in the college, he was soon delivered out of the hands of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAILIFF">bailiff</a>; and took his passage on board a Dutch ship to <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROTTERDAM">Rotterdam</a>, where, after a short stay, he proceeded to <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRUSSELS">Brussels</a>; he then visited great part of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLANDERS">Flanders</a>; and after passing some time at <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-STRASBOURG">Strasbourg</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LOUVAIN">Louvain</a>, where he obtained a degree of bachelor of physic, he accompanied an English <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BERNE">Berne</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENEVA">Geneva</a>. It is undoubtedly fact, that this ingenious unfortunate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> travelled on foot most part of his tour. He had left England with very little money; and being of a philosophical turn, and at that time possessing a body capable of sustaining every fatigue, and a heart not easily terrified at danger, he became an enthusiast to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> he had formed of seeing the manners of different countries. He had some knowledge of the French language and of music, and he played tolerably well on the German <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLUTE">flute</a>; which, from an amusement, became at some times the means of subsistence. His learning produced him a hospitable reception at most of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> houses; and his music made him welcome to the peasants of Flanders and other parts of Germany. "Whenever I approached," he used to say, "a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEASANT">peasant</a>'s house towards night-fall, I played one of my most merry tunes; and that procured me not only a lodging, but subsistence for the next day: but in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> (his constant <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a>), I must own, whenever I attempted to entertain persons of a higher <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a>, they always thought my performance odious, and never made me any return for my endeavours to Goldsmith, please them." On Mr Goldsmith's arrival at Geneva, he was recommended as a proper person for a travelling <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TUTOR">tutor</a> to a young man, who had been unexpectedly left a considerable sum of money by his uncle Mr S——, formerly an eminent pawnbroker near Holborn. This youth, who had been articled to an attorney, on receipt of his fortune determined to see the world; and, on his engaging with his preceptor, made a proviso that he should be permitted to govern himself; and Goldsmith soon found his pupil understood the art of directing in money-concerns extremely well, as avarice was his prevailing <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PASSION">passion</a>. His questions were usually how money might be saved, and which was the least expensive course of travelling; whether anything could be bought that would turn to account when disposed of again in London? Such curiosities on the way as could be seen for nothing he was ready enough to look at; but if the sight of them was to be paid for, he usually asserted that he had been told they were not worth seeing. He never paid a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BILL">bill</a> that he would not observe how amazingly expensive travelling was; and all this, though he was not yet twenty-one. During Goldsmith's continuance in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWITZERLAND">Switzerland</a>, he assiduously cultivated his poetical talent, of which he had given some striking proofs while at the college of Edinburgh. It was here he sent the first sketch of his delightful poem called the Traveller, to his brother the clergyman in Ireland, who, giving up fame and fortune, had retired with an amiable wife, to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a> and obscurity, on an income of only 40l. a-year. From Geneva Mr Goldsmith and his pupil visited the south of France; where the young man, upon some disagreement with his preceptor, paid him the small part of his salary which was due, and embarked at <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARSEILLES">Marseilles</a> for England. Our wanderer was left once more upon the world at large, and passed through a variety of difficulties in traversing the greatest part of France. At length his curiosity being satiated, he bent his course towards England, and arrived at <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOVER">Dover</a> the beginning of the winter 1758. When he came to London, his stock of cash did not amount to two livres. An entire stranger in this <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METROPOLIS">metropolis</a>, his mind was filled with the most gloomy reflections on his embarrassed situation. With some difficulty he discovered that part of the town in which his old acquaintance Dr Sleigh resided. This gentleman received him with the warmest affection, and liberally invited him to share his purse till some establishment could be procured for him. Goldsmith, unwilling to be a burden to his friend, a short time after eagerly embraced an offer which was made him to assist the late Rev. Dr Milner in instructing the young gentlemen at the academy at Peckham; and acquitted himself greatly to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DOCTOR">Doctor</a>'s satisfaction for a short time; but having obtained some reputation by the criticisms he had written in the Monthly Review, Mr Griffith, the proprietor, engaged him in the compilation of it; and, resolving to pursue the profession of writing, he returned to London, as the mart where abilities of every kind were sure of meeting distinction and reward. As his finances were by no means in a good state, he determined to adopt a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> of the strictest economy: and took Goldsmith took lodgings in an obscure court in the Old Bailey, where he wrote several ingenious little pieces. The late Mr Newberry, who at that time gave great encouragement to men of literary abilities, became a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATRON">patron</a> to our young author; and introduced him as one of the writers in the Public Ledger, in which his Citizen of the World originally appeared, under the title of Chinese Letters. Fortune now seemed to take some notice of a man she had long neglected. The simplicity of his character, the integrity of his heart, and the merit of his productions, made his company very acceptable to a number of respectable families; and he emerged from his shabby apartments in the Old Bailey to the politer air of the Temple, where he took handsome chambers, and lived in a genteel style. The publication of his Traveller, and his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VICAR">Vicar</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WAKEFIELD">Wakefield</a>, was followed by the performance of his comedy of the Good-natured Man at Covent Garden theatre, and placed him in the first rank of the poets of the age. Among many other persons of distinction who were desirous to know him was the duke of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTHUMBERLAND">Northumberland</a>; and the circumstance that attended his introduction to that nobleman is worthy of being related, in order to show a striking trait of his character. "I was invited," said the Doctor, (as he was then universally called), "by my friend Mr Percy, to wait upon the duke, in consequence of the satisfaction he had received from the perusal of one of my productions. I dressed myself in the best manner I could; and, after studying some compliments I thought necessary on such an occasion, proceeded to Northumberland house, and acquainted the servants that I had particular business with his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRACE">Grace</a>. They showed me into an antichamber; where, after waiting some time, a gentleman very genteelly dressed made his appearance. Taking him for the duke, I delivered all the fine things I had composed in order to compliment him on the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> he had done me; when, to my great astonishment, he told me I had mistaken him for his master, who would see me immediately. At that instant the duke came into the apartment; and I was so confused on the occasion, that I wanted words barely sufficient to express the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> I entertained of the duke's <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLITENESS">politeness</a>, and went away extremely chagrined at the blunder I had committed." Another feature of his character we cannot help laying before the reader. Previous to the publication of his Deserted Village, the bookseller had given him a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOTE">note</a> for one hundred guineas for the copy, which the Doctor mentioned a few hours after to one of his friends; who observed, it was a very great sum for so short a performance. "In truth," replied Goldsmith, "I think so too; I have not been easy since I received it; therefore I will go back and return him his note;" which he absolutely did; and left it entirely to the bookseller to pay him according to the profits produced by the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALE">sale</a> of the piece, which turned out very considerable. During the last rehearsal of his comedy intitled She stoops to Conquer, which Mr Coleman had no opinion would succeed, on the Doctor's objecting to the repetition of one of Tony Lumpkin's speeches, being apprehensive it might injure the play, the manager with great keenness replied, "Psha, my dear Doctor, do not be fearful of squibs, when we have been sitting almost these two hours upon a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BARREL">barrel</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUNPOWDER">gunpowder</a>." The piece, however, contrary to Mr Coleman's <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPECTATION">expectation</a>, was received with uncommon applause by the audience; and Goldsmith's <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIDE">pride</a> was so hurt by the severity of the above observation, that it entirely put an end to his friendship for the gentleman that made it. Notwithstanding the great success of his pieces, by some of which it is asserted, upon good authority, he cleared £800l. in one year, his circumstances were by no means in a prosperous situation; which was partly owing to the liberality of his disposition, and partly to an unfortunate <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HABIT">habit</a> he had contracted of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-GAMING">gaming</a>; the arts of which he knew very little of, and consequently became the prey of those who were unprincipled enough to take advantage of his simplicity. Just before his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> he had formed a design for executing an Universal <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DICTIONARY">Dictionary</a> of Arts and Sciences, the prospectus of which he actually published. In this work several of his literary friends, (particularly Sir Joshua Reynolds, Dr Johnson, Mr Beauclerc, and Mr Garrick), had undertaken to furnish him with articles upon different subjects. He had entertained the most sanguine expectations from the success of it. The undertaking, however, did not meet with that encouragement from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOOKSELLERS">booksellers</a> which he had imagined it would undoubtedly receive; and he used to lament this circumstance almost to the last hour of his existence. He had been for some years afflicted, at different times, with a violent strangury, which contributed not a little to embitter the latter part of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>; and which, united with the vexations which he suffered upon other occasions, brought on a kind of habitual despondency. In this unhappy condition he was attacked by a nervous fever, which, being improperly treated, terminated in his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISSOLUTION">dissolution</a> on the 4th of April 1774. As to his character, it is strongly illustrated by Mr Pope's line, In <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WIT">wit</a> a man, simplicity a child. The learned leisure he loved to enjoy was too often interrupted by distresses which arose from the liberality of his temper, and which sometimes threw him into loud fits of passion: but this impetuosity was corrected upon a moment's reflection; and his servants have been known, upon these occasions, purposely to throw themselves in his way, that they might profit by it immediately after; for he who had the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOOD_FORTUNE">good fortune</a> to be reproved, was certain of being rewarded for it. The universal esteem in which his poems were held, and the repeated <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> they give in the perusal, is a striking test of their merit. He was a studious and correct observer of nature; happy in the selection of his images, in the choice of his subjects, and in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HARMONY">harmony</a> of his versification; and, though his embarrassed situation prevented him from putting the last hand to many of his productions, his Hermit, his Traveller, and his Deserted Village, bid fair to claim a place among the most finished pieces in the English language. Besides the works already mentioned, he wrote, 1. History of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> and animated nature, 6 vols 8vo. 2. History of England, 4 vols 8vo. 3. History of Rome, 2 vols. 4. Abridgements of the two last, for the use of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a>. 5. A view of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPERIMENTAL_PHILOSOPHY">experimental <a class="</a>xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, 3 vols 8vo; a posthumous work, not esteemed. 6. Miscellanies, &c.

ST GEORGE

Pages 732-732

a fort and town of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PENINSULA">peninsula</a> on this side the Ganges, and on the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of Coromandel, belonging to the British; it is otherwise called <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-MADRAS">Madras</a>, and by the natives Chilipatam. It fronts the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, and has a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> river on its back side, which hinders the fresh water <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a> from coming near the town, so that they have no good water within a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILE">mile</a> of them. In the rainy seasons it is incommodeed by inundations; and from April to September, it is so scorching hot, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the sea breezes did not cool the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a>, there would be no living there. There are two <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, one of which is called the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">White</a> Town, which is walled round, and has several bulwarks and bastions to defend it: it is 400 paces <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> and 150 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, and is divided into regular streets. Here are two churches, one for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a>, and the other for the Papists; as also a good <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOSPITAL">hospital</a>, a town <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HALL">hall</a>, and a prison for debtors. They are a corporation, and have a mayor and aldermen, with other proper officers. The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">Black</a> Town is inhabited by Gentooes, Mahometans, and Portuguese and Armenian <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>, and each <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> has its <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a> and churches. This, as well as the White Town, is ruled by the English governor and his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIAMOND">diamond</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a> are but a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-WEEK">week</a>'s journey from this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, which renders them pretty plentiful, but there are no <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> ones since that <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> diamond was procured by Governor Pitt. This colony produces very little of its own growth <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> manufacture for foreign <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MARKETS">markets</a>, and the trade is in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the Armenians and Gentooes. The <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> things the British <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> in, besides diamonds, are calicoes, chintz, muslins, and the like. In 1794 the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> of the town was estimated at 300,000. Their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICE">rice</a> is brought by sea from Gangam and Orixa, their wheat from <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SURAT">Surat</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BENGAL">Bengal</a>, and their fire wood from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> of Diu; so that an enemy, with a superior force at sea, may easily distress them. The houses of the White Town are built with brick, and have lofty rooms and flat roofs. The houses in the White Town have all green Venetian windows, and are surrounded by gardens. The Black Town consists chiefly of thatched cottages. The <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> power is lodged in the governor and council, who are also the last <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESORT">resort</a> in civil causes. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> have two chaplains, who officiate by turns. They never attempt to make proselytes, but leave that to the Popish missionaries. The salaries of the Company's writers are very small: but if they have any fortune of their own, they may make it up by trade; which must generally be the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>, for they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> grow rich. It was taken by the French in 1764, who restored it at the peace of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIX">Aix</a>-la-Chapelle.

THEOREM II

Pages 696-696

Every triangle ABC is the half of a parallelogram ABCD, having the same base and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ALTITUDE">altitude</a>. For the triangles ABC, ACD are equal (28. i.). Cor. 1. Therefore a triangle ABC is the half of a rectangle BCEF of the same base and altitude. Cor. 2. All triangles having equal bases, and equal altitudes, are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EQUIVALENT">equivalent</a>.

THEOREM III

Pages 696-696

Two rectangles of the same <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ALTITUDE">altitude</a> are to each other as their bases. Let ABCD, AEFD be two rectangles, which have a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> altitude <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AD">AD</a>; the rectangle ABCD shall have to the rectangle AEFD the same ratio that the base <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AB">AB</a> has to the base AE. Let the base AB have to the base AE the ratio of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> p (which we shall suppose 7.) to the number q (which may be 4.), that is, let AB contain p (7.) such equal parts as AE contains q (4.), then, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> perpendiculars be drawn to AB and AE at the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">points</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVISION">division</a>, the rectangles ABCD and AEFD <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be divided, the former into p, and the latter into q rectangles, which will be all equal (1.) for they have equal bases, and the same altitude; thus the rectangle ABCD will also contain p such equal parts as the rectangle AEFD contains q; therefore the rectangle ABCD is to AEFD as the number p to the number q (Ax. 4. 3.), that is, as the base AB to AE.
